title: What’s new
text:
Version 2.1.0 (2024-11-07)

Summary

Time in simulations is now handled by an ss.Time() class, which unifies how time is represented between the Sim and each module.
In addition to networks, there is now a new way of implementing disease transmission via mixing pools.



Time

Time handling now performed by the ss.Time() class. This has inputs similar to before (start, stop, unit, dt, with dur still available as a sim input). However, instead of the previous timevec and abs_tvec arrays, there are now multiple ways of representing time (including datevec and yearvec), regardless of what the inputs were.
Dates are now represented in a native format, ss.date, that is based on pd.Timestamp.



Mixing pools

Adds a new approach to disease transmission called mixing pools. A mixing pool is a “mean field” coupling wherein susceptible agents are exposed to the average infectious agent. The user can create a single mixing pool using the ss.MixingPool class, or create many pools using MixingPools. Such mixing pools could be used to simulate contact matrices, for example as published by Prem et al.
There is a new ss.Route class, which is the base class for ss.Network and ss.MixingPool.



Other changes

Demographic modules have been updated to fix various bugs around different time units.
The method for hashing distribution trace strings into seeds has changed, meaning that results will be stochastically different compared to Starsim v2.0.
Fixed a bug with how timepars were updated in parameters.
There is a new ss.Base class, which both ss.Sim and ss.Module inherit from.
Results now print as a single line rather than the full array. The latter is available as result.disp().
sim.to_df() now works even if different modules have different numbers of timepoints.
The timepars module has been renamed to time.
In demographics modules, units has been renamed rate_units.
There are two new options, ss.options.date_sep and ss.options.license. The former sets the date separator (default ., e.g. 2024.04.0.4), and the latter sets if the license prints when Starsim is imported.

title: What’s new
text:
Version 2.0.0 (2024-10-01)

Summary
Version 2.0 contains several major changes. These include: module-specific timesteps and time-aware parameters (including a day/year unit flag for modules, and ss.dur() and ss.rate() classes for parameters), and changes to module types and integration (e.g. renaming update() and apply() methods to step();).


Time-aware parameters and modules

Added ss.dur(), ss.rate(), and ss.time_prob() classes, for automatic handling of time units in simulations. There are also convenience classes ss.days(), ss.years(), ss.perday(), ss.peryear(), and ss.beta() for special cases of these.
ss.dur() and ss.rate(), along with modules and the sim itself, have a unit parameter which can be 'day', 'week', 'month', or 'year' (default). Modules now also have their own timestep dt. Different units and timesteps can be mixed and matched. Time parameters have a to() method, e.g. ss.dur(1, 'year').to('day') will return ss.dur(365, unit='day').
The ss.Sim parameter n_years has been renamed dur; sim.yearvec is now sim.timevec, which can have units of days (usually starting at 0), dates (e.g. '2020-01-01'), or years (e.g. 2020). sim.abs_tvec is the translation of sim.timevec as a numeric array starting at 0, using the sim’s units (usually 'day' or 'year'). For example, if sim.timevec is a list of daily dates from '2022-01-01' to '2022-12-31', sim.abs_tvec will be np.arange(365).
Each module also has its own mod.timevec; this can be different from the sim if it defines its own time unit and/or timestep. mod.abs_tvec always starts at 0 and always uses the sim’s unit.
There is a new Loop class which handles the integration loop. You can view the integration plan via sim.loop.to_df() or sim.loop.plot(). You can see how long each part of the sim took with sim.loop.plot_cpu().
There are more advanced debugging tools. You can run a single sim timestep with sim.run_one_step() (which in turn calls multiple functions), and you can run a single function from the integration loop with sim.loop.run_one_step().



Module changes

Functionality has been moved from ss.Plugin to ss.Module, and the former has been removed.
ss.Connector functionality has been moved to ss.Module. ss.Module objects can be placed anywhere in the list of modules (e.g., in demographics, networks, diseases, interventions), depending on when you want them to execute. However, ss.Connector objects are applied after Disease.step_state() and before Network.step().
Many of the module methods have been renamed; in particular, all modules now have a step() method, which replaces update() (for demographics and networks), apply() (for interventions and analyzers), and make_new_cases() (for diseases). For both the sim and modules, initialize() has been renamed init().
All modules are treated the same in the integration loop, except for diseases, which have step_state() and step_die() methods.
The Starsim module states.py has been moved to arrays.py, and network.py has been moved to networks.py.



State and array changes

ss.Arr, ss.TimePar, and ss.Result all inherit from the new class ss.BaseArr, which provides functionality similar to a NumPy array, except all values are stored in arr.values (like a pd.Series).
Whereas before, computations on an ss.Arr usually returned a NumPy array, calculations now usually return the same type. To access the NumPy array, use arr.values.
There is a new ss.State class, which is a subtype of ss.BoolArr. Typically, ss.State is used for boolean disease states, such as infected, susceptible, etc., where you want to automatically generate results (e.g. n_infected). You can continue using ss.BoolArr for other agent attributes that you don’t necessarily want to automatically generate results for, e.g. ever_vaccinated.



Results changes

Results are now defined differently. They should be defined in ss.Module.init_results(), not ss.Module.init_pre(). They now take the module name, number of points, and time vector from the parent module. As a result, they are usually initialized via ss.Module.define_results(res1, res2) (as opposed to mod.results += [res1, res2] previously). define_results() automatically adds these properties from the parent module; they can still be defined explicitly if needed however.
Because results now store their own time information, they can be plotted in a self-contained way. Both ss.Result and ss.Results objects now have plot() and to_df() methods.



Demographics changes

Fixed a bug in how results were defined for ss.Births and ss.Deaths.
The ss.Pregnancy module has been significantly rewritten, including: (1) Agents now have a parent which indicates the UID of the parent; (2) Women now track child_uid; (3) On neonatal death, the pregnancy state of the mother is corrected; (4) Pregnancy rates now adjusted for infecund rather than pregnant; (4) Pregnancy now has a burn-in, which defaults to True; (5) Pregnancy has a p_neonatal_death parameter to capture fetal and neonatal death if the mother dies.
Slots now has a minimum, default of 100, to account for small initial population sizes that grow dramatically over time.



Computational changes

There have been several performance improvements. The default float type is now np.float32. Transmission is now handled by a specialized Infection.compute_transmission() method. Several additional functions now use Numba, including fastmath=True, which leverages Intel’s short vector math library.
A new ss.multi_random() distribution class has been added, that allows random numbers to be generated by two (or more) agents. It largely replaces ss.combine_rands() and is 5-10x faster.
A new ss.gamma() distribution has also been added.
Distributions have a new jump_dt method that jumps by much more than a single state update.
ss.parallel() and ss.MultiSim.run() now modify simulations in place by default. Instead of sims = ss.parallel(sim1, sim2).sims; sims[0].plot(), you can now simply do ss.parallel(sim1, sim2); sim1.plot().



Other changes

Data can now be supplied to a simulation; it will be automatically plotted by sim.plot().
ss.Calibration has been significantly reworked, and now includes more flexible parameter setting, plus plotting (calib.plot_sims() and calib.plot_trend()). It also has a debug argument (which runs in serial rather than paralell), which can be helpful for troubleshooting issues.
MultiSim now has display methods brief() (minimal), show() (moderate), and disp (verbose).
sim.export_df() has been renamed sim.to_df().
Most classes now have to_json() methods (which can also export to a dict).
Fixed a bug in how the InfectionLog is added to disease modules.
Sim.gitinfo has been replaced with Sim.metadata (which includes git info).
Infection.validate_beta() is now applied on every timestep, so changes to beta during the simulation are now honored.
sim.get_intervention() and sim.get_analyzer() have been removed; use built-in ndict operations (e.g., the label) to find the object you’re after.
requires has been removed from modules, but ss.check_requires() is still available if needed. Call it manually from init_pre() if desired, e.g. a PMTCT intervention might call ss.check_requires(self.sim, ['hiv', 'maternalnet']).
For networks, contacts has been renamed edges except in cases where it refers to an agent’s contacts. For example, network.contacts has been renamed network.edges, but ss.find_contacts() remains the same.
Networks now have a to_graph() method that exports to NetworkX.
ss.diff_sims() can now handle MultiSim objects.
Sim._orig_pars has been removed.
ss.unique() has been removed.



Regression information

Note: the list here covers major changes only; in general, Starsim v1.0 scripts will not be compatible with Starsim v2.0.
Results from Starsim v2.0 will be stochastically (but not statistically) different from Starsim v1.0.
All duration and rate parameters should now be wrapped with ss.dur() and ss.rate(). Events that represent probabilities over time (i.e. hazard rates) can also be wrapped with ss.time_prob(), although this is similar to ss.rate() unless the value is relatively large.
ss.Plugin has been removed. Use ss.Module instead.
init_results() is now called by init_pre(), and does not need to be called explicitly.
default_pars() has been renamed define_pars().
add_states() has been renamed define_states()
initialize() has been renamed init().
Demographics.update() has been renamed Demographics.step().
Network.update() has been renamed Network.step().
Disease.update_pre() has been renamed Disease.step_state().
Disease.make_new_cases() has been renamed Disease.step().
Disease.update_death() has been renamed Disease.step_die() (which is now called by People.step_die()).
Infection._set_cases() has been renamed Infection.set_outcomes().
Intervention.apply(sim) has been renamed Intervention.step(); ditto for Analyzer.
Module.step() no longer takes sim as an argument (e.g., replace intervention.apply(sim) with intervention.step()).
All modules now have methods for start_step(), finish_step(), init_results(), and update_results().
Network.contacts has been renamed Network.edges.
sim.get_intervention() and sim.get_analyzer() have been removed; simply call directly instead (e.g. replace sim.get_intervention('vaccine') with sim.interventions['vaccine']).
requires is no longer an attribute of modules; call the ss.check_requires() function directly if needed.
People.resolve_deaths() has been renamed People.check_deaths()
ss.unique() has been removed.

title: What’s new
text:
Version 0.5.0 (2024-05-14)

Summary
All inputs to the sim and modules now use a ss.Pars() class, which handles updating and validation. It is now not necessary to ever use pars= (although you still can if you want), so what was previously:
sim = ss.Sim(pars=dict(diseases='sir', networks='random'))
is now just:
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sir', networks='random')
Updates happen recursively, so distributions etc. can be flexibly updated.
This has significantly changed how modules are initialized; what was previously:
def __init__(self, pars=None, **kwargs):

    pars = ss.omergeleft(pars,
        dur_inf = 6,
        init_prev = 0.01,
        p_death = 0.01,
        beta = 0.5,
    )

    par_dists = ss.omergeleft(par_dists,
        dur_inf = ss.lognorm_ex,
        init_prev = ss.bernoulli,
        p_death = ss.bernoulli,
    )

    super().__init__(pars=pars, par_dists=par_dists, *args, **kwargs)
is now:
def __init__(self, pars=None, **kwargs):
    super().__init__()
    self.default_pars(
        beta = 0.5,
        init_prev = ss.bernoulli(0.01),
        dur_inf = ss.lognorm_ex(6),
        p_death = ss.bernoulli(0.01),
    )
    self.update_pars(pars, **kwargs)


Parameter changes

Added a ss.Pars class (and a ss.SimPars subclass) that handles parameter creation, updates, and validation.
Initialization has been moved from sim.py to parameters.py; ss.Sim.convert_plugins() has been replaced by ss.SimPars.convert_modules().
The key method is ss.Pars.update(), which performs all necessary validation on the parameters being updated.



Initialization changes

Previously, the people were initialized first, then the states were initialized and the values populated, then the modules were initialized, and finally the distributions are initialized. This led to circular logic with the states being initialized based on uninitialized distributions. Now, states and modules are linked to the People and Sim objects, but further initialization is not done at this step. This ensures all distributions are created but not yet used. Next, distributions are initialized. Finally, the initial values are populated, and everything is initialized.
New methods supporting these changes include ss.link_dists(), dist.link_sim(), dist.link_module(), sim.init_vals(), people.init_vals(), module.init_vals(),



Module changes

Whereas modules previously initialized a dict of parameters and then called super().__init__(pars, **kwargs), they now call super().__init__() first, then self.default_pars(par1=x, par2=y), then finally self.update_pars(pars, **kwargs).
What was previously e.g. ss.Module(pars=dict(par=x)) is now ss.Module(par=x).
par_dists has been removed; instead, distributions are specified in the default parameters, and are updated via the Pars object.
Modules now contain a link back to the Sim object. This means that all methods that used to have sim as an argument now do not, e.g. self.update() instead of self.update(sim).
ss.module_map() maps different module types to their location in the sim.
ss.find_modules() finds all available modules (including subclasses) in Starsim.
Removed ss.dictmerge() and ss.dictmergeleft (now handled by ss.Pars.update()).
Removed ss.get_subclasses() and ss.all_subclasses() (now handled by ss.find_modules()).
Modules can no longer be initialized with a name key; it must be type (e.g. dict(type='sir') rather than dict(name='sir').
Added to_json() and plot() methods to Module.
Removed connectors.py; connectors still exist but as an empty subclass of Module.



People and network changes

BasePeople has been removed and merged with People.
Time parameters (ti, dt, etc.) have been removed from People. Use sim.ti, sim.dt etc. instead. One consequence of this is that people.request_death() now requires a sim argument. Another is that network methods (e.g. add_pairs()) now take sim arguments instead of people arguments.
SexualNetwork is now a subclass of DynamicNetwork.
Removed ss.Networks (now just an ss.ndict).
Network connectors have been removed.
Person has been implemented as a slice of sim.people[i].
There is a new parameter use_aging; this defaults to True if demographic modules are supplied, and False otherwise.



Other changes

Boolean arrays have new methods true(), false(), and split(), which return the UIDs for the True values (alias to arr.uids), False values, and both sets of values, respectively. ss.bernoulli.split() has been added as an alias of ss.bernoulli.filter(both=True).
All inputs to a sim are now copied by default. To disable, use ss.Sim(..., copy_inputs=False).
There is a new Plugin class, which contains shared logic for Interventions and Analyzers. It has a from_func(), which will generate an intervention/analyzer from a function.
Diseases no longer have a default value of beta=1 assigned; beta must be defined explicitly if being used.
Individual diseases can now be plotted via either e.g. sim.plot('hiv') or sim.diseases.hiv.plot().
Distributions can be created from dicts via ss.make_dist().
A new function ss.check_sims_match() will check if the results of two or more simulations match.
ndict values can be accessed through a call; e.g. sim.diseases() is equivalent to sim.diseases.values().
Merged test_dcp.py and test_base.py into test_other.py.
Renamed test_simple.py to test_sim.py.
Renamed test_dists.py to test_randomness.py.

title: What’s new
text:
Version 0.4.0 (2024-04-24)

Replace UIDArray, ArrayView, and State with Arr, which has different subclasses for different data types (e.g. FloatArr, BoolArr, and IndexArr). States are usually represented by BoolArr (e.g. sir.infected), while other agent properties are represented by FloatArr (e.g. sir.rel_trans).
Arrays that had previously been represented using an integer data type (e.g. sir.ti_infected) are now also FloatArr, to allow the use of np.nan. Integer arrays are supported via IndexArr, but these are only intended for use for slots and UIDs.
Arr objects automatically skip over dead (or otherwise removed) agents; the “active” UIDs are stored in sim.people.auids, which is updated when agents are born or die. This array is linked to each Arr, so that e.g. sim.people.age.mean() will only calculate the mean over alive agents. To access the underlying Numpy array, use sim.people.age.raw.
FloatArr has isnan, notnan, and notnanvals properties. BoolArr has logical operations defined. For example, ~people.female works, but ~people.ti_dead does not; people.ti_dead.notnan works, but people.female.notnan does not.
UIDs used to be NumPy integer arrays; they are now ss.uids objects (which is a class, but is lowercase for consistency with np.array(), which it is functionally similar to). Indexing a state by an integer array rather than ss.uids() now raises an exception, due to the ambiguity involved. To index the underlying array with an integer array, use Arr.raw[int_arr]; to index only the active/alive agents, use Arr.values[int_arr].
Dead agents are no longer removed, so uid always corresponds to the position in the array. This means that no remapping is necessary, which has a significant performance benefit (roughly 2x faster for large numbers of agents).
Renamed omerge to dictmerge and omergeleft to dictmergeleft.

title: What’s new
text:
Version 0.3.0 (2024-03-30)

New RNGs & distributions

Replaces ss.SingleRNG(), ss.MultiRNG(), ss.ScipyDistribution(), and ss.ScipyHistogram() with a single ss.Dist() class. The starsim.random and starsim.distributions submodules have been removed, and starsim.dists has been added.
The ss.Dist class uses np.random.default_rng() rather than scipy.stats by default, although a scipy.stats distribution can be supplied as an alternative. This is up to 4x faster (including, critically, for Bernoulli distributions).
Also removes ss.options.multirng (the new version is equivalent to it being always on).
Removes duplicate logic for transmission (make_new_cases())
Adds new custom distributions such as ss.choice() and ss.delta().
These distributions can be called directly, e.g. dist = ss.weibull(c=2); dist(5) will return 5 random variates from a Weibull distribution.
Instead of being manually initialized based on the name, the Sim object is parsed and all distributions will be initialized with a unique identifier based on their place in the object (e.g. sim.diseases.sir.pars.dur_inf), which is used to set their unique seed.



Other changes

This PR also fixes bugs with lognormal parameters, and makes it clear whether the parameters are for the implicit normal distribution (ss.lognorm_im(), the NumPy/SciPy default, equivalent to ss.lognorm_mean() previously) or the “explicit” lognormal distribution (ss.lognorm_ex(), equivalent to ss.lognorm() previously).

title: SEIR with a realistic infectious period
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
In an SEIR model, people infected first pass through a latent period (E, exposed) before they become infectious. In the simplest SEIR, the time spent in each state is exponentially distributed: many people leave a state almost at once and a few stay a long time, which is rarely realistic. A gamma-distributed (Erlang) period with a few stages is closer to most real infections: each person passes through k stages, each exponential, and the total has the same mean but much less spread. This page compares the two, for the same mean infectious period.
crumbs: SEIR with a realistic infectious period

title: SEIR with a realistic infectious period
text:
The model








Parameter
Value
Meaning




β
0.3 per day
Rate of infection per susceptible person, per unit of the share infectious


Latent period
5 days
Mean time in E (exponential)


Infectious period
10 days
Mean time in I: exponential, or Erlang with 3 stages


R0
3
β × the mean infectious period


Population
100,000



Infectious at the start
0.1%





import starsim as ss

def make_seir(infectious_period):
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection = S >> E @ 0.3*I
    latency   = E >> I @ ss.days(5)
    recovery  = I >> R @ infectious_period
    return ss.Disease(infection, latency, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='seir')

exponential = make_seir(ss.days(10))
erlang = make_seir(ss.erlang(mean=ss.days(10), k=3))

The infection leads to E, so the people infected at the start are put in I with init=dict(I=0.001). The diagram, from diagram():

erlang.diagram()


flowchart LR
    S(["S"])
    E(["E"])
    I(["I"])
    R(["R"])
    S -.->|"infection: 0.3 × I"| E
    E -->|"latency: 5 days"| I
    I -->|"recovery: erlang(k=3, mean=10 days)"| R





flowchart LR
    S(["S"])
    E(["E"])
    I(["I"])
    R(["R"])
    S -.->|"infection: 0.3 × I"| E
    E -->|"latency: 5 days"| I
    I -->|"recovery: erlang(k=3, mean=10 days)"| R








As an ODE, the Erlang period is exact: I is split into three stages, each with a mean of a third of the period, as the equations show:

sim = ss.Sim(erlang, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0)
sim.run()
erlang.equations()

dS/dt   = -beta * S * I / N
dE/dt   =  beta * S * I / N - E / dur_E
dI_1/dt =  E / dur_E - 3 * I_1 / mean(dur_I)
dI_2/dt =  3 * I_1 / mean(dur_I) - 3 * I_2 / mean(dur_I)
dI_3/dt =  3 * I_2 / mean(dur_I) - 3 * I_3 / mean(dur_I)
dR/dt   =  3 * I_3 / mean(dur_I)
crumbs: SEIR with a realistic infectious period

title: SEIR with a realistic infectious period
text:
Result

sims = {
    'Exponential': ss.Sim(exponential, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0),
    'Erlang, 3 stages': ss.Sim(erlang, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('seir')








Both have the same R0, so the same share of people is infected in the end. But with the Erlang period, people infect others over a narrower window of time after they were infected, so the epidemic grows faster, and peaks earlier and higher. A model fitted to the growth of an epidemic with the wrong distribution of the infectious period gets R0 wrong, which is one reason for the stages.

title: Cases, hospitalizations, and deaths, fitted to data
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Data on an epidemic is rarely the number infected: it is reported cases, hospital admissions, or deaths, each a share of infections, some time after infection. In Starsim these are outcomes: results computed from the model’s flows, with a share, a delay, and (for a stay in hospital) a duration, that don’t change the epidemic itself. This page adds three outcomes to an SIR, makes weekly data from the model with a known β, and fits β to it.
crumbs: Cases, hospitalizations, and deaths, fitted to data

title: Cases, hospitalizations, and deaths, fitted to data
text:
The model








Parameter
Value
Meaning




β
fitted, between 0.05 and 1 per day
Rate of infection; the data was made with 0.25


Infectious period
10 days
Mean time in I (exponential)


Cases
50% of infections, 5 days later
Reported cases


Hospitalizations

People in hospital


Deaths

Lognormal delay (mean 14 days, standard deviation 5)


Population
1,000,000



Infectious at the start
0.1%





import starsim as ss

beta = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1.0]) # A parameter to fit, with its starting value and bounds
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
cases     = ss.outcome(0.5*infection, delay=ss.days(5))
hosp      = ss.outcome(0.05*infection, delay=ss.days(7), duration=ss.days(10))
deaths    = ss.outcome(0.2*hosp, delay=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=14, std=5, unit='days'))
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, cases, hosp, deaths, init=dict(I=0.001), name='sir')

pars = dict(total_pop=1e6, start='2020-01-01', stop='2020-06-01')

title: SIR, four ways
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
The SIR model is the starting point of most epidemic modeling: people are susceptible (S), infectious (I), or recovered and immune (R), infection is frequency-dependent (each susceptible person is infected at a rate of β times the share of people who are infectious), and people stay infectious for an exponentially distributed time. This page writes it in each of the ways Starsim accepts, checks that they are the same model, and runs it as a deterministic ODE, as two kinds of stochastic compartmental model, and as agents.

title: SIR, four ways
text:
The model








Parameter
Value
Meaning




β
0.3 per day
Rate of infection per susceptible person, per unit of the share infectious


Infectious period
10 days
Mean time in I (exponential)


R0
3
β × the infectious period


Population
10,000



Infected at the start
0.1%
10 people



Each transition says where people move from and to, and at what rate. These four spellings say the same thing:

import starsim as ss

spellings = {}

# Operators: from >> to @ rate (or duration)
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
spellings['Operators'] = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='sir')

# Each transition written out in full
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
spellings['Explicit'] = ss.Disease(
    ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.3*I, name='infection'),
    ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(10), name='recovery'),
    init_prev = 0.001,
    name = 'sir',
)

# A class, for a disease to reuse or extend
class SIR(ss.Disease):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
spellings['Class'] = SIR(init_prev=0.001, name='sir')

# The whole flow, β S I / N, as most other frameworks write it
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
N = S + I + R
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*S*I/N
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
spellings['Whole flow'] = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='sir')

The same states, transitions, and rates give the same results, whatever the spelling:

for label, disease in spellings.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(disease, total_pop=10_000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0).run()
    print(f'{label:12s} peak infections: {sim.results.sir.I.max():,.0f}')

Operators    peak infections: 3,006
Explicit     peak infections: 3,006
Class        peak infections: 3,006
Whole flow   peak infections: 3,006


The state-transition diagram, from diagram() (the dashed arrow is a transmission):

spellings['Operators'].diagram()


flowchart LR
    S(["S"])
    I(["I"])
    R(["R"])
    S -.->|"infection: 0.3 × I"| I
    I -->|"recovery: 10 days"| R





flowchart LR
    S(["S"])
    I(["I"])
    R(["R"])
    S -.->|"infection: 0.3 × I"| I
    I -->|"recovery: 10 days"| R

title: SIR, four ways
text:
Result
The same model can be run in four ways: as an ODE (the default for this model, since nothing in it is about individual people), as a chain binomial (a random number of people move between states each day), with the Gillespie algorithm (each event at its own random time), and as agents.

sir = spellings['Operators']
sims = {}
for solver in ['ode', 'binomial', 'gillespie', 'abm']:
    sims[solver] = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=10_000, stop=ss.days(150), solver=solver, verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sir')








The three stochastic runs follow the ODE closely, each a little differently by chance. With 10,000 people and 10 infected at the start, chance mostly moves the timing of the peak; with fewer people, or fewer infected at the start, the runs differ more (see The chance of a major outbreak). In all of them about 94% of people are infected in the end, as the final-size equation predicts for R0 = 3 (see Final size):

title: Closing schools
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Closing schools is one of the first measures considered against a new respiratory infection. It removes the contacts children make at school, but not those at home or elsewhere, so whether it helps depends on how much of the spread happens at school, and on when the schools close and reopen. This page models a closure as the loss of one setting’s contacts, adapting the school closure example of the Epidemics R package: an SEIR model of an influenza-like infection in the population of the United Kingdom, in three age groups, with the contact matrices of Prem et al. (2021) for each setting.

title: Closing schools
text:
The model








Parameter
Value
Meaning




β
0.016 per contact
Chance of infection per contact with an infectious person


Latent period
3 days
Mean time in E (exponential)


Infectious period
7 days
Mean time in I (exponential)


Age groups
0–19, 20–39, 40+
With the shares of the United Kingdom’s population


Contacts
Prem et al. (2021)
One matrix each for home, school, work, and the rest of the community


Infectious at the start
One in a million



Closure
Days 200 to 260
School contacts removed; the others go on




import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
flu = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> E @ 0.016*I,
    onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(3),
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(7),
    init      = dict(I=1e-6),
    name      = 'flu',
)
flu.stratify(age=[0, 20, 40])

home, school, work, community = [ss.contacts('United Kingdom', layer=layer) for layer in ['home', 'school', 'work', 'community']]

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/


R0 is about 1.5. The closure is a modifier of the school contacts: from day 200 to day 260 they are multiplied by zero, and when it ends, they are back as they were, since a modifier never changes the contacts themselves.

closure = ss.modify(school, multiply=0, start=ss.days(200), stop=ss.days(260))

title: Closing schools
text:
Result

pars = dict(people=ss.people('United Kingdom'), networks=[home, school, work, community], stop=ss.days(600))
sims = {
    'Schools open': ss.Sim(flu, **pars),
    'Schools closed for 60 days': ss.Sim(flu, interventions=closure, **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('flu_I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Schools open, Schools closed for 60 days)
  Done in 0.76 s









The closure doesn’t prevent the epidemic. It delays the peak by about six weeks and lowers it by about a fifth, which could matter for hospitals, but most of those it spares are infected after schools reopen, since the epidemic resumes among people who are still susceptible: the number infected in all is only about 3% lower.

msim.summarize().loc['flu_infection']








value


scenario





Schools open
3.398707e+07


Schools closed for 60 days
3.288660e+07







By age, the number infectious falls in every group while schools are closed, and most among children, who make most of the contacts at school:

sims['Schools closed for 60 days'].results.flu.I.by('age').plot()








The Epidemics package says a closure another way: as a share by which the contacts of each age group fall (e.g. by half for those under 20). That works in Starsim too, as a modifier of each group’s susceptibility and transmissibility, e.g. ss.modify(flu.rel_sus, multiply=0.5, where=flu.age < 20, start=..., stop=...). Removing the school contacts says more directly what a closure does, when the contacts by setting are known.

title: Final size
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
In a closed SIR epidemic that starts with almost everyone susceptible, the share of people who are ever infected, z, depends only on R0. Kermack and McKendrick (1927) showed that it solves the final-size equation
\[z = 1 - e^{-R_0 z},\]
whatever the infectious period or how fast the epidemic runs. This page checks Starsim’s ODE against the equation for R0 from just above 1 to 4.

title: Final size
text:
The model
An SIR with an infectious period of 10 days, and β = R0 / 10 per day for each value of R0. A population of a million starts with one person in a million infectious, so that almost everyone starts susceptible, as the equation assumes, and each run lasts long enough (2,000 days) for even the slowest epidemic, with R0 just above 1, to end.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

def make_sir(R0):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ (R0/10)*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
    return ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(I=1e-6), name='sir')


make_sir(2).diagram()


flowchart LR
    S(["S"])
    I(["I"])
    R(["R"])
    S -.->|"infection: 0.2 × I"| I
    I -->|"recovery: 10 days"| R





flowchart LR
    S(["S"])
    I(["I"])
    R(["R"])
    S -.->|"infection: 0.2 × I"| I
    I -->|"recovery: 10 days"| R

title: Final size
text:
Result
For each R0, the final size from the model is the share of people recovered at the end:

R0s = np.arange(1.1, 4.01, 0.3)
model = []
for R0 in R0s:
    sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(R0), total_pop=1e6, stop=ss.days(2000), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    model.append(sim.results.sir.R[-1] / 1e6)

The equation has no closed-form solution, but it can be solved by iteration: start from any z between 0 and 1 and apply the right-hand side repeatedly, which converges to the solution when R0 > 1.

R0_curve = np.linspace(1.01, 4, 200)
z = np.ones_like(R0_curve)
for i in range(500):
    z = 1 - np.exp(-R0_curve*z)

plt.plot(R0_curve, z, label='Final-size equation')
plt.plot(R0s, model, 'o', label='Starsim (ODE)')
plt.xlabel('R0')
plt.ylabel('Share of people ever infected')
plt.legend()
plt.show()








The model agrees with the equation to within a few parts in a million, for every R0: about the share of people infectious at the start, which the equation leaves out. Run as agents or stochastically in a large population, the model gives close to the same final size in the runs in which a major outbreak occurs (see The chance of a major outbreak).

title: Final size
text:
Going further

SIR, four ways writes and runs the SIR model this check uses.
Kermack WO, McKendrick AG (1927). A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Proceedings of the Royal Society A 115:700–721.

title: Cholera with a water reservoir
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Cholera spreads mostly through water rather than from person to person: infected people shed bacteria into the water, the bacteria decay over weeks, and susceptible people are infected by drinking it. A model of it needs a state that is not people at all: the amount of bacteria in the water, W. This page models W as a state of the disease that holds a count rather than people, following the model of Codeço (2001).

title: Cholera with a water reservoir
text:
The model
Infection depends on the concentration of bacteria, with a dose-response curve that saturates: the rate is β W / (W + K), where K is the concentration at which the rate is half its maximum.








Parameter
Value
Meaning




β
0.5 per day
Maximum rate of infection, when the water is saturated with bacteria


K
100,000
Concentration of bacteria at which the rate is half its maximum


Infectious period
5 days
Mean time in I (exponential)


Shedding
10 per day
Bacteria shed into the water by each infectious person


Survival of bacteria
30 days
Mean time bacteria survive in the water


Population
10,000



Infectious at the start
0.1%





import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
W = ss.State(people=False) # Bacteria in the water: a count, not people
K = 1e5                    # Concentration at which infection is half its maximum

infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(0.5) * W.n / (W.n + K)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(5)
shedding  = ss.null >> W @ ss.perday(10) * I.n  # Each infectious person sheds 10 a day
decay     = W >> ss.null @ ss.days(30)          # Bacteria survive 30 days on average
cholera = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, shedding, decay, init=dict(I=0.001), name='cholera')

W.n and I.n are counts (the amount of bacteria, and the number of people infectious), where a bare I in a rate would be the share of people infectious. ss.null is outside the model: shedding adds bacteria from nowhere, and decay removes them. title: Severity by age, as a function
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Some parts of a model are easiest to write as a function. Here the chance that an infection is severe enough for hospital depends on age: 10% under 50, and 40% from 50 up. Rather than stratify the disease by age and give a value for each group, the chance is a Python function of the sim, which reads people’s ages. Starsim tries the function on the model’s age groups, and since it works on them, the model still runs as compartments; run as agents, the same function is evaluated for each person.

def severity(sim):

flu = ss.Disease(infection, course, discharge, init=dict(I=0.001), name='flu')

title: Vaccination as a stratification
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
In many compartmental models, vaccination is not part of the disease at all: the population is split into the vaccinated and the unvaccinated, vaccination moves people from one group to the other, and the vaccinated are infected at a lower rate. This is how summer2, Atomica, and many published models write it, and it keeps the disease model the same whatever the vaccination program. This page writes an SIR this way, with a campaign that vaccinates half of the population on day 10, and compares it with no vaccination.

title: Vaccination as a stratification
text:
The model








Parameter
Value
Meaning




β
0.3 per day
Rate of infection of the unvaccinated


Vaccine effect
90%
The vaccinated are infected at 10% of the rate of the unvaccinated


Infectious period
10 days
Mean time in I (exponential)


R0
3
Before vaccination


Campaign
Day 10
Vaccinates 50% of people, whatever their state


Population
10,000



Infectious at the start
0.1%





import starsim as ss

def make_sir():
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
    sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='sir')
    sir.stratify(vaccinated=[False, True], split=[1, 0], adjust={'infection': [1.0, 0.1]})
    return sir

campaign = ss.Delivery(move=dict(vaccinated=True), coverage=0.5, at=ss.days(10), name='campaign')

stratify() splits each state in two, with everyone unvaccinated at the start (split=[1, 0]), and adjust= multiplies the rate of infection by 1 for the unvaccinated and 0.1 for the vaccinated. The campaign is a delivery that moves people to the vaccinated group: it needs no vaccine product, since the effect of vaccination is in the stratification. The diagram, from diagram(), is an SIR’s, since the vaccinated and unvaccinated groups split each state:

make_sir().diagram()

title: An STI on a sexual network
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
A sexually transmitted infection spreads only within partnerships, which form and dissolve over time, and how fast it spreads depends on who partners with whom and for how long, not just on the average number of partners. This needs a model of individual people and their partnerships: a network, and so agents. This page models a curable bacterial STI (an SIS model: people become susceptible again when cured) on Starsim’s sexual network of men and women, with a different chance of transmission per sex act from men to women and from women to men.

title: Age groups and a contact matrix
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
People of different ages mix differently: children have the most contacts, and most of them with other children. An age-structured model splits each state by age group, and a contact matrix says how many contacts a day a person in each group has with people in each other group. With contacts, β is the chance of infection per contact, and the force of infection on group i is β times the sum over groups j of the contacts of i with j times the share of j who are infectious. This page builds an age-structured SIR, as in the age-structured models of Keeling and Rohani (2008, chapter 3).

title: Hospitalization and death
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Two different mechanisms decide what happens to people after a state, and a model needs the right one. In a split on entry, the outcome is decided when people enter the state: here, 10% of infectious people will go to hospital and the rest will recover, each after their infectious period. With competing hazards, two transitions out of a state run at the same time and whichever happens first wins: here, people in hospital are discharged after 10 days on average, but die at a rate of 0.02 per day while they are there, so the share who die depends on both rates. This page puts both in one model, a respiratory infection with hospitalization, and checks the share who die.

import starsim as ss

S, I, R, H, D = ss.states('S I R H D')
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I
course    = ss.Transition(I, [R, H], dur=ss.days(8), p=[None, 0.1])  # Split on entry: 10% to H, the rest to R
discharge = H >> R @ ss.days(10)                                     # Competing hazards: discharge ...
death     = H >> D @ ss.perday(0.02)                                 # ... and death
covid = ss.Disease(infection, course, discharge, death, init=dict(I=0.001), name='covid')

In p=[None, 0.1], None stands for the rest (here, 90%). The diagram, from diagram():

And the equations, in which the split appears as the shares (1 - 0.1) and 0.1 of the flow out of I, and the competing hazards as two flows out of H:

covid.equations()

dS/dt = -beta * S * I / N
dI/dt =  beta * S * I / N - I / dur_I
dR/dt =  (1 - 0.1) * I / dur_I + H / dur_H
dH/dt =  0.1 * I / dur_I - rate_death * H - H / dur_H
dD/dt =  rate_death * H


A rate given as a number is named by its transition, so the rate of death appears as a parameter called rate_death, and a duration by the state it is the time in (dur_I and dur_H). To give it a name of your own, write it as ss.par(ss.perday(0.02), name='mu') (see Parameters).

title: The chance of a major outbreak
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
An epidemic with R0 above 1 doesn’t always take off. Early on, when there are only a few cases, each one infects a random number of others, and by chance all of them can recover before passing the infection on. For an SIR model with an exponential infectious period, started by one infectious person, the chance that this happens (that the outbreak is minor) is 1 / R0, so the chance of a major outbreak is 1 − 1 / R0 (Whittle, 1955). A deterministic model can’t show this, since in an ODE an epidemic with R0 above 1 always takes off; this page checks it with many stochastic runs.
crumbs: The chance of a major outbreak

title: The chance of a major outbreak
text:
The model
An SIR in a population of 1,000, with an infectious period of 10 days and β = R0 / 10 per day, started by a single infectious person. Each model is run 300 times with the Gillespie algorithm, which follows each infection and recovery as an event at its own random time, as the theory does.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

def make_sir(R0):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ (R0/10)*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
    return ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=1), name='sir')


make_sir(2).diagram()


flowchart LR
    S(["S"])
    I(["I"])
    R(["R"])
    S -.->|"infection: 0.2 × I"| I
    I -->|"recovery: 10 days"| R





flowchart LR
    S(["S"])
    I(["I"])
    R(["R"])
    S -.->|"infection: 0.2 × I"| I
    I -->|"recovery: 10 days"| R
crumbs: The chance of a major outbreak

title: The chance of a major outbreak
text:
Result
A run counts as a major outbreak if more than 10% of people are infected; the rest infect at most a few people each, so the exact threshold hardly matters. infection.summarize() gives the infections over the whole of each run:

R0s = [1.25, 1.5, 2, 3, 4]
major = []
for R0 in R0s:
    sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(R0), total_pop=1000, stop=ss.days(365), solver='gillespie', verbose=0)
    msim = sim.run(n_runs=300, verbose=0)
    infections = msim.results.sir.infection.summarize() # One total for each run
    major.append(np.mean(infections > 100))

R0_curve = np.linspace(1, 4.2, 100)
plt.plot(R0_curve, 1 - 1/R0_curve, label='Theory: 1 − 1/R0')
plt.plot(R0s, major, 'o', label='Starsim (300 Gillespie runs each)')
plt.xlabel('R0')
plt.ylabel('Share of runs with a major outbreak')
plt.legend()
plt.show()








Each point is a share of 300 runs, so it is uncertain by about ±0.05 (two standard errors), and within that the runs agree with the theory.
The theory is for continuous time. A chain binomial model (solver='binomial') moves people between states in steps of time, here a day, and gives higher shares for this model (about 0.56 for R0 = 2, against 0.5): in steps of a day, the chance that a person recovers before infecting anyone is lower than in continuous time. With a smaller step (dt=ss.days(0.1)), it agrees with the theory. Agents also take steps of a day, but draw each person’s infectious period from the exponential distribution itself, and agree with the theory at steps of a day.

title: Measles in London, four ways
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Starsim declares most models in a few lines: states, transitions, rates, and the data to fit them to. Sooner or later, though, a model needs something none of these say. This page takes one such model, the measles model of He, Ionides and King (2010), and fits it into Starsim in four ways, each a small step from the last:
None of these needs anything added to Starsim. Each gives up a little of what Starsim knows about the model in return for freedom.

title: Measles in London, four ways
text:
The model
He et al. fitted a stochastic SEIR model to the weekly measles cases reported in London from 1944 to 1965. It is the classic test of methods for fitting stochastic models, and it has four features that Starsim’s declarations don’t have words for:

Noise on the rate of infection. Besides the chance of who is infected each day, the force of infection itself varies at random from day to day (“extra-demographic” noise, gamma-distributed with variance σ²).
Births that enter school together. Most children (55.7%) enter the susceptible pool all at once, on the day school starts in September; the rest enter through the year. The birth rate and the population follow the census.
School terms. Transmission is higher during the four school terms than in the holidays.
A measurement model whose spread grows with the cases. Each week’s reported cases are normal, with mean ρC and variance ρC(1 − ρ + ψ²ρC), where C is the number who recovered that week.

The parameters are those the paper estimated. The census and the cases are two small tables:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.stats as sps
import sciris as sc
import starsim as ss

pars = sc.obj(
    R0=56.8, sigma=28.9/365.25, gamma=30.4/365.25, mu=0.02/365.25, # Latent and infectious periods of about 12 days; deaths per day
    alpha=0.976, iota=2.9, sigma_se=0.0878,  # Mixing, imported infections, and the noise
    amplitude=0.554, cohort=0.557,           # School terms, and the share of births entering at school start
    rho=0.488, psi=0.116,                    # Reporting
    s0=0.0297, e0=5.17e-5, i0=5.14e-5,       # Starting shares
)
start = ss.date('1943-12-31')
stop = start + ss.days(7*1096) # 1,096 weeks of data
terms = [(7, 100), (115, 199), (252, 300), (308, 356)] # School terms, in days of the year

census = pd.read_csv('../tutorials/data/he2010_london_covariates.tsv', sep='\t') # Days from 1944-01-07; the birth rate is per person per year, lagged four years
cases = pd.read_csv('../tutorials/data/he2010_london_cases.tsv', sep='\t')        # Days from the start
data = pd.DataFrame(dict(recovery=cases.weekly_cases.values), index=[start + ss.days(int(t)) for t in cases.time])

def year(date):
    """ The time as He et al. count it: the year, plus the day of the year over 365.25 """
    return date.year + date.dayofyear/365.25

census_years = year(ss.date('1944-01-07')) + census.t.values/365.25
def lookup(column, date):
    """ The census value in force at a date (each month's value holds until the next) """
    i = np.searchsorted(census_years, year(date), side='right') - 1
    return census[column].values[max(i, 0)]

title: Measles in London, four ways
text:
1. Declared, with a little code
The states, transitions and deaths are declared as usual. What they can’t say is written as functions of the sim, which Starsim calls once a step: the force of infection, which reads the calendar for the school terms, and the births, which on day 251 of the year include the cohort entering school. The noise is a value that changes each step, so it is a few lines of a connector, whose step() draws it before the diseases run; the force of infection reads it.

class Noise(ss.Connector):
    """ Gamma noise on the force of infection, with mean 1, drawn once a step """
    def __init__(self, sigma_se):
        super().__init__(name='noise')
        self.var = sigma_se**2*365.25 # The variance of a day's noise
        self.value = 1.0

    def init_post(self):
        super().init_post()
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(self.sim.pars.rand_seed)

    def step(self):
        self.value = self.rng.gamma(1/self.var, self.var)

def force(sim):
    """ The force of infection: school terms, mixing that rises a little more slowly than the number infectious, and the noise """
    doy = sim.now.dayofyear
    school = any(lo <= doy <= hi for lo,hi in terms)
    seas = 1 + pars.amplitude*0.2411/0.7589 if school else 1 - pars.amplitude # The same mean over the year
    beta = pars.R0*seas*(1 - np.exp(-(pars.gamma + pars.mu)))
    I = sim.diseases.measles.I.n
    return ss.perday(beta*(I + pars.iota)**pars.alpha/lookup('pop', sim.now)*sim.connectors.noise.value)

def births(sim):
    """ Births per day; on day 251, also the cohort of the year's births entering school """
    yearly = lookup('pop', sim.now)*lookup('birthrate', sim.now)
    entry = sim.now.dayofyear == 251
    return ss.perday(yearly*((1 - pars.cohort)/365.25 + pars.cohort*entry))

def make_measles():
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    N0 = lookup('pop', start)
    return ss.Disease(
        infection = S >> E @ force,
        latency   = E >> I @ ss.perday(pars.sigma),
        recovery  = I >> R @ ss.perday(pars.gamma),
        births    = ss.null >> S @ births,
        deaths    = ss.death(rate=ss.perday(pars.mu)),
        init_n    = dict(S=round(pars.s0*N0), E=round(pars.e0*N0), I=round(pars.i0*N0)),
        name      = 'measles',
    )

sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(), connectors=Noise(pars.sigma_se), solver='binomial', total_pop=lookup('pop', start),
             start=start, stop=stop, dt=ss.days(1), data=data)
sim.run()

Sim: measles, 2,464,805 people, as a stochastic compartmental model (chain binomial), 1943-12-31 to 1965-01-01
  Note: the initial value of S in "measles" is kept, and the other 2,391,346 people start in R, the only state not given one


  Done in 16.6 s


Sim(n=2464804; 1943-12-31—1965-01-01; diseases=measles; connectors=noise)


The model runs as a chain binomial, a stochastic compartmental model, since nothing in it is about individual people. To compare it with the data, the weekly recoveries are scaled by the reporting rate ρ:

weekly = sim.results.measles.recovery.values[1:].reshape(-1, 7).sum(axis=1) # Days 1-7, 8-14, ..., as the data are
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
plt.plot(data.index, data.recovery, label='Reported', alpha=0.6)
plt.plot(data.index, pars.rho*weekly, label='Model × ρ', alpha=0.8)
plt.ylabel('Cases per week')
plt.legend()








The model’s epidemics come every other year, as London’s did, though not always in the same years: a stochastic model’s timing drifts from the data’s unless it is filtered, as in step 5. describe() shows everything that is declared, and says what is code:

What this costs: the functions run in Python once a step, so the run is taken a step at a time (a few seconds) rather than in one compiled call; and Starsim’s own particle filter, which runs many copies of the kernels at once, can’t take a connector, since each copy would need noise of its own. Everything declared still prints, and the run’s results are ordinary results.

title: Measles in London, four ways
text:
2. A likelihood of your own
He et al.’s measurement model is a normal whose variance grows with the mean, which isn’t one of Starsim’s likelihoods. Any likelihood can be given as a function of the data and the model’s values, returning the log-likelihood of each. Here, as in the paper, it is the chance of the reported number rounded to a whole case:

def reported(observed, recovered):
    """ The log-likelihood of the reported cases, given the recoveries """
    m = pars.rho*recovered
    sd = np.sqrt(m*(1 - pars.rho + pars.psi**2*m)) + 1e-18
    lik = np.where(observed > 0, sps.norm.cdf(observed + 0.5, m, sd) - sps.norm.cdf(observed - 0.5, m, sd), sps.norm.cdf(0.5, m, sd))
    return np.log(lik + 1e-18)

ss.fit.loglik(sim, likelihood=dict(recovery=reported))

-31485.821261718982


The function can be given wherever a distribution is: on an outcome (ss.outcome(..., likelihood=reported)), to sim.fit(likelihood=...), and to the particle filter. For a single stochastic run, the log-likelihood is low, since its epidemics are not in step with the data; a particle filter (step 5) measures the fit properly.

title: Measles in London, four ways
text:
3. Written as code
The most direct way is to write the model as one module, in NumPy, with nothing declared. This is He et al.’s own algorithm, line for line (an Euler-multinomial step each day). Its states are arrays with one value for each of n runs, so one sim can also run many copies of the model at once:

class He2010(ss.Module):
    """ He et al.'s model, as code: n copies of S, E, I and R, advanced each day by the function euler """
    def __init__(self, n=1, euler=None):
        super().__init__(name='he2010')
        self.n = n
        self.euler = euler

    def init_post(self):
        super().init_post()
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(self.sim.pars.rand_seed)
        N0 = lookup('pop', self.sim.t.start)
        self.S, self.E, self.I = [np.full(self.n, np.round(N0*x)) for x in [pars.s0, pars.e0, pars.i0]]
        self.C = np.zeros(self.n) # Recoveries in the last step
        self.recoveries = []

    def step(self):
        p, now = pars, self.now
        pop = lookup('pop', now)
        yearly = pop*lookup('birthrate', now)
        births = np.round(yearly*((1 - p.cohort)/365.25 + p.cohort*(now.dayofyear == 251)))
        seas = 1 + p.amplitude*0.2411/0.7589 if any(lo <= now.dayofyear <= hi for lo,hi in terms) else 1 - p.amplitude
        beta = p.R0*seas*(1 - np.exp(-(p.gamma + p.mu)))
        var = p.sigma_se**2*365.25
        noise = self.rng.gamma(1/var, var, self.n)
        rates = (p.iota, p.alpha, p.sigma, p.gamma, p.mu)
        self.C = self.euler(self.S, self.E, self.I, beta, pop, births, noise, self.rng, rates)
        self.recoveries.append(self.C.mean())

def euler_step(S, E, I, beta, pop, births, noise, rng, rates):
    """ One day for each copy: who leaves S, E and I, and where to (the rest die) """
    iota, alpha, sigma, gamma, mu = rates
    foi = beta*(I + iota)**alpha/pop*noise
    out = []
    for n,rate in [(S, foi), (E, sigma), (I, gamma)]:
        leaving = rng.binomial(n.astype(np.int64), 1 - np.exp(-(rate + mu)))
        out.append((rng.binomial(leaving, rate/(rate + mu)), leaving))
    (inf, nS), (lat, nE), (rec, nI) = out
    S += births - nS
    E += inf - nE
    I += lat - nI
    return rec

def make_coded(n=1, euler=euler_step, **kwargs):
    return ss.Sim(modules=He2010(n, euler), start=start, stop=stop, dt=ss.days(1), verbose=0, **kwargs)

sims = ss.parallel([make_coded(rand_seed=seed) for seed in range(6)]).sims
totals = [pars.rho*np.sum(s.custom.he2010.recoveries) for s in sims]
print(f'Reported cases over 21 years: {np.mean(totals):,.0f} ± {np.std(totals):,.0f}')

Reported cases over 21 years: 539,534 ± 7,494


The module keeps nothing for each person, so the sim has no agents: Starsim runs it as it is, calling its step() once a day and nothing else. (A module that keeps a value for each person, with define_states(), runs as agents instead.) Starsim still gives it the dates, seeds, parallel runs, and anything else it asks of the sim; what it can’t do is show what the module does (describe() lists it by name only), run it under another solver, or fit it with sim.fit(), since there is nothing declared to fit.

title: Measles in London, four ways
text:
4. Compiled
@ss.jit compiles a function with Numba, with no change to what it does. The step above is written for whole arrays, so here it is again as a loop over the copies, which Numba makes fast:

@ss.jit
def euler_loop(S, E, I, beta, pop, births, noise, rng, rates):
    """ The same as euler_step(), one copy at a time """
    iota, alpha, sigma, gamma, mu = rates
    rec = np.zeros(len(S))
    for i in range(len(S)):
        foi = beta*(I[i] + iota)**alpha/pop*noise[i]
        nS = rng.binomial(int(S[i]), 1 - np.exp(-(foi + mu)))
        nE = rng.binomial(int(E[i]), 1 - np.exp(-(sigma + mu)))
        nI = rng.binomial(int(I[i]), 1 - np.exp(-(gamma + mu)))
        inf = rng.binomial(nS, foi/(foi + mu))
        lat = rng.binomial(nE, sigma/(sigma + mu))
        rec[i] = rng.binomial(nI, gamma/(gamma + mu))
        S[i] += births - nS
        E[i] += inf - nE
        I[i] += lat - nI
    return rec

make_coded(euler=euler_loop).run() # The first run compiles it
for label,euler in [('NumPy', euler_step), ('Compiled', euler_loop)]:
    T = sc.timer()
    make_coded(euler=euler).run()
    T.toc(f'One run, {label}')

  Compiling euler_loop() with Numba, estimated time: 1-10 s
One run, NumPy: 1.59 s
One run, Compiled: 1.51 s


The first call compiles it, which takes a few seconds once; after that it is loaded from Numba’s cache. Compiling pays off most for loops that NumPy can’t write as whole arrays. For this model, most of the time of a large run is the random draws themselves. A function that Numba can’t compile (e.g. one that calls Sciris) is an error, which says why; @ss.jit(nopython=False) runs it as Python instead, with a note.

title: Measles in London, four ways
text:
5. A particle filter
The coded model’s copies can be the particles of a filter. At the end of each week, an analyzer weights each copy by how likely that week’s reported cases are under it (the reported() likelihood from step 2), and then draws the copies again in proportion to their weights, so that those that have drifted from the data are dropped. The mean weight, multiplied over the weeks, estimates the likelihood of the data:

class Filter(ss.Analyzer):
    """ A bootstrap particle filter over the copies of He2010 """
    def __init__(self, observed):
        super().__init__(name='pfilter')
        self.observed = observed
        self.loglik = 0.0

    def init_post(self):
        super().init_post()
        self.model = self.sim.custom.he2010
        self.week = np.zeros(self.model.n)
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(self.sim.pars.rand_seed + 1)

    def step(self):
        if self.ti == 0: # Analyzers also run at the start, before the first step
            return
        self.week += self.model.C
        if self.ti % 7:
            return
        weights = np.exp(reported(self.observed[self.ti//7 - 1], self.week))
        self.loglik += np.log(weights.mean())
        n = len(weights)
        chosen = np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(weights/weights.sum()), (self.rng.random() + np.arange(n))/n).clip(max=n - 1)
        for key in ['S', 'E', 'I']:
            setattr(self.model, key, getattr(self.model, key)[chosen])
        self.week[:] = 0

sim = make_coded(n=500, euler=euler_loop, analyzers=Filter(data.recovery.values)).run()
print(f'Log-likelihood: {sim.analyzers.pfilter.loglik:,.1f}')

Log-likelihood: -5,812.2


With 2,000 particles, ten such filters give −5,819 ± 14, against −5,827 ± 13 from pomp, the R package He et al. used; fewer particles give a lower and noisier estimate. A filter like this is the basis of fitting a stochastic model: estimate the likelihood at many parameter values and keep the best (IF2 and particle MCMC are refinements of the same idea).

title: Starsim
Starsim
Starsim
text:
Installation
If you’re new to Python, check out our getting started guide. You can also use our installer, which will install Python along with all required dependencies.

Requirements
Python 3.12-3.14 or R.
We recommend, but do not require, installing Starsim in a virtual environment, such as uv or conda.


Python
Starsim is most easily installed via PyPI:
pip install "starsim[jax]"
starsim init
JAX is recommended, for gradients, fitting with them, and long runs. It is optional since it has no builds for Windows on Arm: there, use pip install starsim, and everything else works. Intel Macs are not supported.
starsim init compiles Starsim (once, which takes a few minutes and makes the first runs faster) and installs its skill for AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex (type /starsim to use it). To do just one of these, run starsim compile or starsim ai.
Or with uv:
uv init example
cd example
uv add "starsim[jax]"
Starsim can also be installed locally (including optional dependencies for testing and documentation). To do this, clone first this repository, then run:
pip install -e .[dev]


R
R-Starsim can be installed with:
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("starsimhub/rstarsim")
library(starsim)
init_starsim()
See r.starsim.org for more information.

title: Starsim
text:
Usage and documentation
Full documentation, including tutorials and an API reference, is available at docs.starsim.org.
You can run a simple demo via:
import starsim as ss
ss.demo()
Here’s how you’d write a minimal compartmental SIR model with an infection rate of 0.3 per step and a mean recovery duration of 10 steps:
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.3*I),
    recovery = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10)
)

sim = ss.Sim(sir).run()
sim.sir.plot()
If you prefer something that looks more like equations rather than code, there’s an even more compact notation available:
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states(3) # Create model states
inf = S >> I @ 0.3*I   # Define infection at rate beta, mediated by I (*S/N implied)
rec = I >> R @ 0.1     # Define spontaneous recovery
ss.Sim(inf, rec).run().plot() # Create, run, and plot the simulation
The code above runs as a compartmental model by default, but you can also run it as an agent-based model (ABM) if you prefer. ABMs come with additional flexibility, such as defining explicit contact networks:
import starsim as ss

# Define the parameters
pars = dict(
    n_agents = 5_000,     # Number of agents to simulate
    networks = dict(      # Networks define how agents interact with each other
        type = 'random',  # Use the built-in 'random' network
        n_contacts = 10   # Each person has 10 contacts with other people  
    ),
    diseases = dict(      # Define the disease dynamics
        type = 'sir',     # Use the built-in SIR disease (including built-in parameters)
        init_prev = 0.01, # Proportion of the population initially infected
        beta = 0.05,      # Probability of transmission between contacts
    )
)

# Make the sim, run and plot
sim = ss.Sim(pars)
sim.run() # Runs as an agent-based model since uses an explicit network
sim.plot() # Plot all the sim results
sim.sir.plot() # Plot the standard SIR curves
Or from R:
library(starsim)
load_starsim()

# Define the parameters
pars <- list(
    n_agents = 5000,
    networks = list(type = 'random'),
    diseases = list(type = 'sir', beta = 0.1)
)

# Create, run, and plot the simulation
sim <- ss$Sim(pars)
sim$run()
sim$diseases$sir$plot()
More usage examples are available in the tutorials and user guide.

title: Gradients
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
For a deterministic model, run as an ODE, Starsim can work out how each result changes as each parameter changes: the gradient, or the derivatives of the results with respect to the parameters. It does this by automatic differentiation with JAX, which follows the calculation of the run step by step, rather than by rerunning the model with slightly different values. Gradients make several things possible:
This page assumes the basics of Fitting a model. Gradients need JAX (pip install "starsim[jax]"), a model that runs as an ODE, and one whose whole run is compiled: a rate that calls a Python function, a module written as code, or a movement register rules them out, and the fit says which when it can’t use gradients. JAX runs on a GPU if it finds one; if it can’t use it (e.g. its CUDA plugin is of another version than JAX), run it on the CPU with ss.options.jax = 'cpu' (or the environment variable STARSIM_JAX=cpu) before it is first used.

title: Gradients
text:
The model
The model is a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000, 90% of whom are immune, with two unknowns: the transmission rate beta and the share of cases reported, report. Reported cases are counts, so their likelihood is a Poisson: it says how the data vary around the model’s value. The data are a year of weekly cases drawn from a run with beta = 1.9 and report = 0.5:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])  # Transmission rate per day
report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1]) # Share of cases reported

infection = S >> E @ beta*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
cases     = ss.outcome(report*onset, likelihood=ss.poisson())
measles = ss.Disease(infection, onset, recovery, cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9))
pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

truth = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=1.9, report=0.5), rand_seed=2, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_data('cases', resample='week')

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/
Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.003 s; measles: 5,856 infections; at most 298 infectious, on 2025-08-05

title: Gradients
text:
The gradient of a result
sim.gradient() gives the derivative of each result, at each time, with respect to each parameter with bounds, at the parameters’ current values. Here, at the true values, for the daily reported cases:

grad = truth.gradient('cases')

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
t = truth.results.timevec
ax.plot(t, grad.beta.measles.cases, label='Change in daily cases per unit of beta')
ax.plot(t, grad.report.measles.cases, label='Change in daily cases per unit of report')
ax.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.5)
ax.legend();

  Compiling the gradient with JAX, estimated time: 0.2-5 s









A higher β brings the epidemic forward: more cases before the peak, and fewer after it, when the susceptible people have already been used up. A higher reporting share scales every week’s cases up in proportion. Because the two parameters change the curve in different ways, the data can tell them apart. Two parameters whose gradients had the same shape could only be fitted as a combination (see Parameter identification).
The result is indexed by parameter, then module, then result: grad.beta.measles.cases is an array with one value per time step.
sim.gradient() also takes a function of the run sim, which can be anything that returns a number or an array, e.g. a total cost. Its gradient is worked out from the same run in JAX, so it needs no JAX of your own:

total = lambda sim: sim.results.measles.cases.sum()
truth.gradient(total)

sc.obj(beta=3076.0809603227817, report=5824.650394379204)

title: Gradients
text:
Many values
A parameter with a value for each level of a stratification (ss.par(ss.by(patch=[...]), bounds=...)), an array, or a time series has a gradient for each value, named as a fit names them. A time series fitted value by value is a way to estimate a transmission rate that changes in time, with no shape assumed for it:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
days = list(range(0, 365, 28)) # A value every four weeks, in between which it changes linearly
beta = ss.par(ss.timeseries(days, [1.5]*len(days), 'linear'), bounds=[0.5, 4])
onset = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
cases = ss.outcome(0.5*onset, likelihood=ss.poisson()) # The share reported, taken as known here
measles_t = ss.Disease(S >> E @ beta*I, onset, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9))
smooth = lambda pars: 100*np.sum(np.diff(pars['beta'].values)**2) # Large changes from one value to the next are unlikely
fit_t = ss.Sim(measles_t, data=data, **pars).fit(penalty=smooth, verbose=False)
fit_t.table[['par', 'best']]

With many values, what the fit minimizes is differentiated in reverse mode, which takes one pass whatever the number of values, and a long run is checkpointed so that the memory it takes grows only as the square root of its length. Neither is a setting.

title: Gradients
text:
The log-density
sim.log_density() gives the log of the posterior density of the fitted parameters (the log-likelihood of the data, plus the log of the priors), as a function of their values, together with its gradient. It is what a sampler or optimizer of your own would use:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **pars)
density = sim.log_density()
print('Parameters:', density.names)
print('At the starting values:', density.x0)
print('Log-density:', density(density.x0))
print('Its gradient:', density.grad(density.x0))

Parameters: ['beta', 'report']

The gradient is positive for both parameters: at the starting values (1.5 and 0.3), increasing either would make the data more likely.

title: Gradients
text:
A best fit with gradients
sim.fit() uses the gradient by default when a deterministic model has three or more fitted parameters ('l-bfgs-b'); with one or two, Nelder–Mead, which needs no gradient, is faster. Either can be asked for:

fit = sim.fit(method='l-bfgs-b')
fit.table

Every data series here has a likelihood, so this is the maximum likelihood estimate. If a parameter has a prior (ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4], prior=ss.normal(2, 0.2))), the best fit is instead the most probable value, given the data and the prior.

title: Gradients
text:
A posterior with NUTS
A best fit is one set of values. A posterior is the whole distribution of values that are consistent with the data, which says how certain each value is, and how the parameters depend on each other. method='nuts' draws from it, given a likelihood for every data series. The priors are each parameter’s prior=, or uniform over its bounds:

post = sim.fit(method='nuts', draws=250, warmup=250)
post.summarize();

Using the likelihood: the sum of the log-likelihoods of cases, treated as independent
Searching on a log scale: report
  Compiling the NUTS sampler with JAX, estimated time: 1-10 s
NUTS: 4 chains on 4 cores, each of 250 warm-up draws and then 250 draws: compiled in 7.0 s, sampled in 1.3 s
Converged: R-hat at most 1.002 and effective sample size at least 541, with 0 divergent draws
The negative log-likelihood is 165.8 at the best values and 4061 at the initial values
Fitted 2 parameter(s) by nuts
Negative log-likelihood: 4061 before, 165.8 after
Converged: R-hat at most 1.002 and effective sample size at least 541, with 0 divergent draws
Posterior: 1,000 draws from 4 chains (best: the draw with the highest posterior density; median, lower, and upper: the median and 95% interval of the posterior)


Each chain of the sampler starts at a different point, spends warmup= draws tuning itself, and then makes draws= draws (500 of each by default; fewer here to keep this page quick). The table gives, for each parameter, the median of the posterior and its 95% interval (lower and upper), with two checks that the chains agree: the R-hat (rhat), which should be at most 1.01, and the effective sample size (ess), the number of independent draws the correlated draws are worth. Fit diagnostics says what to do if they fail.
The draws themselves are in post.samples, one row for each:

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(post.samples.beta, post.samples.report, s=5, alpha=0.5)
ax.scatter(1.9, 0.5, marker='x', s=100, color='red', label='True values')
ax.set_xlabel('beta (per day)')
ax.set_ylabel('report')
ax.legend();








The two are negatively correlated: a slightly higher β gives a slightly larger epidemic, which a slightly lower reporting share brings back to the same number of reported cases.

title: Gradients
text:
Profile likelihoods
A profile likelihood is another way to find a confidence interval for one parameter, without priors: at each value of it, the other parameters are refitted, and the values whose negative log-likelihood is within 1.92 of the lowest form the 95% confidence interval. It also shows whether the data determine the parameter at all: a profile that stays flat up to a bound means they don’t.

prof = ss.fit.profile(sim, 'beta', values=np.linspace(1.86, 1.94, 9))
print('Best value of beta:', round(prof.best, 3))
print('95% confidence interval:', np.round(prof.interval, 3))
prof.table

title: Gradients
text:
Projecting from a posterior
fit.project() runs the fitted model under each scenario, once for each of n draws from the posterior, with the same draws (and seeds) in every scenario. Each draw has a seed of its own, so the spread of the runs is the uncertainty in the fitted values, carried into the projection, together with chance. Here, a vaccination campaign on 1 April that reaches half the town, compared with none:

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.97, coverage=0.5, at='2025-04-01')
proj = post.project({'No campaign': None, 'Campaign': vaccination}, n=50)
proj.plot('measles.cases')

title: Gradients
text:
Other samplers
NUTS is for deterministic models. For a stochastic model, the likelihood can’t be differentiated, and the other posterior methods apply (see Fitting a model):

method='pmcmc', particle MCMC, for a stochastic compartmental model (e.g. solver='binomial') whose data series all have a likelihood: the likelihood at each point is estimated by running many copies of the model (particles) and weighting them by how well they match each data point.
method='abc-smc', approximate Bayesian computation, for any model, including agents: it keeps the values whose runs come closest to the data, and needs no likelihood.
method='if2', iterated filtering, finds the maximum likelihood values of a stochastic compartmental model with particles.

A posterior can also be put together by hand, by sampling-importance resampling, which needs only runs of the model and a likelihood: draw many sets of values from the priors and run each (ss.parallel(sim, priors=True, n_runs=1000), whose msim.runs has the values of each run), work out the likelihood of the data for each run, and resample the runs in proportion to their likelihoods. It is simple and works for any model, but most draws from a wide prior land where the likelihood is negligible, so it needs many runs for few parameters, and fails for many.
How the gradients are computed (the run in JAX, and the steps around it) is explained in Randomness.

title: Starsim models
text:
🧠60% 🤖40%
The Starsim framework serves as a centralized “hub” for storing anything that is typically required to model the spread of diseases, as compartments or among agents. This includes representations of networks, diseases, populations, demographics, interventions, and products, and logic for connecting all of these things together and simulating their interactions over time.

title: Starsim models
text:
Models built with Starsim
Specific models that have been created using the Starsim framework are kept in their own separate repositories. Starsim’s models include the following:
