(If you’ve developed a model and want it included in this list, please get in touch.)
One of the strengths of Starsim is that all of these models are inter-compatible. For example, an HIV-TB coinfection model can be created by combining the HIV module from STIsim and the TB module from TBsim.
These models were written for Starsim 3, and are being ported to Starsim 4; check each model’s own documentation for the version of Starsim it needs. For moving your own Starsim 3 code to Starsim 4, see Starsim v3; much of the rewriting is done by the migration script, python -m starsim.converters.migrate.
Note: the Starsim suite also includes Covasim (for modeling COVID-19). Covasim is built on the same principles as Starsim, but unlike the above tools, it is a separate codebase and is not inter-operable with the other models.

title: Starsim models
text:
The built-in library
Starsim itself comes with a small library of example modules, imported with import starsim.library as ssl: diseases (HIV with CD4 counts, cholera with an environmental reservoir, Ebola, measles), networks (households, networks in space, and theoretical networks such as Erdős–Rényi), and maternal, newborn, and child health (fetal health, neonatal sepsis). They are illustrative rather than validated: their parameter values are indicative, and they are meant to be copied and adapted. See Library: Diseases, Library: Networks, and Library: Maternal-child health.
The core of Starsim also includes the classic compartmental structures, ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR, as declared diseases with named parameters (see Diseases).

title: Starsim models
text:
Choosing a starting model
Start from the smallest model that represents the mechanism your question depends on. An extra compartment, network, or demographic process is worth adding when it changes a quantity relevant to the question, and when it can be supported by assumptions or data. These pages are good starting points for common questions:



Question
Starting point




How does a closed outbreak progress?
SIR, four ways


Does the distribution of the latent or infectious period affect the timing?
SEIR with a realistic infectious period


How many hospital beds will be occupied, and how many people die?
Hospitalization and death


Does an environmental reservoir matter?
Cholera with a water reservoir


Which age groups are most affected?
Age groups and a contact matrix, T4 – Age groups and contacts


What is the effect of vaccination?
Vaccination as a stratification, T5 – Interventions and scenarios


How does infection move between towns?
T6 – Geography and mixing


What do surveillance data say about the parameters?
Cases, hospitalizations, and deaths, fitted to data, T7 – Data and calibration


Do individual partnerships matter?
An STI on a sexual network, A2 – Networks



When adapting a model, first reproduce its baseline, then change one assumption at a time, and compare the results with and without each change. Record where each parameter value came from (ss.par(..., source=...) keeps it with the model; see Parameters), and which outputs were checked against data. If you already have a model in another framework, see Conversion, and check that the translated model gives the same results as the original.

title: Model execution
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Model declaration covered the model as data, and the graph that resolves and checks it when a module is built. This page follows the model into a sim: what sim.init() does, how time works, the loop that runs each step, the objects that hold a run’s state, and how Starsim reports what went wrong or what it assumed. Modules looks at the same loop from the side of one module.

title: Model execution
text:
What sim.init() does
Creating a sim only stores what it was given (as copies, so one sir can go into several sims). The rest happens at sim.init(), which sim.run() and sim.describe() call if needed. In order (Sim.init() in starsim/sim.py, and choose_solver() and the steps that build a declared model in starsim/solvers/choose.py):

Values. Values given by name (pars=dict(beta=0.1)) are set, and each parameter is checked against its bounds (a ValueError).
Groups. The stratifications of the sim and its modules are collected into sim.groups.
Unit. The unit of bare numbers is chosen (below).
Solver. Under solver='auto', Starsim records each ingredient that matters to the choice, lays the model out as compartments (which runs none of its code), and chooses an ODE if every part has a compartmental form, agents otherwise; a compartmental run uses that layout, so it is made once. For a compartmental run, networks become contact rates between groups, and the population becomes one row per group. See Solvers and backends.
Objects. The timeline, the people, and for each declared disease an engine, the object that runs its transitions under the chosen solver. This is the one place where the solver changes which objects exist.
Starting values. Random number streams (Randomness), people’s attributes, then each state’s initial conditions.
Results and the loop. Results are allocated, data is attached to them by name, and the loop’s functions are collected. Parameters are locked, so setting one that doesn’t exist raises an error.
Report. One line saying what will run and how (the modules, the population, the solver, and the span of time), a note for each inference or approximation (kept in sim.notes), and for a compartmental model with transmission, R0 and the number infectious at the start, as a check that the model and its seed are what you meant. When sim.describe() initializes the sim, the line is said when the sim is run instead. The reason for the solver is in sim.solver_reason, and in describe().


import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I,
    recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, start='2020-01-01', stop='2020-07-01')
sim.init()

Sim: sir, 10,000 people, as an ODE, 2020-01-01 to 2020-07-01
  sir: R0 = 3, with 100 infectious at the start


Sim(n=10000; 2020-01-01—2020-07-01; diseases=sir)


Errors are raised at the earliest point that can detect them: a mistake in the model’s structure when the module is built, a value out of bounds at step 1, and a function that asks for something the solver can’t give when it is first called. After sim.init() the sim’s settings are frozen: a changed copy is made with sim.new().

title: Model execution
text:
Units and time
Starsim has four time types: durations (ss.days(10)), hazard rates (ss.perday(0.1)), probabilities per period (ss.probperday(0.1)), and frequencies (ss.freqperday(0.1)). Converting one to a timestep is the type’s job: a hazard r becomes the probability 1 − exp(−r·dt), and a frequency the expected count f·dt. Since mixing them up is a common quiet error, adding a rate to a frequency raises a TypeError. The types are in starsim/time.py, and dates in starsim/dates.py.
A bare number is typed by its slot. Above, 0.3 is a rate and dur=10 a duration. After @ a bare number is always a rate: I >> R @ 10 recovers at 10 a day, while a 10-day dwell time is @ ss.days(10). Its unit is the sim’s unit, from the first of: unit=, the typed values in the model’s diseases, dates for start and stop, a typed dt or stop, years for start and stop, and the typed values in other modules. With none, time is in timesteps, as in a textbook model. The unit is never guessed from the size of a number (0.05 is plausible per day and per year), and when it is inferred, a note says from what:








Sim
Unit
Note




ss.Sim(sir, stop=100), with only bare numbers
none: 100 steps
none, since nothing was guessed


ss.Sim(sir, stop=100, unit='day')
day
none


ss.Sim(sir, start='2020-01-01', stop='2020-06-01')
day
unit='day' (from start and stop dates), kept but not printed, since the dates make it plain


ss.Sim(sir, start=2020, stop=2030)
year
unit='year' (from start and stop years)


ss.Sim(sir, stop=100, dt=ss.weeks(1))
week
unit='week' (from dt)



One time index per step. Step k goes from time point k − 1 to k. Throughout it, in every module, sim.ti is k, where its results go, and sim.now is its start, when values that vary in time are read. At ti == 0 there is no step: the loop records the starting values, and the analyzers run once to see them. See Time.

title: Model execution
text:
The loop
Each step, the loop calls the modules in Starsim’s long-standing order (starsim/internals/loop.py):








Order
Who
What happens




1
sim, then every module
advance() and start_step(): move time and the random number streams on


2
custom modules, then demographics
step(): custom modules; births add agents, and deaths are requested


3
diseases
step_state(): state updates of a disease written as code


4
connectors, networks, interventions
step(): cross-module code, then edges, then deliveries


5
diseases
step(): transmission, and every transition of a declared disease


6
people
step_die(): requested deaths take effect


7
people, then every module
update_results()


8
analyzers
step(), reading the finished step


9
every module, people, sim
finish_step(): dead agents are removed



New agents exist before diseases see them, networks update before interventions so an intervention sees the final network, and interventions run before transmission so someone vaccinated today is protected today. Within a type, modules run in the order given; there are no priorities, phases, or dependency graph. Three rules make this easy to reason about:

Each module sees what the modules before it did. Infection, testing, and treatment can happen in one step. HIV and syphilis can each change the other’s transmission: the order decides who goes first, and its effect shrinks with the timestep (sim.check_dt() measures it).
Order inside one module doesn’t matter. Transitions out of one state compete in one draw: the total hazard decides who leaves, and each one’s share decides where they go, so declaring recovery before death favors neither.
Nobody is removed mid-step. A death is a request that takes effect at step_die(), so arrays never change length partway through a step.

The loop is data. After sim.init(), sim.loop.to_df() lists every call at every time, and sim.loop.insert(fn, label='sir.step') adds a function at any point, or moves a module there. The order can always be printed, and it is the only thing that decides what runs when. Modules shows how to read it.
In a compartmental run, a disease’s own flows have no order: the ODE evaluates them together. If nothing needs a step of its own, the whole run is one call to the kernels (small compiled functions that step the compartments; see Solvers and backends), with no Python loop. sim.kernel_reason() says why a run is stepped instead (for example “it runs as agents”, or the name of an analyzer with a step of its own), and is None for a run taken in one call.

title: Model execution
text:
Per-module timesteps
A module can have its own dt. The loop’s plan is every (time, function) pair of every module on its own timeline, sorted by time and then by the order above, so a daily disease and yearly demographics share one sim, and on the days the demographics are due they run at their usual place. Rates and durations are converted with the dt of the module that uses them. describe() shows the schedule; for a daily disease with ss.Births(dt=ss.years(1)) and ss.Deaths(dt=ss.years(1)):
schedule     every day: sir
             every 365 days: births, deaths

title: Model execution
text:
The runtime objects
These are the objects that hold a run’s state, and that a module written as code reads and writes.

Modules. Diseases, networks, demographics, interventions, connectors, and analyzers are all ss.Module (starsim/internals/modules.py), with one lifecycle: init_pre() and init_post(), then the step functions above, then finalize(). They differ in what they contain, not in how they are scheduled. See Modules.
Engines. A declared disease’s step() hands its transitions to its engine (ss.solvers.make_engine()): Agents or Compartmental, or one that runs nothing for a disease written as code. This is the seam between model and solver: no method of ss.Disease asks which solver it has. A subclass that overrides step() calls super().step(), then does anything else.
People. As agents, sim.people (starsim/people.py) has one entry per agent: age, sex, whether alive, and every module’s states. In a compartmental run it has one row per group, so people.age in a model not stratified by age raises an ss.CapabilityError saying to stratify or run as agents.
Arrays. As agents, a declared state is an ss.BoolState over agents (starsim/internals/arrays.py), beside the ss.FloatArr and others that code adds. arr[uids] reads and writes some agents (ss.uids), and arr.values those alive. Arrays grow as agents are born; the dead leave at the end of the step. Writes by code to a declared state (sir.I[uids] = True) are tracked, so counts see them; writes through .raw, the NumPy array underneath, are not. See Array indexing.

title: Model execution
text:
Errors, warnings, and notes
The policy is: prefer guessing a default and printing it to raising an error. An error is for when there is no sensible guess: a name that doesn’t exist, lengths that don’t match, a request the solver can’t meet. Every message is meant to be read once, by an epidemiologist or by an AI writing a model for one, so it uses the user’s own names, says what exists instead, and says what to do:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.05 * I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(7), init_prev=0.01, name='sir')
sim = ss.Sim(sir, pars=dict(betta=0.2), verbose=0)
try:
    sim.init()
except KeyError as e:
    print(f'{type(e).__name__}: {e}')

KeyNotFoundError: pars= has a value for "betta", which matches no parameter. Parameters are sir.init_prev, sir.beta, sir.dur_I; did you mean sir.beta?


There are three levels:








Level
Type
What happens




Error
a built-in exception: a KeyError for a name that is not found, a TypeError for a value of the wrong kind, a ValueError for the rest
raises; caught by type, e.g. except KeyError


Warning
a RuntimeWarning
issued through Python’s warnings, so filters (and ss.options.warnings='error') apply; the run continues


Note
ss.note()
a line about something assumed or approximated; kept in sim.notes whatever the verbosity, and printed as one line when verbose is 1 or more



A note is said once: the same note isn’t kept twice, and notes made while a sim is being initialized are held and printed after the line that starts the run, so they read as part of it. Since the notes are kept, they survive into a saved sim, and a test can check for them.
Five errors and four warnings are classes of their own, in starsim/internals/errors.py, since code catches or filters them by kind: ss.CapabilityError (the solver asked for can’t run part of the model, which solver='auto' catches to run as agents; it is a ValueError), ss.AlreadyRunError (a sim or module run twice), the distribution errors ss.errors.DistNotInitializedError and DistSeedRepeatError, and BooleanOperationError; and the warnings ss.errors.AtBound (a best fit at a bound), NotConverged, LossyExport, and ImportIncomplete. The tests check each error, warning, and note by its message (tests/devtests/test_errors.py), so a change to a message is a deliberate one.

title: Model execution
text:
Limits

Order between modules is a modeling choice that Starsim won’t make for you. By convention, the module whose accuracy matters most runs last, since it sees the most up-to-date state.
Direct writes by code aren’t recorded. sim.what_modifies(x) lists the declared modifiers on a quantity, not what a step() does to it.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
sim.fit() always returns values. Whether to trust them is a separate question, with several parts: does the model match the data, did the search find the best values, are the values determined by the data, and would the fitted model predict data it hasn’t seen? This page goes through the checks, in the order worth making them. It assumes the basics of Fitting a model.
The examples use a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000, 90% of whom are immune. The data are a year of weekly reported cases, made from the model with a latent period of 10 days (an SEIR model), beta = 1.9, and half of all cases reported:
import starsim as ss

def make_seir():
    """ Measles with a latent period: infected (E), then infectious (I) about 10 days later """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])
    report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])
    onset  = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    cases  = ss.outcome(report*onset)
    return ss.Disease(S >> E @ beta*I, onset, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9), name='measles')

pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
truth = ss.Sim(make_seir(), pars=dict(beta=1.9, report=0.5), rand_seed=2, verbose=0, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_data('cases', resample='week')

title: Fit diagnostics
section: Does the model match the data?
text:
Does the model match the data?
Start by looking. A fit can converge perfectly and still be wrong, if the model can’t produce the pattern in the data. Here the data are fitted with a model that leaves out the latent period, an SIR model:

def make_sir():
    """ Measles without a latent period: infectious as soon as infected """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])
    report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    cases     = ss.outcome(report*infection)
    return ss.Disease(infection, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9), name='measles')

sir_fit = ss.Sim(make_sir(), data=data, **pars).fit()

Searching on a log scale: report
Fitting by nelder-mead (2 fitted parameters, for which it is faster than gradients; override with method=)
Converged: the best two of 3 searches, from points of the scan that are apart, ended within 0.00038 of each other (objective values 0.3833 at beta=1.433, report=1; 0.3833 at beta=1.433, report=1; 0.3833 at beta=1.433, report=1; 193 evaluations)
The goodness of fit is 0.3833 at the best values and 0.6958 at the initial values


/home/cliffk/idm/ssv4/starsim/fit.py:2114: AtBound:


the best-fit value of "report" (1) is at one of its bounds [0.05, 1]; consider widening them



The search converged, but the share reported ended at its upper bound of 1 (with an AtBound warning). fit.plot(residuals=True) shows why: the model’s weekly cases before and after fitting against the data, and below them the difference between the data and the fitted model (the residuals), on the data’s own weeks, as the fit compares them:

sir_fit.plot(residuals=True)








Without a latent period, an epidemic with the same R0 grows much faster, so the SIR model can’t be both as late and as large as the data: it peaks too early and too low, even with every case reported. The residuals have a pattern: too many cases in the model early on, then too few through the peak. Residuals that wander above and below zero at random, as for the right model below, are what a good fit looks like:

seir_fit = ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, **pars).fit(verbose=False)
seir_fit.plot(residuals=True)








A pattern in the residuals points to the structure of the model, or to how the data were defined, not to the fitting: no search will fix it. Some common patterns, and what to look at first:







Pattern
Things to examine




The peak consistently too early or too late
The initial infections and when they are introduced; the latent period; reporting delays


The right shape but the wrong size
The population size; the share reported; whether the data count events (a flow) or people at a time (a stock)


A best value at a bound
The bounds; a missing process that the parameter is making up for; weak identification


Different starts giving different answers
Several optima, too short a search, a noisy objective


A good fit but an unstable projection
Parameters the data can’t tell apart; a change in the epidemic the model doesn’t have



Before blaming the model, check that like is compared with like: incidence with case counts over the same interval, prevalence with a survey at a time, hospital admissions with admissions rather than beds occupied, and dates aligned (a week ending on a Sunday, not starting on one). The fit’s measure (fit.mismatch) helps compare fits to the same data, here 0.38 for the SIR model against 0.10 for the SEIR model, but the plot shows where a model fails.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
Did the search converge?
Every fit says whether it converged, and how it decided, in fit.converged and fit.why, which are also printed:

print(seir_fit.converged)
print(seir_fit.why)

True
the best two of 3 searches, from points of the scan that are apart, ended within 9.6e-05 of each other (objective values 0.09553 at beta=1.9, report=0.4832; 0.09553 at beta=1.9, report=0.4833; 0.09553 at beta=1.9, report=0.4833; 299 evaluations)


What “converged” means depends on the method:








Method
Converged when
If not




SciPy optimizers ('nelder-mead', 'l-bfgs-b')
The searches from the best few starting points of a scan end at the same value
More starting points (scan=) or searches (restarts=); a sign of several local optima, or a ridge


Optuna
The best score improved by less than 1% over the last quarter of the trials
More trials (n_trials=)


NUTS, particle MCMC
The chains agree (R-hat at most 1.01) and no draws diverged
More warm-up (warmup=); check identifiability


Iterated filtering ('if2')
Chains from different starts end within 2 of the best log-likelihood
More iterations or particles



A fit that has not converged is not necessarily wrong, but it can’t be trusted until it has been run longer, or until the reason it didn’t is understood.

title: Fit diagnostics
section: Is a best value at a bound?
text:
Is a best value at a bound?
A best value at the edge of its bounds triggers an AtBound warning, as for the SIR model above. It means one of three things:

The true value is beyond the bound: widen it, if larger (or smaller) values are plausible.
The data don’t determine the parameter, so nothing stops it drifting to the edge (see Parameter identification).
The model is missing something, and the parameter is being pushed to the edge to make up for it, as the reporting share was above. Widening its bounds to allow more than 100% of cases to be reported would make the fit better and the model worse.

title: Fit diagnostics
section: Does the fit give the same answer again?
text:
Does the fit give the same answer again?
A stochastic model is fitted to noisy scores, so a second fit, with another rand_seed=, shows how much the answer depends on chance. Here the model is run as a chain binomial (a stochastic compartmental model), and fitted twice:

import pandas as pd

stochastic = ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, solver='binomial', **pars)
rows = []
for seed in [1, 4]:
    fit = stochastic.fit(n_trials=100, rand_seed=seed, verbose=False)
    rows.append(dict(rand_seed=seed, beta=fit.pars.beta, report=fit.pars.report, converged=fit.converged))
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)








rand_seed
beta
report
converged




0
1
1.899
0.472
False


1
4
1.877
0.514
False







The two fits differ: β by about 1% (1.90 and 1.88, against a true 1.9) and the share reported by about 9% (0.47 and 0.51, against 0.5), and neither says it converged, since the best score was still improving at the end of the search. Even a fit that says it has converged has only stopped improving; that doesn’t make the answer precise. The noise in the scores is large compared with the difference that report makes to them. More trials, or more runs for each trial (n_runs=, 4 by default for a stochastic compartmental model), reduce this; so does a likelihood, which weighs the data by how much they vary. The fit also reruns its best values with the same seeds as the search, and warns when they then score worse than the starting values: the best trial may have been a lucky run.
For a stochastic model, also check the fit against many runs, not one: fit.sim.run(n_runs=20), as in Fitting a model. The data should lie within the range of the runs about as often as the interval says.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
Does the time step matter?
A model run as agents or as a chain binomial takes whole steps, and when its rates are fast compared with the step, the step changes the results (see Solvers and backends), and so the fitted values: a fit with daily steps can find a higher β to make up for the delay the steps add. fit.sim.check_dt() reruns the fitted sim with half the step and shows how much each result changes; if they change by more than the mismatch of the fit, fit again with the smaller step.

title: Fit diagnostics
section: Can the data tell the parameters apart?
text:
Can the data tell the parameters apart?
Starsim notes when two parameters can’t be told apart: when they appear in the model only multiplied together, or (for a posterior) when they are almost perfectly correlated. Even without a note, check that the fit can recover known values from data made by the model itself, as this page’s examples do. Parameter identification covers this in detail.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
Is the posterior reliable?
For a posterior (method='nuts', 'pmcmc', or 'abc-smc'), fit.summarize() prints a table with the posterior’s median and 95% interval for each parameter, and two checks for each:

R-hat (rhat): compares the spread within each chain with the spread between chains. Near 1 means the chains have found the same distribution; above 1.01, they disagree, and the posterior is not yet reliable.
Effective sample size (ess): how many independent draws the correlated draws are worth. A few hundred is enough for a median and a 95% interval.

NUTS also counts divergent draws (fit.diagnostics.divergences), where the sampler’s path went wrong in a region of sharp curvature; even a few mean the posterior may be missing a region. If any of these checks fail, the fit warns (ss.errors.NotConverged). More warm-up (warmup=) sometimes fixes it, but a common cause is a ridge, where the data determine only a combination of parameters: then fix one, or get more data. An example of a posterior with a ridge is in Parameter identification.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
Looking at the search
For a fit by Optuna, fit.study is Optuna’s own record of the search, which its plots take: how the best score improved over the trials (has it levelled off?), which parameters mattered most to the score, and the score over each pair of parameters (a long diagonal valley is a ridge that the data can’t resolve). These need Plotly:
import optuna
optuna.visualization.plot_optimization_history(fit.study)
optuna.visualization.plot_param_importances(fit.study)
optuna.visualization.plot_contour(fit.study, params=['beta', 'report'])
For any method, fit.to_df() has every evaluation, with the values tried and the objective at each, for plots of your own; Parameter identification has one.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
Does the model predict?
A model with more parameters usually fits better, without necessarily being better. A fairer test is how well a model fitted to the start of the data predicts the rest. ss.fit.compare_models() fits each model to all but the last 25% of each data series (holdout=), runs it forward, and scores it on the part held out:

comparison = ss.fit.compare_models({'SIR': ss.Sim(make_sir(), data=data, **pars),
                                    'SEIR': ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, **pars)},
                                   method='nelder-mead')
comparison.summarize();

/home/cliffk/idm/ssv4/starsim/fit.py:2114: AtBound:


the best-fit value of "report" (1) is at one of its bounds [0.05, 1]; consider widening them



held out: the last 25% of each series (cases: 2025-10-08 to 2026-01-01)
fit error and prediction error are the normalized absolute error, on the data fitted to and on the held-out data (lower is better)


The SEIR model fits better and predicts better. folds= repeats the comparison over several cut points, which shows whether the difference is larger than the spread from one cut point to another; comparison.plot() shows each model’s fit and prediction against the data.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
A checklist



Check
How
A problem looks like




The model matches the data
Plot the model against the data, on the data’s own periods, and the residuals (fit.plot(residuals=True))
A pattern in the residuals; a parameter pushed to a bound


The search converged
fit.converged, fit.why
“Not converged”, with the reason


No value is at a bound
The AtBound warning
A best value at the edge


The answer is stable
Fit again with another rand_seed= (stochastic) or from other starting points (scan=)
Different values each time


The parameters are identifiable
A note that they can’t be told apart; recover known values
A ridge, or values that move together


The posterior is reliable
rhat, ess, divergences
R-hat above 1.01, few effective draws, any divergences


The model predicts
ss.fit.compare_models()
A model that fits well but predicts badly


The fit is plausible
Compare the values with what is known from elsewhere
A reporting share above 1, an infectious period of months



The last check matters most, and no software can make it: a fit only finds the values that make this model match these data. Whether those values, and the model, make sense for the disease and the setting is a judgment for the modeler.
When reporting a fit, say enough for someone else to repeat it and judge it: what each data series is and how it was matched to the model (flow or stock, over what periods); the measure of fit or the likelihood; the parameters fitted, with their bounds and priors, and those held fixed and why; the method, its settings, and the seed; the diagnostics above; and the versions of Starsim and of the data.

title: Transmission
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
A disease says who infects whom: S >> I @ beta * I reads “susceptible people become infected at a rate proportional to their contact with infected people”. Everything around it is kept separate. The routes say who meets whom and how often; effects say what changes what; interventions say what is delivered to whom; and results say what comes out. Each of these is a separate object, so changing one (homogeneous mixing to a contact matrix, say, or a vaccine to a test) doesn’t touch the disease. This page covers each of them, and how the engines turn routes and modifiers into who is infected.

title: Transmission
text:
Routes: who meets whom
A bare state in a rate means contact with people in that state, through whatever routes the sim has. With no network, beta * I is the textbook beta * I / N, and beta is a transmission rate. With a network or mixing pool, the route supplies the contacts, and beta becomes a probability per contact (per act, on a sexual network). It is one rule: the hazard is beta times the contact rate times the share of contacts who are infectious, and the default contact rate is 1. Nobody has to write /N, a common mistake in hand-written models.
When a formula needs the number itself, it uses I.n, which is taken literally. This is how environmental and vector-borne transmission are written: a water reservoir or a mosquito population is just a state declared with people=False, and its count appears in the rate (beta * W.n / (W.n + K)). There is no special route type for these.
All routes are passed with networks=, and the disease stays the same object throughout:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.05 * I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10),
    init_prev = 0.01,
    name      = 'sir',
)

routes = {
    'No network':     dict(),
    'Mixing pool':    dict(networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=10)),
    'Contact matrix': dict(networks=ss.contacts('Kenya'), stratify=dict(age=[0, 15, 65])),
    'Random network': dict(networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10)),
}
for label, kw in routes.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(sir, unit='day', stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0, **kw)
    sim.init()
    print(f'{label}: {sim.solver}, since {sim.solver_reason}')

No network: ode, since every part of the model has a compartmental form
Mixing pool: ode, since every part of the model has a compartmental form
Contact matrix: ode, since every part of the model has a compartmental form
Random network: abm, since RandomNet is an individual-level network


Homogeneous mixing, a mixing pool, and a contact matrix have exact compartmental forms, so solver='auto' runs them as an ODE; an individual-level network doesn’t, so the sim runs as agents. auto never approximates the mixing. Ask for solver='ode' on a network and Starsim uses the standard approximation (homogeneous mixing with the same mean contacts for a random network; the Anderson–May partner-change model for lasting partnerships) and prints one line saying so, or raises CapabilityError with approx=False. See Solvers and backends for how the choice is made.
A list of routes is a layered population (ss.contacts('Kenya', layer='school'), and so on), and the force of infection sums over the layers. Space is a stratification by patch (ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)), with an optional mobility model (ss.geo.gravity(), ss.geo.radiation(), or a matrix) that couples the patches by commuting or migration; these run under every solver. Contact tracing and the transmission log need routes that keep individual contacts, so they need agents.

title: Transmission
text:
How the engines compute transmission
The rule above is one, but each engine computes it in its own terms, from the same declaration:

As compartments, the routes are turned into contact rates between groups when the sim is initialized (ss.solvers.Mixing, in solvers/mixing.py): homogeneous mixing is one contact per unit of time, a mixing pool sets the number of contacts, mixing pools between age groups give a contact matrix, and space adds the movement between patches. The force of infection on each group is then beta times the contact rates times the share infectious in each group it meets, which the kernels evaluate as part of the program. Nothing is drawn per contact.
As agents, transmission is drawn over each network’s edges (ss.solvers.Transmission, in solvers/agents.py): for each edge with an infectious person at one end and a susceptible at the other, the chance in the step is 1 − exp(−beta·dt), times the effective rel_trans of the source and rel_sus of the target. A network with acts per partnership works out a hazard per act instead. The routes are taken in the order of sim.networks, and someone reached by several sources is infected by the first, who is recorded as the source in the infection log. A mixing pool as agents is a force of infection on each agent from the share infectious in the pool, with no edges.
A disease written as code (ss.Infection) transmits through the same ss.solvers.Transmission code, so it sees the same modifiers and products, gives the same edges the same random numbers, and attributes infections the same way; a bare beta is a rate in the sim’s unit, as in a declared disease, and on a network with acts a probability per act.

Each edge’s random number is drawn by its source and target, from a stream named after the disease, so adding a network or another disease doesn’t change which edges transmit (see Randomness).

title: Transmission
text:
Effects: what changes what
There are two ways for one module to change another, and both are first-class:

ss.modify, for the common case: while a condition holds, multiply (or add to, or set) a named quantity. ss.modify(hiv.rel_trans, multiply=2.0, where=syphilis.active) reads “for people with active syphilis, multiply HIV transmissibility by 2”.
Ordinary Python in a module’s step(), for everything else: several sources and targets, boolean flags, schedules, memory.

A modifier never overwrites what it changes. Each modifiable quantity has a base value (what its module set) and an effective value (the base with every active modifier applied). Reading sir.rel_sus[uids] gives the base, assigning to it sets the base, and sir.current_value('rel_sus', uids) is what transmission will use (whether the disease is declared or written as code, which share the code that applies it: ss.solvers.Transmission). When a modifier switches off, the quantity is simply back at its base: there is nothing to save or restore, and two modules can’t clobber each other. Several modifiers on one quantity combine by one fixed rule, whatever order they were declared in: set, then multiply, then add.
Conditions (where=) use the sim’s real attributes. Written before the sim exists, ss.ppl.age > 65 is a lazy expression (an ss.conditions.Cond), evaluated each time it’s needed. Nothing is analyzed in advance: a condition is tried on whatever the solver provides, agents or groups. age > 65 works on groups if 65 is an age bin edge; for age > 70 inside a bin, auto runs agents and an explicit solver='ode' stops and says why.
Because modifiers are declared, Starsim can list them all, before anything runs. Products are modifiers too, so a vaccine shows up in the same list:

masks       = ss.modify(sir.rel_sus, multiply=0.6, where=ss.ppl.age > 65, start=ss.days(20))
vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.85, who=ss.ppl.age < 15, coverage=0.7, at=[ss.days(30)])
sim = ss.Sim(sir, interventions=[masks, vaccination], stratify=dict(age=[0, 15, 65]), unit='day', stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0)
sim.what_modifies(sir.rel_sus)

sir.rel_sus
  modifiers
    masks            multiply=0.6   where=(people.age > 65)   start=20
    vaccine          multiply=0.15   where=has_vaccine (acquisition efficacy of vaccine)


Code that writes another module’s arrays directly is allowed, but isn’t tracked. Nothing is accepted and then ignored: a modifier that no solver would apply raises a ValueError when the sim is built. Modules run in Starsim’s ordered loop (Model execution), each seeing the current values, so mutual dependence (HIV raising syphilis susceptibility while syphilis raises HIV transmissibility) needs no special handling; any effect of the order is of order dt, which sim.check_dt() measures.

title: Transmission
text:
Interventions: products and delivery
An intervention has two parts. What is a product (ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, ss.Treatment: nouns) or a change to a quantity (ss.modify). Delivery is who gets it, when, and how many (ss.vaccinate, ss.screen, ss.treat: verbs), given by keywords (who=, coverage=, capacity=, at=, interval=, at_age=), or by one deliver= function when those depend on each other. Routine versus campaign delivery is a keyword, not a class. A delivery takes its product’s keywords and makes the product itself (ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.85, ...) makes an ss.Vaccine); a product is made on its own only when several deliveries give the same one.
A cascade of care is a list of ordinary deliveries, each triggered by the outcome of another:
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.8, specificity=0.95, coverage=0.1, interval=ss.days(7))  # a rapid test
confirm   = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.95, specificity=0.99, who=screening.positive, coverage=0.9) # a follow-up is a step of its own
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.95, who=confirm.positive, capacity=ss.perday(50))                # while stocks last
An outcome such as screening.positive is an event: the people it happened to this step. Events can be joined (a | b), and they remember: screening.positive.ever, .count, and .since work anywhere a condition does. Each step runs after the steps whose events trigger it, whatever order they are listed in, so a follow-up acts on the same step as its trigger. Every delivery has results of its own (delivered, eligible, coverage, …).
The same declarations run under every solver where they can. This cascade runs as an ODE, with the tests as flows thinned by sensitivity and specificity and capacity as a cap on the total flow. Some things need individuals: a test result that comes after a delay=, the joint of two events, .since, trace= (delivery to contacts), or a product whose effect is your own code. Under auto any of these makes the sim run as agents, and the reason it prints names the part.
A rule with memory (“reopen schools only after four weeks below the threshold”) is a small intervention class whose step() keeps a flag, plus a modifier that reads it. A scenario is just a sim with its interventions; ss.parallel({'Baseline': base, 'Masks': masks}) runs several as one ss.MultiSim, labeled by scenario.

title: Transmission
text:
Results
Every state gets a count (I) and every transition a flow of the same name (infection), with no declaration needed. Extra results are declared with the model: a ratio (prevalence = I / N) or an ss.outcome, a weighted, delayed sum of flows for observed quantities (“half of infections are reported, five days later”: ss.outcome(0.5 * infection, delay=ss.days(5))). An outcome moves nobody, and if the model includes testing, the tests’ own positive results are the cases instead.
Each result knows what kind of quantity it is (kind: a flow, a stock, or a ratio), and that one fact does a lot of work: it sets how the result is summarized over time (summarize_by: 'sum' for a flow, 'last' for a stock, 'mean' for a ratio, unless told otherwise); resampling to weeks, or comparing with weekly data, sums a flow but reads a stock at the end of each week, and a ratio is never averaged across groups (its numerator and denominator are summed, then divided). After stratification a result is still one result with extra dimensions, so res.I.select(age='0-14') and res.I.by('age') replace names like I_female_high. Data attaches by column name (data='cases.csv' with a column called cases), which is also all that calibration needs (see Calibration).
A sim is one run. Many runs are an ss.MultiSim, whose results are the same ss.Result objects, each holding every run (an array with a row for each run and a column for each time point), with the scenario and any parameters swept recorded for each run. So the same methods work on one run or many: res.select(scenario=...), res.median() and res.quantiles() at each time point, and res.summarize(), which reduces each run to one value by the result’s kind (a flow to its total, a stock to its final value):

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
small = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.2 * I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(10), init_n=dict(I=3), name='sir')
sim = ss.Sim(small, solver='gillespie', total_pop=1000, unit='day', stop=ss.days(120), verbose=0)
msim = sim.run(n_runs=20)

totals = msim.results.sir.infection.summarize() # The total infections of each run
print('Total infections in each run:', totals)
print('Share of runs with a major outbreak:', (totals > 100).mean())

Total infections in each run: [818. 788. 682. 771.   2. 725. 719. 776. 796. 842. 819.   9. 790. 754.
 797. 823. 769. 811. 762. 811.]
Share of runs with a major outbreak: 0.9


Extinction and bimodality can’t be seen in a median, which is why msim.plot(lines=True) draws every run, and msim.summarize() gives an interval as well as the median.

title: Transmission
text:
Limits

Modifiers on one quantity combine by the one rule above. Protection from several strains a person holds needs a different rule (the strongest, or a capped sum), which is ss.immunity; anything else is step() code.
Functions in where= and ss.modify keep no memory apart from hold=; anything that must remember is a class.

The code is in starsim/networks.py and solvers/mixing.py (routes), connectors.py and internals/conditions.py (effects), interventions.py, products.py and solvers/deliveries.py (interventions), and results.py. For the modeler’s view, see the user guide on contact networks, population data and contact matrices, geography, connectors, products, interventions, results, and scenarios and many runs.

title: Solvers and backends
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
The same declared model can be run five ways: as a deterministic ODE ('ode'), as three kinds of stochastic compartmental model ('binomial', 'gillespie', 'tau'), or as agents ('abm'). This page explains how Starsim chooses between them, the engines that do the work, the backends and kernel sets that make them fast, how approximations are announced, and which tests keep each path honest. For how to choose a solver as a modeler, and how the solvers’ results differ, see Solvers and backends in Running models.

title: Solvers and backends
text:
How solver='auto' chooses
The default, solver='auto', picks the simplest, fastest representation that runs the model without changing what it means: an ODE if every part of the model has a compartmental form, and agents otherwise. The line the sim prints when it is initialized says which it chose, and sim.solver_reason (and describe()) says why:

import starsim as ss

def make_sir(dur=ss.days(10)):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    return ss.Disease(
        infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(0.3) * I,
        recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=dur),
        init_prev = 0.01,
    )

kw = dict(unit='day', stop=100)
sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(), **kw).init()                                       # Homogeneous mixing
print()
sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(), networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10), **kw).init() # A network of individuals
print()
sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(4))), **kw).init() # A lognormal dwell time

Sim: sir, 10,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 100
  sir: R0 = 3, with 100 infectious at the start

Sim: sir, as 10,000 agents, days 0 to 100
  Running as agents: RandomNet is an individual-level network
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.3 per day (per infectious contact), 26% in a step. Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters

Sim: sir, 10,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 100
  sir: R0 = 3, with 100 infectious at the start
  Note: recovery has a lognorm_ex dwell time (nearly fixed, not exponential), approximated by 6 Erlang stages (mean 10 days kept; std 4.08 days, against 4 days given)


The rule behind this is that 'auto' never approximates the mixing and never drops anything individual-level. A model runs as agents if it has any of these:

an individual-level network (ss.RandomNet, ss.SexualNet), or n_agents=;
a function that takes uids, or a per-agent attribute that isn’t a stratification (viral load);
a module written as code that keeps a value for each person (define_states()), or that says compartmental = False; being written as code isn’t a reason by itself, so a module that keeps nothing per person (an ODE of its own, an analyzer) runs beside the compartments, and a sim of such modules has no agents at all;
anything that needs individual histories: contact tracing, the infection log, time in a state, or each person’s mother or children.

Everything else, including contact matrices, stratifications, fixed delays, and interventions that target strata, has a compartmental form.
The one thing 'auto' approximates unasked is a dwell time that isn’t exponential, Erlang or fixed, as in the third example. Sending a simple model to agents over one lognormal would be the bigger surprise, so it uses Erlang stages that keep the mean exactly, and prints the standard deviation they give. A dwell time too variable for stages (a coefficient of variation above 3) makes 'auto' choose agents.
sim.describe() lists each ingredient that matters for the choice and whether it runs as compartments: yes, approx (and how), or no (and why). Code is never analyzed in advance: a function is called with what the solver has (one value per agent, or one per group), and if it asks for something only agents have, the run stops with an ss.CapabilityError that names it.

'auto' only ever chooses ode or abm; a stochastic compartmental solver, or ide, is used only when it is asked for by name. ide runs as the ODE, with each dwell time that is not exponential as a conveyor of whole steps, leaving each slot at the distribution’s own chance rather than through Erlang stages. Any solver can also run the model as a branching process (branching=True): infection takes no one from the uninfected and gives no one back, and as agents, agents are made only for the infected (see Branching and rescaling). A sim is one run whatever the solver, and many runs are an ss.MultiSim (ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=100)).
Some of the conditions in the last column are reported as notes, and sim.check_dt() measures how much a smaller step would change the results.

title: Solvers and backends
text:
Approximations are announced
When a solver is asked for that the model doesn’t natively fit, Starsim uses the standard approximation where one exists, and says so in one line. It stops only when there is no sensible approximation. For example, a random network run as an ODE becomes homogeneous mixing at the network’s mean number of contacts:
>>> ss.Sim(sir, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10), solver='ode', unit='day', stop=100).init()
Sim: sir, 10,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 100
  sir: R0 = 30, with 100 infectious at the start
  Note: RandomNet approximated by homogeneous mixing with 10 contacts per day (its mean number of contacts)
A network model run as an ODE is a coarser model, not an invalid one, and someone who typed solver='ode' asked for it. Each ingredient has one standard approximation (lasting partnerships use a partner-change model; a distribution on beta uses its mean). Things with no compartmental form, such as contact tracing, stop with an ss.CapabilityError before the run, saying what to do instead.
By default each approximation prints a note; approx=True keeps the notes without printing them, and approx=False makes any approximation an error (under 'auto', that sends a lognormal dwell time to agents). Either way the notes are kept in sim.notes, so they survive into saved output.

title: Solvers and backends
text:
The engines
Each declared module gets one engine when the sim is initialized. A module written as code, with no declared states or transitions, gets an empty engine and runs its own step(). Beside the engines, solvers/deliveries.py is what an intervention does differently as compartments (it reaches a share of each group, not a list of agents), and solvers/particles.py steps many runs of one program together for the particle filter.








Engine
Files
What it does




Compartmental
solvers/compartmental.py, solvers/mixing.py, solvers/backends/kernels.py
Expands states into compartments (one per group, branch and Erlang stage) and transitions into a flat list of flows, the program. The kernels (small functions in solvers/backends/kernels.py, compiled with Numba, or their Rust copies) step that program for all four compartmental solvers. mixing.py turns networks and mixing pools into contact rates between groups.


Agents
solvers/agents.py, solvers/agents_*.py, solvers/backends/passes.py
Each state is a boolean array over agents. A dwell time is drawn on entry and the exit scheduled; competing rates out of a state are resolved in one draw; transmission is drawn over each network’s edges. The moves of a step are taken in rounds (below), each a few NumPy passes over the agents who move. The heavy passes over agents and edges are compiled.


Crossing
solvers/crossing.py
Diseases tracked jointly, when a condition in one refers to a state of another (ss.modify(hiv.rel_trans, multiply=3, where=syph.I)). Their compartments are crossed and run as one program, up to a budget (ss.options.max_joint); above it, 'auto' uses agents.



Three details of the compartmental engine explain most of its behavior:

A whole run in one call. If nothing needs Python between steps (no module written as code with a step of its own, such as an intervention, analyzer, or connector, and no modifier with where=, when=, or a function as its amount), the kernels run the whole simulation in one call; otherwise they are called once per step. Values that vary in time (ss.timeseries, ss.seasonal, and ss.by of them, by place or age) are tabulated for every step before the run, and so are deliveries on a schedule to people chosen by state and group (ss.Delivery.tabulated), including a move between states such as a seed (ss.Delivery(move=S >> I, at=...)), so none of these makes a run stepped. The results are the same, and sim.kernel_reason() says why a run is stepped.
Rust, Numba, or plain. The kernels run in Rust, compiled by Numba, or as plain Python, with the same results (see the kernels, below).
JAX for long ODE runs and gradients. internals/gradients.py (ss.gradients) runs the same program with the same RK4 steps in JAX, so results can be differentiated (sim.gradient()) and many parameter sets run at once. ss.solvers.choose_engine() uses JAX for an ODE when the kernels would take more than about half a second (about what JAX takes to start), as estimated from the size of the model alone, so the same model always gets the same engine (and the same results with a seed); sim.engine_reason says which ran, once the sim has been run.

The agent engine takes a step as one sweep over the disease’s transitions, in an order worked out once from the graph (Agents.sweep()): each transition after those that bring people into its source, a trigger (on=) after the event it waits for, and the triggers out of a state ahead of its scheduled exits; a loop of states is broken at the transition declared first. At each transition in turn, those it moves now leave (by its trigger, or because their exit by it is due, including people who arrived in its source earlier in the sweep with a wait that rounds to no steps), and everyone who left by it is sent to their destinations (a transition with several destinations takes one draw for each, and ss.stay puts people back); each arrival is dated, and has its branch, dwell time and exit drawn if its state schedules them. Someone who reaches a transition the sweep has already passed is taken by another sweep, until nobody moves, so the moves with no wait happen in the step that caused them, as in the ODE, and in the order a modeler writing the code by hand would take them (Agents.finish_moves()). The step’s infections are dated at its end, and start a cascade of their own. Every way in from code (an intervention’s move, ss.move(), disease.infect()) is a round of its own.
Each of the engine’s draws is keyed by its stream, the step, and the round (Agents.draw(), Agents.new_round()): each transition of the sweep is a round, as is each way in from code. A draw is not keyed by how many times the stream has been called, so it does not depend on how the work of a round is batched; an agent moves at most once in a round, so each agent’s draws from a stream are its own (STARSIM_CHECK_DRAWS=1 checks it).
The random draws are shared too: solvers/backends/draws.py has exact draws from counter-based uniforms, so a stream doesn’t depend on how work is split across threads. Users’ own code can be compiled with @ss.jit (solvers/backends/jit.py), with the same results as when run as Python.

title: Solvers and backends
text:
The kernels
The same kernels exist as several sets, which give the same numbers (but see plain Python’s in the table, for the chain binomial): Rust’s (solvers/rust/, swapped in by solvers/backends/rust.py), Numba’s (solvers/backends/kernels.py, passes.py, draws.py), and plain Python’s (the compartmental kernels in Numba’s code, run without compiling it; for the ODE, the same steps vectorized in NumPy, solvers/backends/ode.py). ss.options.kernels chooses between them; by default ('auto') it is chosen at run time, as the table says. JAX is not one of these: it is an engine for a whole run of the ODE, chosen by the run (sim.jax).

Numba’s kernels are the reference: a change is made there first, then in Rust’s (solvers/rust/README.md says how), and test_kernel_sets.py checks that every set still gives the same numbers.

text:
Execution paths and the tests that pin them
Each path below is checked against a reference where one exists: the ODE against SciPy and known answers, and the other paths against the ODE or against a path already checked. Files in tests/ are the core tests, run on every change; those marked devtests/ are the slower developer tests in tests/devtests/.

title: Solvers and backends
text:
Limits

Solvers that take whole steps differ from the ODE by an amount of order dt, which is why the agreement tests use a quarter-day step. With whole weekly steps (substeps=1) on an SIR with daily rates, the chain binomial’s peak is about a third higher than the ODE’s; by default it takes enough substeps to stay within a few percent. A compartment holds about x/2 too many people, for x its total rate out times the substep, so Compartmental.binomial_substeps() keeps x to 5%, and near the epidemic threshold (where a small bias in R moves prevalence a lot) to a tenth of |R0 − 1|.
Agreement is tested on simple models. For complex ones (a sexual network as an ODE), solvers are expected to differ; the guarantee is that Starsim says what it approximated.
Gillespie is exact but takes events one at a time; for millions of events in groups that mix, 'tau' is the practical choice.
Gradients exist only for solver='ode' and for rates written as expressions. One model can’t yet mix solvers (an ODE with rare importations as discrete events).

title: People and agents
text:
🧠15% 🤖85%
Every model has a population: how many people there are, their ages and sex, and anything else about them that the model needs, such as where they live. This page covers the size of the population, its ages (including the population of a named country), other properties of people and how a model uses them, and, for a model run as agents, the People object that holds what each agent is and has, and the arrays it keeps them in. Births, deaths, and migration are in Demographics, and who meets whom is in Contact networks.
The examples use the measles model from the tutorials:
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

title: People and agents
text:
How many people
total_pop= is the number of people in the population. A model run as compartments needs nothing else:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0033 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6


Sim(n=100000; 0—50; diseases=measles)


As agents, n_agents= is the number of agents. Given both, each agent stands for total_pop/n_agents people, here 10, and results are given in people, not agents:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: measles, as 10,000 agents, each 10 people, days 0 to 50
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.031 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 78,380 infectious, on day 9









The two runs differ a little, since as agents the epidemic is a stochastic process that takes whole daily steps (see Solvers and backends). Without either total_pop= or n_agents=, a model has 10,000 people. Fewer agents than people make a model faster, but add noise from chance, more so for rare events; see Branching and rescaling.

title: People and agents
text:
Ages and sex
As agents, each person has an age and a sex. Unless told otherwise, Starsim gives agents the ages of the world’s population in 2024, and an even chance of being female. A compartmental model split into age groups without a share for each takes the shares from the same ages, and describe() marks them as guessed.
The population of a country is ss.people(): its size, its ages, and its share of women, from the UN World Population Prospects (or, for a US state, the US Census), which come with Starsim. The sim takes its size from it, so a compartmental model can use a named population as well as agents can:

kenya = ss.people('Kenya', year=2024)
print('Population of Kenya in 2024:', round(kenya.named.total))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, people=ss.people('Kenya', year=2024, n_agents=5000), stop=ss.days(50))
sim.init()
sim.people.plot_ages();

Population of Kenya in 2024: 56571298
Sim: measles, as 5,000 agents, each 11,300 people, days 0 to 50
  Running as agents: people were given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters









In a compartmental model, ages matter only once the model is split into age groups, with measles.stratify(age=[0, 15, 65]), which then takes the share of people in each group from the named population. See Stratification and, for contacts between age groups, Population data. The tutorial T4 – Age groups and contacts builds an age-structured measles model step by step.
Ages can also come from data of your own, with ss.People(n_agents, age_data=...): a table with a column age (the lower edge of each age group) and a column value (the number or share of people in it), or a CSV file with those columns:

ppl = ss.People(5000, age_data='test_data/nigeria_age.csv')
sim = ss.Sim(measles, people=ppl, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.init()
sim.people.plot_ages();

Sim: measles, as 5,000 agents, days 0 to 50
  Running as agents: people were given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters









A sim copies the people it is given when it is built, so look at sim.people afterwards, not at ppl.

title: People and agents
text:
Properties of people
A model refers to a property of people with ss.ppl: ss.ppl.age, ss.ppl.female, or a property of your own. ss.ppl.age < 5 is a condition, which picks out people, for example to say who an intervention reaches:

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.8, where=ss.ppl.age < 5, at=ss.days(10))

A property of your own is given to ss.People as a state, with a value for each agent; it can be drawn from a distribution. Here 30% of people live in towns:

urban = ss.BoolState('urban', default=ss.bernoulli(p=0.3))
ppl = ss.People(10_000, extra_states=urban)

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.9, where=ss.ppl.urban, at=ss.days(1))
base = ss.Sim(measles, people=ppl, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({'No vaccination': base, 'Vaccinating towns': base.new(interventions=vaccination)})
msim.plot('measles.I')
print('Share of people in towns:', msim.sims[1].people.urban.mean())
print('Vaccinated:', msim.results.vaccination.delivered.sum())








Share of people in towns: 0.31
Vaccinated: 2800.0


Vaccinating the 30% of people who live in towns slows the epidemic and lowers its peak, but with an R0 of about 15, measles still reaches nearly everyone else: a reminder that a property such as urban matters only as much as who it picks out.
A property can also be in a rate: infection = S >> I @ beta*(1 + 0.5*ss.ppl.urban)*I has transmission 50% higher in towns. ss.ppl is read when the sim is built, so the property can be given after the model is written.
In a compartmental model, people have no properties of their own, only the groups the model is split into. The same property is a stratification, and the same condition then picks out a group:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles2 = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
measles2.stratify(urban={False: 0.7, True: 0.3}) # 70% rural, 30% in towns

sim = ss.Sim(measles2, interventions=vaccination, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.by('urban').plot()

title: People and agents
text:
States and arrays
As agents, what each person is and has is kept in arrays with one value per agent. A state such as alive, female, or a disease’s I is an ss.BoolState, an array of true or false values; a number, such as age, is an ss.FloatArr (or ss.IntArr for whole numbers). These arrays work like NumPy arrays, with sums, means, comparisons, and arithmetic, but are made for three things nearly every agent-based model needs:

Growth: as people are born or arrive, the arrays grow, in chunks rather than one agent at a time, so that adding agents is cheap.
Indexing: agents who die or leave stay in the arrays, so that what happened to them can still be looked up, but are left out of counts, sums, and means.
Random values: a state’s default can be a distribution, as with urban above, so each new agent draws its own value, with common random numbers so that two runs give each agent the same draw.

Every agent has a UID, its identifier, which never changes and is its position in the full (“raw”) arrays. The UIDs of the agents still taking part (alive and not removed) are people.auids, the active UIDs. Most of the time you won’t need these, but here is how they work, in a population with births and deaths (at default rates) over 20 years:

sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=1000, start='2000', stop='2020', dt=ss.years(1), demographics=True, verbose=0)
sim.init()
ppl = sim.people
print('Agents at the start:', len(ppl))
print('Mean age at the start:', ppl.age.mean())

sim.run()
print('Births:', sim.results.population.births.sum())
print('Deaths:', sim.results.died.sum())
print('Agents at the end:', len(ppl))
print('UIDs used:', ppl.uid.raw.max() + 1)
print('Length of the raw arrays:', len(ppl.age.raw))
print('Mean age of the living:', ppl.age.mean())

Agents at the start: 1000
Mean age at the start: 33.988655
Births: 426.0
Deaths: 199.0
Agents at the end: 1227
UIDs used: 1426
Length of the raw arrays: 1440
Mean age of the living: 39.723263


The number of agents is the number of living agents. The UIDs used include the agents who have died, and the raw arrays are a little longer still, with room for the next births. ppl.age.values gives the values for the active agents, and ppl.age.raw for every slot, including empty ones (which hold NaN). A condition on an array gives the UIDs of the agents who meet it, and those UIDs index any other array:

under5 = (ppl.age < 5).uids
print('Children under 5:', len(under5))
print('Share of them who are female:', ppl.female[under5].mean())
print('UIDs of the first few who died:', ppl.dead.uids[:5])

Children under 5: 101
Share of them who are female: 0.38613861386138615
UIDs of the first few who died: [ 9 14 23 53 54]


For how to pick out agents in code, see Array indexing.

title: People and agents
text:
People as agents
As agents, sim.people holds every agent: its properties, and the states of every module in the sim. Each person has these:







Name
What it is




alive
Whether the agent is alive


female
Whether the agent is female


age
The agent’s age, in years


ti_dead
The step on which the agent died, if it has (NaN otherwise)


ti_removed
The step on which the agent left for another reason, such as emigration


cause_of_death
The cause of each death (its position in people.causes, the names of the causes; -1 for none)


scale
The number of people the agent stands for, relative to the others (1 unless set)



Each module adds its own states, under its name. A declared disease adds a state for each of its states (sim.people.measles.S, .I, .R), the time each agent entered a state (ti_I) and is due to leave it, and each person’s relative susceptibility and transmissibility (rel_sus and rel_trans). To save memory, the time of entering a state is kept only when something reads it: the disease itself (e.g. for a state with a dwell time), or the code of a module in the sim that names it. Reading one that wasn’t kept, e.g. in an analysis after the run, raises an error that says so; ss.State(keep_time=True) keeps it for one state (e.g. for code that reads the time since onset), and ss.options.keep_times = True, set before the sim is built, keeps them all, and the history of every transition (e.g. sir.infection.count).
A time of entering reads as the step the move happened in, so ti_E.isclose(sim.ti) is “entered this step”. The difference of two of them is not always a duration, though: an infection by contact happens at the end of its step, and a scheduled move (such as becoming infectious after a latent period) at the start of its step, so ti_I - ti_E reads one step longer than the latent period was. For the time people spent in a state, use the state’s stays: np.mean(sim.diseases.measles.E.stays) is the mean latent period, a duration in the sim’s unit, over everyone who has entered E and left it. Those still in the state are left out (E.time gives how long they have been there so far). With each state whose time of entering is kept, the time each person last left it is kept too, so stays works for any such state, e.g. one with a dwell time (I.stays in an SIR); for another, keep its time as above.
A module adds its states to the people when the sim is initialized, so they don’t need to be given to ss.People. A property that belongs to one module (such as a disease’s immunity) is best defined in that module, with define_states() (see Custom modules); a property that several modules use (such as urban, or a social determinant of health) is best given to ss.People with extra_states=, as above.

title: People and agents
text:
States with several columns
Sometimes each person needs several values of the same kind, such as their immunity to each of several strains. A state can have columns=, which gives it one row per agent and one column per value. Like any state, it grows as agents are born. Here a module written as code keeps each person’s susceptibility to two strains, and the susceptibility to the second one falls by 10% each year:

class Immunity(ss.Module):
    """ Susceptibility to two strains, with susceptibility to the second falling over time """
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(
            ss.FloatArr('sus', columns=['wild', 'mutant'], default=1.0),
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        self.sus.mutant *= 0.9**(self.t.dt/ss.years(1)) # The second column, for every agent: 10% less each year
        return

sim = ss.Sim(Immunity(), n_agents=1000, demographics=True, start='2000', stop='2005', dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sus = sim.people.immunity.sus
print('Number of agents:', len(sim.people))
print('Shape of the values:', sus.values.shape)

Number of agents: 1045
Shape of the values: (1045, 2)


A column can be read by name as an attribute (sus.mutant), as a key (sus['mutant']), or with sus.col('mutant'); each gives an ordinary array with one value per agent, and writing to it (sus.mutant = 0) changes the state. To index, the first index picks agents and the second picks columns, by name or by position:

uids = ss.uids([0, 1, 2])
print('Both columns, for 3 agents:')
print(sus[uids])
print('The mutant column, for 3 agents:', sus[uids, 'mutant'])
print('Mean susceptibility to the mutant:', sus.mutant.mean())

sus[uids, 'wild'] = 0 # These agents are now immune to the wild type
print('Immune to the wild type:', (sus.col('wild') < 0.5).uids)

Both columns, for 3 agents:
[[1.        0.5904897]
 [1.        0.5904897]
 [1.        0.5904897]]
The mutant column, for 3 agents: [0.5904897 0.5904897 0.5904897]
Mean susceptibility to the mutant: 0.6092101
Immune to the wild type: [0 1 2]


Since a state with several columns has several values per agent, it can’t be turned into UIDs directly; use one column, as above. Some other things to note:

columns=3 gives three unnamed columns, read by position only, and a tuple such as columns=(2, 3) gives more dimensions.
Column names must be unique, and can’t be the name of something an array already has (such as raw or mean).
sus[:, [0, 1]] gives columns 0 and 1 for every active agent.
people.to_df() gives one column of the table per value, e.g. immunity.sus_wild and immunity.sus_mutant (or _0, _1, and so on for unnamed columns).

Strains use states like this to keep each person’s immunity to each strain.

title: People and agents
text:
In a compartmental run
In a compartmental run there are no agents. sim.people then has one row for each group the model is split into, and asking for a property of each person, such as sim.people.age in a model not split by age, raises an error saying to stratify by it or to run as agents. Results, describe(), and conditions such as where=ss.ppl.age < 5 (for a model stratified by age) work the same either way.
The API reference for this page: People, Arrays.
