title: Optimization
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Calibration asks which values of a model’s parameters fit the data. Optimization asks a different question of a calibrated model: given a budget, how should it be divided between programs to do the most good? If testing, bed nets, and vaccination each reduce transmission, with diminishing returns as each reaches more people, there is an allocation of a fixed total between them that averts the most infections, and it is rarely all to the program that looks best on its own. ss.fit.optimize() finds it, using the same machinery as fitting: the spending on each program is a parameter of the model, and the search runs the model at each allocation it tries.
This page covers how spending is put into a model, the search itself, limits on each program, a different total, the least total that reaches a target, and reading the result. Where costs come from, and how to count what interventions cost, is in Costs; fitting the model first is in Fitting a model.

title: Optimization
text:
Spending as parameters
ss.fit.optimize() needs the spending on each program as a named parameter of the model (ss.par), and the model has to say what the spending buys: here, how the share of people a program reaches depends on what is spent on it, and how much that reduces transmission. In this SIR model of an infection with R0 = 2, two programs reduce transmission, each with diminishing returns: the share of people reached rises as 1 − exp(−spend / (cost per person × population)), so the first dollars reach many people and later ones fewer. Testing (and isolating those who test positive) costs $10 a person and, at full reach, cuts transmission by 60%; bed nets cost $5 a person and cut it by 30%. The current budget is $100,000, split evenly:

import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
tests = ss.par(50e3, name='tests') # Spending on testing, in dollars
nets  = ss.par(50e3, name='nets')  # Spending on bed nets

N = (S + I + R).total
reach = lambda spend, cost: 1 - np.exp(-spend/cost/N) # The share of people reached, at a cost per person
beta = ss.perday(0.2)*(1 - 0.6*reach(tests, 10))*(1 - 0.3*reach(nets, 5))
sir = ss.Disease(S >> I @ beta*I.frac, I >> R @ ss.days(10), init_prev=0.001, name='sir')

sim = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=10_000, start=2025, stop=2026, verbose=0) # One year, in daily steps

ss.par(..., name=) gives each parameter the name it is found by. Since the spending is in the rates of the model, a change in it is a change in the model like any other: sim.new(pars=dict(tests=100e3, nets=0)) is the sim with everything spent on testing. Before optimizing, it helps to see the range of outcomes. sir.R at the end of the run is the number of people ever infected:

allocations = {
    'No spending':  dict(tests=0,     nets=0),
    'All testing':  dict(tests=100e3, nets=0),
    'All bed nets': dict(tests=0,     nets=100e3),
    'Even split':   dict(tests=50e3,  nets=50e3),
}
for label, spend in allocations.items():
    run = sim.new(pars=spend).run()
    print(label, round(run.results.sir.R[-1]))

No spending 7972
All testing 3575
All bed nets 5715
Even split 3533


Testing does more for the money than bed nets, but its returns diminish, so the even split does better than either alone.

title: Optimization
text:
Finding the best allocation
ss.fit.optimize() keeps the total fixed (by default, the total of the current values, $100,000 here) and searches over its division between the programs, with minimize= the result to make as small as possible (or maximize= one to make as large as possible):

best = ss.fit.optimize(sim, spend=['tests', 'nets'], minimize='sir.R')
best.summarize()

Optimized sir.R: 3,533.42 to 3,094.7, in 15 runs (0.1 s)
sir.R: 3,533.42 before, 3,094.7 after (15 runs)









before
after




tests
50000.0
75231.627116


nets
50000.0
24768.372884







The best allocation puts about three quarters on testing and a quarter on bed nets, which brings the infections down from about 3,530 with the even split to about 3,090: some 440 infections averted for the same money. The best allocation’s run is best.sim, which can be compared with the others:

compare = ss.MultiSim([
    sim.new(pars=allocations['No spending'], label='No spending').run(),
    sim.new(pars=allocations['Even split'], label='Even split').run(),
    best.sim.new(label='Best allocation').run(),
])
compare.plot('sir.I')








How it works: the search (SciPy’s SLSQP) is over the shares of the total, which sum to 1, and each point it tries is a run of the model; a model that is nothing but compartments is restarted for each run rather than built again, so each run takes milliseconds. The search is local, and assumes that the result changes smoothly with the spending, so:

Use a deterministic model. With a stochastic model, each run of the same allocation gives a different answer, and the search can’t tell a better allocation from a lucky run. Optimize the ODE form of the model (solver='ode'), or give a function of the sim that averages many runs.
Make returns diminish. If every program’s effect grows in proportion to its spending, the best allocation is to put everything into the program with the best ratio; the answer is then obvious, and the search adds nothing. Real programs saturate, and the model should say how.
Check that the answer is not one of several. With more than a few programs, the search can stop at an allocation that is better than those near it but not the best; starting from another allocation (other values of the spending parameters) and comparing is a quick check.

title: Optimization
text:
What to optimize, and when
minimize= and maximize= take the name of a result, as a disease’s ('sir.R', or 'R' for the first disease), whose value at the end of the run is used, or at the time given by at= (a date, or a year). For anything else, they take a function of the run sim, which returns the number to make small or large: here, the height of the peak, for a health system that must not be overwhelmed:

def peak_infectious(sim):
    """ The most people infectious at once """
    return sim.results.sir.I.max()

peak = ss.fit.optimize(sim, spend=['tests', 'nets'], minimize=peak_infectious, verbose=False)
peak.summarize()

peak_infectious: 206.143 before, 162.629 after (12 runs)

The best allocation for the peak is much the same as for the total here, but need not be: a program that delays infections helps the peak more than the total.
start= says when the new allocation takes effect: before it, each program keeps its current spending, and from then on, the allocation being tried. This is the usual question for a program that is already running: given what has been spent until now, how should next year’s budget be divided?

from_april = ss.fit.optimize(sim, spend=['tests', 'nets'], minimize='sir.R', start='2025-04-01', verbose=False)
from_april.summarize()

title: Optimization
text:
Limits on each program
Programs can rarely be cut to nothing or grown without limit: a program may have contracts to honor, or be unable to expand faster than it can hire staff. bounds= gives the least and most each program can have, in dollars, by name, with None for no limit (a program not named has none beyond 0 and the total):

limited = ss.fit.optimize(sim, spend=['tests', 'nets'], minimize='sir.R', bounds=dict(tests=(None, 60e3)), verbose=False)
limited.summarize()

title: Optimization
text:
A different total
total= sets the total to divide, for the question “what if the budget were larger (or smaller)?”; the search starts from the current shares of the spending, scaled to the total. Here, the best allocation of twice the budget:

double = ss.fit.optimize(sim, spend=['tests', 'nets'], minimize='sir.R', total=200e3, verbose=False)
double.summarize()

sir.R: 3,533.42 before, 71.7292 after (21 runs)









before

For a curve of the best result against the budget (the “production function” of the programs together), run it at a range of totals:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

totals = [25e3, 50e3, 100e3, 200e3, 400e3]
infections = []
for total in totals:
    opt = ss.fit.optimize(sim, spend=['tests', 'nets'], minimize='sir.R', total=total, verbose=False)
    infections.append(opt.value)

plt.plot(np.array(totals)/1e3, infections, 'o-')
plt.xlabel('Total budget (thousands of dollars)')
plt.ylabel('People infected, with the best allocation')
plt.ylim(bottom=0);








Each further dollar averts fewer infections until, past a certain budget, transmission is pushed below the threshold (R below 1), and the curve flattens out near the initial infections.

title: Optimization
section: The least total that reaches a target
text:
The least total that reaches a target
The reverse question, how much money is needed to reach a target, is answered with target=: the least total whose best allocation brings the result to the target (at most the target with minimize=, at least with maximize=). The search doubles the total until it reaches the target, then halves the gap between a total that does and one that doesn’t, to within 1%:

needed = ss.fit.optimize(sim, spend=['tests', 'nets'], minimize='sir.R', target=1000, verbose=False)
needed.summarize()

sir.R: 3,533.42 before, 968.425 after (78 runs)
The least total that reaches 1,000: 128,906 (from 100,000)

This assumes that more money never does worse, which is true of any sensible model of spending. A target that no budget can reach (fewer infections than the initial ones, say) is an error.

title: Optimization
text:
Reading the result
ss.fit.optimize() returns an ss.fit.Optimization, which holds:



Attribute
What it is




alloc
The best allocation, by program


value
The result with it


total
Its total (with target=, the least total that reaches the target)


alloc_before, value_before
The current allocation, and the result with it


sim
The sim run with the best allocation


n_runs
The number of runs the search took


converged, why
Whether the search reached its own stopping rule, and its message




best.alloc

{'tests': 75231.62711574533, 'nets': 24768.37288425468}


If the search ends at an allocation worse than the one it started from, the starting allocation is returned. By default (verbose=True, unless ss.options.verbose says otherwise) it prints a line at the end, as in the first example, and with target=, each total it tried.

title: Optimization
text:
Program books from Atomica
An optimization in Atomica starts from a program book: a spreadsheet of programs, their costs, and the coverage and effects they buy. A model imported from Atomica with its program book (see Conversion: Atomica) has a spending parameter for each program, so spend= is not needed, and the same calls work:
sim = ss.import_from('hiv_framework.xlsx', format='atomica', databook='hiv_databook.xlsx', progbook='hiv_progbook.xlsx', programs_start=2020)
best = ss.fit.optimize(sim, start=2020, maximize='all_vs', at=2030)
least = ss.fit.optimize(sim, start=2020, maximize='all_vs', at=2030, target=1.1*best.value) # The least money that reaches 10% more

title: Optimization
text:
Pitfalls

Spending that changes nothing. A spending parameter that doesn’t appear in any rate leaves the result unchanged, and the search returns the starting allocation; check with a few allocations by hand first, as above.
Optimizing a stochastic run. The search compares runs, so chance differences between them become apparent differences between allocations. Use the ODE, or average many runs in a function given as minimize=.
An optimum that is an artifact of the model of costs. The answer is only as good as the curves that say what spending buys; a different saturation (or none) can move the best allocation a long way. Try the plausible range of costs and effects, as for any other uncertain parameter.
A model that wasn’t calibrated. An allocation optimized on an uncalibrated model optimizes the wrong epidemic; fit it first (see Fitting a model).

text:
Further reading

Optima HIV: allocative efficiency studies of HIV programs, the approach ss.fit.optimize() takes

SciPy: Constrained minimization (SLSQP): the search used here

title: Architecture
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
This section explains how Starsim is put together and why. It is for two kinds of reader: a modeler who wants to know what happens when they call sim.run(), and a prospective contributor deciding whether this is a codebase they could work in. You don’t need any of it to use Starsim; the rest of the user guide, starting from What is Starsim?, is the place for that.

title: Architecture
text:
The idea in one paragraph
A model in Starsim is written once, as data: states (S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')), transitions between them (S >> I @ beta * I), and parameters, with the mixing, demography and interventions around them. Each disease checks its own structure when it is made (unknown names, rates of the wrong shape). When the sim is initialized, Starsim reads those objects, fills in what was left out (and records each guess), checks them against each other, and chooses how to run them: as a deterministic ODE, as one of three stochastic compartmental solvers, or as agents. Because the model is data rather than code, everything else is derived from the same objects: the printed description, the equations, the diagram, and the exports to other frameworks. One declared model, several ways to run it, and one source of truth for all of them.
A model can also be written as code, as classes with their own step() methods: these run through the same loop, as agents if they keep a value for each person and otherwise with no agents at all (an ODE of your own runs as just that), and can sit beside declared models in one sim. Modules covers how the two kinds fit together.

title: Architecture
text:
The principles behind it
Every design choice is checked against a short constitution. In order of weight:

Simplicity. Writing and changing a model should be easy for an epidemiologist, not just an engineer. A model ported to Starsim should get shorter.
Performance. As close to custom compiled code as is feasible. This is why compartmental runs go through kernels (small compiled functions that step the compartments) and why agents use compiled passes over their arrays.
Flexibility. Every major modeling feature should be expressible, even if not every one is built in. When a declaration can’t say something, a module’s step() can.
Correctness. The machinery is validated by tests, but over-correctness should not cost simplicity or speed: Euler steps, Erlang stages and other standard approximations are fine, as long as they are announced.

After these come understandability (few concepts, no brittle subsystems), maintainability (solvers should not each reimplement the same thing), composability (use as much or as little of Starsim as you want), short startup (no long compilation before a small run), and being easy for AI tools to work with. The development principles add: no legacy shims, avoid bloat, and think about the whole system before adding a special path for one case.
You’ll see these principles in specific choices throughout this section. For example, solver='auto' picks the simplest representation that runs the model faithfully (simplicity, performance); every approximation prints one line saying what was done (correctness without refusing); and the compiled kernels are optional, with a plain-Python path for short runs (short startup).

title: Architecture
text:
The map
Starsim has five layers. Broadly, each builds on the ones before it, and a contributor can usually work in one layer at a time.






flowchart TD
    D["<b>1. Declaration</b><br/>states, transitions, rates,<br/>parameters, dimensions"]
    G["<b>The graph</b><br/>resolved, completed, checked"]
    O["<b>2. Build and orchestration</b><br/>sim.init(), the loop, modules,<br/>people, networks, results"]
    C{"choose a solver"}
    K["<b>3. Compartmental engine</b><br/>ode, binomial, gillespie, tau"]
    A["<b>3. Agent engine</b><br/>abm"]
    J["<b>4. Speed and alternate backends</b><br/>Numba and Rust kernels, JAX, compiled draws"]
    E["<b>5. Edges</b><br/>fitting, import and export,<br/>presentation, library, geography"]
    D --> G --> O --> C
    C --> K
    C --> A
    K -.-> J
    A -.-> J
    O --- E









Layer
Files in starsim/
What they do




1. Declaration
transitions.py, internals/expressions.py, internals/graph.py, internals/parameters.py, distributions.py, internals/dists.py, internals/time.py, internals/dates.py, internals/conditions.py, internals/dimensions.py, strains.py
The words a model is written in: states and transitions, rates as expressions (beta * I), parameters (ss.par, ss.by), durations and rates with units, conditions for where=, stratifications and strains. internals/graph.py collects one module’s declarations into an ss.graph.Graph, names them, fills in defaults (recording each guess), and checks them.


2. Build and orchestration
sim.py, internals/loop.py, internals/timeline.py, internals/modules.py, people.py, internals/arrays.py, networks.py, diseases.py, demographics.py (including ss.Pregnancy), interventions.py, products.py, connectors.py, analyzers.py, results.py, run.py
The runtime objects. sim.init() builds the population, the modules and the results, and chooses the solver; the loop then calls each module in a fixed, printable order each step. ss.Module is the one base class for diseases, networks, demographics, interventions, connectors and analyzers. run.py runs many sims (ss.MultiSim, ss.parallel).


3. Engines
solvers/choose.py, solvers/engine.py, solvers/compartmental.py, solvers/mixing.py, solvers/agents.py, solvers/crossing.py, solvers/deliveries.py, solvers/particles.py
How a graph is run. choose.py picks the solver and says why. Each declared module gets one engine: Compartmental (which flattens the model into a program of flows that the kernels step) or Agents (boolean arrays over agents). crossing.py tracks several diseases jointly when one refers to another’s states.


4. Speed and alternate backends
solvers/backends/ (kernels.py, ode.py, draws.py, passes.py, rust.py, jit.py, cache.py, memory.py), internals/gradients.py, and the Rust crate in solvers/rust/
The same runs, faster or differentiable. kernels.py holds the Numba kernels that step a compartmental program (ss.kernels), and ode.py the same ODE in NumPy for runs too short to compile for; draws.py the exact random draws everything shares; passes.py the compiled passes over agents and network edges; chain.py the chain binomial and tau-leaping in JAX; rust.py swaps in the Rust copy of all of these; jit.py is ss.jit, for compiling users’ own code; and internals/gradients.py runs the ODE in JAX for gradients and many runs at once. No user needs to read these.


5. Edges
fit.py, internals/display.py, internals/errors.py, geo.py, data.py, converters/, library/
What builds on a run model. Fitting (sim.fit()); describe(), diagram() and equations(); errors, warnings, and notes; places, mobility and data by place name; importers and exporters for other frameworks; and example diseases and networks (import starsim.library as ssl).



Helpers that every layer uses are in settings.py (ss.options), utils.py, internals/debugtools.py (profiling, debugging, and mock objects for tests) and internals/cli.py (the starsim command). Everything in internals/ is also at the top level: ss.graph, ss.expressions, ss.gradients, ss.errors, and so on.
For a sense of scale, the package is about 70,000 lines of Python: about 13,500 in declaration, 19,000 in orchestration, 12,500 in the engines, 8,000 in the speed layer (2,700 of them the Numba kernels), 15,000 at the edges (half of that in converters/, and 3,000 in library/), and 2,000 in the helpers. The Rust copy of the kernels adds another 7,000 lines, outside the installed package. The core that a model passes through on every run is layers 1 to 3.
A few things to notice in the map:

A declaration doesn’t say how it will run. The states, transitions and parameters of layer 1 are the same objects whether the model runs as an ODE or as agents; only when they are evaluated (a rate, a condition) do they see one value per group or one per agent. That is what makes the solver a choice rather than part of the model.
Every compartmental solver steps the same program. The ODE, the chain binomial, Gillespie and tau-leaping all run the flat list of flows that Compartmental builds. The JAX backends, the Rust kernels and the particle filter run that same program too, so a fix in one place is a fix for all of them.
Code is never analyzed in advance. A function in a rate, or a module’s step(), is simply called with what the solver has (one value per agent, or one per group). If it asks for something that only agents have, the run stops and says so.

title: Architecture
text:
The pages in this section

Model declaration: states, transitions, rates and parameters as objects; how the graph resolves, completes and checks them; and how importers turn another framework’s model into the same objects.
Model execution: what sim.init() does, units and time, the order modules run in each step, and the policy on errors, warnings, and notes.
Solvers and backends: how the solver is chosen, the engines that run each one, the kernel sets, and the tests that pin each path.
Transmission: routes (networks and mixing pools), how one module changes another (ss.modify), deliveries, and results.
Randomness: random streams and common random numbers, run identity, and how randomness is handled in fitting.
Modules: what a module is, its lifecycle, declared modules beside modules written as code, and how to read the loop.

How the design is tested (the test suites, and which to run after a change) is in the developer guide.

title: Outcomes
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
What a model tracks is not what is observed. A model of measles tracks who is susceptible, latent, infectious, and immune; a surveillance system sees reported cases, some days after infection, and only some of them. This page covers the results a model has, how to declare more (such as prevalence or the share immune), how to declare outcomes, the reported quantities worked out from the model’s flows (cases, hospital admissions, deaths), and how data is attached to the results by name, so that it can be plotted and fitted.
For a step-by-step introduction, see T7 – Data and calibration.

title: Outcomes
section: The results of a declared disease
text:
The results of a declared disease
Every declared disease has a result for each state and each transition, named after it, with no need to declare them:

a state (S, E, I, R) is a stock: the number of people in it at each time point;
a transition (infection, onset, recovery) is a flow: the number of people who made it during each step. A flow’s running total is .cum.


import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # The end of the latent period
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, onset, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-05-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.measles
print(res.keys())
print('Infections:', round(res.infection.sum()))

['timevec', 'S', 'E', 'I', 'R', 'infection', 'onset', 'recovery']
Infections: 99900


A result has one value for each time point of the sim. A stock at time point t is the number at t; a flow at t is the number during the step that ends at t, so a flow’s first value is 0. See Results for working with results: selecting, resampling, plotting, and exporting them.

title: Outcomes
text:
Declaring more results
A sum or ratio of states, given to the disease as a result, is a result like any other. Nobody is “in” a sum of states, so it makes no new state; as a result, it is the combined count, and a ratio of two is a proportion:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
N = S + E + I + R
infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)

prevalence = (E + I)/N # The share of people infected, latent or infectious
immune     = R/N       # The share immune, as a serosurvey would measure it

measles = ss.Disease(
    transitions = [infection, onset, recovery],
    results     = [prevalence, immune],
    init        = dict(I=0.001),
)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-05-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.diseases.measles.plot('prevalence', 'immune')








Flows can be used the same way: infection/S is the incidence per susceptible person. A ratio is a ratio of sums: by group or over a longer period, its numerator and denominator are each summed, and then divided, never averaged.
A result needs a name of its own. A parameter over time is a result of an expression of it under another name, eir_now = 1*eir; giving the parameter itself (eir=eir) raises an error. In a class, an expression with a value for each person, such as age = ss.ppl.age or duration = affected.time, is a helper for the rates, not a result.

title: Outcomes
text:
Outcomes
An outcome is a reported quantity: a flow worked out from the model’s other flows, which moves nobody. It is how a model says what a surveillance system would see. For measles, the rash appears about 4 days after people become infectious, and suppose half of cases are reported, a tenth of reported cases are admitted to hospital (for 5 days on average), and 2% of those admitted die:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)

cases  = ss.outcome(0.5*onset, delay=ss.days(4))                       # Half of cases reported, at the rash
hosp   = ss.outcome(0.1*cases, delay=ss.days(2), duration=ss.days(5))  # A tenth of those admitted to hospital
deaths = ss.outcome(0.02*hosp, delay=ss.days(5))                       # 2% of those admitted die

measles = ss.Disease(
    transitions = [infection, onset, recovery],
    outcomes    = [cases, hosp, deaths],
    init        = dict(I=0.001),
)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-05-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.measles
print('Reported cases:', round(res.cases.sum()))
print('Hospital admissions:', round(res.hosp.sum()))
print('Most in hospital at once:', round(res.n_hosp.max()))
print('Deaths:', round(res.deaths.sum()))
sim.diseases.measles.plot('cases', 'n_hosp')

Reported cases: 49947
Hospital admissions: 4995
Most in hospital at once: 1163
Deaths: 100










The source is a share of a flow, or a sum of shares of several: 0.5*onset is half of those who become infectious. The share is the probability of being counted. Reporting that depends on severity is a sum: ss.outcome(0.1*mild + 0.6*severe), where mild and severe are transitions.
Outcomes can follow from outcomes: hosp is a share of cases, and deaths a share of hosp, so a chain of events is a line for each.
delay= is the time from the source event to this one: a duration (exponentially distributed, as for any duration), a distribution such as ss.constant(ss.days(4)) or ss.lognorm_ex(...), or a function of the sim.
duration= gives a second result, n_<name>: the number currently in the outcome, here the number in hospital.
A share can be a parameter: ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.1, 0.9]) makes the reporting rate fittable, and ss.by(age=[...]) gives a share for each age group, as for any value (Parameters).

An outcome is worked out from the counts of its source flows, in each group, so it never records which people were counted. In a deterministic run, the share multiplies the flow and the delay spreads it over the following steps; in a stochastic or agent-based run, those counted are a binomial draw from the step’s events, and their delays are drawn too. So the reported cases of a stochastic run vary by chance, as real reporting does.
Infection, onset of symptoms, hospital admission, and a reported case are different events, even when their curves look alike, so define what the data measures before choosing the source and delay: a series of cases dated by onset is not the same as one dated by when the report was received. Check the start and end of the run, too: a delay can move events past the end of the run without changing the number of infections, so the last weeks of an outcome are lower than they will be.
describe() gives each outcome’s definition, under the disease’s transitions, e.g. cases   outcome: 0.5 × onset, after 4 days (exponential).

An outcome, an intervention, or a state
An outcome stands for an observation process that the model doesn’t represent. Which to use depends on what the model contains:



The situation
Use




Testing and reporting aren’t in the model: “about half of cases are reported, four days after onset”
An outcome


Testing is modeled, by interventions
The interventions’ own results: each test reports the diagnoses it made (Products)


Being counted changes what happens to the person (people in hospital are isolated and stop transmitting)
A state, with transitions in and out (Diseases)



An outcome is a result, so anything can read it: an intervention can be triggered when n_hosp passes a threshold. What it can’t do is single out individuals. An outcome belongs to one disease; a total over several diseases is arithmetic on their results after the run (sim.results.measles.cases + sim.results.rubella.cases), which is a result but not a declared one, so data can’t be attached to it.

title: Outcomes
text:
Data attached by name
Data is attached to a sim with data=: a table with a time column (date, year, t, or time) and a column for each result there is data for, named like the result. A column called cases is compared with the result cases, and plotted with it. To try this where the answer is known, make data from the model: to_data() draws weekly counts of reported cases from a run, with Poisson noise as in real reporting, from a sim with its own random seed:

truth = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-05-01', rand_seed=2, verbose=0)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_data('cases', resample='week')

sim.run()
sim.plot('cases')








The plot shows the model’s cases summed over each week of the data, as they are compared in a fit.

Data need not be on the model’s time step. A flow, such as weekly reported cases, is compared with the model’s total over each week of the data; a stock or a ratio, such as the share immune in a serosurvey, with the model’s value on the date of the data. The result already knows which it is.
With several diseases, a column is matched to the one that has a result of that name, or is named with its disease, measles.cases.
Data by group is given in long form: extra columns named after dimensions (age) say which group each row is for, and each row is compared with cases.select(age=...).
A missing value is not a zero. Leave weeks with no report empty (NaN) rather than 0, so that they are left out of the comparison rather than compared with a count of none.
A column that matches no result gets a note that lists the closest names, so a misspelled header is noticed; in a fit, it is an error.

Data is usually read from a file: data='measles_cases.csv' reads it. A file whose headers are not the names of results is read with ss.simdata(), which renames the columns and can drop those that match nothing:
data = ss.simdata('measles_cases.csv', aliases=dict(date='Week ending', cases='Reported measles cases'), ignore_extra=True)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-05-01')
Data attached this way is what calibration fits to: sim.fit() fits every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data.

title: Outcomes
text:
Likelihoods
Nothing needs a likelihood to be compared with data or fitted to it: by default, a fit compares each result with its data by their normalized absolute difference. Where a likelihood is wanted, for example for Bayesian methods, it is given with the outcome, as the distribution of the data around the model’s value:
cases = ss.outcome(0.5*onset, delay=ss.days(4), likelihood=ss.nbinom(n=ss.par(10, bounds=[1, 100])))
The model’s value is the mean of the distribution, and the rest (here the dispersion of a negative binomial) is given, or fitted as a parameter. See Fitting a model and Gradients.

title: Outcomes
text:
Pitfalls

A daily result against weekly data. Compare like with like: res.cases.resample('week') is the model’s weekly cases.
An outcome where a state is needed. If being counted changes what happens to a person, it is a state, not an outcome.
A misspelled data column. A column that matches no result is only noted when the sim is made; read the notes, or use ss.simdata(..., aliases=...) to rename it.

title: Outcomes
text:
Further reading

EpiNow2: estimating epidemic growth from delayed and partly reported cases, with delay distributions, in R
Practical considerations for measuring the effective reproductive number, Rt: why the delays between infection and observation matter, and how to account for them
pomp: stochastic models with an explicit measurement model linking the process to the data, in R
Simulation-based inference for epidemiological dynamics: course notes on measurement models and likelihoods for epidemic data

title: Interventions
text:
🧠5% 🤖95%
An intervention is anything done to change the course of an epidemic. Most are one of two kinds. Some deliver a product to people: a vaccine, a test, or a drug, given to the people who are eligible, at given times or when something happens to them. Others change a quantity in the model, giving nothing to anyone: masks, distancing, and school closures change transmission, faster diagnosis shortens the time people are infectious. This page covers both: how products are delivered (who, when, and how many), and how parameters are changed (when, for whom, and how changes combine), and then interventions written as code, for anything else.
What a vaccine, test, or treatment does is on Products, and what interventions cost on Costs. The same ss.modify() that changes parameters is how one module changes another, on Connectors. The tutorial T5 – Interventions and scenarios compares interventions against measles, and A4 – Interventions uses deliveries that need agents; running the scenarios of a comparison is on Scenarios.
Here are the two kinds side by side, against measles in a town of 100,000: a vaccination campaign that reaches 90% of people on day 5, and distancing that halves transmission from day 5 to day 30:
import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.0001)

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, leaky=False, coverage=0.9, at=[ss.days(5)])                 # Delivers a product
distancing = ss.modify(measles.pars.beta, multiply=0.5, start=ss.days(5), stop=ss.days(30))           # Changes a parameter

kw = dict(total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(measles, **kw),
    'Vaccination':     ss.Sim(measles, interventions=vaccination, **kw),
    'Distancing':      ss.Sim(measles, interventions=distancing, **kw),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')
msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/
















value


scenario





No intervention
99989.974541


Vaccination
51053.731226


Distancing
99963.735147
The campaign (with an all-or-nothing vaccine, leaky=False, as measles vaccine roughly is) protects those it reaches for good, and halves the number infected; by day 5, measles is already spreading fast, and many are infected before it starts. Halving transmission of a disease with an R0 of 15 hardly helps: R0 is still above 7, and when distancing ends, the people it protected are still susceptible. A disease with an R0 of 2, as in the examples below, responds very differently.

title: Interventions
text:
Delivering products
A delivery says who can receive the product, when, and how many. There is one delivery for each kind of product, ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat(), and each takes the product, or the product’s own keywords, as well as how it is delivered. A delivery takes its name from the variable it is assigned to, and has results of its own: the number delivered on each step, the number eligible, and the coverage reached. Its keywords are the same for every product:







Keyword
Meaning




start=, stop=
When delivery starts and stops: dates, or times in the sim’s unit


at=
Deliver in rounds at these times (a campaign)


interval=
Deliver in rounds this far apart, between start and stop


at_age=
Routine delivery to people as they reach an age, e.g. at_age=ss.months(9)


where=
Who can receive it: a condition, or a function of the sim


who=
Who receives it: an event (such as screening.positive or sis.infection), a condition, or both, joined with &


coverage=
The share of eligible people reached


capacity=
The number that can be delivered (per round, per step, or as a rate)


priority=
Who is served first when capacity runs short


queue=
Whether those not served wait their turn (agents only)


delay=
The time from a trigger to delivery (agents only)


trace=
Deliver to the contacts of those selected, on a network (agents only)


when=
Deliver only on steps where a function of the timeline returns True, e.g. lambda t: t.ti % 7 == 0


deliver=
A function of the sim that returns who receives it, instead of where=, coverage=, and the rounds


disease=
The disease the product acts on, if there is more than one



The examples in this section use a curable infection with no lasting immunity, over 20 years, as an SIS model run as agents (since some of what follows depends on each person’s own history):

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peryear(2)*I  # β = 2 per year
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.years(1)      # Infected for a year on average, then susceptible again
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.1)

kw = dict(n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)


Rounds and routine delivery
With at= or interval=, delivery is in rounds: in each round, every eligible person is offered the product once. With neither, delivery is routine: each person is offered it once, at the first step on which they are eligible. at_age= is routine delivery as people reach an age: at_age=ss.months(9) vaccinates children as they turn 9 months old, and not everyone older on the first day.

routine  = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, coverage=0.8, start='2005')                         # Once per person, when first eligible
yearly   = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, coverage=0.2, interval=ss.years(1), start='2005')   # A round every year
campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, coverage=0.6, at=['2005', '2010'])                  # Two rounds

scenarios = {
    'No vaccination':       ss.Sim(sis, **kw),
    'Routine, 80%':         ss.Sim(sis, interventions=routine, **kw),
    'Yearly rounds, 20%':   ss.Sim(sis, interventions=yearly, **kw),
    'Two campaigns, 60%':   ss.Sim(sis, interventions=campaign, **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')








As agents, each person has an age, so at_age= can be any age. As compartments, people have only an age group, and reach an age by aging from the group below it into the one it starts, so at_age= needs age groups with an edge at that age; otherwise it is an error (it never runs the model as agents instead). To compare several ages of delivery with the same compartments, give fine age groups once, with an edge at each age to try:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles = ss.Disease(S, I, R, infection=S >> I @ ss.peryear(500)*I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(8), births=ss.birth(S, rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), init=dict(I=0.001, R=0.85), name='measles')
measles.stratify(age=[0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 5, 15]) # Edges every 3 months up to 18 months

sims = {}
for months in [6, 9, 12, 15]:
    mcv1 = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.85, coverage=0.8, at_age=ss.months(months), name='mcv1')
    sims[f'At {months} months'] = ss.Sim(measles, interventions=mcv1, total_pop=1e6, start=2000, stop=2005, dt=ss.weeks(1), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
for label in sims:
    print(f'{label}: {msim.sims[label].results.measles.infection.sum():,.0f} infections')

At 6 months: 106,247 infections
At 9 months: 106,431 infections
At 12 months: 106,468 infections
At 15 months: 106,476 infections




Coverage and capacity
coverage=0.7 is a share of the eligible people. A typed rate or probability, such as coverage=ss.perday(0.1), is the chance of being reached over the step (or over the round, with interval=), and routine delivery then offers it at every step to those eligible: a rate of seeking care, for example. capacity= is a number available: a bare number is per round for campaigns (or per step, for delivery on events or by a function), and a rate, such as ss.peryear(500), is per unit time, which routine delivery needs. When fewer are available than people who would receive one, those who do are chosen at random, unless priority= says who comes first (e.g. priority=ss.ppl.age, the oldest first). Given together, coverage is applied first, and capacity caps the result:

limited = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, coverage=0.6, at=['2005', '2010'], capacity=500) # At most 500 doses a round
sim = ss.Sim(sis, interventions=limited, **kw)
sim.run()
print('Doses delivered:', sim.results.limited.delivered.sum())

Doses delivered: 1000.0


With queue=True, those not served for lack of capacity wait, longest first, until they are served or are no longer eligible; a duration, such as queue=ss.months(6), limits the wait.


Who is eligible
where= says who can receive the product. It is a condition on people or on the states of a module, written before the sim exists, such as ss.ppl.age < 15 (people under 15), sis.I (people infected), or a combination with &, |, and ~ (and, or, not). A condition is not worked out when it is written, but each time it is needed, in the sim it runs in, so the same condition works in every copy of a sim. Anything else is a function of the sim, returning a boolean array or the UIDs of people:

children = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, coverage=0.9, at=['2005'], where=ss.ppl.age < 15)
adults = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, coverage=0.9, at=['2005'], where=lambda sim: sim.people.age >= 15)

sim = ss.Sim(sis, interventions=[children, adults], **kw)
sim.run()
print('Children vaccinated:', sim.results.children.delivered.sum())
print('Adults vaccinated:', sim.results.adults.delivered.sum())

Children vaccinated: 1067.0
Adults vaccinated: 3408.0


Each of these deliveries makes its own vaccine. The first is named vaccine; since that name is taken, the second is named after its delivery, adults_product.


Delivery when something happens
An event in where= delivers to the people something has just happened to, instead of on a schedule: a transition (the people who went through it on this step), or the outcome of another delivery. A transition can also be given by its path, where='sis.infection'. Here half of people are treated when they are infected, up to 30 treatments a month:

on_infection = ss.treat(cure=0.9, where=sis.infection, coverage=0.5, capacity=30)
sim = ss.Sim(sis, interventions=on_infection, **kw)
sim.run()
sim.plot('sis')








A condition can also be read on someone’s mother: ss.mother(cond, born=True) holds for a person whose mother meets cond. Each event remembers, per person, whether it ever happened (.ever), how often (.count), and how long ago (.since). Here newborns are tested if their mother tested positive at antenatal care within the past year:

pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=ss.freqperyear(100)) # Births a year per 1,000 women
anc = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, where=pregnancy.P, coverage=0.5)
newborn = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, who=pregnancy.birth & ss.mother(anc.positive.since <= ss.years(1), born=True))
sim = ss.Sim(sis, demographics=pregnancy, interventions=[anc, newborn], **kw)
sim.run()
print('Newborns tested:', sim.results.newborn.delivered.sum())

Newborns tested: 1270.0


As agents, every delivery keeps the memory of its events (who it reached, and each outcome), so it can be read after a run: sim.interventions.screening.ever.uids is everyone ever screened, and (sim.interventions.screening.positive.since <= ss.years(1)).uids everyone positive within the past year.
trace= is contact tracing: it delivers to the contacts, on a network, of the people that the event in who= selects. A network with memory= reaches recent past partners too (see Contact networks).


Delivery by a function
When who, when, and how many depend on each other (“treat the 200 oldest people who are infected”), one function says it. It is called every step (within start and stop, if given), and returns the UIDs of the people who receive the product on that step; capacity= may still cap it:

import numpy as np

def oldest_infected(sim):
    """ The 200 oldest people who are infected """
    infected = sim.diseases.sis.I.uids
    order = np.argsort(sim.people.age[infected])
    return infected[order[-200:]]

targeted = ss.treat(cure=0.9, deliver=oldest_infected, start='2005')
sim = ss.Sim(sis, interventions=targeted, **kw)
sim.run()
sim.plot('sis')








when= is a condition on time, a function of the timeline that returns True or False, and delivers only on steps where it is True. A function of the sim goes in where=, e.g. once prevalence passes a threshold (see below).

title: Interventions
text:
Changing parameters

Masks and distancing
Here is a flu-like epidemic in a town of 100,000, with β = 0.4 per day and an infectious period of 5 days (R0 = 2), and two policies: masks worn from day 20 to day 60, which cut transmission by 40%, and distancing that halves transmission from day 20 and then eases to 80% of its usual level from day 60:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I        # β = 0.4 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(5)   # Infectious for 5 days on average
flu = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

masks = ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=0.6, start=ss.days(20), stop=ss.days(60))
distancing = ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=ss.timeseries({ss.days(20): 0.5, ss.days(60): 0.8}), start=ss.days(20))

kw = dict(total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
scenarios = {
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(flu, **kw),
    'Masks': ss.Sim(flu, interventions=masks, **kw),
    'Distancing': ss.Sim(flu, interventions=distancing, **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('flu.I')








flu.pars.beta is the β of the transmission, which a declared disease names beta. Masks delay the epidemic, but once they come off, most of it still happens; distancing, which never fully ends, cuts it by more:

msim.summarize().loc['flu_infection']








value


scenario





No intervention
79615.377937


Masks
65736.554255


Distancing
49626.920011









Changes at given times: ss.timeseries()
ss.modify(target, multiply=ss.timeseries({t1: x1, t2: x2}), start=t1) multiplies a quantity by each value from its time until the next; before start=, the quantity has its own value. Each multiplier is relative to the quantity’s own value, not to the one before. set= gives values instead of multipliers, and one change needs no series: ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, set=0.25, start=ss.days(20)). The times are dates in a sim with dates ('2025-03-01'), durations since the start (ss.days(20)), or numbers in the sim’s unit.


Changes while a condition holds: ss.modify()
ss.modify(target, multiply=...) changes a quantity for as long as it applies: always, between start= and stop=, on the steps a condition on time says so (when=), or where a condition holds (where=), of people, of the population, or a function of the sim. It takes exactly one of:







Keyword
What it does




multiply=
Multiplies the quantity


efficacy=
Removes a share of the risk: the same as multiply=1 - efficacy, for protection such as condoms


add=
Adds to the quantity (parameters only; and an inflow from ss.null, to which it adds an amount per unit time from outside the model, e.g. ss.modify(typhoid.shedding, add=ss.perday(4e6)))


set=
Replaces the quantity (parameters only)



and any of:







Keyword
Meaning




start=, stop=
When it applies (by default, always)


where=
Who it applies to: a condition, or a function of the sim (by default, everyone)


when=
A condition on time: a function of the timeline that returns True on the steps it applies


hold=
Once where= or when= selects someone, it stays on for them for at least this long


share=
With multiply= or efficacy=, the share of acts (or contacts) it applies to, e.g. condom use in 30% of acts


route=
For a change to transmission, the network or networks it applies on (by default, all)



The amount can itself vary: multiply= takes anything a parameter takes, such as ss.seasonal() or ss.timeseries() (see Parameters).

What can be changed
The target of a modifier is any named quantity in the model:








Target
Example
What it changes




A parameter
flu.pars.beta
The parameter, for everyone it applies to


A transition
flu.recovery
The transition’s rate (or its probability, for a branch with p=)


Susceptibility or infectiousness
flu.rel_sus, flu.rel_trans
Each person’s relative chance of infection, or of infecting others (multiply only)


A network or contact layer
school, from ss.contacts('Kenya', layer=[...])
The contacts on it


Any of these by name
'flu.pars.beta', 'school.pars.n_contacts'
The same, written as a path



Here faster diagnosis from day 30 halves the time that people stay infectious, by doubling the rate of recovery, and susceptibility is halved for people aged 65 and over in an age-structured version of the model:

faster = ss.modify(flu.recovery, multiply=2, start=ss.days(30))
sim = ss.Sim(flu, interventions=faster, **kw)
sim.run()
print('Infections with faster diagnosis:', round(sim.results.flu.infection.sum()))

flu_age = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
flu_age.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
older = ss.modify(flu_age.rel_sus, multiply=0.5, where=ss.ppl.age >= 65)

sim = ss.Sim(flu_age, interventions=older, **kw)
sim.run()
sim.results.flu_age.I.by('age').plot()

Infections with faster diagnosis: 53684









Closing schools is a modifier on the school layer of a contact matrix: see Population data.


Who it applies to
where= is a condition on people or on the states of modules, written before the sim exists: ss.ppl.age >= 65, flu.I, or a combination with &, |, and ~ (and, or, not), such as (ss.ppl.age >= 65) & ~flu.R. A condition is worked out each time it is needed, in the sim it runs in, so the same condition works in every copy of a sim made by ss.parallel() or by calibration. Anything else is a function of the sim, returning a boolean array or the UIDs of people: where=lambda sim: sim.people.age >= 65. A condition on a property of people, such as age, can be run as compartments only if the model is stratified by that property, as above; otherwise the model runs as agents.



Changes triggered by the epidemic
A rule such as “close schools when cases pass a threshold” is a function of the sim, given as where=, which returns True on the steps it applies. It can read any result up to the start of the step (sim.ti - 1, since this step’s results aren’t written yet). It has no memory: the modifier is on exactly when the function says so, so a bare threshold switches on and off as the epidemic crosses it. hold= adds the simplest memory: once on, it stays on for at least that long. Here transmission is halved for at least 30 days whenever more than 5,000 people are infectious:

def many_infectious(sim):
    return sim.results.flu.I[sim.ti - 1] > 5000

reactive = ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=0.5, where=many_infectious, hold=ss.days(30))
sim = ss.Sim(flu, interventions=reactive, **kw)
sim.run()
sim.plot('flu')








A condition on a result can also be written with the result itself, which works out the condition for each place (or other group) on its own. Here each of two towns halves its transmission for at least 14 days once its cases over a week pass 200 per 100,000 people:

towns = ss.geo.geography(names=['North', 'South'], pop=[50_000, 50_000], x=[0, 20], y=[0, 0])
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(5)
flu_towns = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0])))
flu_towns.stratify(patch=towns, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=0.001))

weekly = flu_towns.infection.incidence(over=ss.days(7), by='patch') # New infections over the past week, as a share of each town
local = ss.modify(flu_towns.pars.beta, multiply=0.5, where=weekly > 200e-5, hold=ss.days(14))

sim = ss.Sim(flu_towns, interventions=local, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.flu_towns.I.by('patch').plot()








Each town’s measures keep its epidemic near the threshold. Any other rule that remembers what it did (a lockdown that lasts until cases fall below a lower threshold, say) is a module written as code: a subclass of ss.Intervention whose step() decides, and an ss.modify() whose when= reads its decision, so that the base value is never overwritten. See below.


How changes combine
A modifier never overwrites the quantity it changes. The quantity keeps its own base value, and the modifiers active now are applied on top of it to give the effective value, which the model uses:
effective = (the set value, if any, otherwise the base) × every multiplier + every addition
that is, set, then multiply, then add, whatever order the modifiers were given in. Two 40% reductions give a 64% reduction (0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36), the usual assumption for independent effects; the efficacies of products (such as a vaccine’s) are multipliers of the same kind. Since the base is never changed, nothing has to be undone when a modifier stops applying, and modifiers from several sources combine instead of erasing each other. The array itself holds the base: as agents, the effective value of each person, with the modifiers and products that apply now, is dis.current_value(), e.g. sim.diseases.flu_age.current_value('rel_sus'), which is what to record or check (rel_sus itself gives the base values). sim.what_modifies() lists the modifiers on a quantity, with their conditions:

sim = ss.Sim(flu_age, interventions=older, **kw)
sim.init()
sim.what_modifies(sim.diseases.flu_age.rel_sus)

flu_age.rel_sus
  modifiers
    older            multiply=0.5   where=(people.age >= 65)


A modifier can be given to the sim as an intervention (interventions=) or as a connector (connectors=). The two do the same thing, and differ only in where they run in each step; by convention, policies go in interventions= and interactions that are part of the biology (one disease raising the risk of another) in connectors= (see Connectors).


Under compartments and agents
Changes work the same under every solver. As agents, a change to contacts (such as multiply=0.5 on a layer) means each contact happens with that probability in a step; in a compartmental run, the contacts are scaled. where= on a property of people needs either agents, or a model stratified by that property, and a model with neither runs as agents.

title: Interventions
text:
Writing an intervention as code
Deliveries and modifiers cover the common cases. Anything else is a module written as code: a subclass of ss.Intervention with a step() method, which runs on every step and can read and change anything in the sim (see Custom modules, and the tutorial T9 – Custom modules, which writes one for isolating measles cases).
An intervention written as code is best kept to deciding, leaving the change itself to ss.modify(), so that the base value is never overwritten and the change combines with others. Here is a lockdown with memory: it starts when more than 5,000 people are infectious, as the reactive measure above does, but is lifted only once fewer than 1,000 are. The intervention keeps the decision, and records it as a result; the modifier reads it:

class Lockdown(ss.Intervention):
    """ Lock down when more than `on` people are infectious, and lift it only once fewer than `off` are """
    def __init__(self, on=5000, off=1000, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(on=on, off=off)
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.active = False
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(ss.Result('active', label='Lockdown in place'))
        return

    def step(self):
        infectious = self.sim.results.flu.I[self.sim.ti - 1] if self.sim.ti > 0 else 0 # As of the last step
        if not self.active and infectious > self.pars.on:
            self.active = True
        elif self.active and infectious < self.pars.off:
            self.active = False
        self.results.active[self.ti] = self.active
        return

lockdown = Lockdown()
effect = ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=0.5, where=lambda sim: sim.interventions.lockdown.active)

msim = ss.parallel({
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(flu, **kw),
    'Lockdown':        ss.Sim(flu, interventions=[lockdown, effect], **kw),
})
msim.plot('flu.I')
print('Days of lockdown:', msim.sims[1].results.lockdown.active.sum())








Days of lockdown: 38.0


The lockdown stays in place for 38 days, until fewer than 1,000 people are infectious, rather than switching on and off around a single threshold. Once it is lifted, a second wave follows, since most people are still susceptible: the usual result of a measure that ends before immunity has built up, and a reason to run scenarios until their epidemics are over. An intervention that reads results only, as this one does, runs under every solver; one that acts on particular people (e.g. through their states) runs as agents. A product whose effect needs code is a subclass of ss.Product instead: see Products.

title: Interventions
text:
Comparing scenarios
An intervention’s effect is the difference between a run with it and a run without, so every comparison needs a baseline that shares everything else: the same population, parameters, and, for a stochastic model, random numbers. Make the scenarios from one sim, with sim.new(interventions=...), and run them together with ss.parallel(), as on this page. Some things to keep in mind:

Run long enough. An intervention that delays infections can look like one that prevents them if the run ends too soon; run until the epidemics of all scenarios are over, or long enough to see the endemic level.
Run more than once. For a model run as agents or as a stochastic model, the difference between two single runs is partly chance; run each scenario several times (n_runs=), with the same seeds for each, and compare the differences run by run (msim.diff()). See Scenarios.
Count the same thing. Compare the same results in the same units across scenarios: infections in people, not agents, and over the same period.

title: Interventions
text:
Pitfalls

Routine is once per person. Routine delivery offers each person the product once, when they are first eligible; a share of people reached every year is delivery in yearly rounds (interval=ss.years(1)), or routine delivery with a typed coverage (coverage=ss.probperyear(0.5)), a chance at every step for as long as people are eligible.
Coverage is of the eligible. coverage=0.8 with where=ss.ppl.age < 5 reaches 80% of children under 5, not 80% of everyone.
Routine delivery needs a rate of capacity. A bare number as capacity= is per round or per step; routine delivery has neither, so it needs a rate, e.g. ss.peryear(500).
and, or, and not don’t combine conditions. Use &, |, and ~, with brackets: (ss.ppl.age > 15) & ~sis.I.
A multiplier is relative to the base. ss.modify(beta, multiply=ss.timeseries({20: 0.5, 60: 0.8}), start=20) sets transmission to 80% of its base from day 60, not to 80% of the 50% before.
Susceptibility and infectiousness only multiply. add= and set= are for parameters; on rel_sus and rel_trans, use multiply=.
A trigger with no memory flickers. where= on a threshold switches the modifier on and off as the quantity crosses it; give hold= for a measure that stays in place once begun.
Read results from before this step. A function given as where= runs before the step’s results are written; read [sim.ti - 1], not [sim.ti].

The API reference for this page: Interventions, Connectors (for ss.modify()).

title: Interventions
text:
Further reading

Covasim: Interventions: changing transmission, testing, tracing, and vaccination in an agent-based model
epydemix: Modeling interventions: changing contacts over time in a compartmental model
EMOD: Creating campaigns: another framework’s approach to events, eligibility, and coverage of interventions

title: Parameters
text:
🧠10% 🤖90%
The parameters of a model are the numbers in it: transmission rates, durations, shares, and the like. This page covers where they live, their units, how to name them so they can be documented, changed, and fitted, and the forms a value can take: a number, a value for each group, a value that changes over time, or one that varies between people.

title: Parameters
text:
Values live in the model
In a declared disease, a value lives where it is used. There is no separate block of parameters to fill in: each number becomes a parameter, named after its role:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

measles.pars

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/


Pars(init_prev=par(0.001), beta=par(1.9), dur_I=par(days(8)))


The number that multiplies a source of infection is beta (named by its transition, beta_infection, only where two would have the same name). A duration is named by the state it is the time in (dur_E, dur_I), or by its transition if people can leave that state after more than one duration (dur_recovery, dur_death), and a rate by its transition (rate_death). What a number means is given by where it is: after @ and multiplying I, a rate; as init_prev=, a share of the population.

title: Parameters
text:
Units of time
A typed value says its unit: ss.days(8) is a duration, and ss.perday(1.9), ss.peryear(0.02) are rates. A bare number takes the unit of the model, which is the unit of its typed values: here days, from ss.days(8), so β = 1.9 is per day. The rates of births and deaths don’t count, so adding births per year to this model leaves β per day. A model whose other typed values are in different units (a duration in days and another in years) has no single unit for its bare numbers, which is an error that asks for unit=; giving every rate a type avoids it.
Values are converted to the time step of the sim, whatever it is, so the same model can be run with a step of a day or a week. A rate (ss.perday) is a rate, converted exactly. A probability over a period, such as a 10% chance of recovering each day, is written ss.prob(0.1, 'day'), and is converted as a probability: over a week it is 1 − 0.9^7, not 0.7. See Time for durations, rates, and dates.

title: Parameters
text:
Named parameters
When a parameter is to be documented, reused, or fitted, give it a name with ss.par(). It behaves like its value in a rate, so it can be used anywhere a number can:

beta = ss.par(1.9, bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate per day', source='Chosen to give R0 of about 15')
dur  = ss.par(ss.days(8), bounds=[ss.days(6), ss.days(10)], doc='Infectious period', source='About 4 days either side of the rash')

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ dur
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

measles.pars

Pars(
    init_prev = par(0.001),
    beta      = par(1.9, bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate per day'),
    dur       = par(days(8), bounds=[days(6), days(10)], doc='Infectious period'),
)



The name is taken from the variable (beta), or given with name=.
bounds is the range of plausible values. A parameter with bounds can be fitted: sim.fit() fits every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data (Fitting a model). A value outside its bounds is an error.
doc (what it means) and source (where the value came from) are free text. describe() shows them under the transition that uses the parameter, and they are kept when the model is saved.
prior= gives a distribution of belief about the value, used only in calibration (Gradients).


sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.describe()
