title: Parameters
text:
Changing a parameter
A parameter can be changed when the sim is made, by name, without changing the model. This is how a set of values for one setting, or a fitted set, is used:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=1.5), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
print('R0 with beta = 1.5:', round(sim.diseases.measles.R0(), 1))

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 12, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0019 s; measles: 99,899 infections; at most 70,922 infectious, on day 7
R0 with beta = 1.5: 12.0


With several modules, a parameter’s name is given with its module’s, e.g. pars={'measles.beta': 1.5}. A name that matches no parameter is an error, which lists the names there are, so a misspelled parameter is never silently ignored:

try:
    ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(betta=1.5)).init()
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)

KeyNotFoundError pars= has a value for "betta", which matches no parameter. Parameters are measles.init_prev, measles.beta, measles.dur; did you mean measles.beta?


A parameter can also be changed during a run, from a date or when a condition holds, with ss.modify(); see Interventions.

title: Parameters
section: The forms a value can take
text:
The forms a value can take
Where a value is given decides what it means; the form it takes is free. Each of these can be a rate, a duration, a share, or a starting value:








Form
Example
Means




A number
1.9
The same for everyone, always (in the model’s unit of time)


A typed value
ss.perday(1.9), ss.days(8)
The same, in its own unit


A value for each group
ss.by(age=[2.5, 1.9, 1.0])
One value for each age group (or other group)


A time series
ss.timeseries({'2025-01-01': 1.9, '2025-03-01': 1.2})
Changes over time, from given values


A seasonal cycle
ss.seasonal(mean=1.9, amplitude=0.2, peak='March')
A yearly cycle around a mean


A function of the sim
lambda sim: 1.9 if sim.now < ss.date('2025-03-01') else 1.2
Worked out at each step


A distribution
ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(8), std=ss.days(2))
Varies between people


A function of the sim and the people
lambda sim, uids: ...
One value for each person (agents only)



Any of these can be wrapped in ss.par() to give it a name, bounds, or a source. The sections below cover each kind.

Values for each group
ss.by() gives a value for each level of a stratification. Here children (0–14) are the most likely to be infected, and older adults the least:

def make_measles(beta):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the share in each
    return measles

betas = {
    'The same for everyone': 1.9,
    'By age':                ss.by(age=[2.5, 1.9, 1.0]),
}
for label, beta in betas.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(beta), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(30), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    infections = sim.results.measles.infection
    print(label)
    for age in ['0-14', '15-64', '65+']:
        print('  Infected by day 3, aged', age, ':', round(infections.select(age=age).cum[3]))
sim.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()

The same for everyone
  Infected by day 3, aged 0-14 : 5349
  Infected by day 3, aged 15-64 : 10698
  Infected by day 3, aged 65+ : 1783
By age
  Infected by day 3, aged 0-14 : 8032
  Infected by day 3, aged 15-64 : 12652
  Infected by day 3, aged 65+ : 1172









With β by age, children are infected sooner, and older adults later, than with the same β for everyone; with an R0 this high, nearly everyone is infected within a week or two either way. The plot shows new infections by age group with β by age.
Here the values are per day, and mixing is homogeneous, so a higher β means a higher rate of infection for susceptible people in that group. The values can also be given by label (ss.by(age={'0-14': 2.5, ...})), as a table, or for several dimensions at once. See Stratification. They can also come from code, as a function of the sim that gives one value per level, worked out at each step: ss.by(patch=fn), e.g. a biting rate in each place from mosquitoes written as code, whatever other dimensions the sim has.


Values that change over time
Contact patterns, reporting, and treatment change over time, and so do the parameters that stand for them. A value can be a time series (ss.timeseries()), held or interpolated between given dates; a smooth yearly cycle (ss.seasonal()); or a function of the sim, worked out at each step. Each goes wherever a number would, in a rate, a share, or a starting value. Time covers them, with examples of measles with and without school terms. A change made by an intervention, from a date or when a condition holds (ss.change(), ss.modify()), is covered in Interventions.

title: Parameters
text:
Values that vary between people
A distribution, given as a value, gives each person their own value: recovery = I >> R @ ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(8), std=ss.days(2)) gives each person their own infectious period. For durations, a compartmental run represents the distribution with stages; see Durations and Distributions.
A function of the sim and the people, fn(sim, uids), returns one value for each person it is given, and can use anything about them. Here the infectious period is longer for children under 5 (a made-up example):

def dur_fn(sim, uids):
    age = sim.people.age[uids]
    return ss.days(8 + 4*(age < 5)) # 12 days for children under 5, 8 for everyone else

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.constant(dur_fn)) # Each person's own duration, as given
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
same = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9*I, ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.constant(ss.days(8))), init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
base = ss.Sim(same, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
base.run()

print('Still infectious on day 18, with 8 days for everyone:', round(base.results.measles.I[18]))
print('Still infectious on day 18, with 12 days under 5:', round(sim.results.measles.I[18]))

Still infectious on day 18, with 8 days for everyone: 72
Still infectious on day 18, with 12 days under 5: 677


Nearly everyone is infected in the first week or two either way, but with the longer infectious period of young children, the epidemic takes several days longer to end. Children under 5 are only a few percent of the population, so the effect is only as large as the group the function applies to.
A rate is worked out for the people who could take it at each step (everyone in its source state), so a function in a rate is called for them, every step. Multiplied by a condition, it is called only for the people the condition holds for, and is 0 for the others: with rate = ss.par(fn, name='infant')*(ss.ppl.age < 1), fn is given only the children under 1, and need not check their ages itself.
A function that uses uids, or anything else about individual people, needs agents, so a model with one runs as agents. Where the same thing can be said by group (ss.by(age=...) on a stratified model), it runs under every solver.
A distribution in a rate gives each person their own rate: in S >> I @ ss.gamma(a=0.5, scale=3.8)*I, each person has their own transmission rate (the same as ss.Transition(S, I, rate=ss.gamma(a=0.5, scale=3.8)*I)). A distribution on its own after @ is a dwell time; times a state, it is a rate.

title: Parameters
section: Parameters of modules written as code
text:
Parameters of modules written as code
A module written as code (see Custom modules) declares its parameters, and their defaults, in its __init__() with self.define_pars(), and then takes the values it was given with self.update_pars():

class Antibodies(ss.Module):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            half_life = ss.days(60), # How quickly antibodies decline
            boost     = 1.0,         # The antibody level just after recovery
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)

antibodies = Antibodies(half_life=ss.days(90))
print(antibodies.pars)

Pars(half_life=days(90), boost=1.0)


The point of define_pars() is to set the ground truth for what each parameter is. The values given to the module are checked against it, so a misspelled name is an error:

try:
    Antibodies(half_lfe=ss.days(90))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)

ValueError 1 unrecognized argument for antibodies: half_lfe


A value can be given in any form that fits the default. For a parameter whose default is a distribution, a number sets the distribution’s main value, and another distribution replaces it. For example, in the library’s SIR written as code (ssl.AgentSIR), the chance of death is a Bernoulli distribution (a yes or no for each person), so it can be given as a probability or as another Bernoulli distribution, but not as a distribution of another kind, since what the module does with it (picking who dies) needs a yes or no:

import starsim.library as ssl

print(ssl.AgentSIR(p_death=0.02).pars.p_death)                  # A probability: the p of the default
print(ssl.AgentSIR(p_death=ss.bernoulli(p=0.2)).pars.p_death)   # Another Bernoulli distribution
print(ssl.AgentSIR(dur_inf=ss.normal(loc=ss.years(4), scale=ss.years(1))).pars.dur_inf) # Any distribution of durations
try:
    ssl.AgentSIR(p_death=ss.lognorm_ex(4))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)

ss.bernoulli(p=0.02)
ss.bernoulli(p=0.2)
ss.normal(loc=ss.years(4), scale=ss.years(1))
TypeError Bernoulli distributions can only be changed to another Bernoulli distribution or ss.choose_n(): <class 'starsim.distributions.lognorm_ex'> is invalid


A parameter of a distribution can itself be a function of the sim and the people it is drawn for, which is how a module written as code makes a value depend on age, sex, or anything else the sim knows; see Distributions.

title: Parameters
text:
Pitfalls

A bare number in the wrong unit. A bare number is in the model’s unit of time: in a model whose unit is years, I >> R @ 0.125 is 0.125 per year. Typed values (ss.perday(0.125), ss.days(8)) don’t depend on it.
Changing the model instead of the sim. To try another value, give it to the sim (pars=dict(beta=1.5)) rather than changing the disease, which every sim made from it shares.
A distribution as a value or as a prior. A distribution as a value is variation between people. Uncertainty about a single value is a prior, ss.par(1.9, prior=...), used only in calibration.
A function where a time series would do. A function can’t be printed by describe(), exported to another framework, or written out as equations.

title: Parameters
text:
Further reading

epiparameter: a library of epidemiological parameters (incubation periods, serial intervals, and the like) from the literature, in R
Rates and probabilities in economic modelling: converting between rates and probabilities over different periods
pomp: estimating the parameters of stochastic dynamic models, in R

title: Model declaration
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
A disease written as code, as a class whose step() method changes arrays of agents, can be run but not read: Starsim can’t describe the model, draw it, or run it any other way. A declared disease is instead a set of objects (states, transitions, parameters) that describe the model without running it. Everything else is derived from them: the description, the diagram and equations, the stratified model, the exports to other frameworks, and the engines that run it as an ODE, a stochastic compartmental model, or agents.
This page covers those objects, what Starsim does with them when a module is built, how it fills in what you left out, and how models from other frameworks are turned into the same objects. Model execution covers what happens next. For how to write a disease as a modeler, see Diseases and Writing models.

title: Model declaration
text:
States and transitions
A state (ss.State) is something a person can be in: a compartment in an ODE, a boolean array over agents in an agent-based run. A transition (ss.Transition) moves people between states, driven by a rate, a dwell time, a branch probability, or a trigger. There are four ways to write a model, and they build the same objects:
import starsim as ss

# Operators: "S goes to I at rate beta times I"
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10),
)

# Fully explicit, e.g. for building models in a loop or from another language
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(
    ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.3 * I, name='infection'),
    ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(10), name='recovery'),
)

# A class, when there is also behavior that isn't a transition
class SIR(ss.Disease):
    S, I, R   = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)

# A class whose structure depends on its arguments, declared in __init__()
class SIRS(ss.Disease):
    def __init__(self, waning=True, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(ss.states('S I R'))
        self.define_transitions(
            infection = self.S >> self.I @ 0.3 * self.I,
            recovery  = self.I >> self.R @ ss.days(10),
        )
        if waning:
            self.define_transitions(waning=self.R >> self.S @ ss.days(100))
The first three are the same model, and give the same results. This is a rule of the design: a keyword means the same thing in every form, and subclassing adds behavior, not vocabulary. A transition takes the state objects themselves, never their names as strings, so nothing is inferred from a name. In the fourth form, what is declared in __init__() is collected as it is given and built once, when the outermost __init__() returns (built_after() in starsim/diseases.py), so a subclass can add to its parent’s states before anything is built; after that, declaring more raises an error.

title: Model declaration
text:
Rates are expressions
When you write 0.3 * I, nothing is computed. I is a state, so the result is an expression (ss.expressions.Expr, in starsim/internals/expressions.py): a small tree whose leaves are parameters, states, counts (I.n), and properties of people (ss.ppl.age), joined by arithmetic and NumPy functions. Each engine evaluates the same tree in its own terms: a value for each group of a compartmental model, for each agent, or as JAX arrays so a gradient can be taken through the run. This is what lets a model written once be run by any solver.
Two kinds of leaf differ. I.n is the number of people in I, used literally. A bare I means contact with people in I: with no network that’s I.n / N, so beta * I is the textbook beta * S * I / N, and with a network each engine works it out from who actually meets whom, which no single formula can say. Since that is a sum over contacts, a rate must be linear in its bare states (beta * I * I raises a ValueError that suggests the two ways to say what was probably meant). Transmission covers how each engine turns a bare state into a force of infection.
The kind of a transition is derived from its rate, not declared: if the rate mentions a bare state, the transition is contact-mediated and that state is a source of infection; otherwise it is spontaneous. You can see this on the transition itself:
sir.infection.contact     # True: its rate mentions I
sir.infection.terms       # {I: par(0.3)}: the coefficient of each source of infection
sir.recovery.contact      # False

title: Model declaration
text:
Parameters
A number written inline becomes a parameter of the module, named after its slot: above, sir.pars has beta (the coefficient of I) and dur_I (the dwell time of recovery, the mean time in I), with init_prev. A duration is always named by the state it is the time in, or by its transition if people can leave that state after more than one duration (dur_recovery), and a rate by its transition (rate_death); any other name is qualified by its transition only if two would clash (beta_infection). Wrap a value in ss.par() when it needs a name, bounds, or a source; bounds are what make it fittable, since sim.fit() fits every parameter with bounds to every result with data. A value may also vary by group (ss.by(age=[...])), in time (ss.timeseries()), or between people (a distribution): the slot decides what a value means, and the form is free. Setting a parameter the module doesn’t have raises a KeyError that lists the parameters it does have and suggests the nearest, since a misspelling that is silently ignored is one of the hardest bugs to find. See Parameters.

title: Model declaration
text:
Dimensions
Age, sex, place, and risk group are all handled by one operation, stratify(), which takes a finished model and divides it by a property of people:
sim = ss.Sim(sir, stratify=dict(age=[0, 15, 65]))   # or sim.stratify(age=...), for every module
sir.stratify(risk=['low', 'high'], adjust={'infection': [1, 3]})  # one disease's own dimension
Stratifying doesn’t copy the states: sir still has S, I, and R, and the dimension becomes an axis. In a compartmental run each state has one row per group; as agents the property is an array on the people, and the groups are used for adjustments, conditions, and results. The base model and the stratification don’t refer to each other, which is what lets one disease be reused with different structures. A stratified result is still one result (res.I.select(age='0-14'), res.I.by('age')). Properties of people are normally stratified on the sim, because every disease has to agree on them. The code is in starsim/dimensions.py (ss.dimensions.Strat), and the groups a sim ends up with are sim.groups. See Stratification.

title: Model declaration
text:
The graph: resolve, complete, check
When ss.Disease(...) is called, it builds the module’s graph (ss.graph.Graph, in starsim/internals/graph.py). The graph is where the objects you wrote become a model:

Collect and name. It gathers the states, transitions, parameters, and results, and names any that have no name: from the keyword they were passed under, then a name= argument, then the variable they’re bound to in the calling code. A transition with none of these is named infection if it is the disease’s only transmission (as in ss.SIR), and otherwise gets a name built from its endpoints (I_to_R); a state with none raises a ValueError, since a made-up state name would leak into results.
Resolve. It finds which states are people and which are plain counts (a water reservoir, a mosquito population), derives the kind of each transition from its rate, marks the sources of infection, works out which transitions are acquisitions of the disease, and finds the first state (where people start and are born into).
Complete. It turns inline values into named parameters, and groups the exits of each state into those that compete (rates, resolved together in one draw, so declaration order never matters) and those that split on entry (p=).
Check. It checks what can be checked without a sim: the time dimension of every rate, that branch probabilities add up, that exposure is linear, and that keywords name real parameters.

So mistakes in the model’s structure are errors when the disease is built, at the line that made it. What needs the sim (the unit of bare numbers, values against their bounds, the shapes of values by group, the choice of solver) is checked at sim.init().
Picking names up from variables is convenient but implicit, so it happens in one place, once. It can miss (a transition written inline in the call gets the fallback name), and describe() shows the names used.

title: Model declaration
text:
Guessed defaults
Short models leave a lot unsaid: how a dwell time is distributed, how people mix, how many there are. Starsim fills each gap with a default and records the rule that produced it: a guessed default. describe() prints the resolved model with every guess marked, so nothing is assumed silently:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(bounds=[0.1, 1.0], source='to be fitted')
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ beta * I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(3)),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, stop=100)
sim.describe()

Every [guessed: ...] is a choice you didn’t make: 10,000 people, the ODE solver, homogeneous mixing, 11 Erlang stages for the lognormal dwell time, and beta starting at the geometric middle of its bounds. Each guess is tested both ways: a model that makes it has it marked, and one that doesn’t, doesn’t.

title: Model declaration
section: Ways to write a model out
text:
Ways to write a model out
A Starsim model is written as Python, and that code is the model: it is what is kept, shared, and compared (with a diff in a text editor, or by the results it gives). The other forms each hold less:



What
Method
Holds
Read back?




The code
the script itself; for an import, sim.imported.code
the model, as Python
yes, by running it


Results as JSON
sim.to_json()
parameters, summary, and results, for use elsewhere
no


A saved sim
ss.save('run.sim', sim)
the sim itself (a pickle), including partway through a run
yes, with ss.load()


Another framework’s format
ss.export_to(sim, 'odin') or 'sbml'
the compartmental form of the declared diseases
yes, with ss.import_from()



A sim made in Starsim is never written back out as Starsim code: its code is the script that made it. Only an import is written as code, as the next section explains.

title: Model declaration
text:
Importers and exporters
Every importer reads another framework’s model into one intermediate object, ss.converters.Source: its states, parameters, flows as rate expressions, stratifications, outcomes, and what it couldn’t translate. One function, ss.converters.write(), writes a Source as Starsim code (a declared ss.Disease, with its parameters, states, and transitions as variables, ending with sim = ss.Sim(...)), by the same rules for every format, and ss.converters.build() runs that code to make the sim. So there is one path, from a foreign model to code to a sim, and never from a sim back to code; each framework needs only a reader, and there are no framework-to-framework converters. The code is kept as sim.imported.code, for the user to keep and change. A value the writer can’t write as code, such as a network, is given by the importer as ss.converters.Code('...'), the Python that makes it.






flowchart LR
  F["odin, SBML, EMULSION, SimInf,<br>flepiMoP, summer2, Atomica, camdl,<br>EpiModel, epydemix, MEmilio"] --> R[reader] --> S["ss.converters.Source"] --> W["ss.converters.write()"] --> C["Starsim code"] --> Sim[sim]
  Sim --> E["SBML, odin"]






The hardest part of importing is reading rates. Most frameworks write a flow as a total, such as beta * S * I / N; the importer turns it into a per-person rate on a transition, and says how it read each one. A rate divided by the population total is exposure through the routes (beta * I); one without the division is density-dependent and is kept as a count (beta * I.n); anything else is kept literally, as an expression of counts, which is exact under every solver. A Source can also be filled in by hand, which shows each step:

src = ss.converters.Source('sir', format='by hand')
for name, n in dict(S=990, I=10, R=0).items():
    src.add_state(name, init=n)
src.add_par('beta', 0.3)
src.add_par('gamma', 0.1)
src.add_flow('S', 'I', rate='beta * S * I / (S + I + R)', per='total', name='infection')
src.add_flow('I', 'R', rate='gamma * I', per='total', name='recovery')
sim = ss.converters.build(src, stop=100)
print(sim.imported.code)

Imported "sir" from by hand: 3 states, 2 transitions, 2 parameters
  S -> I           beta * S * I / (S + I + R) : S taken out of the flow; exposure to I (divided by the total: frequency-dependent) => beta * I
  I -> R           gamma * I : I taken out of the flow; spontaneous => gamma
# Imported from by hand (an object) by ss.import_from()
#
# How each rate was read:
#   S -> I           beta * S * I / (S + I + R) : S taken out of the flow; exposure to I (divided by the total: frequency-dependent) => beta * I
#   I -> R           gamma * I : I taken out of the flow; spontaneous => gamma

import starsim as ss

# Parameters
beta = ss.par(0.3)
gamma = ss.par(0.1)

# States
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')

# Transitions and outcomes
infection = S >> I @ (beta * I)
recovery = I >> R @ gamma

sir = ss.Disease(
    S, I, R, infection, recovery,
    init_n = dict(S=990, I=10),
    first = 'S',
    name = 'sir',
)

sim = ss.Sim(diseases=[sir], stop=100, total_pop=1000)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sim.run()
    sim.plot()



The flow beta * S * I / (S + I + R) was read as frequency-dependent exposure, and written as beta * I; gamma * I lost its I and became a rate per person. Exporting goes the other way, from the built model:

print(ss.export_to(sim, 'odin'))

## sir, exported from Starsim 4.0.0; time is in days

deriv(S) <- -infection
deriv(I) <- infection - recovery
deriv(R) <- recovery

initial(S) <- 990
initial(I) <- 10
initial(R) <- 0

infection <- beta * S * I / N
recovery <- gamma * I
N <- S + I + R

beta <- user(0.3)
gamma <- user(0.1)



/home/cliffk/idm/ssv4/starsim/converters/export.py:487: LossyExport:


exported to odin: 3 states, 2 transitions, as 3 compartments and 2 flows (time in days)
  not exported: result "prevalence"



An importer keeps the source’s names, marks what it guessed (as [guessed] in describe(), like a hand-written model), keeps going when something doesn’t map onto a built-in piece, and lists what it couldn’t translate by name (ss.errors.ImportIncomplete, also in sim.imported.incomplete). An incomplete import still runs, without the listed parts, and the warning says how to finish it with the import-model skill for AI assistants (in starsim_ai/). Exporters work the other way: SBML and odin are written from the built model (each disease’s graph and engine, in its compartmental form), and each export lists what it left out or changed (ss.errors.LossyExport), one line per declaration. A network, a module written as code, and a function are always listed as left out. ss.converters.to_hub() writes the runs of a MultiSim as a forecast-hub submission.
The code is in starsim/converters/: core.py holds Source, write(), and build(), there is one file per framework, and export.py has the exporters. The files for epydemix, MEmilio, and summer2 also run as scripts in those frameworks’ own environments (needing neither Starsim nor Sciris), where they write the model as JSON for the importer to read; EpiModel’s equivalent is an R script (dump_epimodel.R). Each importer is tested against its framework’s own examples (tests/devtests/io/) and in a scaled-down demo per framework (tests/switching/ in the lingua_franca_design repo). For the modeler’s view, see Import and export and the conversion pages for each framework.

title: Model declaration
text:
The vocabulary
A language nobody can hold in their head is one nobody uses correctly, so the design record lists every public name in one place (17-vocabulary.md), and a name is added only after asking: does Starsim already have one; can it be written with what exists (a bednet is an ss.modify, a metapopulation a stratification by patch); would more than one kind of model use it; is a keyword enough?
The capitalization rule is Starsim’s existing one: modules, containers, and base classes are CamelCase (ss.Sim, ss.Disease, ss.Vaccine); the pieces you put inside them are lowercase (ss.days, ss.normal, ss.modify, ss.vaccinate). The importers are held to the same vocabulary: they write only names that a person would write by hand, which is why every import is ordinary Starsim code.

title: Model declaration
text:
Limits

Code is opaque. A function given as a rate (rate=my_fn) isn’t analyzed in advance; if it needs something only agents have, a compartmental run stops and says what it asked for.
A disease written as code is not data. A disease with its own define_states() of arrays and its own step() runs in the same loop, but describe() shows only its class, arrays, and parameters. A class can mix the two: declared transitions, plus code in step() after super().step(). See Modules.
Some things need agents. A distribution across people or an individual-level network has no compartmental form, so solver='auto' runs the model as agents and says why. See Solvers and backends.
Exports carry less than the code. Only the compartmental form of the declared diseases goes into odin or SBML.

title: Deployment
text:
🧠40% 🤖60%
A study with thousands of runs, or a model that others use through a web page, needs more than a laptop and a notebook. Starsim is plain Python, so it runs anywhere Python does: on one large computer, on a cluster, or behind a dashboard. This page covers moving an analysis from a notebook into a script, and then each of these. Making many sims and comparing them is in Scenarios; this page is about where they run.

title: Deployment
section: From a notebook to a script
text:
From a notebook to a script
An analysis that will be run again (by you next month, by a colleague, or on another computer) is best kept as a script rather than a notebook: inputs explicit, the model made by a function, and the results saved with what is needed to make them again. A script that runs sims in parallel puts the work under if __name__ == '__main__':, so that the worker processes, which import the script, don’t start the analysis again (this is required on Windows and macOS):
# measles_campaign.py
import sciris as sc
import starsim as ss

def make_sim(coverage=0.5, seed=1):
    """ The measles model, with a campaign on day 30 """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    beta = ss.par(1.9)
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=5))
    campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, coverage=coverage, at=ss.days(30))
    return ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180),
                  solver='binomial', rand_seed=seed, label=f'Coverage {coverage}', verbose=0)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sims = [make_sim(coverage) for coverage in [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75]]
    msim = ss.parallel(sims, n_runs=100)
    msim.to_df(quantiles=[0.025, 0.5, 0.975]).to_csv('measles_campaign.csv', index=False)  # The results, as quantiles over the runs
    sc.savejson('measles_campaign_info.json', dict(            # What is needed to make them again
        starsim = ss.__version__,
        git = sc.gitinfo(__file__),
        date = sc.getdate(),
    ))
Keep the computation and the presentation apart: a script (or a cluster job) saves tables, and a notebook makes the figures from them, so a figure can be changed without running everything again. Record the version of Starsim and of your own code (sc.gitinfo() gives the commit), the data, the seeds, and the parameter values; a saved table with these is reproducible long after a saved sim (a pickle, which needs the same versions of the code to load) has stopped loading. Check one run and one small batch before a large one.

title: Deployment
text:
On one large computer
The simplest way to run more is a larger computer, such as a cloud virtual machine with many cores. ss.parallel() already runs sims on all the cores of the computer it is on, so a script that uses it needs no changes. Here, the measles model is run for ten values of β, ten times each:

import numpy as np
import sciris as sc
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=5)) # 90% immune, 5 infectious

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), solver='binomial', verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(beta=np.linspace(1.5, 2.3, 10)), n_runs=10)
msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']

n_cpus= limits the number of cores used (for a shared computer), and parallel=False runs the sims one after another, which is useful for debugging, since an error then comes with its full traceback.
When the sims differ in more than parameter values, make them in a loop, or with a function (see Running sims), and give the list to ss.parallel(). If making each sim is itself slow (reading large data files, or building a large population), make them in parallel too, with sc.parallelize() from Sciris:

def make_sim(seed, coverage):
    campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, coverage=coverage, at=ss.days(30))
    return ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), solver='binomial', rand_seed=seed, label='Campaign', verbose=0)

sims = sc.parallelize(make_sim, iterarg=range(8), coverage=0.5) # One sim for each seed, 0 to 7
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')








Making sims in parallel copies each one back to the main process, which takes time for a large sim; sc.parallelize(..., serial=True) makes them one after another, to check whether parallel is faster. Since the eight sims have the same label, they are runs of one scenario, and the plot shows their median and spread; sims with different labels are scenarios of their own (and so is each sim with no label).






Tip



A remote computer can be used through SSH and a terminal, or from an editor on your own computer: VS Code (and editors based on it, such as Positron), PyCharm, and Spyder all connect to a remote Python. A Jupyter server on the remote computer (such as The Littlest JupyterHub) works too.



Threads for linear algebra
NumPy and SciPy do their linear algebra with a library called BLAS, which can use many threads. Starsim sets it to one thread when it is imported: on the machines we tested, more threads didn’t make Starsim faster, and they slow down starting up and starting workers. More threads can speed up large matrix calculations of your own, so you can change this:
ss.options.num_threads = 4 # For the rest of the session; use 0 to leave BLAS as it is

with ss.options.context(num_threads=4): # Or just for this block
    results = my_matrix_calculation()
Or set it from the shell, with STARSIM_NUM_THREADS=4 python my_script.py. This is separate from ss.options.threads, which sets the threads for Starsim’s own loops over agents.
On Linux, this works at any time. On Windows and macOS, it can’t change BLAS once NumPy has been imported, though workers of ss.parallel() still get it. This rarely matters, but if it does, import Starsim before NumPy, or set OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS (VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS on a Mac) before starting Python.

title: Deployment
text:
On a cluster with Dask
For more runs than one computer can manage, tools such as Dask spread them across many computers. Each task makes and runs a sim and returns it; sim.shrink() first removes the people, so that only the results are sent back. ss.MultiSim() then collects sims that have already run, without running them again. (This and the next example are not run on this page.)
import dask
import dask.distributed as dd
import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

def run_sim(seed, beta):
    """ Make and run one sim, and return it without its people """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=5))
    sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), solver='binomial', rand_seed=seed, label=f'beta={beta}', verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    sim.shrink()
    return sim

if __name__ == '__main__':
    client = dd.Client(n_workers=4)
    tasks = [dask.delayed(run_sim)(seed, beta) for seed in range(10) for beta in [1.5, 1.9, 2.3]]
    sims = list(dask.compute(*tasks))
    msim = ss.MultiSim(sims) # Collects the results of sims that have run
    msim.plot()
Coiled, a paid service built on Dask, runs the same tasks on a cluster in the cloud that grows and shrinks with the work:
import coiled

cluster = coiled.Cluster(n_workers=50, workspace='<your_coiled_workspace>')
client = cluster.get_client()
futures = [client.submit(run_sim, seed, 1.9) for seed in range(1000)]
sims = client.gather(futures)
msim = ss.MultiSim(sims)
msim.plot()
Dask’s workers set MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_ so that freed memory goes back to the system at once, which slows sims down by making them fault in new pages. On Linux with glibc, importing Starsim overrides this, so nothing needs to be set; a task that needs that memory back during a long job can call ss.solvers.backends.release_memory().
The same pattern (a function that makes, runs, and shrinks one sim, given a seed and the values that differ) works with other tools, such as Joblib.

title: Deployment
section: On a cluster with a job scheduler
text:
On a cluster with a job scheduler
On a high-performance cluster run by a scheduler such as Slurm, the usual pattern is a job array: the same script is run many times, each with its own task number, which picks the seed and the scenario. Each job saves its sim (shrunk) or, better, a table of the results it needs, and a final script collects them:
# run_one.py: run as one task of a job array, e.g. with sbatch --array=0-399
import os
import starsim as ss
from measles_campaign import make_sim

task = int(os.environ['SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID'])
coverages = [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75]
coverage, seed = coverages[task % 4], task // 4 + 1  # 100 seeds of each of 4 scenarios
sim = make_sim(coverage=coverage, seed=seed)
sim.run()
sim.save(f'results/sim_{task}.sim')  # Shrunk by default, since it has finished
# collect.py: once every task has finished
import glob
import starsim as ss

sims = [ss.load(filename) for filename in sorted(glob.glob('results/sim_*.sim'))]
msim = ss.MultiSim(sims)  # Collects sims that have already run; sims with the same label are runs of one scenario
msim.summarize()
Three things matter more on a cluster than on a laptop:

One level of parallelism. When the scheduler already runs many tasks at once, don’t have each task start a pool of its own: use ss.parallel(..., parallel=False) within a task, or limit it with n_cpus=. Within one sim, Starsim uses several threads only for passes over very large populations (200,000 agents or more), and never in the workers of ss.parallel(); ss.options.threads = 1 (or the environment variable STARSIM_THREADS=1) turns them off. NumPy’s linear algebra (OpenBLAS or MKL) has threads of its own, which the workers of ss.parallel() divide among themselves; to keep them to one, set SCIRIS_NUM_THREADS=1 in the task’s environment (e.g. in the job script), or call sc.limit_threads(1). None of these limits the Numba threads that Starsim’s passes use; STARSIM_THREADS=1 does.
Compile once, before the runs. Starsim’s compiled code (see Solvers and backends) is compiled on first use and kept on disk. Run starsim compile (or ss.compile()) once after installing, in the shared environment or when building a container image, so that hundreds of tasks don’t each compile it, or wait for each other to.
The same code everywhere. Install the same versions of Starsim and of your own modules on every node (a container image, or a shared environment), since a saved sim needs them to load.

title: Deployment
text:
Interactive dashboards
A model can be put behind a web page, so that others can change its inputs and see the results. There are several tools for this, including Shiny for Python, Voilà, and Panel; one of the simplest is Streamlit. This one has sliders for the share of the town that is immune and the coverage of a vaccination campaign:
import streamlit as st
import starsim as ss

def run_sim(immune, coverage):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=immune), init_n=dict(I=5))
    campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, coverage=coverage, at=ss.days(30))
    sim = ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    return sim

st.title('Measles in a town of 20,000')
immune = st.slider('Share immune at the start', 0.5, 0.99, 0.9)
coverage = st.slider('Coverage of the campaign on day 30', 0.0, 1.0, 0.5)

sim = run_sim(immune, coverage)
st.write('Infections:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))
st.pyplot(sim.diseases.measles.plot())
Saved as app.py, it runs (after pip install streamlit) with streamlit run app.py, which opens the dashboard in a browser. As an ODE, each run takes a fraction of a second, so the page updates as the sliders move.

title: Deployment
text:
Pitfalls

Sending whole sims between computers. A sim with its people can be large; shrink it before returning it (sim.shrink()), as ss.parallel() does by itself.
The same seed in every task. Give each run its own rand_seed, or every run of a stochastic model is the same.
Workers that compete for cores. A pool of processes in each of many tasks on one node runs slower than one; use one level of parallelism.
Code that isn’t on the workers. A module written as code must be importable on every computer that runs it, since sims are sent between them as Python objects (pickles), which need the same code to be read.

title: epydemix
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
This page is for people who use epydemix in Python: age-structured compartmental models written transition by transition, populations and contact matrices loaded by place name, interventions on one contact setting, fits by ABC with no likelihood, and projections from the posterior for scenario hubs. It shows an epydemix model next to the same model in Starsim, how their results agree, how long each takes, and what works and what does not yet, including what fails.

title: epydemix
text:
The same model in both
epydemix’s tutorial on population data: an SIR in Kenya’s population, with contact matrices between five age groups, run 100 times:

from epydemix.population import load_epydemix_population
from epydemix import load_predefined_model
from epydemix.visualization import plot_quantiles

population = load_epydemix_population("Kenya")
model = load_predefined_model("SIR", transmission_rate=0.04)
model.set_population(population)

results = model.run_simulations(start_date="2019-12-01",
                                end_date="2020-04-01",
                                percentage_in_agents=10 / model.population.Nk.sum(),
                                Nsim=100)

df_quantiles_comps = results.get_quantiles_compartments()
ax = plot_quantiles(df_quantiles_comps, columns=["Infected_total", "Susceptible_total", "Recovered_total"], legend_loc="center right")

In Starsim, ss.contacts('Kenya') and ss.people('Kenya') are bundled (Prem 2021 contact matrices and UN population estimates), so nothing is downloaded. solver='binomial' runs the model as a chain binomial, as epydemix does, and use_aging=False keeps people in their age group for the four months:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.04 * I),
    recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, rate=0.1),
    init_n    = dict(I=10),
)
sir.stratify(age=[0, 5, 20, 50, 65])
sim = ss.Sim(sir, networks=ss.contacts('Kenya'), people=ss.people('Kenya', year=2020), start='2019-12-01', stop='2020-04-02',
             solver='binomial', use_aging=False, verbose=0)
msim = sim.run(n_runs=100)

res = msim.results.sir
S, I, R = res.S.mean(), res.I.mean(), res.R.mean() # The mean of the 100 runs, at each time
N = S[0] + I[0] + R[0]
print('Peak:', round(100*I.max()/N, 2), 'percent infected, on day', I.values.argmax(), '(epydemix: 54.46 percent, on day 40)')
print('Final size:', round(100*R[-1]/N, 2), 'percent (epydemix: 99.63 percent)')
msim.plot()

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/
Peak: 53.95 percent infected, on day 36 (epydemix: 54.46 percent, on day 40)
Final size: 99.6 percent (epydemix: 99.63 percent)









msim.results.sir.I.select(age='0-4').quantiles() gives the quantiles over runs for one age group, as get_quantiles_compartments() does.

title: epydemix
text:
How the results agree



Model
Agreement




The Kenya tutorial (above)
Agree: the mean of 100 runs peaks at 54.5% to 54.7% of the population on day 39 (in different sets of runs), against epydemix’s 54.46% on day 40, and the final size is 99.6% against 99.63%. Starsim’s population is the UN’s (52.2 million in 2020) and epydemix’s is 55.9 million; with epydemix’s population, the peak is 54.32%. Imported with ss.import_from() from epydemix’s own script, the peak is 54.41% on day 40


The COVID tutorial (SEIR with an Erlang delay to death, mobility, seasonality, three reopening scenarios)
Agree at fixed values: weekly deaths within 0.9% of the peak, and 10,534 deaths by 2 August against 10,525 (means of 200 runs). This needs substeps=1, so that the chain binomial takes whole days as epydemix does; without it, the Erlang delay makes Starsim substep the model, and there are 6,039 deaths. The fitted values are each inside the original’s 90% range, but the comparison was of a point estimate against a posterior

text:
What works and what does not yet
These are from Starsim’s switching demo for epydemix users (tests/switching/test_epydemix.py in the lingua_franca_design repo), which checks each task against epydemix’s numbers, and from the review it was built from. “Fails” means the demo’s check does not pass today.







Task
Today




The Kenya tutorial from Starsim’s bundled data
Works: peak, its day, and the final size as above


A vaccine by age, written on the disease’s age groups (where=sir.age < 5)
Works: 6.9 million under-5s are vaccinated, the number in Kenya in 2020


Closing one contact setting from a date (schools)
Works: ss.contacts('Kenya', layer=['home', 'school', 'work', 'community']) gives a layer for each setting, and ss.modify(school, multiply=0, start='2020-03-15') closes one


Vaccination, testing, and treatment without copying compartments
Works: a product and a delivery (ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, where=...)), with the disease unchanged


A particle filter on a model whose transmission is a fitted value times a season times a mobility series
Works: the log-likelihood peaks at the true value


A posterior with no likelihood (ABC-SMC, with wmape as the distance), then projections from it under scenarios, as quantile tables
Works: sim.fit(method='abc-smc'), fit.project(scenarios, n=), and .to_df(quantiles=), below


A posterior with a likelihood
Works: particle MCMC for a stochastic model, NUTS for an ODE, with R-hat and ESS


Populations and contact matrices for US states (load_epydemix_population("United_States__Massachusetts"))
Fails until starsim_data publishes them: ss.people('United States:Massachusetts') (US Census, 2023) and ss.contacts('United States:Massachusetts', layer='school') (Mistry et al. 2021) read the 50 states and DC, but the files cannot be downloaded yet


Other solvers: the same model as an ODE, by Gillespie’s method, or as agents
Works: solver='ode', 'gillespie', or 'abm'



A posterior with no likelihood, then projections from it. Here the model is an SIR in a million people whose transmission is a fitted value b times a season times a mobility series, fitted to weekly infections drawn from a run at b = 0.5:

mobility = ss.timeseries({'2020-02-23': 1.0, '2020-05-31': 0.3}, mode='linear') # Falls steadily from 1 to 0.3
season = ss.seasonal(mean=0.9, amplitude=0.1/0.9, peak=ss.days(14))

def make_sim(b, data=None, rand_seed=1):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    sir = ss.Disease(infection=ss.Transition(S, I, rate=b*season*mobility * I), recovery=ss.Transition(I, R, rate=ss.perday(0.25)), init_n=dict(I=100), name='sir')
    return ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=1e6, unit='day', start='2020-02-23', stop='2020-05-31', solver='binomial', data=data, rand_seed=rand_seed, verbose=0)

# The data: weekly new infections from one run at b = 0.5, with a seed of its own; the run is already stochastic, so its counts are used as they are
truth = make_sim(ss.par(0.5), rand_seed=2).run()
data = truth.to_data('infection', resample='week', noise=None) # Compared with the result infection

sim = make_sim(ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.1, 1]), data=data)
fit = sim.fit(method='abc-smc', particles=50, generations=3, rand_seed=1, verbose=0)
fit.table # The posterior median of b and its 95% interval (lower, upper); the true value is 0.5

title: epydemix
text:
Bringing your model in
ss.import_from(source, format='epydemix') reads an epydemix model: either a live EpiModel (if epydemix is installed alongside Starsim) or the JSON written by starsim/converters/epydemix.py run as a script, which runs your script in epydemix’s own environment. Each compartment becomes a state, each mediated transition exposure through the population’s contact matrices (summed over the settings, as epydemix does), each spontaneous transition a rate per day, and the population’s age groups a stratification. The sim runs as a chain binomial in daily steps (solver='binomial', substeps=1), as epydemix does. On the Kenya tutorial, dumping takes about 4 s (it downloads the population), and the import and 100 runs take 0.26 s, with the same results as epydemix; the import is Starsim code you can keep (sim.imported.code).
See Import/export for importing in general: checking an import, keeping it as code, and finishing one that is incomplete.

title: Import/export
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
A model written for another framework can be read into Starsim, and a Starsim model can be written out in formats other tools read. Importing is useful for checking a model against its original, for running it in ways the original can’t (as agents, say, or fitted with gradients), or for building on it in Starsim: adding age groups, interventions, or a fit to data. This page covers how importing works, how to check an import and finish one that is incomplete, the formats, and the exports. The pages for each framework (Starsim v3, odin, EpiModel, and the others in this section) show a model from that framework written both ways, and how closely the results agree; Modeling landscape compares the frameworks.

title: Import/export
text:
Importing a model
ss.import_from() reads a model file into a sim. Here is a measles model written in odin, a language for compartmental models in R: the measles model of the tutorials, with a latent period of 10 days (a rate sigma of 0.1 per day) and an infectious period of 8 days (gamma = 0.125 per day), in a town of 100,000, 90% of whom are immune. The file is written to a temporary folder first:

import os
import tempfile
import numpy as np
import sciris as sc
import starsim as ss

odin_code = '''
deriv(S) <- -beta * S * I / N
deriv(E) <- beta * S * I / N - sigma * E
deriv(I) <- sigma * E - gamma * I
deriv(R) <- gamma * I

initial(S) <- N - I_init - R_init
initial(E) <- 0
initial(I) <- I_init
initial(R) <- R_init

N <- user(100000)    # Population size
I_init <- user(10)   # Number infectious at the start
R_init <- user(90000) # Number immune at the start
beta <- user(1.9)    # Transmission rate, per day
sigma <- user(0.1)   # 1 / latent period (10 days)
gamma <- user(0.125) # 1 / infectious period (8 days)
'''
folder = tempfile.mkdtemp()
filename = os.path.join(folder, 'measles.R')
sc.savetext(filename, odin_code)

sim = ss.import_from(filename, start='2025-01-01', stop=365)

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/
Imported "measles" from odin: 4 states, 3 transitions, 4 parameters
  S -> E           beta * S * I / N : S taken out of the flow; N taken as the total [guessed: N = 100000, the number of people at the start]; exposure to I (divided by the total: frequency-dependent) => beta * I
  E -> I           sigma * E : E taken out of the flow; spontaneous => sigma
  I -> R           gamma * I : I taken out of the flow; spontaneous => gamma


Each deriv() is the rate of change of a compartment, written as the total flows in and out: β S I / N people a day are infected, σ E become infectious, and γ I recover. This is the form of most textbooks and frameworks. The format is told from the file (or given with format='odin'). odin has no time unit, so its numbers are taken to be per day (unit= says otherwise), and odin is told when to stop when it is run, so the sim needs stop=, here 365 days; start= gives it dates, which a forecast hub needs (below). Other arguments change the model as it is read: pars=dict(beta=1.5) gives a parameter another value, and dt= a step.
The importer prints how it read each rate, which is the first thing to check. A Starsim transition is a rate per person (each susceptible person is infected at a rate of β times the share infectious), so each importer turns each total flow into a rate for each person who leaves the state, by dividing by that state, and then classifies what is left:



A flow written as
Is read as




gamma * I
A rate gamma per person in I, whatever anyone else is doing


beta * S * I / N
Frequency-dependent transmission: beta * I, exposure to the share infectious


beta * S * I
Density-dependent transmission: beta * I.n, exposure to the number infectious


Anything else
The expression itself, as a rate of counts, which is exact under every solver

text:
Checking an import
The imported model is an ordinary Starsim sim, and runs like any other:

sim.run()
sim.plot()

  Done in 0.0033 s; measles: 5,856 infections; at most 298 infectious, on 2025-08-05









sim.describe() shows the model as Starsim built it, with each guess marked, as for a model written by hand:

Here the importer guessed the names of the transitions (from their states, such as S_to_E, since odin doesn’t name flows), and the total population N (from the people at the start). The solver is the one odin uses for this model, an ODE, so that the results can be checked against odin’s.
Two models are the same if they give the same results. Here is the import against the same model written in Starsim, as in the tutorials (see T3 – Building a disease), where the rates are written as the durations they stand for:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10, R=90_000), name='measles')
mine = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop=ss.days(365))
mine.run()

theirs = sim.results[sim.diseases[0].name]
print('Largest difference in I:', abs(theirs.I.values - mine.results.measles.I.values).max())

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0033 s; measles: 5,856 infections; at most 298 infectious, on 2025-08-05
Largest difference in I: 0.0


The two differ only in how they are written: the import names its transitions by the states they join, and has a rate of 0.1 a day where the other has an average of 10 days, which is the same exponential distribution. Both run as an ODE, and the numbers agree, so these are the same model. Where two models differ, the describe() of each, side by side, shows how. For an import from a framework that is installed alongside Starsim, the best check is against the original framework’s own results; each conversion page does this for one or two models.
Since the import is an ordinary model, it can then be run in any of the ways Starsim can run a model. sim.new() makes a new sim from the same inputs, with whatever is given changed. Here it is run as agents, which odin can’t do (the solver is given as well as the number of agents, since the import asked for an ODE, to match odin):

agents = sim.new(solver='abm', n_agents=100_000) # One agent per person
agents.run()

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig = plt.figure()
plt.plot(sim.t.datevec, theirs.I, label='ODE (as in odin)')
plt.plot(agents.t.datevec, agents.results[agents.diseases[0].name].I, label='Agents')
plt.ylabel('Number infectious')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Sim: measles, as 100,000 agents, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and S_to_E transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.63 s; measles: 6,030 infections; at most 339 infectious, on 2025-08-10









The agents follow the ODE, as they should in a town of this size, with some noise from chance: with only 10 people infectious at the start, and only 10% of the town susceptible, chance moves the timing of the peak a little from run to run, and whole steps of a day make the peak a little higher (as the note printed by the run says). See Solvers and backends for the solvers.

title: Import/export
text:
Keeping an imported model
An import gives Starsim code: the importer writes the model as Python, and the sim is that code run. The code is kept as sim.imported.code, to be kept, read, and changed like a model written by hand. It says where the model came from and how each rate was read, and ends with anything that wasn’t translated:

print(sim.imported.code)

# Imported from odin (measles.R) by ss.import_from()
#
# How each rate was read:
#   S -> E           beta * S * I / N : S taken out of the flow; N taken as the total [guessed: N = 100000, the number of people at the start]; exposure to I (divided by the total: frequency-dependent) => beta * I
#   E -> I           sigma * E : E taken out of the flow; spontaneous => sigma
#   I -> R           gamma * I : I taken out of the flow; spontaneous => gamma

import starsim as ss

# Parameters
N = ss.par(100000.0)
beta = ss.par(1.9)
gamma = ss.par(0.125)
sigma = ss.par(0.1)

# States
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')

# Transitions and outcomes
S_to_E = S >> E @ (beta * I)
E_to_I = E >> I @ sigma
I_to_R = I >> R @ gamma

measles = ss.Disease(
    S, E, I, R, S_to_E, E_to_I, I_to_R,
    init_n = dict(S=9990, I=10, R=90000),
    first = 'S',
    name = 'measles',
)

sim = ss.Sim(diseases=[measles], solver='ode', unit='day', stop=ss.days(365), start='2025-01-01', total_pop=100000.0)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sim.run()
    sim.plot()



The code is yours, a starting point to edit: a transition can be given a better name (infection rather than S_to_E), a rate can be written as the duration it stands for, and anything Starsim has that the original doesn’t (age groups, interventions, a fit to data) can be added. sc.savetext('measles.py', sim.imported.code) writes it to a file, and ss.converters.convert(filename) imports a model and saves its code in one step (beside the original, with the extension .py, unless filename= is given). Reading some formats takes a while (a large workbook, or a script that has to be run in R first), and the saved code then runs in a fraction of the time. From then on, the file is the model: to compare it with another version, compare their results or their describe(), or the two files in a text editor.

title: Import/export
text:
Finishing an incomplete import
Each framework has features that have no direct counterpart in Starsim, such as code written in the original language, or a formula the importer can’t read. An importer translates what it can, and lists the rest by name rather than guessing: the sim runs without the parts it couldn’t translate, and lists them in a warning (ss.errors.ImportIncomplete) and in sim.imported.incomplete. The import above was complete:

print('Format:', sim.imported.format)
print('Not translated:', sim.imported.incomplete)

Format: odin
Not translated: []


Here is the measles model over 20 years instead, with births, deaths, and seasonal transmission:

seasonal_code = '''
deriv(S) <- mu * N - beta * S * I / N - mu * S
deriv(E) <- beta * S * I / N - sigma * E - mu * E
deriv(I) <- sigma * E - gamma * I - mu * I
deriv(R) <- gamma * I - mu * R

N <- S + E + I + R
beta <- beta0 * (1 + amp * cos(2 * 3.141593 * t / 365)) # Highest at the start of each year

initial(S) <- 7000
initial(E) <- 30
initial(I) <- 30
initial(R) <- 92940

beta0 <- user(1.9)   # Mean transmission rate, per day
amp <- user(0.2)     # Size of the seasonal cycle, relative to the mean
sigma <- user(0.1)   # 1 / latent period (10 days)
gamma <- user(0.125) # 1 / infectious period (8 days)
mu <- user(0.00008)  # Birth and death rate, per day (about 3% a year)
'''
seasonal_file = os.path.join(folder, 'measles_seasonal.R')
sc.savetext(seasonal_file, seasonal_code)

seasonal = ss.import_from(seasonal_file, stop=20*365, dt=7) # A step of a week is plenty over 20 years
seasonal.imported.incomplete

Imported "measles_seasonal" from odin: 4 states, 8 transitions, 5 parameters
  -> S             mu * N : an inflow, from counts => mu * (S.n + E.n + I.n + R.n)
  S ->             mu * S : S taken out of the flow; an outflow => mu
  E -> I           sigma * E : E taken out of the flow; spontaneous => sigma
  E ->             mu * E : E taken out of the flow; an outflow => mu
  I -> R           gamma * I : I taken out of the flow; spontaneous => gamma
  I ->             mu * I : I taken out of the flow; an outflow => mu
  R ->             mu * R : R taken out of the flow; an outflow => mu


/home/cliffk/idm/ssv4/starsim/converters/core.py:862: ImportIncomplete:


2 part(s) of the model were not translated:
  time: an equation uses the time (t, time, or step); a value that changes in time could be an ss.timeseries
  S -> E: the rate "beta * S * I / N" could not be translated ("t" is not a state or parameter of the model)
The sim runs without them. To finish the import, ask an AI assistant with the import-model skill loaded (printed by `starsim ai show import-model`, or starsim_ai/import-model in the Starsim repo; see "Finishing an incomplete import"): "Finish importing measles_seasonal.R (odin) into Starsim: save its code, sim.imported.code, to a file, translate each part listed in sim.imported.incomplete (the code's "Not translated" comments), and check the result against the original with the validate-import skill."



[('time',
  'an equation uses the time (t, time, or step); a value that changes in time could be an ss.timeseries'),
 ('S -> E',
  'the rate "beta * S * I / N" could not be translated ("t" is not a state or parameter of the model)')]


β now depends on the time, t, in a formula the importer doesn’t translate. So the transmission, which uses β, isn’t translated either, and both are listed. The births, deaths, latent period, and recovery are translated. Without the transmission, this sim would run, but with no epidemic, so it has to be finished first. The code of the import lists what wasn’t translated at the end, as comments, and the missing parts can be added to it by hand. A seasonal cycle like this one is ss.seasonal() (see Parameters): a mean, an amplitude, and the time of year of the peak, here the start of the year (peak=0). Births and deaths into and out of every state are shorter written as ss.birth() and ss.death() in demographics= (see Demographics), which is the same model:

beta = ss.seasonal(mean=ss.perday(1.9), amplitude=0.2, peak=0) # Added: β, highest at the start of the year

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ beta*I # Added: the transmission
progression = E >> I @ ss.perday(0.1)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.perday(0.125)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init_n=dict(S=7000, E=30, I=30, R=92940), name='measles')

demographics = [ss.birth(rate=ss.perday(8e-05)), ss.death(rate=ss.perday(8e-05))]
finished = ss.Sim(measles, demographics=demographics, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(20*365), dt=ss.days(7))
finished.run()
finished.plot('measles.I')

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 7294 (the last whole step before 7300)
  measles: R0 = 18.2 (R = 1.29 at the start, with 7% susceptible), with 30 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0052 s; measles: 55,071 infections; at most 263 infectious, on day 1176









This gives the two-year cycle of measles epidemics, as births replenish the susceptible people. Checking it against the original model, run in odin, would be the last step.
For a longer model, with more that isn’t translated, sim.imported.prompt is a prompt for an AI assistant with Starsim’s import-model skill (installed with starsim ai install), which can finish the job in the same way: write the code, translate what is listed, and check the result against the original.

title: Import/export
text:
The formats
ss.import_from() reads these formats, and tells which one a file is from by its contents (or give format=); ss.converters.importers lists them:



Framework
Reads
Notes




Atomica
A framework and databook (.xlsx), and a program book
Programs become parameters of spending, for ss.fit.optimize()


camdl
A .camdl file (compiled with camdlc), or its JSON form
Parameters keep their bounds and priors; observations become outcomes with their likelihoods


EMULSION
A model file (.yaml)
Each state machine becomes a disease


EpiModel
An R script, run first in R by dump_epimodel.R
A fitted network becomes ss.DegreeNet


epipack
A live model, or the JSON written by epipack.py
Each reaction process becomes a flow; a network is read at its mean degree


epydemix
A live model, or the JSON written by epydemix.py
Runs as a chain binomial in daily steps, as epydemix does


epymorph
The JSON written by epymorph.py
Nodes become places; movement clauses are run and averaged into commuting


flepiMoP
A configuration file (.yml), with the files it names
Places become a stratification with commuting between them


MEmilio
The JSON written by memilio.py
Contact matrices with their changes over time; a graph of places


odin
An R file in odin’s language (read without R)
odin 1 and odin2 syntax; arrays become stratifications


SBML
An SBML file (.xml)
Species become states, reactions transitions


SimInf
An R file (read without R), with its initial state and events
Nodes become places; events a movement register


summer2
A live model, or the JSON written by summer2.py
Each stratification, with its mixing matrix



For epipack, epydemix, epymorph, MEmilio, and summer2, Starsim’s importer for that framework (e.g. starsim/converters/memilio.py) also runs as a script in the framework’s own environment, needing neither Starsim nor Sciris there, and writes what it built as JSON for Starsim to read; for EpiModel, starsim/converters/dump_epimodel.R does the same in R. The others are read directly. Each importer is tested against its framework’s own examples. A Starsim 3 script is not imported, but rewritten: see Starsim v3.

title: Import/export
text:
How an import is built
Every importer reads its format into the same intermediate object, ss.converters.Source: its states, parameters, flows as rate expressions, stratifications, outcomes, and what it couldn’t translate. One function, ss.converters.write(), writes a Source as Starsim code (a declared ss.Disease, with its parameters, states, and transitions as variables, ending with sim = ss.Sim(...)), by the same rules for every format, and ss.converters.build() runs that code to make the sim. So there is one path, from another framework’s model to code to a sim; each framework needs only a reader. A value that can’t be written as a simple value, such as a network, is given by the importer as ss.converters.Code('...'), the Python that makes it.






flowchart LR
  F["odin, SBML, EMULSION, SimInf,<br>flepiMoP, summer2, Atomica, camdl,<br>EpiModel, epipack, epydemix,<br>epymorph, MEmilio"] --> R[reader] --> S["ss.converters.Source"] --> W["ss.converters.write()"] --> C["Starsim code"] --> Sim[sim]
  Sim --> E["SBML, odin"]






A Source can also be filled in by hand, to bring in a model from a framework that has no importer (here, an SIR from a spreadsheet or a paper):

src = ss.converters.Source('sir', format='by hand')
for name, n in dict(S=990, I=10, R=0).items():
    src.add_state(name, init=n)
src.add_par('beta', 0.3)
src.add_par('gamma', 0.1)
src.add_flow('S', 'I', rate='beta * S * I / (S + I + R)', per='total', name='infection')
src.add_flow('I', 'R', rate='gamma * I', per='total', name='recovery')
sir = ss.converters.build(src, stop=100)
print(sir.imported.code)

Imported "sir" from by hand: 3 states, 2 transitions, 2 parameters
  S -> I           beta * S * I / (S + I + R) : S taken out of the flow; exposure to I (divided by the total: frequency-dependent) => beta * I
  I -> R           gamma * I : I taken out of the flow; spontaneous => gamma
# Imported from by hand (an object) by ss.import_from()
#
# How each rate was read:
#   S -> I           beta * S * I / (S + I + R) : S taken out of the flow; exposure to I (divided by the total: frequency-dependent) => beta * I
#   I -> R           gamma * I : I taken out of the flow; spontaneous => gamma

import starsim as ss

# Parameters
beta = ss.par(0.3)
gamma = ss.par(0.1)

# States
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')

# Transitions and outcomes
infection = S >> I @ (beta * I)
recovery = I >> R @ gamma

sir = ss.Disease(
    S, I, R, infection, recovery,
    init_n = dict(S=990, I=10),
    first = 'S',
    name = 'sir',
)

sim = ss.Sim(diseases=[sir], stop=100, total_pop=1000)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sim.run()
    sim.plot()



ss.converters.write(src) gives the code without running it. How the importers and exporters are built is described in Architecture.

title: Import/export
text:
Exporting a model
A Starsim model is written as Python, and that code is the model: it is what is kept, shared, and compared. There are other ways to write a model, or its results, out:



What
How
Holds
Read back?




The code
the script itself; for an import, sim.imported.code
the model, as Python
yes, by running it


Results as JSON
sim.to_json()
parameters, summary, and results, for use elsewhere
no


A saved sim
ss.save('run.sim', sim)
the sim itself (a pickle), including partway through a run
yes, with ss.load()


Another framework’s format
ss.export_to(sim, 'odin')
the compartmental form of the declared diseases
yes, with ss.import_from()



ss.export_to() writes a model in SBML (for tools such as COPASI) or odin. Each is written from the model’s compartmental form:

print(ss.export_to(sim, 'odin'))

## measles, exported from Starsim 4.0.0; time is in days

deriv(S) <- -S_to_E
deriv(E) <- S_to_E - E_to_I
deriv(I) <- E_to_I - I_to_R
deriv(R) <- I_to_R

initial(S) <- 9990
initial(E) <- 0
initial(I) <- 10
initial(R) <- 90000

S_to_E <- beta * S * I / N
E_to_I <- sigma * E
I_to_R <- gamma * I
N <- S + E + I + R

beta <- user(1.9)
sigma <- user(0.1)
gamma <- user(0.125)



/home/cliffk/idm/ssv4/starsim/converters/export.py:487: LossyExport:


exported to odin: 4 states, 3 transitions, as 4 compartments and 3 flows (time in days)
  not exported: result "prevalence"



filename= writes it to a file too. A format that can’t carry part of the model (such as a network, a module written as code, or a function) leaves it out, and the export lists what it left out or changed in a warning (ss.errors.LossyExport), one line for each. An exported model can be read back in:

sbml_file = os.path.join(folder, 'measles.xml')
ss.export_to(sim, 'sbml', filename=sbml_file)
again = ss.import_from(sbml_file, start='2025-01-01', stop=365, verbose=False)
again.run()
print('Infections, imported from odin:', round(sim.results.measles.S_to_E.values.sum()))
print('Infections, after a round trip through SBML:', round(again.results.measles.S_to_E.values.sum()))

title: NumPy
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
This page is for people who write their own models as a loop in NumPy: a compartment per variable, a binomial draw per flow each step (a chain binomial), 1 - np.exp(-rate*dt) to turn a rate into a probability, an array axis for each age group or place, and a loop of runs over seeds. It shows such a model next to the same model in Starsim, how their results agree, how long each takes, and what works and what does not yet.

title: NumPy
text:
The same model in both
A stochastic SEIR in daily steps, for a million people, written as a NumPy loop:

import numpy as np

def run_numpy(seed=0, N=1_000_000, I0=10, beta=0.3, sigma=0.2, gamma=0.1, days=365):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    S, E, I, R = N - I0, 0, I0, 0
    out = np.zeros((days+1, 4))
    out[0] = S, E, I, R
    for t in range(days):
        n_SE = rng.binomial(S, 1 - np.exp(-beta*I/N))
        n_EI = rng.binomial(E, 1 - np.exp(-sigma))
        n_IR = rng.binomial(I, 1 - np.exp(-gamma))
        S, E, I, R = S - n_SE, E + n_SE - n_EI, I + n_EI - n_IR, R + n_IR
        out[t+1] = S, E, I, R
    return out

runs = np.array([run_numpy(seed) for seed in range(200)])
print('NumPy, 200 runs: mean peak of I', round(runs[:,:,2].max(axis=1).mean()), 'and mean final R', round(runs[:,-1,3].mean()))

NumPy, 200 runs: mean peak of I 205567 and mean final R 949913


In Starsim, each flow is one line, with its rate; the conversion of rates to probabilities, the bookkeeping of who leaves and enters each state, and the results are done for you. solver='binomial' runs it as a chain binomial, and substeps=1 takes each day whole, as the loop above does (by default, the chain binomial splits a step when more than about 5% of a compartment would leave in it, or fewer near the epidemic threshold):

import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states(4)
seir = ss.Disease(S >> E @ ss.perday(0.3)*I, E >> I @ ss.perday(0.2), I >> R @ ss.perday(0.1), init_n=dict(I=10))
sim = ss.Sim(seir, total_pop=1_000_000, unit='day', stop=365, solver='binomial', substeps=1, verbose=0)

msim = sim.run(n_runs=200)
msim.plot()








msim.summarize() summarizes each result over each run (a state by its final value, unless told otherwise; here I by its peak), then over the runs, with the median, a 95% interval, the mean, and the standard deviation:

summary = msim.summarize(how={'seir_I': 'max'}) # The peak of I in each run
summary.loc[['seir_I', 'seir_R']]

title: NumPy
text:
How the results agree







Model
Agreement




The SEIR above, as a chain binomial
Agree: over 200 runs each, the mean peak of I is 205,517 in Starsim against 205,568 in NumPy (0.02%), and the mean final R is 949,944 against 949,914 (within one standard error of the difference, about 30); the mean of I peaks on day 128 in both


The same model as an ODE (solver='ode')
As expected: a peak of 196,388 on day 120 and a final R of 940,480, the deterministic counterpart of the chain binomial (which has a higher peak since its steps are a day long)


The same model as 100,000 agents (solver='abm'), each standing for 10 people
Agree when the epidemic takes off: peaks of 195,780 and 194,990 and final sizes of 942,370 and 938,490 in two seeds, close to the ODE’s. The 10 initial infections are one agent, so in two of four seeds the epidemic dies out at once, as it should for one case with R0 = 3



These numbers are from runs on 22 October 2026, on a 20-core x86-64 Linux machine shared with other work.

Timings
Lines are lines of model code (not counting blank lines, comments, imports, printing, or plotting, and counting a line over 100 characters twice); times are for one run, on the same machine as above.

Pass: the north star fails a time only if Starsim is more than 2 times slower and more than 1 s slower



A NumPy loop of a few compartments is hard to beat for speed, since it does nothing but the draws. Starsim’s time goes into building the sim (checking the model, choosing the solver, making the results); the run itself is compiled code, so the difference shrinks as the model grows in states, groups, and steps, and many runs are run on all cores by sim.run(n_runs=).

title: NumPy
section: What works and what does not yet
text:
What works and what does not yet
There is no switching demo for NumPy users, since a NumPy model is whatever its author wrote. These are the tasks a NumPy loop is usually written for, and where each stands today.



Task
Today




A chain binomial, an ODE, or agents from one model
Works: solver='binomial', 'ode', 'gillespie', or 'abm', above


An array axis for age or place, with a contact matrix or mixing between places
Works: seir.stratify(age=[0, 5, 18, 65]) and ss.contacts(), or ss.geo.geography() and ss.geo.Mobility() for places; see the odin and LASER pages


Many runs over seeds, with ranges
Works: sim.run(n_runs=) runs them in parallel; msim.summarize() gives the median, an interval, and the mean of each result over the runs, and res.quantiles() the range at each time point


Fitting to data
Works: sim.fit() chooses the method from the model (by gradients for an ODE, by simulation for a stochastic model), and gives a posterior when one is asked for (method='nuts', 'pmcmc', or 'abc-smc')


Anything the loop does that is not a flow between states (a running maximum, a rule in Python)
Works: a module written as code, with a step() in Python; a value it keeps can be read by a function in a rate, which runs under any solver


Speed for a small model run once
Slower: 13 ms against 0.7 ms (above), which is under the north star’s limit but 18 times slower

title: NumPy
text:
Bringing your model in
There is no importer for NumPy code, since a loop can do anything. An AI assistant with Starsim’s import-model skill (starsim_ai/import-model/ in the Starsim repository, or starsim ai show import-model) can translate one, following the mapping above: each binomial draw is a flow (S >> E @ rate), its probability’s rate is the flow’s rate, and each array axis is a stratification.
See Import/export for importing in general: checking an import, keeping it as code, and finishing one that is incomplete.

text:
Further reading

NumPy: random generator: binomial draws, as a chain binomial uses them
