title: Running sims
text:
🧠20% 🤖80%
A sim (ss.Sim) is one model put together with everything needed to run it: the diseases, the population, the time span, how people mix, and any births and deaths, interventions, and analyzers. It runs them in the right order, and holds the results afterwards. This page covers what a sim takes, what it prints, what happens when it is built, and the ways of running it: in full, part of the way, and again with something changed. It ends with saving sims and with the make_sim() pattern that larger projects are built around. T1 – Getting started and T2 – Building a model build and run the measles model used here; running many sims and comparing them is in Scenarios.

title: Running sims
text:
The smallest sim
A sim needs a model and, usually, a population and a time span. Here is a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000 people, run for 50 days:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(1.9)                    # Transmission rate per day
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)       # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.003 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6









A run prints:

What it runs, and how: the diseases, the population, the solver (here an ODE, since nothing in the model needs individual people; see Solvers and backends), and the time span.
R0 of each disease with the number infectious at the start, as a check that the model is the one you meant: here R0 = β × the infectious period = 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15, as for measles. If some people start immune, the line gives the reproduction number at the start too, e.g. “R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible)”.
Notes, if any: something Starsim assumed, approximated, or wants you to check, such as a step that is long for the rates in the model. Notes are kept in sim.notes too.
Progress, for a run that goes a step at a time (as agents, say), rather than all at once.
A closing line: how long it took, the total number of infections, and the size and timing of the peak.

How much is printed is set by verbose, given to the sim or to sim.run(): 0 prints nothing (the usual choice inside loops and fits), 1 the lines above (the default), and 2 everything, including a line for each step. A fraction between 0 and 1 prints the progress of a long run every that share of it: verbose=0.1 every 10%.

title: Running sims
text:
What a sim takes
The settings of a sim are its keywords. The ones most models use:



Setting
What it is




diseases (or the first argument)
The disease or diseases; several are given as a list


total_pop
The size of the population (default 10,000)


n_agents
The number of agents, for a run as agents; giving it makes the sim run as agents (see Branching and rescaling)


start, stop (or dur)
The time span: dates ('2025-01-01'), years (2025), or durations from 0 (ss.days(50))


dt, unit
The time step, and the unit of bare numbers (see Time)


networks
How people mix: a contact matrix (ss.contacts()), a network, or a mixing pool (default: everyone mixes with everyone); see Contact networks


demographics
Births, deaths, and migration (see Demographics)


interventions, analyzers, connectors
Interventions, analyzers, and connectors between modules (see Interventions)


data
Data to compare the results with, by name (see Results)


solver
How to run: 'auto' (the default), 'ode', 'binomial', 'gillespie', 'tau', or 'abm'


rand_seed
The random seed, for a stochastic run (default 1; see Scenarios)


label
A name for the sim, used in plots and comparisons


verbose
How much to print (above)



sim.pars holds all of them after the sim is made, including the ones not given. sim.describe() shows the whole model as Starsim has built it, with each value it chose itself marked (see Writing models).
total_pop and n_agents are separate on purpose. total_pop is the number of people the model stands for, and is the same under every solver; n_agents is how many individuals are followed when the sim runs as agents. Given both, each agent stands for total_pop/n_agents people, which saves time at the cost of coarser random events (see Branching and rescaling):

agents = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50))
agents.run()

Sim: measles, as 10,000 agents, each 10 people, days 0 to 50
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.044 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 78,380 infectious, on day 9


Sim(n=100000 (10000 agents); 0—50; diseases=measles)


The first line now says “as 10,000 agents, each 10 people”. The epidemic is much the same as the ODE’s, but not identical: each agent’s infection is a random event.

Settings in a dict
The settings can also be collected in a dict and passed together, which is handy when several sims share them:

pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-03-01', verbose=0)

town = ss.Sim(measles, **pars)
city = ss.Sim(pars, diseases=measles, total_pop=1_000_000) # The same settings, with one changed

A dict given as the first argument is read as settings, and a keyword given as well overrides the same setting in the dict, as total_pop does for city. In such a dict, a module from Starsim’s library can be given as a dict of its own parameters, with its name as type. This is a shorthand found in many existing scripts, for example for an agent-based SIR on a random network:

pars = dict(
    diseases = dict(type='sir', beta=ss.perday(0.1), dur_inf=ss.days(10)),
    networks = dict(type='random', n_contacts=4),
    n_agents = 2_000,
    start = '2025-01-01',
    stop = '2025-07-01',
)
sim = ss.Sim(pars)
sim.run()

Sim: sir, as 2,000 agents, 2025-01-01 to 2025-07-01


  Done in 0.42 s; sir: 1,929 infections; at most 862 infectious, on 2025-01-23


Sim(n=2000; 2025-01-01—2025-07-01; networks=randomnet; diseases=sir)


It is the same as giving the modules themselves, diseases=ss.SIR(beta=..., dur_inf=...) and networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4). A name on its own (diseases='sir') uses the module’s default parameters.

title: Running sims
section: What happens before the first step
text:
What happens before the first step
Nothing is computed when a sim is made. sim.init(), which sim.run() calls if it hasn’t been called, builds the sim:

It fills in whatever was left out (the unit of time from the values in the model, how long each state lasts beyond its average, how people mix, where people start) and records each choice, so that describe() can show it.
It checks the model: unknown parameter names, values outside their bounds, and shapes that don’t match the model’s groups are errors here, before the run.
It chooses the solver, makes the people (with a default age and sex structure, unless a population is given; see People and agents), adds each module’s states, parameters, and results, sets up the time steps, and starts the random number generators.

Calling sim.init() yourself is useful for looking at the people or the model before a long run, or for finding an error without waiting for one.
A sim copies the modules it is given, so the same disease can be given to several sims. After a run, use the sim’s own copy: sim.diseases.measles, not the variable measles, which is never run.

title: Running sims
text:
Running again, and variants
sim.run() on a sim that has already run runs it again from the start, as it was before it was first run: changes made to a sim once it has been initialized belong to that run only. To run it again with something changed, use sim.new(), which makes a new sim as this one was before it was run, with whatever is given changed. Here the same outbreak with a lower transmission rate, as if contacts were fewer, compared with the original:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), label='Original', verbose=0)
sim.run()
slower = sim.new(pars=dict(beta=1.2), label='Fewer contacts')
slower.run()

msim = ss.MultiSim([sim, slower])
msim.plot('measles.I')








With β = 1.2, R0 is about 10 rather than 15, and the peak comes later and lower. What sim.new() changes can be settings (sim.new(total_pop=1_000_000)), parameters of the model by name (sim.new(pars=dict(beta=1.2)), for a parameter made with ss.par() and so given a name; see Parameters), or modules (sim.new(interventions=campaign)). This is the usual way to make the scenarios of a comparison (see Scenarios).
Three other ways of running again:

sim.copy() makes an exact copy, including the state of a sim part of the way through a run (below).
sim.run(solver='abm') runs the same sim as agents, building it again for the new solver, and sim.run(n_runs=20) runs it 20 times with different seeds, returning the runs together as an ss.MultiSim (see Scenarios).
sim.restart() takes a sim back to its start without building it again, optionally with new parameter values (sim.restart(pars=dict(beta=1.2))). For a model that is nothing but compartments this makes repeated runs many times faster, and sim.run(n_runs=...) and sim.fit() use it where they can.

title: Running sims
text:
Running part of the way
sim.run(until=...) runs up to a given time and stops; a later sim.run() carries on from there. This is useful for looking at the state of a sim in the middle of a run, for changing it before going on, and for running a shared start (a burn-in) once and then branching into scenarios. Here, measles reaches a town in which 90% of people are immune; a month in, the scenarios differ by how much contacts are reduced from then on (by closing schools, say), each a copy of the sim at that point with an ss.modify() added:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(1.9)
measles = ss.Disease(S >> I @ beta*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=10)) # 90% immune, 10 infectious

base = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
base.run(until='2025-02-01')

reductions = {'No change': 0, 'Contacts down by 20%': 0.2, 'Contacts down by 40%': 0.4}
sims = {}
for label, reduction in reductions.items():
    sim = base.copy()
    sim.add_module(ss.modify('measles.pars.beta', multiply=1-reduction))
    sims[label] = sim

msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')








A module added this way (sim.add_module()) acts from the time it is added; its results cover the whole run, but are filled in only from then. Only modules that leave the layout of the model as it is can be added part of the way: a vaccine adds a state for the people who hold it, so ss.vaccinate() must be given when the sim is made (with a start date), and Starsim says so if you try.
A parameter of the copy can also be set directly before it carries on, which here has the same effect as the 40% reduction:

sim = base.copy()
sim.diseases.measles.pars.beta = 1.9*0.6
sim.run()
print('Peak infectious:', round(sim.results.measles.I.max()))

Peak infectious: 76


Copying a sim takes some time too, so a shared start saves time only when it is long compared with the rest of the run, or when there are many scenarios. For a model that runs in a fraction of a second, as here, it is simpler to run each scenario in full with sim.new() and an intervention that starts on the date.

title: Running sims
text:
The order of each step
For a declared model, Starsim works out the order of everything in a step from the model itself. For modules written as code it matters, because each module’s code runs at a fixed point in the step:

Each module’s start_step(), which mostly moves the random number generators on.
Births, deaths, and other demographics.
Progression of each disease (step_state(): recoveries, deaths, and other moves that don’t depend on contact).
Connectors (which change one module according to another).
Networks (contacts form and end).
Interventions.
Transmission (each disease’s step()).
Deaths are carried out (people.step_die()), with each death assigned to one cause, so that every death is counted once.
Results are recorded.
Analyzers (which see the step’s results).
Each module’s, the people’s, and the sim’s finish_step().

So on a single day, a woman who becomes pregnant, develops symptoms, moves house, takes a test, and transmits an infection does them in that order, and transmits to her new household rather than her old one. Putting demographics first means that a child born during a step can be infected during that step (for example, by her mother), and that the effect of an infection during pregnancy is captured. Putting networks before transmission means that a new partnership can transmit in the step it forms, which matters for sexually transmitted infections with short partnerships.
Modules can have time steps of their own (demographics once a year and a disease once a day, say); the sim keeps a plan of which module runs on which step. sim.loop.to_df(), after sim.init(), lists every function called in every step, and sim.loop.plot() draws it. A declared model with nothing but compartments is run in one go rather than step by step, which is why its run is so fast; see Model execution and Custom modules.

title: Running sims
text:
Saving and loading
sim.save() saves a sim to a file, and ss.load() loads it again:

sim.save('my-measles.sim')
loaded = ss.load('my-measles.sim')
loaded.plot('measles')








By default a saved sim that has finished keeps its results but not the people, which makes the file much smaller; a sim saved part of the way through keeps everything, so that it can be loaded and run on (shrink=False keeps everything in either case). A saved sim is a Python pickle, so it needs the same version of Starsim (and of any modules written as code) to load. For the results alone, sim.to_df() gives them as a table, which can be saved as a CSV or Excel file, and sim.to_json() gives the results and settings as JSON (see Results). To write the model itself in another format (SBML, odin), see Import and export.
sim.shrink() does the same in memory: it removes the people and the other per-agent arrays from a finished sim, keeping the results. For a sim of agents this is most of its size, so it is worth doing when keeping many runs. ss.MultiSim and ss.parallel() already shrink the sims they run.

title: Running sims
text:
Larger projects: make_sim()
A project with more than a few scenarios is usually built around one function that makes the sim, with an argument for each thing that varies, so that every scenario, seed, and calibration run is made the same way. A sketch of the pattern, as an HIV project might have it:
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl
import pandas as pd

def make_sim(seed=1, n_agents=10_000, start=1990, stop=2030, scenario='baseline', debug=False):
    """ Make the sim for one scenario and seed """
    if debug: # A quick version for testing the code
        n_agents, stop = 1_000, 2000

    # Population and demography, from data
    people = ss.People(n_agents, age_data=pd.read_csv('data/age_dist_1990.csv'))
    pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=pd.read_csv('data/asfr.csv'))
    deaths = ss.Deaths(death_rate=pd.read_csv('data/deaths.csv'))

    # Networks, disease, and interventions
    sexual = ss.SexualNet()
    maternal = ss.MaternalNet()
    hiv = ssl.HIV(beta={'sexualnet': [0.008, 0.004], 'maternalnet': [0.2, 0]})
    interventions = []
    if scenario == 'treat':
        interventions.append(ssl.ART(year=[2004, 2020], coverage=[0.1, 0.8]))

    sim = ss.Sim(
        people = people,
        diseases = hiv,
        networks = [sexual, maternal],
        demographics = [pregnancy, deaths],
        interventions = interventions,
        start = start,
        stop = stop,
        total_pop = 9.98e6,
        rand_seed = seed,
        label = scenario,
    )
    return sim
The scenarios and seeds are then a loop over its arguments, run together with ss.parallel() (see Scenarios). If making the sim is itself slow (reading large files, say), the sims can be made in parallel too, with Sciris:
import sciris as sc

iterkwargs = [dict(seed=seed, scenario=scen) for seed in range(20) for scen in ['baseline', 'treat']]
sims = sc.parallelize(make_sim, iterkwargs=iterkwargs)
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
Keep anything that differs between scenarios as an argument rather than editing the sim afterwards, and keep debug=True as a quick way to check the code end to end. For running such a project on a cluster or as a web app, see Deployment.

title: Running sims
text:
Pitfalls

Using the module you made rather than the sim’s copy. After a run, sim.diseases.measles has the run’s state; the measles you made does not. Likewise, a function given to a sim should read what it needs from the sim it is given (lambda sim: sim.diseases.measles.I.n), not from a variable.
Changing a setting after the sim is built. Once a sim is initialized its settings belong to that run, and setting one (sim.pars.stop = 30) raises an error; give it to sim.new(stop=30) instead.
Settings given twice. A setting given in a pars dict and again as a keyword takes the keyword’s value, without a word.
A sim that isn’t what you meant. Read the first lines a run prints, and sim.describe(): R0, the unit of time, and the solver catch most mistakes before any result is read. More are in Profiling and debugging.

title: What is Starsim?
text:
Introduction
Starsim is a framework for modeling the spread of diseases, as compartmental models or among agents via dynamic transmission networks. Starsim supports:

Writing a disease as its states and the transitions between them (compartments and the rates of flow between them, as in a textbook model), and running the same model as a deterministic compartmental model, as a stochastic one, or as agents
Co-transmission of multiple diseases at once, capturing how they interact biologically and behaviorally
Non-infectious diseases, either on their own or as factors affecting the transmission or mortality of infectious diseases
Detailed modeling of mother-child relationships starting from conception, allowing investigation of infant and childhood diseases
Multiple types of transmission network, including theoretical (e.g. Erdős–Rényi) and realistic (e.g. age-assortative sexual partnerships)
Different intervention types, such as vaccines or treatments, and showing their impact through different delivery methods such as mass campaigns or targeted outreach
Calibration to data, and common random numbers, so that two scenarios differ by what was changed rather than by chance

Starsim is available for both Python and R, and is fully open-source under the MIT license.

title: What is Starsim?
text:
Types of disease modeling
Starsim models can be compartmental or agent-based (an ABM). A disease written as states and transitions can be run either way: as compartments when the model can be written as compartments, and as agents when something in it needs individuals, such as a network of who is in contact with whom. Starsim chooses which, and says so; it can also be told (see Solvers and backends). Parts of a model written as Python code, such as a custom intervention, run as agents. ABMs are most suitable for questions that are moderately complex, and have medium to large amounts of data available:



Types of model


For simpler questions, statistical or compartmental models are often all that’s needed. For very complex questions, machine learning models may be more suitable. Examples of each type of question are:

Statistical models: “Are people who received the vaccine less likely to get infected?”
Machine learning models: “What behavioral factors influence vaccination uptake?”
Compartmental models: “What is disease prevalence going to be in 5 years given 100% vaccine uptake?”
Agent-based models: “What is disease prevalence going to be in 5 years given realistic assumptions about screening and vaccine coverage?”

Because a declared Starsim model can be run both ways, the choice need not be made up front: a model can start as compartments, and be run as agents once a question needs individuals (and the two can be compared, to see what the individual detail changes). The conceptual overview explains how this works.

title: What is Starsim?
text:
Why Starsim?
Starsim aims to address the limitations of existing ABMs, specifically along the dimensions of usability, capability, and outcome:








Dimension
Starsim
Status quo




Usability
Starsim is fast, has a simple interface, and requires knowledge of Python (or R) only
Many ABMs are slow, complex, or require knowledge of C++/Java


Capability
Starsim supports multiple custom diseases and networks, including co-transmission
Most other disease models are single-disease or hard-coded to a handful of diseases


Outcome
Once you’ve collected your data, modeling your questions with Starsim takes days to weeks
Writing, testing, and calibrating a custom model can take months to years



While of course not all existing ABMs have these limitations, many of them have at least one. (For a good review of general-purpose ABMs, see Antelmi et al. 2023). For how Starsim relates to other modeling frameworks, see the modeling landscape.

title: What is Starsim?
text:
Starsim principles
Starsim’s design philosophy has two parts. First, “Common tasks should be simple”. Examples include:

Defining parameters
Running a simulation
Plotting results

These are things you need to do in every single Starsim analysis, so we’ve tried to make them as easy as possible.
The second part of the philosophy is “Custom tasks can’t always be simple, but they should still be possible”. Examples include:

Introducing a new vaccine
Implementing a new disease
Writing a custom calibration function

If you’re implementing a complicated disease, there will always be some irreducible complexity involved in that. Starsim’s job is to help you where it can, but then get out of the way and let you write your code.

title: What is Starsim?
text:
Should I use Starsim?
Starsim is suitable for many use cases, but not all. Some examples of suitable Starsim use cases are:

If you are currently doing agent-based modeling but your model is too slow/inflexible/hard to use for your research questions

Example: Your model takes 14 hours for a single run, and every year you’re worried that your computing grant won’t be renewed

If you are currently doing compartmental modeling, and want to try out an agent-based model without investing 3-6 months learning how to use it

Example: Your compartmental mpox model has so far been very effective, but you’ve been asked to evaluate an individually-targeted intervention that requires tracking individual agents. In Starsim, the same model can be run as an ODE and as agents, and the two compared

If you want to quickly prototype different diseases or networks before deciding whether to implement them in your full model

Example: You know and love your HIV model, but you want to see what the impact would be of including syphilis co-transmission or a different type of MSM network


However, there are other cases where Starsim may not be suitable. These include:

If you are doing a very simple modeling task, such as a simple SIR or SEIR model, you might as well use plain Python or R. Starsim is fast and concise, but is unlikely to be faster or significantly more concise than well-written custom code. But if your script starts getting longer than about 100 lines, and if you want to do calibration or handle different time units, there is a good chance that Starsim would be able to make things easier.
If your current model is highly specialized to a given context, the switching cost of moving to Starsim may not be worthwhile. Starsim can import models from several other frameworks (see Import and export), and AI tools make translating a model much easier than it used to be, so get in touch if this is of interest to you.

title: What is Starsim?
text:
Finding your way around
These docs are organized by what you want to do:

To see Starsim in action, take the tour, which builds and runs a model in a few minutes, or browse the gallery of complete models.
To learn Starsim, follow the tutorials in order. The core tutorials (T1 to T9) build up one measles model, from a simple SIR to age groups, vaccination, geography, calibration, and custom code; the agent-based tutorials (A1 to A5) cover networks, demographics, and modules that need individuals.
To look something up, use this user guide. Each page is a complete reference for one topic, such as writing models, time, or running scenarios, and links to the tutorial that introduces it. The Architecture pages explain how Starsim works under the hood.
For the exact arguments of a function, see the API reference.
If you are coming from another framework (Starsim 3, EpiModel, odin, epydemix, and others), see Conversion, which has a page for each.

A runnable example is a starting point, not a calibrated model of a particular population: a model’s scientific validity depends on its assumptions, the evidence behind its parameters, and the checks made against data.

title: Time
text:
🧠35% 🤖65%
Every rate in a model is per some unit of time, every duration is in some unit, and a sim runs over a span of time in steps. This page covers how to give each of these, how Starsim converts between them, and the conventions it uses for calendars. The short version: give rates and durations with their units (ss.perday(1.9), ss.days(8)), give the span as dates or durations, and Starsim does the rest.
Starsim’s handling of time is complex, because, well, time is complex. Although time seems intuitive, there are many corner cases where intuition breaks down (and, worse, it might not seem like it has broken down, leading you astray!). Thus, perhaps more than any other part of Starsim, be sure to check your assumptions about time. The decisions Starsim made for the thorny cases are listed under Conventions, below. Units, dates, and steps are introduced in T2 – Building a model.

title: Time
section: The time span and the step
text:
The time span and the step
A sim runs from start to stop (or for dur), in steps of dt. The span can be given in three ways:








Given as
Example
Time is




Dates
start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01'
Calendar dates; results are dated


Years
start=2025, stop=2030
Years, as numbers with dates behind them


Durations
stop=ss.days(50)
Time since the start (day 0, day 1, …)



Here is the measles model over the first two months of 2025:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)       # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-03-01')
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles')

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0055 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on 2025-01-07









The step, dt, is one unit of the model by default (here a day). Results are recorded at every time point, from the start to the stop inclusive, so a run of 59 daily steps has 60 time points: the state at the start, then after each step. A flow, such as infections, at a time point is the number during the step that ends there.
Specifying the length with dur is exactly the same as specifying stop: internally, stop = start + dur, so start=2000, dur=20 is the same as start=2000, stop=2020. Why are the endpoints inclusive? For a range like start=2000, stop=2020, there are three equally valid interpretations:

Inclusive start, exclusive end (2000-01-01 to 2019-12-31), by analogy to np.arange(0, 20) giving 0–19.
Inclusive start, minimally inclusive end (2000-01-01 to 2020-01-01), by analogy to np.linspace(0, 20) giving 0–20, or plt.xlim(left=2000, right=2020).
Inclusive start, maximally inclusive end (2000-01-01 to 2020-12-31).

Starsim uses the second (middle) interpretation. This is mostly for plotting (a sim run from 2000 to 2020 looks odd if the plot ends in 2019) and so that stop and dur are interchangeable: start=2000, dur=20 intuitively runs to 2020, not 2019. Just as with np.arange, the step determines which points fall within the range, and the final point is the last one at or before stop: start='2017-01-01', stop='2024-12-31', dt=ss.datedur(months=1) ends at 2024-12-01, because the next monthly point is past stop.

Choosing the step
For the ODE, Gillespie, and tau-leaping, the step only says how often results are recorded: the ODE takes as many smaller steps inside each one as it needs, and the other two work in continuous time. For agents and the chain binomial, each step is taken whole, so a step that is long compared with the time people spend in a state changes the results. Starsim notes when this may be so, and sim.check_dt() measures it, by running the sim again with half the step and comparing each result. Here is the same measles model run as agents, with daily steps:

agents = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=10_000, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-03-01', verbose=0)
agents.check_dt()

Change in each result when the timestep goes from 1 to 0.5 days (largest difference, as a share of the largest value):
  measles.infection             57.3%   (peak 27610 → 33830)
  measles.recovery              51.4%   (peak 8600 → 9400)
  measles.I                     35.8%   (peak 78380 → 76750)
  measles.S                     30.6%   (peak 99900 → 99900)
  measles.R                     13.2%   (peak 99840 → 99830)


Measles spreads so fast (early on, each infectious person infects 1.9 others a day) that halving a daily step changes the peak in new infections by more than half: for agents, a day is too long a step for measles, and dt=ss.days(0.25) is closer to right. A model of a slower infection, or of a disease over years, can take much longer steps. See Solvers and backends.
A module can have a step of its own, such as yearly births in a model with weekly transmission (ss.Births(..., dt=ss.years(1))), and the modules are run in order of time.

title: Time
Time
text:
Rates, probabilities, and durations
Dates say when things happen, but disease modeling is mostly about durations and rates: how many days from infection to recovery? What is the chance of transmission per week? Starsim calls these unit-aware quantities time parameters, and has four kinds, each with constructors for days, weeks, months, and years (a week is exactly 7 days, and a month exactly 1/12 of a year):








Kind
Means
Constructors




Duration
A length of time
ss.days(8), ss.weeks, ss.months, ss.years, and ss.datedur for calendar arithmetic


Rate
A hazard: events per person per unit of time, happening continuously
ss.perday(1.9), ss.perweek, ss.permonth, ss.peryear


Probability
The chance of an event within a period
ss.prob(0.1, 'day'), and 'week', 'month', 'year'


Frequency
An expected number of events per unit of time, such as sex acts per year (used in modules written as code)
ss.freq(80, 'year')



Converting each to a step is Starsim’s job. Over a step of length Δt, a rate r becomes the probability 1 − exp(−r Δt) of at least one event, a probability p per period T becomes 1 − (1 − p)^(Δt/T), a frequency f becomes f Δt events, and a duration d is used through its rate 1/d. The ODE, Gillespie, and tau-leaping use the rates themselves, with no conversion.
The full family of time parameters is:
TimePar         # All time parameters
├── dur         # Durations, in units of time
│   ├── days, weeks, months, years
│   └── datedur    # Calendar durations
└── Rate        # Everything "per" something
    ├── per        # Rates (hazards) of an event that happens once, e.g. death
    │   └── perday, perweek, permonth, peryear
    ├── prob       # Probabilities, with or without a period
    │   └── probperday, probperweek, probpermonth, probperyear
    └── freq       # Numbers of events, e.g. acts per year
        └── freqperday, freqperweek, freqpermonth, freqperyear
ss.prob(0.1, 'day') and ss.probperday(0.1) are the same, as are ss.freq(80, 'year') and ss.freqperyear(80). Durations add with the left-hand unit taking precedence, and can be converted: ss.years(2) + ss.days(3) is years(2.00822), and ss.years(10).to('days') is days(3650).
The kinds differ in what multiplying by a duration means, which is how each is converted to a step:

A rate times a duration is a probability: ss.peryear(0.8) * ss.years(1) is 1 − exp(−0.8) ≈ 0.55, the chance of the event happening at least once in a year. A rate times a number is a scaled rate (ss.peryear(0.8) * 2 is 1.6 per year), which is how relative risks are applied. A rate need not be below 1: ss.perday(2) is valid.
A probability times a duration is the probability over that duration, worked out through the rate behind it: ss.prob(0.8, ss.years(1)) * ss.years(2) is 0.96, not 1.6 (which is not a probability).
A frequency times a duration is an expected number of events: ss.freqperyear(80) * ss.years(0.5) is 40.

The kinds combine where the result has a meaning:

print(ss.perday(0.1) * ss.days(3))               # The chance of at least one event in 3 days
print(ss.prob(0.1, 'day') + ss.prob(0.1, 'day')) # Two competing risks of 0.1 a day: 0.19 a day
print(1 / ss.days(10))                           # A rate: 0.1 per day
print(2 / ss.perday(0.1))                        # A duration: 20 days

0.2591817793182822
probperday(0.19)
perday(0.1)
days(20)


Where they don’t, it is an error that says why, for example adding a rate to a probability:

try:
    ss.perday(0.1) + ss.prob(0.1, 'day')
except Exception as e:
    print(e)

cannot compute perday(0.1) + probperday(0.1): a rate (ss.perday) + a probability per time (ss.prob) has no meaning. Only rates of the same kind can be combined, e.g. ss.perday + ss.peryear, or ss.prob(0.1, "day") + ss.prob(0.1, "year"); convert one of them first, e.g. with ss.peryear(rate).



Which to use

A rate (ss.peryear(0.01)) for anything that happens to a person once, at some rate: infection, recovery, death. This is what most models use, and what an ODE means by a rate.
A duration (ss.days(8)) for the average time spent in a state; it is the same as the rate 1/duration, and usually easier to read.
A probability per period (ss.prob(0.01, 'year')) when the data is a share of people in a period: for example, 10 deaths in a year among 1,000 people.
A frequency (ss.freq(80, 'year')) for a number of events that can each happen many times, such as contacts or acts.







Tipss.prob vs ss.bernoulli



ss.prob (and ss.probperyear, etc.) is a number: a time-aware value you can multiply and convert between periods. ss.bernoulli is a distribution you sample for each agent: dist.filter(uids) returns the agents for whom the trial succeeded. When you need to decide an outcome for each agent in a module written as code (“who gets infected, who dies, who is vaccinated?”), use ss.bernoulli; use ss.prob when you need the probability itself as a value. See Distributions.


A rate of deaths, such as 10 per 1,000 people per year, is per person-year: people who have died stop contributing person-years. So of 1,000 people with a death rate of ss.peryear(0.1), 95 die in a year (1,000 × (1 − exp(−0.1))), not 100; if 100 is what the data means, it is a probability, ss.prob(0.1, 'year').

title: Time
text:
Dates and the timeline
ss.date is a calendar date, based on pd.Timestamp, and is quite flexible about what it is made from:

import datetime as dt
import pandas as pd

d1 = ss.date(2025)
d2 = ss.date(2025, 1, 1)
d3 = ss.date('2025-01-01')
d4 = ss.date(pd.Timestamp('2025-01-01'))
d5 = ss.date(dt.datetime(2025, 1, 1))
print(d1 == d2 == d3 == d4 == d5)

d = ss.date('2025-01-01')
print(d.years)            # As a year
print(d + ss.days(10))    # Ten days later

True
2025.0
2025-01-11


Dates are interchangeable with years as numbers (float(d) is the same as d.years; unlike a duration, a date has an unambiguous number), although some rounding can occur. A duration added to a date counts time exactly, with a year as 365 days and a month as 1/12 of a year. ss.datedur counts in calendar units instead, which is what “six months later” usually means:

print(d + ss.years(0.5))            # Half of 365 days later
print(d + ss.datedur(months=6))     # Six calendar months later
print(ss.date('2025-07-01') - d)    # The time between two dates, in days

2025-07-02
2025-07-01
days(181)


The two differ because the first half of 2025 is shorter than the second: there are 181 days from 1 January to 1 July, and 184 from 1 July to 1 January. So even though 6/12 is certainly 0.5, date-based and number-based arithmetic give different answers. ss.datedur takes whole numbers of years, months, weeks, and days (it is a thin wrapper of pd.DateOffset, which a date also accepts), and dt=ss.datedur(months=1) steps a sim by calendar months. A sequence of dates is made with ss.date.arange(start='2025-07-01', stop='2025-09-18', step=ss.week).
sim.t (an ss.Timeline) holds the sim’s time points, in several forms: datevec (dates), yearvec (years as numbers), relvec (time since the start, in the unit of the step), and tivec (the number of each time point). timevec is the one that is most natural for the sim (dates for a dated sim, time since the start otherwise), and is what results use. You will rarely need the timeline directly, but it’s what keeps modules with steps of their own in time with each other and with the sim:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-03-01', dt=ss.weeks(1), verbose=0).init()
print(sim.t.datevec[:4])
print(sim.t.yearvec[:4])
print(sim.t.relvec[:4]) # Weeks since the start

[<2025-01-01> <2025-01-08> <2025-01-15> <2025-01-22>]
[2025.         2025.01917808 2025.03835616 2025.05753425]
[0. 1. 2. 3.]

title: Time
Time
text:
Conventions
Time has corners where reasonable choices differ. Some questions Starsim has had to wrestle with:

If you run a simulation from 2000 to 2020 with monthly steps, would you expect the same average number of infections in 2004 (a leap year) and 2005 (not a leap year)? What about February 2012 and March 2012?
Is a year 365 days, 365.25 days, or either 365 or 366 days depending on the year?
Usually years and dates are interchangeable, so start=2000, stop=2020 is the same as start='2000-01-01', stop='2020-01-01'. But what if someone simply wants to run for a number of years, start=0, stop=20, given that there is no year 0?
If an event is scheduled at the fractional year 2025.7, is that the nearest day (2025-09-12), or that exact moment (2025-09-11 16:48)? Will users ever want hours and minutes?
Should units be strict (ss.days(5) != 5) or permissive (ss.days(5) == 5)?
If a mortality rate is “100 deaths per 1,000 people per year”, should 100 of 1,000 people die in a year, or 95 (100 deaths per 1,000 person-years, since people stop accruing person-years once they die)?
What does it mean to multiply a probability? Is ss.prob(0.1)*2 equal to ss.prob(0.2)? If so, what is ss.prob(0.5)*2, or ss.prob(0.9)*2?

These are Starsim’s answers, although different answers would also be valid:

A month is exactly 1/12 of a year, so a monthly rate gives the same number of events in February as in March, and in 2004 as in 2005.
A year is 365 days (with some stretching where needed to make whole years and calendar dates line up).
A number given as start is a year if it looks like one (2025), and a time since the start otherwise (0, or stop=ss.days(50)), in which case results are in time since the start rather than dated. The same goes for any number given as a time, such as at=2030 or a time of an ss.timeseries(): from 1900 on it is a calendar year, even in a sim with dates, and below that a time in the sim’s unit after the start (for 2,000 days, write ss.days(2000)).
Dates are whole days, unless a smaller step is asked for explicitly (dt=ss.days(0.25)).
Units are loose when compared with plain numbers (ss.days(5) == 5 is true), but strict between units (ss.years(1) == ss.days(365) is true).
A rate is per person-time: of 1,000 people with a death rate of ss.peryear(0.1), about 95 die in a year. If 100 is what the data means, it is a probability, ss.prob(0.1, 'year').
A probability stays between 0 and 1: ss.prob(0.5)*2 is 0.75 (the chance of at least one of two events), which also means that ss.prob(0.1)*2 is 0.19, not 0.2.

title: Time
text:
In modules written as code
A module written as code works with time a step at a time. Each time quantity in its parameters knows the module’s step after sim.init(), so:

rate.to_prob() is the probability of an event in one step;
dur.to_dt() is a duration as a number of steps, for comparing with the step numbers that states such as a time of infection hold;
freq.to_events() is the expected number of events in one step.

Convert a rate to a probability as the last step of a calculation, after multiplying it by any relative risks, so that the result is a valid probability:
death_rate = ss.peryear(0.1)
rel_death_age = 3.4 # Older age, higher risk
rel_death_ses = 5.7 # Lower socioeconomic status, higher risk

# Right: multiply first, then convert to a probability
p_death = (death_rate * rel_death_age * rel_death_ses).to_prob()

# Wrong: gives an invalid probability
p_death = death_rate.to_prob() * rel_death_age * rel_death_ses
States such as ti_infected or ti_recovered hold step numbers, not times, so a duration has to be converted to steps before it is added to one:
# Right: the duration as a number of steps (from the step after the infection, which is dated at the end of its step)
self.ti_clearance[uids] = self.ti_infected[uids] + 1 + self.pars.dur_persist.to_dt()

# Wrong: ss.years(100), ss.months(100), and ss.days(100) would all mean "100 steps"
self.ti_clearance[uids] = self.ti_infected[uids] + 1 + self.pars.dur_persist
Declare such a state as an ss.TimeArr, and take the move when self.ti_clearance.due(), which rounds a time between steps up or down at random in proportion, so the duration keeps its mean, as a declared disease’s does (see ss.Infection).
.to_dt() also takes a step, to convert to: ss.years(100).to_dt(ss.months(1)) is 1,200 monthly steps. A duration or rate is never silently a plain number: float(ss.peryear(0.1)) is an error, since ss.peryear(1), ss.permonth(1), and ss.perday(1) would all give 1, though they differ by a factor of 365. Use .to_dt(), .to_prob(), .to('year') (or .years, e.g. to compare with an agent’s age), or .value (the number in its own unit) if you really do want it. Values drawn from a distribution of durations (self.pars.dur_inf.rvs(uids)) are already in steps. See Custom modules.

title: Time
text:
Pitfalls

A bare number after @ is a rate, not a duration. I >> R @ 8 means 8 recoveries per person per unit of time (an infectious period of 1/8 of a day). Write ss.days(8), or ss.Transition(I, R, dur=8); Starsim notes a duration shorter than a step, which usually means this mistake.
Mixed units with bare numbers. A model with typed values in days and births in years can’t tell what a bare β means; give β its unit, or unit=.
A long run with daily steps. Twenty years of daily steps is 7,300 steps; Starsim warns when a sim has very many steps, since a longer step (dt=ss.weeks(1)) is often enough.
Steps of agents and the chain binomial. These take each step whole; check that the step is short enough for the fastest rate in the model.

text:
Further reading

Rates and probabilities in economic modelling: converting between rates and probabilities, and why multiplying probabilities by time goes wrong
Appropriate models for the management of infectious diseases: how the distribution of time spent in a state, not just its mean, shapes an epidemic
pandas: time series and date functionality: dates, offsets, and resampling, on which ss.date and ss.datedur are built
pandas.tseries.offsets.DateOffset: calendar arithmetic, as ss.datedur does it

title: Nonstandard usage
text:
🧠15% 🤖85%
Starsim is built for infectious diseases, but its machinery is general: a population of agents, each with properties kept as arrays over all of them; modules that change those properties at each step; results recorded over time; and random numbers drawn so that runs can be repeated and compared. A module written as code can hold any property of people and any rule for changing it, so Starsim can run agent-based models with no disease at all. This page shows two classic ones: a model of wealth, from economics, and a model of flocking birds, from computer graphics.
Not every model of something other than an infection needs code. States and transitions describe any process in which people move between categories at given rates (smoking, use of contraception, stages of a chronic disease, employment), and a declared model of such a process runs under every solver, with the same interventions as a disease: see Diseases. Some models track things that are not people at all, such as bacteria in water or a population of mosquitoes, as states with people=False in the same model as the people.

title: Nonstandard usage
text:
A model of wealth
This is the “wealth model” of the Mesa tutorial: each of 100 people starts with one unit of wealth, and at each step, everyone who has any gives one unit to someone chosen at random. Though the rule is fair, wealth ends up very unequal.
Each person’s wealth is a state, and whom each giver gives to is drawn from a Starsim distribution, so that runs can be repeated and compared (see Random numbers). The Gini coefficient (0 if everyone has the same, near 1 if one person has everything) is a result:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

class Wealth(ss.Module):
    """ Each person starts with 1 unit of wealth; each step, everyone with any gives 1 unit to someone chosen at random """

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_states(
            ss.FloatArr('wealth', default=1.0, label='Wealth'),
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.recipient = ss.randint(low=0, high=lambda self, sim, uids: len(sim.people)) # Whom each giver gives to
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('gini', label='Gini coefficient'),
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        givers = (self.wealth > 0).uids
        recipients = self.recipient.rvs(givers)
        self.wealth[givers] = self.wealth[givers] - 1
        self.wealth[:] = self.wealth + np.bincount(recipients, minlength=len(self.wealth)) # Each recipient gets 1 unit for each giver who chose them
        return

    def update_results(self):
        super().update_results()
        w = np.sort(self.wealth.values)
        n = len(w)
        self.results.gini[self.ti] = np.sum((2*np.arange(1, n+1) - n - 1)*w)/(n*w.sum())
        return

sim = ss.Sim(Wealth(), n_agents=100, stop=100) # 100 steps
sim.run()
sim.results.wealth.gini.plot()

Sim: wealth, as 100 agents, steps 0 to 100


  Done in 0.043 s









Inequality rises within a few steps and then stays high. The final distribution has many people with nothing and a few with several units:

wealth = sim.people.wealth.wealth
plt.figure()
plt.hist(wealth.values, bins=np.arange(wealth.max() + 2) - 0.5)
plt.xlabel('Wealth')
plt.ylabel('Number of people')
plt.show()








Compared with Mesa, where each agent is an object with its own step(), Starsim keeps each property as one array over all people, so a rule is applied to everyone at once: the code is a little shorter, and faster for large populations.

title: Nonstandard usage
text:
A model of flocking
Boids are the classic model of flocking, in which each bird follows three simple rules about the birds it can see: alignment (steer towards their average heading), cohesion (steer towards their center), and separation (steer away from any that are too close). No bird leads, and nobody tells the flock where to go, but flocks form and fly together.
In Starsim, each boid’s position (x, y) and velocity (vx, vy) are states, starting at random. The world is a unit square whose edges wrap around, so a boid leaving on the right comes back on the left. At each step, the module works out the offset from every boid to every other (the short way round), applies the three rules to all the boids at once, keeps each boid’s speed between a minimum and a maximum, and moves them. How well the flock is aligned is a result: for each boid, the length of the average heading of those it can see (itself included), averaged over all boids, which is 1 when each moves with its neighbors and close to 0 when their headings are random:

class Boids(ss.Module):
    """ Flocking: each boid steers towards the heading and center of the boids it can see, and away from those too close """

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            radius     = 0.1,    # How far a boid can see (the world is a unit square)
            too_close  = 0.03,   # How close is too close
            alignment  = 0.1,    # How strongly a boid steers towards its neighbors' heading
            cohesion   = 0.005,  # ... towards its neighbors' center
            separation = 3e-5,   # ... away from those too close
            speed      = [0.005, 0.01], # The minimum and maximum distance moved in a step
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(
            ss.FloatArr('x',  default=ss.random(), label='Position (x)'),
            ss.FloatArr('y',  default=ss.random(), label='Position (y)'),
            ss.FloatArr('vx', default=ss.uniform(-0.01, 0.01), label='Velocity (x)'),
            ss.FloatArr('vy', default=ss.uniform(-0.01, 0.01), label='Velocity (y)'),
        )
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(ss.Result('aligned', label='Alignment with neighbors'))
        return

    def offsets(self):
        """ The offsets from each boid to every other, the short way round the edges, and the distances """
        x, y = self.x.values, self.y.values
        dx = x[None, :] - x[:, None]
        dy = y[None, :] - y[:, None]
        dx -= np.round(dx)
        dy -= np.round(dy)
        return dx, dy, np.hypot(dx, dy)

    def step(self):
        p = self.pars
        vx, vy = self.vx.values, self.vy.values
        dx, dy, dist = self.offsets()
        np.fill_diagonal(dist, np.inf) # A boid is not its own neighbor
        near = dist < p.radius
        n_near = np.maximum(near.sum(axis=1), 1)
        close = dist < p.too_close

        # The three rules, for all the boids at once
        steer_x = p.alignment*(near @ vx / n_near - vx) + p.cohesion*(near*dx).sum(axis=1)/n_near - p.separation*(close*dx/dist**2).sum(axis=1)
        steer_y = p.alignment*(near @ vy / n_near - vy) + p.cohesion*(near*dy).sum(axis=1)/n_near - p.separation*(close*dy/dist**2).sum(axis=1)
        alone = ~near.any(axis=1) # A boid that sees nobody flies straight on
        vx = vx + np.where(alone, 0, steer_x)
        vy = vy + np.where(alone, 0, steer_y)

        # Keep the speed within limits, then move, wrapping around the edges
        speed = np.hypot(vx, vy)
        factor = np.clip(speed, *p.speed)/speed
        self.vx[:] = vx*factor
        self.vy[:] = vy*factor
        self.x[:] = (self.x + self.vx) % 1
        self.y[:] = (self.y + self.vy) % 1
        return

    def update_results(self):
        super().update_results()
        speed = np.hypot(self.vx.values, self.vy.values)
        hx, hy = self.vx.values/speed, self.vy.values/speed # Each boid's heading
        _, _, dist = self.offsets()
        sees = dist < self.pars.radius # Including itself
        self.results.aligned[self.ti] = (np.hypot(sees @ hx, sees @ hy)/sees.sum(axis=1)).mean()
        return

The rule of alignment is what makes a flock: without it, boids still gather and keep their distance, but each flies its own way. Here 200 boids fly for 200 steps, with and without it:

scenarios = {
    'Flocking': ss.Sim(Boids(), n_agents=200, stop=200),
    'No alignment': ss.Sim(Boids(alignment=0), n_agents=200, stop=200),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, parallel=False)
msim.plot('boids.aligned')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Flocking, No alignment)
  Done in 0.91 s









With alignment, most boids are moving with their neighbors within about 50 steps, and nearly all within 100; without it, their headings stay about as random as at the start. The positions and velocities are states, so the flock can be drawn at any point in a run. Here the sim runs in stages (run(until=...) runs up to a given step, and the next call carries on from there), and each snapshot shows every boid as an arrow along its heading:

sim = ss.Sim(Boids(), n_agents=200, stop=200)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4))
for ax, step in zip(axes, [0, 30, 200]):
    sim.run(until=step)
    boids = sim.custom.boids
    speed = np.hypot(boids.vx.values, boids.vy.values)
    ax.quiver(boids.x.values, boids.y.values, boids.vx.values/speed, boids.vy.values/speed, angles='xy', scale_units='xy', scale=40, width=0.005) # Arrows along each heading
    ax.set_title(f'Step {step}')
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
plt.show()

Sim: boids, as 200 agents, steps 0 to 200


  ──────────────────────────────   0%  step 1  0.0 s


  ──────────────────────────────   1%  step 2  0.0 s


  Done in 0.4 s









From random headings at the start, groups form within a few dozen steps, and by the end the boids fly as a few large flocks (which wrap around the edges of the square), with space between their members. The module is given to the sim as custom (any module that is not a disease, network, demographic module, intervention, analyzer, or connector), and is reached as sim.custom.boids.
As in the wealth model, each rule is applied to every boid at once, as operations on arrays, rather than by looping over the boids. Working out the distance between every pair of boids takes time and memory in proportion to the square of their number, which is fine for hundreds or a few thousand; for many more, a spatial index (such as SciPy’s cKDTree) would find each boid’s neighbors faster.

title: Scenarios
text:
🧠10% 🤖90%
A scenario is a sim with something changed: an intervention added, a parameter set to another value, a different population. Comparing scenarios is how most models answer policy questions: how many infections would a campaign avert, and does it matter when it happens? And since a single stochastic run is one draw of what could happen, most comparisons also need many runs of each scenario. This page covers making scenarios and running them together, running a model many times and reading the spread, comparing scenarios fairly, sweeping a parameter, carrying uncertainty in parameter values into the results, and the random seeds that make it all reproducible. T5 – Interventions and scenarios teaches the same through one example; Running sims covers single sims.

title: Scenarios
text:
Scenarios by label
Here, measles has reached a town of 20,000 people in which 90% are immune, with 50 infectious people on 1 January. The question is what a vaccination campaign that reaches half the town, with a vaccine that protects 95% of those who receive it, would avert, and whether it matters if it happens in February or March:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(1.9)                    # Transmission rate per day
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)       # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=50)) # 90% immune, 50 infectious

base = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01')
february = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, coverage=0.5, at='2025-02-01')
march    = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, coverage=0.5, at='2025-03-01')

sim.new() makes a new sim from the same inputs, with whatever is given changed, so each scenario is the base sim with its intervention. ss.parallel() runs a dict of sims by label, at the same time on the computer’s cores:

scenarios = {
    'No campaign': base,
    'Campaign in February': base.new(interventions=february),
    'Campaign in March': base.new(interventions=march),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (No campaign, Campaign in February, Campaign in March)
  Done in 0.59 s









The result is an ss.MultiSim: the runs of every scenario, with each result holding a row for each run. msim.summarize() gives each result over the whole run for each scenario: the total of each flow (measles_infection is the number of infections) and the final value of each state:

title: Scenarios
text:
Many runs of one model
These runs are ODEs, so each scenario has one answer: what happens on average. To see the outbreaks that could happen, run the model as a stochastic model, in which people move between states at random, and run it many times. Here is measles introduced into the same town by only five infectious people. Each case infects about 1.5 others at the start (R0 of 15 times the 10% who are susceptible). First the ODE, then 50 runs of the same model as an exact stochastic compartmental model (solver='gillespie'; a model that runs as agents is stochastic already; see Solvers and backends for the choices):

measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=5)) # Now 5 infectious
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180))
sim.run();

Sim: measles, 20,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 180
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible), with 5 infectious at the start
  Note: "measles" starts with 5 infected, so whether it takes off is a matter of chance, which solver="ode" does not show; solver="gillespie" with ss.parallel(n_runs=...) does
  Done in 0.0059 s; measles: 1,187 infections; at most 137 infectious, on day 74



msim = sim.run(solver='gillespie', n_runs=50)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 50 runs
  Done in 3.4 s









sim.run(n_runs=50) runs it 50 times, each with its own random seed (the same as ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=50)). The ODE gave one outbreak peaking at about 137 infectious on day 74. The plot of the runs shows their median at each time point, and the range that holds 95% of them. lines=True shows each run instead, which shows what the median hides:

msim.plot('measles.I', lines=True)








Some runs die out at once, and the others take off at different times. With five cases at the start and R = 1.5, branching-process theory gives a chance of (1/1.5)⁵ ≈ 13% that all five chains of transmission end by chance, something the ODE cannot show (the first line the ODE run printed says so). For more on the chance that an introduction takes off, see Branching and rescaling.

The median outbreak has about 1,150 infections, while the interval runs from almost none (the runs that died out) to about 1,330. A summary of a total is a summary over whole epidemics: each run gives one number. interval=0.5 gives the interquartile range instead.
The band in the plot is different: it is the spread of the runs at each time point, taken separately. The median curve is not a typical epidemic, since the runs peak at different times, and at each time point the median mixes runs that are rising, peaking, and over. Its peak is lower than the peak of most runs:

peaks = msim.summarize(how={'measles_I': 'max'}).loc['measles_I'] # The peak of each run, summarized
print('Median of the peaks:', peaks['median'])
print('Peak of the median curve:', msim.results.measles.I.median().max())

Median of the peaks: 137.5
Peak of the median curve: 109.0


So for a question about the size or timing of the peak, summarize the peak of each run (as above), not the median curve; for a question about how many people are infected on a given date, the band at each time point is the answer. The usual summaries of a result over the runs are built in:
res = msim.results.measles.I
res.values                       # Every run: one row per run, one column per time point
res.median()                     # The median at each time point
low, mid, high = res.quantiles() # The 2.5%, 50%, and 97.5% quantiles at each time point
res.quantiles([0.25, 0.5, 0.75]) # Other quantiles
res.mean()                       # The mean at each time point
res.take(3)                      # One run, as the result of a single sim
Each summary is over the runs of each scenario separately. With several scenarios, low, mid, high = res.quantiles() still works: each is a result with a row per scenario, and select(scenario='Campaign in February') picks one. msim.to_df() gives every result as quantiles over the runs at each time, as one long table, for saving or plotting elsewhere.

How many runs
The interval is estimated from the runs, so with few runs its ends are uncertain themselves. The ends of a 95% interval rest on the most extreme 2.5% of runs at each end: one run in 40. With 500 runs:

many = sim.run(solver='gillespie', n_runs=500)
many.summarize().loc['measles_infection']

MultiSim: 500 runs
  Done in 17.9 s


median    1159.000000
low          1.000000
high      1318.150000
mean      1001.738000
std        414.325352
Name: measles_infection, dtype: float64


Here the summary of 50 runs was already close to this. In general, the median settles with a few tens of runs, while the ends of the interval rest on few runs each, and move most from one set of runs to the next. As a rough guide, 20 to 50 runs are enough for a median and the shape of the spread, and a few hundred for the ends of a 95% interval. Stochastic compartmental runs are fast, so many runs are cheap; for agents, it may be worth starting with fewer.

title: Scenarios
text:
Comparing scenarios with many runs
Comparing two scenarios run many times, the question is whether the difference between them is larger than the difference chance alone would make. Starsim helps in two ways.
First, the runs of each scenario use the same seeds in the same order (the first run of each with seed 1, the second with seed 2, and so on), so the first run of the baseline and the first run of the campaign share their random numbers: the same people are infected by the same chains of transmission, until the campaign changes them. Starsim makes sure that a random number goes to the same use in both runs, even when the intervention changes how many draws are made (common random numbers; see Random numbers). The difference between paired runs is then mostly the effect of the intervention, not noise.
Second, msim.diff() gives the difference of each scenario from a baseline, run by run, and msim.summarize(baseline=...) summarizes those differences. Here are the February campaign and the baseline from above, each run 20 times with the chain binomial (solver='binomial'):

scenarios = {
    'No campaign': base.new(solver='binomial', verbose=0),
    'Campaign in February': base.new(solver='binomial', interventions=february, verbose=0),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, n_runs=20)
msim.plot('measles.I')









msim.summarize(baseline='No campaign').loc['measles_infection']

The difference in infections is negative, about −520: the campaign averts about 520 infections, with 95% of runs between about 340 and 630. msim.diff() gives the differences themselves, run by run, as results; here, the infections averted so far at each point in time:

averted = -msim.diff('No campaign')['Campaign in February'].measles.infection.cum # Infections averted so far, in each pair of runs
averted.plot()








To see what pairing buys, compare the paired runs with the same scenarios given different seeds (rand_seed=1000 for the campaign), so that the runs are not paired:

def averted_by(msim):
    """ Infections averted by the campaign by the end, with the 95% interval over the runs """
    averted = -msim.diff('No campaign')['Campaign in February'].measles.infection.cum
    low, mid, high = averted.quantiles()
    print('Infections averted:', round(mid[-1]), 'with 95% of runs between', round(low[-1]), 'and', round(high[-1]))

unpaired = ss.parallel({
    'No campaign': scenarios['No campaign'],
    'Campaign in February': scenarios['Campaign in February'].new(rand_seed=1000),
}, n_runs=20)

print('Paired:  ', end=' '); averted_by(msim)
print('Unpaired:', end=' '); averted_by(unpaired)

Paired:   Infections averted: 516 with 95% of runs between 343 and 631
Unpaired: Infections averted: 514 with 95% of runs between 245 and 603


The estimate of the effect is about the same, but its interval is wider when the runs are not paired, since the difference then includes the chance differences between two unrelated outbreaks. Pairing is what makes a small effect visible in few runs. Paired runs need the same model apart from the intervention: a change to anything else (the population size, the time step) breaks the pairing.

title: Scenarios
text:
Parameter sweeps
To see how a result depends on a parameter, run the sim with each of a set of values. pars= takes a list of values for each parameter, and each value is a scenario of its own, labeled with it. Here the outbreak with β from 1.5 to 2.3 per day (R0 from 12 to 18):

sim = base.new(label='', verbose=0) # Back to 50 infectious at the start; base took the label 'No campaign' from ss.parallel() above
msim = ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(beta=[1.5, 1.9, 2.3]))
msim.plot('measles.I')









msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']








value


scenario





beta=1.5
720.454008


beta=1.9
1189.910076


beta=2.3
1467.045386







The parameter is named as it is in the model: here beta, the name of the ss.par() it was given (describe() lists the names). When there is more than one disease, give the disease too, e.g. pars={'measles.beta': [1.5, 2.3]}. The values become columns of msim.runs, the table of runs, and a result can be picked by value: msim.results.measles.I.select(beta=2.3).
Several parameters given together are taken value by value (the first value of each together, then the second, and so on), so each needs the same number of values; for other sets, give a list of dicts, one per set (pars=[dict(beta=1.5, dur=ss.days(6)), dict(beta=2.3, dur=ss.days(8))], where dur is the infectious period). For a full grid of two parameters, build the list of dicts with a loop. n_runs= runs each set that many times, with the same seeds for each set, so the sets are compared with the same chance events. A seed given in pars= (rand_seed=[1, 2, 1, 2] next to beta=[1.5, 1.5, 2.3, 2.3]) is a run of its scenario, not a scenario of its own.
A sweep gives each value equal space, but that does not say they are equally likely. To carry the uncertainty in a parameter into the results instead, draw its value afresh for each run (next).

title: Scenarios
text:
Uncertainty in parameter values
Chance is one source of uncertainty; not knowing the parameters is another. A parameter declared with ss.par() and bounds (or a prior) can be drawn afresh for each run with priors=True: each run takes a value drawn uniformly between the bounds (or from the prior), and a seed of its own, so the spread of the runs includes both. Here β is between 1.5 and 2.3 per day (R0 between 12 and 18), with the five initial cases from before, compared with the same runs with β fixed:

beta = ss.par(1.9, bounds=[1.5, 2.3]) # β, known to lie between these values
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=5))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), solver='gillespie', verbose=0)
fixed = ss.parallel(sim.new(label='Beta fixed at 1.9'), n_runs=50)
drawn = ss.parallel(sim.new(label='Beta drawn between 1.5 and 2.3'), priors=True, n_runs=50)

After a model is fitted to data, the values found by the fit can be carried into a projection the same way (fit.project(); see Fitting a model). To see how the results depend on each value in turn, rather than all at once, sweep the parameter instead (above).

title: Scenarios
text:
Seeds
Every stochastic run starts from a random seed (rand_seed, 1 by default), and the same seed gives the same run, on any computer:

binomial = base.new(solver='binomial', verbose=0)
a = binomial.new(rand_seed=1).run()
b = binomial.new(rand_seed=1).run()
c = binomial.new(rand_seed=2).run()
print('Infections with seeds 1, 1, and 2:', a.results.measles.infection.sum(), b.results.measles.infection.sum(), c.results.measles.infection.sum())

Infections with seeds 1, 1, and 2: 1264.0 1264.0 1269.0


n_runs=k uses the seeds rand_seed, rand_seed + 1, …, rand_seed + k − 1, so the first of many runs is the same as a single run, and any run can be made again on its own: run i (counting from 0) of a sim with seed 1 is the sim with rand_seed=1 + i. To run particular seeds, give them as a sweep: ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(rand_seed=[1, 5, 9])), which gives three runs of the sim’s scenario (not three scenarios). msim.runs, the table of runs, gives the seed of each run (rand_seed), so a run that stands out can be made again on its own. An ODE has no random numbers, so its seed changes nothing.

title: Scenarios
text:
Combining runs, copies, and memory
msim.combine() adds the runs together into one sim, as if they were one population: counts are summed, and other results (such as prevalence) are averaged, weighted by each sim’s population. It is a way to treat several smaller runs of agents as one larger population, with no uncertainty bounds since the result is a single sim; the people are not joined, so the combined sim cannot be run on. ss.MultiSim.merge(m1, m2) puts the runs of several MultiSims together into one, one after the other, and msim.split() splits them again (or, for a MultiSim that was not merged, into the runs given by inds= or chunks=).
A sim copies the modules it is given, so the same disease or intervention can be given to several sims, as above. ss.parallel(), on the other hand, runs the sims it is given as they are, so after ss.parallel(scenarios), each sim in scenarios has its results (with n_runs=, the runs are new sims, and the sims given are not run). inplace=False runs copies instead. A sim given in a dict takes the label it is given there.
By default, ss.parallel() keeps the results of each run but not the people in it, which keeps memory use down when there are many runs. For many thousands of runs, keep only what you need from each: msim.summarize(), msim.to_df(), or a function of each sim, saved as a table, rather than the MultiSim itself. ss.converters.to_hub() writes runs as the quantile tables that forecasting hubs take.
ss.parallel() runs the sims in separate processes. In a script (rather than a notebook), on Windows and macOS, put the code that runs them under if __name__ == '__main__':, as Python’s multiprocessing requires; and on a system that cannot start processes, ss.parallel(..., parallel=False) runs the same sims one after the other. For larger studies, build the sims with a make_sim() function (see Running sims), and for running them on a cluster, see Deployment.

title: Scenarios
text:
Pitfalls

Scenarios that differ in more than the intervention. Make each scenario from the same base with sim.new(), so that everything else, including the seed, is the same.
Comparing medians instead of differences. The difference between the medians of two scenarios is not the median difference; use msim.diff() for the effect of an intervention, run by run.
The median curve is not a typical epidemic. For the size or timing of the peak, summarize each run’s peak.
Runs that die out pull the summary down. If the question is about outbreaks that take off, look at those runs (e.g. lines=True), and report the chance of dying out separately.
Too few runs for the ends of an interval. Use a few hundred for a 95% interval that you will report.
Reading a band as a confidence interval for a parameter. The band over runs with fixed values is the spread due to chance alone; it says nothing about how well β is known unless the runs drew β too (priors=True).
