title: Modules
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Everything a sim runs, apart from the people themselves, is a module: each disease, network, demographic process, intervention, connector and analyzer. This page explains what a module is, what happens to it from the moment it is given to a sim to the end of the run, how declared modules and modules written as code live side by side, how modules find each other, and how to read the loop that calls them. It is the view from inside; for how to write a module of your own, see Custom modules and the tutorials T9 and A5.

title: Modules
text:
What a module is
A module is an instance of ss.Module (starsim/internals/modules.py), or of a subclass. Every module has the same parts:

a name (sir, randomnet), unique in the sim, and a label for plots;
its parameters, mod.pars (an ss.Pars), given with define_pars() and set from the user’s arguments with update_pars(), which raises an error for one that wasn’t defined;
its timeline, mod.t (an ss.Timeline), which is the sim’s unless the module is given a dt, start or stop of its own;
its distributions, each with a random number stream of its own, found by searching the module when the sim is initialized (Randomness);
its states, arrays with one value per agent (define_states()), which the people grow and shrink with the population;
its results, mod.results, one ss.Result per quantity per time point; every ss.BoolState gets a count of the same name without being declared;
a link to the sim, mod.sim, set when the sim is initialized.

A few attributes are locked (pars, t, sim, dists, results, and each state), so that self.I = ... in a step raises an error instead of quietly replacing the array: the error suggests self.I[:] = ....
What kind of module it is decides only where in each step it is called, and where the sim keeps it. The kinds are the subclasses in ss.modules.module_map(), which is the one place that says what they are:



Kind
Base class
Kept in
Examples




Diseases
ss.Disease
sim.diseases
a declared ss.Disease, ss.SIR, ss.Infection and its subclasses, ssl.HIV


Networks
ss.networks.Route
sim.networks
ss.RandomNet, ss.SexualNet, ss.MixingPool


Demographics
ss.Demographics
sim.demographics
ss.Births, ss.Deaths, ss.Pregnancy


Interventions
ss.Intervention
sim.interventions
ss.vaccinate, ss.screen, ss.treat (deliveries, which hold products)


Connectors
ss.Connector
sim.connectors
ss.modify


Analyzers
ss.Analyzer
sim.analyzers
ss.infection_log, or a function of the sim


Custom
ss.Module, or anything that is none of the above
sim.custom
a module of your own



A module can be more than one kind: ss.Pregnancy is both a demographic module and a declared disease, so it adds people and has states and transitions; a delivery such as ss.screen is an intervention that is also a source of events (the people it reached, screening, and its outcomes, screening.positive), which other deliveries can be triggered by. A product (ss.Vaccine) is a module too, but it has no step of its own: it is held by the delivery that gives it, and listed by sim.products().
Modules can be given to a sim by keyword (diseases=, networks=, …), as positional arguments, which the sim sorts by kind, or by name as strings (diseases='sis', networks='random'), which ss.modules.find_modules() looks up among Starsim’s classes and any registered with ss.register_modules(). A module given no name is named after its class in lower case, and numbered if two would clash (randomnet, randomnet_1).

import starsim as ss

def make_sir():
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    return ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ ss.perday(0.3) * I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(10), init_prev=0.01, name='sir')

sim = ss.Sim(
    make_sir(),
    networks      = ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4),
    demographics  = [ss.Births(), ss.Deaths()],
    interventions = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.5, at=[ss.days(20)]),
    analyzers     = ss.infection_log(),
    n_agents = 2000,
    unit     = 'day',
    stop     = ss.days(60),
    verbose  = 0,
)
sim.init()
for mod in sim.modules:
    print(f'{mod.name:15} {type(mod).__name__}')

births          Births
deaths          Deaths
randomnet       RandomNet
vaccinate       vaccinate
vaccine         Vaccine
sir             Disease
infection_log   infection_log


sim.modules lists every module of the sim in the order they are initialized: demographics, connectors, networks, interventions, products, diseases, custom modules, and analyzers. (The vaccine is there because the delivery made it.)

title: Modules
text:
The lifecycle
A module goes through four stages: it is made, initialized with the sim, stepped, and finalized. Every stage is a method that a subclass can override, calling super() to keep what the base class does.
Made. __init__() stores what the module was given: its parameters, states, and, for a declared disease, its states and transitions, which are built into its graph (Model declaration). Nothing is linked to a sim yet. When a module is given to a sim, the sim copies it, so one module can go into several sims; the copy is the one that runs, which is why a change to the original after the sim is made (adding a callback, say) raises an error saying to make it on sim.diseases.<name> instead.
Initialized. sim.init() (Model execution) chooses the solver first, since that decides which objects exist, and then initializes the modules in two passes:

init_pre(sim), for each module in turn: link it to the sim, set up its timeline, link its time parameters to its dt (so that self.pars.dur.to_dt() works without arguments), check its bare numbers against the sim’s unit, add its parameters to sim.pars and its results to sim.results, add it and its states to the people (sim.people.add_module()), and make its results (init_results()). A declared disease first makes its engine, the object that will run its transitions under the chosen solver.
Then the sim initializes every distribution, gives the people their starting values, and calls init_post() on each module, which gives each state its initial values (and, for a declared disease, its initial conditions: who starts infected).

After that, the loop is built, and the parameters are locked, so setting one that doesn’t exist raises an error.
Stepped. Each step, the loop calls the module’s methods at its kind’s place in the order:








Method
Called for
What it is for




start_step()
every module
moving the random number streams on to this step; a declared disease’s engine prepares the step


step()
custom modules, then demographics
what the module does; births add agents, and deaths are requested


step_state()
diseases
state changes of a disease written as code, before the networks and interventions (a declared disease takes all its transitions in step())


step()
connectors, then networks, then interventions
changes to other modules, edges, deliveries


step()
diseases
transmission, and every transition of a declared disease


step_die(uids)
diseases, through people.step_die()
what happens to the agents who die this step (they leave every state)


update_results()
every module, after the people
recording the step’s results


step()
analyzers
reading the finished step


finish_step()
every module, then the people
tidying up; dead agents are removed



A method that is sure to do nothing in this sim (the base class’s own update_results() for a module with nothing to count, say) is left out of the plan, so it costs nothing. At the first time point there is no step: the loop records the starting values, and the analyzers run once to see them.
Finalized. After the last step, finalize() calls finalize_results() on each module, which scales the results that count people by the number of people each agent stands for. A module can override finalize_results() to work out results from others; it calls super().finalize_results() first. A module that has been finalized can’t be stepped again: running it again raises ss.AlreadyRunError, which says to copy it first.
Forgetting to call super() is the commonest mistake in writing a module, so the base class’s methods that must be called are marked with @ss.required(). After a run, sim.check_method_calls() warns about any that weren’t, naming the method and the module.

title: Modules
section: Declared modules and modules written as code
text:
Declared modules and modules written as code
A disease can be declared (states and transitions), written as code (arrays and a step_state() and step() of its own), or both. The difference is in what the module hands to its engine:

A declared disease’s graph is run by its engine, ss.solvers.Agents or ss.solvers.Compartmental, made by ss.solvers.make_engine(). ss.Disease.step() is three calls to the engine: the transitions that are not contact-mediated, then those that are, then any functions of the model. No method of ss.Disease asks which solver it has.
A disease written as code (an ss.Infection subclass, or an ss.Disease that declares nothing) gets an engine that has nothing to run (ss.solvers.Undeclared), so super().step() is harmless, and its own code does the work. An ss.Infection transmits through the same code a declared disease uses as agents (ss.solvers.Transmission), so modifiers and products act on it in the same way.
A class can be both: declared states and transitions, plus code in step() after super().step() has taken them, reading or writing arrays of its own.

Every other kind of module is written as code (apart from the deliveries and modifiers, which are declared in their own way, by keywords). So a sim is often a mixture, and Starsim has to decide whether it can run as compartments. It never runs code to find out. Instead it looks at what each module written as code keeps (init_capabilities() in starsim/solvers/choose.py):

A module that keeps a value for each person (any array given with define_states()) needs agents, since only agents have one value per person.
So does one that adds and removes agents (ss.Births, ss.Deaths; a declared disease’s ss.birth() and ss.death() are their compartmental form), and an individual-level network.
A module can say for itself: compartmental = True on the class says its code works on groups too, and compartmental = False that it needs agents.
Anything else (code that keeps nothing per person, whatever its kind) runs beside the compartments, called at its place in the loop like any other module. If its code then asks for something only agents have (people.age in a model not stratified by age, say), it raises an ss.CapabilityError that says so.

A sim made only of such modules has no agents at all, so an ODE written by hand in NumPy, as a custom module, runs as just that. Here are two small custom modules beside the same declared SIR: one keeps a single number for the whole population, the other a number for each person:

class Alarm(ss.Module):
    """ Count the days on which more than 5% of people are infectious: nothing per person """
    def __init__(self, threshold=0.05, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_pars(threshold=threshold)
        self.days_over = 0

    def step(self):
        sir = self.sim.diseases.sir
        if sir.I.n > self.pars.threshold*self.sim.people.alive.sum():
            self.days_over += 1

class Exposure(ss.Module):
    """ Count each person's days infectious: one value per person """
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(ss.FloatArr('days_infectious', default=0))

    def step(self):
        infectious = self.sim.diseases.sir.I.uids
        self.days_infectious[infectious] += 1

for mod in [None, Alarm(), Exposure()]:
    sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(), custom=mod, unit='day', stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0)
    sim.init()
    label = type(mod).__name__ if mod else 'No module'
    print(f'{label}: {sim.solver}, since {sim.solver_reason}')

No module: ode, since every part of the model has a compartmental form
Alarm: ode, since every part of the model has a compartmental form
Exposure: abm, since "exposure" (Exposure) keeps a value for each person (days_infectious), which only agents have; if its code works on groups, set compartmental = True on it


The SIR alone and the SIR with Alarm run as an ODE; Exposure makes the sim run as agents, and the reason names it and says how to change that. Alarm still costs something: a compartmental run is usually taken by the kernels in one call, with no Python loop, but a module with a step of its own makes the run go step by step, and sim.kernel_reason() says so:

sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(), custom=Alarm(), unit='day', stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0)
sim.init()
sim.kernel_reason()

'alarm has a step of its own (a module written as code)'


The same Alarm runs as agents too, unchanged: sir.I.n is the number infectious either way, so the module doesn’t need to know which solver it is in.

for kw in [dict(), dict(n_agents=5000)]:
    sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(), custom=Alarm(), unit='day', stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0, **kw).run()
    print(f'{sim.solver}: {sim.custom.alarm.days_over} days with more than 5% infectious')

ode: 49 days with more than 5% infectious
abm: 51 days with more than 5% infectious


The two agree to within a few days, the difference being the chance in a run of 5,000 agents.

title: Modules
text:
How modules find each other
Modules don’t hold references to each other: a module reaches the rest of the sim through self.sim, at run time, which is always the sim’s own copy. The sim offers several ways in, all to the same objects:



To reach
Write
Notes




A module, by kind and name
self.sim.diseases.sir, self.sim.networks.randomnet
the usual way; each kind is an ss.ndict, so sim.diseases[0] works too


A module, by name alone
self.sim.sir
if the name is unique and isn’t an attribute of the sim


A module through the people
self.sim.people.sir
the people hold every module with states


A state by its full name
self.sim.people.states['sir.I']
every module’s states, flat, as <module>.<state>


A property of people
self.sim.people.age, or ss.ppl.age in a condition written before the sim exists
ss.ppl is a lazy reference, evaluated when it is needed


A result
self.sim.results.sir.I, self.sim.diseases.sir.results.I
the same object: a module’s results are nested in the sim’s


The time
self.ti, self.now, self.t.dt
the module’s own; with a timeline of its own, self.ti counts its own steps



States are shared by reading them: any module can read sir.I or another module’s array, and the arrays always have one value per agent alive, in the same order, since the people grow and shrink them all together. A property of people that several modules use (a measure of wealth, say) can be added once with people.add_state() and read by all of them. Writing is a different matter. A module can write into another’s arrays (an intervention that cures people sets sir.I[uids] = False), and for a declared disease the write is tracked so its counts stay right, but Starsim can’t see what was changed or why. The declared alternative is ss.modify, which never overwrites anything: it keeps the quantity’s base value and applies itself on top, so modifiers can’t clobber each other, and sim.what_modifies() can list them (Transmission). To move people between a declared disease’s states, ss.move() does it the same way under every solver.
An array that most agents never change (a relative susceptibility that is 1 until something sets it) can be made with shared=True, which takes no memory per agent until a value is set; ss.Infection’s rel_sus and rel_trans are made this way.

title: Modules
text:
Reading the loop
The loop (sim.loop, an ss.Loop in starsim/internals/loop.py) is built at the end of sim.init() by Loop.collect_funcs(), which walks the sim’s modules in the order above and collects each method to call. Its plan is every (time, method) pair, sorted by time and then by that order; a module with a timeline of its own appears only at its own times. sim.loop.to_df() gives the plan as a table, so the order can always be checked rather than remembered. For the sim above, as agents, one step is:

sim = ss.Sim(
    make_sir(),
    networks      = ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4),
    demographics  = [ss.Births(), ss.Deaths()],
    interventions = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.5, at=[ss.days(20)]),
    analyzers     = ss.infection_log(),
    n_agents = 2000,
    unit     = 'day',
    stop     = ss.days(60),
    verbose  = 0,
)
sim.init()
df = sim.loop.to_df()
df[df.ti == 1][['label', 'module', 'func_name']]

Each row is one call. The rows that are missing are the ones left out because they would do nothing: the analyzer’s start_step(), and every module’s finish_step(), which none of these overrides. The first time point (ti == 0) has only the rows that record the start: the people’s and modules’ results (except the intervention’s, which has done nothing yet) and the analyzer.
Three more tools work on the same plan:

sim.loop.insert(fn, label='sir.step') adds a function of the sim after a given call (or before=True), at every time or only those that match_fn= picks; given a module of the sim instead of a function, it moves that module’s step() there. It is the way to put code at a point that no kind of module runs at.
sim.run(profile=True) times every call, and sim.loop.plot_cpu() shows where the time went, by module and method; sim.loop.plot() draws the plan itself.
sim.check_dt() reruns the sim at half the step, which shows how much the order (and every other effect of the step’s length) moves the results.

A compartmental run that is taken by the kernels in one call doesn’t use the plan at all, which is why it is made only when it is first needed.

title: Modules
text:
Limits

The order between kinds is fixed. There are no priorities or phases; within a kind, modules run in the order given. A module that must run at another point is moved there with sim.loop.insert().
What code does to another module isn’t recorded. describe() and what_modifies() see declarations, not the writes of a step().
Whether code needs agents is decided by what it keeps, not what it does. A module with no states that still reads per-agent values in a compartmental run is caught only when it first asks for them, part way into the run.

title: Modules
text:
In the design record

Objects and construction: ss.Sim, the lifecycle, and the module contract
Execution: the loop, deferred removals, and per-module timesteps
Backends: how a model is laid out for each solver, and what needs agents

title: Modules
text:
Further reading

Mesa: Model and Agent: a general agent-based framework in which behavior lives on agent classes, where Starsim puts it on modules acting on arrays of agents
Vivarium: The builder: how a component-based microsimulation gives each component access to the rest of the simulation during setup
EMOD: Reporter component: how IDM’s agent-based model collects output, the role analyzers play in Starsim

title: Diseases
text:
🧠50% 🤖50%
Core Starsim (import starsim as ss) provides the framework and its generic building blocks: ss.Disease, ss.SIR, ss.RandomNet, ss.Pregnancy, and so on. The Starsim library (import starsim.library as ssl) is a separate collection of specific modules built on those: particular diseases such as measles and cholera (this page), specialized networks such as households (Library: networks), and worked examples of harder modeling patterns such as congenital infection (Library: maternal-child health).
The library ships with Starsim, but is held to a lower bar than the core package. Its modules are illustrative rather than validated: parameter values are indicative, some are placeholders, and their interfaces may change between versions. Treat them as starting points to copy and adapt, not as ready-made models of a particular setting.
Most library modules are written as code (see Custom modules): each has a step() that updates its agents directly, so they run as agents, under the agent-based solver only. The measles of the tutorials, by contrast, is declared as states and transitions, which run under any solver (see Diseases). The library’s ssl.Measles is a fuller agent-based model, with deaths and its own parameters.

title: Diseases
text:
Using library modules
Library classes are available both at the top level and through their submodule; the two are the same objects:

import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

print(ssl.Measles is ssl.diseases.Measles)

True


Otherwise they behave like core modules, and can be mixed freely with them, here a library disease on a core network:

outbreak = dict(start='2000', dur=ss.years(1), n_agents=2000)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.Measles(beta=ss.perday(0.3)), networks=ss.RandomNet(), **outbreak)
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles')

Sim: measles, as 2,000 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2001-01-01


  Done in 0.31 s















ImportantOutbreak diseases need a step of days



The library’s outbreak diseases give their natural history in days: incubation periods of a week or two, and illness lasting days. Starsim chooses a step of a day for them, from the units of their durations. With a step of a year (dt=ss.years(1)), those durations are shorter than a step, and the dynamics are meaningless: ssl.Cholera, for example, then gives no infections at all, because its environmental reservoir never has time to build up. See Time for more on steps.


The library has two groups of diseases. The first, below, are written as code, so they run as agents: five example diseases, from a simple outbreak to a chronic infection and a disease that is not transmitted, plus an SIR, SIS, and SEIR written as code. The second, further down, are declared as states and transitions, each a short version of a published model, so they run as compartments or as agents.



Class
Based on

Measles as an SEIR model, with natural history parameters from the US CDC

Ebola, with severe disease and continued transmission from unburied bodies

Cholera, with symptomatic and asymptomatic infection, plus indirect transmission through a decaying environmental reservoir

HIV, with CD4 counts, deaths that depend on them, and transmission from mother to child

Antiretroviral therapy for ssl.HIV, scaled up over the years given

Records every agent’s CD4 count at every step, for ssl.HIV

A non-communicable disease: a risk factor, the condition, and death from it; not transmitted

title: Diseases
section: Outbreak diseases: measles, Ebola, and cholera
text:
Outbreak diseases: measles, Ebola, and cholera
The three diseases with a latent period build on ssl.AgentSEIR, which moves agents from S to E to I to R. Measles only sets parameter values: a latent period of about 8 days, an infectious period of about 11, and a probability of death of 0.5%. Ebola and Cholera also replace set_progression(), for their fuller natural histories (severe disease and burial; symptoms and shedding), while keeping the transitions between states and the counting of new infections. All three have placeholder values of beta, so give one suited to the network.
Ebola gives each case a chance of severe disease (p_sev) and of death (p_death); severe cases transmit more (sev_factor), and so do the bodies of those who have died until they are buried (unburied_factor), unless they are buried safely, which happens with probability p_safe_bury. Comparing the default, a quarter of burials safe, with every burial safe shows how much the funerals add to an epidemic. Since this epidemic is close to its threshold, chance matters, so each scenario is run 5 times, and the plot shows the median and the range:

ebola = lambda p_safe_bury: ssl.Ebola(beta=ss.perday(0.008), p_safe_bury=p_safe_bury)
scenarios = {
    'A quarter of burials safe': ss.Sim(diseases=ebola(0.25), networks=ss.RandomNet(), **outbreak),
    'Every burial safe':         ss.Sim(diseases=ebola(1.0),  networks=ss.RandomNet(), **outbreak),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, n_runs=5, parallel=False)
msim.plot(['ebola.infectious', 'ebola.infection.cum'])

MultiSim: 10 runs of 2 scenarios (A quarter of burials safe, Every burial safe)
  Done in 4.8 s









In these runs, burying every body safely cuts the infections over the year by about a quarter.
Cholera adds environmental transmission to the usual transmission from person to person, by extending infect(): infectious people shed bacteria into a shared reservoir (at shedding_rate, asymptomatic people much less), the bacteria die off (at decay_rate), and susceptible people are infected by the water with a probability that rises with the concentration, reaching half of beta_env at half_sat_rate. This is the pattern to follow for any waterborne, vector-borne, or otherwise indirectly transmitted disease. Turning off the environmental route (beta_env=0) shows how much of the epidemic it carries:

cholera = lambda **kwargs: ssl.Cholera(beta=ss.perday(0.02), **kwargs)
scenarios = {
    'Person to person and water': ss.Sim(diseases=cholera(),           networks=ss.RandomNet(), **outbreak),
    'Person to person only':      ss.Sim(diseases=cholera(beta_env=0), networks=ss.RandomNet(), **outbreak),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, parallel=False)
msim.plot(['cholera.infectious', 'cholera.infection.cum', 'cholera.env_conc'])

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Person to person and water, Person to person only)
  Done in 0.81 s









With these values, transmission from person to person alone barely sustains itself, and the reservoir turns a small outbreak into a large one. The results env_prev (the share of people shedding) and env_conc (the concentration of bacteria) track the reservoir.

title: Diseases
text:
HIV, treatment, and CD4 counts
ssl.HIV comes with two companion modules that show how a disease, an intervention, and an analyzer fit together:

ssl.ART is an intervention that scales up treatment coverage over the years given, reducing transmission by art_efficacy and raising CD4 counts back towards cd4_max.
ssl.CD4_analyzer is an analyzer that records every agent’s CD4 count at every step, in a dense array of steps by agents (so it suits small sims).

Since deaths from HIV depend on CD4 counts, treatment reduces deaths as well as transmission. Unlike the outbreak diseases above, HIV plays out over years, so steps of a year and a span of decades suit it:

endemic = dict(start='2000', stop='2030', dt=ss.years(1), n_agents=2000)
hiv = lambda: ssl.HIV(beta=ss.peryear(0.05), init_prev=0.05)
net = lambda: ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=ss.poisson(2))
art = ssl.ART(year=[2005, 2015], coverage=[0, 0.9]) # Coverage rising from 0 in 2005 to 90% in 2015

scenarios = {
    'No ART':   ss.Sim(diseases=hiv(), networks=net(), analyzers=ssl.CD4_analyzer(), **endemic),
    'With ART': ss.Sim(diseases=hiv(), networks=net(), analyzers=ssl.CD4_analyzer(), interventions=art, **endemic),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, parallel=False)
msim.plot(['hiv.prevalence', 'hiv.death'])

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (No ART, With ART)
  Done in 0.59 s









The deaths over the whole run, and the prevalence in 2030 (the final value), for each scenario:

summary = msim.summarize()
summary.loc[['hiv_death', 'hiv_prevalence']]

Each sim’s analyzer holds the CD4 counts of every agent. The mean count among those infected falls without treatment, and recovers as treatment is scaled up:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig = plt.figure()
for label, sim in zip(scenarios, msim.sims):
    cd4 = sim.analyzers.cd4_analyzer.cd4 # Steps by agents
    infected = cd4 < sim.diseases.hiv.pars.cd4_max # Uninfected agents keep the maximum count
    mean_cd4 = np.array([row[inf].mean() if inf.any() else np.nan for row, inf in zip(cd4, infected)])
    plt.plot(sim.t.yearvec, mean_cd4, label=label)
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Mean CD4 count of those infected')
plt.legend()
plt.show()














Note



ART offers treatment only to agents infected at least art_delay ago, so it has no effect once an epidemic has saturated and no one is newly infected. If the number on treatment (n_art) stays at zero, check that transmission is still going on when treatment starts.

title: Diseases
text:
A non-communicable disease
ssl.NCD is not transmitted, so it needs no network. Each agent starts at risk with probability initial_risk; those at risk develop the condition after a time drawn from dur_risk, and die of it after a time drawn from prognosis. Its results are the number at risk, the prevalence of the condition, and the deaths from it. Halving the share who start at risk, as a stand-in for a policy on a risk factor such as smoking, halves the cases and deaths that follow:

chronic = dict(start='2000', stop='2040', dt=ss.years(1), n_agents=2000, demographics=[ss.Births(), ss.Deaths()])
scenarios = {
    '30% at risk': ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.NCD(initial_risk=0.3),  **chronic),
    '15% at risk': ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.NCD(initial_risk=0.15), **chronic),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, parallel=False)
msim.plot(['ncd.prevalence', 'ncd.death'])

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (30% at risk, 15% at risk)
  Done in 0.094 s









Only the starting population is ever at risk here, so the condition dies out with them; a model of a real risk factor would put newborns and others at risk too, which is a change of init_post() and step() (see Adapting a library module).

title: Diseases
section: SIR, SIS, and SEIR written as code
text:
SIR, SIS, and SEIR written as code
The core ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR are declared, as states and transitions, so they run under any solver; they are the textbook models, with exponential durations and no deaths unless p_death is given. ssl.AgentSIR, ssl.AgentSIS, and ssl.AgentSEIR are Starsim 3’s versions of the same models, written as code: durations are lognormal (dur_inf=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(6)) by default), and AgentSIR and AgentSEIR have p_death=0.01. They schedule each course in whole steps as the agent engine does a declared disease’s, so each case, seeds included, is infectious for dur_inf on average (in Starsim 3, each case was half a step short, and the seeds half a step long). AgentSIS also has a level of immunity for each agent, boosted by each infection (imm_boost) and waning exponentially (waning), which lowers that agent’s susceptibility. They are the classes to build on for a disease that changes how infection, progression, or recovery happens for each agent, as the outbreak diseases above do; a Starsim 3 subclass of ss.SIR that replaces its methods can build on ssl.AgentSIR instead, unchanged (see Starsim v3).
With the same mean duration and no deaths, the two SIRs differ only in the shape of the duration: the lognormal of AgentSIR (with a standard deviation of one year) makes almost every infection last about 6 years, while the exponential of ss.SIR has many short infections and a few very long ones. Fewer people recover early on, so the epidemic of AgentSIR peaks higher and ends more sharply:

pars = dict(beta=ss.peryear(0.1), init_prev=0.01, p_death=0)
sir_pars = dict(start='2000', stop='2040', dt=ss.months(1), n_agents=2000, networks=ss.RandomNet())
declared = ss.Sim(diseases=ss.SIR(**pars), **sir_pars).run()
as_code = ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.AgentSIR(**pars), **sir_pars).run()

fig = plt.figure()
plt.plot(declared.t.yearvec, declared.results.sir.I, label='ss.SIR (declared, exponential duration)')
plt.plot(as_code.t.yearvec, as_code.results.agentsir.infected, label='ssl.AgentSIR (code, lognormal duration)')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Number infected')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Sim: sir, as 2,000 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2040-01-01
  Running as agents: n_agents was given


  Done in 0.39 s; sir: 1,975 infections; at most 1,102 infectious, on 2007-10-01


Sim: agentsir, as 2,000 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2040-01-01


  Done in 0.3 s









Their results are named differently: the declared model’s are named after its states (I) and transitions (infection), while the version written as code has Starsim 3’s names for its states (infected), and the same infection.

title: Diseases
text:
Declared diseases
The rest of the library’s diseases are declared, as states and transitions (Diseases), so each runs as a compartmental model or as agents. Each is a short version of a published model, with its default parameters from that source, named for the disease rather than for the model, so the source is given here and in each class’s docstring. They are still illustrative: each is the simplest version of its model that shows what makes it interesting, and none has been fitted to a particular place.








Class
What it shows
The model, and where the parameters come from




ssl.Malaria
A vector: people and mosquitoes in one model, the mosquitoes as counts rather than people
The Ross-Macdonald model, in the form of Keeling MJ, Rohani P, Modeling Infectious Diseases in Humans and Animals, Princeton University Press, 2008, Program 4.4, which gives every parameter


ssl.MalariaImmunity
Immunity that builds with exposure: inoculation that saturates, superinfection, and a faster recovery once immune
The Garki model of Dietz K, Molineaux L, Thomas A, Bull World Health Organ 1974;50:347-357, as given in Molineaux L, Gramiccia G, The Garki Project, WHO, 1980, ch. 10, Table 31


ssl.TB
A spectrum of disease, with movement back and forth between states and reinfection
The LSHTM model of Schwalb A et al., PLOS Glob Public Health 2025;5(1):e0005050, in the form of TBsim’s reference ODE (lshtm_ode.R), which gives every parameter


ssl.COVID
A chain of increasingly severe states, each of which some people leave by recovering
The simple SECIR example of MEmilio (Kühn MJ et al., Mathematical Biosciences 2021), which gives every parameter


ssl.Influenza
A yearly cycle in transmission (ss.seasonal) with waning immunity
Natural history from Carrat F et al., Am J Epidemiol 2008;167:775-785; R0 of 1.3 from Biggerstaff M et al., BMC Infect Dis 2014;14:480; the cycle is illustrative


ssl.RSV
Maternal immunity: babies born protected, in a seasonal MSEIRS model
Weber A, Weber M, Milligan P, Math Biosci 2001;172:95-113, for the infectious period, the seasonal form, and R0


ssl.Pertussis
Immunity that wanes over decades, giving epidemics that return every few years
Wearing HJ, Rohani P, PLoS Pathogens 2009;5(10):e1000647, for the natural history, R0, and duration of immunity


ssl.Dengue
Several serotypes, each a disease with its own vector, and partial cross-protection between them
The Ross-Macdonald structure above, with indicative dengue values; cross-protection as found by Reich NG et al., J R Soc Interface 2013;10:20130414


ssl.Typhoid
Chronic carriers: a few people shed for life, at a hundredth of the infectiousness of an acute case
Pitzer VE et al., PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2014;8(1):e2642, for the carriers, waning, and R0 of 2.8


ssl.Polio
A rare outcome as a branch: about 1 infection in 200 causes paralysis
US CDC Pink Book for the paralytic fraction; Fine PEM, Carneiro IAM, Am J Epidemiol 1999;150:1001-1021, for R0


ssl.Syphilis
Stages, with the one thing that cannot be declared (infectiousness that falls with time since the latent stage began) written as code
STIsim’s syphilis module, which cites its own sources


ssl.Gonorrhea
An SIS infection on a sexual network
STIsim’s gonorrhea module



Malaria is the clearest example of what declaring buys: mosquitoes are states like any other, declared with people=False so that they are counts rather than people, and R0() works out the reproduction number from the model itself:

malaria = ssl.Malaria()
print('R0:', round(malaria.R0(), 1))

sim = ss.Sim(malaria, total_pop=10_000, unit='day', stop=600, verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.diseases.malaria.plot('Ih', 'Iv')

R0: 14.6









Starsim’s R0() counts each passage through a mosquito as a generation, so it is the square root of the classical Ross-Macdonald value, m·a²·b·c/(γ·μ_v) = 213.
The Garki model adds immunity, and with it the result the source is known for: malaria dies out below a critical vectorial capacity, (α₁ + δ)/g, which is 0.022 contacts per person per day with these parameters:

critical = 0.022
for C in [0.5*critical, 2*critical, 0.2]:
    sim = ss.Sim(ssl.MalariaImmunity(C=C), total_pop=10_000, unit='day', dt=ss.days(5), stop=365*30, verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    res = sim.results.malariaimmunity
    print(f'Vectorial capacity {C:.3f}: parasite rate {res.prevalence[-1]:.3f}, of which detected {res.detected[-1]:.3f}')

Vectorial capacity 0.011: parasite rate 0.000, of which detected 0.000
Vectorial capacity 0.044: parasite rate 0.313, of which detected 0.311
Vectorial capacity 0.200: parasite rate 0.509, of which detected 0.491


The same declaration runs as agents (n_agents= instead of total_pop=), where the prevalence is the same but each run differs by chance.
Since these are declared, describe(), diagram(), and equations() work on any of them, which is the quickest way to see what a model does (ssl.Dengue is a list of serotypes, so each is shown in its own right, e.g. sim.diseases.den1.diagram()):

ssl.Typhoid().equations()

dS/dt = -birth_rate * S - (beta * S * I / N + beta * rel_carrier * S * C / N) + R / dur_imm + birth_rate * (S + I + C + R).n
dI/dt =  (beta * S * I / N + beta * rel_carrier * S * C / N) - birth_rate * I - I / dur_inf
dC/dt =  p_carrier * I / dur_inf - birth_rate * C
dR/dt =  (1 - p_carrier) * I / dur_inf - birth_rate * R - R / dur_imm


One of them needs agents rather than compartments: ssl.Syphilis, because the falling infectiousness of latent syphilis is a quantity each person carries, set in its step(). The rest run under any solver.

title: Diseases
text:
Adapting a library module
Library modules are ordinary Starsim modules, so they can be changed in the usual ways. The simplest is to change their parameters:

measles = ssl.Measles(beta=ss.perday(0.4), dur_exp=ss.normal(loc=ss.days(10)), p_death=0.01)

For a change to how the disease works, build on the class. Here measles gets waning immunity: recovered agents become susceptible again after a delay, dur_immune. The new class adds a parameter and a state in __init__(), schedules the loss of immunity when each agent is infected (set_prognoses()), and makes the agents whose time has come susceptible again at each step (step_state()):

class WaningMeasles(ssl.Measles):
    def __init__(self, dur_immune=ss.years(1), **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_pars(dur_immune=dur_immune)
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(ss.TimeArr('ti_susceptible', label='Time of losing immunity'))
        return

    def set_prognoses(self, uids, sources=None):
        super().set_prognoses(uids, sources)
        self.ti_susceptible[uids] = self.ti_recovered[uids] + self.pars.dur_immune / self.t.dt
        return

    def step_state(self):
        super().step_state()
        waned = (self.recovered & self.ti_susceptible.due()).uids
        self.recovered[waned] = False
        self.susceptible[waned] = True
        return

scenarios = {
    'Lifelong immunity':     ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.Measles(beta=ss.perday(0.3)), networks=ss.RandomNet(), **outbreak),
    'Immunity for 60 days':  ss.Sim(diseases=WaningMeasles(dur_immune=ss.days(60), beta=ss.perday(0.3), name='measles'), networks=ss.RandomNet(), **outbreak),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, parallel=False)
msim.plot(['measles.susceptible', 'measles.recovered'])

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Lifelong immunity, Immunity for 60 days)
  Done in 0.53 s









Giving the new disease name='measles' keeps its results under the same name as the original’s, so the two can be plotted together. With waning, the recovered agents return to being susceptible, as intended. This alone doesn’t produce a second wave: the outbreak burns out before immunity wanes, so there is no one infectious left to start one. Recurring waves need a continuing source of infection: importation, births (bringing in new susceptible people), or a slower disease.
Copying a library module and editing it is also a good way to use it; that is what these modules are for. See Custom modules for writing modules from scratch, and the tutorial A5 – Custom modules for a worked example.

New library modules are welcome, particularly ones that show a modeling pattern that is otherwise hard to work out. See starsim/library/README.md for its conventions, and How to contribute for the general process.

title: Products
text:
🧠10% 🤖90%
Vaccination, screening, and treatment programs have two parts: what is given (a vaccine, a test, or a drug: a product), and the delivery, which says who gets it, when, and how many. Starsim keeps the two apart, because programs do: an intervention decides who gets something and when, while the product says what happens to a person when they get it. The same vaccine can then be given routinely to infants in one scenario and in a campaign in another, without defining the vaccine again.
This page covers products: vaccines, tests, and treatments, how their protection wanes, and products of your own. Deliveries (routine and campaign delivery, coverage, capacity, eligibility, and delivery triggered by events) and changes to a model’s parameters, such as distancing or school closures, which need no product, are on Interventions. The cost of products is on Costs. The tutorial T5 – Interventions and scenarios uses a vaccine for measles, and A4 – Interventions uses tests and treatment with agents.

title: Products
text:
A vaccination campaign
There is one delivery for each kind of product: ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat(). Each takes the product’s own keywords (a vaccine’s efficacy, a test’s sensitivity) and makes the product, along with how it is delivered. Here a measles campaign reaches 90% of people on day 5 of an outbreak, with a vaccine that cuts the chance of infection by 95%:

import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.0001)

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, coverage=0.9, at=[ss.days(5)])

kw = dict(total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0)
scenarios = {
    'No vaccination': ss.Sim(measles, **kw),
    'Campaign on day 5': ss.Sim(measles, interventions=vaccination, **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('measles.I')








A vaccine protects only those not yet infected, so the sooner the campaign, the more it prevents; coverage (the share reached) and efficacy (the protection of those reached) are separate numbers, and both matter. Interventions are given to the sim with interventions=, singly or as a list. A delivery takes its name from the variable it is assigned to (vaccination here), and has results of its own: the number delivered on each step, the number eligible, and the coverage reached (and cost, if the product has one). Name a delivery after the activity (vaccination, screening, treatment), since the product takes the name of the thing (vaccine, test, drug).

title: Products
text:
Products



Product
Delivered by
Main keywords




ss.Vaccine
ss.vaccinate()
efficacy, waning, leaky, doses, during, cost


ss.Diagnostic
ss.screen()
sensitivity, specificity, delay, detects, results, cost


ss.Treatment
ss.treat()
cure, efficacy, transition, waning, during, cost



A product is made explicitly only where it is the topic, or where one product is given by several deliveries (see below).
The examples below this point use a curable infection with no lasting immunity, over 20 years, as an SIS model run as agents (since some of what follows depends on each person’s own history):

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peryear(2)*I  # β = 2 per year
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.years(1)      # Infected for a year on average, then susceptible again
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.1)

kw = dict(n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)

With R0 = 2 × 1 = 2, half of people are infected at any time once the infection is endemic.

Vaccines
A vaccine’s efficacy is its protection against infection: the chance of infection of everyone who holds it is multiplied by 1 − efficacy. A dict gives efficacy against several things: acquisition (the chance of infection), transmission (how infectious a vaccinated person is if infected), mortality (the chance of dying of the disease), or any named transition of the disease (whose rate it scales).
By default a vaccine is leaky: everyone vaccinated is partly protected. With leaky=False it is all or nothing: a share efficacy of those vaccinated are fully protected, and the rest not at all. The two give the same protection on the first exposure, but differ after many exposures, since under a leaky vaccine everyone vaccinated is still infected eventually. waning= is how protection fades: a duration means it is lost after an exponentially distributed time with that mean. Here are all three, given to half of people in 2010:

kw_vx = dict(coverage=0.5, at=['2010'])
scenarios = {
    'No vaccine':                     ss.Sim(sis, **kw),
    'Leaky (80%)':                    ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, **kw_vx), **kw),
    'All or nothing (80%)':           ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, leaky=False, **kw_vx), **kw),
    'Leaky, waning after 3 years':    ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, waning=ss.years(3), **kw_vx), **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')








doses=[0.85, 1.0] gives a vaccine in doses, with the share of the full protection after each; each delivery to someone who already holds the vaccine gives the next dose.
Protection can also fade by its own shape. ss.box(dur=..., decay=...) is full protection for dur, then (with decay=) an exponential decline with that mean, or none; it runs under every solver. Any other shape is a function of the time since delivery, t, a duration (so t < ss.days(180) and t.years mean the same in any sim), returning the share of protection left; a function of (t, sim, uids) also gets the sim and the people who hold it, e.g. to read their age at vaccination (sim.people.age[uids] - t.years). A function runs as agents only. A dict gives each effect its own waning (waning=dict(acquisition=ss.box(dur=ss.years(1)), transmission=None)). A product given again to someone who holds it restarts a waning by shape or function.

scenarios = {
    'Box of 2 years, then a decline': ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, waning=ss.box(dur=ss.years(2), decay=ss.years(3)), **kw_vx), **kw),
    'Fading linearly over 5 years':   ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, waning=lambda t: np.clip(1 - t.years/5, 0, 1), **kw_vx), **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')








during= holds a product only while people are in some states: ss.Treatment(efficacy=dict(transmission=0.5), during=sis.I) makes people half as infectious while they are infected, and they stop holding it when they recover.
A product’s coverage is also a quantity a rate can read: itn.coverage is the share of the people in the same place who hold it, each counted by the protection they have left, and itn.coverage(fn) counts each by a function of the time since delivery (e.g. the share of mosquitoes a net kills). A disease made with the product can use it in any rate, e.g. Sv >> ss.null @ 1/life + a*kill*itn.coverage.


Tests and what follows them
A test (ss.Diagnostic) has a sensitivity, the chance that someone infected tests positive, and a specificity, the chance that someone not infected tests negative. ss.screen() delivers it, and its positive and negative are the people with each result on that step. What happens to them is another delivery, given them with who=, with its own coverage, so loss to follow-up is explicit. Here half of people are screened each year from 2010, and 80% of those who test positive are treated with a drug that cures 95%:

screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, coverage=0.5, interval=ss.years(1), start='2010')
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.95, who=screening.positive, coverage=0.8)

sim = ss.Sim(sis, interventions=[screening, treatment], **kw)
sim.run()
sim.plot('sis')
print('Positive tests:', sim.results.screening.positive.sum())
print('Treated:', sim.results.treatment.delivered.sum())








Positive tests: 8806.0
Treated: 7060.0


A follow-up can have follow-ups of its own, to any depth. By default a test detects infection with the disease it is given for; detects= takes a condition for anything else. delay= on the test is the time from the test to its result.
A test’s values can be by the states of several diseases ({hpv16.I: 0.9, 'hpv18.CIN': 0.95}), including the boolean states of a disease written as code ('hpv16.cin'). With disease=[...], a value for a state without a disease ('cin') is for that state of each, and someone is tested once, in the most severe state they are in.
A test can have more than two results: results= gives them, most severe first, each with its chance for people in each state (None for people in none of them), and the last result is everyone the others don’t take. Each result is a result of the delivery and an event that can trigger what follows:

cytology = ss.Diagnostic(results=dict(high=dict(I=0.9), low={'I': 0.05, None: 0.02}, normal=None)) # Low grade for 2% of those not infected
screening = ss.screen(cytology, coverage=0.5, start='2010', interval=ss.years(1))
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.8, who=screening.high)

sim = ss.Sim(sis, interventions=[screening, treatment], **kw)
sim.run()
print('High grade:', sim.results.screening.high.sum())
print('Low grade:', sim.results.screening.low.sum())

High grade: 8417.0
Low grade: 759.0




Treatments
A treatment’s cure is the chance that it clears the infection, once, when it is given: the person leaves the infected states by the disease’s recovery (transition= names it, when there are several). Its efficacy is what it does for as long as it is held, as for a vaccine: antiretroviral therapy for HIV is efficacy=dict(transmission=0.96, mortality=0.9). A treatment is given to the people who are infected, unless the delivery says otherwise. cure=dict(cin=0.9) cures by state, of a declared disease or one written as code (which is cured by its clear_infection()).
Here are the two kinds of treatment, each given to infected people at a rate of 50% a year: a cure, and a treatment that cuts how infectious people are by 90% while they are infected (and are treated), without shortening their infection:

cure = ss.treat(cure=0.9, coverage=ss.peryear(0.5))
suppress = ss.treat(efficacy=dict(transmission=0.9), during=sis.I, coverage=ss.peryear(0.5))

scenarios = {
    'No treatment':                ss.Sim(sis, **kw),
    'Cure':                        ss.Sim(sis, interventions=cure, **kw),
    'Less infectious while held':  ss.Sim(sis, interventions=suppress, **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')








Both lower prevalence by about half. A cure does it by shortening infections, and reaches each person afresh each time they are infected; the other keeps people infected, but stops most of them from passing it on.


Costs
Every product takes cost=, the cost of each delivery, which is then a result of the delivery (cost), next to the number delivered. See Costs for costing a program and comparing costs and effects between scenarios.

title: Products
text:
One product, several deliveries
A product made on its own can be given by several deliveries, which then share it: a person vaccinated by either holds the same vaccine, and is not protected twice. Here a vaccine is given routinely to 30% of people, and in a campaign in 2010:

vaccine = ss.Vaccine(efficacy=0.8)
routine  = ss.vaccinate(vaccine, coverage=0.3, start='2005')
campaign = ss.vaccinate(vaccine, coverage=0.5, at=['2010'])

scenarios = {
    'Routine':                ss.Sim(sis, interventions=routine, **kw),
    'Routine and campaign':   ss.Sim(sis, interventions=[routine, campaign], **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')








Each delivery has a name of its own, from its variable or from name=; steps made by a function, with no variable, are numbered (screen, screen_1, …).

title: Products
text:
Under compartments and agents
Products and deliveries work under every solver: as agents, the sim records who holds each product and since when, and in a compartmental run, holding a product becomes a stratification of the model. What follows each person’s own history needs agents: waning given as a function of the time since delivery (an ss.box() runs under every solver, its box as several levels of holding the product), a test’s delay=, queue= and delay= on a delivery, .since and .count (.ever works under every solver), the conditions on mothers, contact tracing, and functions that pick particular people. A model that uses any of these runs as agents unless told otherwise. For any other waning shape under every solver (e.g. two rates in turn), write the protection as states of the disease, and move people into them with the delivery’s move= (e.g. ss.Delivery(move=S >> V, ...); see Diseases). A weighted count ((ss.by(biting=w)*I).n, A.n_trans) and a product’s coverage in a rate are worked out once a step in a compartmental run.

title: Products
text:
Writing a product as code
A product whose effect needs code of its own is a subclass of ss.Product (or of ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, or ss.Treatment) with an administer(uids) method, which is called with the people a delivery gave it to on each step. Like any module, it can have parameters of its own (with define_pars()), states, and results. Here is a vaccine that protects younger people more: 90% at birth, falling to none at 80:

class AgeVaccine(ss.Product):
    """ A vaccine whose protection falls with the age at which it is given """
    def __init__(self, efficacy=0.9, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(efficacy=efficacy)
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        return

    def administer(self, uids):
        age = self.sim.people.age[uids]
        protection = self.pars.efficacy * np.clip(1 - age/80, 0, 1)
        self.sim.diseases.sis.rel_sus[uids] *= 1 - protection
        return

scenarios = {
    'No vaccine':                    ss.Sim(sis, **kw),
    'Vaccine, 90% at every age':     ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.5, at=['2010']), **kw),
    'Vaccine, falling with age':     ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(AgeVaccine(), coverage=0.5, at=['2010']), **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')








A product written as code acts on agents, so a model with one runs as agents. Here administer() changes each person’s susceptibility directly, which lasts for the rest of the run; a protection that should wane, or combine with other products and modifiers without overwriting them, is better given as a vaccine’s efficacy= with waning=, or as an ss.modify() (see Interventions). administer() can also return outcomes, as a test does (dict(positive=uids)), which are then results and events of the delivery. An intervention whose logic is not a product at all is a subclass of ss.Intervention: see Interventions.

title: Products
text:
Pitfalls

One product, one protection. Two deliveries of the same vaccine object share it: someone vaccinated by both is protected once. Two deliveries that make their own vaccines (ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, ...) twice) give two vaccines, whose protections multiply for someone who gets both.
Coverage is not efficacy. Coverage is the share of eligible people who receive a product; efficacy is what it does for those who do. Halving either halves the protection of a leaky vaccine, but they are different questions for a program.

The API reference for this page: Products.

text:
Further reading

epydemix: Vaccinations: vaccination in a compartmental model
