title: Demographics
text:
🧠5% 🤖95%
Over a single outbreak of a few months, the population barely changes, and most models leave out births and deaths. Over years it does change, and that matters for transmission: births bring in people who have never been infected, deaths remove people (including those who are immune), and the population ages. For measles, the rate at which births replenish the susceptible population sets how soon it can spread again after an epidemic.
This page covers births and deaths declared for a population, which work however the model is run; rates from data by country, by age, sex, and year; life tables; migration; pregnancy; and aging. The tutorial A3 – Demographics uses them on a whole country, People and agents covers the population at the start, and Branching and rescaling covers modeling a large population with fewer agents.

title: Demographics
text:
Births and deaths
Births and deaths for the whole population go in demographics=. ss.birth(rate=r) adds people at a crude birth rate r (a typed rate is per person, e.g. ss.peryear(0.03); a bare number is per year, and above 1 per 1,000 people, as ss.Births reads it, so 30 is the same), into the first state of each disease (here S); ss.death(rate=r) removes people from every state at rate r, read the same way. Here is the measles model of the tutorials over 30 years, with 30 births and 10 deaths per 1,000 people a year:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I       # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

demographics = [
    ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), # 30 births per 1,000 people per year
    ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.01)), # 10 deaths per 1,000 people per year
]
pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2000', stop='2030', dt=ss.days(1), verbose=0)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, demographics=demographics, **pars)
msim = ss.parallel({'No births or deaths': ss.Sim(measles, **pars), 'Births and deaths': sim})
fig = msim.plot('measles.I', log=True, do_show=False) # A log scale shows the later epidemics, which are far smaller than the first
fig.axes[0].set_ylim(0.1, 200_000)
fig















log=True plots on a log scale; do_show=False returns the figure without showing it, so it can be changed (here, the range of the axis) before it is shown.
Without births, the first epidemic leaves almost everyone immune, and measles is gone for good. With them, births add susceptible children until there are enough for measles to spread again, and the epidemics recur, smaller each time, until they settle at an endemic level.
The births and deaths are transitions of the disease, so they are among its results (sim.results.measles.births, sim.results.measles.deaths) and in describe(). With several diseases, the same people are born into and die from each of them.
In the ODE, though, a fraction of an infectious person is enough for measles to come back, and the sim says so when it runs:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, demographics=demographics, **pars)
sim.run(verbose=1);

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2000-01-01 to 2030-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Note: the number infected in "measles" falls to 0.91 (at 2000-04-10) and then rises to 2,053; a stochastic run would usually die out there. solver="gillespie" with ss.parallel(n_runs=...) shows how often, in the runs of msim.results.measles.I after that point
  Done in 0.017 s; measles: 208,602 infections; at most 74,135 infectious, on 2000-01-07


The number infectious falls below one person within a few months. In a real town of 100,000 people, measles would have died out by then. A stochastic model, in which people are whole numbers and chance matters, shows this:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, solver='binomial', demographics=demographics, total_pop=100_000, start='2000', stop='2005', dt=ss.days(1), rand_seed=1)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as a stochastic compartmental model (chain binomial), 2000-01-01 to 2005-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0068 s; measles: 100,151 infections; at most 75,827 infectious, on 2000-01-08









Measles dies out after the first epidemic, and only comes back if it is brought in from outside. This is why measles persists without reintroduction only in large populations (above a “critical community size” of a few hundred thousand people). See Solvers and backends for more on when an ODE and a stochastic model differ.
A death from a disease, rather than from every state, is a transition of the disease: ss.death(I, rate=ss.peryear(0.1)) (see Diseases). demographics=True adds births and deaths at default rates (20 births and 10 deaths per 1,000 people a year).
A birth or death rate can also change over time, with ss.timeseries(). By default each value holds until the next; 'linear' interpolates between them. Here the birth rate falls from 40 to 20 per 1,000 a year over 30 years, compared with a birth rate that stays at 40:

deaths = ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.01))
constant = ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.04))
falling = ss.birth(rate=ss.timeseries({'2000-01-01': ss.peryear(0.04), '2030-01-01': ss.peryear(0.02)}, mode='linear'))

pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2000', stop='2030', dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({
    'Constant birth rate': ss.Sim(measles, demographics=[constant, deaths], **pars),
    'Falling birth rate': ss.Sim(measles, demographics=[falling, deaths], **pars),
})
msim.plot(['alive', 'measles.I'])








The population grows more slowly with the falling birth rate, and with fewer susceptible children born each year, the endemic level of measles is lower. The times of a series can also be years ({2000: ..., 2030: ...}): a bare number from 1900 on is a calendar year, and a smaller one a time in the sim’s unit after the start. See Parameters for ss.timeseries() and other parameters that vary over time.

title: Demographics
text:
Rates from data
Birth and death rates usually come as data: crude birth rates by year, and death rates by year, sex, and age. The demographics modules ss.Births and ss.Deaths take these, and the rates of the UN World Population Prospects for a country by name, which come with Starsim. With ss.people() for the population at the start (see People), this is the population of Kenya from 2000:

kenya = dict(
    people = ss.people('Kenya', year=2000, n_agents=20_000),
    demographics = [ss.Births(birth_rate='Kenya'), ss.Deaths(death_rate='Kenya')],
    start = 2000,
    stop = 2030,
    dt = ss.years(1),
)
sim = ss.Sim(**kenya)
sim.run()
sim.results.alive.plot()
sim.people.plot_ages();

Sim: births, deaths, as 20,000 agents, each 1,530 people, years 2000 to 2030
  Note: unit='year' (from dt)


  Done in 0.13 s
















The demographics modules run as agents. They age people, give each newborn a mother of reproductive age (people.parent), and can run on a step of their own (e.g. dt=ss.years(1) for the demographics of a model whose diseases step daily).
The model’s population can be checked against the UN’s own estimates of the population of Kenya:

for year in [2010, 2020, 2030]:
    print(year, 'model:', round(sim.results.alive[year - 2000]), 'UN:', round(ss.people('Kenya', year=year).named.total))

2010 model: 40915919 UN: 41598566
2020 model: 52293624 UN: 52217334
2030 model: 63538032 UN: 63102246


The model follows the UN’s estimates to within 2%. The UN’s rates that come with Starsim are estimates for single years, given every ten years, so ss.Births and ss.Deaths interpolate between them.

Data of your own
Rates of your own are given as a table. Crude birth rates have a column for the year and one for the rate (ss.Births(birth_rate=df)); death rates have columns for the year, sex, age group, and rate (ss.Deaths(death_rate=df)). Each rate holds from its year until the next year given.
Crude birth and death rates are usually given per 1,000 people, and death rates by age per person. A rate above 1 is read as per 1,000, and a rate below 1 as per person; a rate that could be either (from 0.1 to 1, or above 1,000) gives a warning saying which was assumed. rate_units=1000 (per 1,000) or rate_units=1 (per person) says which, and silences it:
births = ss.Births(birth_rate=35)                   # 35 per 1,000 people per year
births = ss.Births(birth_rate=0.035)                # The same, per person
deaths = ss.Deaths(death_rate=df, rate_units=1)     # Death rates by age, per person
Declared rates (ss.birth(), ss.death()) are always per person.


Life tables
A life table says how many of a cohort die at each age. ss.death(lifetable=...) takes one and runs under every solver: as agents, each person’s age at death is drawn from it, given their age; in a compartmental model stratified by age, it gives a death rate for each age group. ss.Deaths(lifetable=...) also takes a table for each sex, and for each year from which it holds:

import numpy as np

ages = np.arange(0, 105, 5) # The lower edge of each 5-year age group
dx = [5, 1, 0.5, 0.5, 1, 1, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 14, 12, 8, 4, 1.5] # Deaths in each group, of a cohort of 100 (an illustrative table)
table = ss.lifetable(ages=ages, deaths=dx)

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2060, dt=ss.years(1), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({
    'Constant death rate': ss.Sim(demographics=[ss.Births(birth_rate=20), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02))], **pars),
    'Life table': ss.Sim(demographics=[ss.Births(birth_rate=20), ss.death(lifetable=table)], **pars),
})
for sim in msim.sims:
    age = sim.people.age
    print(sim.label, '– mean age:', age.mean(), 'share over 90:', (age > 90).mean())

Constant death rate – mean age: 46.556656 share over 90: 0.16842327150084316
Life table – mean age: 34.08276 share over 90: 0.00711615004221445


With a constant death rate, everyone has the same chance of dying each year whatever their age, so many people live implausibly long: after 60 years, a sixth of the population is over 90. With the life table, deaths come mostly in old age, under 1% are over 90, and the population is younger.

title: Demographics
text:
Migration
People arriving from outside are ss.immigration(rate=r), where r is a number of people per unit time (not per person); as agents, they arrive with ages drawn from the population’s. People leaving are ss.emigration(rate=r), a rate per person; as agents, they are recorded as having left (results.emigrated), not as having died. Both go in demographics=:

demographics = [ss.immigration(rate=ss.peryear(500)), ss.emigration(rate=ss.peryear(0.005))]

A run of these over ten years, for a population of 100,000 modeled with 5,000 agents:

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, total_pop=100_000, start=2000, stop=2010, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim = ss.Sim(demographics=demographics, **pars)
sim.run()
print('Population after 10 years:', sim.results.alive[-1])
print('Emigrants:', sim.results.emigrated.sum())

Population after 10 years: 99700.0
Emigrants: 5420.0


About 500 people leave each year (0.5% of 100,000) and 500 arrive, so the population stays near 100,000. For movement between places within a model, see Geography.

title: Demographics
text:
Pregnancy
ss.Pregnancy models pregnancy itself, for models where it matters: mother-to-child transmission, maternal health, or contraception. Women conceive at age-specific fertility rates; a pregnancy ends in a delivery, a miscarriage, a stillbirth, an abortion, or a maternal death; and each delivery adds a child, whose mother is known. It runs as agents. Fertility rates by age come from the UN for a place by name, as for births and deaths (fertility_rate='Nigeria', per 1,000 women in each 5-year age group, by year), or as a table of your own, here also per 1,000 women:

import pandas as pd

fertility = pd.read_csv('test_data/nigeria_asfr.csv') # Age-specific fertility rates by year and single year of age
pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=fertility, rate_units=1000) # Per 1,000 women per year; or fertility_rate='Nigeria'

nigeria = dict(
    people = ss.people('Nigeria', year=2000, n_agents=5000),
    demographics = [pregnancy, ss.Deaths(death_rate='Nigeria')],
    start = 2000,
    stop = 2020,
    dt = ss.months(1),
    verbose = 0,
)
sim = ss.Sim(**nigeria)
sim.run()
sim.results.pregnancy.plot()








Pregnancy is declared, with states NP (not pregnant) and P (pregnant), so its transitions are events that other modules can use, as for a disease: conception, delivery (which happens to the mother), and birth (which happens to the newborn). Each is also a result (sim.results.pregnancy.conception, .birth, .miscarriage, .stillbirth, .abortion). Contraception, for example, is a modifier of conception, and an intervention can reach pregnant women (where=pregnancy.P) or newborns (who=pregnancy.birth; see Interventions):

pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=ss.peryear(0.08), rate_units=1)    # 80 conceptions per 1,000 women a year
contraception = ss.modify(pregnancy.conception, multiply=0.5, start='2005') # Halves conception from 2005

pars = dict(demographics=pregnancy, n_agents=5000, start='2000', stop='2010', dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
scenarios = {
    'No contraception': ss.Sim(**pars),
    'Contraception': ss.Sim(**pars, interventions=contraception),
}
for label, sim in scenarios.items():
    sim.run()
    print(label, 'births:', sim.results.pregnancy.birth.sum())

No contraception births: 1045.0
Contraception births: 818.0


Mother-to-child transmission uses the networks that pregnancy makes between mother and child (ss.PrenatalNet and ss.BreastfeedingNet); see Contact networks. pregnancy.pars lists the other parameters, such as the duration of pregnancy, the chance of a loss, and maternal and infant mortality.

title: Demographics
text:
Aging
People age if the model has births or deaths, and not otherwise; use_aging=True or use_aging=False in the sim says otherwise. As agents, each person’s age goes up with each step. In a compartmental model stratified by age, people move from each age group to the next: if people are spread evenly over the ages in a group, at a rate of one over its width (a group 5 years wide is left at a rate of 1/5 per year), and for a named population, at the rate its age pyramid gives, as agents would age.
The API reference for this page: ss.Births, ss.Deaths, ss.Pregnancy.

title: Demographics
text:
Further reading

EpiModel: Demography in network models: births, deaths, and aging in open-population network models
UN World Population Prospects: the source of the birth rates, death rates, and age structures that come with Starsim

title: Maternal-child health
text:
🧠45% 🤖55%
Transmission from mother to child, and the outcomes of a pregnancy (stillbirth, preterm birth, low birth weight, neonatal death), are harder to model than a standard disease: they depend on the timing of pregnancy, on which module acts first in a step, and on how deaths around birth are counted. The ssl.mnch submodule of the Starsim library (import starsim.library as ssl; see Library: diseases for what the library is) has worked examples of these patterns. All of them build on pregnancy (ss.Pregnancy, which gives each pregnancy as states and transitions, with conception, delivery, and the unborn child as an agent) and on ss.PrenatalNet, the network between a pregnant woman and her unborn child; both are described on Demographics.
Like the rest of the library, these are illustrative: the probabilities and effect sizes are placeholders, chosen to make the effects easy to see. The examples below use a step of a week, since pregnancy outcomes are timed in weeks, and a high fertility rate, so that a small population gives enough births:
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

mnch_pars = dict(start='2000', stop='2005', n_agents=2000, dt=ss.weeks(1))
demographics = lambda: [ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=ss.freqperyear(100), burnin=True), ss.Deaths()]
networks = lambda: [ss.PrenatalNet(), ss.RandomNet()]

title: Maternal-child health
text:
Congenital outcomes
CongenitalDisease is an SIR that is passed from an infected mother to her unborn child through ss.PrenatalNet. For each child infected before birth, it draws an outcome from birth_outcomes (by default stillbirth, congenital infection, or a normal birth, with probabilities 0.3, 0.4, and 0.3), and schedules it for around the time of delivery. An outcome that kills (a stillbirth or miscarriage) is scheduled one step before delivery, so that it happens before birth; otherwise ss.Pregnancy, which runs earlier in each step, would already have delivered the baby, and the loss would be counted as a live birth followed by a neonatal death. Compared with the same population without transmission (beta=0), the extra stillbirths are those the disease causes (and are no longer counted as births):

def congenital(beta):
    disease = ssl.mnch.CongenitalDisease(beta=beta, init_prev=0.2)
    return ss.Sim(diseases=disease, demographics=demographics(), networks=networks(), **mnch_pars)

for label, beta in {'No transmission': 0, 'Transmission': ss.peryear(20)}.items():
    sim = congenital(beta).run()
    preg = sim.results.pregnancy
    print(label)
    print('  Births:', int(preg.birth.sum()))
    print('  Stillbirths:', int(preg.stillbirth.sum()))
    print('  Congenital infections:', sim.diseases.congenitaldisease.congenital.sum())

Sim: congenitaldisease, as 2,034 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2005-01-01
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: pregnancy: women pregnant at the start, conceived over the 40 steps before it (burnin=True)


  Done in 1.0 s


No transmission
  Births: 232
  Stillbirths: 1
  Congenital infections: 0
Sim: congenitaldisease, as 2,034 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2005-01-01
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: pregnancy: women pregnant at the start, conceived over the 40 steps before it (burnin=True)


  Done in 0.98 s


Transmission
  Births: 171
  Stillbirths: 62
  Congenital infections: 91


Among the children infected before birth, the numbers of stillbirths and congenital infections follow the probabilities in birth_outcomes.
To use this in a disease of your own, build on ssl.mnch.CongenitalDisease (or copy its set_congenital() and step_congenital(); ss.Infection calls set_congenital() for each person infected before birth): define birth_outcome_keys and birth_outcomes in its parameters, add a ti_<key> state for each outcome (and a true/false state for each outcome that doesn’t kill), and call self.step_congenital() from step_state(). Outcomes named 'stillborn', 'miscarriage', or 'neonatal_death' are deaths; the first two happen before delivery and the third after it. ssl.HIV (see Library: diseases) also uses set_congenital(), to infect children of infected mothers at birth.

title: Maternal-child health
text:
Neonatal deaths
NeonatalSepsis infects a share of newborns at birth (init_prev, by default 30%), and kills half of them (p_death) within about a week. It shows that neonatal deaths need no special handling: ss.Pregnancy counts any death of a baby aged 0 to 28 days, from any cause, as a neonatal death. The results are therefore in the pregnancy module, not the disease, and comparing with a sim without sepsis gives the deaths it causes:

scenarios = {
    'No sepsis': ss.Sim(demographics=demographics(), networks=networks(), **mnch_pars),
    'Sepsis':    ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.mnch.NeonatalSepsis(), demographics=demographics(), networks=networks(), **mnch_pars),
}
for label, sim in scenarios.items():
    sim.run()
    print(label)
    print('  Births:', int(sim.results.pregnancy.birth.sum()))
    print('  Neonatal deaths:', int(sim.results.pregnancy.neonatal_death.sum()))

Sim: pregnancy, deaths, prenatalnet, randomnet, as 2,034 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2005-01-01
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: pregnancy: women pregnant at the start, conceived over the 40 steps before it (burnin=True)


  Done in 1.1 s


No sepsis
  Births: 232
  Neonatal deaths: 1
Sim: neonatalsepsis, as 2,034 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2005-01-01
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: pregnancy: women pregnant at the start, conceived over the 40 steps before it (burnin=True)


  Done in 1.1 s


Sepsis
  Births: 232
  Neonatal deaths: 36

title: Maternal-child health
text:
Fetal health
FetalHealth doesn’t depend on any particular disease: it tracks a baseline fetal weight percentile for each pregnancy, and has two levers that other modules can pull: bringing delivery forward (the risk of a preterm birth) and adding growth restriction (the risk of a low birth weight). At delivery, it works out the birth weight from the gestational age, the percentile, and the growth restriction, and classifies newborns as of low birth weight (under 2,500 g), very low birth weight (under 1,500 g), small for gestational age, or small vulnerable newborns (any of these, or preterm). Its results are the numbers of each on each step, and the means and rates over each step’s births (e.g. mean_birth_weight, lbw_rate), which are NaN on a step with no births and are left out of a mean over time (res.mean_birth_weight.resample('year')).
The fetal_infection connector pulls those levers when a pregnant woman is infected: each infection brings delivery forward by about 3 weeks (timing_shift) and restricts growth by 15% (growth_penalty). The treat_pregnant intervention treats infected pregnant women (90% of them, p_treat), and reverses 70% of the damage. Both are written as code for an SIR written as code, so the disease here is ssl.AgentSIR, named 'sir'. FetalHealth is given as custom, since it is not a disease, network, demographic module, or intervention. Three scenarios show the baseline, the effect of infection, and how much treatment from 2001 recovers:

def fetal(beta, treat=False):
    treatment = ssl.mnch.treat_pregnant(disease='sir', start_year=2001) if treat else None
    return ss.Sim(
        diseases      = ssl.AgentSIR(beta=beta, name='sir'),
        demographics  = demographics(),
        connectors    = ssl.mnch.fetal_infection(),
        interventions = treatment,
        custom        = ssl.mnch.FetalHealth(),
        networks      = networks(),
        **mnch_pars,
    )

scenarios = {
    'No infection': fetal(beta=0),
    'Infection, untreated': fetal(beta=ss.peryear(20)),
    'Infection, treated from 2001': fetal(beta=ss.peryear(20), treat=True),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, parallel=False)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig = plt.figure()
for label, sim in zip(scenarios, msim.sims):
    res = sim.results.fetal_health
    births = int(res.birth.sum())
    print(label)
    print('  Births:', births)
    print('  Low birth weight (%):', round(100*res.lbw.sum()/births))
    print('  Small vulnerable newborns (%):', round(100*res.svn.sum()/births))
    plt.plot(res.timevec, res.lbw.cumsum(), label=label)
plt.ylabel('Babies born with a low birth weight (cumulative)')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (No infection, Infection, untreated, Infection, treated from 2001)
  Done in 3.7 s


No infection
  Births: 232
  Low birth weight (%): 4
  Small vulnerable newborns (%): 14
Infection, untreated
  Births: 233
  Low birth weight (%): 43
  Small vulnerable newborns (%): 70
Infection, treated from 2001
  Births: 233
  Low birth weight (%): 8
  Small vulnerable newborns (%): 32









Infection in pregnancy raises the share of babies born with a low birth weight several times over, and treatment brings most of it back down. To adapt this to another disease, build on fetal_infection and replace _apply_damage() with the disease’s own effects: for example, a larger growth penalty for severe infections than for mild ones.

title: Maternal-child health
text:
Further reading

WHO: Born too soon: the decade of action on preterm birth, and the definitions of preterm and low birth weight used here
LiST: the Lives Saved Tool: a widely used model of the effect of maternal and child health interventions on mortality

title: Connectors
text:
🧠15% 🤖85%
A connector links modules: it lets one part of a model change another. The common case is an interaction between diseases (people with HIV are more likely to acquire other sexually transmitted infections, and the reverse), but a connector can link any modules, such as pregnancy raising the risk of a disease. Most connectors are a single ss.modify(), the same call that changes parameters, given to the sim with connectors=; anything a modifier can’t say is a connector written as code. The tutorial T8 – Stratification and co-transmission builds up a model of two interacting diseases, and Strains covers several strains of one disease, with immunity between them.

title: Connectors
text:
Two diseases that interact
Measles, the running example of the tutorials, is a poor fit here: its interactions with other infections are not the usual reason to model it. HIV and a curable sexually transmitted infection (STI) are the classic case, since each raises the risk of the other. HIV here is the library’s (ssl.HIV, a disease written as code, with a CD4 count for each person), and the STI is declared, with no lasting immunity. Both pass through a sexual network, with β per sex act (see Contact networks):

import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

hiv = ssl.HIV(beta={'sexualnet': ss.peract(m2f=0.0008, f2m=0.0004)}, init_prev=0.2)

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ dict(sexualnet=ss.peract(m2f=0.1, f2m=0.05))*I
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.years(1) # Infected for a year on average, then susceptible again
sti = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/


Each interaction is one modifier: “for people with a CD4 count below 500, multiply their susceptibility to the STI by 2”, and so on. People with AIDS (a CD4 count below 200) meet both conditions on their susceptibility, so theirs is multiplied by 2 × 2.5 = 5:

interactions = [
    ss.modify(sti.rel_sus,   multiply=2,   where=hiv.cd4 < 500), # People with HIV are 2 times as likely to acquire the STI
    ss.modify(sti.rel_sus,   multiply=2.5, where=hiv.cd4 < 200), # ... and 5 times as likely with AIDS
    ss.modify(sti.rel_trans, multiply=1.5, where=hiv.cd4 < 500), # People with HIV are 1.5 times as infectious with the STI
    ss.modify(sti.rel_trans, multiply=2,   where=hiv.cd4 < 200), # ... and 3 times with AIDS
    ss.modify(hiv.rel_sus,   multiply=2.7, where=sti.I),         # People with the STI are 2.7 times as likely to acquire HIV
    ss.modify(hiv.rel_trans, multiply=2.7, where=sti.I),         # ... and as infectious with it
]

kw = dict(networks=ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.years(1)), n_agents=2000, start=2000, stop=2030, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
scenarios = {
    'Without interactions': ss.Sim([hiv, sti], **kw),
    'With interactions': ss.Sim([hiv, sti], connectors=interactions, **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot(['hiv.infected', 'sti.I'])








Each disease spreads further with the other: the two amplify each other, which neither model shows on its own.

title: Connectors
text:
Modifiers as connectors
ss.modify(target, multiply=..., where=...) reads “for the people who meet the condition, multiply the target by this”. The target is a quantity of one module (here, each person’s susceptibility or infectiousness, rel_sus and rel_trans; or a parameter or a transition), and the condition reads the states of another (hiv.cd4 < 500, sti.I). Interventions has every option of ss.modify(), the targets it takes, and how conditions are written.
Several modifiers on one quantity combine by multiplying (set, then multiply, then add), whatever order they were given in, and none overwrites the quantity’s own value: the multipliers active for each person are applied on top of it. So when a condition stops holding (an STI is cured, say), its effect ends with it, and nothing has to be reset.
Connectors need not be between diseases. Here pregnancy, a module of its own, doubles susceptibility to the STI:

pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=ss.freqperyear(100)) # Births a year per 1,000 women
during_pregnancy = ss.modify(sti.rel_sus, multiply=2, where=pregnancy.P)

scenarios = {
    'No effect of pregnancy': ss.Sim([hiv, sti], demographics=pregnancy, **kw),
    'Susceptibility doubled in pregnancy': ss.Sim([hiv, sti], demographics=pregnancy, connectors=during_pregnancy, **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
for sim in msim.sims:
    print(sim.label, '– share of pregnant women with the STI:', round(sim.diseases.sti.I[sim.demographics.pregnancy.P].mean(), 3))

No effect of pregnancy – share of pregnant women with the STI: 0.426
Susceptibility doubled in pregnancy – share of pregnant women with the STI: 0.447


The share of pregnant women with the STI is only a little higher, at the end of this run: pregnancy is short, the STI is already common, and whether someone is infected depends as much on their partners as on their susceptibility. A modifier gives the effect of a condition on a quantity; how much that matters to the epidemic is for the model to say.
A modifier can be given as a connector (connectors=) or as an intervention (interventions=); the two differ only in where they run in each step. By convention, what is part of the biology goes in connectors=, and policy in interventions=.

title: Connectors
text:
Interactions and interventions together
Because an interaction is a condition, not a value that was set, it follows whatever changes who meets the condition. Here the STI is treated from 2015 on: as each person is cured, they leave sti.I, and their HIV risk falls back with no extra code:

treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.9, disease='sti', coverage=0.8, interval=ss.years(1), start='2015')
scenarios = {
    'With interactions': ss.Sim([hiv, sti], connectors=interactions, **kw),
    'With interactions and STI treatment': ss.Sim([hiv, sti], connectors=interactions, interventions=treatment, **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot(['hiv.infected', 'sti.I'])








Treating the STI also slows HIV, since fewer people have the STI that raises their HIV risk.

title: Connectors
text:
Connectors written as code
A connector written as code is a subclass of ss.Connector with a step() method, which runs on every step (after demographics and the progression of diseases, and before networks, interventions, and transmission) and can read and change anything in the sim. It is for what conditions can’t say. Many things that look as if they need code don’t: a condition can read how long ago something happened (where=sti.I | (sti.recovery.since <= ss.months(3)), as agents), and a multiplier can vary in time (multiply=ss.seasonal(...)).
The safe pattern is for the code to work out a quantity, and for a modifier to apply it, so that nothing is overwritten. Here inflammation from the STI raises the risk of HIV while the STI lasts, and fades with a half-life of three months once it clears; the connector keeps each person’s level of inflammation, and a modifier multiplies HIV susceptibility by the factor it works out:

class Inflammation(ss.Connector):
    """ Inflammation from an STI, which raises the risk of HIV and fades after the STI clears """
    def __init__(self, rel_sus=2.7, half_life=ss.months(3), **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_pars(rel_sus=rel_sus, half_life=half_life)
        self.define_states(
            ss.FloatArr('level', default=0.0),  # 1 while infected, then halving every half-life
            ss.FloatArr('factor', default=1.0), # The resulting multiplier of HIV susceptibility
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        sti = self.sim.diseases.sti
        self.level[:] = self.level[:] * 0.5**(self.t.dt/self.pars.half_life)
        self.level[sti.I.uids] = 1.0
        self.factor[:] = 1 + (self.pars.rel_sus - 1)*self.level[:]
        return

inflammation = Inflammation()
effect = ss.modify(hiv.rel_sus, multiply=inflammation.factor)
sim = ss.Sim([hiv, sti], connectors=[inflammation, effect], **kw)
sim.run()
print('New HIV infections:', sim.results.hiv.infection.sum())

New HIV infections: 355.0


A connector’s parameters (define_pars()) can be changed when it is made, Inflammation(half_life=ss.months(6)), and fitted like any other. Custom modules covers parameters, states, and results of a module’s own.






Warning



A connector that sets an array directly (hiv.rel_sus[uids] = 2.7) erases whatever any other module did to it, such as a vaccine’s protection or another interaction, and has to undo its own change when the condition ends. Let the code work out a value or a state, and let a modifier apply it, as above.

title: Connectors
text:
Under compartments and agents
Modifiers work under every solver. A condition on a disease’s state (sti.I) in a compartmental run needs the diseases to be tracked jointly, so that there is a compartment for each combination of their states; Starsim does this itself when a modifier of one declared disease reads the states of another, and says so in a note (the states of a × b are tracked jointly). A condition on a quantity that only agents have, such as a CD4 count of a disease written as code, or on how long ago something happened, runs as agents. A connector written as code runs as agents.

title: Connectors
text:
Pitfalls

Conditions combine with &, |, and ~, with brackets, not with and, or, and not.
Susceptibility and infectiousness only multiply. add= and set= are for parameters.
Multipliers multiply. Two modifiers whose conditions both hold for someone give the product of their multipliers (2 × 2.5 = 5 above); to give people with AIDS a factor of 5 in all, the second is 2.5, not 5.
Setting arrays in code erases other effects. See the warning above.

The API reference for this page: Connectors.

title: Connectors
text:
Further reading

Covasim: Vaccines and variants: immunity across variants of one virus, the other common kind of interaction between infections
EpiModel Gallery: network models extended with modules of their own, as connectors written as code extend a Starsim model

title: Solvers and backends
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
A model in Starsim says what the compartments are, how people move between them, and at what rates. A solver is the method that turns this into numbers over time. The same model can be solved in six ways, and for most models and questions they give the same answer, so Starsim chooses one for you. This page is about the cases where the choice matters: small numbers of people, outbreaks that die out by chance, steps that are too long for the rates, and contacts between particular people. It ends with speed, and the compiled code (the backends) that runs each solver. How the solvers work inside, and how they are tested against each other, is in Solvers and backends in the architecture section.

title: Solvers and backends
text:
The solvers



Solver
What it computes
Use it for




'ode'
The expected course of the epidemic, as a set of ordinary differential equations: compartments hold fractions of people, and the result is the same on every run
Large populations, comparing scenarios on average, fitting to data, gradients


'ide'
As 'ode', with each dwell time as it is rather than as Erlang stages (an integro-differential model)
Dwell times far from exponential, and renewal-equation models (see Branching and rescaling)


'binomial'
Whole people moving between compartments at random, a step at a time (a chain-binomial model)
Simple stochastic runs, and models that are defined in discrete time


'gillespie'
Whole people moving one at a time, at random times (Gillespie’s exact stochastic simulation algorithm)
Small populations, chance of extinction, exact stochastic dynamics


'tau'
As Gillespie, but taking many events at once (tau-leaping), which is close to exact and much faster when there are many events
Large stochastic runs


'abm'
Individual agents, each with their own state, age, and contacts
Networks, differences between individuals, histories (who infected whom, time since infection)



The first five are compartmental: they only know how many people are in each compartment (or group, if the model is stratified). Agents know who each person is. Any of them can also run the model as a branching process, with depletion turned off (branching=True; see Branching and rescaling).

title: Solvers and backends
text:
How Starsim chooses
By default (solver='auto'), a model runs as an ODE if every part of it can be written as compartments, and as agents if anything in it needs individuals: a contact network, n_agents=, or a module written as code (other than an analyzer). 'auto' never chooses a stochastic compartmental solver; ask for one by name.
Here is a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000 people. Measles has a basic reproduction number R0 of about 15 (β = 1.9 per day, infectious for 8 days), but in this town 90% of people are already immune, so at the start each case infects about 15 × 0.1 = 1.5 others:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=10)) # 90% immune, 10 infectious

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
sim.run();

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0026 s; measles: 5,781 infections; at most 673 infectious, on day 89


The first line of the output says what ran and how: here, as an ODE. The second gives R0, 15.2, and the reproduction number at the start, R = 1.52, the number of people each case infects at the start, which is R0 times the share susceptible. sim.describe() shows the same choice and the reason for it, before anything runs. To use another solver, give solver= to the sim, or to run():
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150), solver='gillespie')
sim.run(solver='abm') # Runs the same sim again, as agents

title: Solvers and backends
text:
The same outbreak five ways
For a large population and a model with nothing individual in it, the solvers agree. Here is the outbreak above with each one, run side by side with ss.parallel(), which takes a dict of sims by label:

sims = {}
for solver in ['ode', 'binomial', 'gillespie', 'tau', 'abm']:
    sims[solver] = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150), solver=solver)
sims['abm'] = sims['abm'].new(n_agents=100_000) # One agent per person: see below

msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 5 runs of 5 scenarios (ode, binomial, gillespie, tau, abm)

By default a sim has 10,000 agents, so here each would stand for 10 people, and the 10 infectious people at the start would be a single agent: an outbreak started by one case, which dies out two times in three (below). When a model’s start is a few people, keep agents at one per person, at least at the start; see Branching and rescaling.
