The classic final-size equation for an SIR model says that a share z of the susceptible people are infected in the end, where z = 1 − exp(−1.5 z): z = 0.58, or about 5,800 of the 10,000 who are susceptible. The ODE is close to that (it is not quite over by day 150), and so are the stochastic runs: the chain binomial, tau-leaping, and agents within a few hundred, and the Gillespie run lower, since its outbreak happened by chance to take off later and is further from over by day 150. Each stochastic run is one draw from many possible outbreaks, so a single run of one is not a better or worse answer than the ODE: to compare them properly, run the stochastic solvers many times (see Scenarios).

title: Solvers and backends
text:
When they disagree

Whether an outbreak takes off
The ODE follows fractions of people, so an outbreak that starts with one infectious person always takes off if R > 1. In reality, that person may recover before infecting anyone, or the first few chains of transmission may end by chance. With one infectious person at the start, the ODE says what it cannot show:

measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1)) # One infectious person
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
sim.run();

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible), with 1 infectious at the start
  Note: "measles" starts with 1 infected, so whether it takes off is a matter of chance, which solver="ode" does not show; solver="gillespie" with ss.parallel(n_runs=...) does
  Done in 0.0092 s; measles: 5,028 infections; at most 667 infectious, on day 124


The note suggests running it many times with a stochastic solver. Here it is run 200 times with Gillespie’s algorithm, and every run is plotted (lines=True):

msim = sim.run(solver='gillespie', n_runs=200)
msim.plot('measles.I', lines=True)

MultiSim: 200 runs
  Done in 0.096 s









Most runs show nothing: the outbreak died out. Counting the runs with fewer than 100 infections:

totals = msim.results.measles.infection.summarize() # The total infections of each run
print('Runs that died out:', sum(totals < 100), 'of', len(totals))

Runs that died out: 140 of 200


Branching-process theory says that an outbreak started by one case dies out with a probability of 1/R = 1/1.52 = 0.66 (for an infectious period that is exponentially distributed, as here). The share of runs that died out is close to that. The runs that took off are each close to the ODE, but later or earlier by chance.
So for a question such as “what is the chance that an imported case starts an outbreak?”, or for the uncertainty in when an outbreak peaks, use a stochastic solver and many runs. The ODE answers a different question: how large and when, on average, if it takes off.


Fade-out between epidemics
Over longer periods, the ODE can carry an infection through a trough in which fewer than one person is infectious, after which it grows again. A stochastic model can’t: when the last infectious person recovers, the infection is gone until it is introduced again. This is why, for measles, small populations see epidemics that end and need new introductions, while large ones keep the infection going (the critical community size).
Here is the same town over 20 years, with births and deaths (20 per 1,000 people a year), which bring in new susceptible children. Since the births and deaths are per year, the rates in the disease are given as typed values (ss.perday(1.9)), so that each has its own unit:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=10))
demographics = [ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02))]

town = ss.Sim(measles, demographics=demographics, total_pop=100_000, start='2000-01-01', stop='2020-01-01', dt=ss.weeks(1))
town.run()
town.plot('measles')

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2000-01-01 to 2019-12-28 (the last whole step before 2020-01-01)
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: the number infected in "measles" falls to 0.82 (at 2000-09-23) and then rises to 427; a stochastic run would usually die out there. solver="gillespie" with ss.parallel(n_runs=...) shows how often, in the runs of msim.results.measles.I after that point
  Done in 0.0036 s; measles: 40,655 infections; at most 783 infectious, on 2000-03-25









The ODE has a first epidemic, a trough in which the number infectious falls below one (which it notes), and then recurring epidemics as susceptible children accumulate, about 40,000 infections in all. Run with tau-leaping, eight times:

msim = town.run(solver='tau', n_runs=8)
msim.plot('measles.I', lines=True)

MultiSim: 8 runs
  Done in 0.17 s










msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']

median    6705.000000
low       6563.675000
high      6974.650000
mean      6735.000000
std        150.399468
Name: measles_infection, dtype: float64


In every stochastic run, measles dies out after the first epidemic, with about 6,700 infections in all: a sixth of the ODE’s. Neither is wrong as a model, but only the stochastic one represents a town in which measles can disappear, and the difference is the whole answer to a question about long-term burden. Where fade-out matters, use a stochastic solver, or add introductions from outside (see Geography).


The length of a step
The ODE takes as many small steps inside each time step as it needs, and Gillespie and tau-leaping work in continuous time, so for these the step only says when results are recorded. Agents, and the chain binomial with substeps=1, take each step whole: everyone’s chance of moving is worked out at the start of the step, and someone infected during a step can’t infect anyone until the next one. When rates are fast compared with the step, this slows the epidemic down. By default the chain binomial splits each step into enough substeps to keep this bias small: no more than about 5% of a compartment leaves it in a substep, and fewer near the epidemic threshold (R0 close to 1), where a small bias in R moves the prevalence a lot. A probability of 1 over a period (e.g. ss.probperyear(1)) moves everyone in the step: as agents, within it, and in compartments, the whole compartment at the start of each step or substep.
Measles in a town with no immunity is such a case: with β = 1.9 per day, the number infected can double in less than half a day. Here it is as an ODE, and as agents with steps of one day and of a quarter of a day:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

ode     = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(30), label='ODE').run()
daily   = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(30), solver='abm', label='Agents, steps of a day').run()
quarter = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(30), solver='abm', dt=ss.days(0.25), label='Agents, steps of a quarter day').run()

Sim "ODE": measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 30
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0019 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6
Sim "Agents, steps of a day": measles, as 10,000 agents, each 10 people, days 0 to 30
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.028 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 78,380 infectious, on day 9


Sim "Agents, steps of a quarter day": measles, as 10,000 agents, each 10 people, days 0 to 30
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.062)): each step is 0.25 days, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 38% in a step. Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.061 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 77,320 infectious, on day 6.75



ss.parallel(ode, daily, quarter).plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (ODE, Agents, steps of a day, Agents, steps of a quarter day)
  Done in 0.33 s









The sims have different steps, so each is plotted against its own time points; what needs their results put together as runs of one thing, such as the median across runs, raises an error saying so.
The ODE peaks on day 6, and agents with steps of a quarter of a day within a day of it; agents with daily steps peak three days later, and higher. The agents’ run notes the size of the step, and sim.check_dt() runs the sim again with half the step and shows how much each result changes:

daily.check_dt()

Change in each result when the timestep goes from 1 to 0.5 days (largest difference, as a share of the largest value):
  measles.infection             57.3%   (peak 27610 → 33830)
  measles.recovery              51.4%   (peak 8600 → 9400)
  measles.prevalence            35.8%   (peak 0.7838 → 0.7675)
  measles.I                     35.8%   (peak 78380 → 76750)
  measles.S                     30.6%   (peak 99900 → 99900)
  measles.R                     14.0%   (peak 94000 → 95270)


A result that changes by more than a few percent when the step is halved depends on the step, and the step should be smaller. The shorter the generation time of an infection compared with the step, the more this matters: measles is extreme, and for an infection with rates of a few percent per step (as for most models with daily steps and durations of weeks), the step makes little difference. See Time for how to set the step.
A state’s count is recorded at the end of each step, so as agents it includes the people infected in that step, who can’t infect anyone until the next one. At a coarse step, a stock therefore reads a little high compared with the ODE, even at equilibrium: an SIS with R0 = 1.25 and 5 days infectious settles at 21.4% infectious with daily steps, against 20% for the ODE, of whom 18.1% are transmitting during a step. The difference shrinks in proportion to the step (20.5% with steps of a quarter of a day), and the average over a step of the number infectious is close to the ODE’s (19.8% with daily steps).
A threshold on a clock acts at the step boundaries, since the clock is read once a step. A rate that applies until 13 weeks of pregnancy (where=preg.P.time < ss.weeks(13)), on monthly steps, applies while the clock reads 0, 1, and 2 months, and someone who arrives during a step spends on average half of it at 0: so it applies for about 2.5 of the 3 months it should, and the event it governs happens less often than the inputs imply (11.9% of pregnancies miscarry against 14.1%, in FPsim’s case). sim.check_dt() shows it, and a shorter step reduces it.


Contacts between particular people
A compartmental model assumes that everyone in a group mixes with everyone else in it at random. A contact network, in which each person has a few fixed contacts, breaks this: once someone’s contacts are infected or immune, they have nobody left to infect, so the epidemic grows more slowly and infects fewer people than random mixing at the same number of contacts. A network needs agents; with solver='ode', Starsim replaces it with random mixing at the network’s mean number of contacts, and notes that it has done so.
Measles spreads so readily that nearly everyone is infected either way, so this example uses a less transmissible infection, with β = 0.05 per contact per day and eight contacts each that never change (dynamic=False):

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
flu = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 0.05*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init_prev=0.001, name='flu')
contacts = ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=8, dynamic=False)

agents = ss.Sim(flu, networks=contacts, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(150), dt=ss.days(0.5)).run()
mixing = ss.Sim(flu, networks=contacts, total_pop=10_000, stop=ss.days(150), solver='ode').run()

Sim: flu, as 10,000 agents, days 0 to 150
  Running as agents: n_agents was given


  Done in 0.26 s; flu: 8,745 infections; at most 2,500 infectious, on day 37


Sim: flu, 10,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  flu: R0 = 3.2, with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: RandomNet approximated by homogeneous mixing with 8 contacts per day (its mean number of contacts)
  Done in 0.0016 s; flu: 9,516 infections; at most 3,241 infectious, on day 28


With random mixing (the ODE), R0 = 0.05 × 8 × 8 = 3.2; on the fixed network, the epidemic peaks later and lower, and fewer people are infected. If the structure of contacts is part of the question (partnerships, households, contact tracing), use agents; if only the average number of contacts matters, compartments are enough. approx=False makes any such approximation an error instead of a note.

title: Solvers and backends
text:
Speed
The compartmental solvers don’t slow down with the size of the population, except Gillespie, which takes one event at a time. A million people, as a chain binomial, tau-leaping, and Gillespie:

for solver in ['binomial', 'tau', 'gillespie']:
    ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=1_000_000, stop=ss.days(50), solver=solver).run()

Sim: measles, 1,000,000 people, as a stochastic compartmental model (chain binomial), days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 1,000 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0013 s; measles: 999,000 infections; at most 760,234 infectious, on day 7
Sim: measles, 1,000,000 people, as a stochastic compartmental model (tau-leaping), days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 1,000 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.002 s; measles: 999,000 infections; at most 758,106 infectious, on day 6
Sim: measles, 1,000,000 people, as a stochastic compartmental model (Gillespie), days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 1,000 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.13 s; measles: 999,000 infections; at most 741,375 infectious, on day 6


Each says how long it took. Gillespie handled about two million events here in well under a second; with tens of millions of events, use tau-leaping. Agents take time in proportion to the number of agents and the number of steps; a population larger than the number of agents is represented by having each agent stand for several people (see Branching and rescaling).

title: Solvers and backends
text:
Backends
Whichever solver is chosen, the numbers are worked out by compiled code rather than by Python, which is why a compartmental run of a million people takes milliseconds. Starsim has three engines, and chooses among them itself; none changes the results, so most users never need this section, except to know why the first run after installing Starsim can be slow.

The kernels are compiled loops: they run compartmental models step by step, the passes over the agents (who is infected, who recovers), and the random draws. There are two copies that give the same numbers bit for bit: one in Numba, which is compiled on first use after installing Starsim (a few minutes, once; it is then kept on disk), and one in Rust, compiled ahead of time and included in the wheels that pip install starsim gets on Linux, macOS, and Windows (from a clone, build it with cd starsim/solvers/rust && ./build). ss.options.kernels chooses: 'auto' (the default) uses Rust if it is there and Numba otherwise, running short compartmental runs as plain Python while Numba has not yet compiled; 'rust' and 'numba' ask for one; 'python' runs the compartmental kernels as plain Python, which is slow but easy to step through in a debugger.
JAX takes a whole run of the ODE when the run is long enough to repay starting JAX (about half a second, once a session): many groups, many steps, or many runs. The choice is made from the size of the model, never from timing, and an ODE run in JAX agrees with the kernels to rounding. Setting sim.jax = True or False before the run forces it either way. JAX is also what computes gradients.
Plain Python and NumPy run the rest: the step loop of agent-based runs, and modules written as code. Your own loops in a module can be compiled with @ss.jit (see Custom modules).

To compile everything at once rather than on first use, run ss.compile() (or starsim compile from the command line): once after installing, when building a Docker image, in continuous integration, or before a long batch of runs on a cluster, so that no run waits for it (see Deployment). With verbose=2, a run says which engine took it and why (e.g. “engine: kernels: a short run, shorter than JAX takes to start”), and why a compartmental run was taken step by step rather than in one call (an intervention that needs its own step, for example).
Two settings of the sim change the numerical method itself rather than the engine. integrator= is the ODE’s scheme: 'rk4' (fourth-order Runge–Kutta, the default) or 'euler'. substeps= is the number of substeps in each time step, for the ODE and the chain binomial; by default there are enough that no compartment turns over by more than a small share in one, and substeps=1 takes each step whole, as discrete-time chain-binomial models in the literature do.

title: Solvers and backends
text:
Which to use



If the question is about
Use




The expected course of an epidemic in a large population
'ode' (the default for a compartmental model)


Fitting a model to data, or gradients
'ode' (see Calibration)


The chance that an outbreak takes off or dies out, or the spread of possible outbreaks
'gillespie' (or 'tau' for large populations), with many runs


The same for one introduction into a large population, or chains of who infected whom
branching=True, with 'gillespie', or 'abm' for chains, and until= to stop the runs that take off (Branching and rescaling)


A model written in discrete time, such as a chain-binomial model from the literature
'binomial' with substeps=1


Networks, contact tracing, individual histories, or differences between people that groups can’t hold
'abm' (chosen for you when the model has them)

title: Solvers and backends
text:
Pitfalls

One stochastic run is not a result. Compare a stochastic solver with the ODE over many runs, not one.
A long step changes agents and the chain binomial. When the sim notes that many people leave a state in one step, check with sim.check_dt(), and shorten the step if the results change.
An ODE with fewer than one person infected. The ODE notes when the number infected falls below one and then rises again; a stochastic model would usually die out there.
Approximations under 'ode'. A network, or anything else that needs agents, is replaced by its standard compartmental form when you ask for 'ode', with a note; read the notes (they are also kept in sim.notes).

title: Solvers and backends
text:
Further reading

Keeling & Ross: On methods for studying stochastic disease dynamics: ODEs, chain binomials, Gillespie, and tau-leaping compared
GillesPy2 documentation: a library of Gillespie and tau-leaping solvers for the same kind of model
Epiverse epidemics: deterministic and stochastic compartmental models in R
odin.dust: one model compiled as an ODE or as a stochastic discrete-time model

title: Custom modules
text:
🧠15% 🤖85%
Most of a Starsim model is declared: its states, its transitions and their rates, the interventions given to it, and the results it reports. Some parts of a model are easier to say as code: a quantity that each person carries and that changes continuously (an antibody level, a CD4 count, a viral load), a rule of behavior of your own, or a result worked out in a way of your own. A module written as code is a Python class with a step() method, which Starsim calls once each step. It can read and change the rest of the sim, and it sits in the same sim as declared diseases.
This page covers when to write a module as code, a worked example, the parts of a module, the order in which Starsim calls them, and modules made from a single function. T9 – Custom modules builds one up a step at a time, A5 – Custom modules does the same for modules among agents, and Model execution explains the loop that calls them.

title: Custom modules
text:
Before writing code
Many things that once needed a module of their own are declared, and a declared part has two advantages: it runs under every solver (as an ODE, as a stochastic compartmental model, or as agents), and describe(), diagram(), and equations() show it. So before writing a module, check whether one of these does the job:



To model
Declare it with
See




A disease that moves people between states
ss.Disease() with states and transitions
Diseases


Vaccination, testing, or treatment
ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), ss.treat()
Products


Protection that wanes
ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, waning=ss.years(5), ...), or a state people leave (R >> S @ ss.years(5))
Products


Contact tracing
a delivery with trace=
Products


A change to a parameter for some people or some time (masks, school closures)
ss.modify()
Interventions


One disease changing the risk of another
ss.modify(sti.rel_sus, multiply=3, where=hiv.I)
Connectors


A number to report, such as cases from infections
ss.outcome()
Outcomes



Write a module as code when the model needs something none of these can say. A module that keeps a value for each person, like the one below, works on agents, so a sim with one runs as agents by itself (n_agents= says how many); it works with declared diseases in the same sim. A module that keeps nothing per person, such as an ODE of its own, runs with no agents, and costs the loop only its own methods; A5 – Custom modules works through an example, from declared to compiled code.

title: Custom modules
section: An example: immunity that fades gradually
text:
An example: immunity that fades gradually
In a declared SIRS model, immunity is all or nothing: people are fully protected in R until they move back to S, and then not protected at all. For many respiratory infections, protection fades gradually as antibodies decline, so each person’s susceptibility depends on how long ago they recovered. That is a per-person quantity that changes continuously, which is what code is for.
(Measles, the example in the tutorials, is a poor fit here: immunity to measles lasts for life. This page uses a generic respiratory infection instead.)
Here is the infection, with no immunity at all: people go back to S when they recover (an SIS model). Its R0 is 0.4 per day × 7 days = 2.8:

import starsim as ss

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I       # β = 0.4 per day
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.days(7)  # Infectious for 7 days on average
cold = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/


The module holds each person’s antibody level. It is 1 just after recovery and halves every half_life:

class Antibodies(ss.Module):
    """ Each person's antibody level: 1 on recovery, then halving every half_life """

    def __init__(self, half_life=ss.days(60), **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            half_life = half_life,
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(
            ss.FloatArr('level', default=0.0, label='Antibody level'),
        )
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('mean_level', label='Mean antibody level'),
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        decay = 0.5**(self.t.dt/self.pars.half_life) # The share left after one step
        self.level[:] = self.level*decay
        recovered = self.sim.diseases.cold.recovery.uids # Those who recovered in the last step
        self.level[recovered] = 1.0
        return

    def update_results(self):
        super().update_results()
        self.results.mean_level[self.ti] = self.level.mean()
        return

The module keeps the level, and a modifier says what it does: it multiplies each person’s susceptibility to the infection by what the antibodies leave of it. A modifier never overwrites the quantity it changes, so the disease’s own rel_sus is kept, and describe() lists the modifier as part of the model:

def susceptibility(sim):
    """ Each person's susceptibility: 1 minus their antibody level """
    return 1 - sim.custom.antibodies.level

protection = ss.modify(cold.rel_sus, multiply=susceptibility)

To compare, run the infection with no immunity, with all-or-nothing immunity that lasts 60 days on average (a declared SIRS), and with antibodies that halve every 60 days:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sirs = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(7),
    waning    = R >> S @ ss.days(60), # Fully immune, then fully susceptible
    init_prev = 0.01,
    name = 'cold',
)

pars = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(365))
sims = {
    'No immunity': ss.Sim(cold, **pars),
    'All or nothing': ss.Sim(sirs, **pars),
    'Antibodies that fade': ss.Sim(cold, Antibodies(), connectors=protection, **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold_I')

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (No immunity, All or nothing, Antibodies that fade)
  Done in 0.93 s









With no immunity, the infection settles at once at an endemic level. With either kind of immunity, the first wave leaves many people protected, so the number infectious falls and then rises again as protection is lost. With antibodies that fade, people regain some susceptibility soon after recovering, instead of none at all until they lose their protection entirely, so the later waves are larger and the infection settles at a higher level.
ss.parallel() runs the sims in place, so each one has its results. The module’s result is among them, under the module’s name:

sims['Antibodies that fade'].results.antibodies.mean_level.plot()

title: Custom modules
text:
Choosing a base class
A module subclasses one of Starsim’s module types, so that it runs at the right point in each step and ends up in the right place in the sim:



Base class
Use for
Given to the sim as




ss.Module
Anything that doesn’t fit the others, like the antibodies above
custom= (or as a positional argument)


ss.Disease
A disease: declared, written as code, or both (see Diseases)
diseases=


ss.Infection
A disease whose transmission between agents is written as code
diseases=


ss.Network
Who has contact with whom
networks=


ss.Demographics
Births, deaths, and migration
demographics=


ss.Intervention
Actions that change the course of the epidemic
interventions=


ss.Analyzer
Recording results without changing anything
analyzers=


ss.Connector
Links between modules, such as interactions between diseases
connectors=



The sim keeps each kind in its own list, e.g. sim.custom.antibodies and sim.interventions[0]. A module is named after its class in lower case (antibodies), unless it is given name=.

title: Custom modules
text:
Parameters: define_pars() and update_pars()
In __init__(), call super().__init__() first, with no arguments; then give the parameters and their defaults with define_pars(); then apply the values the user gave with update_pars():
def __init__(self, half_life=ss.days(60), **kwargs):
    super().__init__()
    self.define_pars(
        half_life = half_life,
    )
    self.update_pars(**kwargs)
update_pars() raises an error for a parameter that define_pars() didn’t give, which catches misspelled names. The parameters are in self.pars. Give rates and durations as Starsim’s time parameters (e.g. ss.days(60), ss.peryear(0.1)), so that they mean the same whatever the step of the sim: self.t.dt/self.pars.half_life above is a number of half-lives per step, whether the step is a day or a week.

title: Custom modules
text:
States: define_states()
A state of a module is an array with one value for each agent. Give the module’s states with define_states(), as ss.FloatArr (numbers), ss.BoolState (true or false), or ss.IntArr (whole numbers). (ss.State is different: it is a state of a declared disease.)
self.define_states(
    ss.FloatArr('level', default=0.0, label='Antibody level'),
    ss.BoolState('vaccinated', label='Vaccinated'),
)
Each state becomes an attribute of the module (self.level) and is added to the people (sim.people.antibodies.level). States grow as agents are born, and a dead agent’s values are kept but left out of sums and means. Keep every value that belongs to a person in a state, never in a plain NumPy array of your own, which wouldn’t grow with the population. Each ss.BoolState also gives a result of the same name, the number of people for whom it is true. A state can also have several columns, e.g. immunity to each of several strains: see People. To read and write states, see Array indexing.
A property of each person that several modules read, rather than a state of one module (e.g. a social determinant of health that two conditions depend on), is added to the people themselves, from init_pre(), with sim.people.add_state(ss.BoolArr('housing', default=ss.bernoulli(0.2))). Adding one that is there already returns it, so each module that reads it can add it. A declared rate reads it as ss.ppl.housing, or as ss.ppl.get('housing', 0) to have a value when no module adds it.
Code reads the same names a declaration does: a condition or an event’s memory of a running sim, indexed by UID, gives its values, e.g. preg.since_birth[uids] (the time since each woman’s last live birth) or (hiv.I & preg.P)[uids], and .values gives them for everyone alive. A declared transition’s current rate for some agents, with its modifiers, is dis.death.hazard(uids).

Aliases
define_aliases() gives a name that stands for something else: the name of another state, or a function of the module.
self.define_aliases(infectious='infected') # Another name for a state
self.define_aliases(asymptomatic=lambda self: self.infected & ~self.symptomatic) # Worked out from other states
Keyword arguments to define_states() are passed on to define_aliases(), so a module can give its states and aliases together. An alias is used only when the module has no attribute of that name, so a base class can use one as a default that a subclass replaces by defining a state of the same name; this is how ss.Infection counts everyone infected as infectious unless a subclass says otherwise (see Diseases). An alias given as a function is worked out each time it is read, can’t be written to, and gives a result (its count). To replace an inherited state or alias, pass overwrite=True to define_states(); to remove one, name it in reset=.

title: Custom modules
text:
Results: define_results()
To report a result of your own, override init_results() and give it with define_results(). A result has one value for each time point of the sim:
def init_results(self):
    super().init_results()
    self.define_results(
        ss.Result('mean_level', label='Mean antibody level'),
        ss.Result('n_protected', kind='stock', label='Number protected'),
    )
kind= says how the result is summed over time and compared with data: 'flow' for a number of events in each step (e.g. new infections), 'stock' for a quantity at each time point (e.g. the number infected), and 'ratio' for a share or a mean. If it isn’t given, it is guessed from the name (new_... is a flow, n_... a stock) or else the type (an integer is a count, guessed to be a flow; anything else is a ratio). A flow or stock is a count, which is multiplied by the number of people each agent stands for when the population is rescaled; a ratio (a share, a mean, or a level) isn’t. scale= overrides this. Fill results in update_results(), at self.ti.

title: Custom modules
text:
The work: step()
step() is called once each step, and is where the module does its job. Inside it:

self.sim is the whole sim: its people (self.sim.people), diseases (self.sim.diseases.cold), and so on. A plain ss.Module given as modules= is in self.sim.custom (sim.modules is every module of the sim, of every kind).
self.pars are the module’s parameters. A time parameter stays one (self.pars.half_life), as above. A value that varies, in time (ss.timeseries, ss.seasonal) or by level (ss.by(node=[...])), is its value now in arithmetic and NumPy (self.pars.emergence*n, np.exp(-self.pars.k), float(self.pars.k)): a number in the sim’s unit, or one for each level. If its values are typed, its value now is typed too, so self.pars.rate.to_prob() works whether rate is ss.peryear(0.1) or ss.timeseries({2000: ss.peryear(0.1), 2010: ss.peryear(0.2)}). So is a parameter of a declared disease, with what modifies it applied (acts*(1 - hiv.pars.eff_condom)).
self.t.dt is the length of a step, self.now is the date or time the step starts from, and self.ti is the index of the time point at the step’s end, where what happens during the step is recorded.
A transition of a declared disease says who went through it: disease.recovery.uids is the agents who recovered in the last step. disease.recovery.ever, .count, and .since say whether, how often, and how long ago each person did; to save memory, a disease keeps this history only for the transitions something in the model reads, so to read one after the run (e.g. sir.infection.count.values), set ss.options.keep_times = True before the sim is built.
To move people between the states of a declared disease, use ss.move(): ss.move(sir.I, sir.R, p=0.5) cures half of those infectious, ss.move(sir.S, sir.I, n=5) makes five susceptible people infectious, ss.move(sir.S, sir.R, p=0.8, where=ss.ppl.age < 5) protects 80% of the susceptible children under 5 (a condition on a group, as in where= elsewhere), and sir.move(uids, sir.R) moves particular agents from wherever they are (as agents only; the arguments can come in any order, with the source before the destination, so ss.move(sir, uids, 'R') is the same). It runs the same under every solver, and since people are moved rather than made or lost, every disease keeps the same people; the number in a state of people (sir.I.n) is read, not set. A count that is not people (mosquitoes, ss.State(people=False)) can also be set (W.n = 0) or moved from and to outside the model (ss.move(ss.null, mosq.Sv, n=1000)).

A module written as code that is not a disease runs before the diseases in each step, so what it does (protecting someone, say) applies to the transmission in the same step. Model execution lists the full order.

Exits and arrivals within a step
As agents, a module written as code takes each step whole, as Starsim’s own solvers do, and two habits keep its results from depending on the length of the step (see Solvers). Draw competing exits from a state together: if a mosquito can die or become infectious, draw one exit with the total rate and then which one it was (in proportion to the rates), rather than first the deaths and then the progression of the survivors, which counts the second against a smaller group. And let those who arrive in a state during a step face only the rest of the step: a mosquito that emerges or is infected mid-step should have, on average, half a step’s chance of leaving it, not a whole one. Both biases are of the order of the rate times the step, so they matter when rates are a sizable fraction of a step; sim.check_dt() shows them.
For anything random, give the module a distribution in __init__() (e.g. self.p_isolate = ss.bernoulli(p=0.5)) and draw from it in step() (self.p_isolate.filter(uids)), rather than calling NumPy’s random numbers. Each distribution then has its own stream of random numbers, so the module’s draws don’t change when the rest of the model does, and comparisons between scenarios stay free of noise from the random numbers: see Random numbers.

title: Custom modules
text:
When each method is called
When a sim is built and run, each module goes through these stages:

__init__(): the module is made; its parameters and states are given.
init_pre(sim): called once when the sim is built. It links the module to the sim and the people, sets up its time steps, and calls init_results(). Override it rarely, and call super().init_pre(sim) if you do.
init_post(): called once the people exist and their states have their initial values; for setup that needs them.
step(): called once each step.
update_results(): called each step after every module has stepped, to record the step’s results.
finalize() and finalize_results(): called once at the end of the run, e.g. to work out a result from others.

Always call the base class’s method (super().init_results(), super().update_results(), and so on) when you override one that the base class has.

title: Custom modules
text:
Modules from functions
For a quick piece of logic, a function of the sim is enough: it becomes the module’s step(), called once each step. A function given as interventions= becomes an ss.Intervention, one given as analyzers= an ss.Analyzer, and one given as custom= an ss.Module, named after the function. A common use is a check while a model is being built, such as that everyone is in one state of a disease at each step:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

def check_states(sim):
    """ Check that everyone alive is in exactly one state of measles """
    m = sim.diseases.measles
    in_states = m.S.sum() + m.I.sum() + m.R.sum()
    assert in_states == len(sim.people), f'{in_states} people in states, but {len(sim.people)} alive'
    return

sim = ss.Sim(measles, analyzers=check_states, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()
print(sim.analyzers[0].name)

check_states


A function module is called at every step, so it has to check the time itself if it should act only at some (e.g. if sim.now >= ss.date('2025-03-01'):). Its keyword arguments with defaults are its parameters, passed to it at each call, so one given as ss.par with bounds can be fitted and set by name like any other parameter (def close_schools(sim, start=2025, share=ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.2, 0.8])):; see Fitting a model). It has no states or results of its own; as soon as it needs them, write a class instead. ss.Intervention.from_func(fn) (and likewise for the other types) makes the module from a function explicitly. For analyzers, see Analyzers.

title: Custom modules
text:
Pitfalls

Writing code for something that is declared. Check the table at the top of this page first: a declared part runs under every solver and shows in describe().
Forgetting super(). Call super().__init__() with no arguments as the first line of __init__(), and the base class’s method whenever you override init_results(), update_results(), init_post(), and the like.
Keeping per-person values outside a state. A plain array doesn’t grow when agents are born; a state does, and appears in sim.people.to_df().
Keeping a reference to another module. A sim copies the modules it is given when it is built, so reach the rest of the sim through self.sim in step() (e.g. self.sim.diseases.cold), not through an object kept from before.
Comparing self.ti across modules with their own timelines. A module given start=, stop=, or a dt= of its own runs only on its own steps, and its self.ti counts those steps, not the sim’s. To compare times between modules, use dates or durations (self.now), not step indices.
Writing into another module’s arrays at your own ti. Write into another module’s results and time arrays at its index, not yours: disease.results.treated[disease.ti], and disease.ti_recovered[uids] = disease.ti. With a yearly sim and a monthly disease, self.ti is the wrong row.
Using NumPy’s random numbers. Draw from Starsim’s distributions instead, as above, so that runs can be repeated and scenarios compared without noise from the random numbers.
Reading rel_sus without its modifiers. A disease written as code that is not transmitted (not an ss.Infection with a beta) and reads its own rel_sus or rel_trans reads them with self.current_value('rel_sus', uids), which applies ss.modify(dis.rel_sus, ...) and products, and says so in its class, allow_modifiers = ('rel_sus',); otherwise a modifier of them is refused, since nothing would apply it.
Reading a parameter that differs between people. ss.modify(dis.pars.rate, ...) works on a disease written as code, and self.pars.rate is the modified value while it applies. That is one value, so a modifier with where= needs self.current_value('rate', uids) and allow_modifiers = ('rate',); otherwise it is refused.
Several causes of death in one step. If several modules request the death of the same person in a step (sim.people.request_death(uids, cause=self)), one cause is chosen at random; give each claim its hazard (hazard=) to choose in proportion to them.
Writing to .raw. Write to states by UID (self.level[uids] = 1); see Array indexing.

title: Custom modules
text:
Further reading

Mesa: agents and their step methods in a general-purpose agent-based modeling framework in Python
LASER: fast spatial agent-based disease models, with per-agent properties updated in compiled code
NetLogo: a classic environment for agent-based models, with many example models
Covasim: Starsim’s predecessor, whose custom interventions and analyzers work much as modules do here

title: Analyzers
text:
🧠10% 🤖90%
An analyzer records something during a run that the results don’t keep, without changing the model. It is called at the end of each step, after everything else has been updated, and reports on the state of things then. Most quantities don’t need one: every state and transition of a declared disease has a result, ratios and outcomes are declared with the model (see Results and Outcomes), and results by age or any other group come from stratifying the model. An analyzer is for the rest: something about individual agents (their ages when infected, who infected whom), or a quantity worked out from several modules at once.

title: Analyzers
text:
When an analyzer runs
An analyzer runs at the start (time point 0) and then at the end of each step, after the step’s results have been recorded. In the analyzer, sim.ti (or self.ti in a class) is the time point at the end of the step, where the step’s results go. A declared disease dates each infection at the end of the step in which it happened, in its state ti_I, so the people infected during this step are those with ti_I.isclose(ti) (== raises for a time, since a time drawn between steps never equals one exactly). An analyzer that acts every few steps (if self.ti % 7 == 0, at the end of each week) also acts at time point 0, before anything has happened, unless it skips it (if self.ti == 0: return).

title: Analyzers
text:
A function as an analyzer
The simplest analyzer is a function of the sim, given in analyzers=. This one records the mean age of the people infected in each step, which is a common measure for measles (where vaccination of children raises it). It needs individual ages, so the sim runs as agents:

import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

ages = []
def age_at_infection(sim):
    new = sim.diseases.measles.ti_I.isclose(sim.ti) # People infected during this step
    ages.append(sim.people.age[new].mean() if new.any() else np.nan)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(30), dt=ss.days(0.25), analyzers=age_at_infection, verbose=0)
sim.run()
print('Mean age at infection, by step:', np.round(ages[1:9], 1))

Mean age at infection, by step: [15.2 37.1 32.5 32.5 31.9 42.4 32.9 28.4]


Here people mix at random, so the mean age at infection is close to the mean age of the population (34); with a contact matrix in which children mix most, it is not (see below).
A function is quick to write, but what it records lives outside the sim: it is not plotted or exported with the results, and when the sim is run in another process (by ss.parallel()), the list in this process stays empty. For anything kept, use a class.

title: Analyzers
text:
An analyzer as a class
An analyzer written as a class (a subclass of ss.Analyzer) declares results of its own, which are then stored, plotted, and exported with the sim’s other results. This one records the mean age at infection, and the new infections among children and adults, as one result with a column for each:

class AgeAtInfection(ss.Analyzer):
    """ The mean age of the people infected in each step, and the number of them who are children and adults """
    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('mean_age', label='Mean age at infection'), # An average (a ratio), so not scaled by the people each agent stands for
            ss.Result('new_infections', columns=['children', 'adults'], label='New infections'),
        )

    def step(self):
        new = self.sim.diseases.measles.ti_I.isclose(self.ti)
        if new.any():
            age = self.sim.people.age
            self.results.mean_age[self.ti] = age[new].mean()
            self.results.new_infections[self.ti] = [np.count_nonzero(new & (age < 15)), np.count_nonzero(new & (age >= 15))]
        else:
            self.results.mean_age[self.ti] = np.nan # No infections, so no mean age (rather than 0)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(30), dt=ss.days(0.25), analyzers=AgeAtInfection(), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.ageatinfection.new_infections.plot()








The analyzer’s results are under its name in lower case, sim.results.ageatinfection. A result with columns has each as a result of its own (res.new_infections.children), and each is a column of sim.to_df():

sim.to_df().columns.tolist()

['time',
 'measles_S',
 'measles_I',
 'measles_R',
 'measles_infection',
 'measles_recovery',
 'ageatinfection_mean_age',
 'ageatinfection_new_infections_children',
 'ageatinfection_new_infections_adults',
 'alive',
 'female',
 'new_deaths',
 'new_emigrants',
 'cum_deaths']


An analyzer is a way to compare what the results don’t show. Here the same analyzer is added to two versions of the model: the one above, with homogeneous mixing, and one with a contact matrix in which children have the most contacts, mostly with each other (the matrix of Population data, with β per contact chosen to give a similar epidemic):

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.15*I       # β = 0.15 per contact
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles_ages = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 4, 0.5], [2, 8, 0.5], [1.5, 3, 2]]) # Contacts a day

kw = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(20), dt=ss.days(0.25), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({
    'Homogeneous mixing': ss.Sim(measles, analyzers=AgeAtInfection(), **kw),
    'Contact matrix by age': ss.Sim(measles_ages, networks=contacts, analyzers=AgeAtInfection(), **kw),
})
msim.plot('ageatinfection.mean_age')








With homogeneous mixing, the mean age at infection stays near the mean age of the population throughout. With the contact matrix, children are infected first, and the mean age rises as the epidemic goes on, until the last people infected are mostly older adults, who have the fewest contacts. Nearly everyone is infected by measles in the end either way, so a result such as the total number infected would not show this.
A result that is a count (a flow or a stock) is multiplied by the number of people each agent stands for when the run ends; an average or a share (a ratio, which mean_age is guessed to be from its name) is not. scale= overrides this.

title: Analyzers
text:
The infection log
The infection log records each infection: when it happened, who was infected, and, where there is a network, by whom. It needs agents and a contact network, since otherwise nobody is the source of a particular infection: an infection by a mixing pool (ss.MixingPool), a contact matrix, or mixing with everyone comes from the share infectious in a group, not from a particular person, so its source and network are NaN (seeds have a source of -1). Give analyzers='infection_log':

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
flu = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 0.05*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init_prev=0.002, name='flu')

sim = ss.Sim(flu, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=8), n_agents=5_000, stop=ss.days(100), analyzers='infection_log', verbose=0)
sim.run()
log = sim.analyzers.infection_log.log
df = log.to_df()
df.tail()

Each row is one infection: the time (t), the infected agent (target), and the agent who infected them (source, which is −1 for the people infected at the start). The log also plots who infected whom over time, and log.to_graph() gives the chains of transmission as a NetworkX graph:

sim.analyzers.infection_log.plot()








animate() shows the same infections as they happen, one frame per time point: each agent infected is a dot on a grid, colored by when it was infected. It draws each frame in turn, so run it in a Python session rather than a notebook:

sim.analyzers.infection_log.animate(framerate=20)

From the log, the generation interval (the time from a person’s infection to the infection of each person they infect) is the time of each infection minus the time its source was infected:

infected_at = df.set_index('target').t        # When each agent was infected
df['generation'] = df.t - df.source.map(infected_at)
print('Mean generation interval:', round(df.generation.mean(), 1), 'days')

Mean generation interval: 5.5 days


If a person’s contacts all stayed susceptible, the mean would be the mean infectious period, 8 days. It is shorter because they don’t: on a network, a person’s contacts are soon infected by others or immune, so people infect fewer of them late in their infectious period.
A disease written as code can add data to each infection, such as the variant (log.add_entries(uids, sources, time, variant=variants)), or to each agent’s latest infection later on, such as a diagnosis (log.add_data(uids, diagnosed=True)). See Custom modules.

title: Analyzers
text:
Analyzers in a compartmental run
An analyzer can be given to a model that runs as compartments, as any module written as code can that keeps nothing for each person. There, it sees the number of people in each compartment, not individuals: sim.diseases.measles.I.n is the number infectious. The run then goes a step at a time, so it is slower; for a quantity that can be worked out from the results after the run, such as the effective reproduction number R0 × S/N, compute it from the results instead.

title: Analyzers
text:
Pitfalls

An analyzer must not change the model. To change something during a run, use an intervention.
Results kept outside the sim are lost when the sim runs in another process (ss.parallel()); declare results in a class.
Counts of agents are scaled; averages are not. A result’s kind decides this: a flow or stock is scaled, a ratio is not. Give kind= (or scale=) when the guess from the name is wrong.
Check whether a result already exists. Stratifying the model gives results by age or any other group, under every solver, with no analyzer.

title: Modeling landscape
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
There are many tools for modeling infectious diseases, and most modelers already use one. This page sets out the kinds of model and of tool, where Starsim fits among them, and when another tool is the better choice. It ends with a comparison of Starsim with the frameworks that have a conversion page: a model from each, written both ways, with how their results agree, how long each takes, and what works and what does not yet.

title: Modeling landscape
text:
Kinds of model
Mechanistic models of transmission (models of how infection passes between people, as opposed to statistical models that forecast cases from past cases) come in a few kinds, which differ in how they represent the population:

Deterministic compartmental models divide the population into compartments (susceptible, infectious, recovered, and so on, often stratified by age, sex, or place) and follow the number in each as an ordinary differential equation (ODE) or difference equation. They are fast, smooth, and easy to fit, and they give the expected course of a large epidemic; they have no chance, so they say nothing about fade-out or the spread of outcomes in small populations.
Stochastic compartmental models have the same compartments, but move whole numbers of people between them at random: a chain binomial in discrete time, or the Gillespie algorithm in continuous time. They capture chance (outbreaks that die out, variation between runs) at little more cost than an ODE, and are the usual basis of particle filters.
Metapopulation models are compartmental models in each of many places (towns, districts, farms) linked by movement or commuting. They capture the geography of spread without following individuals.
Network models follow individuals and their contacts: partnerships for sexually transmitted infections, households, or contact graphs. They are needed when who meets whom matters (concurrency, clustering, contact tracing), and often estimate the network from survey data.
Agent-based models follow every individual, each with their own states (age, infection, immunity, treatment, history), contacts, and events. They are the most flexible (any rule that can be written about a person can be modeled) and the most costly, both to run and, often, to write and check.

The same disease can usually be written in more than one of these, and the choice is about the question: an ODE for the expected size of an epidemic in a large population, a stochastic or agent-based model where chance, heterogeneity, or individual histories matter.

title: Modeling landscape
text:
Kinds of tool
The tools differ as much in how a model is written as in what it can represent:

Written by hand, in a general-purpose language: a loop in NumPy, or an ODE solver such as R’s deSolve or Julia’s DifferentialEquations. Complete freedom, and nothing done for you: stratification, interventions, calibration, and checking are all yours to write.
Model languages compiled to fast code: odin (R, compiled to C++), and camdl. A model is a short list of equations; the tool runs it fast, and often fits it (odin’s companions for particle filters and MCMC).
Configuration files: flepiMoP and EMULSION in YAML, Atomica in spreadsheets. A model is data rather than code, which suits teams and non-programmers, and pipelines that run many models the same way.
Libraries of compartmental models, used from Python: summer2 (stratifications and JAX), epydemix (populations and contact matrices by country, and fitting by approximate Bayesian computation), MEmilio (a C++ core, with ODE, integro-differential, metapopulation, and agent-based models), and SimInf in R (stochastic models in thousands of linked herds).
Network and agent-based frameworks: EpiModel (R, with networks estimated by exponential random graph models), LASER (fast agent-based models at national scale), Starsim v3 and Covasim, EMOD, and general-purpose agent-based tools such as Mesa and NetLogo.
Statistical tools that fit mechanistic models to data: pomp (partially observed Markov processes), Stan and PyMC (Bayesian inference), and the packages of the R Epidemics Consortium and the Epiverse for outbreak analytics.

title: Modeling landscape
text:
Where Starsim fits
Starsim’s distinctive feature is that one model runs in more than one of these ways. A disease declared as states and transitions (S >> I @ beta*I; see Writing models) is data that Starsim can read, so the same declaration runs as an ODE, as a stochastic compartmental model, or as agents, chosen by a single argument (see Solvers and backends). A model can start as an ODE, be fitted fast, and then run as agents to add a network, a household structure, or an intervention that targets individuals, without being written twice. Where the declaration can’t express something, a module written as code in Python (see Custom modules) adds it, at the cost of running only as agents.
Around that core are the parts most models need: stratification by age, sex, place, or anything else (Stratification); populations and contact matrices by country (Population data); networks (Contact networks); demographics and pregnancy (Demographics); vaccines, treatments, and other interventions (Interventions); costs (Costs); and calibration, including gradients through the model (Fitting a model). Models from many of the tools above can be read in, and Starsim models written out (Import/export).
Starsim is a Python library. It suits modelers who write code (or are willing to), who want one tool from a quick compartmental model to a detailed agent-based one, and who want to compare the two.

title: Modeling landscape
section: When another tool is the better choice
text:
When another tool is the better choice
Starsim is not the best tool for every job, and the comparisons below say where it falls short. Another tool is likely to serve better:

For networks estimated from survey data with exponential random graph models (terms such as nodemix, absdiff, or gwesp): EpiModel, which builds on statnet. Starsim’s networks target degrees and matching, not general ERGM terms.
For the fastest agent-based runs at national scale (tens of millions of agents): LASER, which is built for speed per agent above all; Starsim is close on one thread, but slower on many.
For many small stochastic runs, and fits by particle MCMC with filtered trajectories: odin with its companion packages, whose compiled models start faster.
For models of livestock in thousands of herds driven by a register of movements: SimInf, which is faster for small models of this kind.
For models built and used in spreadsheets, with budget optimization: Atomica, whose users need no code at all.
For a full pipeline of scenario projections for a hub, on a cluster: flepiMoP, which has the batch jobs and post-processing that Starsim lacks.
For teaching with a graphical interface: NetLogo, where students can watch and change a model without writing Python.
For estimating the reproduction number or forecasting cases from surveillance data: statistical tools such as EpiNow2 and the Epiverse packages, rather than a mechanistic model of transmission.
For statistical models that are not about transmission: Stan or PyMC directly.

If the team already has a working model in another tool, that is often reason enough to keep it; the conversion pages show what moving would gain and lose.

title: Modeling landscape
text:
How these numbers were made
The models. Each framework’s examples were taken from its own documentation or repository, run in that framework’s own environment, and translated into Starsim by hand. The original, the translation, and a script that compares them are kept in the lingua franca design repository (examples/ and vignettes/), with the original’s reference results. These are the models on each page.
Lines and times. Starsim’s north-star script, tests/north_star/north_star.py in the lingua_franca_design repo, reads every translation and writes a table of lines of model code and run time, the original against Starsim, with the rows that fail. Starsim’s lines are counted from the translation: not counting blank lines, comments, docstrings, imports, or the if __name__ == '__main__' block, and counting a line over 100 characters twice. The original’s lines are those of its model file (rows of spreadsheets for Atomica, lines of YAML for flepiMoP and EMULSION). Starsim fails on lines if it has more than the original. Time is two numbers: the first run in a new process, and the best of 5 repeated runs, each building and running the sim. A time fails if Starsim is more than 2 times slower and more than 1 s slower. The originals were timed in their own environments (what each time includes, such as starting R or compiling, is said on each page). The script was run twice on 18 October 2026, on a 20-core x86-64 Linux machine shared with other work: once with the originals’ recorded times, and once with the originals run again where that could be done.
What works and what does not yet. Starsim’s switching demos (tests/switching/ in the lingua_franca_design repo) take each task that a user of that framework does every week, written in that field’s terms and scaled down to run in seconds, and check it against the original framework’s numbers. Of their 50 checks, 41 pass today, 8 fail, and one needs a framework that cannot be installed alongside Starsim. Each failing check names what blocks it. The demos were built from a review in which an experienced user of each framework tried their routine work in Starsim at their real scale (on 17 October 2026). Numbers on the pages that are not from the demos or the north star are from the translations’ own comparisons (13 and 14 October 2026) or from that review; a time from the review is given with its date. The NumPy page has no translation or demo: its numbers are from its own code, which is run when the docs are built. Starsim’s numbers are for the development version of Starsim.

title: Fitting a model
text:
🧠10% 🤖90%
Disease models usually need to be fitted to a particular setting before they can answer “what if” questions about it. Calibration is fitting a model’s parameters to data: finding the values for which the model’s results match what was observed. A model of a measles outbreak, for example, may know how long people are infectious from the literature, but not how fast measles spreads in this particular town, or what share of cases were reported. Those are the parameters to estimate from the data.
There are many approaches to calibration, from tuning parameters by hand to fully Bayesian methods. For many applications an optimization-based approach, which looks for the single set of values that fits best, is enough for a first exploration: it avoids the tedium of tuning by hand, and costs much less than a Bayesian method. The optimizer chooses values, the model is run with them, its results are compared with the data, and a measure of the mismatch tells the optimizer where to look next, until it settles on the values that fit best. When the question needs the uncertainty in the values too, a posterior (the distribution of values consistent with the data) can be fitted instead.
In Starsim, calibration needs two things, each stated where it belongs:
sim.fit() then fits every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data. There is no function to write that puts each value into the model, and none that pulls out the results to compare: the model already knows where each parameter is used and what each result is.
This page covers the options. The calibration tutorial goes through one fit step by step; Parameter identification is about whether the data can determine the parameters at all; Gradients covers posteriors and profile likelihoods; Fit diagnostics covers what to check afterwards; and Optimization uses the same machinery to allocate a budget.

title: Fitting a model
text:
The smallest example
The model is a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000 people, 90% of whom are already immune by vaccination. People are infected (S to E), become infectious about 10 days later (E to I), when the rash appears, and recover after about 8 days (I to R). The reported cases are a share of the people whose rash appears, report. Two parameters are unknown: the transmission rate beta and the share reported, report:

import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])    # Transmission rate per day: unknown
report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])   # Share of cases reported: unknown

infection = S >> E @ beta*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # The rash appears about 10 days after infection
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
cases     = ss.outcome(report*onset) # Reported cases: a share of the onsets
measles = ss.Disease(infection, onset, recovery, cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9))

pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/


The value given to each parameter (1.5 and 0.3) is where the search starts, and the bounds are the range it searches.
To check that calibration works, it helps to fit data for which the right answer is known. to_data() draws data from a run of the model, as if it had been observed: here, weekly reported cases from a run with beta = 1.9 and report = 0.5, as counts with random (Poisson) noise. The true sim gets its own random seed, rand_seed=2, so that its noise is not shared with any run being fitted:

truth = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=1.9, report=0.5), rand_seed=2, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_data('cases', resample='week')
data.head()

title: Fitting a model
text:
What is fitted
Every parameter with bounds is fitted, wherever it is: a rate, a share, a duration, a parameter of a network or an intervention. A duration’s bounds are in its own unit, e.g. ss.par(ss.days(8), bounds=[5, 12]) for between 5 and 12 days.

pars= fits only the parameters named, keeping the others at their values: sim.fit(pars=['beta']).
Wide positive bounds (where the high end is 10 or more times the low end) are searched on a log scale, since going from 0.05 to 0.1 matters as much as going from 0.5 to 1. The fit says which parameters it searches this way.
A prior, ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4], prior=ss.normal(2, 0.3)), is used by the methods that use likelihoods: a best fit is then the most probable values rather than the maximum likelihood, and a posterior uses it as its prior. Without one, the prior is uniform over the bounds.
In a module written as code, a parameter given as ss.par is fitted and its code sees the value, including a value in a dict parameter, e.g. cin_fn=dict(k=ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.1, 0.5])), fitted as cin_fn.k. A parameter with the same name in several modules is fitted with its module’s name, e.g. hpv16.rel_beta and hpv18.rel_beta; pars= and ss.Sim(pars=...) take either name.
A modifier’s amount, ss.modify(hiv.rel_sus, multiply=ss.par(2.7, bounds=[1, 4])), is fitted as multiply (or with the modifier’s name, if it is a parameter of a declared disease).
A parameter whose value is an array, with bounds for each element, has each element fitted, as curve[0], curve[1], …, except those whose low and high bounds are equal, which stay as they are: ss.par(np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.2]), bounds=[np.array([0, 0, 0.2]), np.array([1, 1, 0.2])]). A time series with bounds, ss.par(ss.timeseries(days, [0.3]*10), bounds=[0.05, 1]), has each of its values fitted in the same way, named by its times (beta[0], beta[14], …), and fit.pars has the time series whole. Either has a gradient for each value, so a deterministic model is fitted by gradients. penalty= adds a function of the values to what a best fit minimizes, e.g. to keep a curve smooth: sim.fit(penalty=lambda pars: 10*np.sum(np.diff(pars['curve'], 2)**2)).


A value that isn’t a parameter
A value set in code, such as a setting of an intervention that its constructor doesn’t take, or anything the model works out from it, is fitted by writing a function that sets it, with the value as a keyword argument given as ss.par, and giving the function as a module. A function given as an intervention is called at every step, with its keyword arguments as the module’s parameters:
def set_testing(sim, symp_prob=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 0.5])):
    sim.interventions.testing.symp_prob = symp_prob
    sim.interventions.testing.asymp_prob = symp_prob/10

sim = ss.Sim(..., interventions=[set_testing, testing], data=data)
fit = sim.fit() # Fits symp_prob, with the others
The value is a parameter like any other: fit.pars.symp_prob, ss.Sim(pars=dict(symp_prob=0.2)), sim.sensitivity(), and ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(symp_prob=[0.1, 0.2])) all find it by name. A module added after the sim was made (e.g. sim.pars.analyzers += my_analyzer) is kept by sim.new(), and so by the runs of a fit.

title: Fitting a model
text:
The data
The data has a time column (date, year, t, or time; an integer year is a calendar year) and one column for each data series, named like the result it is compared with: here cases. With several modules, a column that could match more than one result is named with its module, e.g. measles.cases. Any result can have data, including an analyzer’s (by_age.cancers_0_15), a result nested deeper in sim.results (hpv.genotype.cancers), and a column of a result with columns (sis.infection.alpha), so gof= is needed only for targets worked out from the results, such as a share.
The data need not be on the model’s time step, and nothing needs to say how to line the two up, since each result knows what kind of quantity it is:

A flow, like reported cases, is summed over each interval of the data: weekly data is compared with each week’s total.
A stock (like the number infectious) or a ratio (like prevalence) is compared with the model’s value at the data’s time.
Data by calendar year is compared over the year it names: a flow summed over it, and a stock or ratio averaged over it.

data= takes a dataframe or a file name. Real files rarely arrive with matching headers, so ss.simdata() renames columns on the way in, and can ignore the columns not needed:
data = ss.simdata('town_cases.csv', aliases=dict(cases='Reported cases (weekly)', date='Week ending'), ignore_extra=True)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **pars)
A column that matches no result gets a note listing the closest result names when the sim is initialized, and is an error when the fit compares the data with the results, so a typo in a header is caught. weights= gives series different weights, e.g. sim.fit(weights=dict(cases=1, deaths=5)).

title: Fitting a model
text:
Measuring the fit
Without a likelihood, the measure of fit is the normalized absolute error: for each data series, the mean absolute difference between the model and the data, divided by the mean of the data. It needs no assumptions about the noise in the data, and puts series of different sizes on one scale. gof='rmse' uses the root mean squared error instead, and gof= can also be a function of the sim that returns the mismatch to minimize (lower is better), e.g. to bring data of its own:
def peak_error(sim):
    """ How far the model's peak week is from the observed peak, in weeks """
    weekly = sim.results.measles.cases.resample('week')
    return abs(weekly.values.argmax() - data.cases.values.argmax())

fit = sim.fit(gof=peak_error)
A likelihood says how the data vary around the model’s value: the model’s value is the mean of the distribution, and the likelihood supplies the rest. It can be declared on the outcome, where it is used by every fit, or given to the fit by the name of the data series:
cases = ss.outcome(report*onset, likelihood=ss.poisson()) # On the outcome
fit = sim.fit(likelihood=dict(cases=ss.nbinom(n=10)))     # Or for one fit
The likelihoods are:



Likelihood
For data that are




ss.poisson()
Counts, such as reported cases


ss.nbinom(n=...)
Counts that vary more than a Poisson, with n the dispersion (a smaller n is more variable); n can itself be an ss.par with bounds, and is then fitted too


ss.normal(scale=...)
Continuous values, with the standard deviation scale


ss.lognorm_ex(std=...)
Positive continuous values, with the standard deviation std


ss.binom(n=...)
The number who test positive out of n people surveyed (the data column holds the number positive), with the model’s value, a share such as a prevalence, as the probability


ss.bernoulli()
Yes or no outcomes



When every data series has a likelihood, the fit maximizes the sum of their logs (the maximum likelihood estimate), and the methods that give a posterior can be used.

fit_lik = sim.fit(likelihood=dict(cases=ss.poisson()), verbose=False)

title: Fitting a model
text:
How the fit is found
By default a fit is a best fit (a single set of values), by a method that suits the model, which sim.fit() prints with its reason. A posterior (the distribution of values consistent with the data) is always asked for by name:








The model
The default method (a best fit)
A posterior, by name




Deterministic (an ODE)
'l-bfgs-b', a gradient-based optimizer; 'nelder-mead' for one or two parameters, or when the model can’t be differentiated
'nuts' (the No-U-Turn sampler), given a likelihood for every series


Stochastic compartmental
'optuna'
'pmcmc' (particle MCMC), given a likelihood for every series


Agent-based
'optuna'
'abc-smc' (approximate Bayesian computation), which needs no likelihood



'powell' and 'slsqp' (two more methods of scipy.optimize.minimize) can also be given, as can 'if2' (iterated filtering, for a stochastic compartmental model). Fitting methods compares them all, with the settings of each and an example. A list, such as method=['optuna', 'nelder-mead'], runs each method in turn, each starting from the best values the one before found, and stops at a method that doesn’t converge.
The gradient-based methods and their posteriors are covered in Gradients.

title: Fitting a model
text:
A stochastic model
A stochastic model gives a different result on each run, so each set of values gives a noisy score. Starsim fits a stochastic model with Optuna, a library for searching over parameters, which tries values, scores them by running the model, and uses the scores to choose where to try next. Here is the same model as a stochastic compartmental model (a chain binomial, in which the number of people who move between states each day is random):

sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, solver='binomial', **pars)
fit = sim.fit(n_trials=100, rand_seed=5)
fit.summarize()

Searching on a log scale: report
Fitting by optuna (a stochastic sim; override with method=)

The estimates are less precise than those of the ODE: each score is noisy, so the search can settle anywhere in a region of similar scores, and a fit with another rand_seed gives somewhat different values (in particular of report). Fit diagnostics shows how to check how much this matters.
The options that matter for a stochastic fit:

n_trials= is the number of sets of values to try (100 by default). Use more for more parameters.
n_runs= is the number of runs that each set of values is scored by: 4 by default for a stochastic compartmental model, and 1 for agents. Each trial uses fresh random seeds, so that the search averages over chance rather than fitting one run’s luck; the best fit is then the trial among the best tenth whose neighbors score best, rather than the luckiest. reseed=False scores every trial with the same seeds instead, e.g. for a rare outcome, where fresh seeds let the search favor values whose runs were lucky.
rand_seed= makes the fit itself reproducible.
n_workers=4 runs the trials in 4 processes at once, and storage='fit.log' keeps the trials in a file, so that calling fit() again with the same file carries on where it stopped.
fit.study is Optuna’s study, for its plots, e.g. optuna.visualization.plot_param_importances(fit.study).

Agents are fitted the same way, e.g. ss.Sim(measles, data=data, n_agents=20_000, **pars).fit(n_trials=200). With agents each run is slower, and with few people in the model the noise is larger, so a fit usually needs more trials.
fit.sim is one run with the best values. Since the model is stochastic, it is more useful to run it many times, and see whether the data lie within the range of the runs:

msim = fit.sim.run(n_runs=20)


msim.plot('measles.cases')








The plot shows the median and 95% of the 20 runs, as weekly totals, against the data.

title: Fitting a model
text:
Using the fit
The calibrated sim is the starting point for scenarios. sim.new() makes a new sim from the same inputs, with whatever is given changed; from fit.sim, that includes the fitted values. Here, a vaccination campaign on 1 April that reaches half the town, compared with none:

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.97, coverage=0.5, at='2025-04-01')
scenarios = {
    'No campaign': fit.sim.new(),
    'Campaign':    fit.sim.new(interventions=vaccination),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, n_runs=20)
msim.plot('measles.cases')

title: Fitting a model
text:
Which parameters matter
Before calibrating, it helps to know which parameters the results depend on at all, since a parameter that does not matter cannot be fitted either. sim.sensitivity() needs no data: it samples the parameters over their bounds, runs the model at each sample, and gives the partial rank correlation of each parameter with a summary of each result. Near 1 or -1, the result goes up or down with the parameter (with the others held fixed); near 0, it doesn’t depend on it:

sens = sim.sensitivity(n=50, verbose=False)
sens[['measles.I peak', 'measles.cases total']]

title: Fitting a model
text:
Allocating a budget
The same machinery answers a different question: given the spending on each program as parameters of the model, how should a fixed total be divided between them to make a result as small (or as large) as possible? ss.fit.optimize() does this; see Optimization.

title: Fitting a model
text:
Pitfalls

A best value at a bound. The fit warns (AtBound) when a best value is at the edge of its bounds: the best value may lie beyond it, so widen the bounds, or check that the parameter means what you think it does.
Parameters the data can’t tell apart. Two parameters that only ever appear multiplied together (such as a contact rate and a chance of infection per contact) can’t be fitted separately; the fit notes this. See Parameter identification.
A lucky trial. In a stochastic fit, the best trial may simply have been a lucky run. The fit reruns the best values with the same seeds, and says so if they then score worse than the starting values; use more trials, or more runs per trial (n_runs=).
A column that matches nothing. Data columns are matched to results by name; a column that matches no result is an error when fitting, with the closest names suggested.
Too few runs to judge. One run of a stochastic model, with the best values, says little about whether the model fits; compare the data with many runs, as above.

More checks are in Fit diagnostics. How the fitting works, and how the method is chosen, is explained in Randomness.
