title: Profiling and debugging
text:
🧠10% 🤖90%
A model can go wrong in three ways: it stops with an error, it runs but gives an answer that looks wrong, or it runs too slowly. This page goes through the tools Starsim has for each, in roughly the order to reach for them, and then the mistakes that are known to catch people out, most of which don’t raise an error at all. Most of the examples use the measles model from the tutorials: an SIR with β = 1.9 per day and an infectious period of 8 days, so R0 = 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15.
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0023 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6


Sim(n=100000; 0—50; diseases=measles)
Where to look first, by symptom:

title: Profiling and debugging
section: Errors and what a run prints
text:
Errors and what a run prints
When Starsim can’t build or run a model, it raises an error that names what is wrong in the terms of the model, and says what to do about it. Here the parameter β is misspelled:

try:
    ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(betta=2.0), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50)).run()
except KeyError as error:
    print(error)

pars= has a value for "betta", which matches no parameter. Parameters are measles.beta, measles.dur_I; did you mean measles.beta?


Most errors are Python’s own: a KeyError for a name that is not found, as here, a TypeError for a value of the wrong kind, and a ValueError for the rest. The message is what says what went wrong, so search for it, or catch the error by its type as above. The few that code may want to catch by kind are classes of their own, such as ss.CapabilityError, raised when the solver asked for can’t run part of the model. Most mistakes are caught when the sim is built (sim.init(), which sim.run() calls first), before any time step is taken, so an error usually comes at once rather than after a long run.
A run prints what it is running and how, the R0 of each disease, any notes, and a closing line with the size and timing of the peak. Read these first: most surprises are explained there. A note is something Starsim assumed or noticed that is worth knowing, and doesn’t stop the run. For example, in an SEIR model, init_prev puts people in E, where a new infection starts, so nobody is infectious at first:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
latency   = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
seir = ss.Disease(infection, latency, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
seir_sim = ss.Sim(seir, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(100))
seir_sim.run()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 100
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 0 infectious at the start
  Note: init_prev seeds E of "measles", where a new infection starts, so nobody is infectious at the start; to seed infectious people, use init=dict(I=...) (a share) or init_n= (a number)
  Done in 0.0023 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 29,177 infectious, on day 33


Sim(n=100000; 0—100; diseases=measles)


The notes are kept in sim.notes, even when nothing is printed (verbose=0):

seir_sim.notes

["unit='day' (from the typed values in the model)",
 'init_prev seeds E of "measles", where a new infection starts, so nobody is infectious at the start; to seed infectious people, use init=dict(I=...) (a share) or init_n= (a number)']


Some messages are warnings rather than notes: the run continues, but something probably needs attention (for example, a fitted parameter that ended at one of its bounds). To stop at the first warning instead, so that a script can’t carry on past one unnoticed, turn warnings into errors:
ss.options(warnings='error')

Checking the model

other = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')

Checking the numbers
A few numbers can be checked by hand. The run prints R0, which for an SIR is β × the infectious period; if it is far from what you expected, a rate or a duration is wrong, often in its units (see Rates, durations, and units below). In a closed population, the share of people ever infected depends only on R0 (it is about 80% for R0 = 2, and all but a few for measles), and the peak comes later the fewer people start infected.
Another check is to run the same model in another way. The ODE is the average course of the epidemic; run as agents, the model should follow it closely when there are many people, and differ by chance when there are few. A large difference that doesn’t shrink with more people points to the size of the time step, or to something in the model that only one of them does. Here the same model is run both ways, as the scenarios of ss.parallel():

ode = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
agents = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=20_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({'ODE': ode, 'Agents': agents})
msim.plot('measles.I')








With total_pop=100_000 and n_agents=20_000, each agent stands for five people, so the results of the two are on the same scale. The two reach about the same peak, but the agents reach it a few days later. With 20,000 agents and 20 infected at the start, that is not chance; the next section shows that it is the time step. Solvers and backends says when to expect the solvers to differ, and why.


Checking the time step
Agents, and stochastic compartmental models, take whole time steps: each step, people move between states with a probability worked out from the rates over that step. When the rates are high compared with the step (for measles, β = 1.9 per day against a step of 1 day), a smaller step can change the answer. sim.check_dt() runs the model with the step it has and with a step half as long, and shows how much each result changes:

agent_sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=20_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
agent_sim.check_dt()

Change in each result when the timestep goes from 1 to 0.5 days (largest difference, as a share of the largest value):
  measles.infection             74.0%   (peak 5384 → 6859)
  measles.recovery              51.6%   (peak 1707 → 1789)
  measles.I                     47.2%   (peak 15681 → 15558)
  measles.S                     41.0%   (peak 19980 → 19980)
  measles.R                     15.2%   (peak 19890 → 19913)


Each line is the largest difference between the two runs at any time, as a share of the result’s largest value. The height of the peak of infectious people hardly changes, but the epidemic runs faster with the shorter step, so on a given day the counts differ by much more. The reason is that someone infected during a step can only infect others from the next step on: with R0 = 15 and an infectious period of 8 days, measles doubles in well under a day at first, so steps of a day hold it back. If the timing of the peak matters, use the smaller step (dt=ss.days(0.5)), and check again. For a stochastic run, part of each change is the difference between two runs, so a change of a few percent can be chance. (An ODE adjusts its own steps within each time step, so its results hardly depend on dt.)


Finding what changes a parameter
Interventions and connectors change parameters while the model runs. When a parameter doesn’t seem to have the value you expect, sim.what_modifies() lists everything that changes it:

masks = ss.modify(measles.pars.beta, multiply=0.6, start=ss.days(10))
masked = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), interventions=masks, verbose=0)
masked.what_modifies(measles.pars.beta)

measles.pars.beta
  modifiers
    masks            multiply=0.6   start=10

title: Profiling and debugging
text:
Common pitfalls
These are mistakes that have actually caught people out, collected from questions, reviews, and tests in which modelers new to Starsim wrote models for tasks with known answers. Most of them don’t raise an error: the model runs and gives a wrong answer. Starsim prints a note for many of them. The examples use a version of the measles model with weekly reported cases (half of infections), made by a function so that each example starts afresh:

import starsim as ss

def make_measles(beta=1.9):
    """ The measles SIR of the tutorials, with weekly reported cases (half of infections) """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    cases     = ss.outcome(0.5*infection)
    return ss.Disease(infection, recovery, cases, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')


Rates, durations, and units
A number after @ is a rate, not a duration. I >> R @ ss.days(8) means that people stay in I for 8 days on average, but I >> R @ 8 means that they leave at a rate of 8 per unit of time, so after an eighth of a day. Starsim notes when a duration comes out shorter than the time step, which is almost always this mistake:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ 8   # Meant: 8 days
wrong = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
ss.Sim(wrong, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50)).run()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 0.238, with 100 infectious at the start
  Note: unit='day' (from start and stop)
  Note: recovery has a mean dwell of 0.12 days, shorter than the step; a duration is written dur=, or ss.days(10)
  Done in 0.0034 s; measles: 31 infections; at most 100 infectious, on day 0


Sim(n=100000; 0—50; diseases=measles)


R0 comes out at 0.24 instead of 15, and the outbreak never starts. Give a duration with its unit (ss.days(8)), or as dur= in ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8)).
A plain number is in the sim’s unit of time. The unit is taken from the values that have one (here, ss.days(8)), and describe() says where it came from. Every plain number is then in that unit: β = 1.9 is per day, and so is stop. So stop=2, meant as two years, is two days:

ss.Sim(make_measles(), total_pop=100_000, stop=2).run()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 2
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0016 s; measles: 3,486 infections; at most 3,352 infectious, on day 2


Sim(n=100000; 0—2; diseases=measles)


Give times with their units (stop=ss.years(2)), or as dates (start='2025-01-01', stop='2027-01-01'). If nothing in a model has a unit, time is counted in steps, and the run says “steps” where it would say “days”.
A number as a time is a year, or a time since the start. A number from 1900 on is a calendar year, as in start=2025: at=2026 is the start of 2026, and at=2026.5 the middle of it. Any other number is a time in the sim’s unit after the start, so at=30 means 30 days after the start of a sim in days (for 2,000 days, write ss.days(2000)). Starsim stops with an error when a time falls outside the sim:

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.5, at=2026)
try:
    ss.Sim(make_measles(), interventions=vaccination, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01').run()
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)

a round of "vaccination" (2026) is outside the sim (2025-01-01 to 2025-07-01); a number from 1900 on is a calendar year, and any other number a time in the sim's unit (days) since the start.


A date within a year is written as a string: at='2025-02-01'.
A rate times a duration is not a rate. A rate of 0.1 per year times 3 days is the chance of an event over those 3 days, a plain number, not a rate. Starsim raises an error rather than guess what was meant:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
try:
    ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9*I, I >> R @ ss.peryear(0.1)*ss.days(3))
except TypeError as error:
    print(error)

the rate of the transition "I_to_R" is a plain number (a rate times a duration), not a rate:
       rate = peryear(0.1) * days(3)
     A rate times a duration is a probability over that duration, not a rate; give the rate itself, e.g. rate=ss.peryear(0.1).




Starting the epidemic
init_prev puts people where an infection starts, not where they are infectious. In an SIR model that is I, but in an SEIR model it is E, so nobody is infectious at the start and the epidemic starts a latent period late. The run says so:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
latency   = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
seir = ss.Disease(infection, latency, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
ss.Sim(seir, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(100)).run()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 100
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 0 infectious at the start
  Note: init_prev seeds E of "measles", where a new infection starts, so nobody is infectious at the start; to seed infectious people, use init=dict(I=...) (a share) or init_n= (a number)
  Done in 0.0021 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 29,177 infectious, on day 33


Sim(n=100000; 0—100; diseases=measles)


To start people infectious, give the share in each state with init (init=dict(I=0.001)), or the number with init_n (init_n=dict(I=100)).
An ODE always takes off. An ODE is the average course of an epidemic, so if R0 is above 1 it takes off from any number of infected people, even a fraction of one. A real outbreak that starts with one or two cases dies out by chance quite often: with R0 = 3, a third of the chains of infection started by one case end without a major outbreak. Starsim notes this when a model starts with only a few infected:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=2), name='sir')
ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(200)).run()

Sim: sir, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 200
  sir: R0 = 3, with 2 infectious at the start
  Note: "sir" starts with 2 infected, so whether it takes off is a matter of chance, which solver="ode" does not show; solver="gillespie" with ss.parallel(n_runs=...) does
  Done in 0.0035 s; sir: 94,046 infections; at most 30,047 infectious, on day 58


Sim(n=100000; 0—200; diseases=sir)


To see how likely an outbreak is, run the model stochastically, many times (see Runs and chance).


Runs and chance

The median of sir_infection (the number of new infections over the run) is a large outbreak, but the low end of its interval is 0, and the mean is between the two: some runs died out before the two people infected at the start infected anyone. The infections in each run show the split directly:

msim.results.sir.infection.summarize()

array([   0., 4689.,    0., 4727., 4688., 4713., 4719., 4700., 4700.,
       4670., 4699., 4716., 4682., 4683., 4730., 4721., 4705., 4711.,
       4684., 4684.])


When the question is whether there is an outbreak at all, count the runs with one, and summarize the size of the outbreak over those runs only. A single stochastic run is one possible outcome, and two scenarios compared with one run each can differ by chance alone; see Scenarios.
n_agents= runs the model as agents. Giving a number of agents asks for agents, so a model that would run as an ODE is run as agents instead, with the chance and time steps that come with them. To set the size of the population in a compartmental model, use total_pop=. With both, each agent stands for several people (total_pop=100_000, n_agents=10_000 makes each agent ten people), and the results are scaled to the whole population. describe() says which solver was chosen and why.
A time step can be too long for a fast disease. Agents and stochastic compartmental models take whole steps, and someone infected during a step can only infect others from the next one. For a disease that spreads as fast as measles, steps of a day slow the epidemic down by a few days. Starsim suggests a shorter step when transmission or leaving a state is fast compared with the step (and says which is fastest), and sim.check_dt() shows how much a smaller step changes the results; see Checking the time step above.


Mixing and stratification
With contacts, β is per contact. Without a network or contact matrix, everyone mixes with everyone, and β is the rate at which a susceptible person is infected per unit of the share infectious (as if each person had one contact a day). With a contact matrix, β is the chance of infection per contact, so R0 is multiplied by the number of contacts. Adding a contact matrix with about 15 contacts a day to the measles model, with β left at 1.9, gives an R0 of about 210:

stratified = make_measles()
stratified.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]])
ss.Sim(stratified, networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50)).run()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 214, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0033 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 91,233 infectious, on day 1


Sim(n=100000; 0—50; diseases=measles)


When contacts are added to a model, scale β down to keep the same R0; here, β = 0.12 per contact gives R0 ≈ 14. describe() says what β is per (beta on contacts: 1.9 per day per contact).
stratify() changes the disease itself. It works in place, and returns the disease too. Run the same notebook cell twice and the second stratify() does nothing (with a note); stratify the same disease again by the same property in a different way, and it raises an error, since its states are already split:

stratified = make_measles()
stratified.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
try:
    stratified.stratify(age={0: 0.5, 20: 0.5})
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)

"measles" is already stratified by "age", in another way. stratify() works in place, so the stratification can be given once; to change it, build the model again.


To try several stratifications, build the disease again each time, as make_measles() does here.


Interventions
Vaccines are leaky unless told otherwise. A vaccine with efficacy=0.9 reduces each vaccinated person’s chance of infection by 90% (a leaky vaccine). A vaccine that fully protects 90% of those vaccinated and does nothing for the rest (all or nothing) is leaky=False. For a disease that spreads as fast as measles, the difference is large: a leaky vaccine only slows infection, and with an R0 of 15, many vaccinated people are infected in the end. Here 90% of people are vaccinated at the start with each kind:

leaky = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.9, at=ss.days(0))
all_or_nothing = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, leaky=False, coverage=0.9, at=ss.days(0))
sims = {}
for label, vaccination in {'Leaky': leaky, 'All or nothing': all_or_nothing}.items():
    sims[label] = ss.Sim(make_measles(), interventions=vaccination, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']








value


scenario

Measles vaccine protection is close to all or nothing, as are many live vaccines; choose the kind that matches the evidence for the vaccine being modeled.


Data
Data is matched to results by name. A column of data is compared with the result of the same name, so a column called reported is not compared with the result cases. When a sim is built, Starsim notes a column that matches no result, and sim.fit() stops with an error:

truth = ss.Sim(make_measles(), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), rand_seed=2, verbose=0).run()
data = truth.to_data('cases', resample='week')
data = data.rename(columns={'cases': 'reported'}) # As it might come from elsewhere
ss.Sim(make_measles(), data=data, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50)).init()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Note: The data column "reported" matches no result. The closest results are recovery, R, cases.
     Rename it with ss.simdata(..., aliases=dict(recovery='reported')), or drop it with ss.simdata(..., ignore_extra=True). It is not compared with the results.


Sim(n=100000; 0—50; diseases=measles)


Rename the column to match the result (data.rename(columns={'reported': 'cases'})), or say which result it is: data=ss.simdata(data, aliases=dict(cases='reported')).
Counts over a period are compared with totals over the same period. A result that counts events, such as infections or reported cases, is compared with the data as its total since the previous data point, so weekly data is compared with weekly totals, whatever the model’s time step. A result that counts people at a time, such as the number infectious, is compared at the time of each data point. Data on prevalence (people infectious at a time) given as a count of events, or the other way round, fits the wrong thing; check which kind each column is. Fitting a model has more on data.

To see what happens during a run, a function of the sim can be inserted into the loop, after (or, with before=True, before) any call in it. Here it prints the number infectious every ten days, just after the disease has taken its step:

def show_infectious(sim):
    if sim.ti % 10 == 0:
        print('Day', sim.ti, 'infectious:', sim.diseases.measles.I.sum())

probed = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=20_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
probed.init()
probed.loop.insert(show_infectious, label='measles.step')
probed.run()

Day 20 infectious: 4331

Day 40 infectious: 368
Day 50 infectious: 110


Sim(n=20000; 0—50; diseases=measles)


A function given as an analyzer (analyzers=show_infectious) does the same without touching the loop, but always runs last in the step; inserting it gives control over where. For anything more than a quick look, use an analyzer, which runs at the end of each step and can keep results of its own. Breakpoints and print statements in a module written as code work as in any Python program. A compartmental model that Starsim runs whole (an ODE with nothing that needs to happen between steps) has no loop to look into; inserting a function or adding an analyzer makes it run one step at a time, with the same results, and describe() says so (under plan).
sim.loop.plot() draws the loop as a diagram, which is most useful when modules have time steps of their own (demographics once a year and a disease once a week, say), to see which runs when. sim.run_one_step() takes a single step, for stepping through a run by hand in a debugger.

title: Profiling and debugging
text:
Profiling
Compartmental models run in well under a second, so profiling is mostly for models run as agents, especially with networks or modules written as code. Start with how long each part of each step takes: run with profile=True, and plot the time spent in each call of the loop:

big = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=50_000, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10), stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
big.run(profile=True)
big.loop.plot_cpu()








Here the network (randomnet.step, which pairs people up afresh each day) takes a large share of the time, as much as the disease. To see which lines of a function take the time, follow it with sim.profile(), which runs a copy of the sim with a line-by-line profiler on the functions given:

big = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=50_000, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10), stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
prof = big.profile(follow=ss.RandomNet.add_pairs, plot=False)

The function names are those of the code actually run, which for an inherited method is the class that defines it (a module that inherits its step() from ss.Infection shows as Infection.step). The same works for a method of a module you wrote, which is where the time usually goes in a slow model: a loop over people in Python, where an operation on the whole array would do. sim.cprofile() profiles every function the run calls, which is useful when you don’t yet know where to look. Only functions called during the run can be followed this way; for anything else, such as the building of the sim, use sc.profile() from Sciris directly.
When the time is in your own code, the usual remedies, roughly in order of how much they help:

Work on arrays, not people. A loop over agents in Python is a hundred times slower than the same operation on the whole array (disease.I[uids] = True, (age > 15).uids); see Array indexing.
Compile a loop that can’t be written as array operations with @ss.jit (see Custom modules).
Use fewer agents. Many questions are answered as well with each agent standing for several people (see Branching and rescaling), or without agents at all: a declared model that needs no individuals runs as compartments, in milliseconds (see Solvers and backends).
Record less. Analyzers that store something for every agent at every step, and very long runs with short steps, use memory and time.

A fit runs the model thousands of times, so a model that takes a second becomes a fit that takes hours: profile the model first, then see Fitting a model for making the fit itself cheaper.

title: Parameter identification
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
A parameter is identifiable if the data determine its value. A fit always returns some value for each parameter, but that value is only meaningful if the data could not equally well be explained by quite different values. There are two ways this can fail:
The way to check is to fit data for which the right answer is known: data made from the model itself, with known values. If the fit doesn’t recover those values, it won’t recover the truth from real data either. This page shows that check, and what the fit tells you when identification fails. It assumes the basics of Fitting a model.

title: Parameter identification
text:
Recovering known values
The model is a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000, 90% of whom are immune, with three unknowns: the transmission rate beta, how long people stay infectious, dur_inf, and the share of cases that are reported, report. The reported cases are counts, so their likelihood is a Poisson:

import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta    = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])             # Transmission rate per day
dur_inf = ss.par(ss.days(6), bounds=[3, 15])       # Infectious period, in days
report  = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])            # Share of cases reported

infection = S >> E @ beta*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ dur_inf
cases     = ss.outcome(report*onset, likelihood=ss.poisson())
measles = ss.Disease(infection, onset, recovery, cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9))
pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

The data are a year of weekly reported cases, drawn from a run with beta = 1.9, dur_inf = 8 days, and report = 0.5. The true sim has its own random seed, so its noise is not shared with any run being fitted:

true_values = dict(beta=1.9, dur_inf=ss.days(8), report=0.5)
truth = ss.Sim(measles, pars=true_values, rand_seed=2, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_data('cases', resample='week')

sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **pars)
fit = sim.fit()

title: Parameter identification
text:
Which combinations the data determine
A best fit is a single point; it doesn’t show how far the values could move and still fit nearly as well. One way to see that is to look at many values and how well each fits. Plotting beta against dur_inf for each trial, colored by how much worse its negative log-likelihood is than the best:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

worse = np.log10(1 + trials.objective - trials.objective.min()) # 0 at the best trial
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
points = ax.scatter(trials.beta, trials.dur_inf, c=worse, cmap='viridis_r', s=15)
d = np.linspace(4, 15, 50)
ax.plot(d, 1.9*8/d, 'k--', label='beta × dur_inf = 15.2 (the true R0)')
ax.scatter(1.9, 8, marker='x', s=100, color='red', zorder=10, label='True values')
ax.set_xlabel('beta (per day)')
ax.set_ylabel('dur_inf (days)')
ax.set_ylim(3, 15)
plt.colorbar(points, ax=ax, label='How much worse than the best (log10)')
ax.legend();








The good fits lie along a curve on which β × the infectious period, the basic reproduction number R0, stays about the same. The data determine R0 well: it sets how many people the outbreak reaches. They determine β and the infectious period separately much less well, through the timing of the epidemic alone. This is a practical limit, not a structural one: the full data still pick out the right point on the curve, but a little more noise, or less data, and they wouldn’t.

title: Parameter identification
text:
Less data
Suppose the outbreak is being fitted while it is still growing: 16 weeks of data, before the peak. Early growth is set by the rate at which the epidemic grows, which many combinations of β and the infectious period give:

early = sim.fit(data=data.iloc[:16], method='nelder-mead')
early.table

Using the likelihood: the sum of the log-likelihoods of cases, treated as independent
Searching on a log scale: report
Not converged: the 3 searches, from points of the scan that are apart, ended at different objective values (41.19 at beta=1.195, dur_inf=15, report=0.5946; 48.67 at beta=3.4, dur_inf=5.017, report=0.1253; 59.11 at beta=4, dur_inf=5.04, report=0.05; 1414 evaluations), so the best may be a local optimum; try a larger scan (scan=) or more searches (restarts=)
The negative log-likelihood is 41.19 at the best values and 564 at the initial values

The searches from different starting points end at different values and different scores, so it reports that it did not converge; the infectious period ends at its upper bound (with an AtBound warning), which here doesn’t mean the true value is beyond the bound, only that nothing in the data stops it from going there; and the values are far from the truth. Wider bounds would not help. What helps is more information: more data, data of another kind (such as a serosurvey of who was infected), or fixing a parameter that is known from elsewhere. Measles’ infectious period is well known, so in practice it would be fixed rather than fitted:

early_fixed = sim.fit(data=data.iloc[:16], pars=['beta', 'report'], verbose=False)

title: Parameter identification
text:
Parameters that appear only together
Some models can’t separate two parameters whatever the data. Here transmission is written as the number of contacts a day times the chance of infection per contact, and both are fitted:

contacts = ss.par(10, bounds=[2, 30])   # Contacts per day
p_infect = ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 0.5]) # Chance of infection per contact

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection = S >> E @ contacts*p_infect*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
cases     = ss.outcome(0.5*onset)
measles2 = ss.Disease(infection, onset, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9))

fit2 = ss.Sim(measles2, data=data, **pars).fit()

Searching on a log scale: contacts, p_infect
Fitting by nelder-mead (2 fitted parameters, for which it is faster than gradients; override with method=)
  Note: "contacts" and "p_infect" appear in the model only multiplied together, so the data can determine only their product (1.9), not each of them; fit one and fix the other
Converged: the best two of 3 searches, from points of the scan that are apart, ended within 9.7e-05 of each other (objective values 0.09673 at contacts=13.07, p_infect=0.145; 0.09673 at contacts=20.52, p_infect=0.09237; 0.09674 at contacts=30, p_infect=0.06319; 239 evaluations)
The goodness of fit is 0.09673 at the best values and 0.9933 at the initial values


The fit converges, since every search reaches the same best score, but at different values; Starsim notes that the two parameters appear only multiplied together, so the data determine only their product (here 1.9, the true β). The remedy is to fit one and fix the other, or to write the model with their product as one parameter.

title: Parameter identification
text:
Noise in the data
Even when the parameters are identifiable, a real epidemic is one realization of a chance process, and a different realization would give somewhat different estimates. To see how much, make several data sets from a stochastic version of the model (a chain binomial, solver='binomial'), each with its own seed, and fit each one with the deterministic model. Here the infectious period is fixed at its true value, 8 days, and β and the share reported are fitted:

import pandas as pd

known = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(dur_inf=ss.days(8)), **pars) # The infectious period fixed at its true value
rows = []
for seed in range(1, 7):
    epidemic = ss.Sim(measles, pars=true_values, solver='binomial', rand_seed=seed, verbose=0, **pars).run()
    epidemic_data = epidemic.to_data('cases', resample='week', seed=seed)
    est = known.fit(data=epidemic_data, pars=['beta', 'report'], verbose=False)
    rows.append(dict(seed=seed, total_cases=epidemic_data.cases.sum(), beta=est.pars.beta, report=est.pars.report))

A posterior gives this uncertainty from a single data set; see Gradients.

title: Parameter identification
text:
Summary








Sign
Likely cause
What to do




A note that two parameters appear only together
Structural: only their product (or ratio) matters
Fit one and fix the other, or use their product as one parameter


A note that two parameters are almost perfectly correlated in the posterior
Practical: the data determine a combination
More data, or data of another kind; or fix one from other evidence


Searches from different starts end at different values with similar scores
A ridge or a flat region
As above; look at the trials, or a profile likelihood


A best value at a bound
The data don’t constrain it, or the bounds are too narrow
Check the trials; widen the bounds only if larger values are plausible


Estimates from known data far from the truth
Too little data, or the wrong data
Recover known values before fitting real data



Starsim notes the first two cases itself. To draw values from the priors of the parameters (or uniformly over their bounds) and run the model for each, for a Bayesian workflow of your own, use ss.parallel(sim, priors=True, n_runs=200). Fit diagnostics covers the other checks to make after a fit, and Gradients the profile likelihood, which shows how well the data determine one parameter at a time.

title: Branching and rescaling
text:
🧠20% 🤖80%
Many questions are about a small part of a large population: the first cases of an outbreak in a city, or an epidemic in a country of tens of millions. Simulating every person is then often unnecessary and slow. There are two ways round it. While an outbreak is small compared with the population, the susceptible people are hardly depleted, and it can be treated as a branching process: each case infects a random number of others, independently of every other case, and the rest of the population hardly matters. Once an epidemic is large, a run as agents can instead let each agent stand for several people: population rescaling. This page covers both. A compartmental model holds numbers of people, so it can be any size at no cost; a branching process can be run by any solver, and population rescaling is for runs of agents.

title: Branching and rescaling
text:
Branching processes
Early in an outbreak, each case infects a random number of others, its offspring. If the offspring of each case are independent of everyone else’s (as they are while nearly everyone is susceptible), the outbreak is a branching process, and a few of its properties follow from the offspring distribution alone:

The chance that an introduction dies out. Even with R0 above 1, the first few chains of transmission can all end by chance. For an SIR model with an exponentially distributed infectious period, started by one case, the chance is 1/R0; started by n cases, (1/R0)^n.
Chains and generations. Who infected whom, how many generations a chain lasts, and how large it gets before it dies out or takes off.
Overdispersion. If some cases infect many more people than others (superspreading), the offspring distribution has a long tail, and more introductions die out, even at the same R0.

In Starsim, a branching process is not a different model, but the same model run with depletion turned off: ss.Sim(branching=True). Infection then takes no one from the uninfected, and gives no one back, so the susceptible side stays as it would be with no infection, however large the outbreak gets. It works with every solver:







Solver
What it gives




'ode'
The expected course: exponential growth at the rate that goes with R0


'ide'
The same, with each dwell time as it is, which is the renewal equation (below)


'gillespie', 'binomial', 'tau'
A branching process of counts: the chance of extinction, and the distribution of chain sizes


'abm'
A branching process of individuals: who infected whom, and differences between people



With solver='auto', the solver is chosen as it would be without branching. What is held is the uninfected side: the states people can be in without having been infected. The model’s other flows act on it as usual, so vaccination (S >> V) still takes people from S. A flow back to the uninfected side, such as waning immunity, takes people out of the process instead, with a note. In a rate, N is the number of people on the uninfected side, so each case’s offspring average R0 however many cases are seeded.

The chance that an outbreak dies out
Here is an influenza-like infection with R0 = 2 (β = 0.2 per day, infectious for 10 days), introduced by one case into a city of a million people. An ODE always takes off, so the question needs a stochastic solver and many runs (see Solvers and backends). Gillespie’s algorithm is exact for this model, and as a branching process its cost is the number of events, not the size of the population. Each run stops once 100 people have been infected, by when its chain has taken off:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.2*I        # β = 0.2 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)  # Infectious for 10 days on average: R0 = 2
flu = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=1), name='flu') # One imported case

sim = ss.Sim(flu, total_pop=1e6, stop=ss.days(100), solver='gillespie', branching=True, verbose=0)
msim = sim.run(n_runs=100, until=flu.I.n + flu.R.n >= 100)
b = msim.branching
print(f'Share of introductions that died out: {b.p_extinct:.2f} (95% interval {b.p_extinct_ci[0]:.2f} to {b.p_extinct_ci[1]:.2f}; theory: 1/R0 = 0.5)')

Share of introductions that died out: 0.48 (95% interval 0.38 to 0.58; theory: 1/R0 = 0.5)


until= stops a run once a condition holds: an expression of the model, as here, or a function of the sim, checked at the end of each step. It works for any run, not only a branching process; the results after the stop are NaN, and sim.stopped is the time point the run stopped at. Without it, a branching process that takes off grows without limit. msim.branching.plot() shows how large the chains got, and the gallery page The chance of a major outbreak does the same over a range of R0.


Chains and offspring, as agents
For chains of transmission, run the same model as agents. A branching process of agents makes agents only for the people infected, so a city of 10 million costs no more than a village: here, 100 imported cases, followed for 60 days:

flu = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=100), name='flu') # 100 imported cases, for enough chains to count
sim = ss.Sim(flu, total_pop=10e6, stop=ss.days(60), solver='abm', branching=True, verbose=0)
sim.run()
b = sim.branching
print(f'{len(sim.people):,} agents for {sim.pars.total_pop:,.0f} people; {b.length} generations')

60,239 agents for 10,000,000 people; 21 generations


sim.branching has, for each agent, its infector (−1 for the imported cases), its generation, the time point it was infected (ti), and the number it infected (offspring). Since the most recent cases are still infecting others, only the offspring of the cases infected long enough before the end are counted in full (complete):

n = b.offspring[b.complete]
print('Cases:', len(n), ' Mean offspring:', n.mean().round(2), ' Variance:', n.var().round(1), ' Share with none:', (n == 0).mean().round(2))

Cases: 432  Mean offspring: 2.13  Variance: 7.6  Share with none: 0.32


The mean is close to R0 = 2. With an exponential infectious period, the offspring distribution is geometric, with a variance of R0(1 + R0) = 6 and a third of cases infecting nobody: one reason why so many introductions die out.
To give the cases different infectiousness, give the disease rel_trans as an attribute drawn for each person, ss.attr(). With a fixed infectious period, a gamma distribution with mean 1 and shape k gives a negative binomial offspring distribution with dispersion k; k = 0.2 is about what has been estimated for SARS and other infections with superspreading. Comparing the offspring with and without it, each over 20 runs:

k = 0.2
offspring = {}
for label, extra in [('Same infectiousness', {}), (f'Overdispersed (k = {k})', dict(rel_trans=ss.attr(ss.gamma(a=k, scale=1/k))))]: # Each person's infectiousness, with mean 1
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    flu_k = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 0.2*I, I >> R @ ss.constant(ss.days(10)), init_n=dict(I=20), name='flu', **extra)
    sim = ss.Sim(flu_k, total_pop=10e6, stop=ss.days(60), solver='abm', branching=True, verbose=0)
    msim = sim.run(n_runs=8)
    b = msim.branching
    offspring[label] = b.offspring
    print(f'{label}: R = {b.R:.2f}, k = {b.k:.2g}')

bins = np.arange(0, 16)
plt.hist(list(offspring.values()), bins=bins, density=True, label=list(offspring.keys()))
plt.xlabel('Number of people infected by each case')
plt.ylabel('Share of cases')
plt.legend();

Same infectiousness: R = 1.98, k = 1.1e+02
Overdispersed (k = 0.2): R = 2.07, k = 0.21









With the same infectiousness and a fixed infectious period, the offspring are Poisson (k is infinite). With overdispersion, most cases infect nobody and a few infect many, so the outbreak grows more erratically, and more introductions die out: by theory, about 80% from one case, against 20% with the same infectiousness. msim.branching.R and .k are a negative binomial fitted by maximum likelihood, and are fitted only from runs of a fixed length: a run stopped by until= stops because its chain is large, so its cases had more offspring than most.


The renewal equation
solver='ide' is the deterministic solver that takes each dwell time as it is, rather than as the Erlang stages that 'ode' uses: an integro-differential model. As a branching process, it is the renewal equation that EpiEstim, EpiNow2, and epidemia are built on, with the generation interval that the model’s latent and infectious periods give:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
seir = ss.Disease(S >> E @ 0.4*I, E >> I @ ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(5), std=ss.days(3)), I >> R @ ss.days(5), init_n=dict(I=10), name='seir')
sims = {solver: ss.Sim(seir, total_pop=1e6, branching=True, solver=solver, stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0) for solver in ['ide', 'ode']}
ss.parallel(sims).plot('seir.I')








The latent period here is lognormal. 'ide' keeps it as it is, as a conveyor of whole steps with the distribution’s own chance of leaving after each one; 'ode' approximates it with Erlang stages that match its mean and standard deviation, so the two are close but not the same. For a reproduction number that varies in time, give beta as an ss.timeseries, which sim.fit() can fit.

title: Branching and rescaling
text:
Population rescaling

Population size and number of agents
Two settings say how big the population is:

total_pop is the size of the population being modeled. As compartments, it is the total of the compartments; as agents, it is the number of people the agents stand for.
n_agents is how many agents are simulated. It is a computational choice, like the time step, and giving it makes the sim run as agents.

If neither is given, the population is 10,000. If only n_agents is given, total_pop is the same. If only total_pop is given and the sim runs as agents, there are as many agents as people, up to 10,000.
Here is an influenza-like infection (R0 = 0.3 per day × 10 days = 3) in a city of a million people, as compartments and as 10,000 agents. (This page uses a slower infection than measles, whose fast rates need short steps when run as agents; see Solvers and backends.)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I        # β = 0.3 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)  # Infectious for 10 days on average
flu = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

ode    = ss.Sim(flu, total_pop=1e6, stop=ss.days(150)).run()               # A million people, as compartments
agents = ss.Sim(flu, total_pop=1e6, stop=ss.days(150), solver='abm').run() # The same, as 10,000 agents
print('People per agent:', agents.pars.pop_scale)

Sim: flu, 1,000,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  flu: R0 = 3, with 1,000 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0037 s; flu: 939,538 infections; at most 300,623 infectious, on day 38
Sim: flu, as 10,000 agents, each 100 people, days 0 to 150
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.3 per day (with everyone infectious), 26% in a step. Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.072 s; flu: 941,300 infections; at most 312,800 infectious, on day 41


People per agent: 100.0


Each agent stands for 100 people, and the counts in the agents’ results are multiplied by 100. The two agree on the size of the epidemic and of its peak; the peak comes a few days later as agents, partly by chance and partly because agents take whole daily steps.


Static scaling
The number of people each agent stands for is pop_scale, which is total_pop / n_agents unless it is given itself. Results that are counts (such as I) are multiplied by it when the run ends; results that are shares or averages (such as prevalence) are not.
The cost is resolution. With 5,000 agents for a million people, each agent is 200 people, so an epidemic can’t start from fewer than 200 people, and an outbreak started by 10 people can’t be represented at all:

flu = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10)) # 10 people infectious at the start
static = ss.Sim(flu, total_pop=1e6, n_agents=5_000, stop=ss.days(150), label='Static')
static.run();

Sim "Static": flu, as 5,000 agents, each 200 people, days 0 to 150
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.3 per day (with everyone infectious), 26% in a step. Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters
  Note: "flu" starts with one agent in I (200 people): its initial number is 0.05 agents at 200 people per agent, which rounds to 0. For the number given, give more agents (n_agents=), or rescale=True


  Done in 0.12 s; flu: 943,200 infections; at most 333,600 infectious, on day 49


Starsim notes the problem: 10 people are 0.05 of an agent, so the run starts with one agent infectious, which is 200 people, and its epidemic is that of 200 cases, not 10. The initial infections can instead be given as a number of agents, with ss.choose_n(), here 10 agents, each of whom stands for 200 people, so 2,000 people are infectious at the start:

flu = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=10) # 10 agents infectious at the start
static = ss.Sim(flu, total_pop=1e6, n_agents=5_000, stop=ss.days(150), label='Static')
static.run();

Sim "Static": flu, as 5,000 agents, each 200 people, days 0 to 150
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.3 per day (with everyone infectious), 26% in a step. Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters
  Note: "flu" starts with one agent in I (200 people): its initial number is 0.05 agents at 200 people per agent, which rounds to 0. For the number given, give more agents (n_agents=), or rescale=True


  Done in 0.12 s; flu: 943,200 infections; at most 333,600 infectious, on day 49




Dynamic rescaling
With rescale=True, each agent starts by standing for one person, and the number grows as the epidemic does, up to pop_scale. At the end of each step, the sim:

checks the share of agents who are no longer naive (who have left the first state of any disease);
if that share is more than rescale_threshold (5% by default), multiplies the number of people per agent by at least rescale_factor (1.2 by default), without going past pop_scale;
makes enough of the agents who are not naive naive again (if the number of people per agent doubles, half of them), so that the infected people are spread over fewer agents.

So every agent always stands for the same number of people, and agents are freed to stand for the part of the population that has not been infected yet. With dynamic rescaling, the 10 agents infectious at the start are 10 people:

dynamic = ss.Sim(flu, total_pop=1e6, n_agents=5_000, stop=ss.days(150), rescale=True, label='Dynamic')
dynamic.run()
dynamic.results.pop_scale.plot()

Sim "Dynamic": flu, as 5,000 agents, each 200 people, days 0 to 150
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.3 per day (with everyone infectious), 26% in a step. Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.12 s; flu: 931,555 infections; at most 311,400 infectious, on day 72









The number of people per agent (sim.results.pop_scale) starts at 1, and grows as the epidemic does, to 200. Here are the three runs:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ten = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10), name='flu') # 10 people infectious, as compartments
ode = ss.Sim(ten, total_pop=1e6, stop=ss.days(150), label='ODE', verbose=0).run()

for sim in [ode, static, dynamic]:
    res = sim.results.flu.I
    plt.plot(res.timevec, res.values, label=sim.label)
plt.xlabel('Day')
plt.ylabel('Number infectious')
plt.legend();








The static sim starts with 2,000 people infectious, so its epidemic peaks weeks earlier. The dynamic sim starts with 10, like the ODE here; it may take off later or earlier than the ODE by chance, since the ODE always takes off at once, while a few agents can take a while to start a chain of transmission (see Scenarios, and branching processes above).

Results count the people no agent stands for yet
While each agent stands for fewer people than pop_scale, part of the population is not represented by any agent. The sim counts these people as one number, sim.results.unrepresented: at the start, pop_scale − 1 for each agent; at each rescaling, from s to s′ people per agent, it falls by s′ − s for each agent alive then, who now stands for that many more. An agent who dies is the scale people it stands for, and one who is born adds that many, so neither changes it. The number alive is scale people for each agent alive, plus these. They are like the agents, and have never been infected, so a declared disease counts its share of them in its first state; another declared module, such as ss.Pregnancy, shares them out over its states as the agents are. The results are of the whole population from the start, and so is any share of it, such as prevalence:

res = dynamic.results
print('Alive at the start:', res.alive[0])
print('Susceptible at the start:', res.flu.S[0])
print('Infectious at the start:', res.flu.I[0])

Alive at the start: 1000000.0
Susceptible at the start: 999990.0
Infectious at the start: 10.0




Diseases written as code
Dynamic rescaling needs to know which agents are naive, and to make agents naive again. A declared disease does both by itself. A disease written as code that transmits (a subclass of ss.Infection) counts the agents who have ever been infected (ti_infected) as not naive, and its make_naive() puts each of its states back to its default value, except rel_sus and rel_trans, which other modules (such as vaccines) often change. A disease that keeps something else, or that sets rel_sus itself, overrides it:
class MyDisease(ss.Infection):
    def make_naive(self, uids, skip_states=None):
        super().make_naive(uids, skip_states=['rel_trans']) # Reset rel_sus too
        self.my_custom_value[uids] = 0 # And anything not kept as a state
A count that is added up during the run would mix steps with different numbers of people per agent, so work out a running total in finalize_results(), after the results have been scaled; a declared disease’s running totals (res.infection.cum) are worked out from the scaled flows when they are asked for.

title: Branching and rescaling
text:
Pitfalls

Too few agents for the start of an epidemic. Starsim notes when the initial number of people rounds to too few agents; use more agents, ss.choose_n(), or rescale=True.
Results during a run are in agents. Counts are scaled when the run ends; an analyzer that reads a count during the run sees agents.
Rare events. An event that happens to fewer people than an agent stands for (a rare complication) happens to whole agents or not at all; such a model needs more agents.
Too few agents for a few seeds. A model started by a few people, run with each agent standing for several, starts from fewer agents than people, or from none: give n_agents equal to total_pop at least until the outbreak is large, or use rescale=True.
Dynamic rescaling and diseases written as code. The people no agent stands for yet are in the results of a declared module (for a disease, in its first state) and in alive, but not in those of a module written as code, whose counts and shares are of the people the agents stand for.
Dynamic rescaling with births and deaths. An agent who dies early, while it stands for few people, is few deaths, and the people no agent stands for are not born and do not die, so with many deaths or births before the scale reaches pop_scale, the population is not that of a run with each agent standing for pop_scale from the start. With more agents born than die before then, the count of people no agent stands for can fall below 0, as the agents come to stand for more people than there are.
Treating a depleting run as a branching process. Chains and offspring counted from a run in which a sizable share of people have been infected are biased down; count them only while the outbreak is small compared with the population.
A stochastic branching process with no until=. A chain that takes off grows without limit, and each step gets slower; give until=, or a short stop=.
R and k from runs stopped by until=. They are not fitted, since such runs are not a fair sample of cases; run for a fixed stop= instead.
Networks in a branching process of agents. It mixes in groups and places; a contact network raises a CapabilityError. A compartmental solver takes a random network’s mean number of contacts.

title: Branching and rescaling
text:
Further reading

Epiverse: superspreading: offspring distributions, overdispersion, and the probability that an outbreak takes off
Epiverse: epichains: simulating and fitting transmission chains as branching processes
Lloyd-Smith et al. (2005): Superspreading and the effect of individual variation on disease emergence: the negative binomial offspring distribution and its dispersion k

title: Contact networks
text:
🧠15% 🤖85%
A disease model says how infectious people are; the mixing says who meets whom, and how often. This page covers the ways of giving the mixing in Starsim: homogeneous mixing, mixing pools, and networks of individual contacts (random, sexual, mother-to-child, and household networks). Contact matrices between groups, such as age groups, are in Population data, and several places with movement between them in Geography. The tutorial A2 – Networks builds up the same material as a single worked path, and T4 – Age groups and contacts uses a contact matrix in a compartmental model.

title: Contact networks
text:
Choosing how people mix
The disease and the mixing are separate: changing from homogeneous mixing to a network does not change the disease. Each way of mixing is a route (a path by which infection can pass), given to the sim with networks=, which takes networks and mixing pools alike, singly or as a list:

No route given: homogeneous mixing, the assumption of the standard ODE models. Everyone is equally likely to meet everyone else, and the transmission rate β (beta) is a rate per unit time: in S >> I @ beta*I, each susceptible person is infected at a rate of β times the share of people who are infectious.
A mixing pool, ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=10): homogeneous mixing with 10 contacts per unit time. β is then the probability that a contact with an infectious person infects, so β × the number of contacts is the transmission rate.
A contact matrix, ss.contacts(...): mixing between groups, such as age groups, with a number of contacts for each pair of groups (see Population data).
A network, such as ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10) or ss.SexualNet(): contacts between particular people, with β per contact (or per sex act, on a network with acts).

Here is the same disease under three kinds of mixing. With no route, β = 0.05 per day and an infectious period of 10 days give R0 = β × the infectious period = 0.5, so there is no epidemic. With 10 contacts a day, R0 = 0.05 × 10 × 10 = 5, and the mixing pool and the random network give nearly the same epidemic:

import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.05*I       # β = 0.05: per day with no route, per contact with one
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)  # Infectious for 10 days on average
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)

kw = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(120), verbose=0)
scenarios = {
    'Homogeneous mixing':    ss.Sim(sir, **kw),
    'Mixing pool (10 contacts a day)': ss.Sim(sir, networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=10), **kw),
    'Random network (10 contacts a day)': ss.Sim(sir, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10), **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sir.I')








Transmission along every route is frequency-dependent: a person’s number of contacts is fixed, and what matters is the share of them who are infectious. This is the usual assumption for infections passed directly between people. A density-dependent rate, which grows with the number of people infected rather than their share, is written with the count itself, S >> I @ ss.perday(3e-5)*I.n (see Diseases).

Which solver runs it
A model whose mixing has a compartmental form (no route, a mixing pool, or a contact matrix) runs as an ODE unless it is given agents, as the first and second sims above would without n_agents. A network is about particular people, so a model with a network runs as agents. A compartmental solver can still be asked for (solver='ode'); it then approximates the network, and says so in one line:



Route
As agents
As compartments

the partner-change model (partnerships formed at a rate, each with the chance it transmits over its whole length), which needs the model stratified by sex for ss.SexualNet



The approximations are rough where the network matters most: homogeneous mixing with the same mean number of contacts loses the variation between people, and the partner-change model counts at most one transmission in each partnership. Solvers and backends has the details. Anything that needs to know who a person’s contacts are (contact tracing, partner notification, the transmission tree) needs a network, and so agents.

title: Contact networks
text:
Random networks
ss.RandomNet pairs people at random, with n_contacts contacts per person (a number, or a distribution such as ss.poisson(lam=5)). By default the contacts are redrawn every step. dur= makes them last, dynamic=False makes them once at the start and keeps them (people born or added later get none), and age_range=[20, 65] restricts the network to people of those ages. Several networks can be given together, each with its own name, as a layered population: here contacts at home (fully connected households of about three people, ssl.ClusterNet) and contacts at work among adults:

households = ssl.ClusterNet(name='households', cluster_size=ss.poisson(3))
work = ss.RandomNet(name='work', n_contacts=10, age_range=[20, 65], dynamic=False)

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ 0.02*I       # Per contact, per day
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.days(10)  # No lasting immunity
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)

def make_sim(networks):
    return ss.Sim(sis, networks=networks, n_agents=2000, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0)

msim = ss.parallel({'Work only': make_sim(work), 'Households and work': make_sim([households, work])})
msim.plot('sis.I')
print('Number of households:', msim.sims[1].networks.households.n_clusters)








Number of households: 669


Adding households raises the number infected at the endemic level: they reach children and older people, who have no contacts at work, and give each person a few more contacts. Each network’s transmission is counted separately, so the same β applies on every layer unless it is given by route (see below).
ssl.HybridNet gives the four layers of Covasim in one: households (h), schools (s), and workplaces (w), each a ssl.ClusterNet limited by age where it should be, and the community (c), a random network. Once in a sim, it becomes four networks, each reached (and changed) on its own, e.g. sim.networks.s; a dt, start, or stop given to it is passed to all four:

hybrid = ss.Sim(sis, networks=ssl.HybridNet(household_size=3), n_agents=2000, stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0)
hybrid.run()
for net in hybrid.networks():
    print(net.label, 'edges:', len(net))

Households edges: 3113
Schools edges: 5654
Workplaces edges: 8694
Community edges: 19868

title: Contact networks
text:
Sexual networks
ss.SexualNet is a network of partnerships between two groups of people: by default a man and a woman, or two men (between='mm'), or any two groups by name, such as female sex workers and their clients (between=('fsw', 'client')). A partnership lasts dur, and has acts sex acts per unit time. Partnerships and acts are separate numbers, with separate sources of data (numbers of partners from surveys, how long partnerships last, how often partners have sex), so that a probability of transmission per act means what it says.
By default, people with no partner are paired on every step, so nobody has more than one partner at a time. With n_contacts=, the mean number of partners at a time is a target instead, and so are concurrency= (the share with two or more), max_contacts=, and match= (the share of partnerships between people at the same level of a property, e.g. match=dict(risk=0.8)). People then look for partners at the rates that make those targets the network’s stable state. net.check() runs the sim again (three times by default) and compares the network it makes with each target:

net = ss.SexualNet(n_contacts=1.2, concurrency=0.1, dur=ss.years(2))
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, networks=net, start=2000, stop=2010, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.networks.sexualnet.check(output=True)

ss.SexualNet is ss.DegreeNet between men and women, with an age of debut and participation. Partnerships that are not sexual, such as needle sharing among people who inject drugs, are ss.DegreeNet itself, which takes the same targets among anyone (or the people that where= gives, or between two groups with between=), with a target of one partner each by default.

title: Contact networks
text:
Transmission that differs by route
Infectiousness belongs to the disease, and contact to the routes, but how infectious someone is can itself depend on the route: HIV passes far more readily through a shared needle than through sex, and more readily from men to women than the reverse. The disease then gives one β for each route, as a dict keyed by the route’s name (the network’s class in lowercase, unless it was given a name=). On a network with directions, β takes a value for each: ss.peract(m2f=..., f2m=...) is a probability per act from men to women and from women to men. Every route needs a value, so that none is left out by mistake.
Here an infection passes through a random network of social contacts and through a sexual network:

S, I = ss.states('S I')
beta = dict(randomnet=ss.peryear(0.2), sexualnet=ss.peract(m2f=0.01, f2m=0.005))
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.years(1)
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

sim = ss.Sim(sis, networks=[ss.RandomNet(), ss.SexualNet()], n_agents=2000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.plot('sis')

title: Contact networks
text:
Mother-to-child networks
Transmission from mother to child needs pregnancy (ss.Pregnancy), which adds and removes the edges between mother and child: ss.PrenatalNet while the child is in the womb, ss.BreastfeedingNet while the mother breastfeeds, and ss.PostnatalNet for a period after birth (dur=). Their direction is one way, from mother to child. Here a chronic infection (one with no recovery) passes through partnerships and to children before birth, with β a probability per contact on the prenatal network:

S, I = ss.states('S I')
beta = dict(sexualnet=ss.peract(m2f=0.01, f2m=0.005), prenatalnet=0.3)
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
chronic = ss.Disease(infection, init_prev=0.1)

pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=ss.freqperyear(100)) # Births a year per 1,000 women
deaths = ss.Deaths(death_rate=ss.peryear(0.01))
sim = ss.Sim(chronic, networks=[ss.SexualNet(), ss.PrenatalNet()], demographics=[pregnancy, deaths],
             n_agents=2000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.plot('chronic')








See Demographics for pregnancy and births.

title: Contact networks
text:
Mixing pools
A mixing pool is homogeneous mixing among a group of people: no individual contacts, but each person has an effective number of contacts in the pool (n_contacts: a number is the same for everyone, and a distribution is drawn once for each person and kept for the whole run). With no groups, a pool is everyone, as in the first example on this page. src= and dst= restrict it to the people who can infect (the sources) and the people who can be infected (the destinations), so a pool can be one-way. Each is a condition on people, a function of the sim returning a boolean array or UIDs, or ss.AgeGroup(low, high), which works out who is in an age group once for each step and so is faster when there are many pools:

pool = ss.MixingPool(
    src = ss.AgeGroup(low=0, high=15),     # Children infect ...
    dst = ss.AgeGroup(low=15, high=None),  # ... adults, but not each other
    n_contacts = ss.poisson(lam=5),        # 5 contacts a day on average
)
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.05*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, networks=pool, n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(120), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.plot('sir')








On each step, the force of infection in the pool is the mean infectiousness of the sources (the share of them infectious, weighted by each one’s rel_trans), and each susceptible destination has a hazard of β × that mean × their number of contacts × their rel_sus, so is infected in the step with probability 1 − exp(−hazard × dt). This is the term β × S × I/N of the ODE, applied to each person.
Of the 5,000 people, 250 start infected, and the epidemic goes no further than the adults whom children infect: it dies out once the infected children recover, since nobody infects children in this pool and adults infect nobody. ss.MixingPools (plural) is a set of pools between groups, with src and dst as dicts of groups and n_contacts as a matrix, sources by row and destinations by column. A matrix of numbers is much faster than one of distributions, which needs a pool for each pair of groups and a draw for each pair for each person born; to have the number of contacts differ between people, use a distribution, e.g. ss.poisson(lam=2), in the matrix. For mixing by age, the usual case, ss.contacts() makes the ss.MixingPools from a contact matrix and a stratified model gives results by group: see Population data.
In a declared disease, β belongs to the transmission, not to the pool: a pool’s own beta must be left at its default of 1, and any other value raises an error that says to give it to the transmission instead (e.g. dict(mixingpool=...)).

title: Contact networks
text:
Working with edges
A network keeps its edges as arrays: p1 (the first person in each edge), p2 (the second), and beta (a multiplier for each edge, 1 by default), reached as net.edges or as net['p1']. net.find_contacts(uids) gives the contacts of some people, net.to_df() the edges as a table, and net.remove_edges() removes edges by index or by a boolean array. A network can also be made from a table of edges with from_df():

sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=1000, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4), stop=ss.days(10), verbose=0)
sim.run()
net = sim.networks.randomnet
print('Edges:', len(net))
print('Contacts of person 0:', net.find_contacts([0]))

custom = ss.Network(name='custom').from_df(dict(p1=[0, 1, 2], p2=[1, 2, 3]))
custom.to_df()

Edges can be removed by a condition on them or by position, and net.eligible() gives the people who can form edges (alive, and within an age range if given), here on the community layer of the hybrid network above:

net = hybrid.networks.c
print('Community edges:', len(net))
net.remove_edges(net['p1'] < 100) # Remove the edges whose first person has a UID below 100
net.remove_edges([0, 1, 2])       # Remove the first three edges
print('After removing some:', len(net))
print('People of school age:', net.eligible(age_range=[6, 22]).sum())

Community edges: 19868
After removing some: 18840
People of school age: 543


Changing the edges of a network in the middle of a run is the job of an intervention (see Interventions), such as closing schools; the edges of a network that is redrawn each step come back on the next step.
A network of partnerships forgets a partnership when it ends. With memory=, it keeps those that ended within that time, so that net.find_contacts(), and so contact tracing (the trace= of a delivery: see Interventions), also reaches recent past partners, as for partner notification of the past year’s partners:

net = ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(1), std=ss.years(1)), memory=ss.years(1))
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, networks=net, start=2000, stop=2005, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
net = sim.networks.sexualnet
uids = ss.uids(range(200))
print('Current partners of 200 people:', len(ss.Network.find_contacts(net, uids)))
print('Including those of the past year:', len(net.find_contacts(uids)))

Current partners of 200 people: 126
Including those of the past year: 217
