False







The campaigns cost more than routine vaccination, and avert more infections, but each extra infection they avert costs more than with the routine program alone: the campaigns mostly reach children whom routine vaccination has already protected, or who would not have been infected anyway. Whether that is worth paying for is a judgment the model informs but does not make; it depends on what else the money could buy. ssl.Costs gives each sim a result for the cost of each delivery, and their total, costs.total. ssl.ICER totals the cost and the outcome named (any result: infections, deaths, or a model’s DALYs) for each scenario, takes the outcome averted from that of the baseline (the first scenario, unless baseline= names another), and orders the scenarios by cost. Each is compared with the next cheaper one, except that a program that costs more and averts no more than a cheaper one is dominated, and has no ratio. It works the same for any number of programs, for a dict or list of sims as well as a MultiSim, and with several runs of each scenario compares their means. A table that needs more than this, such as extended dominance or a different measure of effect, can be built the same way from the results.
With several runs of each scenario, icer.plot() shows each one on the cost-effectiveness plane, icer.plot_ceac() shows how often each scenario is the best at each willingness to pay, and icer.best(wtp=1000) gives the best scenario at one value.

title: Costs
text:
Disability-adjusted life years
ssl.DALYs counts disability-adjusted life years as results: the time people spend in a state, multiplied by its disability weight, plus the years of life lost to deaths. ssl.ICER compares these by default, so the outcome doesn’t need naming:
analyzers = [ssl.Costs(), ssl.DALYs(weights={'hiv.I': 0.2})]
msim = ss.parallel({'No treatment': ss.Sim(..., analyzers=analyzers), 'Treatment': ss.Sim(..., analyzers=analyzers)})
ssl.ICER(msim).df
With agents, the years of life lost come from each person’s age at death and a standard life table. Compartmental runs don’t record ages at death, so they take a number: ssl.DALYs(weights=..., life_lost=30).

title: Costs
text:
Comparing during a run
ssl.ICER can also be an analyzer, after ssl.Costs and ssl.DALYs. The sim then counts as one more scenario, compared at each step with the finished sims it is given, over the same period, so that a sim can act on the result: for example, an intervention can follow sim.analyzers.icer.best(wtp=1000). window=1 compares the latest step alone.

title: Costs
text:
Costs with uncertainty
A model run as agents, or as a stochastic model, gives different costs and effects in each run, so a cost per outcome averted needs several runs, and an interval. Give each scenario the same seeds (as n_runs= does), so that the runs can be paired, and the difference between scenarios is not lost in the differences between runs. Here a test-and-treat program for a curable infection with no lasting immunity, as on Products, costs $4 a test and $20 a treatment, and each scenario is run 8 times:

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peryear(2)*I  # β = 2 per year
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.years(1)      # Infected for a year on average, then susceptible again
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.1)

screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, coverage=0.5, interval=ss.years(1), start='2010', cost=4.0)
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.95, who=screening.positive, coverage=0.8, cost=20.0)

base = ss.Sim(sis, n_agents=5000, total_pop=100_000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({'No program': base, 'Test and treat': base.new(interventions=[screening, treatment])}, n_runs=8)

res = msim.results
cost = res.screening.cost.values.sum(axis=1) + res.treatment.cost.values.sum(axis=1) # The cost of each run of the program
averted = -res.sis.infection.diff('No program')['Test and treat'].values.sum(axis=1)  # The infections it averted, run by run
ratio = cost / averted

print('Cost of the program ($), median:', round(np.median(cost)))
print('Infections averted, median:', round(np.median(averted)))
print('Cost per infection averted ($), median and range:', np.round(np.median(ratio), 1), np.round([ratio.min(), ratio.max()], 1))

Cost of the program ($), median: 4815920
Infections averted, median: 84740
Cost per infection averted ($), median and range: 56.7 [50.8 58.9]


The costs of each run are scaled to the population, as all results are: with 5,000 agents standing for 100,000 people, each test given to an agent counts as 20 tests. The cost varies little between runs, since it follows the number tested, but the infections averted vary more, so the ratio does too. Eight runs give a rough range; more give a better one, and Scenarios covers how many. The uncertainty here is only from chance: uncertainty in the parameters (the sensitivity of the test, the cost of each treatment) needs runs with values drawn from their priors as well (ss.parallel(sim, priors=True, n_runs=...); see Scenarios).

title: Costs
text:
Discounting and other costs
Economic evaluations usually discount costs and outcomes in later years, at 3% a year for example, since a cost paid later, or an infection averted later, counts for less than one now. A result is an array over time, so discounting is a weight for each time point, (1 + rate)**-(t - start) for a time t in years after start. ssl.discount() applies it to a result, and gives back a result. Here the routine measles program from the first example, discounted at 3% a year from 2010:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, interventions=routine, **pars)
sim.run()
no_vx = ss.Sim(measles, **pars)
no_vx.run()

cost = ssl.discount(sim.results.routine.cost, 0.03, start=2010).sum()
averted = ssl.discount(no_vx.results.measles.infection - sim.results.measles.infection, 0.03, start=2010).sum()
print('Discounted cost ($):', round(cost))
print('Discounted infections averted:', round(averted))
print('Discounted cost per infection averted ($):', round(cost/averted, 2))

Discounted cost ($): 1871913
Discounted infections averted: 316968
Discounted cost per infection averted ($): 5.91


Other costs work the same way, with the results that drive them. A cost that does not depend on deliveries, such as running a program (staff, cold chain, training), is an amount per year over the years the program runs. The cost of the disease itself, such as care for each case, is a cost per infection (or per case, if the model declares one), times the infections; the infections averted then save that cost, and the net cost of a program is its cost less the savings. ssl.Costs takes both: fixed=, a cost per year from start=, and unit_costs=, the cost of each event of any result, by its path. Here the program costs $20,000 a year to run from 2010, and each infection $50 of care, in both scenarios, so that the difference between them is the net cost:

care = {'measles.infection': 50} # $50 of care for each infection
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No vaccination': ss.Sim(measles, analyzers=ssl.Costs(unit_costs=care), **pars),
    'Routine':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=routine, analyzers=ssl.Costs(unit_costs=care, fixed=20_000, start=2010), **pars),
})
df = ssl.ICER(msim, outcome='measles.infection', rate=0.03, start=2010).df # Discounted, as above
print(df[['cost', 'averted']].round())
net = df.cost['Routine'] - df.cost['No vaccination']
print('Net cost per infection averted ($):', round(net/df.averted['Routine'], 2))

                      cost   averted
scenario                            
Routine         79604237.0  316968.0
No vaccination  93278380.0       0.0
Net cost per infection averted ($): -43.14


A net cost below zero means a program saves more than it costs; ssl.ICER then marks the scenario without it as dominated.

title: Costs
text:
Optimizing spending
The examples above cost given programs. The reverse question, how best to divide a budget between programs, is an optimization: ss.fit.optimize() allocates a total between programs whose spending is a parameter of the model, to maximize or minimize a result, or finds the least total that reaches a target. The spending parameters, and how spending turns into coverage, come from the model: from a program book imported with the model (as from Atomica), or from parameters you write. See Optimization.

title: Costs
text:
Under compartments and agents
Costs work the same under every solver. In a compartmental run, the number delivered on a step is a number of people, and the cost is that number times the cost of each delivery. As agents, the cost is counted per agent and scaled, like any count, by the number of people each agent stands for. A cost of a test is per test given (whatever its result), and a cost of a treatment per treatment given; a delivery that offers a product but doesn’t give it (to someone not eligible, or beyond its capacity) costs nothing.

title: Costs
text:
Pitfalls

The cost is per delivery. cost= is the cost of each product given, including what it takes to give it; costs that don’t grow with the number delivered are added separately, as above.
Count every delivery. A program of several steps (a test, then treatment) has a cost for each; add them up.
Compare like with like. Take costs and outcomes from the same runs, over the same period, in the same units; with chance in the model, pair the runs of each scenario by seed.
The horizon matters. Infections averted after the end of the run are not counted, and a program that starts late in a run has had little time to avert any.

The API reference for this page: Products, ss.fit.

title: Costs
text:
Further reading

WHO: Making choices in health, a guide to cost-effectiveness analysis: the methods behind cost per outcome averted
Atomica: Optimization: allocating spending between programs in a compartmental framework built around program costs
Optima HIV: allocation of HIV budgets with program costs and coverage

title: Diseases
text:
🧠10% 🤖90%
A disease in Starsim is declared the way a compartmental model is drawn: as the states people can be in (the compartments) and the transitions between them (the flows), each with what drives it, a rate or a duration. This page is the reference for writing them: the ways to write a transition, transmission and other rates, durations and their distributions, branching, how an epidemic starts, births and deaths, quantities that are not people, and susceptibility. A disease declared this way runs as a compartmental model or as agents, unchanged.
For a step-by-step introduction, see T2 – Building a model and T3 – Building a disease; for diseases among agents, A1 – Diseases. A disease that needs more than states and transitions can be written as code (below).

title: Diseases
text:
A disease in brief
The simplified measles model used throughout these pages is an SIR model:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # From S to I, at a rate of 1.9 per day times the share infectious
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # From I to R, after 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

measles.equations()

dS/dt = -beta * S * I / N
dI/dt =  beta * S * I / N - I / dur_I
dR/dt =  I / dur_I


ss.states() makes the states, named in one string. A transition is written source >> destination @ driver: “S goes to I at 1.9 times I”. What follows @ is one of:

a rate, per person in the source state per unit of time, such as ss.perday(0.125), or an expression of states and parameters, such as 1.9*I;
a duration, such as ss.days(8): the average time people spend in the source state before they take this transition. A duration of 8 days and a rate of 1/8 per day are the same transition.

A bare number in a rate takes the model’s unit of time, here days, from ss.days(8); see Parameters. Names come from the variables: the states are S, I, and R, the transitions infection and recovery, and the disease measles, and so are their results (sim.results.measles.infection).

title: Diseases
text:
Ways to write a transition
There is one kind of transition, ss.Transition, and the operators are a short way to write it. These build the same model:

# Operators: the usual form
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init_prev=0.001)

# Named by keyword, e.g. when the transitions are written inline
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8),
    init_prev = 0.001,
)

# Fully explicit, e.g. to build a model in a loop, or from R
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles = ss.Disease(
    ss.Transition(S, I, rate=1.9*I, name='infection'),
    ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8), name='recovery'),
    init_prev = 0.001,
    name = 'measles',
)

A transition that has no variable or keyword to be named by is named infection if it is the disease’s only transmission, and otherwise gets a name from its states (I_to_R). A disease can also be written as a class, which is the form for a disease that goes into a library (below).

title: Diseases
text:
Transmission
A bare state in a rate, like I in 1.9*I, means contact with the people in that state. With no contacts given (homogeneous mixing), that is the share of the population in it, I/N, so S >> I @ beta*I is the textbook frequency-dependent transmission, with a flow of β S I / N. With a contact matrix or a network, the same rate is worked out from whom each person actually meets, and β is the rate per contact (see Stratification and Population data). A transition whose rate contains a bare state is contact-mediated, and that state is a source of infection.
For density-dependent transmission, in which the number of contacts grows with the size of the population (as is often assumed for animal or vector populations), write the count itself, I.n. The flow is then β S I:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles_density = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9e-5*I.n, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init_prev=0.001)
measles_density.equations()

dS/dt = -1.9e-05 * I.n * S
dI/dt =  1.9e-05 * I.n * S - I / dur_I
dR/dt =  I / dur_I


A rate can also be written as the whole flow, as in the equations of other frameworks: S >> I @ beta*S*I/N (with N = S + I + R) is the same frequency-dependent model as beta*I, and beta*S*I the same density-dependent model as beta*I.n.
Several sources of infection are a sum: S >> E @ beta*(I + 0.5*A) says that people in A (say, without symptoms) are half as infectious as those in I. A rate must be linear in its bare states, since exposure on a network is a sum over contacts; anything nonlinear is written with counts (I.n).

title: Diseases
text:
Other rates
Anything that is not transmission is a rate per person, or a duration:








After @
Means
Example




a duration
the mean time in the source state
I >> R @ ss.days(8)


a distribution of durations
the time in the source state, with that distribution
I >> R @ ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(8))


a rate, or a bare number
a rate per person per unit of time
R >> S @ ss.peryear(0.1), R >> S @ 0.1


a probability per period
the chance of moving in each period, as a rate
I >> R @ ss.prob(0.12, 'day')


an expression with a bare state
transmission
S >> I @ beta*I


an expression of counts
a rate that depends on how many people are in each state
S >> I @ beta*W.n/(W.n + K)


a function of the sim
a rate worked out at each step
S >> I @ my_rate



A bare number after @ is always a rate, never a duration: I >> R @ 8 means a rate of 8 per day, so that people stay infectious for an eighth of a day. A duration is always typed (ss.days(8)), or given as dur= (ss.Transition(I, R, dur=8)).
Transitions out of the same state that are driven by rates (or durations with an exponential distribution) compete: the total rate of leaving is their sum, and each takes its share of those who leave. The order in which they are written doesn’t matter.

title: Diseases
text:
Durations
A single duration is the mean of an exponential distribution, as in an ODE model, and describe() marks this as a guess. An exponential distribution has a lot of spread: with a mean of 10 days, a third of people leave within 4 days, and one in twenty stays more than 30. The real latent period of measles (from infection to becoming infectious) is about 10 days in nearly everyone. A distribution with less spread is given in its place:

import numpy as np

def make_measles(latent):
    """ Measles with a latent period: S -> E -> I -> R """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
    onset     = E >> I @ latent
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    return ss.Disease(infection, onset, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

latents = {
    'Exponential':      ss.days(10),
    'Erlang, 4 stages': ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10)),
    'Fixed':            ss.constant(ss.days(10)),
}
sims = {label: ss.Sim(make_measles(latent), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0) for label, latent in latents.items()}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')
for label, sim in sims.items():
    I = sim.results.measles.I
    print(label, '- peak infectious:', round(I.max()), 'on day', np.argmax(I.values))








Exponential - peak infectious: 29215 on day 28
Erlang, 4 stages - peak infectious: 32506 on day 41
Fixed - peak infectious: 36718 on day 48


All three have the same mean, and so the same R0, but with an exponential latent period some people become infectious within days, which brings the epidemic forward. The more realistic the distribution, the later and higher the peak.
The distributions most used for durations are:








Distribution
Use
Example




Exponential
The ODE default; a constant rate of leaving
ss.days(10)


Erlang (a gamma distribution with a whole number of stages, k)
A duration with less spread: the standard deviation is the mean divided by √k
ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10))


Fixed
Everyone stays exactly this long, e.g. a reporting delay
ss.constant(ss.days(10))


Lognormal
A duration given by its mean and standard deviation, e.g. from a study
ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(2))



Any other distribution of durations works too; see Distributions. As agents, each person draws their own time in the state. As compartments, an Erlang distribution is run exactly, as k stages in a row; a fixed duration is run exactly too (as one compartment for each step people have been in the state); and any other distribution is run as Erlang stages with the same mean and standard deviation, with a note that says so. stages=k on a transition (ss.Transition(E, I, dur=ss.days(10), stages=4)) says how many stages to use, under every solver.

title: Diseases
text:
Branching
Some people go one way and some another: most people with measles recover, but a small share die. There are two ways to say this, and they differ in when the branch is decided.
Separate transitions with p= are decided when people enter the state, and each branch can have its own duration. Here 0.2% of people with measles die, and ss.null is outside the model:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8), p=0.998)
death     = ss.Transition(I, ss.null, dur=ss.days(8), p=0.002)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, death, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()
print('Deaths:', round(sim.results.measles.death.sum()))

Deaths: 199


One transition with several destinations, given as a list with p= for the share going to each, is decided when people leave. Its result is the total, and each destination has a result of its own, <transition>.<state>. Here the dead are kept as a state, D, so that they can be counted:

S, I, R, D = ss.states('S I R D')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
outcome   = ss.Transition(I, [R, D], p=[0.998, 0.002], dur=ss.days(8))
measles = ss.Disease(infection, outcome, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.measles
print('Deaths:', round(res['outcome.D'].sum()))
print('Dead at the end:', round(res.D[-1]))

Deaths: 199
Dead at the end: 199


The shares out of one state must add up to 1; one of them can be left as None, for the rest. A share can vary by age group or in time, like any other value (Parameters).

title: Diseases
text:
How the epidemic starts
Three options say who is in which state at the start, and everyone not placed elsewhere starts in the first state (S):

init_prev= is the share of people who start infected (the initial prevalence). They start in the state that an infection leads to: I in an SIR model, but E in an SEIR model, where nobody is then infectious at the start (a note says so). A number above 1 is a number of people.
init= is the share of people who start in each state, e.g. init=dict(I=0.001, R=0.9) for an outbreak in a population that is 90% immune.
init_n= is the number of people who start in each state, e.g. init_n=dict(I=10).

If nothing is given, a disease with transmission starts with 1% of people infected (init_prev=0.01), which describe() marks as a guess. Values can also be given by group, with ss.by(); see Stratification.

title: Diseases
section: Births and deaths in a disease
text:
Births and deaths in a disease
Births and deaths of everyone are usually given to the sim, as demographics=, so that the same people are born into and die from every disease (Demographics). With one disease, they can also be declared in it: ss.birth(S, rate=...) is a crude birth rate into S (a typed rate is per person; a bare number is per year, and above 1 per 1,000 people), and ss.death(rate=...) with no state is a death rate in every state, read the same way. A death from one state, ss.death(I, rate=...), is a rate like any other: a bare number is in the model’s unit.
New births are the supply of susceptible people that keeps measles endemic. Here is measles in a city of a million, starting from a population in which it has circulated before, so that only 7% of people are still susceptible. Since this model has values in both days and years, the unit of a bare number can’t be known, so β is given as ss.perday():

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8),
    births    = ss.birth(S, rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), # 20 births per 1,000 people per year
    deaths    = ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)),    # The same death rate, so the population is stable
    init      = dict(S=0.07, I=0.0001),             # The rest start in R, immune
)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=1_000_000, start='2000-01-01', stop='2020-01-01', dt=ss.days(1))
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.resample('month').plot()

Sim: measles, 1,000,000 people, as an ODE, 2000-01-01 to 2020-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.07 at the start, with 7% susceptible), with 100 infectious at the start
  Note: the initial value of S in "measles" is kept, and the other 929,900 people start in R, the only state not given one
  Done in 0.0095 s; measles: 377,978 infections; at most 1,136 infectious, on 2000-09-02









(The sim prints R0 = 15.2 and, since 93% start immune, R = 1.07 at the start; see The reproduction number.) Each epidemic uses up the susceptible people faster than births replace them, and then dies down until births have built them up again. So epidemics recur, here about every two years, and get smaller, towards a steady endemic level at which births balance infections. The period is close to the classical approximation 2π√(AD), with A ≈ 1/(μ(R0 − 1)) ≈ 3.6 years the mean age at infection (for a death rate μ of 0.02 per year) and D = 8 days the infectious period. In this deterministic model the epidemics damp out; Parameters over time shows how seasonal contacts keep them going. In a stochastic model the infection can also die out between epidemics in a small population; see Solvers.

title: Diseases
text:
States that are not people
Some of what a model tracks is not people: bacteria in water, or a population of mosquitoes. These are states too, declared with people=False. They are counts, not people: they are never agents, aren’t counted in the population, and are used in rates as counts (W.n). Here is a cholera model with bacteria shed into the water by infectious people (after Codeço, 2001):

beta = 0.5 # Rate of infection per day at a high concentration of bacteria
K    = 1e5 # Concentration of bacteria (cells/mL) that gives half that rate
xi   = 10  # Cells/mL shed per infectious person per day

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
W = ss.State(people=False) # Bacteria in the water: a count, not people
cholera = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ beta * W.n/(W.n + K),
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(5),
    shedding  = ss.null >> W @ xi*I.n,    # An inflow: the total per day
    decay     = W >> ss.null @ ss.days(30), # The mean lifetime in the water
    init      = dict(I=0.001),
)
sim = ss.Sim(cholera, total_pop=100_000, unit='day', stop=365, verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.diseases.cholera.plot('I', 'W') # The infectious, and the bacteria in the water








Since nobody catches cholera from a person here, the infection is spontaneous (its rate has no bare state), but it is still the acquisition of the disease: it is what a vaccine or a lower susceptibility acts on.
A count can weight each person: (ss.by(biting=[0.5, 1, 2])*I).n counts each infectious person by how much they are bitten (in a model stratified by biting), and I.n_trans by how infectious they are (their rel_trans, with any product or modifier on it), so a treatment that halves infectiousness also halves what the treated shed: shedding = ss.null >> W @ xi*I.n_trans. A weighted count works under every solver, worked out once a step in a compartmental run.

title: Diseases
text:
Susceptibility and infectiousness
A state can make the people in it less susceptible, or less infectious, than others, with rel_sus and rel_trans. For example, people vaccinated against measles (V) are 97% protected:

def make_measles(coverage):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    V = ss.State(rel_sus=0.03) # Vaccinated: 3% as susceptible as others
    infection = S + V >> I @ 1.9*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    return ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(V=coverage, I=0.0001), name='measles')

for coverage in [0.85, 0.90, 0.95]:
    sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(coverage), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    print('Coverage', coverage, '- infections in a year:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))

Coverage 0.85 - infections in a year: 23005
Coverage 0.9 - infections in a year: 14834
Coverage 0.95 - infections in a year: 3919


S + V >> I is one transition from either state. Even 95% coverage doesn’t stop the outbreak: with R0 ≈ 15, the share of people who must be immune to stop spread (the herd immunity threshold, 1 − 1/R0) is 93%, and 95% coverage with a vaccine that is 97% effective protects 92%.
Each person also has their own rel_sus and rel_trans, which interventions and connectors change: a vaccine lowers the rel_sus of those who get it (Products), and ss.modify(hiv.rel_sus, ...) can make one disease change the risk of another (Connectors). These act on the transitions that are an acquisition of the disease: every transmission, and any other transition out of the first state if the disease has no transmission (as for cholera above). To say otherwise, give acquisition=True or False to the transition; describe() lists which transitions it took as acquisitions.

title: Diseases
text:
Built-in SIR, SIS, and SEIR
ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR are declared diseases with named parameters: beta, dur_inf, init_prev, p_death (0 by default), and dur_exp for the SEIR. Their results are the same as any declared disease’s, a result for each state and transition, plus a prevalence that each declares as a ratio of its states (prevalence = I/(S + I + R) in the SIR, (E + I)/(S + E + I + R) in the SEIR):

sir = ss.SIR(beta=ss.perday(1.9), dur_inf=ss.days(8), init_prev=0.001)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()
print(sim.results.sir.keys())

['timevec', 'S', 'I', 'R', 'infection', 'recovery', 'death', 'prevalence']

title: Diseases
text:
Diseases as classes
A disease can also be a class, with its states, parameters, and transitions in the class body. This is the form for a disease that goes into a library, or that is made many times with different values. Its parameters can then be given when it is made:

class Measles(ss.Disease):
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    beta      = ss.par(ss.perday(1.9), bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate', source='Gives R0 of about 15')
    infection = S >> E @ beta*I
    onset     = E >> I @ ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10))
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)

measles = Measles(beta=1.5, init=dict(I=0.001)) # Named "measles", after the class
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.plot()








The starting values can also go in the class body (init = dict(I=0.001)), as defaults that init= given to the disease replaces. A count can start from the number of people, e.g. init = dict(W=10*N), with N = (S + I + R).n.
A class can also have methods, for behavior that isn’t a transition: override step(), and call super().step() to run the declared transitions (Custom modules).

Declaring in __init__()
A class body runs once, for the class, so it can’t hold a state or transition that only some versions of the model have. Such a model declares them in its __init__(), on self, with define_states(), define_transitions(), and define_results(). Each one is an attribute at once (self.R), and they are built together once the model is made:

class SIRS(ss.Disease):
    def __init__(self, waning=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(init=dict(I=0.001), **kwargs)
        beta = ss.par(ss.perday(0.3))
        self.define_states(ss.states('S I R'))
        self.define_transitions(
            infection = self.S >> self.I @ beta*self.I,
            recovery  = self.I >> self.R @ ss.days(10),
        )
        if waning is not None: # Immunity wanes only if asked for
            self.define_transitions(waning=self.R >> self.S @ waning)
        self.define_results(prevalence=self.I.frac) # A share of everyone in the model

for waning in [None, ss.days(90)]:
    sim = ss.Sim(SIRS(waning=waning), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    print('Waning:', waning, '- prevalence after a year:', round(sim.results.sirs.prevalence[-1], 4))

Waning: None - prevalence after a year: 0.0
Waning: days(90) - prevalence after a year: 0.0666


States and transitions can also be given as lists, or one at a time with name= (e.g. in a loop over strains); overwrite=True replaces one that was declared already, e.g. with its rate changed.

title: Diseases
text:
Strains
A disease can have several strains that share its states: a person has one course through the states, carrying one strain or several, and each strain has its own values, given as multipliers on the transitions and on rel_trans. ss.immunity() gives the protection between them, here against infection in people who have recovered:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
strains = ss.Strains(['wild', 'variant'], rel_trans=[1, 1.5], immunity=ss.immunity(due_to=R, rel_sus=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]))
flu = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ ss.peryear(8)*I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.years(0.1), waning=R >> S @ ss.years(1), init=dict(I=0.01), name='flu', strains=strains)
sim = ss.Sim(flu, total_pop=100_000, start=2000, stop=2005, verbose=0).run()
sim.results.flu.I.by('strain').plot();








With max_strains=2, people can carry two at once; ss.Strains lists the other options.

Strains with courses of their own
Some diseases don’t fit this, because each strain moves through the states on its own: someone can have CIN from one HPV genotype and be clearing another. Starsim tried one way of writing that, ss.strains.Family, in which the strains of one disease each followed their own course, with immunity between them, and with results over all of them. It was tested on HPVsim, its main use case, and it isn’t part of Starsim: the results were similar to HPVsim’s coded genotypes, but a declared genotype took about 2.5 ms a step against about 0.75 ms coded, which made the whole model about 1.5× slower, and it needed agents anyway once the strains protected each other.
If the strains can share one course, use ss.Strains as above. Otherwise, make each strain a disease of its own, and connect them with a connector. For protection that depends only on which states people are in, that is one ss.modify() for each strain:

def serotype(name):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    return ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ ss.perday(0.3)*I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(7), init=dict(I=0.001), name=name)

den1, den2 = serotype('den1'), serotype('den2')
cross = [ss.modify(den1.rel_sus, multiply=0.7, where=den2.R), ss.modify(den2.rel_sus, multiply=0.7, where=den1.R)]
sim = ss.Sim([den1, den2], connectors=cross, n_agents=5_000, unit='day', stop=200, verbose=0).run()
print(sim.results.den1.infection.sum(), sim.results.den2.infection.sum())

3650.0 3891.0


Each strain then has its own results (sim.results.den1), and a delivery can act on several (disease=[den1, den2]). ssl.Dengue is built this way. Anything more involved, such as a matrix of protection from each person’s antibody levels, is a connector written as code; this is how HPVsim’s cross_genotype.py works.

title: Diseases
text:
Diseases written as code
A disease that needs something states and transitions can’t say, such as a quantity that each person carries and that changes continuously (a CD4 count, a viral load, or an immunity level that wanes), is written as a Python class, with arrays for each person and methods that update them. It runs as agents, and can sit in the same sim as declared diseases. There are two base classes:

ss.Disease, for a disease with no transmission between people, such as a non-communicable disease.
ss.Infection, for a transmitted disease. It adds the states susceptible and infected, each agent’s relative susceptibility and infectiousness (rel_sus and rel_trans), and transmission over the sim’s networks with a beta for each, which is rarely worth writing again. ssl.AgentSIR and ssl.AgentSEIR (import starsim.library as ssl) are complete examples, and good bases for a disease of your own.

A disease written as code fills in some of these methods:



Method
What it does
When to override it




__init__()
Gives the parameters (define_pars()) and states (define_states())
Always


set_prognoses(uids, sources)
Sets what happens to the people just infected: when they recover, whether they die
Always, for an ss.Infection; call super().set_prognoses() first


step_state()
Moves people between states each step, before transmission (e.g. those whose recovery is due)
When the disease has states of its own


step_die(uids)
Clears the states of people who died
When the disease has states of its own


infect()
Transmission over the networks
Rarely: the built-in version handles the networks, beta, rel_sus, and rel_trans



In transmission, the chance that infection passes along a contact from an infectious person to a susceptible one is, in essence, β × rel_trans of the source × rel_sus of the target, where β is the transmission rate of that network. rel_sus and rel_trans are 1 by default, and are the levers that the rest of a model pulls: a vaccine lowers rel_sus, a treatment lowers rel_trans, and a connector between two diseases can raise one disease’s rel_sus in people infected with the other. Because they are ordinary arrays, they can also be set directly. Here everyone under 20 is fully protected (rel_sus = 0), and compared with no protection:

import starsim.library as ssl

for protect in [False, True]:
    sir = ssl.AgentSIR(beta=ss.perday(0.03), dur_inf=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(3)), p_death=0, init_prev=0.01)
    sim = ss.Sim(sir, networks='random', n_agents=2000, stop=ss.days(120), verbose=0)
    sim.init()
    sir = sim.diseases.agentsir # The sim's copy of the disease
    young = (sim.people.age < 20).uids
    older = (sim.people.age >= 20).uids
    if protect:
        sir.rel_sus[young] = 0.0 # Under-20s can't be infected
    sim.run()
    ever_infected = sir.ti_infected.notnan
    print('Under-20s protected:', protect)
    print('  Ever infected, under 20:', ever_infected[young].sum(), 'of', len(young))
    print('  Ever infected, 20 and over:', ever_infected[older].sum(), 'of', len(older))

Under-20s protected: False
  Ever infected, under 20: 632 of 676
  Ever infected, 20 and over: 1241 of 1324
Under-20s protected: True
  Ever infected, under 20: 7 of 676
  Ever infected, 20 and over: 1031 of 1324


The few under-20s infected even when protected were infected at the start (init_prev). Protecting them also protects older people, a little under a third of whom now escape infection, since there are fewer people to pass it on. In a model with a vaccine, the same protection would come from a product, and between diseases from a connector, rather than by setting rel_sus by hand.
Infected and infectious are different things once a disease has a latent period. In ssl.AgentSEIR, people in E and I are both infected (and count towards prevalence), but only those in I are infectious; infectious drives transmission, and infected is worked out from the two. A disease whose latent people transmit too would give the exposed a rel_trans above 0 instead.
The parts of a module written as code (its parameters, states, results, and the order in which Starsim calls its methods) are covered in Custom modules, and A1 – Diseases builds a disease among agents step by step.

title: Diseases
text:
Pitfalls

A bare number after @ is a rate. I >> R @ 8 is a rate of 8 per day, not 8 days; write ss.days(8).
A rate with no state in it is not transmission. S >> I @ 0.2 infects everyone in S at 0.2 per day whether or not anyone is infectious. Transmission names its source: S >> I @ beta*I.
init_prev in an SEIR model starts people in E. To start some people infectious, give init=dict(I=...).

title: Diseases
text:
Further reading

Appropriate models for the management of infectious diseases: how exponential and less variable (Erlang) durations change the course and control of an epidemic
Endemic and epidemic dynamics of cholera: the role of the aquatic reservoir: the cholera model with bacteria in the water used above
Compartmental models in epidemiology: SIR, SEIR, SIS, and models with births and deaths
EpiModel: compartmental and network disease models in R
Epicookbook: the same textbook models written in several languages

title: Distributions
text:
🧠25% 🤖75%
Distributions appear in a model in three ways: as the distribution of a duration (how long people stay in a state, or the delay before an event is reported), as variation between people (each person’s own value of a parameter), and, in modules written as code, as the random draws that decide what happens to each person (who is infected, who tests positive). This page covers the distributions Starsim has, how to choose one for a duration, and how to use them in each of these ways.
Uncertainty about a single value, such as a parameter being fitted, is not variation between people; it is a prior, given with ss.par(..., prior=...) and used only in calibration.

title: Distributions
text:
Distributions of durations
A duration given as a single value, such as I >> R @ ss.days(8), is the mean of an exponential distribution, as in an ODE model. The shape of the distribution matters: with the same mean, it changes when an epidemic peaks and how fast it grows (Durations). These are the distributions most used for durations, each with a mean of 10 days:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

durations = {
    'Exponential':       ss.expon(scale=ss.days(10)),
    'Erlang, 4 stages':  ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10)),
    'Lognormal, std 2':  ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(2)),
}
plt.figure()
for label, dist in durations.items():
    draws = dist.rvs(10_000) # In days, the unit it was given in
    print(label, '- share under 4 days:', np.mean(draws < 4).round(2))
    plt.hist(draws, bins=np.arange(0, 40), histtype='step', lw=2, label=label)
plt.xlabel('Days')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/
Exponential - share under 4 days: 0.33
Erlang, 4 stages - share under 4 days: 0.08
Lognormal, std 2 - share under 4 days: 0.0









With an exponential distribution, a third of people leave within 4 days, and a few stay for a month or more. An Erlang distribution with k stages (a gamma distribution with a whole-number shape) has less spread, a standard deviation of the mean divided by √k, and a lognormal is given by its mean and standard deviation directly, as a study would report them. A fixed duration, ss.constant(ss.days(10)), has no spread at all.
In a model, a distribution of durations goes after @, or as dur=:
onset    = E >> I @ ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10))
recovery = I >> R @ ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(8), std=ss.days(2))
recovery = I >> R @ ss.lognorm_ex(mean=8, std=2, unit='days') # The same: the unit given once
A distribution’s unit is given on its parameters, as typed durations, or once with unit=, which applies to every parameter of it that is a time. As agents, each person draws their own duration when they enter the state. As compartments, there are no individuals to draw for, so an Erlang distribution is run exactly as k compartments in a row (stages), a fixed duration as one compartment for each step people have been in the state, and any other distribution as Erlang stages with the same mean and standard deviation, with a note that says how many.

title: Distributions
text:
Variation between people
A distribution given as a parameter’s value gives each person their own value of it. A distribution of durations is one example; a share (p=), or the rate of a transition, can vary between people too. A model whose parameters vary between people, other than durations, needs individuals to hold their values, so it runs as agents.
A value that differs by group, rather than at random between people, is better given with ss.by() (Parameters): it is the same for everyone in a group, and runs under every solver.

title: Distributions
text:
A fixed number of people
Some things are a number of people, not a share: to start an outbreak with exactly 5 infectious people, give a number (init_n=dict(I=5), or init_prev=5, since above 1 it is a number of people):

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=5)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.init()
print('Infectious at the start:', sim.diseases.measles.I.sum())

Infectious at the start: 5


ss.choose_n() can be used wherever a Bernoulli distribution can: filter() gives the people chosen, split() both those chosen and the rest, and rvs() a true-or-false value for each person. It can weight people (weights=, a value or a function of the people), so that some are more likely to be chosen. Unlike choosing at random from a list, it picks mostly the same people in two sims that differ slightly, which keeps comparisons between scenarios precise (Random numbers). Here the same choice of 5 people out of 20, made with and without person 3 (one of those chosen), picks the same people apart from person 3, who is replaced by one other; and a choice weighted by age picks older people:

sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=20, verbose=0).init()
uids = sim.people.auids

choose_a = ss.choose_n(5, name='Choose 5').init(sim=sim) # Two identical distributions, as if in two sims
choose_b = ss.choose_n(5, name='Choose 5').init(sim=sim)
print('Chosen from everyone:', choose_a.filter(uids))
print('Chosen without person 3:', choose_b.filter(uids.remove(3)))

by_age = ss.choose_n(5, weights=lambda self, sim, uids: sim.people.age[uids], name='Choose by age').init(sim=sim)
chosen, not_chosen = by_age.split(uids)
print('Mean age of those chosen:', sim.people.age[chosen].mean().round(1))
print('Mean age of the rest:', sim.people.age[not_chosen].mean().round(1))

Chosen from everyone: [ 3  4  5 12 15]
Chosen without person 3: [ 4  5 11 12 15]
Mean age of those chosen: 57.3
Mean age of the rest: 30.2

title: Distributions
text:
Working with a distribution
A distribution can be made, drawn from, and looked at on its own. Outside a sim, one with a unit draws in that unit, here days, and shows what it was made from:

dist = ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(5), std=ss.days(2))
print(dist)
print(dist.rvs(5)) # Five draws, in days
print('Mean:', dist.dist.mean())
print('95% of draws are between', dist.dist.ppf([0.025, 0.975]).round(2))
draws = dist.plot_hist(n=1000, bins=30) # Returns the draws

ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(5), std=ss.days(2))
[2.23074401 4.8888378  7.10934066 4.58126451 5.30768619]
Mean: 5.0
95% of draws are between [2.18 9.88]









In a sim, the same distribution draws in steps of its module instead, and from the sim’s random numbers (Random numbers). One with no unit, such as ss.normal(0, 1), draws outside a sim when made with strict=False, which says it need not use the sim’s random numbers.
dist.dist is the SciPy distribution with its parameters, for its mean, quantiles (ppf), density, and so on.
A distribution can round what it draws, which matters for numbers that must be whole, such as a duration in steps: round=True rounds each value up or down at random in proportion to how close it is (so the mean is kept), and round='nearest' rounds to the nearest whole number. Either can be given when the distribution is made, or when drawing. Here a duration of about 5 days, in a sim with steps of a day, drawn for 10 people three ways (reset=True uses the same random numbers each time):

sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=10, dt=ss.days(1), start='2025-01-01', dur=ss.days(30), verbose=0).init()
dur = ss.lognorm_ex(ss.days(5), ss.days(2), round='nearest', name='Rounded duration')
dur.init(sim=sim)

print('Not rounded:', dur.rvs(sim.people.uid, round=False, reset=True).round(2))
print('Nearest:    ', dur.rvs(sim.people.uid, reset=True)) # As set when it was made
print('At random:  ', dur.rvs(sim.people.uid, round=True, reset=True))

Not rounded: [ 5.54  4.27  6.27 12.1   6.    6.62  6.16  4.88  4.33  3.39]
Nearest:     [ 6  4  6 12  6  7  6  5  4  3]
At random:   [ 5  4  7 12  6  6  6  5  5  4]


The parameters of a distribution that is already made, such as the default of a library module, can be changed with set(): ssl.Measles().pars.p_death.set(p=0.05) (see Library: diseases).

title: Distributions
section: Distributions in modules written as code
text:
Distributions in modules written as code
In a module written as code, a distribution is made once, as a parameter (in define_pars()) or an attribute (in __init__()), and drawn from at each step for the people it is about:

dist.rvs(uids) gives one value for each of the people given (by their IDs, or a true-or-false array over people).
For a Bernoulli distribution, dist.filter(uids) gives the people for whom it came out true, and dist.split(uids) both those and the rest.

Drawing for people, rather than a number of values, is what lets each person keep their own random numbers across scenarios, so that two sims differ only where their scenarios do (Random numbers). Making a distribution at every step instead of once breaks this.
A distribution’s parameters can be functions, of the module, the sim, and the people (fn(self, sim, uids)), worked out each time it is drawn from, for the people it is drawn for. The function returns one value for each person (or a single value for all of them), and can use anything the sim knows: their ages, their states, the time.
Here an intervention written as code vaccinates susceptible people against measles on the first day, each with probability p_vx, a Bernoulli distribution made once, as a parameter. A perfect vaccine is given by moving those vaccinated from S to R (a change by UID to a state of a declared disease, which its counts see). The probability can be a single value, or a function of the people: here, 90% of children under 15 and 10% of adults, against 30% of everyone. Measles spreads mostly among school-age children (10 contacts a day in school, 2 in the community), so the two campaigns use about the same number of doses, but with very different effects:

class Campaign(ss.Intervention):
    """ Vaccinate susceptible people against measles on one day, each with probability p_vx (a perfect vaccine) """
    def __init__(self, p_vx=0.3, day=1, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_pars(p_vx=ss.bernoulli(p=p_vx), day=day) # The distribution is made once, here
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(ss.Result('n_vaccinated', dtype=int, label='Vaccinated'))
        return

    def step(self):
        if self.ti == self.pars.day:
            measles = self.sim.diseases.measles
            vaccinated = self.pars.p_vx.filter(measles.S.uids) # Draw for the susceptible people only
            measles.S[vaccinated] = False
            measles.R[vaccinated] = True
            self.results.n_vaccinated[self.ti] = len(vaccinated)
        return

def p_by_age(self, sim, uids):
    """ 90% for children under 15, 10% for everyone else """
    return np.where(sim.people.age[uids] < 15, 0.9, 0.1)

def make_sim(campaign=None):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    measles = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 0.04*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init_prev=0.01, name='measles')
    school = ss.RandomNet(name='school', n_contacts=10, age_range=[5, 15])
    community = ss.RandomNet(name='community', n_contacts=2)
    return ss.Sim(measles, networks=[school, community], interventions=campaign, n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(200))

scenarios = {
    'No vaccination': make_sim(),
    '30% of everyone': make_sim(Campaign(p_vx=0.3)),
    '90% of children, 10% of adults': make_sim(Campaign(p_vx=p_by_age)),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, parallel=False)
for label, sim in zip(scenarios, msim.sims):
    doses = sim.results.campaign.n_vaccinated.sum() if 'campaign' in sim.results else 0
    print(label, '- doses:', int(doses), '- largest number infectious:', int(sim.results.measles.I.max()))
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (No vaccination, 30% of everyone, 90% of children, 10% of adults)
  Done in 3.4 s


No vaccination - doses: 0 - largest number infectious: 379
30% of everyone - doses: 1506 - largest number infectious: 167
90% of children, 10% of adults - doses: 1452 - largest number infectious: 50









With the same number of doses, vaccinating the children who carry most of the transmission stops the outbreak, while spreading the doses over everyone only slows it. In a module, init() is done for each of its distributions when the sim is initialized; a distribution used on its own, outside a module, needs dist.init(sim=sim) first, as in the examples above. See Custom modules for whole modules, and Interventions for vaccination as it is usually given, with ss.vaccinate(), which works under every solver.

title: Distributions
text:
Pitfalls

A distribution as a value or as a prior. A distribution as a parameter’s value is variation between people; uncertainty about one value is a prior.
The exponential default. A single duration is exponential, with a lot of spread. For a latent or infectious period, an Erlang or lognormal distribution is usually closer to the data.
A unit given twice, or not at all. Give a distribution’s unit on its parameters or with unit=; a bare number takes the model’s unit.
Making distributions at every step in a module written as code, which breaks common random numbers. Make them once.

title: Distributions
text:
Further reading

SciPy: statistical functions: the distributions that Starsim’s are built on, with their parameters
NumPy: random generator: how random numbers are drawn from them
Stan functions reference: positive continuous distributions: the lognormal, gamma, Weibull, and others, with their parameterizations

title: Population data
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
A model of a particular setting needs data about its people: how many there are and of what ages, how fast they are born and die, and who has contact with whom. Starsim has these for every country, by name, and takes data of your own in the same forms. This page covers the data that comes with Starsim, contact matrices (by age and by other groups, under compartments and agents), and using data of your own.
These data describe a setting; they don’t set the disease’s parameters, and a model that uses them still needs checking against data on the disease itself (see Fitting a model). Networks of individual contacts are on Contact networks, places and the movement between them on Geography, and the tutorial T4 – Age groups and contacts uses a contact matrix for measles.

title: Population data
text:
Data by place
Starsim has data for each country, from the package starsim_data: populations by age and sex, birth and death rates, contact matrices, and administrative units (counties, provinces, and states). What is small and common (the contact matrices of 177 countries, populations, and the first two administrative levels of every country) is bundled with it; the rest is downloaded on first use. The model objects that use a place take its name, and ss.data gives the data itself, for looking at or using elsewhere:








What
In a model
The data itself




Population by age and sex (UN World Population Prospects)
ss.people('Kenya')
ss.data.population('Kenya'), ss.data.age('Kenya')


Contact matrix by 5-year age group (Prem et al. 2021)
ss.contacts('Kenya')
ss.data.contacts('Kenya')


Birth and death rates by year (and by age and sex, for deaths)
ss.Births(birth_rate='Kenya'), ss.Deaths(death_rate='Kenya')
ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'births'), ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'deaths')


Administrative units, with their populations and positions
ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)
ss.data.geography('Kenya', level=1)



A named population gives the sim its size (total_pop) and the share of people in each age group, so a model stratified by age needs no shares of its own; as agents, it gives the agents their ages and sex (see People and agents). Birth and death rates are on Demographics, and administrative units on Geography.
ss.people() and ss.contacts() take a year and a source: ss.people('Kenya', year=2030) (from 1950 to 2100, with the years between the UN’s decadal values interpolated), and ss.contacts('Kenya', source='mistry2021') for the matrices of Mistry et al. (2021), by single year of age, for 36 countries. A US state is named with its country, ss.people('United States:Massachusetts') and ss.contacts('United States:Massachusetts'), from the US Census and Mistry et al. The data is given as tables (dataframes), with the age groups labeled as a stratification by age labels them ('0-4', '5-9', …, '100+') and where the data came from in .attrs['ref']:

import starsim as ss

births = ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'births') # Crude birth rates per 1,000 people, by year
print(births.head())

pop = ss.data.population('Kenya', year=2024) # Women and men by 5-year age group
print(pop.head())
print('Population of Kenya in 2024:', round(pop.values.sum()))
print('Source:', pop.attrs['ref']['study'])

   Time        CBR
0  1950  49.337002
1  1960  55.183998
2  1970  52.540001
3  1980  48.210999
4  1990  43.930000
          female       male
age                        
0-4    3586313.4  3638635.6
