title: Results
text:
Pitfalls

The flow at a time point is the step that ends there. The peak in infections dated 10 March is the infections during 9 March, with daily steps.
A ratio is not a mean over groups. Use res.prevalence.select(age='65+'), not the mean of the prevalence in each group.
Agents’ results are scaled. With each agent standing for several people, counts are multiplied by that number when the run ends; a count read in the middle of a run is in agents (see Branching and rescaling).

pandas: time series and date functionality: resampling and dates, as to_series() gives them

title: Fitting methods
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
sim.fit() chooses a method that suits the model, so most fits don’t need to name one. This page is for choosing one yourself: what each method gives, what it needs, and what its settings are. Fitting a model covers the data, the parameters, and the goodness of fit, which are the same for every method.

title: Fitting methods
text:
Choosing a method











Method
Gives
The model
Likelihood needed?
Use it when
Avoid it when

Best fit

No

There are many parameters, where it gets slow


'l-bfgs-b'
Best fit
ODE with gradients; default for three or more parameters
No
Many parameters of a deterministic model
The model is stochastic


'optuna'
Best fit
Any; default for stochastic models and agents
No
Runs are noisy, or there is no better option
You need a posterior, or a precise optimum (follow it with 'nelder-mead')


'if2'
Maximum-likelihood best fit
Stochastic compartmental
Yes
You want the maximum likelihood of a stochastic model, whose noise makes a local search unreliable
A parameter has several values (by group, or a time series), or you need a posterior


'nuts'
Posterior
ODE with gradients
Yes
You need a posterior of a deterministic model; it’s the most efficient sampler here
The model is stochastic or has no gradients


'pmcmc'
Posterior
Stochastic compartmental
Yes
You need a posterior of a stochastic model, with its process noise counted
The model runs as agents, or is deterministic (use 'nuts')


'abc-smc'
Approximate posterior
Any, including agents
No
You need a posterior but have no likelihood, or the model runs as agents
A likelihood-based posterior is possible, which is usually sharper



A “stochastic compartmental” model has solver='binomial', 'gillespie', or 'tau', and is one that the kernels run from start to finish, which sim.kernel_only() checks. If it doesn’t, 'if2' and 'pmcmc' raise an error that gives the reason.
Two more methods of scipy.optimize.minimize can also be named: 'powell' (no gradients) and 'slsqp' (gradients, when the sim has them). A list runs methods in turn: see below.
A setting that the method doesn’t take is an error, so a mistyped name can’t be ignored by accident.

title: Fitting methods
text:
The model
Every example fits the transmission rate of the same SIR model, with half of infections reported, to weekly cases drawn from a run with beta=0.5. The likelihood says how the reported cases vary around what the model gives, here Poisson.

import starsim as ss

beta = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.1, 1])
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
cases = ss.outcome(0.5*infection)
sir = ss.Disease(infection, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.01), name='sir')

pars = dict(total_pop=10_000, unit='day', stop=60)
data = ss.Sim(sir, pars=dict(beta=0.5), solver='binomial', rand_seed=2, **pars).run().to_data('cases', resample='week')

deterministic = ss.Sim(sir, data=data, verbose=0, **pars)
stochastic = ss.Sim(sir, data=data, solver='binomial', verbose=0, **pars)
likelihood = dict(cases=ss.poisson())

Sim: sir, 10,000 people, as a stochastic compartmental model (chain binomial), days 0 to 60
  sir: R0 = 4, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0078 s; sir: 9,709 infections; at most 4,114 infectious, on day 16

title: Fitting methods
text:
Best fits

SciPy: 'nelder-mead', 'l-bfgs-b', and others
These search from the best few points of a scan over the bounds. The gradient-based methods take their gradients from JAX (see Gradients). The fit has converged if the two best searches end at the same value.








Setting
Default
Meaning




scan
10 per parameter, at most 100
The number of points tried over the bounds


restarts
3 (1 for one parameter of a deterministic model)
The number of searches, each from one of the best points that are apart


Others
SciPy’s
The method’s own options, e.g. maxiter=500; see scipy.optimize.show_options()




fit = deterministic.fit(method='nelder-mead', scan=5, restarts=2, maxiter=200, verbose=False)
fit.pars

sc.obj(beta=0.489589109536295)




Optuna: 'optuna'
Optuna learns where to look from the scores so far, which suits noisy scores: each trial takes fresh random seeds, so the search averages over chance.








Setting
Default
Meaning




n_trials
100
The number of sets of values to try


n_workers
1
The number of processes running trials at once


storage
None
A file or database URL that keeps the trials, so a fit that stopped can be resumed


Others
Optuna’s
The keywords of study.optimize(), e.g. timeout=600




fit = stochastic.fit(method='optuna', n_trials=50, verbose=False)
fit.pars

sc.obj(beta=0.5053382226999229)




Iterated filtering: 'if2'
Iterated filtering (IF2; Ionides et al. 2015) finds maximum-likelihood values of a stochastic model. It runs a particle filter many times. Each particle has its own parameter values, which take a small random step at each data point, and particles that fit the data well are kept along with their values. The steps shrink from one pass of the filter to the next, so the particles settle on the best values. It’s the method of the pomp package for R.
Each of several chains starts from its own point, and the fit has converged if they end within 2 of each other in log-likelihood. If they don’t, try more passes or more particles, as the message says.








Setting
Default
Meaning




particles
1000
The number of particles in each pass; more gives a less noisy likelihood


iterations
50
The number of passes of the filter in each chain


chains
4
The number of chains, each from its own start


sd
0.05
The first size of a random step, on the scale searched on (the logit of a value’s place between its bounds, of its log for wide bounds)


cooling
0.5
The share of the first step size that is left after 50 passes (pomp’s cooling.fraction.50)




fit = stochastic.fit(method='if2', likelihood=likelihood, particles=100, iterations=25, verbose=False)

Posteriors
A posterior uses each parameter’s prior= if it has one, and otherwise a uniform prior over its bounds. Its draws are in fit.samples, and fit.table adds the median, the 95% interval, and for chains R-hat and the effective sample size. Fit diagnostics covers how to read them. The examples below take few draws so that this page runs quickly, so they can report that they have not converged; a real fit should use the defaults or more.

title: Fitting methods
text:
Several methods in turn
With a list, each method starts from the best values of the one before, and the list stops at a method that doesn’t converge. A broad search followed by a local one is the usual pairing. A setting goes to the stages that take it, and an entry can be a dict to give one stage its own settings:

fit.pars

title: Gallery
text:
Library modules
Starsim also comes with a library of example modules, written as code, which are illustrative rather than validated: their parameter values are indicative, and some are placeholders. Use them as starting points to copy and adapt. They are imported with import starsim.library as ssl:

Diseases (ssl.diseases): HIV with CD4 counts (with ssl.diseases.ART for treatment), cholera with an environmental reservoir, Ebola with transmission from unburied bodies, measles as an SEIR, and a non-communicable disease.
Networks (ssl.networks): households from survey data, people who move in space and connect to those nearby (DiskNet), and theoretical networks such as Erdős–Rényi.
Maternal, newborn, and child health (ssl.mnch): fetal health, neonatal sepsis, and congenital disease.

Library modules in the user guide describes them, and how to use them.

title: Gallery
text:
Scripts in the repository
A few longer examples are kept as scripts in the docs/examples folder of the repository, to read and adapt:

An embedding network (networks/embedding.py): pairs people by their closeness in a continuous space of traits.
One model in several languages (translations/): the same simple SIS model written in plain Python, Numba, JAX, Julia, and Rust, next to the Starsim version, for comparing their speed.
LASER (laser/): a LASER example and its Starsim equivalents, with scripts to time them.

title: Starsim v3.0 to v3.1 migration guide
text:
This guide describes the breaking changes introduced in Starsim v3.1.0 and the steps required to migrate code from Starsim v3.0.x. It was mostly written by an LLM, and is mostly written for other LLMs.
Most of the changes are in the Pregnancy module and maternal networks. If your code does not use ss.Pregnancy, ss.MaternalNet, ss.PrenatalNet, or ss.PostnatalNet, you may only need to check the general changes in sections 1-3.
Note: If you are an LLM reading this, perform each of the following migrations one at a time and confirm with the user after each step.





Previously, people.sir returned a proxy object that exposed only module states (e.g. people.sir.infected). Now it returns a direct reference to the module itself, so all attributes – including dynamically computed @property values – are accessible.
What to change: In most cases, no change is needed – people.sir.infected still works. However, if your code relied on people.sir being a state-only namespace, be aware that it is now the full module object.
# v3.0 -- worked for states, but not for properties
people.sir.infected      # OK
people.sir.infectious    # AttributeError

# v3.1 -- both work
people.sir.infected      # OK (state)
people.sir.infectious    # OK (property)



These boolean attributes have been removed. Type checking is used instead.
What to change: Replace attribute checks with isinstance() checks.
# v3.0
for nw in sim.networks.values():
    if nw.prenatal:
        ...
    if nw.postnatal:
        ...

# v3.1
for nw in sim.networks.values():
    if isinstance(nw, ss.PrenatalNet):
        ...
    if isinstance(nw, ss.PostnatalNet):
        ...



The arguments mother_inds and unborn_inds have been renamed to mother_uids and unborn_uids. The dur, start, and end arguments have been removed – edge lifespans are now managed by the Pregnancy module.
What to change: Update argument names and remove dur/start/end arguments.
# v3.0
net.add_pairs(mother_inds=mothers, unborn_inds=babies, dur=dur_preg, start=ti)

# v3.1
net.add_pairs(mother_uids=mothers, unborn_uids=babies)



PostnatalNet is no longer a subclass of MaternalNet. It is now a DynamicNetwork that accepts an optional dur parameter for the postnatal period. Its add_pairs() method now takes mother_uids and infant_uids (not unborn_uids).
What to change: Update how you construct and interact with PostnatalNet.
# v3.0
postnatal = ss.PostnatalNet()
# Pairs were added by Pregnancy with dur/start/end

# v3.1
postnatal = ss.PostnatalNet(dur=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(0.5), std=ss.years(0.5)))
# Pairs are automatically added at delivery by Pregnancy



A new ss.BreastfeedingNet is available for modeling breastfeeding transmission. It automatically tracks breastfeeding status from the Pregnancy module. This is additive – no migration is required – but if you were previously using PostnatalNet to model breastfeeding transmission, consider switching.
# v3.1
sim = ss.Sim(
    demographics=ss.Pregnancy(),
    networks=[ss.PrenatalNet(), ss.BreastfeedingNet()],
    diseases=ss.SIR(),
)






Previously fecund was a BoolState that was manually set to True/False. It is now a read-only @property that dynamically computes fecundity based on age and sex.
What to change: Remove any code that sets fecund directly.
# v3.0
pregnancy.fecund[uids] = False  # Manually mark as infecund
pregnancy.fecund[uids] = True   # Manually mark as fecund

# v3.1
# fecund is now read-only, computed from age, sex, and min_age/max_age
# Use pregnancy.infertile to mark agents as unable to conceive
pregnancy.infertile[uids] = True



The postpartum BoolState and associated dur_postpartum / ti_postpartum states have been removed. Breastfeeding is now tracked separately.
What to change: Replace postpartum references with breastfeeding or use PostnatalNet with a dur parameter.
# v3.0
pregnancy.postpartum         # BoolState
pregnancy.dur_postpartum     # FloatArr
pregnancy.ti_postpartum      # FloatArr

# v3.1
pregnancy.breastfeeding      # BoolState (mothers currently breastfeeding)
pregnancy.dur_breastfeed     # FloatArr (duration of breastfeeding)
pregnancy.ti_stop_breastfeed # FloatArr (time breastfeeding stops)
pregnancy.breastfed          # BoolState (newborns who were breastfed)



The child_uid FloatArr has been removed. Unborn children are now found dynamically via people.parent.
What to change: Use pregnancy.find_unborn_children(parent_uids) instead.
# v3.0
child = pregnancy.child_uid[mother_uid]

# v3.1
children = pregnancy.find_unborn_children(mother_uids)



The method and associated distribution have been renamed.
What to change: Rename method calls and references.
# v3.0
p = pregnancy.make_p_fertility(eligible_uids)
pregnancy.pars.p_fertility  # Bernoulli distribution

# v3.1
p = pregnancy.make_p_conceive(eligible_uids)
pregnancy._p_conceive  # Bernoulli distribution (now private)



The semantics have been inverted and the name clarified. Despite its name, p_neonatal_death in v3.0 was only applied when a mother dies during pregnancy – it was the probability that the neonate also dies conditional on maternal death. It was never a general neonatal mortality parameter.
In v3.1, p_survive_maternal_death makes this conditional relationship explicit: it is the probability that an unborn child survives the mother’s death (default 0, meaning unborn children do not survive maternal death).
Note: Neither v3.0 nor v3.1 includes a built-in parameter for general neonatal mortality (e.g. from prematurity or birth complications). To model that, override the process_newborns() hook in a Pregnancy subclass.
What to change: Rename the parameter and invert the probability value.
# v3.0
pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(p_neonatal_death=ss.bernoulli(0.8))  # 80% chance neonate dies given maternal death

# v3.1
pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(p_survive_maternal_death=ss.bernoulli(0.2))  # 20% chance unborn survives maternal death



Previously, dur_pregnancy was a fixed value (default ss.years(0.75)). It is now an ss.choice distribution that draws from gestational weeks 32-42, and duration is assigned per-agent.
What to change: If you were relying on a fixed pregnancy duration or accessing self.pars.dur_pregnancy.years, update accordingly.
# v3.0
pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(dur_pregnancy=ss.years(0.75))
# Internally: self.pars.dur_pregnancy.years was a single float

# v3.1
# Default draws from weeks 32-42; to override with a fixed duration:
pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(dur_pregnancy=ss.choice(a=ss.weeks(np.arange(38, 43))))
# Per-agent durations are stored in: pregnancy.dur_pregnancy[uids]  (a FloatArr)



The set_prognoses() method has been removed. Its functionality is now split across make_pregnancies(), process_delivery(), and set_breastfeeding().
What to change: If you had a subclass that overrode set_prognoses(), move the logic to the appropriate new method.
# v3.0
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def set_prognoses(self, uids):
        super().set_prognoses(uids)
        # Custom logic for new pregnancies

# v3.1
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def make_pregnancies(self, uids):
        embryo_counts = super().make_pregnancies(uids)
        # Custom logic for new pregnancies
        return embryo_counts



The step() method no longer delegates to do_step() and update_states(). The burn-in logic has also been moved from step() to init_post(). The new step() calls a sequence of smaller, overridable methods.
What to change: If you had a subclass that overrode do_step() or update_states(), restructure to override the new methods.
# v3.0 step flow
step() -> do_step() -> update_states() + make_pregnancies() + make_embryos()

# v3.1 step flow
init_post()           # Burn-in happens here now
step():
    updates_pre()           # Set base states, check breastfeeding
    progress_pregnancies()  # Advance gestational clock
    process_delivery()      # Handle births
    set_rel_sus()           # Update susceptibility
    select_conceivers()     # Find who conceives
    make_pregnancies()      # Set pregnancy states
    make_embryos()          # Create embryo agents
    update_maternal_deaths()# Handle maternal deaths
Use the _post_delivery() hook for custom post-delivery logic:
# v3.1
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def _post_delivery(self, mother_uids, newborn_uids):
        # Custom post-delivery logic here
        pass



make_embryos() now returns a tuple (conceive_uids_with_repeats, new_uids) instead of just new_uids. The first element accounts for multiple embryos per pregnancy (e.g. twins).
What to change: Update any code that captures the return value.
# v3.0
new_uids = pregnancy.make_embryos(conceive_uids)

# v3.1
conceive_uids_with_repeats, new_uids = pregnancy.make_embryos(conceive_uids, embryo_counts)



The old make_pregnancies() both selected who conceives and set prognoses. These are now separate: select_conceivers() returns UIDs of women who will conceive, and make_pregnancies() sets pregnancy states and durations for those UIDs.
What to change: If you overrode make_pregnancies() in a subclass, split the logic.
# v3.0
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def make_pregnancies(self):
        # Custom selection + prognosis logic

# v3.1
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def select_conceivers(self, uids=None):
        # Custom selection logic
        return conceive_uids

    def make_pregnancies(self, uids):
        # Custom prognosis logic
        embryo_counts = super().make_pregnancies(uids)
        return embryo_counts

Parameter
Default
Description




p_infertile
ss.bernoulli(p=0)
Primary infertility probability


dur_breastfeed
ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(0.75), std=ss.years(0.5))
Breastfeeding duration


p_breastfeed
ss.bernoulli(p=1)
Probability of breastfeeding


embryos_per_pregnancy
ss.choice(a=[1,2], p=[1.0, 0.0])
Number of embryos (twins support)


rr_ptb
ss.normal(loc=1, scale=0.1)
Baseline relative risk of pre-term birth


rr_ptb_age
Age-dependent array
Relative risk of pre-term birth by age


p_survive_maternal_death
ss.bernoulli(0)
Probability unborn survives mother’s death


trimesters
[ss.weeks(13), ss.weeks(26)]
Trimester boundaries






The following results are now available. No migration is required.



Result
Description




maternal_deaths
Number of maternal deaths per timestep


mmr
Maternal mortality rate (per 100,000 births)


tfr
Total fertility rate


n_fecund
Number of fecund women


n_fertile
Number of fertile women


n_susceptible
Number of susceptible (non-pregnant fertile) women



Age-specific fertility rates are available via pregnancy.asfr (a 2D array, not a standard Result).

title: Starsim v3.0 to v3.1 migration guide
text:
This guide describes the breaking changes introduced in Starsim v3.1.0 and the steps required to migrate code from Starsim v3.0.x. It was mostly written by an LLM, and is mostly written for other LLMs.
Most of the changes are in the Pregnancy module and maternal networks. If your code does not use ss.Pregnancy, ss.MaternalNet, ss.PrenatalNet, or ss.PostnatalNet, you may only need to check the general changes in sections 1-3.
Note: If you are an LLM reading this, perform each of the following migrations one at a time and confirm with the user after each step.

title: Starsim v3.0 to v3.1 migration guide
text:
Previously, people.sir returned a proxy object that exposed only module states (e.g. people.sir.infected). Now it returns a direct reference to the module itself, so all attributes – including dynamically computed @property values – are accessible.
What to change: In most cases, no change is needed – people.sir.infected still works. However, if your code relied on people.sir being a state-only namespace, be aware that it is now the full module object.
# v3.0 -- worked for states, but not for properties
people.sir.infected      # OK
people.sir.infectious    # AttributeError

# v3.1 -- both work
people.sir.infected      # OK (state)
people.sir.infectious    # OK (property)



These boolean attributes have been removed. Type checking is used instead.
What to change: Replace attribute checks with isinstance() checks.
# v3.0
for nw in sim.networks.values():
    if nw.prenatal:
        ...
    if nw.postnatal:
        ...

# v3.1
for nw in sim.networks.values():
    if isinstance(nw, ss.PrenatalNet):
        ...
    if isinstance(nw, ss.PostnatalNet):
        ...



The arguments mother_inds and unborn_inds have been renamed to mother_uids and unborn_uids. The dur, start, and end arguments have been removed – edge lifespans are now managed by the Pregnancy module.
What to change: Update argument names and remove dur/start/end arguments.
# v3.0
net.add_pairs(mother_inds=mothers, unborn_inds=babies, dur=dur_preg, start=ti)

# v3.1
net.add_pairs(mother_uids=mothers, unborn_uids=babies)



PostnatalNet is no longer a subclass of MaternalNet. It is now a DynamicNetwork that accepts an optional dur parameter for the postnatal period. Its add_pairs() method now takes mother_uids and infant_uids (not unborn_uids).
What to change: Update how you construct and interact with PostnatalNet.
# v3.0
postnatal = ss.PostnatalNet()
# Pairs were added by Pregnancy with dur/start/end

# v3.1
postnatal = ss.PostnatalNet(dur=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(0.5), std=ss.years(0.5)))
# Pairs are automatically added at delivery by Pregnancy



A new ss.BreastfeedingNet is available for modeling breastfeeding transmission. It automatically tracks breastfeeding status from the Pregnancy module. This is additive – no migration is required – but if you were previously using PostnatalNet to model breastfeeding transmission, consider switching.
# v3.1
sim = ss.Sim(
    demographics=ss.Pregnancy(),
    networks=[ss.PrenatalNet(), ss.BreastfeedingNet()],
    diseases=ss.SIR(),
)

title: Starsim v3 to v4 migration guide
text:
Starsim 4 adds a way to write a disease as declared states and transitions, which can then be run as an ODE, as a stochastic compartmental model, or as agents. This guide maps Starsim 3 code to Starsim 4, job by job, and lists what changes meaning on the way. It is written for both humans and LLMs.
Starsim 3 code is of two kinds, and they migrate differently:

Modules written as code (ss.Module, ss.Disease and ss.Infection subclasses with define_states(), set_prognoses(), and step_state(), custom networks, ss.Intervention and ss.Analyzer subclasses, ss.Births, ss.Deaths, ss.RandomNet, and ss.MFNet, now ss.SexualNet) are still part of Starsim 4. They run unchanged, as agents, and can sit in the same sim as declared diseases. ss.Disease is the base of every disease, as in Starsim 3, whether it is declared, written as code, or both in one class; ss.Infection adds transmission written as code. Per-agent quantities that change continuously (a CD4 count, a level of immunity, time since an event) have no declared form, and keeping them as code is a supported choice.
Starsim 3 spellings that Starsim 4 replaces (the library ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR as code; ss.routine_vx, ss.campaign_vx, ss.routine_screening, ss.treat_num, and the products ss.Vx, ss.Dx, ss.Tx; ss.seasonality) have been removed, as have ss.Calibration with its components, and ss.Samples and ss.Dataset. Use the table of jobs below to port them.

The migration script makes the mechanical changes for you and lists, by file and line, what needs a person: python -m starsim.converters.migrate mymodel.py --check lists what it would change, and without --check it rewrites the files (or folders) in place. Read its diff afterwards. A removed name used in Starsim 4 also raises an error that says what replaced it.
Note: If you are an LLM reading this, migrate one module at a time, run the model after each step, compare it with the Starsim 3 results (allowing for the changes in the next section), and confirm with the user before going on.



Read this first: each of these changes results without an error.


Results now follow the convention of other modeling frameworks, for modules written as code too. <state>[0] (e.g. infected[0]) is the number at the start, before any step; a flow at index 0 is 0; and <state>[ti] is the number after ti steps. A sim with stop=T ends at T, so it takes one step fewer than in Starsim 3. The same script, with Starsim 3’s SIR (ssl.AgentSIR in Starsim 4; see 5), gives:
                  infected[:4]            new_infections[:2]
Starsim 3.7.2     53, 99, 186, 356        26, 46
Starsim 4         31, 64, 128, 240        0, 33
(ss.Sim(n_agents=3000, diseases=ss.SIR(beta=0.1), networks='random'), with ssl.AgentSIR(beta=0.1) in Starsim 4.) The whole curve is one step later, and the random draws differ after that, so results agree statistically (over several seeds), not number for number. For a model with yearly steps, a peak moves a year later. To reproduce published Starsim 3 numbers exactly, use pip install starsim==3.7.2.
With coarse steps, a model can also differ by more than one step. In Starsim 3, a person could pass through several states within one step (e.g. infected, then latent, then active, all in the same step); in Starsim 4, someone who enters a state in a step leaves it in the next step at the earliest (unless the exit is immediate, with no rate= or dur=), as in the compartmental solvers. So with long steps, people wait longer in each state. For tbsim with dt=0.1 years, latent TB is 36% higher and active TB 13% higher than in Starsim 3; at dt=0.005 they agree. If results differ at a coarse step, check them at a smaller dt (sim.check_dt() says whether the step is too long for the model’s rates).



During the step from time point k-1 to k, sim.ti (and self.ti) is k in every module and every phase, from step() to update_results() and the analyzers, and self.now is the time the step starts, at which it reads inputs that change in time, as in Starsim 3. So Starsim 3’s self.results.x[self.ti] = v is right wherever it is written, and a time stamped as self.ti in step() matches self.ti in update_results(). What changes is the first step: time point 0 is the start of the run, recorded before any step, so the first step is ti == 1, and code that does something if self.ti == 0 in step() never does it (an analyzer’s step() also runs at the start, at ti == 0). Do it in init_post(), or test self.ti == 1:
# Starsim 3
def step(self):
    if self.ti == 0: # The first step
        self.seed()
    ...
    self.results.new_cases[self.ti] += len(cases) # Unchanged in Starsim 4

# Starsim 4
def step(self):
    if self.ti == 1: # The first step; time point 0 is the start of the run
        self.seed()
    ...
    self.results.new_cases[self.ti] += len(cases)
A declared disease dates a move between states at the start of the step (ti - 1) and an infection at its end (ti), so a time in a declared state worked out by hand during a step (sim.ti - dis.ti_P) is one step long; its clocks (dis.P.time) are right. For how long people stayed in a state, use dis.P.stays.
A disease written as code dates its initial infections at the start of the run (self.ti is 0 in set_prognoses()), as a declared disease dates its seeds, where Starsim 3 dated them by the first step. So in a Starsim 3 disease that schedules recovery at self.ti + dur and takes it when ti_recovered <= self.ti, the seeds are infectious for one step less than in Starsim 3, as long as later cases are. Both are about half a step short of dur on average; to give every case dur steps on average, as a declared disease does, schedule from the step after the infection and round as the engine does: ss.TimeArr('ti_recovered'), self.ti_recovered[uids] = self.ti + 1 + dur, and self.ti_recovered.due() (see ss.Infection; ssl.AgentSIR and the others do this).



In Starsim 3, beta=0.05 is a rate per year, but beta={'randomnet': 0.05} is a probability per step, used as it is. In Starsim 4 both are rates per unit time, so a dict copied verbatim is too low by a factor of about 1/dt: 12 times at monthly steps, 52 times at weekly ones (5 infections instead of 22,000 in an SIS on a random network at monthly steps). Give each value its Starsim 3 meaning explicitly:







Starsim 3 (monthly steps)
Starsim 4




beta={'randomnet': 0.05}
beta={'randomnet': ss.prob(0.05, 'month')}


beta={'mf': [0.008, 0.004]}
beta={'sexual': ss.peract(m2f=0.008, f2m=0.004)}



Use ss.prob(..., 'week') or ss.prob(..., 'day') for weekly or daily steps. Starsim 4 warns when a dict of bare numbers reaches a declared transmission with a step shorter than its unit; a typed value silences the warning. On ss.SexualNet (Starsim 3’s ss.MFNet), which has acts, a beta is a probability per act, the same at any step: Starsim 3’s pair, [men to women, women to men], is ss.peract(m2f=..., f2m=...), and the network is sexual in a beta dict, not mf.



Starsim 3’s ss.routine_vx(prob=0.05, start_year=2005) gives each eligible person a 5% chance of vaccination every year. Starsim 4’s routine delivery, ss.vaccinate(..., coverage=0.05, start='2005'), offers the vaccine once, when a person first becomes eligible. In an SIS model with 5,000 agents from 2000 to 2020, the first reaches about half the population and the second about 5%. The Starsim 3 behavior is delivery in yearly rounds:
ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, coverage=0.05, interval=ss.years(1), start='2005')



In a disease you declare with ss.Disease(...) (or a class with states and transitions), a duration given as a number (dur=ss.years(1)) is the mean of an exponential distribution, as in an ODE; describe() marks this as a guess. Starsim 3’s library diseases used ss.lognorm_ex(). To keep a distribution, give it: I >> R @ ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(6)). (A distribution that is not exponential runs as Erlang stages in a compartmental run, with a note.)
This includes the library ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR, which are now declared, with Starsim 3’s keywords but the textbook defaults: dur_inf (and dur_exp) given as a number or an ss.dur is the mean of an exponential (a number is in years, as before), where Starsim 3 had a lognormal with a standard deviation of 1 in the same unit (nearly fixed); and nobody dies of the infection unless p_death is given, where Starsim 3 had p_death=0.01. The shape matters: an SIR with R0 = 2.5 and a 7-day infectious period, with beta cut by 40% from day 30 to 90, infects 715,000 of a million with the exponential and 786,000 with Starsim 3’s nearly fixed period. Starsim 3’s models, with their defaults, are ssl.AgentSIR, ssl.AgentSIS, and ssl.AgentSEIR (import starsim.library as ssl): use them to keep Starsim 3’s model, or give ss.SIR(dur_inf=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(6), std=ss.years(1)), p_death=0.01).



A declared disease’s results are named after its states and transitions: I, not n_infected (a module written as code also counts each state under its own name: infected, and sim.results.alive, not n_alive); the flow of a transition is named after it (infection, recovery, with the cumulative total res.infection.cum); and new_infections and cum_infections are infection and infection.cum, for a disease written as code too. Map the names before comparing with Starsim 3 results.
The results of demographics follow the same rule: ss.Births and ss.Deaths have the flows birth and death (were new), with totals birth.cum and death.cum (were cumulative); ss.Pregnancy has preterm, very_preterm, and unborn (were n_preterm, n_very_preterm, and n_unborn), and maternal_death and neonatal_death (were plural).



Write calendar dates as strings (start='2000', stop='2030-06-30'), and step sizes with a unit (dt=ss.months(1), not dt=1/12). A bare start=2000 is still read as a year today, but bare numbers are being changed to mean times in the sim’s unit.




Each row is one job, with the Starsim 3 spelling and the Starsim 4 one. In the Starsim 4 column, sir is a declared disease.





Job
Starsim 3
Starsim 4




Starsim 3’s SIR, with its numbers
ss.SIR(beta=0.1, dur_inf=10) (a lognormal dur_inf, p_death=0.01)
ssl.AgentSIR(beta=0.1, dur_inf=10), and ssl.AgentSIS, ssl.AgentSEIR (agents only); ss.SIR(...) is now the textbook SIR, with an exponential dur_inf and no deaths


An SIR
ss.SIR(beta=0.1, dur_inf=10, init_prev=0.01)
S, I, R = ss.states(3), then infection = S >> I @ ss.peryear(0.1) * I, recovery = I >> R @ ss.years(10), and sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)


An SIS
ss.SIS(beta=0.05, dur_inf=10)
S, I = ss.states(2), then ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ ss.peryear(0.05) * I, recovery=I >> S @ ss.years(10), init_prev=0.01, name='sis') (no waning immunity: add an R state and R >> S for that)


An SEIR
ss.SEIR(dur_exp=ss.days(5), dur_inf=ss.days(10))
S >> E @ beta * I, E >> I @ ss.days(5), I >> R @ ss.days(10) (the state in the rate, I, says who infects)


A disease given as a dict
diseases=dict(type='sir', beta=0.1)
the module itself: ss.Sim(sir)


Parameters
define_pars(beta=ss.peryear(0.1)), pars=dict(beta=...)
beta = ss.par(ss.peryear(0.1), bounds=[0.01, 0.5]), used in the rate; bounds make it fittable


Initial infections
init_prev=ss.bernoulli(0.01)
init_prev=0.01, or init_n=dict(I=100) for a number of people (init=dict(I=0.01) is a share); init_prev= seeds the state a new infection enters (E in an SEIR), and init= and init_n= name the state


Where people start
a state whose default is True (ss.BoolState('susceptible', default=True))
one named with first='N' (in a class, first = 'N' in its body), else the state named S or susceptible, else the first state made


Population size
n_agents=10_000 (with total_pop= to scale)
total_pop=1e6 for any solver; n_agents= makes solver='auto' run as agents (and is used as total_pop in a compartmental run if that is not given)


A new state, by subclassing
an ss.Infection subclass with define_states(), set_prognoses(), and step_state()
a class with states and transitions in its body (below), or keep it as code


Moves scheduled with ti_<event>
set_prognoses() draws dur_inf; step_state() moves people whose ti_recovered <= ti
I >> R @ dur_inf (a duration after @ is a time in the state)


Competing exits
self.transition(uids, to={A: rate_a, B: rate_b})
one transition per exit: X >> A @ rate_a, X >> B @ rate_b

p_death=0.01, drawn at infection
two transitions with the same dur and p=: ss.Transition(I, R, dur=dur, p=0.99) and ss.Transition(I, ss.null, dur=dur, p=0.01)


A rate scaled per agent
rel_sus[uids] *= 2 in step()
a stratification with adjust=, or ss.modify(sir.rel_sus, multiply=2, where=...)



A disease written as a class, when it needs a method as well as transitions:
class SEIR(ss.Disease):
    S, E, I, R = ss.states(4)
    beta     = ss.par(ss.perday(0.3), bounds=[0.1, 1])
    exposure = S >> E @ beta * I
    onset    = E >> I @ ss.days(5)
    recovery = I >> R @ ss.days(10)

seir = SEIR(init_prev=0.01) # Named "seir", after the class






Job
Starsim 3
Starsim 4




Homogeneous mixing
a ss.RandomNet() with many contacts
no network (ss.Sim(sir)); this runs as an ODE


A contact matrix by age
a custom network or mixing pools
sir.stratify(age=[0, 15, 65]) and networks=ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=matrix) (ages= gives the lower edge of each of the matrix’s age groups), or ss.contacts('Kenya')


A network
ss.RandomNet(), ss.MFNet(), networks='random'
the same, with ss.MFNet() now ss.SexualNet() (between men and women by default; ss.MSMNet() is ss.SexualNet(between='mm')); a network makes the sim run as agents


Births and deaths
ss.Births(birth_rate=20), ss.Deaths(death_rate=15), or ss.Sim(birth_rate=20, death_rate=15) (per 1,000 per year)
for the population: ss.Sim(demographics=[ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.015))]) (per person; under every solver); or keep the modules (agents only). birth_rate= and death_rate= on the sim are removed


Pregnancy
ss.Pregnancy(), written as code, with methods to override (make_embryos(), …) and arrays (pregnant, ti_pregnant, ti_delivery)
ss.Pregnancy() is now declared, with Starsim 3’s arguments: the states NP and P and transitions (preg.conception, preg.delivery, preg.birth, …), under every solver. preg.pregnant is preg.P, ti_pregnant is ti_P, the scheduled delivery is ti_exit_P, and the results pregnancies, births, miscarriages, and stillbirths are its flows conception, birth, miscarriage, and stillbirth. A subclass that overrides Starsim 3’s methods raises: use its seams instead: its three rates, fertility=, loss_rate=, and infant_rate= (each a rate, or a function of (sim, uids); fertility is conception_rate() by default), ss.modify() of its transitions, since_birth and preg.lactating (breastfeeding) after a birth, and ss.on(preg.birth) or, from code, preg.add_callback(preg.birth, fn) (Starsim 3’s add_conception_callback(fn) and add_delivery_callback(fn) are removed). ss.PregnancyPars is removed too: ss.Pregnancy().pars has the parameters


The children of some parents
sim.people.find_children(uids)
ss.uids(ppl.auids[np.isin(ppl.parent, uids)]) (People.find_children() is removed)


An age range
ss.parse_age_range('[15, 25)'), ss.apply_age_range()
a condition, (ppl.age >= 15) & (ppl.age < 25), or a stratification, sim.stratify(age=[15, 25, 50]) (both functions moved to STIsim)









Job
Starsim 3
Starsim 4




A vaccine
ss.simple_vx(efficacy=0.8), ss.Vx(...)
the product’s keywords on its delivery, ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, ...), or the product itself, ss.Vaccine(efficacy=0.8), when one product is given by several deliveries. It is leaky, as ss.simple_vx was by default (everyone vaccinated has their chance of infection cut by 80%); for all-or-nothing (Starsim 3’s leaky=False: 80% of those vaccinated are fully protected, the rest not at all), leaky=False


Routine vaccination, p a year
ss.routine_vx(product=vx, prob=0.05, start_year=2005)
ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, coverage=0.05, interval=ss.years(1), start='2005') (see item 4 above)


A campaign
ss.campaign_vx(product=vx, years=[2020], prob=0.6)
ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, at=['2020'], coverage=0.6)


Who is eligible
eligibility=lambda sim: sim.people.age < 15
where=lambda sim: sim.people.age < 15, or a condition: where=sir.age < 15 when sir is stratified by age


Screening and treatment
ss.routine_screening(product=ss.Dx(...), prob=0.1) with a treatment intervention
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, coverage=0.1, interval=ss.years(1)) and ss.treat(cure=0.95, who=screening.positive, coverage=0.8)


Treatment with limited capacity
ss.treat_num(product=ss.Tx(...), max_capacity=10)
ss.treat(cure=0.95, where=sir.infection, capacity=10)


A parameter change at a time
an ss.Intervention that edits sim.diseases.sir.pars.beta in step()
ss.modify(sir.pars.beta, multiply=0.5, start='2010')


A change while something holds
the same, with a test in step()
ss.modify(sir.pars.beta, multiply=0.6, start='2020-03-15', stop='2020-06-01')


Seasonality
ss.seasonality(...)
beta=ss.seasonal(mean=ss.peryear(0.5), amplitude=0.4, peak='January')


One disease changing another
an ss.Connector that writes sis.rel_sus from hiv’s states
connectors=ss.modify(sis.rel_sus, multiply=3, where=hiv.I)


A custom intervention
an ss.Intervention subclass with step()
keep it (agents), or ss.vaccinate(..., deliver=fn) with a function returning who receives it



A connector that sets an array (sis.rel_sus[:] = 1.0, then raises it for some people) also erases what other modules set, such as a disease’s own immunity. ss.modify() multiplies a base value that it never overwrites, so modifiers from several modules combine.






Job
Starsim 3
Starsim 4




Many runs of one sim
ss.MultiSim(sim, n_runs=10).run(), then msim.mean()
msim = sim.run(n_runs=10) (or ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=10)), then msim.summarize() (a table of the median, a 95% interval, the mean, and the standard deviation of each result over the runs), msim.plot() (the median and 95% interval), or msim.results.sir.I.median() and .quantiles() at each time, for any sim; msim.reduce(), mean(), and median() are gone


Scenarios
ss.parallel(sim1, sim2)
ss.parallel({'Baseline': sim1, 'Masks': sim2}), labeled as you like, and msim.diff('Baseline')


A parameter sweep
a loop over ss.Sim(pars=...)
ss.parallel(sim, pars={'sir.beta': [0.2, 0.3, 0.4]})


A result
sim.results.sir.n_infected
sim.results.sir.I


A result by group
an analyzer
sim.results.sir.I.by('age'), .select(age='0-14')


The modules given to a sim
ss.Sim(..., copy_inputs=False), so that sir.results is the sim’s
a sim always copies the modules it is given (copy_inputs= is removed; the migration script removes it and lists the line): read them, and their results, from the sim (sim.diseases.sir, sim.results.sir)


A copy with changes
sc.dcp(sim), then edit
sim.new(n_agents=5000), a new sim from the same inputs with what is given changed; to run the same sim again with another solver, sim.run(solver='abm') (a sim that has run is run again from the start)


Calibration
ss.Calibration(sim, calib_pars=dict(beta=dict(low=0.01, high=0.3, guess=0.1)), build_fn=..., components=[ss.Normal(...)], total_trials=100), then calib.fit()
beta=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 0.3]) in the model, ss.Sim(sir, data=df) with a column named after a result (prevalence), then fit = sim.fit() (n_trials=100 for Optuna, used for agents)


A likelihood
ss.Normal(...), ss.BetaBinomial(...) components
sim.fit(likelihood=dict(prevalence=ss.normal(scale=0.02))), or likelihood= on an ss.outcome()


Data shared by two diseases
an extract_fn per component
name the column after the disease too: sis.prevalence







A published model does not have to move all at once. Keep the hard disease as code and declare the easy one: the mixed sim runs as agents, and sim.new(), ss.parallel() scenarios and sweeps, msim.diff(), and sim.fit() work on the whole sim.
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

hiv = ssl.HIV(beta={'sexual': ss.peract(m2f=0.008, f2m=0.004), 'random': 0}, init_prev=0.05) # Starsim 3's module, written as code (see 3 for its beta)
S, I = ss.states('S I')
sis = ss.Disease( # Newly declared
    infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=dict(sexual=0, random=ss.par(ss.prob(0.005, 'month'), bounds=[0.001, 0.05])) * I),
    recovery  = ss.Transition(I, S, dur=ss.years(2)),
    init_prev = 0.05,
    name = 'sis',
)
susceptible = ss.modify(sis.rel_sus, multiply=3, where=hiv.infected)
sim = ss.Sim([hiv, sis], networks=[ss.SexualNet(), ss.RandomNet()], connectors=susceptible,
             n_agents=2000, start='2000', stop='2020', dt=ss.months(1))

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, disease=sis, coverage=0.05, interval=ss.years(1), start='2010')
msim = ss.parallel({'Baseline': sim, 'Vaccine': sim.new(interventions=vaccination)}, n_runs=3)
msim.diff('Baseline')
Two things to know in a mixed sim:

A condition can name the arrays of a module written as code (where=hiv.infected, where=hiv.cd4 < 200), or be a function of the sim (where=lambda sim: sim.diseases.hiv.infected).
ss.modify() and ss.vaccinate() act on a module written as code too, as agents, if it has what they change (such as rel_sus); give disease= when there are several diseases. Its Starsim 3 connectors and interventions also still run.

To validate each step, run the Starsim 3 version and the ported one over several seeds (sim.run(n_runs=10)) and compare means and spreads, after mapping the result names and allowing for the one-step shift.






Works on any module
Needs a declared disease




Running as agents, networks, ss.Births/ss.Deaths, analyzers, ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=...) with msim.results across the runs, sim.new(), scenarios and sweeps with ss.parallel(), sim.fit() (with bounds on a parameter), ss.modify() and ss.vaccinate() targets (as agents), sim.describe() (in brief)
The ODE and stochastic compartmental solvers, describe() in full, equations()



The compartmental solvers need every module of the sim to have a compartmental form, so a sim with a disease written as code runs as agents.

title: Starsim v3 to v4 migration guide
text:
Starsim 4 adds a way to write a disease as declared states and transitions, which can then be run as an ODE, as a stochastic compartmental model, or as agents. This guide maps Starsim 3 code to Starsim 4, job by job, and lists what changes meaning on the way. It is written for both humans and LLMs.
Starsim 3 code is of two kinds, and they migrate differently:

Modules written as code (ss.Module, ss.Disease and ss.Infection subclasses with define_states(), set_prognoses(), and step_state(), custom networks, ss.Intervention and ss.Analyzer subclasses, ss.Births, ss.Deaths, ss.RandomNet, and ss.MFNet, now ss.SexualNet) are still part of Starsim 4. They run unchanged, as agents, and can sit in the same sim as declared diseases. ss.Disease is the base of every disease, as in Starsim 3, whether it is declared, written as code, or both in one class; ss.Infection adds transmission written as code. Per-agent quantities that change continuously (a CD4 count, a level of immunity, time since an event) have no declared form, and keeping them as code is a supported choice.
Starsim 3 spellings that Starsim 4 replaces (the library ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR as code; ss.routine_vx, ss.campaign_vx, ss.routine_screening, ss.treat_num, and the products ss.Vx, ss.Dx, ss.Tx; ss.seasonality) have been removed, as have ss.Calibration with its components, and ss.Samples and ss.Dataset. Use the table of jobs below to port them.

The migration script makes the mechanical changes for you and lists, by file and line, what needs a person: python -m starsim.converters.migrate mymodel.py --check lists what it would change, and without --check it rewrites the files (or folders) in place. Read its diff afterwards. A removed name used in Starsim 4 also raises an error that says what replaced it.
Note: If you are an LLM reading this, migrate one module at a time, run the model after each step, compare it with the Starsim 3 results (allowing for the changes in the next section), and confirm with the user before going on.

title: Starsim v3 to v4 migration guide
text:
Read this first: each of these changes results without an error.


Results now follow the convention of other modeling frameworks, for modules written as code too. <state>[0] (e.g. infected[0]) is the number at the start, before any step; a flow at index 0 is 0; and <state>[ti] is the number after ti steps. A sim with stop=T ends at T, so it takes one step fewer than in Starsim 3. The same script, with Starsim 3’s SIR (ssl.AgentSIR in Starsim 4; see 5), gives:
                  infected[:4]            new_infections[:2]
Starsim 3.7.2     53, 99, 186, 356        26, 46
Starsim 4         31, 64, 128, 240        0, 33
(ss.Sim(n_agents=3000, diseases=ss.SIR(beta=0.1), networks='random'), with ssl.AgentSIR(beta=0.1) in Starsim 4.) The whole curve is one step later, and the random draws differ after that, so results agree statistically (over several seeds), not number for number. For a model with yearly steps, a peak moves a year later. To reproduce published Starsim 3 numbers exactly, use pip install starsim==3.7.2.
With coarse steps, a model can also differ by more than one step. In Starsim 3, a person could pass through several states within one step (e.g. infected, then latent, then active, all in the same step); in Starsim 4, someone who enters a state in a step leaves it in the next step at the earliest (unless the exit is immediate, with no rate= or dur=), as in the compartmental solvers. So with long steps, people wait longer in each state. For tbsim with dt=0.1 years, latent TB is 36% higher and active TB 13% higher than in Starsim 3; at dt=0.005 they agree. If results differ at a coarse step, check them at a smaller dt (sim.check_dt() says whether the step is too long for the model’s rates).



During the step from time point k-1 to k, sim.ti (and self.ti) is k in every module and every phase, from step() to update_results() and the analyzers, and self.now is the time the step starts, at which it reads inputs that change in time, as in Starsim 3. So Starsim 3’s self.results.x[self.ti] = v is right wherever it is written, and a time stamped as self.ti in step() matches self.ti in update_results(). What changes is the first step: time point 0 is the start of the run, recorded before any step, so the first step is ti == 1, and code that does something if self.ti == 0 in step() never does it (an analyzer’s step() also runs at the start, at ti == 0). Do it in init_post(), or test self.ti == 1:
# Starsim 3
def step(self):
    if self.ti == 0: # The first step
        self.seed()
    ...
    self.results.new_cases[self.ti] += len(cases) # Unchanged in Starsim 4

# Starsim 4
def step(self):
    if self.ti == 1: # The first step; time point 0 is the start of the run
        self.seed()
    ...
    self.results.new_cases[self.ti] += len(cases)
A declared disease dates a move between states at the start of the step (ti - 1) and an infection at its end (ti), so a time in a declared state worked out by hand during a step (sim.ti - dis.ti_P) is one step long; its clocks (dis.P.time) are right. For how long people stayed in a state, use dis.P.stays.
A disease written as code dates its initial infections at the start of the run (self.ti is 0 in set_prognoses()), as a declared disease dates its seeds, where Starsim 3 dated them by the first step. So in a Starsim 3 disease that schedules recovery at self.ti + dur and takes it when ti_recovered <= self.ti, the seeds are infectious for one step less than in Starsim 3, as long as later cases are. Both are about half a step short of dur on average; to give every case dur steps on average, as a declared disease does, schedule from the step after the infection and round as the engine does: ss.TimeArr('ti_recovered'), self.ti_recovered[uids] = self.ti + 1 + dur, and self.ti_recovered.due() (see ss.Infection; ssl.AgentSIR and the others do this).



In Starsim 3, beta=0.05 is a rate per year, but beta={'randomnet': 0.05} is a probability per step, used as it is. In Starsim 4 both are rates per unit time, so a dict copied verbatim is too low by a factor of about 1/dt: 12 times at monthly steps, 52 times at weekly ones (5 infections instead of 22,000 in an SIS on a random network at monthly steps). Give each value its Starsim 3 meaning explicitly:







Starsim 3 (monthly steps)
Starsim 4




beta={'randomnet': 0.05}
beta={'randomnet': ss.prob(0.05, 'month')}


beta={'mf': [0.008, 0.004]}
beta={'sexual': ss.peract(m2f=0.008, f2m=0.004)}



Use ss.prob(..., 'week') or ss.prob(..., 'day') for weekly or daily steps. Starsim 4 warns when a dict of bare numbers reaches a declared transmission with a step shorter than its unit; a typed value silences the warning. On ss.SexualNet (Starsim 3’s ss.MFNet), which has acts, a beta is a probability per act, the same at any step: Starsim 3’s pair, [men to women, women to men], is ss.peract(m2f=..., f2m=...), and the network is sexual in a beta dict, not mf.



Starsim 3’s ss.routine_vx(prob=0.05, start_year=2005) gives each eligible person a 5% chance of vaccination every year. Starsim 4’s routine delivery, ss.vaccinate(..., coverage=0.05, start='2005'), offers the vaccine once, when a person first becomes eligible. In an SIS model with 5,000 agents from 2000 to 2020, the first reaches about half the population and the second about 5%. The Starsim 3 behavior is delivery in yearly rounds:
ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, coverage=0.05, interval=ss.years(1), start='2005')



In a disease you declare with ss.Disease(...) (or a class with states and transitions), a duration given as a number (dur=ss.years(1)) is the mean of an exponential distribution, as in an ODE; describe() marks this as a guess. Starsim 3’s library diseases used ss.lognorm_ex(). To keep a distribution, give it: I >> R @ ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(6)). (A distribution that is not exponential runs as Erlang stages in a compartmental run, with a note.)
This includes the library ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR, which are now declared, with Starsim 3’s keywords but the textbook defaults: dur_inf (and dur_exp) given as a number or an ss.dur is the mean of an exponential (a number is in years, as before), where Starsim 3 had a lognormal with a standard deviation of 1 in the same unit (nearly fixed); and nobody dies of the infection unless p_death is given, where Starsim 3 had p_death=0.01. The shape matters: an SIR with R0 = 2.5 and a 7-day infectious period, with beta cut by 40% from day 30 to 90, infects 715,000 of a million with the exponential and 786,000 with Starsim 3’s nearly fixed period. Starsim 3’s models, with their defaults, are ssl.AgentSIR, ssl.AgentSIS, and ssl.AgentSEIR (import starsim.library as ssl): use them to keep Starsim 3’s model, or give ss.SIR(dur_inf=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(6), std=ss.years(1)), p_death=0.01).



A declared disease’s results are named after its states and transitions: I, not n_infected (a module written as code also counts each state under its own name: infected, and sim.results.alive, not n_alive); the flow of a transition is named after it (infection, recovery, with the cumulative total res.infection.cum); and new_infections and cum_infections are infection and infection.cum, for a disease written as code too. Map the names before comparing with Starsim 3 results.
The results of demographics follow the same rule: ss.Births and ss.Deaths have the flows birth and death (were new), with totals birth.cum and death.cum (were cumulative); ss.Pregnancy has preterm, very_preterm, and unborn (were n_preterm, n_very_preterm, and n_unborn), and maternal_death and neonatal_death (were plural).



Write calendar dates as strings (start='2000', stop='2030-06-30'), and step sizes with a unit (dt=ss.months(1), not dt=1/12). A bare start=2000 is still read as a year today, but bare numbers are being changed to mean times in the sim’s unit.

Job
Starsim 3
Starsim 4




Starsim 3’s SIR, with its numbers
ss.SIR(beta=0.1, dur_inf=10) (a lognormal dur_inf, p_death=0.01)
ssl.AgentSIR(beta=0.1, dur_inf=10), and ssl.AgentSIS, ssl.AgentSEIR (agents only); ss.SIR(...) is now the textbook SIR, with an exponential dur_inf and no deaths


An SIR
ss.SIR(beta=0.1, dur_inf=10, init_prev=0.01)
S, I, R = ss.states(3), then infection = S >> I @ ss.peryear(0.1) * I, recovery = I >> R @ ss.years(10), and sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)


An SIS
ss.SIS(beta=0.05, dur_inf=10)
S, I = ss.states(2), then ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ ss.peryear(0.05) * I, recovery=I >> S @ ss.years(10), init_prev=0.01, name='sis') (no waning immunity: add an R state and R >> S for that)


An SEIR
ss.SEIR(dur_exp=ss.days(5), dur_inf=ss.days(10))
S >> E @ beta * I, E >> I @ ss.days(5), I >> R @ ss.days(10) (the state in the rate, I, says who infects)


A disease given as a dict
diseases=dict(type='sir', beta=0.1)
the module itself: ss.Sim(sir)


Parameters
define_pars(beta=ss.peryear(0.1)), pars=dict(beta=...)
beta = ss.par(ss.peryear(0.1), bounds=[0.01, 0.5]), used in the rate; bounds make it fittable


Initial infections
init_prev=ss.bernoulli(0.01)
init_prev=0.01, or init_n=dict(I=100) for a number of people (init=dict(I=0.01) is a share); init_prev= seeds the state a new infection enters (E in an SEIR), and init= and init_n= name the state


Where people start
a state whose default is True (ss.BoolState('susceptible', default=True))
one named with first='N' (in a class, first = 'N' in its body), else the state named S or susceptible, else the first state made


Population size
n_agents=10_000 (with total_pop= to scale)
total_pop=1e6 for any solver; n_agents= makes solver='auto' run as agents (and is used as total_pop in a compartmental run if that is not given)


A new state, by subclassing
an ss.Infection subclass with define_states(), set_prognoses(), and step_state()
a class with states and transitions in its body (below), or keep it as code


Moves scheduled with ti_<event>
set_prognoses() draws dur_inf; step_state() moves people whose ti_recovered <= ti
I >> R @ dur_inf (a duration after @ is a time in the state)


Competing exits
self.transition(uids, to={A: rate_a, B: rate_b})
one transition per exit: X >> A @ rate_a, X >> B @ rate_b


Death from infection
p_death=0.01, drawn at infection
two transitions with the same dur and p=: ss.Transition(I, R, dur=dur, p=0.99) and ss.Transition(I, ss.null, dur=dur, p=0.01)


A rate scaled per agent
rel_sus[uids] *= 2 in step()
a stratification with adjust=, or ss.modify(sir.rel_sus, multiply=2, where=...)



A disease written as a class, when it needs a method as well as transitions:
class SEIR(ss.Disease):
    S, E, I, R = ss.states(4)
    beta     = ss.par(ss.perday(0.3), bounds=[0.1, 1])
    exposure = S >> E @ beta * I
    onset    = E >> I @ ss.days(5)
    recovery = I >> R @ ss.days(10)

seir = SEIR(init_prev=0.01) # Named "seir", after the class






Job
Starsim 3
Starsim 4




Homogeneous mixing
a ss.RandomNet() with many contacts
no network (ss.Sim(sir)); this runs as an ODE


A contact matrix by age
a custom network or mixing pools
sir.stratify(age=[0, 15, 65]) and networks=ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=matrix) (ages= gives the lower edge of each of the matrix’s age groups), or ss.contacts('Kenya')


A network
ss.RandomNet(), ss.MFNet(), networks='random'
the same, with ss.MFNet() now ss.SexualNet() (between men and women by default; ss.MSMNet() is ss.SexualNet(between='mm')); a network makes the sim run as agents


Births and deaths
ss.Births(birth_rate=20), ss.Deaths(death_rate=15), or ss.Sim(birth_rate=20, death_rate=15) (per 1,000 per year)
for the population: ss.Sim(demographics=[ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.015))]) (per person; under every solver); or keep the modules (agents only). birth_rate= and death_rate= on the sim are removed


Pregnancy
ss.Pregnancy(), written as code, with methods to override (make_embryos(), …) and arrays (pregnant, ti_pregnant, ti_delivery)
ss.Pregnancy() is now declared, with Starsim 3’s arguments: the states NP and P and transitions (preg.conception, preg.delivery, preg.birth, …), under every solver. preg.pregnant is preg.P, ti_pregnant is ti_P, the scheduled delivery is ti_exit_P, and the results pregnancies, births, miscarriages, and stillbirths are its flows conception, birth, miscarriage, and stillbirth. A subclass that overrides Starsim 3’s methods raises: use its seams instead: its three rates, fertility=, loss_rate=, and infant_rate= (each a rate, or a function of (sim, uids); fertility is conception_rate() by default), ss.modify() of its transitions, since_birth and preg.lactating (breastfeeding) after a birth, and ss.on(preg.birth) or, from code, preg.add_callback(preg.birth, fn) (Starsim 3’s add_conception_callback(fn) and add_delivery_callback(fn) are removed). ss.PregnancyPars is removed too: ss.Pregnancy().pars has the parameters


The children of some parents
sim.people.find_children(uids)
ss.uids(ppl.auids[np.isin(ppl.parent, uids)]) (People.find_children() is removed)


An age range
ss.parse_age_range('[15, 25)'), ss.apply_age_range()
a condition, (ppl.age >= 15) & (ppl.age < 25), or a stratification, sim.stratify(age=[15, 25, 50]) (both functions moved to STIsim)









Job
Starsim 3
Starsim 4




A vaccine
ss.simple_vx(efficacy=0.8), ss.Vx(...)
the product’s keywords on its delivery, ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, ...), or the product itself, ss.Vaccine(efficacy=0.8), when one product is given by several deliveries. It is leaky, as ss.simple_vx was by default (everyone vaccinated has their chance of infection cut by 80%); for all-or-nothing (Starsim 3’s leaky=False: 80% of those vaccinated are fully protected, the rest not at all), leaky=False


Routine vaccination, p a year
ss.routine_vx(product=vx, prob=0.05, start_year=2005)
ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, coverage=0.05, interval=ss.years(1), start='2005') (see item 4 above)


A campaign
ss.campaign_vx(product=vx, years=[2020], prob=0.6)
ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, at=['2020'], coverage=0.6)


Who is eligible
eligibility=lambda sim: sim.people.age < 15
where=lambda sim: sim.people.age < 15, or a condition: where=sir.age < 15 when sir is stratified by age


Screening and treatment
ss.routine_screening(product=ss.Dx(...), prob=0.1) with a treatment intervention
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, coverage=0.1, interval=ss.years(1)) and ss.treat(cure=0.95, who=screening.positive, coverage=0.8)


Treatment with limited capacity
ss.treat_num(product=ss.Tx(...), max_capacity=10)
ss.treat(cure=0.95, where=sir.infection, capacity=10)


A parameter change at a time
an ss.Intervention that edits sim.diseases.sir.pars.beta in step()
ss.modify(sir.pars.beta, multiply=0.5, start='2010')


A change while something holds
the same, with a test in step()
ss.modify(sir.pars.beta, multiply=0.6, start='2020-03-15', stop='2020-06-01')


Seasonality
ss.seasonality(...)
beta=ss.seasonal(mean=ss.peryear(0.5), amplitude=0.4, peak='January')


One disease changing another
an ss.Connector that writes sis.rel_sus from hiv’s states
connectors=ss.modify(sis.rel_sus, multiply=3, where=hiv.I)


A custom intervention
an ss.Intervention subclass with step()
keep it (agents), or ss.vaccinate(..., deliver=fn) with a function returning who receives it



A connector that sets an array (sis.rel_sus[:] = 1.0, then raises it for some people) also erases what other modules set, such as a disease’s own immunity. ss.modify() multiplies a base value that it never overwrites, so modifiers from several modules combine.






Job
Starsim 3
Starsim 4




Many runs of one sim
ss.MultiSim(sim, n_runs=10).run(), then msim.mean()
msim = sim.run(n_runs=10) (or ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=10)), then msim.summarize() (a table of the median, a 95% interval, the mean, and the standard deviation of each result over the runs), msim.plot() (the median and 95% interval), or msim.results.sir.I.median() and .quantiles() at each time, for any sim; msim.reduce(), mean(), and median() are gone


Scenarios
ss.parallel(sim1, sim2)
ss.parallel({'Baseline': sim1, 'Masks': sim2}), labeled as you like, and msim.diff('Baseline')


A parameter sweep
a loop over ss.Sim(pars=...)
ss.parallel(sim, pars={'sir.beta': [0.2, 0.3, 0.4]})


A result
sim.results.sir.n_infected
sim.results.sir.I


A result by group
an analyzer
sim.results.sir.I.by('age'), .select(age='0-14')


The modules given to a sim
ss.Sim(..., copy_inputs=False), so that sir.results is the sim’s
a sim always copies the modules it is given (copy_inputs= is removed; the migration script removes it and lists the line): read them, and their results, from the sim (sim.diseases.sir, sim.results.sir)


A copy with changes
sc.dcp(sim), then edit
sim.new(n_agents=5000), a new sim from the same inputs with what is given changed; to run the same sim again with another solver, sim.run(solver='abm') (a sim that has run is run again from the start)


Calibration
ss.Calibration(sim, calib_pars=dict(beta=dict(low=0.01, high=0.3, guess=0.1)), build_fn=..., components=[ss.Normal(...)], total_trials=100), then calib.fit()
beta=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 0.3]) in the model, ss.Sim(sir, data=df) with a column named after a result (prevalence), then fit = sim.fit() (n_trials=100 for Optuna, used for agents)


A likelihood
ss.Normal(...), ss.BetaBinomial(...) components
sim.fit(likelihood=dict(prevalence=ss.normal(scale=0.02))), or likelihood= on an ss.outcome()


Data shared by two diseases
an extract_fn per component
name the column after the disease too: sis.prevalence

title: Starsim v3 to v4 migration guide
text:
A published model does not have to move all at once. Keep the hard disease as code and declare the easy one: the mixed sim runs as agents, and sim.new(), ss.parallel() scenarios and sweeps, msim.diff(), and sim.fit() work on the whole sim.
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

hiv = ssl.HIV(beta={'sexual': ss.peract(m2f=0.008, f2m=0.004), 'random': 0}, init_prev=0.05) # Starsim 3's module, written as code (see 3 for its beta)
S, I = ss.states('S I')
sis = ss.Disease( # Newly declared
    infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=dict(sexual=0, random=ss.par(ss.prob(0.005, 'month'), bounds=[0.001, 0.05])) * I),
    recovery  = ss.Transition(I, S, dur=ss.years(2)),
    init_prev = 0.05,
    name = 'sis',
)
susceptible = ss.modify(sis.rel_sus, multiply=3, where=hiv.infected)
sim = ss.Sim([hiv, sis], networks=[ss.SexualNet(), ss.RandomNet()], connectors=susceptible,
             n_agents=2000, start='2000', stop='2020', dt=ss.months(1))

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, disease=sis, coverage=0.05, interval=ss.years(1), start='2010')
msim = ss.parallel({'Baseline': sim, 'Vaccine': sim.new(interventions=vaccination)}, n_runs=3)
msim.diff('Baseline')
Two things to know in a mixed sim:

A condition can name the arrays of a module written as code (where=hiv.infected, where=hiv.cd4 < 200), or be a function of the sim (where=lambda sim: sim.diseases.hiv.infected).
ss.modify() and ss.vaccinate() act on a module written as code too, as agents, if it has what they change (such as rel_sus); give disease= when there are several diseases. Its Starsim 3 connectors and interventions also still run.

To validate each step, run the Starsim 3 version and the ported one over several seeds (sim.run(n_runs=10)) and compare means and spreads, after mapping the result names and allowing for the one-step shift.

title: Starsim v3 to v4 migration guide
text:
Works on any module
Needs a declared disease




Running as agents, networks, ss.Births/ss.Deaths, analyzers, ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=...) with msim.results across the runs, sim.new(), scenarios and sweeps with ss.parallel(), sim.fit() (with bounds on a parameter), ss.modify() and ss.vaccinate() targets (as agents), sim.describe() (in brief)
The ODE and stochastic compartmental solvers, describe() in full, equations()



The compartmental solvers need every module of the sim to have a compartmental form, so a sim with a disease written as code runs as agents.

title: Starsim 4: the full changelog
text:
Every change made in developing Starsim 4, in detail, as recorded during development. The summary is in CHANGELOG.md, and the guide to moving code from Starsim 3 is v3_v4.md. Changes that may result in differences in model output are flagged with the term “Regression”; changes that may require updates to downstream code are flagged with the term “Migration”.
This version adds a way to write a model as declared states and transitions, which can then be run as an ODE, as a stochastic compartmental model, or as agents. Models written as code (ss.SIR, custom step() methods, etc.) still run, but their results are one step later than in Starsim 3 (see Regression below), so they agree with Starsim 3 statistically, not number for number. The migration guide (docs/migration/v3_v4.md) maps Starsim 3 code to Starsim 4.



ss.TimeArr (float32 step numbers, NaN for never, with due() and .years) replaces ss.arrays.StepArr for every time of agents: the engine’s times of entering and leaving states, people.ti_dead and people.ti_removed. Results are unchanged; reading, writing and comparing them through the array is 2–10× faster (no conversion from 16-bit integers); memory is 2 bytes more per agent per time (LASER’s model: 51 to 66 bytes per agent). arr.due() gives whose time has come, e.g. mask = self.exposed & self.ti_infectious.due() in a disease written as code.
== and != on an ss.TimeArr raise, since a time drawn between steps never equals one exactly, so ti_x == ti quietly missed nearly everyone: ti_x.isclose(ti) gives whose time is at the step nearest ti (the rule due() uses, so for a declared state’s time of entering it is “entered this step”), and ti_x.eq(t) exact equality.
A time between steps is rounded the same way in a disease written as code and in a declared one run as agents: up or down at random in proportion, by each agent’s phase (ss.People.phase(), spread evenly over the slots and shifted by the seed: a time t is taken at step floor(t + phase)), so its mean is kept. ti_x.due() and isclose() use it, where due() took the nearest step (which loses the mean of a dwell shorter than a few steps), and the agent engine rounds its dwell times by it in place of a draw for each (one distribution fewer for each state, delay and transfer, and no memory per agent). For plain arithmetic, compare the times: ti_x < ti + 0.5 is the nearest step. Results of agent runs change, by chance alone.
A second module with a default name is numbered (clip_edges_1) with no warning, as a second modifier already was; a product renamed this way still warns, and two names the user gave still raise. ss.move() on a disease written as code says to set its states in code, and pars= with a key in a sim that has no parameters it can set says so (it raised a ValueError from the suggestion of names).
A sim setting given as ss.par with bounds (e.g. ss.Sim(n_agents=ss.par(5000, bounds=[1000, 20000]))) is fitted by sim.fit() like any parameter, with a new sim built for each value, and taken by name in pars= (sim.new(pars=fit.pars)); a setting given as a plain value in pars= raises, saying to give it to sim.new() or as ss.par. A number of agents that is not whole (as a fit chooses) is rounded to the nearest, for people made in advance too (it was truncated, and raised against people made in advance). Arithmetic between a typed value and a parameter that holds one keeps the unit (ss.weeks(40) - preg.pars.loss_threshold is weeks(20); it was 39.6 weeks, from the threshold’s value in years taken as weeks). After sim.shrink(), a disease written as code no longer holds the sim through its engine.
ss.by keeps one table of values for groups and agents: a value by groups is the table at each group’s position, and a value by people’s properties the table at each agent’s, so lookup_grid() and binned_grid() are gone (lookup(uids=) looks up some agents). Results unchanged.
Migration: there is no model spec. sim.to_code(), ss.diff(), sim.hash(), sim.to_spec() (and each module’s to_spec()), ss.save('model.py', sim), and ss.spec are removed: a model is its code, and two models are compared by their results, describe(), or a text diff of their code. An import still gives code: ss.import_from() writes the model as Starsim code (ss.converters.write()), kept as sim.imported.code, and the sim is that code run; a value an importer cannot write is given as ss.converters.Code. The exporters (SBML, odin) read the built model. A constant function in an imported rate (-log(1 - 0.1)) is now a number, so describe() shows it as a dwell time, with the same results.
Migration: ss.strains.Family is removed, with ss.Strains of diseases, shared=, and ss.immunity(rel_trans=, dur=) or from an attribute: strains with courses of their own are one disease per strain, connected by a connector (see Strains). It was about 1.5× slower than HPVsim’s coded genotypes. ssl.Dengue() is now a list of serotypes, with results sim.results.den1 and so on.
Migration: less machinery, with one way to do each thing: ss.Event, ss.child, ss.Transition(before=) (write rate*(X.time < d)), operator=, protection by memory (strains.last/.ever, ss.immunity(scale=, curve=, p=)), cross_immunity=, the clock dimension, ss.Loop(steps=) with no sim, Loop.plot_step_order(), the options license, date_sep, numba_indexing, jax_cache and check_method_calls, sim.to_yaml(), Module.requires, ss.save(format=) (use ss.export_to()), the Mermaid export, method='asd', and ss.jit on methods and classes are removed. ss.errors keeps 5 error classes (CapabilityError, AlreadyRunError, DistNotInitializedError, DistSeedRepeatError, BooleanOperationError) and 4 warnings; every other error is a built-in exception (ValueError, KeyError, …) with the same message. summarize_by= is the only spelling for how a result is summarized (kind= is gone, and ss.Result() raises on an unknown keyword).
One mechanism for each job: sim.new() is a copy of the sim as it was when init() started, plus the changes given to it (edits to an initialized sim belong to that run); a declared model’s layout is built once; every module reads a parameter’s current value (units, time, modifiers, level) the same way, and a coded module reads typed parameters with no conversion by hand; agents and coded diseases share one transmission (dis.current_value('rel_sus', uids)), so the same model written either way gives the same results, and a coded ss.Infection(strains=ss.Strains(...)) follows the same rules as a declared one; diseases tracked jointly are views of one set of compartments. ss.choice takes a row of p per agent (FPsim’s method choice 27–126 times faster), and ss.Result(..., groups=True) is counted by group from sim.groups.count() (STIsim takes 4.7 s, was 6.6). ss.par shows its label= in its repr and in describe(). dt=ss.datedur(months=1) runs with declared diseases, and monthly dates from the 31st stay at the end of each month.
The speed tests compare Starsim’s time, normalized to the reference machine with sc.benchmark() (tests/timing.py), with its own reference, and fail above 1.5 times it, as the performance guard does; another framework’s time is printed, not asserted, so the tests pass on a busy or slower machine.
Migration: an ss.Infection written as code transmits in transmit() (was infect()) and transmit_route() (was infect_route()); disease.infect(uids) infects those people now for every disease, declared or written as code (ssl.AgentSIR().infect(uids) raised a TypeError). The migration script renames overrides.
Migration: ss.contacts() takes one matrix and says what it is over: ss.contacts(M) for the model’s age groups (was age=M), ages=[0, 15, 65] for the matrix’s own age groups, dims='risk' or dims=['sex', 'risk'] for other stratifications (was risk=M), and a dict for a product of one matrix per stratification (ss.contacts(dict(age=A, area=B)), was age=A, area=B).
Migration: lactation is part of ss.Pregnancy (preg.lactating), and ss.Lactation, lactation='auto', and Module.link() are removed; ss.BreastfeedingNet reads preg.lactating.
Migration: the first state, where people start, is first= if given, else the state named S or susceptible, else the one state transmission infects people from, else the first state made (it raised); describe() says when it was guessed.
Births and deaths declared for the whole population with no disease (demographics=[ss.birth(...), ss.death(...)]) are a declared module like any other, so solver='auto' chooses for them as for any declared model (they were always agents); their results are sim.results.population.
ss.birth(rate=) and ss.death(rate=) of everyone (with no state given) read a bare number as ss.Births and ss.Deaths do: per year, and above 1 per 1,000 (ss.birth(rate=30) is 30 per 1,000 a year), with a note.
describe() shows each parameter’s bounds, each outcome’s definition, each stratification’s split and adjustments, and distributions as they were given (erlang(k=3, mean=10 days)), in plain words (“transmission, from I”, “time in I ~ …”); its solver plan is shown with verbose=True, and it leaves out step timing under the ODE, Gillespie, and tau-leaping. sim.describe() before a run no longer prints the run’s start line.
diagram() draws in a notebook and in Quarto, with values on the arrows (recovery: 8 days); str() of it is still the Mermaid text.
A MultiSim shows its progress: nothing for runs under a second, a bar for each of up to 10 slow runs, and otherwise one bar with the number of runs done; a line every tenth when the output is a file.
Dates print as 2000-01-07; a plot in a notebook no longer also prints Figure(640x480).
n_agents=None means not given (the default); n_agents=0 raises a clear error.
The Sim class holds less: building a declared model is in ss.solvers (choose.py), and the body of describe() is in display.py (sim.py is 1,840 lines, was 2,620).
Each built-in module’s docstring says whether it keeps common random numbers (“Note: CRN safe.”), and spec 11 lists them; test_crn_pairing now tests CRN directly, on ss.RandomNet(method='safe').
A run prints one line saying what it runs (Sim: sir, 10,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 100), R0, its notes, a progress bar redrawn in place, and a closing line with the time taken and each disease’s infections and peak; a MultiSim prints two lines. sim.describe() is in sections, in color in a terminal, as tables in a notebook, and as plain text otherwise.
Running a sim again runs it from the start, with any parameters changed since: sim.run() on a finished sim, and sim.run(solver='binomial', n_runs=20) on a sim built for another solver, need no sim.new(); sim.restart() builds the sim again where it can’t restart it.
Migration: sim.calibrate() is sim.fit(), and ss.contacts(bands=...) is ss.contacts(ages=..., matrix=...).
Shares by level as a dict: sir.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) (a dict was read as its keys, and its shares were dropped); ss.Disease(..., stratify=dict(age=...)).
A delivery makes its product from the product’s keywords: ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.8, at='2025-02-01'), ss.treat(cure=0.95, ...), ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, ...); an explicit product is still given for one product shared by several deliveries.
ss.parallel() takes a dict of sims by label ({'No intervention': s1, 'Vaccine': s2}); msim.summarize() is a table of each result over the runs (median, a 95% interval, mean, and standard deviation, by scenario); sim.to_data('cases', resample='week') draws data from a run, as Poisson counts, in the form ss.Sim(data=...) takes.
Docstrings, notes and error messages no longer mention Starsim 3, outside the migration tools; notes are plainer (e.g. the large-step note says how long people stay and how long a step is).
Regression: R0 (printed when a run starts, and from R0()) is the basic reproduction number, with everyone not infected susceptible; when people start immune, the run also says R at the start (R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible)).
A flow plotted against data at a longer period (weekly cases from a daily model) is shown as its totals over the data’s periods, as the fit compares them, in sim.plot(), msim.plot() (which shows the data too) and fit.plot(); msim.summarize(baseline='No intervention') gives each scenario’s difference from a baseline, run by run.
Building a second disease from the same states and transitions is safe and independent (a disease copies what another already owns); a module keeps the name of the variable it was made as, and a product made by a delivery is named vaccine (or <delivery>_product), with no warning.
sim.init() on a sim already initialized returns it; msim.sims['label']; by(...).summarize() is labeled by group; sim.hash(), ss.diff() and to_code() build a sim quietly; to_code() writes one-call deliveries and leaves out defaults.
ss.Sim(infection, recovery) (or a list of transitions, or diseases=) makes one disease from them, whose results are also at the top (sim.results.I); every module is also sim.<name> (e.g. sim.sir).
A rate can be written as the whole flow, as most other frameworks write it: S >> I @ beta*S*I/N (frequency-dependent) is beta*I, and beta*S*I (density-dependent) is beta*I.n.
