Migration: the count of each state is the result named after the state, for every module: sim.results.sir.I (was n_I), sim.results.alive (was n_alive), and res.infected for a module written as code (was n_infected); the migration script renames Starsim’s own.
Regression: a disease with a transmission seeds 1% of people by default (init_prev=0.01), unless a state is given an initial value.
Whatever is compiled says so as it starts, with how long it takes (Compiling the agent solver with Numba, estimated time: 2-10 s): for Numba only when it is not in Numba’s cache, and for JAX once a session. A first ODE run no longer compiles a helper only to time a step (1.6 s, with nothing in the cache).
The test suite is split: the core tests (tests/test_*.py, about 300, under 15 s in parallel) are what ./run_tests runs, and the slower developer tests (contracts, inference, the spec, errors, importers and exporters, and the slower tests of each feature) are in tests/devtests/, run nightly in CI. JAX runs on the CPU in the tests.
A module’s plot() takes 'states' (the default), 'flows', 'all', or the names of results, in Starsim’s style; sim.plot() leaves out results that never change.
Migration: ss.PregnancyPars is removed (ss.Pregnancy defines its own parameters, in ss.Pregnancy().pars), as are Starsim 3’s pregnancy callbacks: add_conception_callback(fn) is preg.add_callback(preg.conception, fn), and add_delivery_callback(fn) is preg.add_callback(preg.birth, fn), called with the newborns. People.find_children() is removed (ss.uids(ppl.auids[np.isin(ppl.parent, parents)])), and ss.parse_age_range() and ss.utils.apply_age_range() moved to STIsim (an age band is a condition, (ppl.age >= 15) & (ppl.age < 25), or a stratification). The migration script flags each of these.
Migration: ss.PartnerNet (a Starsim 4 prerelease) is ss.DegreeNet, of which ss.SexualNet is a subclass (adding debut and participation), so both take the same targets; ss.Requires and sim.requires(), msim.outbreaks(), and back= and cap= of ss.geo.Mobility are removed.
Regression: a compartmental pars= sweep gives one scenario per value, as agents do (it was one scenario); a draw from a posterior or prior is a run within its scenario. One object used in several places (e.g. one ss.peryear(...) in two transitions) is one parameter, and pars=dict(dur=...) sets the sim’s dur unless the model has a parameter of that name.
Migration: removed root names say what replaced them (ss.Calibration → sim.fit()), with no misleading closest-name hint; ss.uids.cat()/concat() are removed (use concatenate()); ss.MultiSim.make_run() is a method, and a subclass adds its own run options with run_options. The migration script rewrites preg.breastfeeding, uniform_targets= and ss.State(infectious=), and flags compute_transmission(), the congenital death keys, ss.People() without ages, and nested follow-ups in a test that isn’t assigned.
Migration: ss.Strains(transmit='fittest') is removed; strains are carried only in the states of an infection and those that lead back to one, so a reinfection after clearance is with the new strain alone (describe() lists them); split= takes shares by label, including sets ({'DS': 0.5, 'DS+INH': 0.5}); strains.move((A, B), (A, C)) moves between sets.
Migration: ss.Disease is again the base of every disease, declared, written as code (Starsim 3’s class X(ss.Disease) works unchanged), or a mix of both; ss.Infection(ss.Disease) adds only transmission written as code. DiseaseBase is removed.
Regression: the time index is the same in every phase of a step (sim.ti == k throughout step k, with sim.now its start), so self.results.x[self.ti] is right wherever it is written; the loop records index 0. Deliveries’ results moved one index later, run(until=) includes the step that starts at until, and ti_entry is removed.
Migration: init= is shares of people and init_n= numbers of people; the first state is first=, else a state named S/susceptible, else the first state made.
Migration: strains are part of the disease, ss.Disease(strains=ss.Strains(...)), with ss.immunity(due_to=...) replacing protected=; arrow strings are gone (move=DS >> RIF, ss.Delivery(move=S >> V), ss.transfer(risk=('low', 'high'))).
Migration: ss.SexualNet(between=) replaces sides= ('mf', 'mm', or two groups, with n_contacts by group and match=).
sim.current_scale is public again, verbose takes a fraction again, module lists take one level of nesting, and Results.flatten() keeps case.
Starsim 3’s calibration (ss.Calibration, ss.CalibComponent and its likelihoods), interventions and products (ss.RoutineDelivery, ss.CampaignDelivery, ss.BaseTest and the other base classes, ss.treat_num, ss.Dx/Tx/Vx), ss.Samples/ss.Dataset, ss.Debugger, ss.check_version, msim.extinction()/outbreaks(), sim.R0(), sim.solvers() (now part of describe()), Starsim 3’s attributes and result names of ss.Pregnancy (pregnant, ti_delivery, tri1_uids, births, n_fecund, …; set_delivery() reschedules a delivery), and the aliases and error messages kept for Starsim 3 and prerelease names are removed; the migrate-starsim3 skill and python -m starsim.converters.migrate (moved from starsim.migrate) cover each. msim.to_hub() is ss.converters.to_hub(msim). Also removed: stock targets (target=, above=, ss.share), ss.Resource, ss.cascade (give the steps as a list), ss.visit (ss.Delivery(who=...) with no product), and count_events=.
Regression: code is no longer run on a throwaway sim to choose the solver. An analyzer, a plain ss.Module, a function given as a module, and a declared disease’s own step() and functions run beside the compartments without changing it from an ODE; a function that needs agents says so when it runs, and compartmental = False on a module says it needs agents.
A sim always copies the inputs it is given, together, when it is made (copy_inputs= is removed), and no longer rewrites the functions given to it: a function reads modules from the sim it is given (lambda sim: sim.diseases.sir.I.n), not from a variable.
Regression: a smaller set of declared features has a compartmental form; the rest run as agents under auto, and a compartmental solver asked for stops before the run: fetal levels, ss.mother(), ss.Lactation, rates that read the time in a state, clocks, ss.attr, ss.update, queues, delays, .since/.count, waning by a function, events combined, deliveries to several diseases, and coupled ss.Strains. ss.Pregnancy keeps a small compartmental form when a compartmental solver is named. A follow-up of a cure got about 11% too few people as compartments.
import starsim no longer imports starsim.library; import it to use it. Another framework’s model is read with ss.import_from() and written with ss.export_to(); ss.load() and ss.save() are for Starsim’s own objects.
ss.Loop(steps=[...], times=...) runs ordinary functions with no sim (step(t, dt), and record(t) at each time point), at shared or separate times.
A sim written only as code honors unit= (it ran in years); an unknown keyword to any module names the module.
ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR no longer have new_infections and cum_infections, which repeated their infection flow and its total (res.infection, res.infection.cum); their prevalence is declared in the class as a ratio of states, as any model’s is. standard_results is removed, and a data column called new_infections is no longer matched to a declared disease’s transmission. Diseases written as code (ss.Infection, ssl.AgentSIR) keep both.
In a sim with dates, a whole year within the sim given as a number (at=2005, start=1980) is that year, since a time that long after the start would be outside the sim. A product whose delivery took its name from their shared variable is named for its kind (bcg_vaccine, not bcg_bcg), and a module passed through a helper’s interventions variable keeps its default name. ss.pars() takes a value that varies in time or by level in place of a rate or duration. Reading a result from a module given to a sim (which ran its own copy) says where the result is. The migrate script also rewrites the code cells of .ipynb, .qmd, and .md files, renames solver='stochastic', and flags f'n_{state}' and quoted 'n_<state>' names.
Migration: ss.options.kernels ('auto', 'rust', 'numba' or 'python'; STARSIM_KERNELS) replaces ss.options.compile: 'always' is 'numba', and 'never' is 'python'. @ss.jit raises when Numba can’t compile a function, rather than running it as Python, unless given nopython=False.





A binomial or Poisson draw with a NaN input or a count too large for exact draws (2^53 or more, on the side of the draw: n·p or n·(1−p) for a binomial) gives NaN: binomial(inf, p) looped forever, poisson(1e19) gave -2^63, and a NaN n or p gave 0.
A modifier’s set= of a dwell time that is a distribution gave different results run to run with the same seed (its stream’s seed held a memory address).
S >> I @ ss.gamma(...)*I works (it raised WrongDimension), as does ss.by(herd=np.array(...)) (it raised ShapeError); a one-destination split (ss.Transition(I, [F], p=[1.0], rate=...)) is a plain transition, so several compete as rates (it raised BadBranchSplit).
ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=0) makes no edges (it raised ZeroDivisionError); several Mobilitys on one dimension give a clear error; a non-reciprocal contact matrix is noted as agents too.
Density-dependent transmission (S >> I @ beta*I.n) has an R0 (R0() raised “Singular matrix”), and describe() no longer counts recovered people as infected.
Regression: each posterior draw in priors= and fit.project() has its own seed (all ran with the sim’s), so quantiles include chance; seeds in a pars= sweep are runs within a scenario, and msim.runs has a rand_seed column.
Regression: whether JAX or the kernels take a compartmental run, and whether the kernels are compiled, depend only on the model’s size, never on timing a step or on Numba’s cache (a seeded ODE run could differ at float rounding from run to run).
Regression: infectious people placed at the start transmit for their whole stay on a network, a mixing pool or beta*I well mixed (they lost the first step, and with a one-step stay never transmitted).
Regression: a declared disease’s time of entering a state (ti_X) reads as the index of the step the move happened in, for a progression as for an infection, so ti_X == self.ti is “entered this step” in code (a progression read a step early, so STIsim’s ANC testing found nobody); a scheduled exit (ti_exit_X) reads as the step it will be taken in, so np.ceil(preg.ti_exit_P) is the step of the delivery. No model’s dynamics change: the engine keeps its own times (internal()), and the clocks are unchanged. ss.Pregnancy’s ti_delivered and ti_live_birth are the step’s index, and set_delivery(uids, ti) takes the step of the delivery.
Regression: with strains.ever, agents’ protection on the course of an infection (p=, dur=, rel_trans) counted the infection’s own strain, so first infections were protected; and the traits of people made by code with people.grow() and no age= (as Starsim 3’s pregnancy and STIsim’s and HPVsim’s migration do) were drawn from a default age, so newborns got adults’ traits: they are now drawn at the next step, from the age the code set.
In a disease with strains, a rate on counts (beta*I.frac, beta*I.n) is refused with ss.errors.StrainsByCount, since new cases took the split’s strain rather than the infector’s; write beta*I. sim.new(solver=...) puts substeps= back to the new solver’s default unless it is given too, so an importer’s whole steps for the chain binomial don’t become one Runge-Kutta step for the ODE.
Regression: the chain binomial takes substeps by default so that about a tenth of a compartment at most leaves in one (substeps=1 for whole steps; the importers of discrete-time models ask for it); with a stay of about a step it was far from the ODE. The ODE no longer gives a negative flow for a count growing within a step, nor takes millions of substeps for a strain only starting to emerge.
Regression: silent wrong answers fixed in strains (ss.immunity(due_to=) of a non-infectious stage, seeding through every transmission), pregnancy (a death of another cause loses the pregnancy whether or not fetuses are agents; ss.Deaths no longer applies to fetuses), an infinite rate (now certain within the step), declared modules’ counts of their own ss.BoolStates, ss.by() of histograms, derived attributes before the first step, priority=[due, ss.ppl.age], levels outside a dimension’s where=, and calibration (parameters changed after the sim was made, one ss.par held twice, bounds lost in a package’s Pars, a time column beside the data’s index).
solver='auto' runs agents for a Weibull or gamma dwell scaled by group whose spread is too wide for stages, and for a condition on a property that is not a dimension; a per-agent read of a state in a compartmental run raises CapabilityError; JAX’s chain binomial runs on a machine whose JAX defaults to a GPU; a compartmental map between groups too big for memory is refused with its size.
preg.P.time read from code is a duration in the sim’s unit, NaN outside the state, so preg.P.time < ss.weeks(13) is right (it was true for nearly everyone).
Regression: a modifier, change or product that nothing would apply raises ss.errors.Unapplied when the sim is built; products now act on a coded disease that overrides infect(), and changes on inflows apply under the ODE.
Regression: as agents, drawn dwells are rounded to whole steps at random, keeping the mean (dur=0 stays instant); a country’s contact matrix is contacts a day whatever the sim’s unit (it was 365× too low in a sim in years).
Regression: silent wrong answers fixed in births (lost births with short dwells, ss.null parents, newborns’ ages and traits, ss.histogram draws), crossings (the ODE lost people with a fixed dwell), counts at long steps (substepped), weighted agents’ coded results, products shared between deliveries, ss.by keys, dwells after a change of level, STIsim’s aging (a setting changed before init() was overwritten), and calibration (calendar-year data, bounds lost in Pars.update(), “converged” at the start).
Many crashes in expressions (ss.by arithmetic, ratios of flows, ss.ppl in modifiers) are fixed, with one table-driven test over every solver.
Regression: a duration drawn from ss.choice of typed values (ss.choice(a=ss.weeks([...])), as dur_pregnancy is) was read as bare numbers in the sim’s unit, so it was right only when that unit was the values’ own; it is now converted.
Regression: a drawn attribute (ss.attr(dist, on=)) with typed values was drawn in steps rather than in the sim’s unit, so a comparison with a clock (preg.P.time >= anc_ga) was off by the step size.
A distribution with a named parameter (ss.bernoulli(ss.par(0.6, name='sero'))) can be drawn in an attribute (it raised a TypeError); the parameter is a parameter of the module, so pars= and a calibration set it.
A modifier that reads an attribute with init= no longer raises ClockOutsideDomain in a sim with births: the check for a NaN amount looked at the spare slots in the arrays, for people not yet born, as well as at the people alive. The error now says what has no value (a clock, or an attribute with no init=), and how to give it one.
A newborn’s level of a dimension called sex now follows the sex drawn at birth by ss.birth() (they could disagree).
ss.Pregnancy and ss.Lactation no longer set the unit of a model’s bare numbers from their own typed defaults (weeks and years), which made a model with a bare beta and a pregnancy raise IncompatibleTypes.





Interop: ss.import_from() reads two more frameworks. epipack’s reaction processes become flows, keeping how it divides by a fixed population; epymorph’s RUMEs become a stratification by place, with their parameters as resolved and their movement clauses run and averaged into commuting. Both are written as JSON by the importer, run as a script in the framework’s own environment.
Command line: starsim init after pip install starsim sets Starsim up: starsim compile compiles everything ahead of time (ss.compile(), which now also covers the agents’ code), and starsim ai installs a short starsim skill for AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code, and others), which loads the guide and skills of the installed version when used (starsim ai show). The skills are in starsim_ai/ (was ai/), installed alongside starsim. Until Starsim is compiled, importing it says so (STARSIM_UNCOMPILED_WARNING=0 to hide).
Fitting: ss.fit.profile(sim, 'beta') gives the profile likelihood of a parameter and its confidence interval (for deterministic fits); the scan before a search is capped at 100 runs by default (ss.fit.max_scan), with a note; ss.fit.optimize(target=...) finds the least total spending that reaches a target, and bounds=dict(testing=(1e5, None)) bounds each program; priors= takes the draws themselves; fit.project() runs the best fit with its own seeds when a method gives no posterior.
Interop: ss.converters.to_hub() uses the hubverse columns (origin_date=, output_type='quantile'|'sample', a scenario_id per scenario, and 'cum X' and 'peak size X' targets); the odin importer reads odin2 (capitalized draws, a built-in dt, zero_every, and data() with ~); exporting a sim that has been run (to SBML or odin) writes its initial state; sim.to_code() writes a distribution that is not Starsim’s by its name, listing it as one to define, and keeps a delivery’s when=; the EpiModel importer reads nodefactor and acts=.
Layout: the starsim/ folder holds what a modeler would read; the machinery is in starsim/internals/ (graph, presentation, spec, expressions, gradients, errors, debugtools, the command line, and the fonts in assets/) and starsim/solvers/ (the engines, with the kernels in backends/, e.g. ss.solvers.backends.passes and draws, and their Rust copy’s source in rust/, which is not part of the installed package). Importing and exporting is in starsim/converters/, where each framework’s importer, run as a script in that framework’s environment, also writes its model as JSON (EpiModel’s is dump_epimodel.R). The names are unchanged (ss.errors, ss.spec, ss.kernels, …), except that pregnancy is in demographics.py (ss.Pregnancy as before; ss.pregnancy.X is now ss.demographics.X) and Matplotlib’s handling of dates in time.py (ss.timeplot is gone). Fonts are loaded once on import (they were loaded twice).
Modeling: a declared disease whose structure depends on its arguments (a state or transition only some versions have, or transitions made in a loop) declares them in its __init__() on self, with define_states(), define_transitions(), and define_results(), which are built once it is made; define_states() still defines the arrays of a disease written as code. A sim given a stop and a dur starts at stop − dur under any unit (init_unit() set the start to 0), and a start, stop, and dur that disagree raise (the dur was dropped when a start and stop were given, so dur=10 could run 35 years).
Modeling: doc= and source= of a state, transition, or parameter are shown in describe(); memory= on a dynamic network keeps the partnerships that ended within it, so contact tracing (trace=) reaches past partners; ss.modify() acts on a contact matrix (ss.contacts('Kenya', layer='school')), and ss.contacts(place, layer=[...]) gives one per setting; an incidence in a rate raises an ss.CapabilityError that says what to write instead; a transition on= a birth (e.g. a split of newborns by the mother’s state) fires whichever module makes the children; net.check() of a network of partnerships compares it with its targets, with a row for each level; Network.mean_contacts() and Disease.states; equations() says what its symbols stand for (a contact matrix or rate, a parameter that varies in time).
Places: ss.geo.radiation(), a movement model with no parameters to fit, alongside ss.geo.gravity(); ss.geo.geography() from a GeoDataFrame or a .shp, .geojson, or .gpkg file (with geopandas); a US state by name ('United States:Massachusetts') in ss.people(), ss.contacts(), and ss.data.
ss.pars(), Disease.strats, Disease.count() (under every solver), Disease.add_callback(), .ever/.count/.since on declared transitions, a product class’s .held (e.g. where=ss.Vaccine.held), and sim.groups.level(); a compartmental sim has n_alive, new_deaths, new_emigrants and cum_deaths. compile='auto' decides from a timed plain step. ss.Births/ss.Deaths note when data’s years are more than 5 apart during the run.
ss.immunity(due_to=strains.last) and strains.ever run under the compartmental solvers too: what people remember of the strains is a dimension of the disease’s people, so Keeling and Rohani’s two strains with partial cross-immunity are exact (only scale= stays agents only); ss.Delivery(move=S >> E, strain='alpha') imports a strain on a date, under every solver; a trait (ss.attr(dist)) runs under a compartmental solver at its mean, with a note.
Two or more non-exponential dwell times out of one state for the same people (e.g. clearance against care seeking) run under the compartmental solvers: their Erlang stages race, a compartment for each combination, which is exact for the share leaving by each.
Faster: ss.by tables are built once and indexed with NumPy (FPsim-style deaths 24× faster), time-varying values are tabulated once per run, and counts run as agents do less work per step; people.auids are 64-bit again.
compile='auto' counts substeps and compiles when that would save time, saying so in one line even at verbose=0.
sim.fit() takes n_workers= and storage= (resume), fits coded modules’ settings given as ss.par, and runs one search for a deterministic one-parameter fit.
Waning shapes Starsim doesn’t build in (a box then a decay, two rates) are written as declared states in user code and run under every solver; a delivery’s move= takes several sources, and products whose waning is a function are re-dosed.
ss.Pregnancy(infant_rate=) (infant mortality); ss.State(people=False) is checked for (a forgotten one raises); describe() states the timing contract.
A beta for each route may give default, the value of the routes it does not name, e.g. beta=dict(mfnet=ss.peract(0.01), msm=ss.peract(0.1), default=0); the names that are not routes of the sim are then not used, with a note. Without default, a beta dict still names every route and no other. Under every solver, in describe(), the model spec, and ss.to_code(), and for diseases written as code (e.g. ss.SIS(beta=dict(...))). A bare zero in a rate (e.g. ss.par(0.0)) no longer needs unit= when the typed values have different units.
Migration: ss.Pregnancy is the declared pregnancy (NP and P, conception, abortion, losses by gestational age, under every solver), with fetuses as agents when something reads them (fetus='auto', ss.mother(), ss.child), ss.Lactation, burn-in, tfr/asfr, preterm births (rr_ptb, rr_ptb_age, gestation_at_birth, preterm), and Starsim 3’s attributes (a writable ti_delivery reschedules deliveries), results (with mmr, n_fecund, n_fertile, n_susceptible) and callbacks; women pregnant at the start count that pregnancy in n_pregnancies. Starsim 3’s pregnancy written as code is removed: ss.LegacyPregnancy raises an error pointing to ss.Pregnancy, and python -m starsim.converters.migrate rewrites it (and flags overrides of the old module’s methods).
ss.mother(cond, born=True) reads a condition on the mother of anyone who has one, not only the unborn: who=preg.birth & ss.mother(anc.positive.since <= ss.years(1), born=True) reaches the newborns of mothers who tested positive in the last year. No mother is false; a dead mother is in none of her states, but her memory is still read. Agents only. Memory and events read inside ss.mother() are now kept, and ss.mother() prints.
An attribute drawn at an event with bins= (ss.attr(dist, on=..., bins=3, combine='max'), e.g. antibodies at clearance) runs under the compartmental solvers, as levels of a dimension that its events move people between. Other attributes are still agents only.
Births driven by a flow (ss.birth(per=preg.delivery)) run under the compartmental solvers, so the declared ss.Pregnancy does too (losses by gestational age, abortion, deliveries over a distribution of durations, parity as a counter, and other modules’ ss.on(preg.conception)). Burn-in, ss.Lactation, and the unborn run too: what ss.mother() reads is a fetal level of the pregnant compartments, moved between by the fetal transitions, and routed at delivery and birth (stillbirths, neonatal deaths, or the state children are born into). Transmission over MaternalNet runs as a fetal transition; over BreastfeedingNet it is still agents only.
The time in a state (P.time) runs under the compartmental solvers where an exit out of that state reads it (as P.dwell does), e.g. the declared pregnancy’s losses by gestational age; read anywhere else, it still runs as agents.
A test with several results (ss.Diagnostic(results=...)) also has the outcomes positive (any result but the last) and negative (the last), so a step after it reads the same as after a test with two.
Triggers (ss.on()) on states and strata under the compartmental solvers: where one holds, arrivals pass straight through, including on another disease’s state (tracked jointly); ss.on(other.tr) and ss.on(other.tr.to(X)) are synchronized flows. ss.spread seeds as compartments; ss.attr and ss.func (values per person, functions at events) and ss.birth(per=) as agents; undriven=True on a transition; ss.state('mod.X').enter; save and load mid-run as agents.
dur=0 on a transition is immediate under every solver (a junction holds nobody, and costs nothing as an ODE); dur=0 with where= and on= a condition pass people straight through under the compartmental solvers, and on= an event of the same disease moves them at the end of each step. An immediate split with only p= raises saying to give it dur=0.
delay= on any triggered step: the people triggered receive it after the delay if still eligible, under every solver (agents: also a distribution). ss.screen(delay=) is the step’s delay; the time to a test’s result is ss.Diagnostic(delay=).
disease= of a delivery takes a list, and a disease written as code (as agents: tests detect infected, cures call clear_infection(), vaccines scale rel_sus and rel_trans).
The standard prevalence of the library’s diseases can be selected by group, as a ratio (ss.SIS(...).prevalence.select(risk='high')).
ss.transfer(dur=<distribution>) draws each person’s time on reaching the level it moves from (agents), as Erlang stages under compartmental solvers; ss.transfer(method=('none', ['pill', 'iud']), p=[0.6, 0.4], dur=...) moves people to one of several levels.
Several non-exponential dwell times out of one state run under compartmental solvers when each has a where= for other people, e.g. by sex.
after= an event (after=preg.delivery), with dur= for a time after it, for an exact dwell until something else happens (agents); dur=fn warns that it is exponential and points to ss.constant(fn).
ss.Deaths(lifetable=) takes life tables by year and sex; ss.peryear(fn) for a function whose numbers are per year.
A fitted movement between places (ss.geo.Mobility(away=ss.par(...)), gravity k, a, b, c) is worked out again on sim.restart(pars=...), so run(n_runs=), ss.parallel(pars=), PMCMC, IF2 (away=), NUTS and sim.gradient() work with it (before, the restart raised).
ss.DegreeNet(match=dict(risk=0.9, region=0.7)): a share within each of several properties (results match_<name>), and the share is now kept at its target despite people left over.
ss.SexualNet and lasting ss.DegreeNet run under the ODE, binomial, and Gillespie solvers by the partnership approximation (sides by sex need sim.stratify(sex=['female', 'male'])): close to agents for risk groups with short partnerships, 25% high for long monogamous ones, and far too low with concurrency (0.13 to 0.19 of agents for a gonorrhea-like model).
ss.immunity(due_to=R, rel_sus=m, combine='max'|'sum'|'multiply'|fn): protection between strains, combined by a rule, for ss.Strains.
init_prev= takes a function of the sim (and the agents) or an ss.by over people’s own properties (as agents), for a disease with any number of destinations.
ss.peract: a probability per act on networks with acts (ss.SexualNet, ss.DegreeNet(acts=...)), the same at any time step, with directions named from the network’s sides (ss.peract(m2f=0.3, f2m=0.15), or {('m', 'f'): 0.3}; net.directions lists them).
ss.modify(..., efficacy=, share=, route=), for condoms, microbicides and needle programs (ss.modify(ng.infection, efficacy=0.9, share=use, route='mfnet')); ss.contacts(matrix, dims=['sex', 'risk']); ss.DegreeNet(where=) and ss.SexualNet(between=(a, b)) for networks among some people and two-mode networks.
Counters: increment= on transitions, deliveries and transfers (increment='parity' adds 1, increment=dict(parity=2) for twins); clocks: stratify(since_birth=ss.months([0, 3, 12]), kind='clock'), set with move=dict(since_birth=0); p= entries with a to axis normalized over the destinations. Exact under every solver.
Care cascades as steps: ss.screen(who=due, what=cytology, ...), ss.treat(who=screening.positive, what=ablation, ...); who= takes conditions, events, |, &, or a list with operator=; ss.Delivery(who=...) is a step with no product. Every delivery, outcome, product and ss.Event has memory, .ever, .count, and .since. ss.Pregnancy fires conception, delivery and loss. cure= takes a number or a dict by state.
Steps of a cascade can be served in an order and limited: priority= (conditions in tiers, or a score highest first), and queue= (people not served wait, up to a time, then are the outcome never_ran).
ss.Treatment(moves=...) moves people along named (often undriven, cure = A + C >> S) transitions of one or several diseases, with results for each; a transition triggered by an outcome (ss.Transition('I -> R_res', on=drug.failed, p=0.05)) moves those people when it happens, under every solver.
ss.Diagnostic(results=dict(high_grade=..., ascus=..., normal=None)) for tests with several results (each an event and a result), sensitivity by states of several diseases with combine='worst'|'max', and a delay for each result; ss.Vaccine(efficacy=dict(hpv16=0.95, hpv18=0.9)) and doses=[0.6, 1.0]; vx.held as a condition.
From the v4-rs branch: events of transitions and states (tr.to(B), X.enter, (A | B).exit), clocks (X.time, X.progress), ss.on() triggers, ss.stay, distributions with ss.by parameters (ragged Erlang stages as compartments), typed coverage (ss.probperyear(0.5)), routine delivery once per spell of being eligible (ss.Delivery.spells), and a declared pregnancy (now ss.Pregnancy, above).
Regression: as agents, exits are scheduled when people enter a state, and people entering in the state-change row face half a step of its hazards; results at a step as long as a dwell move (e.g. an SIS with a one-year dwell at a step of a year), and random streams move.
A death has one cause per person, kept in people.cause_of_death; when several modules claim the same person in a step, one is chosen at random.
Each destination of a transition with several has a flow result of its own, res.<transition>.<state> (e.g. res.cin.X, also res['cin.X'] and res.cin.select(to='X')), under every solver and by group, summing to the transition’s flow. It can be the source of an outcome (ss.outcome(0.8*cin.X)) and a data column (cin.X) for fitting.
A state’s time in it, P.dwell, can be read in p= of a transition with several destinations out of it (decided as people leave) and in the rate of a transition out of it, e.g. ss.Transition(P, [C, R], dur=..., p=[1 - np.exp(-k*P.dwell), None]), under every solver. Under the compartmental solvers the state becomes a conveyor of whole steps by time in it, exact to the step; describe() says how many compartments. A function reads the same time as disease.P.dwell[uids].
ss.ppl.<name> refers to any property of people, in conditions and now in rates: a property is each person’s value and a condition is 1 or 0, so a regression is an expression (rate=ss.peryear(1)*expit(b0 + b_urban*ss.ppl.urban); SciPy’s expit is allowed). A property that is not a dimension runs as agents (with a note), and raises CapabilityError under an explicit compartmental solver. ss.People.age still works.
ss.by over a property of people: values by label (ss.by(sex=dict(female=..., male=...)), with or without a sex dimension), tables whose numeric column is lower bin edges (averaged over each group in a compartmental run, with a note), a None row for people with no value, outer products of ss.by over different dimensions, and a dwell given as an ss.by of distributions. ss.by(sex=[a, b]) without a sex dimension raises MissingDimension naming the keyed form.
The movement between places can be fitted: ss.geo.Mobility(away=ss.par(...)) and the gravity model’s k, a, b, c; each value tried builds the mixing again (before, a TypeError at init). sim.restart(pars=...) with a new value of one raises.
acquisition=True/False on ss.Transition, ss.progression(), and ss.transmission() says outright whether a transition is an acquisition. ss.states(n, people=False).
One destination of a transition with several can be modified or protected against: ss.modify('hpv.progression.C', multiply=0.5) or ss.Vaccine(efficacy={'progression.C': 0.5}) scales the chance of going to C, not the rate of leaving.
ss.Disease is the one disease class: a subclass that declares no states, transitions, or outcomes is written as code and runs as Starsim 3’s ss.Disease did (super().__init__(), then define_pars(), define_states(), step()); one with no states and no step() or step_state() raises ss.CapabilityError at init. ss.Infection subclasses ss.Disease.
python -m starsim.converters.migrate <path> rewrites Starsim 3 code for Starsim 4 in place (renames, the network’s name with ss.PrenatalNet, a fractional verbose, annualize(), the bases of diseases written as code, and the time index in step(), update_results(), and analyzers), and lists what needs a person; the migrate-starsim3 skill starts from it.
Removed methods of Starsim 3 (Result.annualize(), MultiSim.reduce(), mean(), median(), reset()) raise an error that says what to write instead, rather than a bare AttributeError.
Delays: a fixed delay (ss.constant as a dwell time) is exact in compartmental runs, as a conveyor of whole steps rather than 50 Erlang stages: odin’s 14-day SEIR agrees with odin within 0.25% at a step of a day (1.6% with 200 stages before), in milliseconds rather than seconds. after= and before= (minimum stays) run as compartments by the same conveyor, and the chain binomial agrees with agents step for step. ss.update(count, value) sets a count each step to a value worked out from the model at the start of the step, as odin’s update() of a variable that is not a flow (a lag, a running maximum), in the kernels, in JAX, and as agents.
Inference: method='if2' gives the maximum-likelihood values of a stochastic compartmental sim by iterated filtering (Ionides et al. 2015, as pomp’s mif2() and camdl): each particle of the filter carries its own parameter values, perturbed by a shrinking random walk; four chains from different starts, with fit.converged when they end at the same log-likelihood. On camdl’s SIR it gives camdl’s estimates in about the same time. Parameters of how the data are observed, and of the starting values, are not fitted by IF2 yet (the error points to method='pmcmc').
ss.ppl.age < 15 (and .female, .alive) is a condition written with no people made (ss.People.age is removed).
Docs: “Starsim 4 in ten minutes” (docs/ten_minutes.qmd), the whole workflow on one page, with using Starsim from R; a Starsim 3 to 4 migration guide (docs/migration/v3_v4.md); the tutorials and user guide ported to Starsim 4; and a “Coming from” page for each of 13 frameworks (docs/coming_from/), with its failing rows. The ‘Coming from’ pages have a page for models written as NumPy loops, in place of the measles metapop page.
Programs and budgets: the Atomica importer reads a program book (progbook=, programs_start=): each program’s spending is a parameter, its coverage is the people its spending reaches over everyone it targets, and the parameters it affects move towards its outcomes with coverage. ss.fit.optimize(sim, maximize=..., at=..., start=...) reallocates spending between programs to maximize (or minimize) a result, keeping the total; on Atomica’s HIV demo it finds Atomica’s optimum in about as long. (S + I).total is the number in some states in the whole population (every place, where .n is the same place).
Inference: method='abc-smc' gives a posterior without a likelihood; method= a list runs staged fitting, each stage starting from the last; sim.sensitivity() gives partial rank correlations over samples within the bounds; ss.binom() and ss.bernoulli() are likelihoods; ss.parallel(sim, priors=True) draws the parameters from their priors; fit.project(scenarios) runs scenarios with the posterior’s draws; msim.to_df(quantiles=) and msim.to_hub() write runs as quantiles and as a forecast hub submission; Optuna fits give the spread of their best trials as an indication of uncertainty; sim.log_density() gives the log-density in JAX as a function, with its gradient by reverse mode. A parameter with a value per level (ss.par(ss.by(patch=[...]), bounds=)) is fitted level by level, with the same bounds and prior (fit.pars.beta is an ss.by; one level can be set by name, pars={'beta[a]': 0.3}); so are a modifier’s amount given as an ss.par (which can then be set by name), and typed values with typed bounds (ss.par(ss.days(8), bounds=[ss.days(3), ss.weeks(4)])).
States and transitions: ss.Disease can now be built from ss.State and ss.Transition objects, written with operators (S >> I @ beta * I) or explicitly (ss.Transition(S, I, rate=beta * I)). Also ss.states(), ss.null (for inflows and outflows), ss.birth(), ss.death(), ss.immigration() (a number arriving per unit time, at ages like the population’s) and ss.emigration() (as ss.death(), but agents are recorded as emigrants), and ss.par() (a named parameter with bounds). States that no transition connects to the first state (e.g. a water reservoir) are counts, not people, and are real numbers under every solver. A rate can use NumPy functions of counts (np.clip(0.5 * I.frac, 0, 0.02)) and comparisons (Q.n < 20); a set of states is their sum (Ih / (Ia | Is | Ih)); where= on a transition limits it to some people.
Solvers: ss.Sim(solver=...) runs these models with 'ode', 'binomial', 'gillespie', or 'abm'; the default, 'auto', uses an ODE if every part of the model has a compartmental form, and agents otherwise. Dwell times that are not exponential are run as Erlang stages in a compartmental run, with a note. ss.erlang() and ss.truncnorm() are new distributions. Values can vary in time (ss.timeseries(), ss.seasonal()); the ODE takes them at each stage of a step. The first run after installing says that the solver kernels are being built (one or two minutes, once).
Sim: the first argument of ss.Sim can be the model (a module or a list of modules). If nothing in a declared model has a unit, time is counted in timesteps; unit= sets the unit of bare numbers (if the typed values have different units and there are no bare numbers, the smallest is used, with a note, ss.errors.UnitInferred; bare numbers alongside typed values in different units raise ss.errors.IncompatibleTypes, asking for unit=). New methods: sim.describe() (which also says which solvers can run the sim), sim.hash(), sim.to_spec() (the normalized form of a declared model, for sim.hash() and ss.diff()), sim.new(), and (for diseases) describe(), diagram(), equations(), R0(), and transitions.
Stratification: sir.stratify(age=[0, 15, 65], adjust=...), sim.stratify(), and ss.transfer() split a model by a property of people; ss.contacts(ages=..., matrix=...) makes mixing pools from a contact matrix; result.select() and result.by() read stratified results; ss.by() gives a value per level, for one or several dimensions (as a product, a table, or an array with named axes, any of whose values can be a time series, with arithmetic), and split=ss.by(...) splits the population over several dimensions at once (or, for a dimension of some states only, gives the share entering each level for each level of another, e.g. severity by age); adjust= can also scale rel_trans and rel_sus by level; where= stratifies some groups only (sir.stratify(age=[15, 25, 35, 50], where=dict(sex='female'))), and people outside them have no level of it, so selecting a level leaves them out. People age between age groups.
Strains: ss.Disease(strains=ss.Strains(...)) gives a disease strains, which people can carry several of at once (max_strains=2, with sets such as 'DS+INH'). Someone who carries several passes on each in proportion to its infectiousness, and someone infected with a strain they do not carry carries it as well, e.g. through a transmission that leaves people in their state (superinfection = L >> L @ beta*I). A transition can also change a person’s strains with move= (move=DS >> (DS, RIF)), and ss.immunity(due_to=...) gives the protection between strains.
Places: a stratification by place (sir.stratify(patch=ss.geo.geography(...))) mixes people within each place, with commuting, visiting, or migration between places from a movement model (ss.geo.gravity(), ss.geo.radiation()) or a matrix (ss.geo.Mobility()), or with the force of infection itself moving between places, as in LASER (kind='force'). A contact matrix by age acts within each place; as agents, so do a contact matrix, a mixing pool of everyone, and a random network, as in a compartmental run (people contact others where they live, or where they commute to). ss.geo.Mobility(data=...) is a register of people moved between places (or between states, with to_states), added, and removed on given dates, as in SimInf’s scheduled events. away= rescales movement so that every place has that share of its people’s time away.
Partnerships: ss.DegreeNet() is a network of partnerships that form and dissolve, described by targets for the number of partners people have at a time (n_contacts, concurrency, max_contacts), the share of partnerships between people at the same level of a property (match=dict(risk=0.9)), and how long partnerships last, as in EpiModel (allowing for partnerships ended by deaths); net.check() compares the network it makes with the targets. ss.DegreeNet(n_contacts=ss.by(risk=[...])) gives each level its own number of partners, as EpiModel’s nodefactor, and net.check() also reports how long partnerships last; with acts=, beta is per act, as EpiModel’s act rate. ss.SexualNet takes the same targets for the number of partners (n_contacts, concurrency, max_contacts, match=), between men and women (or men, between='mm'). Networks can be given by name (networks=dict(main=..., casual=...)).
Results and fitting: a transition divided by something in a result is its flow (incidence = infection / S), by group too. ss.outcome() declares reported quantities (with a weight, delay, duration, and reporting period), which are stratified like the flows they come from; ss.simdata() matches data to results by name; sim.fit() fits every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data, wherever it is used (in a rate, an initial count, or a seasonal value), returning an ss.fit.Fit. A likelihood on an outcome (likelihood=ss.nbinom(n=k)) or given to sim.fit(likelihood=...) makes the fit maximize the likelihood, fitting the likelihood’s own parameters too; ss.fit.compare_models() compares models by how well they predict held-out data. A stochastic compartmental sim (solver='binomial', 'tau', or 'gillespie') whose data series all have a likelihood is fitted by particle MCMC (method='pmcmc'): a random-walk Metropolis sampler on the likelihood as estimated by a particle filter (ss.fit.ParticleFilter), which samples the exact posterior; the particles are stepped together by the kernels, each chain chooses how many it needs in its warm-up, and the chains run in parallel. An agent-based sim is fitted by Optuna, as before (a best fit, not a posterior).
Modifiers and conditions: ss.modify() changes a named quantity (a parameter, a transition’s rate, sir.rel_sus, or sir.rel_trans) while a condition holds, for everyone or for the people selected by where=; ss.change() changes one at given times; sim.what_modifies() lists what acts on a quantity. hold= keeps a modifier on for someone for a while once its condition holds for them, and tr.incidence(over=, by=) is a condition on how many went through a transition over a window, as a share of the people at the same level of a stratification, so that each place can apply a rule on its own (MEmilio’s dynamic NPIs). A modifier that depends only on time, and on who it applies to only through states and stratifications (where=hiv.acute), is worked out before the run, as is a transfer at a constant rate, so a compartmental run stays in one call to the kernels. Conditions are written against the people and modules themselves ((ppl.age > 65) & sir.S) and are evaluated when the sim runs (ss.conditions.Cond), or are functions of the sim. A condition in one disease on a state of another (ss.modify(hiv.rel_trans, multiply=3, where=syph.I)) also works in a compartmental run: the states of the two diseases are then tracked jointly, as a dimension of the sim for each (so hiv.results.n_I.by('syph') splits HIV by syphilis state), and the two have the same people, as agents do. A dimension of some states of one of them (e.g. a strain of its infected states) is allowed. As an ODE, diseases tracked jointly take a whole run together (each taking each step in turn, as they do step by step), so they can be restarted, differentiated, and fitted by NUTS. A modifier on a transition chosen with p= (one of several branches out of a state) changes its probability, and the other branches share the rest; a vaccine’s efficacy against such a transition (efficacy=dict(severe=0.75)) does the same. ss.modify('school.pars.n_contacts', multiply=0.2) changes the contacts of a network, under every solver (as agents, each contact then happens with that probability in a step). As agents, sir.current_value('rel_sus') gives the values with the active modifiers applied (reading sir.rel_sus gives the base), and with ss.Sim(track_writes=True), sim.what_modifies() also lists the modules that assigned rel_sus or rel_trans directly.
Modifiers of coded parameters: ss.modify() works on the parameters of a disease written as code, which reads the modified value from self.pars; where it differs between people, the disease reads self.current_value('x', uids) and lists the parameter in allow_modifiers. current_value() also works on the parameters of a declared disease.
Interventions: ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, and ss.Treatment are products, delivered by ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat() in rounds, routinely, on an event (on=sir.infection), or by a function, with where=, coverage=, and capacity=; a follow-up is a step of its own (ss.treat(..., who=screening.positive)). trace= delivers to the contacts, in a network, of the people selected, for contact tracing and partner notification (agents only). ss.transfer() with delivery keywords moves people along a stratification; a transfer can be the target of ss.modify(). A delivery’s results can be selected by stratum. These run under every solver: holding a product is a per-agent property in an agent-based run and a stratification in a compartmental one. A test’s delay= and a product whose protection fades by a function of time (waning=lambda t: ...) now work in a compartmental run too: people wait for their result, or hold the product, in levels of one or more steps. ss.death(lifetable=ss.lifetable(ages, deaths)) draws each person’s age at death once from a life table as agents, and is a death rate for each age group in a compartmental run stratified by age; a delivery with move= and capacity= seeds a number of people on a schedule. As agents, a transition can wait for a minimum stay in its source state (after=), apply only during one (before=, as EMULSION’s escape), and ss.birth(NB, per=tr, n=3) gives each person who goes through a transition newborns; the EMULSION importer translates minimum stays as after=. ss.vaccinate(move=S >> V) moves the people reached from one state to another (a one-off campaign), ss.Vaccine(leaky=False) fully protects a share efficacy of those who receive it and leaves the rest unprotected, and at_age= delivers routinely as people reach an age.
Scenarios and runs: ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=100), sim.run(n_runs=100), and ss.parallel(baseline=..., vaccine=...) return a MultiSim whose results have a run dimension (msim.results.sir.n_I.quantiles(), or by group, msim.results.sir.n_I.select(age='0-4')); msim.diff('baseline') gives the difference of each scenario from a baseline. ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(beta=[0.2, 0.3, 0.4])) runs a sim with each set of parameter values (msim.run_pars has the values of each run).
Importing models: ss.import_from(file, format=...) reads a model from EMULSION, odin, SBML, SimInf, flepiMoP, summer2, Atomica, camdl, EpiModel, epydemix, or MEmilio (its ODE models) into a sim (the format is told from the file where it can be), prints how each rate was read, and lists what it could not translate (ss.errors.ImportIncomplete, also in sim.imported). sim.to_code() writes any sim as a Python file that builds it again, and ss.diff(a, b) compares two models in their own terms. The import-model and validate-import skills (in starsim_ai/) cover what does not map one to one, and check a port against its original.
Exporting models: ss.export_to(sim, 'sbml', 'sir.xml') writes a sim as SBML or odin, and lists what the format cannot carry (ss.errors.LossyExport); SBML and odin exports read back with ss.import_from().
Named data: ss.people('Kenya', year=2024) gives a country’s population (its size, age structure, and sex ratio, from the UN World Population Prospects), for agents or as the size and age split of a compartmental model; ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1) gives a country’s administrative units (names, populations, centroids, distances, and borders) for a spatial stratification, and ss.contacts('Kenya', layer='home') its contact matrix by age, both from starsim_data, bundled for every country at the first two levels (finer levels and other years are fetched). Where the data came from is in describe(), the model spec, and the hash.
JAX and gradients: an ODE can be run in JAX (the same RK4 steps as the kernels; JAX is a dependency), which sim.gradient(), sim.log_density(), gradient fits, and ss.parallel() with many sets of values use without being asked. sim.gradient() gives the derivative of results with respect to parameters, by automatic differentiation of the run, and sim.fit() on an ODE now fits by L-BFGS-B with these gradients (Nelder-Mead for one or two parameters, or where the run has no gradient). ss.parallel(sim, pars=...) with many sets of values takes all the runs in one call to JAX. sim.fit() on an ODE whose data series all have a likelihood now gives a posterior, from the No-U-Turn sampler (BlackJAX; method='nuts', or method='l-bfgs-b' for the maximum likelihood, as before): the log-density (the run, the results with data, the likelihood, and the priors) is one function in JAX, differentiated in forward mode, so the whole of the sampling is compiled, and the chains run on cores of their own (Starsim gives JAX a device for each core when it imports it). The priors are the parameters’ prior= (uniform over their bounds by default), and the fit has the draws (fit.samples), each parameter’s median, 95% interval, rank-normalized R-hat, and bulk effective sample size, and a band over the posterior in fit.plot(). The log-density covers several diseases, including diseases tracked jointly, and outcomes that people stay in; a model it does not cover yet is sampled with Python in the loop, which is much slower. Data by stratum is given in long form, with columns named after dimensions (age) saying which stratum each row is for; each result and stratum is a series (n_I[age=0-14]), compared with res.n_I.select(age='0-14'). A fit notes parameters that the data cannot tell apart (ss.errors.Unidentifiable): ones that appear in the model only multiplied together (or one divided by the other), with the product the data determine; ones almost perfectly correlated over a posterior; and, for a fit by gradients, ones that change the fitted results in almost the same way at the best fit. What JAX compiles is kept for later sessions, in ~/.cache/starsim/jax (unless JAX_COMPILATION_CACHE_DIR says otherwise). In the JAX run, flows are added up with matrices rather than at indices, which makes a gradient about twice as fast.
Births and deaths: births, deaths, and migration of everyone are declared once for the population, in ss.Sim(demographics=[ss.birth(rate=...), ss.death(rate=...)]), and run under every solver; the same people are born into and die from every disease. Births or deaths of everyone declared in more than one disease raise DuplicateDeclaration. birth_rate= and death_rate= on ss.Sim are removed; demographics=True is declared births and deaths at 20 and 10 per 1,000 per year.
Deliveries: a delivery’s schedule and target use the keywords of ss.change and ss.modify: at= (was years=/dates=) and where= (was eligible=); on= takes events only. ss.vaccinate(), ss.treat(), and ss.screen() can make their own product from its keywords (ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.7, at=[2025])). A move delivered to some people is ss.Delivery(move=dict(...), coverage=..., at=[...]); ss.transfer() is movement at a rate, part of the model.
Several sources: a transition with several sources is written with a sum, S + I + R >> D @ mu (no parentheses needed); | on states is a condition (where=sir.I | sir.R), and (S | I) >> D or 0.3*(Ia | Is) raises an error that says to write the sum. ss.states() always returns a list (S, = ss.states(1)). Arrow strings keep | ('S | I -> D').
Fits and plots: fit.divergences, fit.acceptance, and fit.band are fit.diagnostics.divergences, .acceptance, and .band; the column of fit.trials that holds what was minimized is objective (it was mismatch; fit.measure says what it is). sim.plot() and msim.plot() are drawn by one function, sim.results.plot(): msim.plot() has sim.plot()’s titles and figure size, and sim.plot() matches data columns to results as fit() does. Inside, fit() is a Problem and a registry of methods (ss.calibration.methods), and the code for data and results is in results.py.
Code layout: Starsim’s internal modules are reorganized, with every ss. name unchanged: solvers.py is a package (engine, mixing, compartmental, crossing, agents, choose), transitions.py is split into expressions.py, transitions.py, graph.py, display.py, and dimensions.py (with ss.by, ss.timeseries, and ss.seasonal in parameters.py, and ss.geo, ss.gravity, and ss.Mobility in networks.py), and dates are in dates.py; ss.solvers.X still finds every name it did, and the names moved out of transitions.py are spelled by their new modules (ss.expressions.Expr, ss.graph.Graph, ss.dimensions.Strat). A sim’s stratifications and groups are sim.groups (ss.dimensions.Groups), and the solver is chosen by ss.solvers.choose_solver(sim); sim.strats, sim.n_groups, sim.group_levels, sim.group_coords, sim.dim_index(), and sim.level_raw() still work, and the other group attributes and methods (e.g. sim.groups_changed()) are now on sim.groups.
Namespace: the engines and other internals are reached through their submodules (ss.solvers.Compartmental, ss.solvers.Agents, ss.solvers.Crossing, ss.expressions.Expr, ss.graph.Graph, ss.dimensions.Strat, ss.conditions.Cond, ss.diseases.InfectionLog, ss.run.MultiResults), not ss.. What ss. exports is the vocabulary of the specification, the classes and helpers that modules written as code use, and the error classes, checked by tests/test_spec.py. Internal helpers are no longer at the top level: ss.link_dists, make_dist, dist_list, scale_types, rand_raw, Dists (now ss.distributions.X), load_fonts (ss.settings), module_map, module_types, find_modules (ss.modules), linear_interp, linear_accum, step_containing (ss.calibration), load_pars (ss.parameters), validate_sim_data (ss.results), metadata (ss.debugtools), apply_age_range, find_contacts (ss.utils). python -m starsim.converters.migrate rewrites the old names. The phases of Sim.init() that no package overrides are private (sim._init_time(), _init_dists(), _init_rescale(), _init_modules_pre(), _init_people_vals(), _init_modules_post(), _init_solver(), _init_unit(), _init_flows(), _init_named_people(), _init_lifetables()). init_people(), init_module_attrs(), init_results(), and init_data() stay public.
One spelling each: ss.stratify(model, ...) is removed (use model.stratify(...)), and stratifying again in the same way does nothing, with a note. ss.RandomExactNet is ss.RandomNet(method='exact') and uniform_targets=True is method='uniform'; ss.RandomSafeNet is ss.RandomNet(method='safe'); ss.ClusterNet, ss.HybridNet, and ss.MSMNet moved to the library (ssl.), and ssl.HybridNet makes schools and workplaces clusters by default (clustered=False for random networks); the ss.Route export is removed (ss.MaternalNet is kept); ss.MFNet(duration=) is dur=. ss.contacts(matrix, age=edges) is ss.contacts(matrix, bands=edges). track_writes= is removed (sim.what_modifies() lists the declared modifiers), and current_value() of a per-person quantity in a compartmental run raises an error that says only agents have it. The migrate-starsim3 skill maps each old spelling.
E.stays: how long each person who has been through a state stayed there (e.g. np.mean(seir.E.stays), the mean latent period), by default for any state whose time of entering is kept, and right when people later return by another path (e.g. a relapse). ss.options.keep_times = True also keeps each transition’s history (sir.infection.count, .since, .ever).
ss.move(where=) moves only the people a condition holds for (e.g. where=ss.ppl.age < 5), under every solver; ss.RandomNet(remove_self_loops=).
starsim.library.econ: ssl.Costs (an analyzer adding up delivery, per-event and fixed costs as results, with a total), ssl.DALYs, ssl.discount(), and ssl.ICER (incremental cost-effectiveness ratios across scenarios, after they have run or as a sim runs).
ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate='Nigeria') reads a country’s age-specific fertility rates from the UN World Population Prospects, as ss.Births and ss.Deaths read theirs (ss.data.rates(place, 'fertility')); this needs starsim_data 2.1.0.
A delivery takes a transition by its path in on= (on='measles.births'), and one whose where= names a disease’s own groups (where=measles.age < 15) is for that disease without disease=.
ss.parallel() runs sims with different steps, plotting each on its own time axis; what needs the runs put together (medians, bands, summaries) raises an error saying why.
sim.results.I finds a result in a sim’s only disease, and msim.results.I and msim.plot('I') in each sim’s one disease, even when the diseases are named differently (sir, seir); msim.sims.items(), and the sims of a sweep are labeled by their values.
sim.summarize('sir.infection') and msim.summarize('sir.infection') give one result’s summary; res.df is res.to_df(); for the runs of several scenarios, res.summarize() is a dict by scenario.
Plots of results return the figure when not shown (also in Jupyter), plot into a figure given with fig=/ax= so results can be overlaid, and take filename= and log=True; fit.plot() and comparison.plot() use Starsim’s style and date ticks.
ss.options.jax (or STARSIM_JAX) chooses the platform JAX runs on, e.g. 'cpu' for a GPU that JAX can’t use.
sim.summarize() and msim.summarize() take how='max' and how='min', and an unknown how= is an error rather than N/A in the table.
fit.plot(residuals=True) adds the residuals (data minus model, lined up as the fit compares them) below each result.
In a starting value (init, init_n, init_prev), an ss.by dict by label may leave levels out, which start at 0, e.g. init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch={'Nairobi': 10})); a rate or other parameter by label still needs every level, and a key that is not a level is an error.
ss.data.population() and ss.data.contacts() return dataframes labeled by age group (e.g. ss.data.contacts('Kenya', layer='school').loc['10-14', '10-14']), with where the data came from in .attrs['ref'], instead of tuples; ss.contacts() takes such a table.
A distribution with a unit draws in that unit outside a sim with no setup (ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10)).rvs(1000) is in days), plot_hist() labels its axis with the unit, and its repr shows what it was made from (ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10))).
A stratification named like places (patch, region, district, …) given only names and no contacts by it, so that its levels mix as one population, gives a note saying how to make them places (kind='space', or a geography).
The note for a data column that matches no result gives the code to rename it, with the closest result filled in (aliases=dict(cases='reported')).





Regression: as agents, the engine’s draws are keyed by stream, step, and round of moves (not by how many times a stream has been called), so a run doesn’t depend on how a round’s work is batched; results with a seed differ from before, and agree statistically. STARSIM_CHECK_DRAWS=1 checks that no agent is drawn twice from a stream in a round.
Regression: as agents, people infected by transmission have half a step of exits at their first draw, as other arrivals do, so a model in which infection leads straight to an infectious state no longer runs as if R0 were R0 × (1 − γ·dt/2) at coarse steps (an SIR with an 8-day recovery at an 8-day step: an attack rate of 0.77, was 0.07; the ODE’s is 0.80). Models with a latent state are unchanged. The recorded prevalence reads about γ·dt/2 high at coarse steps, since stocks are recorded after the step’s infections.
on_positive=/on_negative= are removed (a follow-up is a step of its own: who=screening.positive); ss.Test is now ss.Diagnostic, and the result diagnosed is positive. ss.People.age etc. are removed: use ss.ppl.age. python -m starsim.converters.migrate rewrites nested follow-ups and mf beta pairs.
On networks with acts, rel_trans, rel_sus, source weights and modifiers multiply the hazard of each act (beta 0.03 with rel_trans=10 gives 0.263 per act); ss.MFNet’s acts are a rate (lognormal, mean 80 a year), kept as real acts per step, so results no longer depend on the time step; a typed rate as beta on such a network (including ss.SIS’s and ss.SIR’s defaults on ss.MFNet) raises WrongDimension; a beta pair in a declared disease raises. Mother-to-child networks transmit one way.
ss.Deaths and ss.Births hold each period’s rate until the next (not the nearest year); ss.Births picks parents from women aged 15 to 49; ss.Pregnancy gives women 46 to 49 the 45–49 rate, reads p_loss per week of pregnancy, and applies rr_ptb to the preterm share; the unborn are left out of the people counts (results.pregnancy.n_unborn) and are not seeded; deaths claimed by two modules in a step are counted once.
Newborns are born in their mother’s place, and a sex dimension follows the newborn’s sex; a split over age and another dimension given as shares within each age group keeps people’s ages.
adjust= on a branch chosen with p= scales its probability (as ss.modify does), not its dwell; as agents, a product’s efficacy against a dur= transition now acts.
The ODE’s fixed delays (ss.constant) let the state’s other exits act on the people due to leave until they leave, so a competing exit acts over the whole delay (it missed half a step: a 12-day incubation with mortality 0.1 a day kept 5% too many).
Clearer errors where the model reviews hit crashes: one transition with several destinations, p=, and no rate or duration says to write a transition for each destination; a sum of states as a transition’s source says to write a list; a function in p= that gives a row per person is refused; a modifier named like a property of people says to rename it; a network asked for by name in a compartmental run points to sim.all_networks(); a coded module’s update_results() that fails at the first time point says it now runs there, before any step; ss.par(<several values>, bounds=) is refused; a parameter with no name gets a sensible example name.
Fixed crashes: a branch share by level (p=[ss.by(risk=...), None]) at seeding as agents (it also seeds each group at its own share, not the mean); ss.change on a beta for each route with a pair of directions; a coded module’s array as a modifier’s amount (multiply=coded.factor); ss.diff() of modules written as code; a module-level ss.par used in the class form keeps its name; a comparison such as Q.n < 20 as where=; ssl.MSMNet gives newcomers a debut.
A remainder branch (p=None) can sit beside a timed exit for other people: the remainder is the timed exit with the same where= as the branches (women split between CIN and clearance, men only clear).
New: ss.move(src, dst, p=, n=, uids=) (also disease.move()), a one-off move of people between states of a declared disease from code, the same under every solver (the number of people in a state of people, sir.I.n, is read, not set); .n (people) and .count() on states under every solver; ss.Births(birth_rate='nigeria') and ss.Deaths(death_rate='nigeria') load the UN rates; people.n in a compartmental run gives each group’s size, and repr(sim.people) says groups; a swept set of values is a scenario of its own ('beta=0.1'); .by() across runs returns levels that .plot() draws together; conditions keep their modules by name, which makes many modifiers faster (88 lazy modifiers: 0.43 s against 0.55 s).
During a run, float(par) is the parameter’s value with its modifiers applied (e.g. ss.change), so a function in a rate that reads it sees the change (it saw the value without it: 3,501 starts after a change to stop them, against 0); par.value and par.raw stay the value without modifiers, and a note says so when a modified parameter is read in a function.
In a compartmental run, a product whose protection fades by a function of time has as many levels of time since delivery (10 to 40) as keep the protection within 2% across each (a 180-day box then a decay over a year was 6.2% off agents at day 729 with 10; now 0.5%).
A note when every time of an ss.timeseries is outside the run (days of the year beside calendar years gave a flat value).
People hold the values of a numeric dimension, binned into its levels: stratify(wealthquintile=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) gives people the values 1 to 5 (they held 0 to 4, binned by the edges 1 to 5, so the top level was empty). A property people already have (ss.People(extra_states=[...])) is kept and binned, not overwritten from the split, and split= for it raises.
A bare dt beside calendar-year start and stop is in years, with a warning, when the model’s typed values are in another unit (dt=1/12 with durations in months gave 1/12 of a month). ss.choice and ss.histogram take unit=, and ss.choice takes typed values (a=[ss.months(9), ss.months(10)]), so either can be a dwell time. A note when a dwell’s distribution gets its numbers from a function and has no unit; a note for an age group nobody can be in (an edge of 100 or more); verbose above 2 is documented as everything.
A transition with offspring= turns aging on (as births do), and each newborn’s people.parent is the person who went through it (people did not age, and newborns had no parent).
ss.seasonal(peak=) refuses a number outside 0 to 1 (a peak of 142 was taken as 0.0, January), and takes a time of year, peak=ss.days(142).
Notes when solver='auto' runs agents with each agent standing for more than 1,000 people, and when a sim is stratified but none of its modules is declared (so no results are by group).
A note when ss.PartnerNet(match=...) matches partners by a property but everyone has the same number of partners (n_contacts=ss.by(...) gives more at some levels), and when a contact matrix by a dimension is not reciprocal for the dimension’s split (N_i·C_ij against N_j·C_ji); both are used as given.
A note that a transfer’s dur= distribution is realized at the constant rate of its mean; the BadBranchSplit error says when an exit with a rate and no p= is why the branches do not sum to 1; the msim.reduce() error says res.quantiles() pools every run.
As agents, a dwell time drawn when someone entered a state follows them when they move to a level where the transition runs at a different speed (adjust= by a dimension people move along: a transfer, a move=, age, or migration); they kept the dwell drawn at the first level (with recovery ten times slower in the level moved to, 0.37 still infected at day 20 against the ODE’s 0.83; now 0.82). About 4% slower for agent models with such an adjustment.
As agents, a state left only by branches with no wait (ss.Transition(J, A, p=0.3) and ss.Transition(J, B, p=0.7)) is passed through at once, as in the ODE; people were held in it for a step (HPVsim review HP2).
People infectious at the start (in a state an infection puts people into) have been so for the first step, as if infected in the step before: as agents their ti_I is -1, and in a compartmental run with a fixed delay they start one slot along. A seeded case with a fixed stay of one step was infectious for two steps under every solver, so the Reed-Frost model’s chance of no further case was 0.013 against the exact 0.131 (canon review CR4).
ss.MFNet draws the age of debut for anyone who has none on each step (newborns, and people who arrive at any age, who before were never given one and so never joined), and draws whether a person takes part when they reach their debut, so a participation probability by age is read at that age (it was drawn at birth, at age 0). ssl.MSMNet does the same. People born during a run now join the network at their debut (about 16 by default), so long runs with births have more partnerships (the baseline’s 20-year run: mfnet_n_edges +8.8%). With n_contacts=, in an open population people look for partners more (or less) often by a factor that keeps the mean number of partners at the target, since partners die and newcomers start with none (with 20-year partnerships and births and deaths, 0.86 against a target of 0.87; it was 0.65). mean_degree and concurrency are per person, so no longer multiplied by the population scale (0.551 became 110.1 with total_pop=1e6).
res.resample('year') and resample('month') on a sim with dates put the point on 1 January (or the 1st of the month) in the period before, since it closes the step that ends there, so a run from 2000 to 2003 has three years, not four with the last of one point; use_years=True labels each year by the year it covers.
res.resample('year') of a stock (n_alive, n_infected) gives its value at the end of each year, where Starsim 3’s annualize() gave the mean over the year; summarize_by='mean' gives the mean.
The time between two dates (ss.date(2010) - ss.date(1990)) is ss.days (here ss.days(7305)), not ss.datedur. ss.datedur is a thin wrapper of pd.DateOffset, taking whole numbers of years, months, weeks, and days (ss.datedur(months=1)); a fraction (ss.datedur(years=0.5)) raises an error that points to ss.years(0.5), and a time before year 1 is ss.years, not ss.datedur.
ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR are the textbook models: dur_inf and dur_exp are the means of exponentials (a number is in years), and p_death defaults to 0. Starsim 3’s models, with a lognormal dur_inf and p_death=0.01, are ssl.AgentSIR, ssl.AgentSIS, and ssl.AgentSEIR. dur_inf=[mean, std] now raises an error, and python -m starsim.converters.migrate flags each use of ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR.
An agent-based fit scores each point by one run (n_runs= for more), as Optuna’s search already learns from nearby points; stochastic compartmental fits keep four runs a point. Under Optuna each point takes fresh seeds, so the search averages over chance rather than fitting one seed’s realization, and the best values are those of the trial whose neighbors score lowest (a kernel average), since the single lowest trial is the luckiest; local methods such as Nelder-Mead keep the same seeds at every point. EpiModel’s fit (test_epimodel_fit) goes from 23.4% to 30.4% prevalence against the 30% fitted to.
A data series that is all zero is scaled by the model’s mean in the default goodness of fit, so it adds at most 1 instead of its raw counts (before, 420 deaths a week swamped a fit to cases).
NUTS chains start at optima found from the best points of a scan, so they no longer agree on a mode far below the best (1.75% of two-parameter fits in a simulation-based calibration).
The ODE’s automatic substeps also follow how fast a compartment grows through its inflows, not only how fast it is left, so a fast epidemic at a daily step is within about 1e-4 of the exact solution (Keeling and Rohani’s program 2.1 was 2.5% off); about 1.0 to 1.2 times the run time. The camdl and flepiMoP importers take one RK4 step a step, as those programs do.
An initial value given for the first state is kept: init=dict(S=0.1, I=1e-4) starts 10% susceptible, with the rest in the one state given no value (it put everyone else in S); if no single state is left for the rest, it is an error.
Any transition out of a disease’s first state is an acquisition, whatever its rate, unless a contact-mediated one leaves that state: rel_sus, a scalar vaccine efficacy, and ss.treat now act on infections by a bite rate, an EIR, or a reservoir (they did nothing). The infected states of a vector model include those whose count infects the vector (Eh, Ih in Ross-Macdonald), so ss.treat reaches them, and R0() of a vector model is the next-generation value at the vector’s disease-free equilibrium (it was 0).
As agents, counts (mosquitoes, a reservoir) take substeps as the ODE does, so they no longer die out or grow without bound at a long step; modifiers of their transitions apply (they were ignored); and people’s rates that use a count take it once advanced, as specified.
As agents, a dwell time already drawn follows a later change to its duration or rate (a modifier or ss.change() on the duration parameter, or a duration or rate that varies in time), as the ODE does; before, only a modifier on the transition was followed (a halved duration gave 825 infected on day 25 against the ODE’s 498).
As agents, where= on a transition with a dwell time takes effect for people already waiting once it holds (people who turned 30 during a run never left).
As agents, a rate competing with a dwell time acts over the whole dwell for people who entered by a progression (it missed the first step: a one-month dwell with a competing rate of 1 per year lost nobody to it, against 8%).
Compartmental runs follow a modifier or ss.change() on a parameter in a branch probability (p=); before, the share stayed at its starting value (0.2 against 0.8 as agents). Separate transitions with p= are decided on entry, one transition with several destinations at exit, with p evaluated then (now documented).
A fixed delay (ss.constant as a dwell time) in a compartmental run is a conveyor of whole steps, not 50 Erlang stages, so it is exact rather than approximate.
The particle filter draws each particle’s random numbers from a stream of its own, so its estimates for a given seed differ from before (statistically the same), and do not depend on the number of threads.
With several declared diseases, births or deaths reach every disease under the compartmental solvers (before, the other diseases had a fixed population); demographics=True with a declared disease runs births and deaths as its transitions (the same model, other random draws).
Time names: the time vocabulary is ss.dur, ss.per, and ss.prob, with ss.days to ss.years and ss.perday to ss.peryear; a probability per period is ss.prob(0.1, 'day') (and prints so). ss.probperday to ss.probperyear, ss.freq and ss.freqperday to ss.freqperyear, and the one-unit instances ss.day to ss.year stay. Removed: the Starsim 2 names ss.rate, ss.time_prob, and ss.rate_prob, deprecated in Starsim 3. A name that Starsim no longer exports raises an error that says what to write instead. ss.dur(3) and ss.per(2) need a unit (they were years).
Docs: the design specification (docs/design/ in the lingua_franca_design repo) matches the code: departures folded in, promised-but-absent features struck or moved to docs/admin/deferred.md, settled open questions closed; its code blocks (every chapter), error catalog, and vocabulary counts are checked by tests/test_spec.py. The best-practices documents keep only their argument, with links to the design for the specification.
Saved forms: a model is saved as code with ss.save('model.py', sim) (which writes sim.to_code()), and a sim with its results with ss.save('run.sim', sim); the model spec (sim.to_spec(), and disease.to_spec(), which disease.to_json() also gives) is the normalized form for sim.hash() and ss.diff() and is no longer read back (ss.from_spec() and ss.load() of a spec are removed). An outcome’s likelihood is written in the spec as its distribution and parameters (not a string), so to_code() writes it too.
Results by group: results by group are kept at every step only while they fit in about 100 MB a module (500 MB over the runs of sim.run(n_runs=)); beyond that they are kept every week, four weeks, quarter, and so on (a flow added up over the period, a state at its end), with a note, and totals are still kept at every step. ss.Sim(results=['n_I', 'cases']) keeps only the named results by group. A stochastic run with mixing between places, or with results kept every few steps, draws in a different order, so its runs differ from before (equally likely); across many runs, outcomes by group are worked out from the flows by group.
Dependencies: seaborn is no longer installed with Starsim (only Starsim 3’s ss.Calibration plots use it, and import it when they are made); starsim_data (named data) is installed with Starsim, and so is openpyxl (for Atomica’s workbooks), through Sciris.
Many runs: a MultiSim is its results: msim.results.<module>.<result> is an ss.Result with a run axis first, however the runs were made, with select(run=, scenario=, <swept parameter>=), quantiles(), median(), mean(), diff(), resample(), to_df(), and plot(); len(msim) is the number of runs. ss.parallel() is the one way to run many sims, and sim.run(n_runs=) its shortcut for one; pars= takes arrays. Removed: msim.reduce(), msim.mean(), msim.median(), msim.reset(), ss.MultiResult, and ss.multi_run() (iterpars= is pars=).
Flow names: a flow has one name, its transition’s (sim.results.sir.infection), and its running total is .cum, computed when asked for; new_infections, cum_infections, and prevalence are kept on ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR, and not added to a disease declared with ss.Disease(); a data column new_infections matches the flow of a declared disease’s one transmission.
Typed arithmetic: arithmetic on a finished transition is about its flow, never its rate: 0.5 * infection given to a disease is an outcome (half its flow), not a second transition at half the rate (L25).
Time during a step: in every module, sim.ti is the time point at the start of the step (the first step has ti == 0, as in Starsim 3), and sim.advance() moves it to the end before results are recorded; a result written during a step goes at ti + 1.
