The fit finds β close to 0.16 and a reported share close to 40%, the values the data was made with, and the mismatch falls from 0.29 with the starting guesses to 0.04. Second, look at the model against the data, before and after fitting:

fit.plot()








The fitted model (“After”) follows the rise, the peak, and the start of the fall of the data, and the data scatters around it about as much as Poisson counts should; the model with the starting guesses (“Before”) peaks too late. Look for departures that are systematic rather than random: a peak that comes too early or too late, a fall that is too slow, or residuals that are all on one side for weeks at a time. Third, check what the values imply. R0 is in proportion to β, so with β = 0.16 rather than 0.14, R0 is about 16 × 0.16 / 0.14 ≈ 18, at the top of the range usually given for measles (12 to 18). If a value had ended at the edge of its bounds, or had implied an R0 of 50, the model or the bounds would need another look.
The fit here is good because the data was made with this model. With real data, the model is never exactly right, and these checks are how you find out where it falls short. Fit diagnostics in the user guide goes further.

title: T7 – Data and calibration
section: Testing the fit on data it wasn’t given
text:
Testing the fit on data it wasn’t given
A model that matches the data it was fitted to may still predict badly: with two free parameters, many curves can pass near a dozen points. A stronger test is to fit the model to the data up to some date, and see how well it predicts the weeks after it, which it wasn’t given. Here, the model is fitted to the data up to 12 March (during the rise) and up to 26 March (around the peak), and each fit is run with all the data attached, so that its predictions can be compared with the weeks it didn’t see:

cutoffs = {
    'Fitted to 12 March': '2025-03-12',
    'Fitted to 26 March': '2025-03-26',
}
sims = {}
for label, cutoff in cutoffs.items():
    early = ss.Sim(measles, data=data[data.date <= cutoff], **settings).fit(verbose=False)
    print(label, '- beta:', round(early.pars.beta, 3), '- reported:', round(early.pars.reported, 2))
    sims[label] = ss.Sim(measles, pars=early.pars, data=data, **settings)

msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.cases')

Fitted to 12 March - beta: 0.19 - reported: 0.19
Fitted to 26 March - beta: 0.159 - reported: 0.43
MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Fitted to 12 March, Fitted to 26 March)
  Done in 0.17 s









Both fits match the data they were given, but they don’t agree about what comes after. Fitted to the rise alone, the model finds a higher β and only 19% of infections reported, and predicts that the outbreak peaks within a week, at about 280 cases a week, when it went on to peak at about 470. Once the data includes the peak, the fit is close to the true values, and predicts the following weeks well.
The reason is that while an outbreak is growing, its rate of growth depends mostly on β, but the number of cases reported depends on both how many people are infected and the share of them reported: a smaller outbreak with more of it reported gives nearly the same rise as a larger outbreak with less of it reported. The outbreak turns when susceptible people run out, so only the peak says how many people have been infected, and so what share of them were reported. When two parameters can trade off like this, the data can’t tell them apart (they are not identifiable from it); Parameter identification shows how to check for this before trusting a fit.

title: T7 – Data and calibration
text:
Projecting from the fit
The data ends in mid-April, but the fitted sim, fit.sim, runs to the end of the year, so it projects the rest of the outbreak. To ask what a vaccination campaign on 1 May would do, make a scenario from it. sim.new() makes a new sim from the same inputs as an existing one, with whatever is given changed: here, the fitted sim with a campaign added.

campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, where=measles.age < 15, coverage=0.8, at='2025-05-01')

sims = {
    'No intervention': fit.sim,
    'Campaign':        fit.sim.new(interventions=campaign),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)

To see the whole year, plot the cases with the data. Since the data is weekly, the plot shows the model’s weekly totals, as the fit compares them, over the weeks with data and the rest of the year:

msim.plot('measles.cases')









msim.summarize().loc['measles_cases']








value


scenario





No intervention
3843.774907


Campaign
3727.499232







By 1 May, the outbreak has already peaked, so the campaign prevents only about 120 reported cases, 3% of them, much less than a campaign on 1 March did in T5. The data says how far the outbreak has gone, and so how much is left for an intervention to prevent.
These projections use the best-fitting values only. Other values fit the data nearly as well, so a projection is uncertain too; Fitting a model in the user guide shows how to find the range of values that fit (a posterior), and how to carry it into projections with fit.project(). It also covers fitting stochastic and agent-based models, likelihoods, and other ways to measure the mismatch.

title: T7 – Data and calibration
text:
Exercises

Start the fit from different guesses, e.g. β = 0.3 and 20% reported (ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=0.3, reported=0.2), data=data, **settings)). Does it find the same values? Then fit to the data up to 12 March from both starting points. What does the difference say?
Fit only β, keeping the reported share at 50% (sim.fit(pars=['beta'])). How does the fit look, and how does the projected size of the outbreak compare with that of the fit of both parameters?
Project a campaign on 1 April instead of 1 May (using the fit of the data to mid-April). How many reported cases would it have prevented?

title: A1 – Diseases
text:
🧠25% 🤖75%
Diseases are the cornerstone of almost any Starsim analysis. In the core tutorials (T1–T9), the measles model ran as compartments: the numbers of people in S, E, I, and R. This tutorial runs the same disease as agents, where each person has their own state, their own times of moving from one state to the next, and, if you want, their own infectiousness and susceptibility. The model is written exactly as before; what changes is what you can ask of it.
By the end of this tutorial, you’ll understand how to:

title: A1 – Diseases
text:
Step 1: A disease as agents
Here is the SEIR measles model from T3. Giving the sim n_agents= instead of total_pop= runs it as agents (solver='abm' says so explicitly); here there are 5,000 of them, each a person:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001))

sims = {
    'Compartments (ODE)': ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=5000, stop=ss.days(150)),
    'Agents':             ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(150)),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Compartments (ODE), Agents)
  Done in 0.36 s









The two agree closely: with 5,000 people and 5 infectious at the start, chance plays only a small part, and the agents give nearly the same epidemic as the ODE. They differ a little because agents take whole daily steps (the run prints a note saying how much this can matter), and because each agent’s course is drawn at random. Everything you learned in the core tutorials (describe(), results, interventions, scenarios) works the same way for agents.
Starsim also has a few diseases ready-made. Much like sims or networks, a disease can be customized by passing in parameters. Here is the library SIR model, with parameters close to measles:

sir = ss.SIR(dur_inf=ss.days(8), beta=ss.perday(1.9), init_prev=0.001, p_death=0.002)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(60))
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: sir, as 5,000 agents, days 0 to 60
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.027 s; sir: 4,995 infections; at most 3,941 infectious, on day 9









Notice how we modified several key parameters:

dur_inf=ss.days(8): how long people stay infectious (8 days, on average)
beta=ss.perday(1.9): the transmission rate
init_prev=0.001: starting with 0.1% of the population infected
p_death=0.002: 0.2% of infected people die

The results are stored in sim.results.sir, and can also be directly accessed via sim.diseases.sir.results. ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR are the textbook models, with exponential durations. For more detail on any of the diseases in the Starsim library of diseases (import starsim.library as ssl), please refer to the Diseases page of the model library.

Step 2: Looking at individual people
As agents, the sim keeps each person’s state, and the time they entered and are due to leave it. sim.people.to_df() gives a table with a row for each person and a column for each of these (measles.ti_E is the step on which each person was infected, and measles.ti_I the step on which they became infectious):

sim = sims['Agents']
df = sim.people.to_df()

sim.people.person(uid) gives everything about one person, and a state gives the IDs (UIDs) of the people in it: measles.R.uids are those who have recovered. Since each person draws their own latent period, you can look at the spread of them directly. In T3, an Erlang latent period changed the course of the epidemic, compared with an exponential one of the same average; as agents, you can see why, person by person:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
progression = E >> I @ ss.erlang(k=10, mean=ss.days(10)) # Latent for 10 days on average, with less spread
measles_erlang = ss.Disease(S >> E @ 1.9*I, progression, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')
sim_erlang = ss.Sim(measles_erlang, n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
sim_erlang.run()

plt.figure()
for label, s in {'Exponential': sim, 'Erlang (k = 10)': sim_erlang}.items():
    latent = s.diseases.measles.E.stays # How long each person who has been through E stayed there: their latent period, in days
    print(f'{label}: mean latent period {np.mean(latent):.1f} days')
    plt.hist(latent, bins=np.arange(0, 40), alpha=0.5, label=label)
plt.xlabel('Latent period (days)')
plt.ylabel('Number of people')
plt.legend();

Exponential: mean latent period 10.2 days
Erlang (k = 10): mean latent period 10.1 days









With an exponential latent period, short latent periods are the most common, and many people take three weeks or more (the longest are off the chart); with an Erlang distribution, most people become infectious between about 6 and 17 days after infection. Both average about 10 days, as declared. The times are whole days, since agents move between states in whole steps. E.stays covers everyone who has entered E and left it (the seeded cases, who started in I, never did), and leaves out those still in it. Subtracting the times of entering (m.ti_I - m.ti_E) would give a day more, since an infection happens at the end of its step and becoming infectious at the start of one; see People and agents. Array indexing shows the other ways to pick out people, and People and agents what each person has.

title: A1 – Diseases
section: Step 3: Chance, and the first case
text:
Step 3: Chance, and the first case
In a compartmental model, an infection that starts with R above 1 always takes off. In reality, the first few cases may recover before infecting anyone, and the outbreak dies out by chance. Agents capture this, since each person’s infections and recovery are drawn at random.
Take the town of T5, where 90% of people are already immune, and suppose one infectious person arrives. Each case then infects about 1.9 × 8 × 0.1 ≈ 1.5 others, on average. Here are 20 runs as agents, each with its own random seed, shown one line each (lines=True), and the ODE for comparison:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1)) # 90% immune, and 1 case

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(ss.Sim(measles, **pars), n_runs=20)
msim.plot('measles.I', lines=True)

ode = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=5000, stop=ss.days(365), solver='ode', verbose=0)
ode.run()
ode.plot('measles.I')















The ODE always gives an outbreak, of the same size. As agents, some runs give an outbreak about as large as the ODE’s, and the rest die out after a handful of cases. Counting the runs with fewer than 20 infections in all:

total = msim.results.measles.infection.values.sum(axis=1) # Total infections in each run
print('Share of introductions that die out:', np.mean(total < 20))

Share of introductions that die out: 0.6


For a simple epidemic model with an exponential infectious period, theory says that one case dies out with a chance of 1/R, here about 2 in 3, which is close to what the runs give. The number of runs is small, so the share varies from one set of runs to the next. This matters for any question about introductions: how likely an imported case is to start an outbreak, or how long a place stays free of a disease.

title: A1 – Diseases
text:
Step 4: People who differ: superspreading
So far, every infectious person is equally infectious. For many diseases they are not: most cases infect few others or none, and a few infect many (superspreading). The usual way to describe this is to give each person an infectiousness drawn from a gamma distribution with a mean of 1; its shape parameter, k, is the dispersion. The smaller k is, the more transmission is concentrated in a few people (estimates for SARS in 2003 put k near 0.16); a very large k gives everyone the same infectiousness, as above.
A value that each person has is an attribute, ss.attr(): here, one drawn once for each person when they are made (a trait). ss.modify() then multiplies each person’s infectiousness (rel_trans) by it:

def make_sim(k=None):
    """ The measles model, with the infectiousness of each person drawn from a gamma distribution with shape k """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    if k is None: # Everyone equally infectious
        measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1))
        return ss.Sim(measles, **pars)
    infectiousness = ss.attr(ss.gamma(a=k, scale=1/k)) # A mean of 1, and a shape (dispersion) of k
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, infectiousness=infectiousness, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1))
    superspreading = ss.modify(measles.rel_trans, multiply=infectiousness)
    return ss.Sim(measles, connectors=superspreading, **pars)

for label, k in {'Everyone equally infectious': None, 'k = 1': 1, 'k = 0.2': 0.2}.items():
    msim = ss.parallel(make_sim(k), n_runs=40)
    total = msim.results.measles.infection.values.sum(axis=1)
    print(label, '- share that die out:', np.mean(total < 20), '- median size of the outbreaks that take off:', np.median(total[total >= 20]))

Everyone equally infectious - share that die out: 0.65 - median size of the outbreaks that take off: 319.5
k = 1 - share that die out: 0.7 - median size of the outbreaks that take off: 299.0
k = 0.2 - share that die out: 0.775 - median size of the outbreaks that take off: 215.0


The average number each case infects is the same in all three, about 1.5, but the more transmission is concentrated, the more often an introduction dies out: with k = 0.2, about 4 in 5 do, since the first case is most likely one of the many who infect nobody. The outbreaks that do take off are of a similar size in all three. For control, this is the good news of superspreading; the bad news is that the outbreaks that occur can start explosively, from a single event. A compartmental model can’t say this, since it has no individuals to differ.
ss.attr() can also draw a value when something happens to a person (e.g. a severity at infection, with on=infection), or record one; see Diseases. A person’s susceptibility can differ in the same way, with ss.modify(measles.rel_sus, ...).

title: A1 – Diseases
text:
Step 5: Immunity that wanes
Measles leaves lifelong immunity, but many infections don’t. Let’s turn an SIR model into an SIRS model, where immunity wanes: recovered agents eventually become susceptible again. This is what lets a disease settle into endemic transmission rather than burning through the population once and disappearing. It is one more transition, from R back to S. Here it is for a generic respiratory infection, with an R0 of 0.4 × 7 = 2.8, and immunity that lasts 6 months on average, compared with the same infection without waning:

def make_cold(waning):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I        # β = 0.4 per day
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(7)   # Infectious for 7 days on average
    infections = ss.attr(1, on=infection, combine='sum', init=0) # The number of times each person has been infected
    transitions = dict(infection=infection, recovery=recovery)
    if waning:
        transitions['waning'] = R >> S @ ss.days(180) # Immune for 6 months on average
    return ss.Disease(**transitions, infections=infections, init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

pars_cold = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(3*365), verbose=0)
sims = {
    'SIR (lasting immunity)': ss.Sim(make_cold(waning=False), **pars_cold),
    'SIRS (immunity wanes)':  ss.Sim(make_cold(waning=True), **pars_cold),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold.I')








With lasting immunity, there is one epidemic and then the infection is gone. When immunity wanes, the pool of susceptible people is continually replenished, so the infection comes back in waves that settle at an endemic level.
The attribute infections counts the times each person has been infected (combine='sum' adds 1 at each infection). This is a history of each person, which only agents have. After three years with waning immunity:

counts = sims['SIRS (immunity wanes)'].people.cold.infections.values
plt.figure()
plt.hist(counts, bins=np.arange(counts.max() + 2) - 0.5)
plt.xlabel('Number of infections in 3 years')
plt.ylabel('Number of people');








Everyone is infected at least once, most people 3 to 5 times, and the number varies by chance from person to person, even though everyone here is alike. A person’s history can be read in a model too: e.g. ss.modify(cold.rel_sus, multiply=0.5, where=cold.infection.count >= 2) would halve the susceptibility of people who have been infected at least twice.

title: A1 – Diseases
text:
Writing a disease as code
Every disease above is declared: its states and transitions, as in the core tutorials. A disease can also be written as Python code, a class with methods that say what happens to each agent at each step. This is how diseases were written in Starsim 3, and it is still the way to write a disease whose course is easier to say in code than in transitions (e.g. a CD4 count that falls continuously). A5 shows how. Several diseases in one sim, and how they affect each other, are covered in T8.

title: A1 – Diseases
text:
Exercises

Parameter exploration: Try different durations of immunity in the SIRS model (e.g. 1, 6, and 24 months). How do they affect the epidemic curve, and the number of times people are infected?
SEIRS model: Add a latent period of 2 days to the SIRS model, to make an SEIRS model. Does it change the endemic level?
Superspreading and control: In the town with 90% immune, increase the share susceptible to 20% (init=dict(R=0.8)), so that each case infects about 3 others. What share of introductions die out now, with and without superspreading (k = 0.2)?

text:
Further reading

Covasim: getting started: an agent-based model of COVID-19, built on similar ideas
Superspreading and the effect of individual variation on disease emergence: the paper that introduced the dispersion k
EpiModel: introduction: deterministic, individual contact, and network versions of the classic models, in R

title: T8 – Stratification and co-transmission
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Who is the outbreak in, and does it make other infections worse?
T4 split the measles model into age groups. Age is rarely the only way in which people differ that matters for an outbreak. Whether someone is vaccinated decides whether they can be infected, and whom they mix with decides whom they can infect. Measles outbreaks in countries with high vaccination coverage happen mostly in communities where coverage is low, and spread from there. And measles doesn’t only harm people while they have it: for a few years afterwards, it leaves them more vulnerable to other infections.
This tutorial has two halves. The first stratifies the measles model by more than age: by vaccination status, and by membership of a close-knit community with low coverage. The second runs measles together with a second disease, with an interaction between them. By the end, you will be able to:

title: T8 – Stratification and co-transmission
text:
The model so far
This is the measles model from T5 – Interventions and scenarios: an SEIR model in a town of 100,000 people in three age groups, who mix according to a contact matrix, with 10 people infectious on 1 January. In T5, the people already immune started in R; here, their immunity comes from vaccination, which is added below as a dimension of its own. Since each section stratifies the model in a different way, the model is made by a function, so that each section can start from a new copy:

import starsim as ss

def make_measles():
    """ The SEIR model of measles, by age, with nobody immune yet """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection   = S >> E @ 0.14*I       # β = 0.14 per contact per day
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Latent for 10 days on average
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10), name='measles')
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+
    return measles

age_contacts = [[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]] # Contacts a day, between age groups
settings = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

title: T8 – Stratification and co-transmission
text:
Vaccination status as a dimension
In most places, most people are vaccinated against measles, and two doses of the vaccine protect about 97% of people. One way to model this is to stratify by vaccination status: everyone is either vaccinated or not, and the vaccinated are 97% less susceptible. T5 modeled vaccination as an intervention, given on a date; a dimension is the natural way to give the immunity that a population already has when the model starts, and it lets the results be read for the vaccinated and the unvaccinated separately.
Coverage often differs by age. Here 85% of children are vaccinated, 92% of adults aged 15 to 64, and 95% of people 65 and over. A share that differs by another dimension is given as an ss.by() over both: a row for each age group, and a column for each level of vaccination, each row adding up to 1. So each age group keeps its size, and the rows say how it is split:

coverage_by_age = ss.by([[0.15, 0.85],  # 0-14: 15% unvaccinated, 85% vaccinated
                         [0.08, 0.92],  # 15-64
                         [0.05, 0.95]], # 65+
                        dims=['age', 'vaccinated'])

measles = make_measles()
measles.stratify(vaccinated=[False, True], split=coverage_by_age, states=['S'], adjust={'rel_sus': [1, 0.03]})

sim = ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=age_contacts), **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('vaccinated').plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 2.34, with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0035 s; measles: 15,155 infections; at most 1,301 infectious, on 2025-05-12









adjust multiplies a quantity in each level: rel_sus, the relative susceptibility, is 1 for the unvaccinated and 0.03 for the vaccinated. The run prints an R0 of about 2.3, rather than 16: since vaccination is a dimension of the model, the vaccinated are part of the population that this R0 is worked out for, and most of them are protected. The outbreak is much smaller than with nobody immune:

res = sim.results.measles
print('Infections:', round(res.infection.sum()))
print('Among the vaccinated:', round(res.infection.select(vaccinated=True).sum()))
print('Among unvaccinated children:', round(res.infection.select(vaccinated=False, age='0-14').sum()))

Infections: 15155
Among the vaccinated: 6242
Among unvaccinated children: 4362


Even with a vaccine that protects 97% of people, about two in five of the people infected are vaccinated, because there are so many more of them than of the unvaccinated. This is a common finding in real outbreaks, and doesn’t mean that the vaccine is failing: each vaccinated person is still far less likely to be infected than each unvaccinated one.
states=['S'] stratifies only the susceptible state by vaccination. This is partial stratification: vaccination matters only for whether someone is infected, and once they are, a vaccinated person is in this model the same as anyone else, so people infected from S enter E with no level of vaccination. Splitting E, I, and R as well would add compartments that behave the same. With states=['S'], the model has 3 × 2 = 6 compartments for S, and 3 each for E, I, and R. Results by a dimension count only the states that have it, so res.I.by('vaccinated') raises an error here, since I has no level of vaccination; the flow out of S, res.infection.by('vaccinated'), says who was infected. A dimension that people mix by (with a contact matrix) can’t be partial, since everyone who can infect or be infected needs a level of it to mix as. See Stratification for this and for where=, which narrows a dimension to some groups rather than some states (e.g. pregnancy, for women only).

title: T8 – Stratification and co-transmission
text:
An under-vaccinated community
Overall coverage says little about an outbreak if the unvaccinated are clustered together. Suppose that 5% of the town’s people belong to a close-knit community in which only 60% are vaccinated (for simplicity, at every age), while 98% of everyone else is. Overall, 96% of the town is vaccinated, and about 93% protected, close to the 94% that would prevent an outbreak (the herd immunity threshold, 1 − 1/16). The community’s members make 70% of their contacts with each other, at school, at church, and at home, and 30% with the rest of the town. This is a third dimension, community, with a share of the population in each level, as for age, and coverage by community is an ss.by() over community and vaccination, as above:

coverage_by_community = ss.by([[0.02, 0.98],  # General: 2% unvaccinated, 98% vaccinated
                               [0.40, 0.60]], # Close-knit community
                              dims=['community', 'vaccinated'])

def make_community_measles():
    """ The measles model, by age, community, and vaccination """
    measles = make_measles()
    measles.stratify(community={'general': 0.95, 'close-knit': 0.05})
    measles.stratify(vaccinated=[False, True], split=coverage_by_community, states=['S'], adjust={'rel_sus': [1, 0.03]})
    return measles

The contacts are now between groups of two dimensions. With a matrix for each, the contacts between two groups are the product of the entries for each: a child in the community has 10 contacts a day with children, and 70% of a community member’s contacts are within the community, so 7 of them are with children in the community. The rest of the town makes 1.6% of its contacts with the community. (The two are consistent: there are 19 times as many people outside the community, so the total contacts each way are the same: 0.95 × 0.016 ≈ 0.05 × 0.3.)
To see what the clustering does, compare it with the same people mixing as if the community weren’t close-knit, so that everyone makes 5% of their contacts with its members, its share of the town. The coverage of each group, and so of the town as a whole, is the same in both:

clustered = ss.contacts(dict(age=age_contacts, community=[[0.984, 0.016], [0.3, 0.7]]), ages=[0, 15, 65])
mixed     = ss.contacts(dict(age=age_contacts, community=[[0.95, 0.05], [0.95, 0.05]]), ages=[0, 15, 65])

sims = {
    'Mixing with everyone': ss.Sim(make_community_measles(), networks=mixed, **settings),
    'Close-knit':           ss.Sim(make_community_measles(), networks=clustered, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.infection')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Mixing with everyone, Close-knit)
  Done in 0.3 s









The coverage is the same in both, but the outbreaks are not. Mixed with everyone, each unvaccinated person in the community is surrounded mostly by vaccinated people, and transmission barely sustains itself: the outbreak smolders, growing slowly all year. Clustered together, the community has a reproduction number of about 16 × (0.4 + 0.6 × 0.03) ≈ 7 within itself, against about 16 × (0.02 + 0.98 × 0.03) ≈ 0.8 in the rest of the town, too low to sustain an outbreak on its own. So the community has an explosive outbreak within weeks, which spills over into the rest of the town. select() picks out any combination of groups, leaving the dimensions not named summed over:

for sim in msim.sims:
    res = sim.results.measles
    print(sim.label, '- in the community:', round(res.infection.select(community='close-knit').sum()), '- elsewhere:', round(res.infection.select(community='general').sum()))
sim = msim.sims['Close-knit']
sim.results.measles.I.by('community').plot()

Mixing with everyone - in the community: 118 - elsewhere: 269
Close-knit - in the community: 2420 - elsewhere: 1720









With the clustering, there are about ten times as many infections in the year, and the community, 5% of the town, has more than half of them. Its outbreak peaks first; the rest of the town’s follows, fed by the contacts between them, and lasts longer, since without the community’s cases it would die out. A model that averaged coverage over the town would miss all of this, and with it where vaccination would do the most good.

title: T8 – Stratification and co-transmission
text:
Moving between groups
So far, nobody changes group: each person stays in their community and their vaccination status, and (with no births or deaths) in their age group. ss.transfer() moves people from one level of a dimension to another at a rate, without changing their disease state. Suppose an outreach program offers catch-up vaccination to unvaccinated people in the community, reaching them at a rate of 2 a year (so that about 85% of them are reached within a year, if the outbreak doesn’t reach them first). ss.transfer(vaccinated=True, rate=...) moves people to the level True from any other, here at a rate that is given for each community, and is 0 outside the community. A transfer belongs to the dimension it moves people along, so it is given to that dimension’s stratify() call, by name:

catchup = ss.transfer(vaccinated=True, rate=ss.peryear(ss.by(community=[0, 2])), states=['S'])

measles = make_measles()
measles.stratify(community={'general': 0.95, 'close-knit': 0.05})
measles.stratify(vaccinated=[False, True], split=coverage_by_community, states=['S'], adjust={'rel_sus': [1, 0.03]}, catchup=catchup)

sims = {
    'No catch-up': msim.sims['Close-knit'],
    'Catch-up':    ss.Sim(measles, networks=clustered, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.infection')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (No catch-up, Catch-up)
  Done in 1.9 s










res = msim.sims['Catch-up'].results.measles
print('Doses given:', round(res.catchup.sum()))
msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']

Doses given: 605









value


scenario





No catch-up
4139.959253


Catch-up
3124.760506







A transfer is a transition, so it has a result of its own, by its name (catchup), and can be changed by an intervention like any other. About 600 doses prevent about 1,000 infections, nearly two for each dose, since each is given where the outbreak is. (Exercise 2 asks what the same doses would do given to the rest of the town.) Three kinds of movement between groups are easy to confuse:



Movement
What it is
How it is given




A transfer
People move steadily, at a rate (catch-up or routine vaccination, migration, a change of risk group)
ss.transfer(), in stratify()


A delivery
People move at given times, with a coverage (a vaccination campaign)
ss.vaccinate() or ss.Delivery(move=...), as an intervention (T5)


Aging
People move up the age groups as they get older
Automatic, when people are born or die



As compartments, each state has a compartment for each combination of levels, so the dimensions multiply: here S has 3 age groups × 2 communities × 2 levels of vaccination = 12 compartments, and E, I, and R have 6 each. Sixteen age groups, five communities, and two levels of vaccination in every state would be 640. Large models still run quickly, but are hard to check; sim.describe() lists each dimension, its levels, the states it applies to, and its adjustments. Every stratification works the same way when the model is run as agents (see A1 – Diseases): each agent then has a value of each dimension, the transfers change those values, and the results are counted by group in the same way.

title: T8 – Stratification and co-transmission
text:
A second disease
Measles damages the immune system’s memory of other infections. For two to three years after recovering, children who have had measles are more likely to fall ill and die from other infections, and in places where measles was common, a large share of all childhood deaths from infection have been put down to this “immune amnesia”. So a measles outbreak leaves a wake of other infections, and preventing it prevents them too. To model this, the model needs a second disease, and the two need to interact.
The second disease here is pneumococcus, a bacterium that many children carry in the nose and throat for a few weeks at a time, usually without harm, and that is a leading cause of pneumonia. It is modeled as an SIS model: people acquire it (S to C, for carrying) through contact with carriers, and clear it after a month on average, after which they can acquire it again. With these values, about a quarter of children and a sixth of adults carry it at any time, about as it would settle on its own, so it starts there.
Measles needs one new state: to know who is affected by immune amnesia, the model has to remember who has had measles recently. In a compartmental model, what a person has been through has to be a state, so recovery from measles now leads to A (recovered, with amnesia), and people leave A for R after two years on average. Both are immune to measles; they differ only in their effect on the other disease. Since the model now has durations in years as well as in days, unit='day' says that the bare numbers (the values of β) are per day. The run is three years long, so that the wake can be seen, and goes back to the model of T5, with immunity in R by age. The diagram (T3) shows the new state:

ages = {0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=age_contacts)
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2028-01-01', unit='day')

S, E, I, A, R = ss.states('S E I A R')
infection   = S >> E @ 0.14*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> A @ ss.days(8)   # Recovered, with immune amnesia
restored    = A >> R @ ss.years(2)  # Immune memory of other infections restored after 2 years on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, restored,
    init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The share immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),
    name = 'measles',
)
measles.stratify(age=ages)

S, C = ss.states('S C')
acquisition = S >> C @ 0.003*C     # Acquired through contact with carriers
clearance   = C >> S @ ss.days(30) # Carried for a month on average
pneumococcus = ss.Disease(acquisition, clearance,
    init = dict(C=ss.by(age=[0.25, 0.17, 0.17])), # The share carrying it in each age group
    name = 'pneumococcus',
)
pneumococcus.stratify(age=ages)
measles.diagram()

title: T8 – Stratification and co-transmission
text:
An interaction
ss.modify() changes a quantity for the people a condition selects. Each disease has a relative susceptibility (rel_sus, how likely each person is to be infected, compared with others) and a relative transmissibility (rel_trans, how likely each person is to infect others), both 1 to begin with, so an interaction between two diseases is a change to one of these, for the people in some state of the other. Here, while people have measles and for as long as they have amnesia, they are twice as likely to acquire pneumococcus (an illustrative value):

amnesia = ss.modify(pneumococcus.rel_sus, multiply=2, where=measles.I | measles.A)

It reads as a sentence: for people infectious with measles or recovered with amnesia (where=measles.I | measles.A), multiply their susceptibility to pneumococcus by 2. The condition is evaluated as the sim runs, so it applies to people while they are in those states, and stops when they reach R; a modifier never overwrites the quantity it changes, so nothing has to be restored. Interactions that are part of the biology are given to the sim as connectors= (an intervention would go in interventions=; the two differ only in when they act in each step). To see what the interaction does, run the two diseases with and without it:

sims = {
    'Independent': ss.Sim([measles, pneumococcus], **settings),
    'Interacting': ss.Sim([measles, pneumococcus], connectors=amnesia, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot(['measles.I', 'pneumococcus.C'])

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Independent, Interacting)
  Done in 0.76 s










msim.summarize().loc['pneumococcus_acquisition']








value


scenario





Independent
706696.485662


Interacting
812411.679520







The measles outbreak is the same in both, since pneumococcus doesn’t affect it. Without the interaction, pneumococcus carries on at its usual level. With it, the number of carriers rises by about a fifth over the year of the outbreak, and stays high for years after measles has gone, as the people with amnesia slowly recover their immunity. The effect is larger than the 9% of people who had measles would suggest: they carry pneumococcus more often, and so pass it to more people, including people who never had measles. Since a share of carriers develop pneumonia, a measles outbreak would cause more pneumonia for years after it.

title: T8 – Stratification and co-transmission

Diseases tracked jointly
To work out the rate at which carriers infect people, a compartmental model of pneumococcus alone needs only the number of carriers. But with the interaction, it needs to know how many of the susceptible people have measles amnesia, which a separate set of compartments for each disease can’t say. So Starsim tracks linked diseases jointly: it makes a compartment for each combination of their states (S for measles and S for pneumococcus, A and C, and so on), and each disease’s transitions move people between the combinations. describe() shows how:

The number of joint states is the product of the diseases’ numbers of states, so it grows quickly; Starsim tracks diseases jointly up to a limit (ss.options.max_joint, 10,000 compartments by default), and above it a model run with the default solver runs as agents, in which each agent simply has a state in each disease. Diseases that don’t refer to each other’s states are not tracked jointly, so linking only the diseases that do interact keeps a model small. Exercises

In the community model, raise coverage in the community from 60% to 80%. How many fewer infections are there in the rest of the town, where coverage hasn’t changed? Why?
Give the same number of catch-up doses (about 600) to unvaccinated people outside the community instead, using a transfer whose rate is 0 in the community. How many infections do they prevent, compared with the doses given in the community?
In the model with two diseases, add a vaccination campaign against measles in children on 1 February (ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, where=measles.age < 15, coverage=0.8, at='2025-02-01')); with two diseases in the sim, the vaccine is for the one whose age groups where= names (measles.age), and disease= says which one if it names none (e.g. where=ss.ppl.age < 15). How many pneumococcus acquisitions does it prevent over the three years, with and without the interaction? What does this mean for working out the benefit of measles vaccination?

title: T1 – Getting started
text:
🧠10% 🤖90%
Starsim is a framework for modeling the spread of disease, and the health of populations more generally. A model in Starsim is written the way an epidemiologist would describe it: the states people can be in, the transitions between them, and the rates of those transitions. Starsim then runs it, either as a compartmental model (a set of equations for the number of people in each state) or as agents (one simulated person at a time).
These tutorials follow one example throughout: a deliberately simplified outbreak of measles in a town of 100,000 people. The numbers are typical of measles, but the model is for teaching, not a calibrated model of any real outbreak. This first tutorial asks the simplest question about it: how does an outbreak grow, and why does it stop? It writes the simplest model that can answer this, runs it, and shows how to check what was built. Tutorial 2 goes through the same model in more depth, Tutorial 3 gives the disease a more realistic course, and later tutorials add age groups, vaccination, several towns, and data.
You need only basic Python: variables, numbers, and function calls. By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

title: T1 – Getting started
text:
Installing Starsim
Starsim is a Python package. To install it, type pip install starsim in a terminal (or %pip install starsim in a notebook). Then, in Python:

import starsim as ss

title: T1 – Getting started
text:
An SIR model of measles
In an SIR model, each person is in one of three compartments: susceptible (S), infectious (I), or recovered and immune (R). People move between them along two transitions:

Infection, from S to I. Each susceptible person is infected at a rate of β times the share of people who are infectious. So the number of new infections per day is β S I / N, where N is the size of the population: the more infectious people there are, the faster the infection spreads.
Recovery, from I to R. People with measles are infectious for about 8 days, so here they recover after 8 days on average.

For measles, β is about 1.9 per day: someone who is infectious, in a population where everyone is susceptible, infects about 1.9 people a day. Over the 8 days they are infectious, they infect 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15 people. This is the basic reproduction number, R0, and 15 is a typical value for measles, one of the most contagious diseases known.
In Starsim, the compartments are states, and each transition says where people move from, where they move to, and at what rate (after @):

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # From S to I, at a rate of β = 1.9 per day times the share infectious
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # From I to R, after 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

Read S >> I @ 1.9*I as “from S to I, at a rate of 1.9 × I”. A state in a rate, like I in 1.9*I, is the share of people in that state. A duration, like ss.days(8), is the average time spent in a state before leaving it. The rate 1.9 has no unit of its own, so it takes the unit of the duration: 1.9 per day. ss.Disease puts the transitions together into a disease, and init_prev=0.001 starts the outbreak with 0.1% of people infectious (100 people in a town of 100,000), and everyone else susceptible.
The disease is named measles, after its variable. These are the standard equations of an SIR model, which equations() prints:

measles.equations()

dS/dt = -beta * S * I / N
dI/dt =  beta * S * I / N - I / dur_I
dR/dt =  I / dur_I


Here dur_I is the infectious period (8 days), the mean time in I, so I / dur_I is the rate of recovery.

title: T1 – Getting started
text:
Running the model
To run the model, give it to a sim (ss.Sim), with the size of the population and how long to run for, here 50 days:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0031 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6









The run prints three lines: what it ran (the disease, 100,000 people, as an ODE, from day 0 to day 50), R0 (15.2, as worked out above), and what happened: how many people were infected, and the size and day of the peak.
Starsim chose to run this model as an ODE (a deterministic compartmental model, solved as a set of differential equations), since nothing in it needs individual people. The plot shows each state (S, I, and R), and each transition as the number of people who made it each day (infection and recovery).
The curves answer the question we started with. At first, almost everyone is susceptible, so each infectious person infects about 15 others, and the number infectious grows several times over in a few days. But each infection uses up a susceptible person. Once most of the town has been infected, an infectious person meets mostly people who are already immune, and infects fewer than one other person before recovering: then the number infectious falls, even though β has not changed. The outbreak stops because it runs out of susceptible people, not because the disease becomes less contagious.
With an R0 of 15 and nobody immune, almost everyone in the town is infected, and the outbreak peaks within a week. This is far faster than real measles outbreaks, because the model has no latent period: people are infectious from the moment they are infected, whereas with measles they are infected for about 10 days before they can infect anyone else. Tutorial 3 adds this.

Checking the model
To build a model that runs, Starsim fills in whatever it is not given: here, for example, how people mix (everyone with everyone else equally, since no contacts were given), and how the time spent infectious varies between people (exponentially, as in the standard ODE). describe() shows the whole model as Starsim has built it: every state, transition, and setting, with each value that Starsim chose itself marked as guessed, so that nothing about the model is hidden:

It is worth reading describe() for every new model, to check that it is the model you meant. describe(verbose=True) adds how the model is run (as compiled code or as agents) and what each rate is per step.

title: T1 – Getting started
text:
The same model as agents
Starsim can also run the same model as agents: one simulated person at a time, each with their own state, who are infected and recover by chance. Giving n_agents= says how many agents to simulate. Here, 10,000 agents stand for the 100,000 people of the town, so each agent stands for 10 people. To compare the two, ss.parallel() runs several sims, each with a label, and plots any of their results together, here the number infectious:

agents = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50))
msim = ss.parallel({'ODE': sim, 'Agents': agents})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (ODE, Agents)
  Done in 0.45 s









The epidemic is much the same: almost everyone is infected, and the peak is about as high. It comes a few days later as agents, though, and the run prints a note saying why. Agents move one step of time at a time (by default, a day), and this outbreak is so fast that a day is a long step: the number of infectious people grows several times over in a day. With a shorter step, such as dt=ss.days(0.25), agents follow the ODE closely; Tutorial 2 shows how.
Agents are what a model needs when people differ in ways that compartments can’t hold, such as each person’s own contacts in a network. For a model like this one, where everyone mixes with everyone else, both give the same answer when the step is short enough. The model is written the same way either way. The core tutorials (T1 to T9) mostly use the ODE, since it is fast and gives the expected epidemic, and say where agents would give something different; the agent-based tutorials (A1 to A5) go further with agents.

title: T1 – Getting started
text:
Exercises

Suppose people with measles were infectious for only 5 days, with the same β. What would R0 be? Change the model, run it, and check the R0 the run prints. How does the epidemic change?
Run the agent version of the model with 1,000 agents instead of 10,000 (each standing for 100 people). What changes in the plot, and why?
Using the output of describe(), find out how Starsim assumes that people mix, and how long people stay infectious (the distribution as well as the average).

title: T6 – Geography and mixing
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Can an outbreak in one town seed another? Measles brought into one town doesn’t stay there. People travel to the next town to work, to shop, or to visit family, and some of them carry it with them. Each town then has its own outbreak, with its own timing, and the towns’ outbreaks are linked by the people who move between them. This is a metapopulation model: several populations, each mixing mostly within itself, coupled by movement.
This tutorial takes the measles model from one town to four. By the end, you will be able to:

title: T6 – Geography and mixing
text:
The model so far
This is the model from T5 – Interventions and scenarios: measles in a town of 100,000 people in three age groups, who mix according to a contact matrix, most of them already immune. Since this tutorial makes the disease several times, with different places and movement, the parts that stay the same are made once, and make_measles() puts them together, with the number of people infectious at the start given:

import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5]) # The rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day
infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10) # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)  # Infectious for 8 days on average
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups

def make_measles(init_n=10):
    """ The measles model, by age, with the number infectious at the start given """
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
        init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The share immune in each age group
        init_n = dict(I=init_n),
        name   = 'measles',
    )
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+
    return measles

sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(), networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles.I')

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.8 (R = 2.46 at the start, with 11% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0081 s; measles: 8,795 infections; at most 934 infectious, on 2025-04-27

title: T6 – Geography and mixing
text:
Several towns
The town, Riverton, has three smaller neighbors. A geography (ss.geo.geography()) gives the places: their names, their populations, and where they are (here, positions on a map in kilometers, from which Starsim works out the distance between each pair):

towns = ss.geo.geography(
    names = ['Riverton', 'Hillside', 'Lakeview', 'Fairfield'],
    pop   = [100_000, 40_000, 20_000, 10_000],
    x     = [0, 20, 35, 60], # Kilometers east of Riverton
    y     = [0, 10, -15, 5], # Kilometers north of Riverton
)
towns.distances.round()

array([[ 0., 22., 38., 60.],
       [22.,  0., 29., 40.],
       [38., 29.,  0., 32.],
       [60., 40., 32.,  0.]])


Places are a stratification, as age groups are: stratify(patch=towns) splits each state by town (a “patch” is a place in a metapopulation model), so that each town has its own susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered people, and the contact matrix applies within each town. The populations of the towns give the population of the model, so total_pop isn’t needed. The outbreak starts in Riverton only: ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0, 0]) gives the number infectious at the start in each town.
Without movement, each town is a separate model:

alone = make_measles(init_n=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0, 0])) # 10 people infectious in Riverton, none elsewhere
alone.stratify(patch=towns)

settings = dict(networks=contacts, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
sim = ss.Sim(alone, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('patch').summarize().round()

Sim: measles, 170,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.8 (R = 2.46 at the start, with 11% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.003 s; measles: 8,795 infections; at most 934 infectious, on 2025-04-27


Riverton     8795.0
Hillside        0.0
Lakeview        0.0
Fairfield       0.0
Name: infection, dtype: float64


Riverton has its outbreak, the same as before, and measles never leaves it.

title: T6 – Geography and mixing
text:
Movement between towns
How much people move between places, and where they go, is often not known in detail. A gravity model is the usual first guess: the movement from one place to another grows with the population of the place people go to (a larger town draws more visitors) and falls with the square of the distance between them. The amount of movement is given separately, as the share of their time that people spend in other towns, away, here 1% (about a quarter of an hour a day, or a day out of every three months):

away = ss.par(0.01, bounds=[0.001, 0.1]) # People spend 1% of their time in other towns
measles = make_measles(init_n=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0, 0]))
measles.stratify(patch=towns, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=away))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.by('patch').plot()

Sim: measles, 170,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.8 (R = 2.46 at the start, with 11% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0033 s; measles: 14,957 infections; at most 1,370 infectious, on 2025-05-11









The movement here is commuting: the people of each town keep their home town, but spend a share of their time in the others, where they can be infected by the people there, and infect them. Commuting changes who is exposed where without changing anyone’s home. (Migration, in which people move home, is kind='migrate', with rates of moving rather than shares of time.)
With movement, the outbreak peaks first in Riverton, at the end of April, and then in each other town in turn: in Hillside, the nearest, in late May, then in Lakeview, and last in Fairfield, the smallest and farthest, in mid-June, six weeks after Riverton. Since the towns have the same immunity, each outbreak infects about the same share of its town, about 9%. select() picks one place’s result, as it does an age group’s:

round(sim.results.measles.infection.select(patch='Fairfield').sum())

880


When the movement between places is known, from a survey or from mobile phone data, it can be given as a matrix instead, with ss.geo.Mobility(matrix=..., kind='commute'): row i, column j is the share of their time that the people of place i spend in place j. Geography covers this, the radiation model, and coupling places through the force of infection rather than through movement.

title: T6 – Geography and mixing
text:
How much movement matters
The share of time away is the least certain number in this model. To see how much it matters, run the model with several values of it. ss.parallel() with pars= runs a sim once for each value given (a parameter sweep), labeling each run with its value:

msim = ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(away=[0.001, 0.01, 0.05]))
msim.results.measles.I.select(patch='Fairfield').plot()

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (away=0.001, away=0.01, away=0.05)
  Done in 0.036 s









With 5 times as much movement, Fairfield’s outbreak comes about three weeks earlier; with 10 times less, about five weeks later. The size of the outbreak doesn’t change: in this model, measles always reaches Fairfield in the end.
That last part isn’t realistic. In an ODE, a small fraction of an infectious person can travel to Fairfield on the first day and start an outbreak there; in reality, measles reaches Fairfield only if a whole infectious person does, and then only if the chains of infection they start don’t die out by chance. To see this, run the model as a stochastic model (as in T5), with little movement, many times:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(away=0.001), solver='binomial', **settings)
msim = sim.run(n_runs=30)
msim.results.measles.I.select(patch='Fairfield').plot(lines=True)

MultiSim: 30 runs
  Done in 2.2 s










fairfield = msim.results.measles.infection.select(patch='Fairfield').summarize() # The infections in Fairfield in each run
print('Runs with an outbreak in Fairfield:', sum(fairfield > 100), 'of', len(fairfield))

Runs with an outbreak in Fairfield: 27 of 30


In about one run in ten, measles never takes off in Fairfield: either no infectious person goes there while the other towns’ outbreaks last, or the few infections they cause die out. In the others, the outbreak comes at very different times, from May to the end of the year, when some are still going. For a small place that is weakly linked to others, whether an outbreak arrives at all is a matter of chance, and a model that ignores this overstates how surely it spreads.

title: T6 – Geography and mixing
text:
As agents
The same model runs as agents, each with a home town, with n_agents=. Here there is one agent for each of the 170,000 people:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=170_000, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.by('patch').plot()

Sim: measles, as 170,000 agents, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.14 per day (per infectious contact), 13% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 3.1 s; measles: 14,959 infections; at most 1,371 infectious, on 2025-05-26









Each agent has a home town, and is exposed in the other towns for the share of their time spent there, as in the compartmental model. The outbreaks spread from town to town as in the compartmental model, a little later (the run notes that agents taking whole days can lag the ODE), and with the variation of a stochastic model: in this run, Fairfield’s outbreak happens to come before Lakeview’s. With fewer agents than people, each agent stands for several people, and the 10 people infectious at the start can be as few as one agent, so the outbreak can die out at the start by chance alone.

title: T6 – Geography and mixing
text:
Real places
Places can also be a country’s regions, by name: ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1) gives Kenya’s 47 counties, with their populations, positions, and which share a border. Movement can come from a gravity model, from the radiation model (ss.geo.radiation(), which needs no parameters), from a matrix of movement you supply, or from a register of moves on given dates (e.g. of livestock between farms), and it can be commuting, as here, or migration. See Geography and Population data.

title: T6 – Geography and mixing
text:
Exercises

Lakeview’s children are less often vaccinated: only 65% of them are immune. Give the share immune by age and town (ss.by() with both, multiplied together: e.g. ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98], patch=[1, 1, 0.8125, 1])), and run the model. How does Lakeview’s outbreak compare with the others’?
A campaign that vaccinates 80% of children under 15 in Riverton only, on 1 March (where=(measles.age < 15) & (measles.patch == 'Riverton')): how many infections does it prevent in Riverton, and how many in the other towns? Why so few in the other towns, in this model?
Replace the gravity model with the radiation model (ss.geo.radiation(away=away)). Which towns’ outbreaks come earlier or later, and why?

Solutions · Next: T7 – Data and calibration

text:
Further reading

epydemix: Populations: the populations and contact data of real places, in another Python framework
Xia, Bjørnstad and Grenfell (2004): Measles metapopulation dynamics: a gravity model for epidemiological coupling and dynamics: the gravity model fitted to measles in England and Wales
Simini et al. (2012): A universal model for mobility and migration patterns: the radiation model

title: T5 – Interventions and scenarios
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
How much difference could a vaccination campaign make? Most models are built to answer a question about an intervention: how many infections would a campaign prevent, and would it prevent more than another way of spending the same effort? This tutorial adds vaccination to the measles model, compares a one-off campaign with routine vaccination and with a public health response that cuts transmission, and runs them side by side as scenarios. It then adds one more thing that changes over time, the school calendar, and runs the scenarios many times, to see how sure the answer is.
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

title: T5 – Interventions and scenarios
text:
The model so far
This is the measles model from T4 – Age groups and contacts: an SEIR model in a town of 100,000 people in three age groups, who mix according to a contact matrix in which children have the most contacts. Most people are already immune, but only 80% of children, and 10 people are infectious on 1 January 2025. With these contacts and this immunity, each case at the start infects about 2.5 others:

import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5]) # The rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day

infection   = S >> E @ beta*I       # Infection, at a rate of β times the contacts with infectious people
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The share immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),                           # 10 people infectious at the start
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the share of people in each

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

sim = ss.Sim(measles, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/
Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.8 (R = 2.46 at the start, with 11% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0027 s; measles: 8,795 infections; at most 934 infectious, on 2025-04-27









With R0 = 16, an outbreak can only be prevented if more than 1 − 1/16, or about 94%, of people are immune (the herd immunity threshold). Here about 89% are, so the outbreak infects about 8,800 people over the year, most of them children.

title: T5 – Interventions and scenarios
text:
A vaccination campaign
A vaccine has two parts in a model: the product, what the vaccine does to the people who get it (here, it cuts their chance of infection by 93%, about what one dose of measles vaccine does), and the delivery, who gets it and when. ss.vaccinate() takes both: the vaccine’s efficacy, and the group (where=), the share of that group reached (coverage=), and when (at=, for a campaign on given dates).
Suppose the town’s health office runs a campaign on 1 March, two months into the outbreak, that reaches 80% of children under 15. A scenario is a sim with its own interventions; to compare scenarios, make a sim for each, labeled with a name that says what it is, and run them together with ss.parallel():

campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, where=measles.age < 15, coverage=0.8, at='2025-03-01')

msim = ss.parallel({
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(measles, **settings),
    'Campaign':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, **settings),
})
msim.plot('measles.infection')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (No intervention, Campaign)
  Done in 0.3 s









Both scenarios start from the same town and the same 10 cases, and are the same until 1 March; the campaign scenario is a separate run, not a continuation of the other. After the campaign, the outbreak peaks within a few weeks (people already infected still fall ill) and then dies away: it is cut to about a quarter of its size, from about 8,800 infections to 2,200.
A campaign reaches children whether or not they are already immune, as real campaigns do, so most of its doses go to children who were protected already; what matters is the share of the susceptible children it reaches. Vaccination also doesn’t cure anyone already infected. Each delivery has results of its own, such as the doses delivered:

print('Doses delivered:', round(msim.sims['Campaign'].results.campaign.delivered.sum()))

Doses delivered: 24000


The vaccine here protects everyone vaccinated by 93% (it is “leaky”). Vaccines can also protect some people fully and others not at all, wane over time, be given in several doses, or protect against transmission rather than infection; see Products.

title: T5 – Interventions and scenarios
section: Routine vaccination, and changing a parameter
text:
Routine vaccination, and changing a parameter
A campaign reaches many people on one day. Routine vaccination reaches them over time, for example as children come to a clinic. Without at=, a delivery is routine: each person is offered the vaccine once, when they first become eligible. With a rate as the coverage, they are reached at that rate for as long as they are eligible. Here, children under 15 are reached at a rate that would vaccinate 80% of them in a year (ss.probperyear(0.8) is a probability of 0.8 over a year, which Starsim converts to the probability for each day of the run):

routine = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, where=measles.age < 15, coverage=ss.probperyear(0.8))

Some interventions don’t give people anything, but change how the disease spreads: isolating cases, tracing their contacts, or keeping unvaccinated children home from school. In a model, these are changes to a parameter. ss.modify() changes a parameter from a given date (and, with stop=, until another); it never overwrites the parameter, so when it stops, the parameter has its own value again. Here, an outbreak response from 1 March cuts transmission by 30%:

response = ss.modify(measles.pars.beta, multiply=0.7, start='2025-03-01')

A time series does the same at several dates, each value holding until the next: for example, ss.modify(measles.pars.beta, multiply=ss.timeseries({'2025-03-01': 0.7, '2025-06-01': 0.9}), start='2025-03-01') cuts transmission by 30% from March, and by 10% from June, as the response is scaled down. Interventions covers the other options, such as changing a parameter only for some people, or only while cases are high.

title: T5 – Interventions and scenarios
text:
Comparing scenarios
With four scenarios, ss.parallel() runs them at the same time on the computer’s cores:

sims = {
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(measles, **settings),
    'Campaign':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, **settings),
    'Routine':         ss.Sim(measles, interventions=routine, **settings),
    'Response':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=response, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 4 runs of 4 scenarios (No intervention, Campaign, Routine, Response)
  Done in 0.91 s









Routine vaccination of the same children helps less than the campaign, since by the time most are reached, the outbreak has passed its peak. The response slows the outbreak from the same date, but the outbreak goes on, since the response doesn’t make anyone immune.
msim.summarize() gives each result over the whole run for each scenario: the total of a flow, such as infections, and the value at the end of a state, such as the number recovered. .loc[...] picks out one result, here the total infections:

summary = msim.summarize()
summary.loc['measles_infection']








value


scenario





No intervention
8795.480637


Campaign
2209.958402


Routine
5468.051569


Response
6683.434300







How a scenario is judged depends on the question. The campaign prevents the most infections, but it needs the most doses at once; the response prevents fewer, but needs no vaccine. A model can’t make that choice, but it can say what each option buys. Two cautions in reading such a table: compare the peak and timing as well as the totals, and run long enough. An intervention can delay infections beyond the end of the run, so a lower total over a short run is not the same as infections prevented for good.

title: T5 – Interventions and scenarios
text:
School terms
Transmission of measles is not the same all year. Before vaccination, measles epidemics in England and Wales followed the school calendar: transmission among children rose when schools opened and fell in the holidays. To add this to the model, split the contacts into those at school and the rest. Suppose that of children’s 10 contacts a day with other children, 6 are at school. Each set of contacts is its own ss.contacts(), with a name, and they are given to the sim together; they add up to the same matrix as before. ss.timeseries() gives a value on each of a set of dates, each holding until the next: here, 1 in term and 0 in the holidays (a simplified calendar), repeating every year (period=ss.years(1)). ss.modify() multiplies the school contacts by it:

school = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[6, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]], name='school')
other  = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[4, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]], name='other')
terms = ss.timeseries({
    '2025-01-01': 0, # New Year holidays
    '2025-01-06': 1, # Spring term
    '2025-04-07': 0, # Spring holidays
    '2025-04-21': 1, # Summer term
    '2025-07-21': 0, # Summer holidays
    '2025-09-01': 1, # Autumn term
    '2025-12-19': 0, # Winter holidays
}, period=ss.years(1))
holidays = ss.modify(school, multiply=terms)

The holidays are part of how the town works, not a policy, so they are given to the sim as a connector (connectors=) rather than as an intervention, though they work the same way. Their effect depends on when the outbreak happens, so suppose measles is brought into the town on 1 May instead, and compare the model with and without the holidays:

calendar = dict(networks=[school, other], total_pop=100_000, start='2025-05-01', stop='2026-05-01')
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No school holidays': ss.Sim(measles, **calendar),
    'School holidays':    ss.Sim(measles, connectors=holidays, **calendar),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (No school holidays, School holidays)
  Done in 0.69 s









The summer holidays come just as the outbreak is growing fastest. They don’t stop it, but flatten it: the peak is about half as high, and the outbreak lasts into the winter, with a second rise when schools reopen in September. The total number infected hardly changes, since in the end it is set by the immunity in the town, but the load on clinics at any one time is much lower. A calendar like this matters most over many years, when it sets the timing of epidemics from one year to the next.
A smooth yearly cycle is another way to give transmission a season: ss.seasonal(mean=0.14, amplitude=0.2, peak='January'), used in place of β, rises and falls 20% either side of 0.14 each year. A time series can also hold a rate, a duration, or the coverage of an intervention, and be read from a file. See Time and Parameters.

title: T5 – Interventions and scenarios
text:
Many runs
So far each scenario has been run once, as an ODE, which gives the expected course of the outbreak. But two towns with the same people, contacts, and immunity don’t have the same outbreak: who happens to meet whom, and when, differs, and this matters most when cases are few. Is the campaign’s effect as certain as one run makes it look?
A stochastic model draws at random the number of people who move between states each day. Run with solver='binomial' (a chain-binomial model), it is the same model, with the same states, rates, and contacts; only how it is solved changes. n_runs=30 runs each scenario 30 times, each with its own random numbers:

msim = ss.parallel({
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(measles, solver='binomial', **settings),
    'Campaign':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, solver='binomial', **settings),
}, n_runs=30)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 60 runs of 2 scenarios (No intervention, Campaign)
  Done in 0.11 s









For each scenario, the plot shows the median of the runs at each time, and the band that holds 95% of them (msim.plot('measles.I', lines=True) shows every run instead). Without the campaign, the outbreaks differ mainly in their timing, peaking from April to June. With it, they differ in size too: the campaign falls on the same date in every run, but some outbreaks have grown further by then than others, and the further an outbreak has grown, the less a campaign can prevent. The band is a summary at each time: since the runs peak on different days, the median curve is lower and broader than the curve of any one outbreak, and is not the course of a typical one.
To ask how many infections a scenario has, first total each run, then summarize the totals. msim.summarize() does this for every result: the median of the runs, the range that holds 95% of them (low and high), the mean, and the standard deviation:

msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']

Each scenario’s runs use the same random numbers as the other’s: run 1 of each starts with the same draws, run 2 with the same draws, and so on. So until 1 March, each pair of runs is the same outbreak, and the difference between them afterwards is the effect of the campaign, not of chance. summarize(baseline=...) gives these differences, run by run (a negative difference is a fall, here infections averted):

msim.summarize(baseline='No intervention').loc['measles_infection']

The campaign averts between about 5,500 and 7,500 infections in 95% of the pairs of runs, about 6,700 in the median pair. The uncertainty here is only the chance in who meets whom: every run has the same β, the same immunity, and the same contacts. Uncertainty in those, which is often larger, comes from varying them too, as in T7 – Data and calibration.
The random numbers of a run come from its random seed, rand_seed (by default 1), and n_runs=30 uses the seeds 1 to 30. The same model with the same seed gives the same result every time, on any computer, so a run that looks odd can be looked at again. Keep the seed fixed while checking a change to a model, and use many seeds before drawing a conclusion. For more on many runs, seeds, and summaries, see Scenarios and Random numbers.

title: T5 – Interventions and scenarios
text:
Exercises

The campaign above is run on 1 March. How many infections does it prevent if it is run on 1 February instead, or on 1 May? What does this say about how quickly a campaign should follow the first cases?
Add a scenario that combines the campaign and the response (interventions=[campaign, response]). Is its effect the sum of the two on their own? Why not?
Start the outbreak with 2 infectious people rather than 10 (init_n=dict(I=2)), and run the model with no intervention 50 times as a stochastic model. In what share of runs does the outbreak die out? Compare this with (1/R)², where R ≈ 2.5 is the reproduction number at the start: roughly the chance that the chains of infection started by both people die out.
