title: A5 – Custom modules
text:
🧠25% 🤖75%
Most of the science in a Starsim model lives in its modules. Diseases, networks, demographics, interventions, analyzers, and connectors are all modules, and they all share the same structure. Most of a model can be declared: states, transitions, rates, deliveries, and modifiers, as in the tutorials so far. Sooner or later, though, a model of individual people needs something none of these say: a quantity that each person carries and that changes continuously, a rule of your own for who meets whom, or a disease whose course is easiest to say step by step. Then you write a module as code: a Python class whose methods Starsim calls at each step, which can read and change anything in the sim.
T9 wrote an analyzer and an intervention as code. This tutorial writes the other kinds that agent-based models most often need, each a small step from what can be declared:
Each gives up a little of what Starsim knows about the model (what describe() can show, which solvers can run it) in return for freedom.

title: A5 – Custom modules
text:
Choosing a base class
Rather than subclassing ss.Module directly, you almost always want to subclass one of the module types, so that your module is run at the right point in the simulation loop and ends up in the right place on the sim:



Base class
Use for
Added to the sim via




ss.Disease, ss.Infection
Disease natural history and transmission
diseases=


ss.Network
Who contacts whom
networks=


ss.Demographics
Births, deaths, migration
demographics=


ss.Intervention
Actions that change the simulation
interventions=


ss.Analyzer
Recording results without changing anything
analyzers=


ss.Connector
Interactions between modules
connectors=


ss.Module
Anything that doesn’t fit the others
custom= (or as a positional argument)

title: A5 – Custom modules
text:
A disease written as code
In A1, immunity that wanes was one more declared transition, R >> S. Here is the same SIRS model written as code. Rather than starting from a blank page, the easiest approach is usually to inherit from a template and change only what’s different. ssl.AgentSIR is the SIR model written as code (it is Starsim 3’s ss.SIR); its states are per-agent arrays, susceptible, infected, and recovered, and its methods move agents between them:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

class SIRS(ssl.AgentSIR):
    def __init__(self, pars=None, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            dur_imm = ss.expon(scale=ss.days(180)), # How long immunity lasts after recovery
        )
        self.update_pars(pars, **kwargs)

        # SIR states are added automatically; here we add the time of losing immunity
        self.define_states(
            ss.TimeArr('ti_susceptible', label='Time of becoming susceptible again'),
        )
        return

    def set_progression(self, uids):
        """ Schedule recovery and death as usual, then schedule the waning of immunity """
        super().set_progression(uids)
        recovering = uids[np.isfinite(self.ti_recovered[uids])] # Agents who are going to die have ti_recovered = NaN
        self.ti_susceptible[recovering] = self.ti_recovered[recovering] + self.pars.dur_imm.rvs(recovering)
        return

    def step_state(self):
        """ Do the usual SIR transitions, then return agents whose immunity has waned to susceptible """
        super().step_state()
        waning = (self.recovered & self.ti_susceptible.due()).uids # Those whose time has come
        self.recovered[waning] = False
        self.susceptible[waning] = True
        return

The new class includes the following main changes:

In __init__() we added the extra parameter (dur_imm) and state (ti_susceptible) that the model needs. We don’t need to redefine the SIR states, since we inherit them.
ssl.AgentSIR.set_prognoses() does two things: it calls set_infection() to make the agents infectious, then set_progression() to schedule what happens to them next. Waning immunity is part of the second, so that’s the only one we extend: we call super() to do the usual scheduling, then sample a waning time for everyone who is going to recover. Agents who are going to die instead have ti_recovered set to NaN, which is how we filter them out.
step_state() likewise calls super() and adds only the recovered → susceptible transition.

Here it is next to the declared SIRS of A1, with the same R0 (0.4 per day × 7 days = 2.8) and durations. A disease whose transmission is written as code transmits over the sim’s networks, so both are given a mixing pool in which everyone has one contact a day, which is the same as homogeneous mixing with β = 0.4 per day:

coded = SIRS(beta=ss.perday(0.4), dur_inf=ss.expon(scale=ss.days(7)), p_death=0, init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
declared = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I,          # A chance of infection of 0.4 per contact per day
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(7),
    waning    = R >> S @ ss.days(180),
    init_prev = 0.01,
    name      = 'cold',
)

pars = dict(networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=1), n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(2*365), verbose=0)
sim_coded = ss.Sim(coded, **pars)
sim_declared = ss.Sim(declared, **pars)
sim_coded.run()
sim_declared.run()

plt.figure()
plt.plot(sim_declared.results.cold.timevec, sim_declared.results.cold.I, label='Declared')
plt.plot(sim_coded.results.cold.timevec, sim_coded.results.cold.infected, label='Written as code')
plt.ylabel('Number infectious')
plt.legend();








The two are the same model, and give the same epidemic, up to chance: a large first wave, and then smaller waves as immunity wanes. They work out the chance of infection in a step the same way (the rate times the share of people who are infectious, turned into a chance), and round each duration to whole steps the same way, so they agree at any step: over four seeds at daily steps, the first wave peaks at 3032 people infectious when coded, and 3015 when declared. What differs is what Starsim knows about them. The declared disease can be shown (describe(), diagram(), equations()), run as an ODE or a stochastic compartmental model as well as agents, and fitted with sim.fit(); its results are named after its states and transitions. The coded one is a set of methods: it runs only as agents, and Starsim can’t show what it does. So for a model that can be declared, declare it. Write a disease as code when its course is easier to say in code than in transitions, or to keep a Starsim 3 model as it was (a Starsim 3 subclass of ss.SIR can subclass ssl.AgentSIR unchanged).

title: A5 – Custom modules
text:
The parts of a module
The class above shows the parts that most modules have:

Parameters. In __init__(), call super().__init__() first, then declare the parameters with their defaults with self.define_pars(), then apply any user-supplied overrides with self.update_pars(), which raises an error for a parameter that wasn’t declared (catching typos early). Rates and durations should use Starsim’s time parameters (e.g. ss.days(), ss.peryear()), so they scale correctly with the timestep.
States. Per-agent arrays that persist across timesteps, declared with self.define_states(): ss.BoolState for true or false, ss.FloatArr for a number, and ss.TimeArr for a time, as a step number (due() gives those whose time has come, rounding a time between steps up or down at random in proportion, so durations keep their mean). Each becomes an attribute (self.ti_susceptible); it grows as agents are born, and each ss.BoolState gives a result, the number of people for whom it is true. Track per-agent data this way, never as a plain Python attribute or a hand-built array.
Results. Time series of your own, declared in init_results() with self.define_results() and filled in each step at self.ti.
The work. step() (or, for a disease, step_state() and the methods it calls), which Starsim calls once per timestep. Inside it, self.sim gives access to the whole simulation, self.ti is the current timestep, and self.t.dt is the module’s timestep. Use self.sim rather than a variable from outside the class, since the sim works on its own copy of each module.
Randomness. For anything random, use a Starsim distribution (e.g. ss.expon, ss.bernoulli, ss.normal) as a parameter or an attribute, rather than calling np.random directly, so your results stay reproducible and scenarios differ only where they should; see Random numbers.

title: A5 – Custom modules
section: A quantity for each person: immunity that fades
text:
A quantity for each person: immunity that fades
In both versions above, immunity is all or nothing: people are fully protected until they move back to S, and then not protected at all. For many respiratory infections, protection fades gradually as antibodies decline, so each person’s susceptibility depends on how long ago they recovered. That is a per-person quantity that changes continuously, which a declared model has no words for, but which is a few lines of code.
The module holds each person’s antibody level. It is 1 just after recovery and halves every half_life. It is an ss.Module, since it is neither a disease nor an intervention, and it reads who recovered in the last step from the declared disease (recovery.uids):

class Antibodies(ss.Module):
    """ Each person's antibody level: 1 on recovery, then halving every half_life """

    def __init__(self, half_life=ss.days(90), **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            half_life = half_life,
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(
            ss.FloatArr('level', default=0.0, label='Antibody level'),
        )
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('mean_level', label='Mean antibody level'), # A mean (a ratio), so not scaled by the number of people per agent
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        decay = 0.5**(self.t.dt/self.pars.half_life) # The share left after one step
        self.level[:] = self.level*decay
        recovered = self.sim.diseases.cold.recovery.uids # Those who recovered in the last step
        self.level[recovered] = 1.0
        return

    def update_results(self):
        super().update_results()
        self.results.mean_level[self.ti] = self.level.mean()
        return

The infection itself has no immunity here: people go back to S when they recover (an SIS model), and the antibodies are its only protection. The module keeps the level, and a modifier says what it does: it multiplies each person’s susceptibility by what the antibodies leave of it. A modifier never overwrites the quantity it changes, so the disease’s own rel_sus is kept, and describe() lists the modifier as part of the model:

S, I = ss.states('S I')
sis = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.4*I, recovery=I >> S @ ss.days(7), init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

def susceptibility(sim):
    """ Each person's susceptibility: 1 minus their antibody level """
    return 1 - sim.custom.antibodies.level

protection = ss.modify(sis.rel_sus, multiply=susceptibility)

To compare, here are the infection with antibodies that halve every 90 days, the same infection with no immunity at all, and the all-or-nothing SIRS, whose protection lasts 180 days on average, about as long as the antibodies take to halve twice:

sims = {
    'No immunity':          ss.Sim(sis, **pars),
    'All or nothing':       ss.Sim(declared, **pars),
    'Antibodies that fade': ss.Sim(sis, Antibodies(), connectors=protection, **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold.I')








With no immunity, the infection settles at once at an endemic level. With either kind of immunity, the first wave leaves many people protected, so the number infectious falls and then rises again as protection is lost. With antibodies that fade, people regain some susceptibility soon after recovering, instead of none at all until they lose their protection entirely, so the second wave comes sooner and is larger, and the infection settles at about twice the level it does with all-or-nothing immunity. The module’s own result is among the sim’s results, under the module’s name:

msim.sims['Antibodies that fade'].results.antibodies.mean_level.plot()








A module that keeps a value for each person works on agents, so a sim with one runs as agents, and declared diseases in the same sim run as agents too, with no change to how they are written.

title: A5 – Custom modules
text:
A network written as code
The networks of A2 pair people at random, or as partners. Suppose instead that people mostly meet others of a similar age: children at school, adults at work, older people with each other. A network written as code is a subclass of ss.Network (or of one of its subclasses) that overrides how edges are made: add_pairs() makes them, and step(), called every step, here removes the day’s contacts and makes new ones. self.append() adds edges, given as the UIDs of the two people in each (p1 and p2) and a transmission multiplier for each (beta).
To pair people of similar ages, sort them by their age plus a little random noise (with a standard deviation of spread), and connect each person with their neighbors in that order:

class AgeNet(ss.Network):
    """ Contacts each day with people close in age """

    def __init__(self, n_contacts=4, spread=ss.years(2), **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            n_contacts = n_contacts, # The number of contacts each person has each day (an even number)
            spread = spread,         # How far apart in age contacts tend to be
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.noise = ss.normal(0, 1) # A Starsim distribution, so that the draws are reproducible
        return

    def add_pairs(self):
        uids = self.sim.people.alive.uids
        age = self.sim.people.age[uids] + self.pars.spread.years*self.noise.rvs(uids) # Each person's age, blurred a little
        order = uids[np.argsort(age, kind='stable')] # Everyone, from youngest to oldest
        p1, p2 = [], []
        for k in range(1, self.pars.n_contacts//2 + 1): # Each person, with the k-th next person in the order
            p1.append(order[:-k])
            p2.append(order[k:])
        p1 = np.concatenate(p1)
        p2 = np.concatenate(p2)
        self.append(p1=p1, p2=p2, beta=np.ones(len(p1)))
        return

    def step(self):
        self.remove_edges(np.ones(len(self), dtype=bool)) # Yesterday's contacts end...
        self.add_pairs()                                  # ...and today's begin
        return

Before using a network, check that it makes what you meant. Here, the ages of the two people in each contact should be nearly the same, and each person should have about 4 contacts:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
cold = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.1*I, # A chance of infection of 0.1 per contact per day: with 4 contacts, R0 = 0.1 × 4 × 7 = 2.8
                   recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(7), init_prev=0.001, name='cold')

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(250), verbose=0)
sim = ss.Sim(cold, networks=AgeNet(), **pars)
sim.init()
df = sim.networks.agenet.to_df()
age = sim.people.age
print('Correlation of the ages of contacts:', round(np.corrcoef(age[ss.uids(df.p1)], age[ss.uids(df.p2)])[0, 1], 3))
print('Contacts per person:', round(2*len(df)/len(sim.people), 2))

Correlation of the ages of contacts: 0.992
Contacts per person: 4.0


Now compare it with a random network with the same number of contacts:

sims = {
    'Random contacts':       ss.Sim(cold, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4), **pars),
    'Contacts close in age': ss.Sim(cold, networks=AgeNet(), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold.I')








The number of contacts is the same, but when they are close in age, the epidemic is slower and flatter. The infection still reaches about as many people in the end, but each case’s contacts overlap more with those of the person who infected them (people of the same age meet each other), so it can’t jump straight across the population, and spreads more slowly. A contact matrix with many narrow age groups would give much the same, under every solver (T4): a network written as code is worth it when the rule is about individuals, such as who is in which household, school, or partnership, rather than about groups.

title: A5 – Custom modules
text:
Which to use




What you write
What Starsim still does
What is given up




Declared
States, transitions, deliveries, modifiers
Everything: describe(), every solver, fitting
Nothing, if it can say what you need


Declared, with a little code
A function of the sim as a rate, a condition, or a modifier’s amount
Results, solvers that can take the function, fitting
Speed (the function runs once a step), and showing what the function does


A module written as code
A class with step() (and states, results, parameters)
Time, people, random numbers, parallel runs, its results
Showing what the module does, and solvers other than agents if it keeps a value for each person


A disease or network written as code
A subclass of ss.Infection or ss.Network
The same, and transmission over the sim’s networks
The same, and fitting its structure



Start declared, and move down the table only for the part that needs it. Here, the SIRS model didn’t need code at all; the antibodies needed a module, but only for the antibody level itself, with a declared disease and a modifier for the rest; and the network needed code for its rule of who meets whom. When code is slow, because it loops over agents in Python, @ss.jit compiles a function with Numba, with no change to what it does; see Custom modules in the user guide, which also covers the order in which Starsim calls a module’s methods, demographics and connectors written as code, and the pitfalls.

title: A5 – Custom modules
text:
Exercises

Change the half-life of the antibodies to 30 days and to 365 days. How does each change the endemic level of infection, compared with no immunity and with the all-or-nothing SIRS?
Give AgeNet a parameter p_random, the share of each person’s contacts that are with anyone at random rather than with people close in age (hint: shuffle a share of the order before pairing, or add a second, random network). How large does it have to be before the epidemic looks like the one with random contacts?
The SIRS class schedules each person’s loss of immunity at recovery. Write an SIRS in which immunity is lost instead with a constant chance each step (an exponential duration, drawn step by step), using an ss.bernoulli distribution in step_state(). Does it give the same epidemic?

T1 – Getting started

import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)


Exercise 1
Suppose people with measles were infectious for only 5 days, with the same β. What would R0 be? Change the model, run it, and check the R0 the run prints. How does the epidemic change?
R0 = β × the infectious period = 1.9 × 5 = 9.5, which the second run prints. With a shorter infectious period, people recover sooner, so fewer are infectious at once, and the peak is lower; but since R0 is still well above 5, almost everyone is still infected.

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery8 = I >> R @ ss.days(8) # Infectious for 8 days, as in the tutorial
recovery5 = I >> R @ ss.days(5) # Infectious for 5 days instead
measles8 = ss.Disease(infection, recovery8, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
measles5 = ss.Disease(infection, recovery5, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')

sim8 = ss.Sim(measles8, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim5 = ss.Sim(measles5, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
msim = ss.parallel({'Infectious for 8 days': sim8, 'Infectious for 5 days': sim5})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Infectious for 8 days, Infectious for 5 days)
  Done in 0.13 s











Exercise 2
Run the agent version of the model with 1,000 agents instead of 10,000 (each standing for 100 people). What changes in the plot, and why?
Surprisingly little: in an epidemic this large, which infects almost everyone, even 1,000 agents follow the same course, and the two curves differ by little more than chance. What changes is the detail. Each agent now stands for 100 people, so the results move in steps of 100, and chance plays a larger part with fewer agents (try another rand_seed= to see how much the curve moves). This matters most when following small numbers, such as the first or last few cases of an outbreak.

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

many = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50))
few  = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=1_000, stop=ss.days(50))
msim = ss.parallel({'10,000 agents': many, '1,000 agents': few})
msim.plot('measles.I')

title: Solutions
text:
T2 – Building a model

import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)


Exercise 1
A town of 2,000 people has had no measles for many years, and 70% of its people are immune. Five people arrive with measles. Using init and init_n, model the outbreak over a year. How many people are infected? Is the reproduction number at the start above or below 1?
With 30% of people susceptible, the reproduction number at the start is 15.2 × 0.3 ≈ 4.6 (which the run prints after R0, as R = 4.56 at the start), well above 1. Almost all of the 600 susceptible people are infected. The run also notes that with only 5 people infected at the start, whether an outbreak takes off is partly a matter of chance, which the ODE doesn’t show; as the note says, running the model many times with a stochastic solver (solver='gillespie', with ss.parallel(n_runs=...)) does.

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.7), init_n=dict(I=5))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=2_000, stop=ss.days(365))
sim.run()
print('Infections:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))

Sim: measles, 2,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 365
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 4.56 at the start, with 30% susceptible), with 5 infectious at the start
  Note: "measles" starts with 5 infected, so whether it takes off is a matter of chance, which solver="ode" does not show; solver="gillespie" with ss.parallel(n_runs=...) does
  Done in 0.002 s; measles: 588 infections; at most 270 infectious, on day 14
Infections: 588




Exercise 2
Using the final size relation, a model with R0 = 1.5 should infect about 58% of people. Choose β to give R0 = 1.5 with an infectious period of 8 days, run the model for long enough for the outbreak to end, and check.
β = R0 / the infectious period = 1.5 / 8 ≈ 0.19 per day. The outbreak is much slower than with R0 = 15, so it needs about two years to end.

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ (1.5/8)*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(730))
sim.run()
print('Share infected:', round(sim.results.measles.R[-1] / 100_000, 2))

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 730
  measles: R0 = 1.5, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0016 s; measles: 58,292 infections; at most 6,369 infectious, on day 91
Share infected: 0.58




Exercise 3
Change the model to density-dependent transmission (I.n), choosing β so that R0 is still 15 in a town of 100,000. Then run it in a town of 10,000 and of 1,000,000. How does the outbreak change with the size of the town, and how does this differ from the frequency-dependent model?
With density-dependent transmission, R0 = β N × the infectious period, so for R0 = 15.2 in a town of 100,000, β = 15.2 / (100,000 × 8) = 1.9 × 10⁻⁵ per infectious person per day. In a town of 10,000, R0 is then only 1.5, so the outbreak is slow and infects about 60% of people; in a town of 1,000,000, R0 is 152, and almost everyone is infected within days. With frequency-dependent transmission, R0 and the shares infected would be the same in towns of every size. Each run prints its R0 as it starts, with verbose=1, and sim.diseases.measles.R0() gives it.

beta = 1.9e-5 # Per infectious person per day
for pop in [10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000]:
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I.n
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10))
    sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=pop, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    res = sim.results.measles
    print('Town of', pop, ' share infected:', round(res.R[-1] / pop, 2), ' peak infectious:', round(res.I.max()))

Town of 10000  share infected: 0.6  peak infectious: 673
Town of 100000  share infected: 1.0  peak infectious: 75229
Town of 1000000  share infected: 1.0  peak infectious: 951751

title: Solutions
text:
T3 – Building a disease

import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)


Exercise 1
Measles has a latent period of 10 to 12 days. Run the SEIR model with a latent period of 12 days, using pars=. Does R0 change? How do the timing and height of the peak change?
R0 doesn’t change (15.2), since it depends only on β and the infectious period. A longer latent period makes the generation time longer, so the epidemic grows more slowly: it peaks about 3 days later, and a little lower.

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta           = ss.par(1.9, bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate per day')
dur_latent     = ss.par(ss.days(10), bounds=[ss.days(7), ss.days(14)], doc='Average latent period')
dur_infectious = ss.par(ss.days(8), doc='Average infectious period')
infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
progression = E >> I @ dur_latent
recovery    = I >> R @ dur_infectious
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001))

latent10 = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
latent12 = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(dur_latent=ss.days(12)), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
msim = ss.parallel({'Latent period of 10 days': latent10, 'Latent period of 12 days': latent12})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Latent period of 10 days, Latent period of 12 days)
  Done in 0.16 s











Exercise 2
Give the infectious period an Erlang distribution too, with k=4. Using R0() and a plot of I, check whether R0 or the course of the epidemic changes.
R0 is unchanged, since the average infectious period is still 8 days. The epidemic peaks a few days sooner and higher: with an exponential infectious period, some people stay infectious for a long time, which spreads their infections out, whereas with an Erlang distribution most people are infectious for close to 8 days.

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001))
exponential = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(8)) # An Erlang infectious period
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001))
erlang = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
erlang.run()
print('R0:', round(erlang.diseases.measles.R0(), 1))

msim = ss.parallel({'Exponential': exponential, 'Erlang': erlang})
msim.plot('measles.I')

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0016 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 36,390 infectious, on day 25
R0: 15.2
MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Exponential, Erlang)
  Done in 0.16 s











Exercise 3
About 1 in 10 people with measles in this town are admitted to hospital, after 4 days of being infectious on average, and stay for 7 days. Add a state for people in hospital (assume they don’t transmit), and find the largest number of people in hospital at once.
People leaving I now branch: 10% go to hospital (H) after 4 days on average, and 90% recover after 8. People in hospital are not in I, so they don’t transmit, which is why R0 falls a little, to 14.4: those admitted are infectious for 4 days instead of 8.

S, E, I, H, R = ss.states('S E I H R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
admission   = ss.Transition(I, H, dur=ss.days(4), p=0.1) # 10% go to hospital...
recovery    = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8), p=0.9) # ...and the rest recover
discharge   = H >> R @ ss.days(7)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, admission, recovery, discharge, init=dict(I=0.001))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
sim.run()
print('Most people in hospital at once:', round(sim.results.measles.H.max()))
sim.results.measles.H.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  measles: R0 = 14.4, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0018 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 27,872 infectious, on day 28
Most people in hospital at once: 2440

title: Solutions
text:
T4 – Age groups and contacts
Each solution starts from the model of the tutorial: measles in a town of 100,000 people in three age groups, with immunity by age and a contact matrix.

import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

def make_measles(immune=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])):
    """ The measles model of T4, with the share immune in each age group given """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5])
    infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(R=immune), init_n=dict(I=10), name='measles')
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
    return measles

matrix = [[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]
settings = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)

1. Fewer contacts between children.

measles = make_measles()
open_schools   = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=matrix)
closed_schools = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[5, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]])
for label, contacts in {'Schools open': open_schools, 'Schools closed': closed_schools}.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(measles, networks=contacts, label=label, **(settings | dict(verbose=1))) # verbose=1 to print R at the start
    sim.run()
    print(sim.results.measles.infection.by('age').summarize().round())

Sim "Schools open": measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.8 (R = 2.46 at the start, with 11% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0017 s; measles: 8,795 infections; at most 934 infectious, on 2025-04-27
0-14     5461.0
15-64    3208.0
65+       127.0
Name: infection, dtype: float64
Sim "Schools closed": measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 13.4 (R = 1.57 at the start, with 11% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0014 s; measles: 6,720 infections; at most 366 infectious, on 2025-07-29
0-14     3867.0
15-64    2745.0
65+       107.0
Name: infection, dtype: float64


The reproduction number at the start (R, in the line each run prints as it starts) falls from about 2.5 to about 1.6, and the outbreak is about a quarter smaller (6,700 infections rather than 8,800), and peaks three months later, at the end of July. Most of the infections prevented are in children, but adults and older adults have fewer infections too, though their own contacts have not changed: they are infected by children, and with fewer children infected, there are fewer infectious children for them to meet. (The matrix with fewer contacts between children is still reciprocal, since only the contacts of children with each other changed.)
2. The same immunity in every age group.

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=matrix)
msim = ss.parallel({
    'Immunity by age': ss.Sim(make_measles(), networks=contacts, **settings),
    '90% immune at every age': ss.Sim(make_measles(immune=0.9), networks=contacts, **settings),
})
msim.plot('measles.infection')
for sim in msim.sims:
    print(sim.label, '- infections:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))








Immunity by age - infections: 8795
90% immune at every age - infections: 5856


In the town of the tutorial, 0.3 × 80% + 0.6 × 92% + 0.1 × 98% ≈ 89% of people are immune, about the same as 90% at every age. Yet with the same immunity at every age, the reproduction number at the start is about 1.6 rather than 2.5, and the outbreak is a third smaller (5,900 infections rather than 8,800), though the number of people susceptible is almost the same. Where the susceptible people are matters, not only how many there are: a gap in immunity among children, who have the most contacts, gives measles far more chances to spread than the same gap spread evenly over the town. This is why measles programs track coverage by age and birth cohort, not only overall.
3. A higher birth rate.

demographics = lambda rate: [ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(rate)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02))]
long = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, unit='day', dt=ss.weeks(1), start='2025-01-01', stop='2045-01-01', verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({
    '30 births a year per 1,000': ss.Sim(make_measles(), demographics=demographics(0.03), **long),
    '45 births a year per 1,000': ss.Sim(make_measles(), demographics=demographics(0.045), **long),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')








With more births, the outbreaks after the first come sooner and closer together, and settle sooner to a higher level of infection. Susceptible children are born faster, so the number needed for the next outbreak builds up sooner. (The population also grows faster, by 2.5% a year rather than 1%, which is why the level of infection keeps rising.)

title: Solutions
text:
T5 – Interventions and scenarios
Each solution starts from the model of the tutorial:

import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

def make_measles(init_n=10):
    """ The measles model of T5, with the number infectious at the start given """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5])
    infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
        init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
        init_n = dict(I=init_n),
        name   = 'measles',
    )
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
    return measles

measles = make_measles()
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]])
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)

1. The timing of the campaign. Run the campaign on each date, and compare the infections with those of no intervention:

sims = {'No intervention': ss.Sim(measles, **settings)}
for date in ['2025-02-01', '2025-03-01', '2025-05-01']:
    campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, where=measles.age < 15, coverage=0.8, at=date)
    sims['Campaign on ' + date] = ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, **settings)
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')
msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']

A campaign on 1 February prevents about 90% of the outbreak; on 1 March, about three quarters of it; on 1 May, when the outbreak is near its peak, only about one infection in eight. Every month of delay lets the outbreak grow by a large factor, so a campaign does the most good if it follows the first cases quickly.
2. The campaign and the response together.

campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, where=measles.age < 15, coverage=0.8, at='2025-03-01')
response = ss.modify(measles.pars.beta, multiply=0.7, start='2025-03-01')
sims = {
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(measles, **settings),
    'Campaign':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, **settings),
    'Response':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=response, **settings),

averted.round()

Together, they prevent more than either alone, but less than the sum of what each prevents on its own. Both act on the same outbreak: once the campaign has cut it to a fraction of its size, there are fewer infections left for the response to prevent.
3. Outbreaks that die out. Count the runs with fewer than 100 infections:

sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(init_n=2), solver='binomial', **settings)
msim = sim.run(n_runs=50)
totals = msim.results.measles.infection.summarize() # The total infections in each run
print('Outbreak died out in', sum(totals < 100), 'of 50 runs; (1/R)^2 =', round((1/2.46)**2, 2))

Outbreak died out in 7 of 50 runs; (1/R)^2 = 0.17


With 2 people infectious at the start, the outbreak dies out in about one run in seven, close to (1/R)² ≈ 17%. For the outbreak to die out, the chains of infection started by each of the first cases must all die out, and each does so with a chance of roughly 1/R. The match is only rough, since R = 2.46 is an average over the age groups: a first case who is a child, with many contacts, is more likely to start an outbreak than an adult, so who the first cases are matters as well as how many there are. In the runs that do take off, the size of the outbreak hardly varies; chance matters at the start, when cases are few.

title: Solutions
text:
T6 – Geography and mixing
Each solution starts from the model of the tutorial, in four towns:

import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

towns = ss.geo.geography(
    names = ['Riverton', 'Hillside', 'Lakeview', 'Fairfield'],
    pop   = [100_000, 40_000, 20_000, 10_000],
    x     = [0, 20, 35, 60],
    y     = [0, 10, -15, 5],
)

def make_towns(immune=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98]), mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=0.01)):
    """ The measles model of T6, in four towns, with the share immune and the movement given """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5])
    infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
        init   = dict(R=immune),
        init_n = dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0, 0])),
        name   = 'measles',
    )
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
    measles.stratify(patch=towns, mobility=mobility)
    return measles

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]])
settings = dict(networks=contacts, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)

1. Lower immunity in Lakeview. The share immune is the product of the values by age and by town, so a factor of 0.8125 for Lakeview gives 0.8 × 0.8125 = 65% of its children (and 75% of its adults under 65, and 80% of older adults):

sims = {
    'Same immunity':        ss.Sim(make_towns(), **settings),
    'Less immune Lakeview': ss.Sim(make_towns(immune=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98], patch=[1, 1, 0.8125, 1])), **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.results.measles.I.select(patch='Lakeview').plot()
for label, sim in zip(sims, msim.sims):
    print(label, '- infections in each town:')
    print(sim.results.measles.infection.by('patch').summarize().round())








Same immunity - infections in each town:
Riverton     8795.0
Hillside     3521.0
Lakeview     1760.0
Fairfield     880.0
Name: infection, dtype: float64
Less immune Lakeview - infections in each town:
Riverton     8818.0
Hillside     3531.0
Lakeview     5429.0
Fairfield     884.0
Name: infection, dtype: float64


With less immunity, Lakeview has a much larger outbreak, about 5,400 infections (over a quarter of the town) rather than 1,800, which comes earlier and peaks higher: with more susceptible people, each case there infects more others, so the outbreak grows faster once it arrives. The other towns’ outbreaks hardly change, since their own immunity is unchanged: Lakeview’s larger outbreak sends a few more infectious visitors to them, but the size of an outbreak in each town is set mostly by that town’s own susceptible people.
2. A campaign in Riverton only.

measles = make_towns()
campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, where=(measles.age < 15) & (measles.patch == 'Riverton'), coverage=0.8, at='2025-03-01')
sims = {
    'No intervention':      ss.Sim(measles, **settings),
    'Campaign in Riverton': ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
for label, sim in zip(sims, msim.sims):
    print(label, '- infections in each town:')
    print(sim.results.measles.infection.by('patch').summarize().round())

No intervention - infections in each town:
Riverton     8795.0
Hillside     3521.0
Lakeview     1760.0
Fairfield     880.0
Name: infection, dtype: float64
Campaign in Riverton - infections in each town:
Riverton     2367.0
Hillside     3479.0
Lakeview     1751.0
Fairfield     878.0
Name: infection, dtype: float64


The campaign prevents about three quarters of the infections in Riverton, but almost none in the other towns. By 1 March, a little measles has already reached them, and as an ODE, the model has an outbreak in every town it reaches, as large as that town’s own immunity allows; fewer cases in Riverton only delay it. A stochastic run (as in the tutorial) would show whether fewer travelers from Riverton make it less likely that measles takes off in the smaller towns at all.
3. The radiation model.

sims = {
    'Gravity':   ss.Sim(make_towns(), **settings),
    'Radiation': ss.Sim(make_towns(mobility=ss.geo.radiation(away=0.01)), **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
for label, sim in zip(sims, msim.sims):
    peaks = sim.results.measles.I.by('patch').values.argmax(axis=0)
    print(label, '- day of the peak in each town:', peaks)

Gravity - day of the peak in each town: [118 141 152 161]
Radiation - day of the peak in each town: [118 142 152 156]


The outbreaks come at about the same times, except in Fairfield, where it peaks five days earlier with the radiation model. In the gravity model, travel falls with the square of the distance, which puts Fairfield, the farthest town, far from everyone. In the radiation model, the share of travelers who go to a place depends on how many people live nearer than it, not on the distance itself, so a far place with few people in between is less cut off than under the gravity model.

text:
T7 – Data and calibration

import starsim as ss
import pandas as pd

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5])
reported = ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.05, 1])
infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
cases       = ss.outcome(reported*infection)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, cases,
    init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
    init_n = dict(I=10),
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]])
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)
data = pd.read_csv('data/measles_cases.csv')

1. Different starting guesses.

early = data[data.date <= '2025-03-12']
for label, df in [('All the data', data), ('Data to 12 March', early)]:
    for guess in [dict(beta=0.14, reported=0.5), dict(beta=0.3, reported=0.2)]:
        fit = ss.Sim(measles, pars=guess, data=df, **settings).fit(verbose=False)
        print(label, '- starting from', guess, '- beta:', round(fit.pars.beta, 3), '- reported:', round(fit.pars.reported, 3), '- mismatch:', round(fit.mismatch, 4))

All the data - starting from {'beta': 0.14, 'reported': 0.5} - beta: 0.162 - reported: 0.409 - mismatch: 0.0368
All the data - starting from {'beta': 0.3, 'reported': 0.2} - beta: 0.162 - reported: 0.409 - mismatch: 0.0368
Data to 12 March - starting from {'beta': 0.14, 'reported': 0.5} - beta: 0.19 - reported: 0.189 - mismatch: 0.0304
Data to 12 March - starting from {'beta': 0.3, 'reported': 0.2} - beta: 0.19 - reported: 0.189 - mismatch: 0.0304


From either starting point, the fit to all the data finds the same values (β ≈ 0.162, 41% reported): the fit starts by scanning the whole range within the bounds, and then searches from the best few points of the scan, so it doesn’t depend much on the starting guesses. Fitted to the data up to 12 March, both starting points also agree, but on the wrong values (β ≈ 0.19, 19% reported), and with a smaller mismatch than the fit to all the data. Searches that agree show that the search has found the best fit to the data it was given, not that the data pin the values down: here the rise of the outbreak alone fits equally well with more infections and less of them reported, and the search settles on one of many nearly equal answers.
2. Fitting β only.

fit_both = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **settings).fit(verbose=False)
fit_beta = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **settings).fit(pars=['beta'], verbose=False)
for label, fit in [('Both fitted', fit_both), ('Reported fixed at 50%', fit_beta)]:
    res = fit.sim.results.measles
    print(label, '- beta:', round(fit.pars.beta, 3), '- mismatch:', round(fit.mismatch, 3), '- infections:', round(res.infection.sum()), '- reported cases:', round(res.cases.sum()))
fit_beta.plot()

Both fitted - beta: 0.162 - mismatch: 0.037 - infections: 9400 - reported cases: 3844
Reported fixed at 50% - beta: 0.152 - mismatch: 0.141 - infections: 9159 - reported cases: 4580









With the reported share fixed at 50%, too high, the fit finds a smaller β (about 0.152) and fits about four times worse: with too many of its infections reported, the model can’t match both the rise of the data and its peak: it overshoots the peak, and falls too slowly after it. It projects about the same number of infections over the year, since here the size of the outbreak is set mostly by the immunity in the town, but about a fifth more reported cases than the fit of both parameters. A fit that is much worse than another with one more parameter free is a sign that a fixed value is wrong.
3. A campaign on 1 April.

sims = {'No intervention': fit_both.sim}
for date in ['2025-04-01', '2025-05-01']:
    campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, where=measles.age < 15, coverage=0.8, at=date)
    sims['Campaign on ' + date] = fit_both.sim.new(interventions=campaign)
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.summarize().loc['measles_cases']

title: Solutions
text:
T8 – Stratification and co-transmission

import starsim as ss

def make_measles():
    """ The SEIR model of measles, by age, with nobody immune yet """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection   = S >> E @ 0.14*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10), name='measles')
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
    return measles

def make_community_measles(coverage=0.6, rate=None):
    """ The measles model by age, community, and vaccination, with the coverage in the community and a catch-up rate in each community """
    split = ss.by([[0.02, 0.98], [1-coverage, coverage]], dims=['community', 'vaccinated'])
    transfers = {}
    if rate is not None:
        transfers['catchup'] = ss.transfer(vaccinated=True, rate=ss.peryear(ss.by(community=rate)), states=['S'])
    measles = make_measles()
    measles.stratify(community={'general': 0.95, 'close-knit': 0.05})
    measles.stratify(vaccinated=[False, True], split=split, states=['S'], adjust={'rel_sus': [1, 0.03]}, **transfers)
    return measles

age_contacts = [[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]
clustered = ss.contacts(dict(age=age_contacts, community=[[0.984, 0.016], [0.3, 0.7]]), ages=[0, 15, 65])
settings = dict(networks=clustered, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)

1. Higher coverage in the community.

for coverage in [0.6, 0.8]:
    sim = ss.Sim(make_community_measles(coverage=coverage), **settings).run()
    res = sim.results.measles
    print('Coverage in the community', coverage, '- infections in the community:', round(res.infection.select(community='close-knit').sum()), '- in the rest of the town:', round(res.infection.select(community='general').sum()))

Coverage in the community 0.6 - infections in the community: 2420 - in the rest of the town: 1720
Coverage in the community 0.8 - infections in the community: 1233 - in the rest of the town: 997


With 80% coverage in the community, there are about 700 fewer infections in the rest of the town (about 1,000 rather than 1,700), although nothing has changed there. Since the rest of the town can’t sustain an outbreak on its own (its reproduction number is about 0.8), its infections are mostly seeded from the community, and each infection prevented in the community prevents the chains of infection that would have followed from it in the rest of the town. This is an indirect benefit of vaccination: a model that counted only the infections prevented in the people vaccinated would miss it.
2. The same doses outside the community.

sims = {
    'No catch-up':                ss.Sim(make_community_measles(), **settings),
    'Catch-up in the community':  ss.Sim(make_community_measles(rate=[0, 2]), **settings),
    'Catch-up outside it':        ss.Sim(make_community_measles(rate=[0.5, 0]), **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
for sim in msim.sims:
    res = sim.results.measles
    doses = res.catchup.sum() if 'catchup' in res else 0
    print(sim.label, '- doses:', round(doses), '- infections:', round(res.infection.sum()))

No catch-up - doses: 0 - infections: 4140
Catch-up in the community - doses: 605 - infections: 3125
Catch-up outside it - doses: 593 - infections: 3932


A rate of 0.5 a year outside the community gives about the same number of doses (about 600), but prevents only about 200 infections, against about 1,000 for the doses given in the community: five times fewer for each dose. Outside the community, most unvaccinated people are surrounded by vaccinated ones and are unlikely to be infected anyway; in the community, each dose removes someone from where the outbreak is spreading. Stratifying by community is what lets the model show this.
3. A measles campaign, and pneumococcus.

ages = {0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=age_contacts)
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2028-01-01', unit='day', verbose=0)

S, E, I, A, R = ss.states('S E I A R')
infection   = S >> E @ 0.14*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> A @ ss.days(8)
restored    = A >> R @ ss.years(2)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, restored,
    init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
    init_n = dict(I=10),
    name = 'measles',
)
measles.stratify(age=ages)

S, C = ss.states('S C')
acquisition = S >> C @ 0.003*C
clearance   = C >> S @ ss.days(30)
pneumococcus = ss.Disease(acquisition, clearance, init=dict(C=ss.by(age=[0.25, 0.17, 0.17])), name='pneumococcus')
pneumococcus.stratify(age=ages)

amnesia = ss.modify(pneumococcus.rel_sus, multiply=2, where=measles.I | measles.A)
campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, where=measles.age < 15, coverage=0.8, at='2025-02-01', disease='measles')

sims = {}
for label, connectors in [('Independent', None), ('Interacting', amnesia)]:
    sims[label] = ss.Sim([measles, pneumococcus], connectors=connectors, **settings)
    sims[label + ', campaign'] = ss.Sim([measles, pneumococcus], connectors=connectors, interventions=campaign, **settings)
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
summary = msim.summarize()
print(summary.loc['measles_infection'])
summary.loc['pneumococcus_acquisition']

scenario                          
Independent            8795.505567
Independent, campaign   850.697309
Interacting            8795.505567
