The campaign prevents about 7,900 of the 8,800 measles infections, the same with or without the interaction. Without it, the campaign prevents no pneumococcus at all, since the two diseases are independent. With it, the campaign also prevents about 97,000 pneumococcus acquisitions over the three years (nearly all of the extra ones that measles caused), about 12 for each measles infection prevented, both among the children spared measles and among the people they would have passed pneumococcus to. An evaluation of measles vaccination that counted only measles would miss this benefit, which is why the estimates of immune amnesia matter for the case for measles vaccination.

title: Solutions
text:
T9 – Custom modules

import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 0.16*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
cases       = ss.outcome(0.4*infection)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, cases,
    init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
    init_n = dict(I=10),
    name = 'measles',
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]])
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)

class VaccineDemand(ss.Intervention):
    """ Unvaccinated people seek vaccination at a rate that rises with the outbreak cases they remember """

    def __init__(self, memory=ss.days(30), half=300, max_rate=ss.perweek(0.1), capacity=None, efficacy=0.93, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(memory=memory, half=half, max_rate=max_rate, capacity=capacity, efficacy=efficacy)
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.remembered = 0.0
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('doses', kind='flow', scale=False, label='Doses given'),
            ss.Result('remembered', kind='stock', scale=False, label='Cases remembered'),
        )
        return

    def share(self):
        """ The share of the highest demand, from the cases remembered """
        return self.remembered/(self.remembered + self.pars.half)

    def step(self):
        measles = self.sim.diseases.measles
        dt = self.t.dt
        self.remembered += self.sim.results.measles.cases[self.ti-1] - self.remembered*(dt/self.pars.memory)
        doses = (self.pars.max_rate*self.share()).to_prob(dt)*measles.count(measles.S)
        if self.pars.capacity is not None:
            doses = min(doses, self.pars.capacity.to_events(dt))
        ss.move(measles.S, measles.R, n=doses*self.pars.efficacy)
        self.results.doses[self.ti] = doses
        self.results.remembered[self.ti] = self.remembered
        return

The module is the one from the tutorial, with the share of the highest demand as a method of its own (share()), so that exercise 2 can use it too.
1. How long people remember.

baseline = ss.Sim(measles, **settings).run().results.measles.infection.sum()
sims = {str(days) + ' days': ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(memory=ss.days(days)), **settings) for days in [10, 30, 90]}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
for sim in msim.sims:
    res = sim.results
    doses = res.vaccinedemand.doses.sum()
    prevented = baseline - res.measles.infection.sum()
    print('Memory of', sim.label, '- doses:', round(doses), '- infections prevented:', round(prevented), '- per dose:', round(prevented/doses, 2))

Memory of 10 days - doses: 3454 - infections prevented: 3104 - per dose: 0.9
Memory of 30 days - doses: 4916 - infections prevented: 3961 - per dose: 0.81
Memory of 90 days - doses: 6093 - infections prevented: 4342 - per dose: 0.71


The longer people remember, the more doses are sought (about 3,500 with a memory of 10 days, 4,900 with 30, and 6,100 with 90), and the more infections are prevented (about 3,100, 4,000, and 4,300). But each extra dose prevents fewer: about 0.9 infections a dose with a memory of 10 days, and 0.7 with 90. A longer memory adds doses mostly after the peak, when people still remember the outbreak but most of those it would infect have already been infected; a dose given then protects someone who was unlikely to be infected anyway.
2. Avoiding contact as well.

def avoidance(sim):
    """ Susceptibility falls by up to 30% as people remember more cases """
    return 1 - 0.3*sim.interventions.vaccinedemand.share()

sims = {
    'Vaccine demand':               ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(), **settings),
    'Vaccine demand and avoidance': ss.Sim(measles, interventions=[VaccineDemand(), ss.modify(measles.rel_sus, multiply=avoidance)], **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')
msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']















value


scenario





Vaccine demand
5396.516150


Vaccine demand and avoidance
4396.978646







Avoiding contact as well makes the outbreak about a fifth smaller again (about 4,400 infections rather than 5,400). The function reads the module from the sim (sim.interventions.vaccinedemand), not from a variable outside it, since the sim works on its own copy of each module; and since neither the module nor the modifier keeps anything for each person, the sim still runs as an ODE.
3. As agents.

sims = {
    'ODE':    ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(), **settings),
    'Agents': ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(), n_agents=100_000, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
for sim in msim.sims:
    res = sim.results
    print(sim.label, '(' + sim.solver + ') - infections:', round(res.measles.infection.sum()), '- doses:', round(res.vaccinedemand.doses.sum()))

ODE (ode) - infections: 5397 - doses: 4916
Agents (abm) - infections: 5469 - doses: 4802


The module runs unchanged as agents, and the two agree to within a few percent; the agents are one run of a random process, so they differ a little from run to run. The module needs no change because it uses only what works under every solver: a result of the sim (cases), the number of people in a state (measles.count(measles.S)), and ss.move() with a number of people, which as agents moves that many agents (chosen at random) from S to R. A module that picked out particular people, e.g. with measles.S.uids, would run only as agents (A5).

title: Solutions
text:
A1 – Diseases
These solutions build on the SIRS model from the tutorial, so we define it again here, with the duration of immunity and the latent period as arguments:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

def make_cold(dur_imm=ss.days(180), dur_latent=None):
    """ A respiratory infection with waning immunity: SIRS, or SEIRS with a latent period; β is 0.4 per day """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    if dur_latent is None: # SIRS
        transitions = dict(infection=S >> I @ ss.perday(0.4)*I)
    else: # SEIRS
        transitions = dict(infection=S >> E @ ss.perday(0.4)*I, progression=E >> I @ dur_latent)
    transitions['recovery'] = I >> R @ ss.days(7)
    transitions['waning'] = R >> S @ dur_imm
    infections = ss.attr(1, on=transitions['infection'], combine='sum', init=0)
    states = [S, I, R] if dur_latent is None else [S, E, I, R]
    return ss.Disease(*states, **transitions, infections=infections, init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(3*365), dt=ss.days(1), verbose=0)


Question 1
Q: Try different durations of immunity in the SIRS model (e.g. 1, 6, and 24 months). How do they affect the epidemic curve, and the number of times people are infected?
A: The shorter immunity is, the faster the susceptible pool is replenished, so transmission settles at a higher endemic level, and people are infected more often. With long-lasting immunity the model behaves much more like SIR: a single epidemic, followed by a long gap before the next wave:

sims = {
    '1 month':   ss.Sim(make_cold(ss.months(1)), **pars),
    '6 months':  ss.Sim(make_cold(ss.months(6)), **pars),
    '24 months': ss.Sim(make_cold(ss.months(24)), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold.I')

for label, sim in sims.items():
    print(label, '- mean number of infections per person:', round(sim.people.cold.infections.values.mean(), 1))








1 month - mean number of infections per person: 18.9
6 months - mean number of infections per person: 4.3
24 months - mean number of infections per person: 0.9




Question 2
Q: Add a latent period of 2 days to the SIRS model, to make an SEIRS model. Does it change the endemic level?
A: The latent period slows each generation of infections, so the first epidemic comes later and has a lower peak, and the waves that follow are out of step with those of the SIRS model. The endemic level of people infectious changes little, since it depends mostly on R0 and the duration of immunity, which are the same:

sims = {
    'SIRS':  ss.Sim(make_cold(), **pars),
    'SEIRS': ss.Sim(make_cold(dur_latent=ss.days(2)), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold.I')










Question 3
Q: In the town with 90% immune, increase the share susceptible to 20% (init=dict(R=0.8)), so that each case infects about 3 others. What share of introductions die out now, with and without superspreading (k = 0.2)?
A: Without superspreading, a share of about 1/R ≈ 1/3 die out. With superspreading, many more do, since most cases still infect nobody:

def make_sim(k=None, immune=0.8):
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    init = dict(init=dict(R=immune), init_n=dict(I=1))
    sim_pars = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
    if k is None:
        measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, **init)
        return ss.Sim(measles, **sim_pars)
    infectiousness = ss.attr(ss.gamma(a=k, scale=1/k))
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, infectiousness=infectiousness, **init)
    superspreading = ss.modify(measles.rel_trans, multiply=infectiousness)
    return ss.Sim(measles, connectors=superspreading, **sim_pars)

for label, k in {'Everyone equally infectious': None, 'k = 0.2': 0.2}.items():
    msim = ss.parallel(make_sim(k), n_runs=100)
    total = msim.results.measles.infection.values.sum(axis=1)
    print(label, '- share that die out:', np.mean(total < 20))

Everyone equally infectious - share that die out: 0.33
k = 0.2 - share that die out: 0.82

title: Solutions
text:
A2 – Networks

Exercise 1
Q: Repeat the comparison of contacts for a less infectious disease, with a chance of infection of 0.083 per contact per day. How much does it matter now that people meet the same contacts every day, and why?
A: With a chance of infection of 0.083 per contact per day and 3 contacts a day, R0 is about 0.083 × 3 × 8 ≈ 2 with random mixing:

import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl
ss.options(jupyter=True)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.083*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
disease = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='disease')

pars = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(200))
sims = {
    'Well mixed':              ss.Sim(disease, networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=3), **pars),
    'New contacts each day':   ss.Sim(disease, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3), **pars),
    'Same contacts every day': ss.Sim(disease, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3, dynamic=False), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('disease.I')
msim.summarize().loc['disease_infection']

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (Well mixed, New contacts each day, Same contacts every day)
  Done in 0.44 s
















value


scenario





Well mixed
7851.0


New contacts each day
7669.0


Same contacts every day
1421.0







Now it matters a great deal: with random mixing, most people are infected, but with the same 3 contacts every day, far fewer (how many varies a lot from one run to the next, since the outbreak can stall early or find its way through). Over a contact that lasts for the whole infectious period, the chance of passing the infection on is only about 1 − e^(−0.083 × 8) ≈ 50%, and one of each person’s 3 contacts is usually the person who infected them, so each case infects on average not much more than one new person. Measles passes along nearly every link, so for measles the network changed the timing but not the size of the outbreak.


Exercise 2
Q: Give the network with partnerships of a year n_contacts=1 and concurrency=0.2. Does the infection persist?

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peract(m2f=0.1, f2m=0.05)*I
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.months(6)
sti = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2030, dt=ss.months(1))
sims = {
    'One partner at a time': ss.Sim(sti, networks=ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.years(1)), **pars),
    '20% with more than one': ss.Sim(sti, networks=ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.years(1), n_contacts=1, concurrency=0.2), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (One partner at a time, 20% with more than one)
  Done in 0.8 s









A: Yes: with 20% of people having more than one partner at a time, the infection persists. Someone with two partners can pass the infection from one partnership to the other without waiting for either to end, which is why concurrency matters so much for sexually transmitted infections.


Exercise 3
Q: Add transmission between men, with a second network ss.SexualNet(name='msm', between='mm', dur=ss.months(3)) and a β for each network. How much does it add?
A: β is given as a dict, with a value for each network by name. Between men, the chance per act is the same in both directions, so it is a single number:

S, I = ss.states('S I')
beta = dict(
    sexualnet = ss.peract(m2f=0.1, f2m=0.05), # Between men and women
    msm       = ss.peract(0.1),               # Between men
)
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.months(6)
sti = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2030, dt=ss.months(1))
mf  = ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.months(3))
msm = ss.SexualNet(name='msm', between='mm', dur=ss.months(3))
sti_mf = ss.Disease(S >> I @ ss.peract(m2f=0.1, f2m=0.05)*I, recovery, init_prev=0.05, name='sti')
sims = {
    'Between men and women only': ss.Sim(sti_mf, networks=mf, **pars),
    'Also between men':           ss.Sim(sti, networks=[mf, msm], **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Between men and women only, Also between men)
  Done in 0.99 s









The network between men adds its own chains of transmission, and the infection settles at a much higher level, more than twice as many infected. Who is in it, and how many partners they have, matters as much as the chance per act: in a model of a real setting, the share of men who take part (participation=) would be much smaller than the default.


Exercise 4
Q: Add households to the measles model, with a community mixing pool with 2 contacts a day. How much do households add?

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.19*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

households = ssl.ClusterNet(cluster_size=ss.poisson(4))
pars = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(100))
sims = {
    'Community only': ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=2), **pars),
    'Households and community': ss.Sim(measles, networks=[households, ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=2)], **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')
msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Community only, Households and community)
  Done in 0.28 s
















value


scenario





Community only
9417.0


Households and community
9940.0







A: The community alone gives an R0 of 0.19 × 2 × 8 ≈ 3, and infects most people. Households make the epidemic faster and infect nearly everyone, but they add less than their number of contacts suggests: once one person in a household is infected, the others are soon infected too, so most household contacts after that are wasted.

title: Solutions
text:
A3 – Demographics

Exercise 1
Q: In Niger, the crude birth rate is 45 and the crude death rate is 9. Assuming these rates stay constant, and starting with its population in 2020, how many people will there be in 2040? Compare this with its UN birth and death rates.
A: We can build a simple demographic model with these rates, and another with the UN’s rates, then run them and compare the results:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

pars = dict(start=2020, stop=2040)
constant = ss.Sim(people=ss.people('Niger', n_agents=5000), demographics=[ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.045)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.009))], **pars)
un = ss.Sim(people=ss.people('Niger', n_agents=5000), demographics=[ss.Births(birth_rate='Niger'), ss.Deaths(death_rate='Niger')], **pars)
msim = ss.parallel({'Constant rates': constant, 'UN rates': un})
msim.plot('alive')

for label, sim in zip(['Constant rates', 'UN rates'], msim.sims):
    print(label, '- population in 2040:', round(sim.results.alive[-1]/1e6, 1), 'million')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Constant rates, UN rates)
  Done in 0.24 s









Constant rates - population in 2040: 47.6 million
UN rates - population in 2040: 42.6 million


With a constant 45 births and 9 deaths per 1,000, the population roughly doubles in 20 years. The UN expects the birth rate to fall (and its death rates differ by age), so the two projections differ.


Exercise 2
Q: How does the time between epidemics in the ODE change if the birth rate (and the death rate) is 20 per 1,000 per year instead of 30? Does it agree with the theory?

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

demographics = [ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02))]
sim = ss.Sim(measles, demographics=demographics, total_pop=20_000, start='2000-01-01', stop='2030-01-01', dt=ss.days(1))
sim.run()

res = sim.results.measles
plt.figure()
plt.semilogy(res.timevec, res.I)
plt.ylim(bottom=0.01)
plt.ylabel('Number infectious');

Sim: measles, 20,000 people, as an ODE, 2000-01-01 to 2030-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 20 infectious at the start
  Note: the number infected in "measles" falls to 0.94 (at 2000-03-26) and then rises to 374; a stochastic run would usually die out there. solver="gillespie" with ss.parallel(n_runs=...) shows how often, in the runs of msim.results.measles.I after that point
  Done in 0.01 s; measles: 29,919 infections; at most 14,822 infectious, on 2000-01-07









A: The epidemics are further apart, and the honeymoon after the first epidemic is longer: with fewer births, it takes longer to build up enough susceptible people for the next epidemic. The theory agrees: with a life expectancy of L = 1/0.02 = 50 years, the average age at infection is about 50/14 ≈ 3.5 years, and the time between epidemics is about 2π√(3.5 × 0.022) ≈ 1.7 years, rather than 1.4.


Exercise 3
Q: In the town with importations, how often do epidemics come if the town has 50,000 people instead? Does measles ever persist between them?

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles = ss.Disease(
    infection   = S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I,
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8),
    importation = S >> I @ ss.peryear(0.001),
    init_prev   = 0.001,
    name        = 'measles',
)
demographics = [ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.03))]
pars = dict(demographics=demographics, start='2000-01-01', stop='2020-01-01', dt=ss.days(1), verbose=0)

plt.figure()
for label, n in {'20,000 people': 20_000, '50,000 people': 50_000}.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=n, **pars)
    sim.run()
    plt.semilogy(sim.results.measles.timevec, sim.results.measles.I, label=label)
plt.ylim(bottom=0.5)
plt.ylabel('Number infectious')
plt.legend();








A: In the larger town, more children are born each year, so the susceptible people build up faster, and imported cases (which also come more often, since there are more susceptible people to be infected outside the town) start epidemics sooner: they come more often, and are larger. Measles still dies out between most of them, though: a town of 50,000 is still well below the critical community size of measles.


Exercise 4
Q: Add contraception (ss.modify(pregnancy.conception, multiply=0.7, start=2010)) to the Nigeria model with pregnancy. How many fewer people are there in 2030?

import pandas as pd

fertility = pd.read_csv('test_data/nigeria_asfr.csv')
pars = dict(start=2000, stop=2030, dt=ss.months(1))

sims = {}
for label in ['Baseline', 'Contraception']:
    pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=fertility)
    contraception = ss.modify(pregnancy.conception, multiply=0.7, start=2010) if label == 'Contraception' else None
    people = ss.people('Nigeria', n_agents=5000)
    sims[label] = ss.Sim(people=people, demographics=[pregnancy, ss.Deaths(death_rate='Nigeria')], interventions=contraception, **pars)

msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('alive')
for label, sim in zip(sims, msim.sims):
    print(label, round(sim.results.alive[-1]/1e6), 'million in 2030')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Baseline, Contraception)
  Done in 2.6 s









Baseline 268 million in 2030
Contraception 227 million in 2030


A: Cutting conception by 30% from 2010 leaves about 40 million fewer people in 2030 (about 227 million rather than 268 million).

title: Solutions
text:
A4 – Interventions
These solutions use the model and interventions from the tutorial, so we define them again here:

import numpy as np
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peract(m2f=0.1, f2m=0.05)*I
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.months(6)
sti = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

settings = dict(
    networks     = ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.months(1), memory=ss.years(1)),
    demographics = [ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02))],
    n_agents     = 5000,
    start        = 2000,
    stop         = 2020,
    dt           = ss.months(1),
    verbose      = 0,
)

drug = ss.Treatment(cure=0.95)
care = ss.treat(drug, on=sti.infection, coverage=0.3, delay=ss.uniform(ss.weeks(1), ss.months(2)))
young = (ss.ppl.age >= 15) & (ss.ppl.age < 30)
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, where=young, coverage=0.5, interval=ss.months(6), start='2010')
treatment = ss.treat(drug, who=screening.positive)
notification = ss.treat(drug, who=screening.positive, trace='sexualnet', coverage=0.5)


Question 1
Q: What happens if the partners of people who seek care are notified too (a second notification, with who=care)? Is the effect larger than notifying the partners of those found by screening?
A: A delivery is an event too, so who=care is the people treated after seeking care. Notifying their partners starts in 2000, rather than 2010, and starts from far more people than screening finds, so it has a much larger effect: here it keeps the infection at a low level from the start, and nearly eliminates it once screening begins.

care_notification = ss.treat(drug, who=care, trace='sexualnet', coverage=0.5)

scenarios = {
    'Screening and notification':  [care, screening, treatment, notification],
    'Also notifying after care':   [care, screening, treatment, notification, care_notification],
}
sims = {label: ss.Sim(sti, interventions=interventions, **settings) for label, interventions in scenarios.items()}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')
msim.summarize().loc['sti_infection']















value


scenario





Screening and notification
35921.0


Also notifying after care
7970.0









Question 2
Q: How much does the effect change if screening reaches everyone aged 15 to 49? Which gives more infections prevented per test?
A: We compare each with treatment when seeking care alone (without partner notification, so that the effect is that of screening):

adults = (ss.ppl.age >= 15) & (ss.ppl.age < 50)
screening_adults = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, where=adults, coverage=0.5, interval=ss.months(6), start='2010', name='screening')
treatment_adults = ss.treat(drug, who=screening_adults.positive, name='treatment')

sims = {
    'Treatment when seeking care': ss.Sim(sti, interventions=care, **settings),
    'Screening 15-29':             ss.Sim(sti, interventions=[care, screening, treatment], **settings),
    'Screening 15-49':             ss.Sim(sti, interventions=[care, screening_adults, treatment_adults], **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')

baseline = msim.sims['Treatment when seeking care'].results.sti.infection.sum()
for label in ['Screening 15-29', 'Screening 15-49']:
    sim = msim.sims[label]
    prevented = baseline - sim.results.sti.infection.sum()
    tests = sim.results.screening.delivered.sum()
    print(label, '- tests:', tests, '- infections prevented:', prevented, '- per 100 tests:', round(100*prevented/tests, 1))








Screening 15-29 - tests: 9268.0 - infections prevented: 3456.0 - per 100 tests: 37.3
Screening 15-49 - tests: 20685.0 - infections prevented: 10183.0 - per 100 tests: 49.2


Screening everyone aged 15 to 49 takes a little over twice as many tests, and prevents about three times as many infections, so it prevents more per test. In this model, partnerships don’t depend on age beyond sexual debut, so people over 30 are as much at risk as younger people; in a real setting, where infection is concentrated in young people, the answer could well be the reverse. Since each run is a single stochastic run, the infections prevented are uncertain; with several runs of each (n_runs=), the comparison per test would be clearer.


Question 3
Q: Add a catch-up campaign in 2010 for everyone aged 15 to 29. How much sooner does vaccination make a difference, and how many more doses does it take?
A: The two deliveries share one vaccine, so that nobody is protected twice:

vaccine = ss.Vaccine(efficacy=0.35)
vaccination = ss.vaccinate(vaccine, at_age=15, coverage=0.8, start='2010')
catch_up = ss.vaccinate(vaccine, where=young, coverage=0.8, at=['2010'])

sims = {
    'Treatment when seeking care': ss.Sim(sti, interventions=care, **settings),
    'And vaccination at age 15':   ss.Sim(sti, interventions=[care, vaccination], **settings),
    'And a catch-up campaign':     ss.Sim(sti, interventions=[care, vaccination, catch_up], **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')
sim = msim.sims['And a catch-up campaign']
print('Doses at age 15:', sim.results.vaccination.delivered.sum())
print('Doses in the catch-up campaign:', sim.results.catch_up.delivered.sum())








Doses at age 15: 538.0
Doses in the catch-up campaign: 824.0


The catch-up campaign protects many of the people at risk at once, rather than waiting for them to be replaced by vaccinated cohorts, so the effect comes years sooner, for about two and a half times as many doses in all.

title: Solutions
text:
A5 – Custom modules

Question 1
Q: Change the half-life of the antibodies to 30 days and to 365 days. How does each change the endemic level of infection, compared with no immunity and with the all-or-nothing SIRS?
A: We define the infection and the Antibodies module from the tutorial again, and run them with each half-life:

import numpy as np
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl
ss.options(jupyter=True)

class Antibodies(ss.Module):
    """ Each person's antibody level: 1 on recovery, then halving every half_life """
    def __init__(self, half_life=ss.days(90), **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_pars(half_life=half_life)
        self.define_states(ss.FloatArr('level', default=0.0, label='Antibody level'))
        return

    def step(self):
        self.level[:] = self.level*0.5**(self.t.dt/self.pars.half_life)
        self.level[self.sim.diseases.cold.recovery.uids] = 1.0
        return

S, I = ss.states('S I')
sis = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.4*I, recovery=I >> S @ ss.days(7), init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

def susceptibility(sim):
    return 1 - sim.custom.antibodies.level

pars = dict(networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=1), n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(2*365), verbose=0)
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sirs = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.4*I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(7), waning=R >> S @ ss.days(180), init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

sims = {'No immunity': ss.Sim(sis, **pars), 'All or nothing': ss.Sim(sirs, **pars)}
for label, half_life in {'Half-life of 30 days': ss.days(30), 'Half-life of 365 days': ss.days(365)}.items():
    protection = ss.modify(sis.rel_sus, multiply=susceptibility)
    sims[label] = ss.Sim(sis, Antibodies(half_life=half_life), connectors=protection, **pars)
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold.I')








The longer the antibodies last, the lower the endemic level. With a half-life of 30 days, people regain most of their susceptibility within a couple of months, so the infection settles at about a quarter of its level with no immunity, but well above its level with the all-or-nothing SIRS (whose protection lasts 180 days on average). With a half-life of a year, almost everyone is still well protected long after the first wave, and the infection dies out.


Question 2
Q: Give AgeNet a parameter p_random, the share of each person’s contacts that are with anyone at random. How large does it have to be before the epidemic looks like the one with random contacts?
A: The simplest way is to keep AgeNet as it was, and add a random network beside it, splitting the 4 contacts a day between the two:

class AgeNet(ss.Network):
    """ Contacts each day with people close in age """
    def __init__(self, n_contacts=4, spread=ss.years(2), **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(n_contacts=n_contacts, spread=spread)
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.noise = ss.normal(0, 1)
        return

    def add_pairs(self):
        uids = self.sim.people.alive.uids
        age = self.sim.people.age[uids] + self.pars.spread.years*self.noise.rvs(uids)
        order = uids[np.argsort(age, kind='stable')]
        p1 = np.concatenate([order[:-k] for k in range(1, self.pars.n_contacts//2 + 1)])
        p2 = np.concatenate([order[k:] for k in range(1, self.pars.n_contacts//2 + 1)])
        self.append(p1=p1, p2=p2, beta=np.ones(len(p1)))
        return

    def step(self):
        self.remove_edges(np.ones(len(self), dtype=bool))
        self.add_pairs()
        return

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
cold = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.1*I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(7), init_prev=0.001, name='cold')

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(250), verbose=0)
sims = {
    'All random':           ss.Sim(cold, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4), **pars),
    'All close in age':     ss.Sim(cold, networks=AgeNet(n_contacts=4), **pars),
    'Half at random':       ss.Sim(cold, networks=[AgeNet(n_contacts=2), ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=2)], **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold.I')








With half of the 4 contacts at random, the epidemic is almost the same as with all contacts random: a few long-range contacts are enough to carry the infection across the ages, as in a “small-world” network. (AgeNet pairs each person with an even number of neighbors, so to try smaller shares, give it more contacts and the random network fewer, keeping the total the same, e.g. 6 and 2.)


Question 3
Q: Write an SIRS in which immunity is lost with a constant chance each step, using an ss.bernoulli distribution in step_state(). Does it give the same epidemic?
A: A constant chance each step gives an exponential (or, in whole steps, geometric) duration of immunity, with the same mean as ss.expon(scale=ss.days(180)) if the chance per day is 1/180, so the waning works the same way. Run with daily steps, the first wave is smaller than in the tutorial, which used steps of a quarter of a day, for the reason given there:

class SIRS(ssl.AgentSIR):
    def __init__(self, pars=None, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(p_wane=ss.bernoulli(p=1/180)) # The chance of losing immunity each day
        self.update_pars(pars, **kwargs)
        return

    def step_state(self):
        super().step_state()
        waning = self.pars.p_wane.filter(self.recovered.uids) # Each recovered agent loses immunity with this chance
        self.recovered[waning] = False
        self.susceptible[waning] = True
        return

coded = SIRS(beta=ss.perday(0.4), dur_inf=ss.expon(scale=ss.days(7)), p_death=0, init_prev=0.01, name='cold')
sim = ss.Sim(coded, networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=1), n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(2*365), dt=ss.days(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.cold.infected.plot()








The chance is per step, so it is only right for a step of one day; a version that works for any step would convert a rate to a chance per step (e.g. ss.peryear(2).to_prob()), or schedule the time of waning at recovery, as the tutorial’s version does.

title: T9 – Custom modules
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
When people hear about an outbreak, some of them go and get vaccinated. How much does that slow the outbreak down, and what limits it?
Most of a Starsim model is declared: its states and transitions, the interventions given to it, and the results it reports. Declared parts run under every solver, and describe(), diagram(), and equations() show them. But some parts of a model are easier to say in code: a rule of behavior of your own, a quantity with dynamics of its own, or a result worked out in a way of your own. A module written as code is a Python class with a step() method, which Starsim calls once at each step, and which can read and change the rest of the sim. It sits in the same sim as the declared diseases.
A module written as code doesn’t make a model agent-based. A module that keeps a value for each person (whether each person has been vaccinated, say) needs agents, and a sim with one runs as agents; A5 – Custom modules writes modules like that. A module that keeps only numbers for the whole population, like the one in this tutorial, runs with the rest of the model as compartments, as an ODE. By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:
Before writing a module, check the table at the top of Custom modules in the user guide: many things that look as if they need code (vaccination, testing, treatment, contact tracing, and changes to parameters) can be declared.

title: T9 – Custom modules
text:
The model so far
This is the measles model from T7 – Data and calibration, with the values that the fit found: β = 0.16, and 40% of infections reported. It runs for a year from 1 January, in a town of 100,000 people in three age groups, about 11% of whom are susceptible:

import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 0.16*I         # β = 0.16 per contact per day
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)   # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)    # Infectious for 8 days on average
cases       = ss.outcome(0.4*infection) # Reported cases: 40% of infections
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, cases,
    init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The share immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),                          # 10 people infectious at the start
    name = 'measles',
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

sim = ss.Sim(measles, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles.cases')

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 18.1 (R = 2.81 at the start, with 11% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0043 s; measles: 9,358 infections; at most 1,140 infectious, on 2025-04-12

title: T9 – Custom modules
text:
Vaccine demand
During measles outbreaks, demand for vaccination rises: parents who had put off vaccinating their children hear about cases in the news or from neighbors, and take them to a clinic. This is an intervention that nobody plans, and the model so far leaves it out. To add it, we need a rule for how many unvaccinated people seek vaccination each day. A simple one: the more cases people have heard about recently, the more of them seek it, up to some limit. Here, of the people still susceptible, a share seek vaccination each day that rises with the number of cases reported in the last week, reaching half of its highest value (10% a week) when 300 cases have been reported in a week.
None of the declared parts says this, so it is written as code. The smallest module is a function of the sim, which Starsim calls once each step; given as interventions=, it becomes an intervention. Inside it, sim.results has the results so far, and sim.ti is the index of the current time point, so the reported cases of the last 7 days are the last 7 values of the result cases. ss.move() moves people between the states of a declared disease, the same way under every solver: here, it moves the people vaccinated (93% of those who get a dose are protected) from S to R:

def vaccine_demand(sim):
    """ The unvaccinated seek vaccination at a rate that rises with the cases reported in the last week """
    measles = sim.diseases.measles
    last_week = sim.results.measles.cases[max(sim.ti-7, 0):sim.ti].sum()      # Cases reported in the last 7 days
    share = last_week/(last_week + 300)                                       # From 0 to 1, a half at 300 cases a week
    seeking = (ss.perweek(0.1)*share).to_prob(sim.t.dt)                       # The chance of seeking vaccination in this step
    ss.move(measles.S, measles.R, p=seeking*0.93)                             # Those vaccinated and protected become immune
    return

sims = {
    'No response': ss.Sim(measles, **settings),
    'Vaccine demand': ss.Sim(measles, interventions=vaccine_demand, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
print('Solver:', msim.sims['Vaccine demand'].solver)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (No response, Vaccine demand)
  Done in 1.6 s


Solver: ode









The sim still runs as an ODE ('ode'), since the function keeps nothing for each person. Demand for vaccination rises with the outbreak, and makes it smaller. But the function has problems that show as soon as we want to use it. Its numbers (300 cases, 10% a week, 93%) are fixed inside it, so a scenario with other values needs another function. It has no results of its own, so we can’t say how many doses were given. And its memory of the outbreak is a window of exactly 7 days, after which a case is forgotten at once, which isn’t how people remember news.

title: T9 – Custom modules
text:
A module as a class
A module written as a class fixes all three. It inherits from one of Starsim’s module types (here ss.Intervention), and has:

Parameters, given with their defaults in __init__() with define_pars(), and changed by name when the module is made (update_pars() raises an error for a name it doesn’t know, which catches misspellings). Rates and durations are given as Starsim’s time parameters (e.g. ss.days(30), ss.perweek(0.1)), so that they mean the same whatever the length of the step.
A state of its own: here, a single number for the whole population, the cases that people remember. Rather than a fixed window, it is a memory that fades: each step, the new reported cases are added, and a share of what is remembered is forgotten, so that a case is remembered for memory (30 days) on average. This is a small ODE of the module’s own, dM/dt = cases − M/memory, solved a step at a time.
Results of its own, given in init_results() with define_results(), and filled in at each step at self.ti. kind='flow' says that doses are events in each step (so they are summed over time), and kind='stock' that the cases remembered are a quantity at each time point.
A step() method, which does the work. In it, self.sim is the sim, self.t.dt the length of a step, and self.pars the parameters.

A module can also limit what it does, which a rule of behavior often needs: here, the clinics can give at most capacity doses a day (none by default), and people who can’t be served stay susceptible, and seek a dose again the next day:

class VaccineDemand(ss.Intervention):
    """ Unvaccinated people seek vaccination at a rate that rises with the outbreak cases they remember """

    def __init__(self, memory=ss.days(30), half=300, max_rate=ss.perweek(0.1), capacity=None, efficacy=0.93, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            memory   = memory,   # How long a reported case is remembered, on average
            half     = half,     # The number of cases remembered at which demand is half its highest
            max_rate = max_rate, # The highest rate at which unvaccinated people seek vaccination
            capacity = capacity, # The most doses the clinics can give, as a rate (None for no limit)
            efficacy = efficacy, # The share of those vaccinated who are protected
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.remembered = 0.0 # The cases that people remember, for the whole population
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('doses', kind='flow', scale=False, label='Doses given'),
            ss.Result('remembered', kind='stock', scale=False, label='Cases remembered'),
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        measles = self.sim.diseases.measles
        dt = self.t.dt

        # Remember the cases reported in the last step, and forget a share of those remembered
        new_cases = self.sim.results.measles.cases[self.ti-1]
        self.remembered += new_cases - self.remembered*(dt/self.pars.memory)

        # The doses sought, limited by what the clinics can give
        share = self.remembered/(self.remembered + self.pars.half)
        seeking = (self.pars.max_rate*share).to_prob(dt)
        doses = seeking*measles.count(measles.S)
        if self.pars.capacity is not None:
            doses = min(doses, self.pars.capacity.to_events(dt))

        # Those protected become immune
        ss.move(measles.S, measles.R, n=doses*self.pars.efficacy)
        self.results.doses[self.ti] = doses
        self.results.remembered[self.ti] = self.remembered
        return

measles.count(measles.S) is the number of people in S now, under every solver, and ss.move(..., n=...) moves a number of people rather than a share. self.sim.results.measles.cases[self.ti-1] is the reported cases of the last step: a module that is not a disease steps before the diseases, so the cases of the step now being run aren’t known yet. Because the module keeps only numbers for the whole population, the sim runs as an ODE, as before. Given to the sim, the module is named after its class in lower case, so its results are in sim.results.vaccinedemand.

title: T9 – Custom modules
text:
Comparing scenarios
With parameters, the same module can be used for each scenario: here, with no response (nobody seeks vaccination: a highest rate of 0), with demand that is met in full, and with clinics that can give at most 30 doses a day, about what a few clinics in a town of 100,000 might manage on top of their usual work:

sims = {
    'No response':           ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(max_rate=ss.perweek(0)), **settings),
    'Demand met in full':    ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(), **settings),
    'At most 30 doses a day': ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(capacity=ss.perday(30)), **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot(['measles.I', 'vaccinedemand.doses'])

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (No response, Demand met in full, At most 30 doses a day)
  Done in 1.0 s










msim.summarize().loc[['measles_infection', 'vaccinedemand_doses']]

With demand met in full, the outbreak infects about 5,400 people rather than 9,400: about 4,900 doses prevent about 4,000 infections. The doses rise with the cases, and peak in mid-March, during the steep rise of the outbreak, when each person protected breaks the most chains of infection; after that, fewer people are left susceptible to seek a dose, although people remember more cases than ever until April. With clinics that can give at most 30 doses a day, they run at capacity for two months, from late February to late April, and the people who can’t be served in March, when it matters most, are often infected while they wait: about 6,600 people are infected, and fewer doses are given, since fewer people are left to seek them. Even met in full, the demand prevents less than half of the infections, because it is driven by the outbreak, and so only starts once the outbreak is under way; vaccination before an outbreak, or a campaign at its start (T5), doesn’t have to wait for it.
sim.describe() lists the module, but can’t say what it does, since that is in its code; this is the price of writing a part of the model as code. A module’s parameters can be fitted to data like any other (T7), if they are given as ss.par with bounds, e.g. VaccineDemand(half=ss.par(300, bounds=[50, 2000])).

title: T9 – Custom modules
section: What changes with a module written as code
text:
What changes with a module written as code

The solver. A module that keeps only numbers for the whole population, like this one, runs under every solver, and the sim runs as an ODE unless something else needs agents. A module that keeps a value for each person (a state made with define_states(), such as whether each person has sought a dose) runs only as agents, and a sim with one runs as agents by itself, with the declared diseases in it unchanged: see A5 – Custom modules. If a module’s code asks for individual people (e.g. measles.I.uids) in a run without agents, the run stops and says so.
The order. In each step, a module that is not a disease runs before the diseases, so what it does (here, protecting people) applies to the transmission in the same step, and it sees the results of the previous step.
The sim’s own copy. The sim works on its own copy of each module. To reach a disease or another module from a module, use self.sim in step() (e.g. self.sim.diseases.measles), not a variable from outside the class.

Custom modules in the user guide covers the rest: the other kinds of module (analyzers, connectors, networks, demographics, and diseases written as code), states for each person, the order in which Starsim calls a module’s methods, and the pitfalls. Analyzers covers analyzers, modules that record something without changing the model.

title: T9 – Custom modules
text:
Exercises

How much does it matter how long people remember the cases they hear about? Run VaccineDemand() with a memory of 10 days and of 90 days, and compare the infections and doses with the 30 days above. Does each extra dose prevent as many infections as the ones before? Why not?
People who hear about an outbreak may also avoid contact with others. Add a second effect of the cases remembered: a modifier, ss.modify(measles.rel_sus, multiply=...), whose multiply= is a function of the sim that returns 1 − 0.3 × the share used for demand (so contacts fall by up to 30%). Read the cases remembered from the module, as sim.interventions.vaccinedemand.remembered. How much smaller is the outbreak?
Run the model with demand met in full as agents, one for each person (n_agents=100_000), and compare the infections and doses with those of the ODE. Does the module need any change? Why not?

Further reading

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
The SIR model of Tutorial 1 and Tutorial 2 leaves out much of what happens in a measles infection, and its outbreak is over within a few weeks, far faster than real measles. Tutorial 2 found that R0 and prior immunity decide how many people are infected. This tutorial asks the other half of the question: what decides how fast an outbreak spreads? It adds, one at a time, the pieces of structure that most models of infectious disease need, and compares the epidemic with and without each:
It then names the parameters of the model, and checks the finished disease with describe(), its equations, and its diagram. By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
A latent period
After someone is infected with measles, there are about 10 days before they become infectious (and about two weeks before the rash appears). In an SEIR model, people in this latent period are in a compartment of their own, E (exposed): infected, but not yet infectious. Infection now moves people from S to E, and a new transition, progression, moves them from E to I after the latent period.
Here is the SIR model of Tutorial 2 next to the SEIR model, both run for 150 days. Each disease is named measles, so that the two runs’ results have the same names and can be plotted together:

import starsim as ss

# The SIR model of Tutorials 1 and 2
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

# The SEIR model: infection leads to E, not I
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I        # Infected by contact with infectious people, I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Infectious after a latent period of 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Recovered after 8 days on average
seir = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

sir_sim  = ss.Sim(sir,  total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
seir_sim = ss.Sim(seir, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
msim = ss.parallel({'SIR': sir_sim, 'SEIR': seir_sim})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (SIR, SEIR)
  Done in 0.41 s









The rate of infection is still β times the share of people in I, not E, since people in E don’t transmit: a state is infectious only if it appears in the rate of infection. Both outbreaks start with 0.1% of people infectious (init=dict(I=0.001)). init_prev=0.001 would instead put them in E, where an infection leads, so that nobody would be infectious until the first of them had been through the latent period (Tutorial 2).
R0 is the same in both, 15.2, as the runs print: it depends on how many people each infectious person infects (β = 1.9 a day, for 8 days), not on how long it takes them to become infectious. But the outbreak is very different. With a latent period, the time from one infection to the next (the generation time) is about 18 days instead of 8, so the epidemic grows more slowly: it peaks on day 28 rather than day 6, and lower, with about 29,000 people infectious at once rather than 74,000. Almost everyone is still infected in the end, since that depends on R0. So the first answer to this tutorial’s question is the generation time: for the same R0, a longer generation time means a slower, flatter epidemic.

title: T3 – Building a disease
section: How long people stay in a state
text:
How long people stay in a state
A duration such as ss.days(10) is an average. By default, the time each person spends in the state is exponentially distributed with this average, as in the standard ODE model. An exponential distribution is a poor description of most latent periods, though: with an average of 10 days, it has 10% of people becoming infectious within a day, and 12% still not infectious after three weeks. The latent period of measles varies much less than this.
A duration can be given as any distribution instead. An Erlang distribution (a gamma distribution with a whole-number shape, k) is the usual choice in compartmental models. With k=10, the latent period has the same average, 10 days, and a standard deviation of about 3 days. Here it is, compared with the exponential latent period above:

progression = E >> I @ ss.erlang(k=10, mean=ss.days(10))  # 10 days on average; 95% between 5 and 17
seir_erlang = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

erlang_sim = ss.Sim(seir_erlang, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
msim = ss.parallel({'Exponential latent period': seir_sim, 'Erlang latent period': erlang_sim})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Exponential latent period, Erlang latent period)
  Done in 0.37 s









The epidemic has the same R0 again, but grows more slowly still: it peaks about two weeks later, on day 44, and higher, with about 35,000 people infectious at once rather than 29,000. With an exponential latent period, the few people who become infectious within a day or two start new chains of infection early, and this speeds up the whole epidemic; with an Erlang one, almost nobody becomes infectious early, so growth is slower, but more of the town is infected at about the same time. So the distribution of a duration, not just its average, sets how fast an epidemic grows. This is worth knowing when a model is fitted to the early growth of an outbreak.
As an ODE, Starsim runs an Erlang distribution as k stages that people go through one after another, each exponential, with an average of 1/k of the whole. The stages are not separate conditions of the disease, only a way of giving the time spent in E a narrower distribution. The same can be written by saying how many stages to use: ss.Transition(E, I, dur=ss.days(10), stages=10) is the same model as E >> I @ ss.erlang(k=10, mean=ss.days(10)). equations() shows the stages, as E_1 to E_10:

seir_erlang.equations()

dS/dt    = -beta * S * I / N
dE_1/dt  =  beta * S * I / N - 10 * E_1 / mean(dur_E)
dE_2/dt  =  10 * E_1 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_2 / mean(dur_E)
dE_3/dt  =  10 * E_2 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_3 / mean(dur_E)
dE_4/dt  =  10 * E_3 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_4 / mean(dur_E)
dE_5/dt  =  10 * E_4 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_5 / mean(dur_E)
dE_6/dt  =  10 * E_5 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_6 / mean(dur_E)
dE_7/dt  =  10 * E_6 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_7 / mean(dur_E)
dE_8/dt  =  10 * E_7 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_8 / mean(dur_E)
dE_9/dt  =  10 * E_8 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_9 / mean(dur_E)
dE_10/dt =  10 * E_9 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_10 / mean(dur_E)
dI/dt    =  10 * E_10 / mean(dur_E) - I / dur_I
dR/dt    =  I / dur_I


As agents, each person draws their own time from the distribution instead. Other distributions, such as ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(2)), are covered in Distributions. The rest of the tutorials keep to exponential durations, for simplicity.

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Waning immunity
In the models so far, people who recover are immune for life, as they are after measles. For many other infections, such as pertussis, RSV, or cholera, immunity wanes: after some time, people become susceptible again. This is a transition from R back to S, which makes an SEIRS model. To see what it does, suppose (unlike real measles) that immunity lasted 2 years on average, and run both models for 5 years:

progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Back to an exponential latent period
waning      = R >> S @ ss.years(2)  # Susceptible again after 2 years on average
seirs = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, waning, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

lifelong = ss.Sim(seir,  total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.years(5), unit='day')
waning_sim = ss.Sim(seirs, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.years(5), unit='day')
msim = ss.parallel({'Lifelong immunity': lifelong, 'Immunity lasting 2 years': waning_sim})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Lifelong immunity, Immunity lasting 2 years)
  Done in 1 s









The model now has durations in days and in years, so unit='day' says which unit the bare number β = 1.9 is in (Tutorial 2). The first outbreak is the same in both. With lifelong immunity, it is the only one: the town is left immune, and the disease dies out. With waning immunity, people return to S and new, smaller waves follow, which settle down to a steady level of about 1,000 people infectious at any time: the disease becomes endemic. A supply of new susceptible people, whether from waning immunity or from births (Tutorial 4), is what lets an infection persist in a population rather than burn out.

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Deaths: a branch
Most people with measles recover, but a small share die, from complications such as pneumonia. How many varies widely between settings, from 1 in 1,000 cases or fewer in high-income countries to several in 100 in some low-income settings. Suppose it is 2 in 1,000 here. People leaving I then go one of two ways, a branch: 99.8% recover and 0.2% die. A branch is a transition with p=, the share of people that take it:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8), p=0.998)        # 99.8% recover...
death       = ss.Transition(I, ss.null, dur=ss.days(8), p=0.002)  # ...and 0.2% die
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, death, init=dict(I=0.001))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
sim.run()
print('Deaths:', round(sim.results.measles.death.sum()))

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0027 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 29,216 infectious, on day 28
Deaths: 200


ss.null is outside the model: people who die leave the population. Each branch has its own result, named after it (recovery and death), and could have its own duration (if, say, people who die did so sooner). Since almost everyone in the town is infected, about 0.2% of 100,000 people die; with so few deaths, the epidemic itself is all but unchanged. The equations show how a branch works: who goes which way is decided when people enter I, so I is in two parts, I_1 for those who will recover and I_2 for those who will die:

measles.equations()

dS/dt   = -beta * S * I / N
dE/dt   =  beta * S * I / N - E / dur_E
dI_1/dt =  p_recovery * E / dur_E - I_1 / dur_recovery
dI_2/dt =  p_death * E / dur_E - I_2 / dur_death
dR/dt   =  I_1 / dur_recovery


A branch is not the only way for two transitions to leave one state. Two transitions out of a state with rates (or durations), and no p=, are competing risks: both act on everyone in the state, and whichever happens first moves them. Then the share that goes each way is set by the rates. A branch says the share directly, which is how the share of cases that die (the case fatality ratio) is usually known. Use whichever matches what you know about the disease.
The next tutorials leave deaths out, since they are few and change little else in this model.

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Naming the parameters
Starsim names the parameters of a model itself (beta, dur_E, …), as Tutorial 2 showed. To name them yourself, and to say more about them, write them with ss.par(). Each takes its name from its variable, and can have a description (doc=), where its value comes from (source=), and bounds, the range of values it could plausibly take:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta           = ss.par(1.9, bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate per day')
dur_latent     = ss.par(ss.days(10), bounds=[ss.days(7), ss.days(14)], doc='Average latent period', source='Assumed for this tutorial')
dur_infectious = ss.par(ss.days(8), doc='Average infectious period')

infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
progression = E >> I @ dur_latent
recovery    = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=dur_infectious, p=0.998)
death       = ss.Transition(I, ss.null, dur=dur_infectious, p=0.002)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, death, init=dict(I=0.001))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))

One parameter can be used in several places, as dur_infectious is here, and changing it changes it everywhere: ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(dur_latent=ss.days(12)), ...) runs the model with a latent period of 12 days. The bounds are what calibration uses: sim.fit() searches for the values of every parameter with bounds that best match data. Parameters in the user guide has more, including priors.

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Checking the disease
The disease now has four states and four transitions, and it is worth checking that it is the disease you meant before using it. There are three ways to look at it. describe() lists every state, transition, and parameter as Starsim has built it: which states are infectious (I, since it is in the rate of infection), the distribution of each duration, each parameter with its value, bounds, description, and source (beta = 1.9 per day, between 1 and 3), and every value that Starsim chose itself, marked as guessed:

equations() prints the disease as the ODEs it stands for, with the names of the parameters. It is the quickest way to check that every flow leaves one state and enters another, and that the force of infection is what you meant:

measles.equations()

dS/dt   = -beta * S * I / N

diagram() draws the states and transitions as a flowchart, with the transmission dashed, the empty circle for ss.null, and each arrow labeled with its value and, for a branch, the share that takes it:

The diagram is written in Mermaid, a language for diagrams that JupyterLab, Quarto, GitHub, and many other tools draw; print(measles.diagram()) gives its text.
This disease is written as states and transitions, the way the rest of the tutorials write diseases. A disease can also be written as a class, with its states, parameters, and transitions in the class body; this is worth doing for a disease that will be used in several models, or shared with others, since then it can be made with different values of its parameters, like the diseases in Starsim’s library (e.g. Measles(beta=1.5)). Diseases in the user guide shows how, along with other kinds of transition, such as those triggered by an event. Tutorial 4 takes the SEIR model of this tutorial (without deaths) and splits the town into age groups.

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Exercises

Measles has a latent period of 10 to 12 days. Using the model with named parameters, run it with a latent period of 12 days, using pars=. Does R0 change? How do the timing and height of the peak change?
Give the infectious period an Erlang distribution too, with k=4. Using R0() and a plot of I, check whether R0 or the course of the epidemic changes.
About 1 in 10 people with measles in this town are admitted to hospital, after 4 days of being infectious on average, and stay for 7 days. Add a state for people in hospital (assume they don’t transmit), and find the largest number of people in hospital at once.
