title: A3 – Demographics
text:
🧠15% 🤖85%
Over an outbreak of a few weeks or months, the population hardly changes, so the core tutorials left births and deaths out. Over years, it does: births bring in new people who have never been infected, deaths remove people who are immune, and the population grows and ages. These change the course of an infection, and for an infection like measles, which leaves lifelong immunity, births are what let it come back at all.
This tutorial covers births and deaths at constant rates, and what they do to measles, first as an ODE and then as agents, where measles can die out; the population of a real country, with birth and death rates from UN data; pregnancy; and how a few thousand agents can stand for a population of millions.

title: A3 – Demographics
text:
Starting point
The measles model from the core tutorials, in a town of 20,000 people:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles.I')

Sim: measles, 20,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 20 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0029 s; measles: 19,980 infections; at most 14,822 infectious, on day 6









R0 = 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15, so the outbreak infects nearly everyone, and since nobody new is born, that is the end of it.

title: A3 – Demographics
text:
Births and deaths
There are a few basic ways to add vital dynamics to your model. The simplest is ss.birth() and ss.death(), which give births and deaths at a constant rate per person: a crude birth rate of 30 per 1,000 people per year is ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)). People are born into each disease’s first state (S) and die from every state at the same rate, so with equal rates the population stays the same size. They are given to the sim in demographics=. You can even simply set demographics=True to use default rates. By default, agents age if and only if the population has births or deaths; you can override this by setting use_aging, e.g. ss.Sim(use_aging=False).
Births and deaths are rates per year, while β and the infectious period are per day. When a model’s rates have different units, Starsim needs every rate to say its own, so β is written ss.perday(1.9); the sim then steps by one day (dt=ss.days(1)). Here is the measles model with births and deaths, as an ODE, over 20 years:

def make_measles(importation=False):
    """ Measles, optionally with infections brought in from outside the town """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    transitions = dict(
        infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I, # β = 1.9 per day
        recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8),
    )
    if importation:
        transitions['importation'] = S >> I @ ss.peryear(0.001) # Each susceptible person is infected outside the town at 0.001 per year
    return ss.Disease(**transitions, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')

demographics = [
    ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), # 30 births per 1,000 people per year
    ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), # 30 deaths per 1,000 people per year
]
pars = dict(demographics=demographics, start='2000-01-01', stop='2020-01-01', dt=ss.days(1))
ode = ss.Sim(make_measles(), total_pop=20_000, **pars)
ode.run()

res = ode.results.measles
res.I.plot(log=True); # On a log scale, since the first epidemic is so much larger than the rest

Sim: measles, 20,000 people, as an ODE, 2000-01-01 to 2020-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 20 infectious at the start
  Note: the number infected in "measles" falls to 0.91 (at 2000-03-27) and then rises to 374; a stochastic run would usually die out there. solver="gillespie" with ss.parallel(n_runs=...) shows how often, in the runs of msim.results.measles.I after that point
  Done in 0.0059 s; measles: 29,856 infections; at most 14,822 infectious, on 2000-01-07









After the first epidemic, there is a “honeymoon” of a few years with very little measles, while births slowly rebuild the number of susceptible people. Once there are enough of them for each case to cause more than one more, measles returns, in a series of smaller epidemics that settle toward a steady endemic level. These match the classic theory of an SIR model with births:

At the endemic level, each case causes one more, so the share of people who are susceptible is 1/R0, about 7%.
The average age at infection is about L/(R0 − 1), where L is the life expectancy (1/0.03 = 33 years here): about 2.4 years, so measles becomes a disease of young children.
The time between epidemics is about 2π√(A × D), where A is the average age at infection and D is the infectious period (8 days, or 0.022 years): about 1.4 years.


print('Share susceptible at the end:', round(res.S[-1]/20_000, 3))

Share susceptible at the end: 0.067


Births and deaths are transitions of the disease, like infection and recovery, so they have results of their own (res.births and res.deaths), and they work under every solver.

title: A3 – Demographics
section: Measles as agents: dying out, and coming back
text:
Measles as agents: dying out, and coming back
The sim also printed a note: between the epidemics, the number of infectious people in the ODE falls below one. An ODE can recover from a fraction of a person, but a real town can’t: once the last case recovers, measles is gone until someone brings it back. Agents show this. Here is the same model as 20,000 agents, and again with a few infections brought in from outside the town (about one or two a year, since each susceptible person is infected outside at 0.001 per year):

sims = {
    'Agents': ss.Sim(make_measles(), n_agents=20_000, **pars),
    'Agents, with importations': ss.Sim(make_measles(importation=True), n_agents=20_000, **pars),
}
for sim in sims.values():
    sim.run()

plt.figure()
plt.semilogy(res.timevec, res.I, label='ODE')
for label, sim in sims.items():
    plt.semilogy(sim.results.measles.timevec, sim.results.measles.I, label=label)
plt.ylim(bottom=0.5)
plt.ylabel('Number infectious')
plt.legend();

Sim: measles, as 20,000 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2020-01-01
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 11.2 s; measles: 20,018 infections; at most 15,820 infectious, on 2000-01-10


Sim: measles, as 20,000 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2020-01-01
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 8.0 s; measles: 29,263 infections; at most 15,838 infectious, on 2000-01-10









As agents, measles dies out after the first epidemic, and with no one to bring it back, it is gone for good, however many susceptible children are born. With importations, it comes back, but not as the ODE does: each imported case finds either too few susceptible people, and fizzles out, or enough, and starts an epidemic. So the epidemics come every few years, as large as the first of the ODE’s later ones, and they don’t settle down to an endemic level, since between them the town has no measles at all. This is why measles persists only in cities of several hundred thousand people or more (its critical community size), and why in smaller places it comes and goes with each new introduction. The share of introductions that take off is the subject of A1.

title: A3 – Demographics
text:
A country’s population
Constant rates are enough for a town over a few years. For more realistic demographics, birth and death rates change from year to year, and death rates differ by age and sex. Starsim includes the UN World Population Prospects for every country: ss.people('Nigeria') gives agents with the ages, sex ratio, and size of Nigeria’s population in the year the sim starts; ss.Births(birth_rate='Nigeria') gives births at Nigeria’s crude birth rate in each year; and ss.Deaths(death_rate='Nigeria') gives deaths at its death rates by year, age, and sex.
To check the model, compare its population with the UN’s, for the same years. A result is compared with data of the same name, so a column called alive is plotted with the result alive:

years = [2000, 2010, 2020, 2030]
population = [ss.people('Nigeria', year=year).named.total for year in years] # The UN's population in each year
data = dict(date=years, alive=population)

people = ss.people('Nigeria', n_agents=5000)
demographics = [ss.Births(birth_rate='Nigeria'), ss.Deaths(death_rate='Nigeria')]
sim = ss.Sim(people=people, demographics=demographics, start=2000, stop=2030, data=data)
sim.run()
sim.plot('alive')

Sim: births, deaths, as 5,000 agents, each 25,300 people, years 2000 to 2030
  Note: unit='year' (from start and stop years)


  Done in 0.032 s









The population grows from 126 million to about 260 million, as the UN projects. The ages change too, and sim.people.plot_ages() shows the age pyramid at the end of the run:

sim.people.plot_ages()








If you want to use realistic demographics for a setting that isn’t in the UN data, or with rates of your own, ss.Births() and ss.Deaths() also take your own data: one rate, rates by year (a table with a column for the year and one for the rate), or for deaths, rates by year, age, and sex. There are examples of these files in the test_data folder (e.g. nigeria_deaths.csv), and ss.People(n_agents, age_data=...) takes the ages of the population from a file. Crude birth and death rates are usually given per 1,000 people, and these modules read a rate above 1 as per 1,000 and a rate below 1 as per person; give rate_units=1000 or rate_units=1 to say which (they warn when a rate could be either). See Demographics in the user guide.

title: A3 – Demographics
text:
Pregnancy
ss.Births() adds babies to the population as a whole. ss.Pregnancy() instead gives women of reproductive age pregnancies, at age-specific fertility rates, which last about nine months and end in a birth (or a miscarriage, a stillbirth, or a maternal death, at rates that can be set). This is what a model needs when something depends on pregnancy itself: infection passed from mother to child (see A2), testing in antenatal care, or the effects of a disease on pregnancy. Pregnancy is itself declared as states (NP, not pregnant, and P, pregnant) and transitions (conception, delivery, and so on), so other modules can use them, e.g. where=pregnancy.P, and each transition is a result. As per standard definitions, fertility_rate is defined per woman, whereas a birth rate is defined per person.
As with births and deaths, ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate='Nigeria') reads Nigeria’s age-specific fertility rates from the UN: births per 1,000 women in each 5-year age group, by year. Pregnancy takes months, so the sim steps by a month:

pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate='Nigeria')
deaths = ss.Deaths(death_rate='Nigeria')

sim = ss.Sim(people=ss.people('Nigeria', n_agents=5000), demographics=[pregnancy, deaths], start=2000, stop=2030, dt=ss.months(1), data=data)
sim.run()
sim.plot('alive')

Sim: pregnancy, deaths, as 5,000 agents, each 25,300 people, years 2000 to 2030
  Running as agents: people were given
  Note: unit='month' (from dt)
  Note: pregnancy: women pregnant at the start, conceived over the 9 steps before it (burnin=True)


  Done in 1.6 s









The population grows much as it did with crude birth rates, but now each birth comes from a pregnancy of a particular woman, so it can be linked to her: her age, her infections, and the care she receives. The pregnancy model supplies the births, so don’t also add ss.Births() (or ss.birth()) unless it stands for a separate source of people: the same births would be counted twice.
Rates of your own work too: fertility_rate takes a table with a column for the year, one for the age, and one for the rate, e.g. pd.read_csv('test_data/nigeria_asfr.csv') (columns Time, AgeGrp, and ASFR), or one rate, e.g. ss.freqperyear(100).

title: A3 – Demographics
text:
Agents standing for many people
Even though we’ve been simulating populations of a few thousand agents, the results reflect a much larger population. You can think of this as a kind of statistical sampling approximation. Nigeria has well over 100 million people, and it would be much too computationally intensive to simulate one agent for each of them. Instead, each agent stands for many people: the sim takes the size of the population from ss.people('Nigeria') (or from total_pop=, e.g. ss.Sim(total_pop=200e6, n_agents=50e3) for 200 million people as 50,000 agents, each standing for 4,000), and divides it by the number of agents, so above each agent stands for about 25,000 people. Results that count people, such as alive and births, are multiplied by this, so they are in people, not agents.
Agents are a sample of the population, so results made from few of them are noisy. Here are births each year, with 1,000 agents and with 20,000:

pars = dict(demographics=[ss.Births(birth_rate='Nigeria'), ss.Deaths(death_rate='Nigeria')], start=2000, stop=2030)
sims = {
    '1,000 agents': ss.Sim(people=ss.people('Nigeria', n_agents=1000), **pars),
    '20,000 agents': ss.Sim(people=ss.people('Nigeria', n_agents=20_000), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('births.birth')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (1,000 agents, 20,000 agents)
  Done in 0.41 s









With 1,000 agents, about 40 are born each year, and the number varies by chance by about the square root of that, around 6, or 15%; with 20,000 agents, the variation is about 4%. As a rule of thumb, use enough agents that the events you care about are counted in the hundreds: for births in a whole country, a few thousand agents is plenty, but for the cases of a rare disease, or the deaths in one age group, it may take many more. And for anything that depends on chance in small numbers, such as whether measles dies out in a town, the agents must be people, one each, not a sample of them. Branching and rescaling shows how to add agents as a rare infection grows.

title: A3 – Demographics
text:
Exercises

In Niger, the crude birth rate is 45 and the crude death rate is 9. Assuming these rates stay constant, and starting with its population in 2020 (ss.people('Niger', n_agents=5000)), how many people will there be in 2040? (You do not need to include any diseases in your model.) Compare this with its UN birth and death rates.
In the measles model with births, how does the time between epidemics in the ODE change if the birth rate (and the death rate) is 20 per 1,000 per year instead of 30? Does it agree with the theory above?
In the town of 20,000 with importations, how often do epidemics come if the town has 50,000 people instead (and so more births each year)? Does measles ever persist between them?
Contraception lowers the rate of conception: ss.modify(pregnancy.conception, multiply=0.7, start=2010) cuts it by 30% from 2010. Add it to the Nigeria model with pregnancy as an intervention. How many fewer people are there in 2030?

title: A3 – Demographics
text:
Further reading

UN World Population Prospects: the data behind ss.people(), ss.Births(), and ss.Deaths()
EMOD: demographics: demographics files for an agent-based disease model
Vivarium: documentation: a framework for microsimulation of populations, with births and deaths

title: A4 – Interventions
text:
🧠15% 🤖85%
Understanding the impact of interventions is one of the most common reasons to use a disease model. T5 showed how to vaccinate a group of people and change a parameter from a date, for measles in a town. This tutorial is about interventions that reach particular people because of what has happened to them: treating people when they seek care, screening a group and treating those who test positive, notifying their partners, and vaccinating people as they reach an age. Each of these depends on individuals, their infections, their test results, and their partners, so they run as agents.

title: A4 – Interventions
text:
Products and interventions
Starsim contains products, which can be thought of as the actual test, diagnostic, treatment, or vaccine product being used, as well as interventions (deliveries), which are responsible for delivering the products to the population. Starsim includes three basic types of product, ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, and ss.Treatment, and a delivery for each: ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat(). A delivery says who receives the product (where= for who is eligible, who= or on= for something that has happened to them), when (at=, interval=, start=, at_age=), and how many (coverage=, capacity=). These are general enough that they rarely need to be tailored to a particular disease, and you can just use them directly. That being said, you are always welcome to write your own, to capture particular features of the intervention you’re modeling (see A5).

title: A4 – Interventions
text:
Starting point
Measles has no treatment, so this tutorial uses the sexually transmitted infection from A2: a simplified curable bacterial infection, such as gonorrhea, that lasts 6 months on average untreated and leaves no immunity (an SIS model), on a sexual network in which partnerships last about a month. The network remembers partnerships for a year after they end (memory=), which partner notification will use. Births and deaths keep the population turning over, so that people age into the groups that interventions reach. It runs as 5,000 agents for 20 years, in monthly steps:

import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peract(m2f=0.1, f2m=0.05)*I  # Chance of infection per act
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.months(6)                    # Infected for 6 months on average, untreated
sti = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

settings = dict(
    networks     = ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.months(1), memory=ss.years(1)), # Partnerships of about a month, remembered for a year
    demographics = [ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02))],
    n_agents     = 5000,
    start        = 2000,
    stop         = 2020,
    dt           = ss.months(1),
    verbose      = 0,
)
sim = ss.Sim(sti, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.plot('sti.I')

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/









The infection is endemic, with about a third of people infected at any time.

title: A4 – Interventions
text:
Treating people who seek care
Some people with the infection notice symptoms and seek care. Suppose 30% of people seek care within a month of infection, on average, and are treated with a drug that cures 95% of them. The drug is the product; ss.treat() delivers it. on=sti.infection delivers it to the people who were just infected, coverage=0.3 to 30% of them, and delay= a time after their infection, drawn for each person:

drug = ss.Treatment(cure=0.95) # Cures 95% of the people it is given to
care = ss.treat(drug, where=sti.infection, coverage=0.3, delay=ss.uniform(ss.weeks(1), ss.months(2)))

The treatment is given when it is due, whether or not the person is still infected by then; for someone who has recovered already, it does nothing.

title: A4 – Interventions
section: Screening, and treating those who test positive
text:
Screening, and treating those who test positive
People without symptoms don’t seek care, so they can only be found by screening. Here people aged 15 to 29, who have the most partners, are screened every 6 months from 2010, with a test that finds 90% of infections (its sensitivity) and gives a false positive for 2% of those not infected (its specificity). Half of the people eligible are reached in each round. Those who test positive (screening.positive) are treated:

young = (ss.ppl.age >= 15) & (ss.ppl.age < 30) # Who is eligible: a condition on each person, worked out when it is needed
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, where=young, coverage=0.5, interval=ss.months(6), start='2010')
treatment = ss.treat(drug, who=screening.positive)

where= takes any condition on people or on the states of a module, combined with & (and), | (or), and ~ (not): young & ~sti.I would screen only young people who aren’t infected, for example (which would be pointless, but possible).

title: A4 – Interventions
text:
Notifying partners
A person who tests positive was infected by someone, and may have infected others. Partner notification reaches their partners, with trace=: it delivers the product to the contacts, on the named network, of the people the event in who= selects. Since the network remembers partnerships for a year, this reaches the partners of the past year, not only the current ones. Here half of the partners of those who test positive are reached, and treated without being tested (as in expedited partner therapy):

notification = ss.treat(drug, who=screening.positive, trace='sexualnet', coverage=0.5)

Now compare these, each scenario adding one more intervention to the last:

scenarios = {
    'No treatment':             [],
    'Treatment when seeking care': [care],
    'And screening':            [care, screening, treatment],
    'And partner notification': [care, screening, treatment, notification],
}
sims = {label: ss.Sim(sti, interventions=interventions, **settings) for label, interventions in scenarios.items()}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')








Treating people who seek care cuts the number infected by about a third, since it shortens the infections it reaches. Screening from 2010 cuts it further, and notifying partners further still: each finds infections that the others miss. The summary gives the total number of infections over the 20 years in each scenario:

msim.summarize().loc['sti_infection']








value


scenario





No treatment
58589.0


Treatment when seeking care
45280.0


And screening
41824.0


And partner notification
35921.0







The deliveries have results of their own, such as the number of people screened, the number who tested positive, and the number of partners treated:

sim = msim.sims['And partner notification']
print('Screened:', sim.results.screening.delivered.sum())
print('Tested positive:', sim.results.screening.positive.sum())
print('Treated after testing positive:', sim.results.treatment.delivered.sum())
print('Partners treated:', sim.results.notification.delivered.sum())

Screened: 9242.0
Tested positive: 1453.0
Treated after testing positive: 1453.0
Partners treated: 5462.0


Everyone who tests positive is treated, including the few whose positive result is false. Partner notification treats several times as many people as screening finds, since each person who tests positive has had several partners in the past year; many of them are infected, and it is those it cures that make the difference.

title: A4 – Interventions
text:
Individual histories
As agents, every delivery remembers, for each person, whether its event happened to them (.ever), how many times (.count), and how long ago (.since). This gives individual histories after the run, e.g. how many times each person tested positive:

screening = sim.interventions.screening
times_positive = screening.positive.count.values
print('Number of people who tested positive 0, 1, 2, ... times:', np.bincount(times_positive.astype(int)))

Number of people who tested positive 0, 1, 2, ... times: [4290  370  231   95   35   10]


About half of the people who tested positive did so more than once, since curing an infection doesn’t protect against the next one; in practice this is a reason to retest people some months after treatment. A history can also decide who receives something: where=screening.positive.since <= ss.months(6) would make a delivery to people who tested positive in the past 6 months (e.g. a retest), and where=~treatment.ever to people never treated.

title: A4 – Interventions
section: Vaccination as people reach an age
text:
Vaccination as people reach an age
There is no vaccine for gonorrhea in routine use, but a meningococcal vaccine appears to give some protection, perhaps 30–40%. Suppose one that is 35% effective is given to 80% of people as they turn 15, from 2010. at_age= is routine delivery as people reach an age: each person is offered it once, on the step on which they reach it, and not everyone older on the first day:

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.35, at_age=15, coverage=0.8, start='2010')

sims = {
    'Treatment when seeking care': ss.Sim(sti, interventions=care, **settings),
    'And vaccination at age 15':   ss.Sim(sti, interventions=[care, vaccination], **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')
print('Doses:', msim.sims['And vaccination at age 15'].results.vaccination.delivered.sum())








Doses: 538.0


The vaccine makes little difference by 2020: after 10 years, it has reached only the people who were 15 or younger in 2010, a small share of those at risk, and it protects each of them only partly. Vaccination as people reach an age pays off over decades, as each cohort replaces an unvaccinated one. By default a vaccine is leaky: everyone vaccinated is 35% less likely to be infected at each exposure. With leaky=False it is all or nothing instead (35% fully protected, the rest not at all), and waning= makes protection fade; see Products.

title: A4 – Interventions
text:
Interventions of your own
These deliveries cover most programs. When who receives something depends on a rule of your own, deliver= takes a function of the sim that returns the UIDs of the people who receive it on each step; and an intervention that does something no product does is a module written as code, a class with a step() method. T9 and A5 show how, and Interventions in the user guide covers the rest: capacity, priority, queues, and delays.

title: A4 – Interventions
text:
Exercises

In the scenario with partner notification, what happens if the partners of people who seek care are notified too (a second notification, with who=care)? Is the effect larger than notifying the partners of those found by screening?
Screening reaches people aged 15 to 29. How much does the effect change if it reaches everyone aged 15 to 49 instead, and how many more tests does it take? Which gives more infections prevented per test?
Add a catch-up campaign to the vaccination at age 15: a single round in 2010 () for everyone aged 15 to 29, with the same vaccine. How much sooner does vaccination make a difference, and how many more doses does it take?

title: A4 – Interventions
text:
Further reading

EpiModel: network modeling for epidemics: a course on network models, including interventions, in R
Covasim: interventions: testing, tracing, and quarantine in an agent-based model
WHO: guidelines for the management of sexually transmitted infections: treatment and partner services in practice

title: T4 – Age groups and contacts
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Who gets measles, and why? So far, everyone in the model town mixes with everyone else equally. In reality, children have many more contacts than adults, mostly with other children, at school and at home; and in a town where most people have been vaccinated, the children who missed out are the ones still susceptible. This tutorial splits the measles model into age groups, gives each group its own immunity, describes how the groups mix with a contact matrix, and reads the results by age. It then adds births and deaths, and uses the population and contacts of a real country.
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

title: T4 – Age groups and contacts
text:
The model so far
This is the SEIR model from T3 – Building a disease, with a latent period of 10 days and an infectious period of 8, in a town of 100,000 people. R0 is β times the infectious period, 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15:

import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0062 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 29,215 infectious, on day 28

title: T4 – Age groups and contacts
section: Age groups, each with its own immunity
text:
Age groups, each with its own immunity
stratify() splits each state of a disease into groups: here, by age, into three groups, 0–14, 15–64, and 65 and over. Each group is given by its lower edge, with the share of the population in it, here 30%, 60%, and 10%. The model then has a compartment for each state in each age group: S for children, S for adults, and so on.
On its own, this changes nothing about the epidemic: everyone still mixes with everyone else equally, so each group is infected at the same rate, in proportion to its size. Age groups matter when something differs between them. The first thing that differs in a real town is immunity. Suppose the town has had a vaccination program for years, so that 92% of adults under 65 and 98% of older adults are immune (from vaccination or from past infection), but only 80% of children, since coverage has slipped recently. ss.by() gives a value for each level of a stratification, and init gives the share of each group that starts in a state; init_n starts 10 people infectious, as if measles had just been brought into the town by travelers. The run is for a year, from 1 January 2025:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The share immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),                           # 10 people infectious at the start
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the share of people in each

settings = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
equal = ss.Sim(measles, label='Everyone mixes equally', **settings)
equal.run()
equal.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()

Sim "Everyone mixes equally": measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.67 at the start, with 11% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0035 s; measles: 7,438 infections; at most 462 infectious, on 2025-07-06









About 90% of the town is immune, so each case at the start infects about 1.7 others on average (the run prints this as R at the start, after R0): an outbreak, but a modest one, which peaks in early July. Since everyone still mixes equally, the outbreak is spread over the age groups in proportion to the number of susceptible people in each.

title: T4 – Age groups and contacts
text:
Contacts between age groups
A contact matrix gives the number of contacts a day that a person in each age group has with people in each age group: row i, column j is the number of contacts that one person in group i has with people in group j. Contact surveys, such as POLYMOD in Europe, measure these. In the matrix below, children have 10 contacts a day with other children, 6 with adults, and 1 with people 65 and over, 17 in all; adults and older adults have 12 each. (These numbers are illustrative, but have the shape of real surveys: children mix most, and mostly with each other.)









Contacts a day, of a person aged…
…with people 0–14
…with people 15–64
…with people 65+




0–14
10
6
1


15–64
3
8
1


65+
3
6
3



A contact between a child and an adult is a contact for both of them, so the matrix is reciprocal: the children, 30% of the town, have 6 contacts each with adults, and the adults, twice as many, have 3 each with children, the same number of contacts in all. (Starsim notes a matrix that isn’t.)
ss.contacts() takes the matrix, with the lower edge of each of its age groups (ages=), and is given to the sim as how people mix (networks=). With contacts, β means something different: it is the rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day, and the matrix supplies how many contacts there are. People here have about 13.5 contacts a day on average, so a β of 1.9 a day under equal mixing is about 0.14 per contact. Reusing a β of 1.9 here would multiply transmission by 13.5: a β fitted under one assumption about mixing generally has to be fitted again under another.

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5]) # The rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day

infection   = S >> E @ beta*I       # At a rate of β times the contacts with infectious people
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
    init_n = dict(I=10),
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups
sim = ss.Sim(measles, networks=contacts, label='Contact matrix', **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()

Sim "Contact matrix": measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.8 (R = 2.46 at the start, with 11% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0039 s; measles: 8,795 infections; at most 934 infectious, on 2025-04-27









With contacts, Starsim works out R0 from the matrix (as the largest eigenvalue of the next-generation matrix), so it depends on who meets whom, not only on the average number of contacts. R0 is about the same as before, 16, but the reproduction number at the start is much higher, about 2.5 rather than 1.7. The susceptible people are concentrated among children, and children are exactly the people with the most contacts, mostly with each other. To compare the two runs, ss.parallel() runs them together and plots them on the same axes:

msim = ss.parallel([equal, sim])
msim.plot('measles.infection')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Everyone mixes equally, Contact matrix)
  Done in 0.34 s









With the contact matrix, the outbreak peaks two months sooner, at the end of April, twice as high, and infects about 8,800 people rather than 7,400; the extra infections are all in children. A model that assumed equal mixing would underestimate an outbreak in a town like this one, where the gaps in immunity are in the group that mixes most.

title: T4 – Age groups and contacts
text:
Results by age group
Every result of a stratified model is kept for each group, and the totals over all groups are as before (res.infection is the infections of all ages). by('age') splits a result into one series for each age group, as in the plots above, and select() picks one group, named by its ages ('0-14', '15-64', '65+'):

res = sim.results.measles
children = res.I.select(age='0-14')
print('Peak number of children infectious:', round(children.max()))
print('Infections in people 65 and over:', round(res.infection.select(age='65+').sum()))

Peak number of children infectious: 616
Infections in people 65 and over: 127


summarize() gives the total over the whole run of each group at once. Counts depend on the size of a group as well as on its risk: dividing by the number of people in each group gives the share of each group infected (the attack rate), which is the risk:

infections = res.infection.by('age').summarize()
print(infections.round())
print('Share of each group infected:')
print((infections / [30_000, 60_000, 10_000]).round(3))

0-14     5461.0
15-64    3208.0
65+       127.0
Name: infection, dtype: float64
Share of each group infected:
0-14     0.182
15-64    0.053
65+      0.013
Name: infection, dtype: float64


Children have nearly two thirds of the infections, though they are under a third of the town: 18% of them are infected, more than three times the share of adults.

title: T4 – Age groups and contacts
text:
Births, deaths, and aging
Over a year, a town’s population hardly changes. Over decades, though, children are born susceptible, and this is what makes measles come back: an epidemic leaves too few susceptible people for the next one, until enough children have been born since. Births and deaths are given to the sim as demographics. ss.birth() takes a crude birth rate, here 30 births a year per 1,000 people, and ss.death() a death rate, here 20 deaths a year per 1,000 people at every age (a simplification; A3 – Demographics uses death rates by age, from data). Children born into S move up the age groups as they grow older. Here is the model over 20 years, with and without births and deaths:

demographics = [
    ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), # 30 births a year per 1,000 people
    ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), # 20 deaths a year per 1,000 people
]
long = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, unit='day', dt=ss.weeks(1), start='2025-01-01', stop='2045-01-01')

msim = ss.parallel({
    'No births or deaths': ss.Sim(measles, **long),
    'Births and deaths':   ss.Sim(measles, demographics=demographics, **long),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (No births or deaths, Births and deaths)
  Done in 0.44 s









A few things are new in this run:

The birth and death rates are per year, and the other rates in the model per day, so unit='day' says which unit the bare numbers of the model (β) are in (T2 – Building a model).
dt=ss.weeks(1) records the results once a week, since daily results over 20 years are more than needed. As an ODE, the model is still solved finely in between.

Without births, there is one outbreak, and then measles is gone for good: nobody new is susceptible. With births, the first outbreak is followed by a series of smaller ones, a year or two apart, settling down to a steady level of infection, which grows slowly as the town does. This is the classic pattern of measles where too few children are vaccinated: births replenish the susceptible people faster than vaccination removes them (in this model, newborns are not vaccinated at all). In the troughs between outbreaks, there are only a handful of infectious people in the whole town, and in reality measles would often die out there until it was brought in again. An ODE can’t show this, since it follows the expected numbers, which never reach zero; T5 – Interventions and scenarios runs the model by chance instead.

title: T4 – Age groups and contacts
text:
A real population
For a model of a real place, the share of people in each age group, and the contacts between them, can come from data. ss.people('Kenya') is the population of Kenya, by age and sex (from the UN World Population Prospects), and ss.contacts('Kenya') is a contact matrix for Kenya, by 5-year age group (from Prem et al., 2021). Given these, stratify() needs only the age groups, and takes the share of people in each from the population; Starsim adds up the contact matrix into the model’s age groups. total_pop keeps the model to a town of 100,000 people, rather than the whole country:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
    init_n = dict(I=10),
)
measles.stratify(age=[0, 15, 65]) # The share in each group comes from the population

kenya = ss.Sim(measles, people=ss.people('Kenya'), networks=ss.contacts('Kenya'), **settings)
kenya.run()
kenya.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 17.4 (R = 2.44 at the start, with 12% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: contact matrix "contacts" aggregated from 16 age groups to the model's 3 (0-14, 15-64, 65+)
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass use_aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0033 s; measles: 10,401 infections; at most 1,125 infectious, on 2025-04-27









Kenya has a young population: about 37% of people are under 15, and 3% are 65 or over. The run notes that the contact matrix was added up into the model’s three age groups. With the same β, R0 is a little higher, about 17, since people in Kenya have more contacts a day than in the made-up matrix above; and with more children, the outbreak is larger, about 10,400 infections, nearly two thirds of them in children. These data are inputs, not a calibrated model: check the year, the age groups, and how contacts were defined in the survey before relying on them. Population data explains what data there are and how they fit together.
Everything in this tutorial works the same way when the model is run as agents (with n_agents=, as in T1 – Getting started): each agent has an age, and so belongs to an age group, and agents age, are born, and die. For more on stratification, such as several dimensions at once, see T8 – Stratification and co-transmission and Stratification; for births and deaths, see Demographics.

title: T4 – Age groups and contacts
text:
Exercises

Closing schools roughly halves the contacts between children. Change the matrix so that children have 5 contacts a day with other children instead of 10. How do the reproduction number at the start and the number of children infected change? Which other age groups are affected, and why?
Give every age group the same immunity, 90%, keeping the contact matrix. How large is the outbreak now, compared with the town above, in which the same overall share of people (about 90%) is immune? What does this say about where gaps in immunity matter most?
In the model with births and deaths, raise the birth rate to 45 a year per 1,000 people, as in some countries with young populations. How does the time between outbreaks change, and why?

Solutions · Next: T5 – Interventions and scenarios

title: T4 – Age groups and contacts
text:
Further reading

POLYMOD: Social contacts and mixing patterns relevant to the spread of infectious diseases: the contact survey in eight European countries behind most age-structured models
Prem et al. (2021): Projecting contact matrices in 177 geographical regions: the source of ss.contacts('Kenya')
socialmixr: Social mixing matrices for infectious disease modeling: an R package for building contact matrices from survey data
epydemix: Modeling with population data: age-structured models with the population and contact matrices of real countries, in another Python framework

title: A2 – Networks
text:
🧠15% 🤖85%
Many infectious diseases transmit when people come into contact with one another, and who infects whom depends on who meets whom. In the core tutorials, people mixed at random: each contact was with someone new, drawn from the whole population (or from an age group). That is a good description of a disease like measles, which spreads through many brief contacts. For other diseases it is not: a sexually transmitted infection spreads between partners, who stay together for months or years, and HIV passes from a mother to her child. What matters then is the pattern of contacts itself, who is linked with whom and for how long, and that is what a network describes.
Starsim contains two different approaches to disease transmission between people:
Contact networks and mixing pools can be used together in a single simulation. This tutorial shows when a network changes the course of an epidemic, how to look inside one, and how to use the three kinds of network Starsim provides: random networks, sexual networks, and the network between mothers and children. It ends with mixing pools. A network links individual people, so a model with one runs as agents.

title: A2 – Networks
text:
Starting point
The measles model from the core tutorials, run as agents (see A1):

import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles.I')

Sim: measles, as 10,000 agents, days 0 to 50
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.049 s; measles: 9,990 infections; at most 7,838 infectious, on day 9









With no network, mixing is homogeneous: β = 1.9 per day is the rate at which one infectious person infects others in a fully susceptible population, and R0 = 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15.

title: A2 – Networks
section: Contacts, and the chance of infection per contact
text:
Contacts, and the chance of infection per contact
A rate like β can be split into two parts: the number of contacts each person has per day, and the chance that a contact between an infectious and a susceptible person passes the infection on. With 3 contacts a day, a chance of 0.63 per contact per day gives the same β of 3 × 0.63 = 1.9, and the same R0. Once there are contacts, β in the transition is the chance per contact: a β fitted with homogeneous mixing can’t be reused with a network without checking what it means.
There are several ways to arrange those 3 contacts a day, and each says something different about how people meet:

ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=3): everyone mixes at random, with 3 contacts a day. This is the same model as homogeneous mixing, with β split into contacts and a chance per contact.
ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3): each person has 3 contacts, with new people each day.
ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3, dynamic=False): each person has the same 3 contacts every day, for the whole run.


infection = S >> I @ 0.63*I       # A chance of infection of 0.63 per contact per day
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

pars = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(100))
sims = {
    'Well mixed':              ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=3), **pars),
    'New contacts each day':   ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3), **pars),
    'Same contacts every day': ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3, dynamic=False), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (Well mixed, New contacts each day, Same contacts every day)
  Done in 0.64 s









When people meet someone new each day, the epidemic is nearly the same as with random mixing. When they meet the same people every day, it is slower and its peak is lower, since contacts are wasted: an infectious person keeps meeting the person who infected them, and the contacts they have already infected. The infection has to spread outward through the network, one link at a time.
Even so, almost everyone is infected in the end, because measles is so infectious that it passes along nearly every link. For measles in a town, then, the pattern of contacts changes the timing more than the size of the outbreak, and the core tutorials’ random mixing (or mixing by age, with a contact matrix) is a reasonable choice. A network matters most when each person has few contacts, the contacts last, and the chance of infection over a contact is well below one: the situation of sexually transmitted infections.

title: A2 – Networks
text:
Looking inside a network
A network stores two very important things: the list of contacts (its edges) and the parameters that determine how they form and dissolve. Like all components of Starsim, it needs to be initialized within a sim before the contacts get made. Here is the network with the same contacts every day, for 30 people, so that it can be plotted:

small = ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3, dynamic=False), n_agents=30, stop=ss.days(10), verbose=0)
small.init()
net = small.networks.randomnet
net.plot()








All networks are stored in sim.networks, and individual networks can be found at their class name after conversion to lower case, here randomnet. Each edge has the UIDs of the two people (p1 and p2), a per-edge transmission multiplier (beta), and a duration (dur). Networks provide some basic functionality, for example to find contacts, and the edge list can be converted to a pandas dataframe (to_df()) or a NetworkX graph (to_graph()) for further analysis:

print('Contacts of agent 0:', net.find_contacts([0]))

df = net.to_df()
df.loc[(df.p1 == 0) | (df.p2 == 0)] # The edges involving agent 0

title: A2 – Networks
text:
Sexual networks
Measles is a poor example of a sexually transmitted infection, so this section uses a simplified curable bacterial infection, such as gonorrhea: an SIS model, in which people become susceptible again when they recover (here after 6 months on average, untreated). ss.SexualNet() is a network of partnerships between men and women. Each partnership lasts for a time (dur=) and has a number of sex acts per year (by default, 80 on average), and the chance of infection is given per act with ss.peract(), separately from men to women (m2f) and from women to men (f2m): for many sexually transmitted infections, transmission is more likely from men to women than the other way. The time unit of this model is a month, so it runs for 30 years in monthly steps.
A key question for a sexually transmitted infection is how often people change partners. Here are three networks that differ only in how long partnerships last:

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peract(m2f=0.1, f2m=0.05)*I  # Chance of infection per act
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.months(6)                    # Infected for 6 months on average
sti = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2030, dt=ss.months(1))
sims = {}
for label, dur in {'1 month': ss.months(1), '3 months': ss.months(3), '1 year': ss.years(1)}.items():
    network = ss.SexualNet(dur=dur) # How long partnerships last, on average
    sims[label] = ss.Sim(sti, networks=network, **pars)

msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (1 month, 3 months, 1 year)
  Done in 1.6 s









The chance of infection per act and the number of acts are the same in all three, but the outcome is not. When partnerships are short, people have many partners in a year, and the infection becomes endemic. When they last a year, a couple infects each other and then has no one else to infect: by the time the partnership ends, the infection has usually cleared, and it dies out. This is why partner change, and having more than one partner at a time (concurrency), drive the spread of sexually transmitted infections, and why they are modeled with a network.
It is worth checking the contact process before reading the epidemic, since two networks with the same average number of contacts can behave very differently. Here, at any moment, the three networks look alike: about two in three people have a partner, and nobody has more than one. degrees() gives the number of partners each person has now:

for label, sim in zip(sims, msim.sims):
    net = sim.networks.sexualnet
    partners = net.degrees(sim.people.auids) # The number of partners of each person alive
    print(label, '- people with 0, 1, 2, ... partners now:', np.bincount(partners))

1 month - people with 0, 1, 2, ... partners now: [1694 3306]
3 months - people with 0, 1, 2, ... partners now: [1694 3306]
1 year - people with 0, 1, 2, ... partners now: [1694 3306]


What differs is only how often partners change, which a snapshot doesn’t show. ss.SexualNet() has options for partnerships between men (between='mm'), for the number of partners people have at a time (n_contacts=) and the share who have more than one (concurrency=), for the age of sexual debut (debut=), and for the share of people who take part (participation=); see Contact networks.

title: A2 – Networks
text:
Mothers and children
Some infections, such as HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B, can pass from a mother to her child during pregnancy or birth. ss.MaternalNet() links each pregnant woman with her unborn child, so it needs pregnancy in the model: ss.Pregnancy() gives women of reproductive age pregnancies that end in births (and ss.Deaths() keeps the population from growing without limit; see A3). As new agents are born, they are linked to their mothers automatically.
Here is a simplified HIV model, with infection for life (no deaths from HIV or treatment, to keep it short). Its β is given for each network: per act on the sexual network, and as a rate per month of pregnancy on the maternal network, so that about 24% of the children of mothers with HIV are infected. Splitting the disease by age (stratify(), as in T4) gives results for children. To compare, a second sim adds prevention of mother-to-child transmission, which is 90% effective: an ss.modify() of the infection on the maternal network only (route=):

S, I = ss.states('S I')
beta = dict(
    sexualnet   = ss.peract(m2f=0.005, f2m=0.0025), # Chance of infection per sex act
    maternalnet = ss.permonth(0.03),                # Rate of infection per month of pregnancy
)
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
hiv = ss.Disease(infection, init_prev=0.1)
hiv.stratify(age=[0, 15]) # Children (0-14) and adults (15+)

prevention = ss.modify(hiv.infection, efficacy=0.9, route='maternalnet')

pars = dict(
    networks     = [ss.SexualNet(), ss.MaternalNet()],
    demographics = [ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=ss.peryear(150)), ss.Deaths(death_rate=ss.peryear(10))],
    n_agents     = 5000,
    start        = 2000,
    stop         = 2020,
    dt           = ss.months(1),
)
sims = {
    'No prevention': ss.Sim(hiv, **pars),
    'Prevention in pregnancy': ss.Sim(hiv, interventions=prevention, **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.results.hiv.I.select(age='0-14').plot()

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (No prevention, Prevention in pregnancy)
  Done in 3.4 s









The children who had HIV at the start (10% of them, as for everyone) grow older and leave the 0-14 group within 15 years, so the children with HIV after that were infected by their mothers. With prevention in pregnancy, there are very few. Starsim also has ss.PrenatalNet(), ss.PostnatalNet(), and ss.BreastfeedingNet(), for when infection before and after birth need to be told apart.

title: A2 – Networks
text:
Mixing pools
A mixing pool is a group whose members mix at random: everyone in it is equally likely to meet everyone else. Unlike a network, it doesn’t list who is in contact with whom, so it can give people many contacts at no extra cost. It suits large groups in which who meets whom doesn’t matter, such as a school or a town, while a network suits small groups in which it does, such as households and partnerships.
src= and dst= say who is in a pool: the people who can infect others in it and the people who can be infected. Here measles spreads through two pools: a school, in which children aged 5 to 14 have 10 contacts a day with each other, and the community, in which everyone has 2 contacts a day:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.19*I       # A chance of infection of 0.19 per contact per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
measles.stratify(age=[0, 5, 15]) # Ages 0-4, 5-14, and 15+, for the results

school    = ss.MixingPool(name='school', src=ss.AgeGroup(5, 15), dst=ss.AgeGroup(5, 15), n_contacts=10)
community = ss.MixingPool(name='community', n_contacts=2)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, networks=[school, community], n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(100))
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()

Sim: measles, as 10,000 agents, days 0 to 100
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.19 per day (per infectious contact), 17% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.09 s; measles: 9,553 infections; at most 3,841 infectious, on day 16









The epidemic starts in the school-age children, who have the most contacts, and spreads from them to the rest of the community. A set of mixing pools by age is a contact matrix, which is how T4 models mixing by age: ss.contacts() makes one pool for each pair of age groups. Mixing pools can be used for any groups, not only ages.

title: A2 – Networks
text:
Choosing how people mix
