Agents



Networks and mixing pools can be used together, as a list, and a disease can have a different β on each. Contact networks in the user guide covers the other networks Starsim provides, including households (ssl.ClusterNet) and the library’s networks. To make your own network, with your own rules for who pairs with whom, see A5.

title: A2 – Networks
text:
Exercises

In the section on contacts, measles reaches almost everyone whether contacts repeat or not. Repeat the comparison for a less infectious disease, with a chance of infection of 0.083 per contact per day (so R0 is about 2 with random mixing). How much does it matter now that people meet the same contacts every day, and why?
In the sexual network with partnerships that last a year, the infection dies out. Give the network n_contacts=1 and concurrency=0.2, so that 20% of people have more than one partner at a time. Does the infection persist?
Multi-network STI model: Adapt the STI model to include transmission between men as well, with a second network ss.SexualNet(name='msm', between='mm', dur=ss.months(3)) and a β for each network. How much does the second network add to the number infected?
Add households to the measles model: import starsim.library as ssl, then ssl.ClusterNet(cluster_size=ss.poisson(4)) gives households of about 4 people, everyone in each in contact with everyone else. Run measles with households and a community mixing pool with 2 contacts a day, and compare it with the community pool alone. How much of the epidemic do households add?

title: A2 – Networks
text:
Further reading

EpiModel: network modeling for epidemics: a course on stochastic network models, including sexually transmitted infections, in R
NetworkX: tutorial: building and analyzing graphs in Python, which net.to_graph() gives
Covasim: people and data: households, schools, workplaces, and community as contact layers
LASER: documentation: spatial agent-based models with mixing between patches

title: How to contribute
text:
🧠40% 🤖60%
Welcome! We are thrilled you are interested in contributing to Starsim. There are many ways to help: asking a question, reporting a bug, suggesting a feature, improving the docs, or contributing code or models.

title: How to contribute
text:
Reporting a problem
A minimal reproducible example is the shortest complete script that shows a problem: anyone can copy it, run it as it is, and see the same thing. It is the most useful thing to include when asking for help or reporting a bug, and making one often finds the cause on the way, since each part removed either matters or doesn’t.

How to make one

Start from what fails, in a fresh session. Restart the notebook’s kernel (or run the script from the command line) and check that the problem is still there. A notebook can hold values from cells that were changed or deleted since, and a disease that was stratified twice.
Remove what doesn’t matter, one thing at a time. Take out interventions, analyzers, extra diseases, networks, and data, and after each removal check that the problem is still there. Put back the last thing removed if it goes away: that is part of the cause.
Make it small and quick. Use fewer agents (or none: if the problem shows in an ODE, use that), a shorter run, and plain numbers in place of values read from files.
Replace private data with made-up data. A few rows typed in, or data drawn from a run of the model with sim.to_data(), show the same problem without sharing anything.
Fix the random seed (rand_seed= in ss.Sim), so that a stochastic run gives the same numbers every time.
Say what you expected, and what you got. Print the numbers, or include the plot, and give the reason you expected something else (a known result, another model, a calculation by hand).



An example
A report that a vaccine works less well than expected might come down to this script, which runs in a second:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.9, at=ss.days(0))
sim = ss.Sim(measles, interventions=vaccination, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(100), rand_seed=1)
sim.run()

# Expected: at most 19,000 infections (the 10% not vaccinated, plus the 10% of the vaccinated whom the vaccine doesn't protect)
print('Infections:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 100
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0022 s; measles: 67,440 infections; at most 13,315 infectious, on day 34
Infections: 67440


It has the model, the intervention, and the numbers, and nothing else. (The answer, in this case, is that the vaccine is leaky: see Profiling and debugging.)


When the model is spread out
When a model is built by several functions or read from files, copy the parts that matter into one script, with the values written in, and check that it still shows the problem. A model imported from another framework is already one script: its code is sim.imported.code (see Import/export).


What to include
When reporting a problem, for example as an issue at github.com/starsimhub/starsim/issues, include:

the script;
what it printed, including any notes, and the whole error message if there is one;
what you expected, and why;
the versions of Starsim, Python, and the main libraries, which this prints:


ss.debugtools.metadata().versions

sc.obj(
    python     = '3.13.9',
    numpy      = '2.4.6',
    numba      = '0.65.1',
    pandas     = '3.0.5',
    sciris     = '3.6.2',
    matplotlib = '3.11.1',
    starsim    = '4.0.0',
)

title: How to contribute
text:
Contributing code
Pull requests should be made against main. Please follow the house style guide (Starsim more or less follows Google’s Python style guide, but with some exceptions), make sure the tests pass, and add an entry to the changelog. The developer guide has the details.
Models and modules are welcome too: a disease, network, or intervention that others could use may belong in the model library, and a complete model may belong in the gallery. Open an issue first to discuss it.
If you have any other questions, please reach out to us: info@starsim.org. Thank you!

title: Developer guide
text:
🧠15% 🤖85%
This guide is for people changing Starsim itself: how to set up, how the code is organized, how it is tested, and how changes are recorded and released. To understand how Starsim works inside, see the architecture section of the user guide.

title: Developer guide
text:
Setting up
Clone the repository and install it in editable mode, with the optional dependencies for testing and the docs:
git clone https://github.com/starsimhub/starsim
cd starsim
pip install -e .[dev]
starsim compile # Optional: compile the Numba kernels now, rather than on the first run
Starsim’s compiled kernels have two copies that give the same numbers bit for bit: Numba’s (the reference, compiled on first use and cached) and Rust’s (compiled ahead of time, so a first run takes no compiling). To build the Rust copy, install Rust and run ./build in starsim/solvers/rust. With the default ss.options.kernels = 'auto', Starsim uses the Rust kernels whenever they have been built. To change a kernel, change the Numba code first, then the Rust copy to match, and run tests/test_kernel_sets.py; starsim/solvers/rust/README.md has the details.

title: Developer guide
text:
How the code is organized
The package is in starsim/. Each file holds one area, named as users meet it (sim.py, people.py, diseases.py, networks.py, interventions.py, fit.py, …); its classes and functions are at the top level (ss.Sim, ss.SIR). The rest is in subfolders:

solvers/: the engines that run declared models (compartmental.py, agents.py), who meets whom in a compartmental run (mixing.py), and how the solver is chosen (choose.py); solvers/backends/ has the compiled kernels (Numba, JAX, and the loader for Rust), and solvers/rust/ the Rust copies.
internals/: how Starsim works under the hood: the graph of a declared module (graph.py), expressions in rates (expressions.py), how a model is shown (display.py), gradients (gradients.py), errors (errors.py), and debugging tools (debugtools.py).
converters/: importers and exporters for other frameworks, and the Starsim 3 migration script (python -m starsim.converters.migrate).
library/: example and reference modules (import starsim.library as ssl), which build on core Starsim but are not part of it.

A compact index of the whole public API is in docs/llms.txt, built by python make_api.py in docs/ (and at starsim.org/v4/llms.txt).

title: Developer guide
text:
Testing
Tests come in three kinds:

Asserted: the test fails if the behavior is wrong (a modifier restores the base value when it ends; reordering competing exits changes nothing).
Recorded: the result is a number or a table rather than a pass or fail (how far an ODE approximation of a network model is from the agents).
Measured against the original: lines of code and run time for a model translated from another framework, compared with that framework.


The suites
The tests are in tests/, in two sets. The core tests (tests/test_*.py, about 300) are quick, cover each feature, and are what ./run_tests runs. The developer tests (tests/devtests/) are the slower and more exhaustive ones: the contracts, inference, gradients, the spec, every error, the importers, and the slower tests of each feature, in a file with the same name as its core file (devtests/test_networks.py has the rest of the network tests). They run every night in CI, and on demand. Most of the tests run on a shared set of small models, the corpus in tests/corpus.py: 23 functions, each returning an unrun sim that runs in seconds, with the solver as a keyword (corpus.sir(solver='binomial')). They range from a plain SIR to cholera with a water reservoir, Ross-Macdonald malaria, two diseases that modify each other, and a TB model with drug resistance.



Suite
What it guards




test_contracts.py
Properties every model and solver must have, over the corpus: people are conserved, the order of competing exits doesn’t matter, the chain binomial, Gillespie and agents agree with the ODE on simple models, random streams are independent, and every guess is marked in describe(). A failure here usually means a silent wrong answer somewhere else.


test_contracts_inference.py
The same for fitting: the JAX log-density equals the sim’s log-likelihood, the particle filter matches direct runs, and each fitting method recovers known values from simulated data.


test_kernels.py, test_gradients.py
The compartmental engine’s paths agree with each other: a whole run with a stepped run, compiled kernels with plain Python, and JAX with the kernels. Gradients agree with finite differences.


test_fast_draws.py, test_jit.py
The exact random draws match their distributions, and the same uniforms give the same draws compiled or not; ss.jit gives the same results as the code run as Python.


test_baselines.py
A standard agent-based sim (two diseases, three networks, births and deaths) gives exactly its recorded results (baseline.yaml); and test_performance_guard fails if any of a set of timed cases is more than 1.5 times slower than its record (perf_guard.yaml).


Feature tests
One file per area (test_transitions.py, test_deliveries.py, test_dimensions.py, …), and test_composition.py for plain NumPy modules beside declared ones.


devtests/io/
Each importer and exporter against the framework it reads or writes. Tests that need R, or the repository of translated examples, are skipped when it isn’t available.


switching/
Thirteen acceptance demos, each in the terms of a framework Starsim is compared with: bring the model in, describe it, fit it, ask a policy question, and run it another way. Each asserts the original’s reference numbers; one that doesn’t pass yet is marked xfail, with the reason.


north_star.py
The north star: a model should never be easier to write without Starsim than with it. For each translated example (kept in a separate repository), a table of lines of model code and run time, original against Starsim, published on the Coming from pages.



The agreement between solvers is layered from exact to statistical. Conservation is checked to 1e-9; the ODE is checked against SciPy and the analytic final size of an SIR; the JAX ODE against the kernels to 1e-9; and the chain binomial, Gillespie and agents against the ODE, as the mean over a few runs at a quarter-day step, within 5% (or a wider tolerance, given with its reason in the test). Solvers and backends has the table of execution paths and the test that pins each one.

Running them
cd tests
./run_tests                                         # The core tests, in test_*.py, in parallel
pytest devtests -n auto                             # The developer tests
pytest devtests/test_contracts.py                   # One suite
STARSIM_SLOW=1 pytest devtests/test_contracts.py             # The agreement test over every compartmental corpus model, not just the simple ones
pytest switching -rxX                               # The switching demos, with the reason for each xfail
pytest test_baselines.py::test_performance_guard    # The performance guard, which is skipped in parallel runs
The performance guard is timing-sensitive, so run it on its own on a quiet machine. After an intended change to results or speed, ./update_baseline.py and ./update_benchmarks.py record the new values, and the change shows up in review as a diff of the .yaml files.



What to run after a change








If you change
These parts see it
Run at least




How states, transitions or rates are declared (transitions.py, expressions.py, graph.py)
Every engine, describe(), the importers’ code, and the exporters
test_transitions.py, test_contracts.py


Parameters, time or units (parameters.py, time.py, dates.py)
Every engine, fitting (which reads bounds and priors), and the spec
test_time.py, test_transitions.py, test_contracts_inference.py


Stratification or strains (dimensions.py, strains.py)
The compartment layout, mixing, agents’ properties, and results by group
test_dimensions.py, test_contracts.py


The compartmental engine or the kernels (solvers/compartmental.py, kernels.py)
All four compartmental solvers, the JAX runs that follow the kernels step for step, and the particle filter
test_kernels.py, test_gradients.py, test_contracts.py


The agent engine or the passes (solvers/agents.py, solvers/backends/passes.py)
Declared models as agents, networks, and births
test_contracts.py, test_baselines.py, test_networks.py


Random draws (distributions.py, solvers/backends/draws.py)
Every stochastic solver, common random numbers, and every recorded result
test_fast_draws.py, test_randomness.py, test_contracts.py::test_streams, test_baselines.py


Solver choice (solvers/choose.py)
What 'auto' picks, the notes, and describe()
test_transitions.py::test_auto, test_contracts.py, test_sim.py


Interventions and modifiers (interventions.py, products.py, connectors.py, solvers/deliveries.py)
Both engines, the loop order, and whether a whole compartmental run is possible
test_deliveries.py, test_interventions.py, test_products.py


The loop or module lifecycle (loop.py, modules.py, sim.py)
Every sim, including modules written as code
test_loop.py, test_sim.py, test_baselines.py


Fitting (fit.py, gradients.py)
sim.fit() and every fitting method
test_contracts_inference.py, test_calibration.py, test_gradients.py


The importers’ code writer or the exporters (converters/core.py, converters/export.py)
Every import, and every export
devtests/io/, switching/


An importer or exporter (converters/)
That framework’s users, and its switching demo
its file in devtests/io/, and its demo in switching/


An error, warning or note
Its message
test_errors.py


Anything on a hot path
Run time
test_baselines.py::test_performance_guard



Files are named by area, so test_networks.py means both tests/test_networks.py and tests/devtests/test_networks.py. When in doubt, run both sets: ./run_tests, then pytest devtests -n auto.


What the tests don’t show

That a model is a good model. Nothing here checks the epidemiology.
That a fit converged. Each fit reports whether it did (fit.converged), and why not.
That an approximation is good enough for your question. Starsim says what was approximated; the judgment is the modeler’s.
That complex models agree across solvers. Only simple ones are asserted to; for the rest, the differences are expected.

title: Developer guide
text:
Building the docs
The docs are built with Quarto; the tutorials and user guide are notebooks, executed when they are built, so their examples always run against the current code. In docs/:
./render                                        # Build the whole site into _site/
./quickrender t3                                # Build one page (any unique part of its name)
./check_notebooks.py tutorials/t3_disease.qmd   # Run pages without building them
./preview                                       # Build and serve, rebuilding pages as they change
./render also builds the API reference from the docstrings (with quartodoc), so a docstring is documentation: write it in the Google style, with an example. Every page has a note at the top of how much of it was written by humans and how much by AI (the authorship: field in its front matter); please keep it current when you change a page.

title: Developer guide
text:
Changelog entries
Every pull request should add an entry to CHANGELOG.md. Changes that alter model output, or that are needed to run an old parameter set with the current version, should be flagged with Migration or Regression.
For any backwards-incompatible change, write the entry so that a human (or an LLM) could perform the migration from the changelog alone. Include the concrete before/after call. For example, instead of:

ss.foo() and ss.bar() are deprecated; use ss.cat() instead.

write:

ss.foo() and ss.bar() have been replaced by ss.cat(). Instead of ss.foo(x=1) and ss.bar(y=2), use e.g. ss.cat(z=[1, 2]).

The extra specificity (which arguments map to which, with example values) is what makes the entry actionable.

title: Developer guide
text:
The design record
The design record is in the lingua_franca_design repository. It has three parts that matter today:

The constitution (docs/admin/constitution.md): the principles every choice is checked against, summarized on the architecture overview.
The spec (docs/design/, files 00 to 19): what the language is and how each part behaves, with a reason for each choice and a list of what was rejected. This section of the docs is a short translation of it.
What was set aside (docs/admin/deferred.md): ideas deferred or decided against, so they aren’t proposed again without new reasons.

When a design changes, the spec is changed first, and then the code to match it. The user documentation is executed when it is built, so its examples run against the current code too.

title: Developer guide
text:
Release procedure
This assumes you’re about to release version 4.1.1.

Merge all pull requests into the release candidate branch (rc4.1.1).
Update the version in version.py from 4.1.1.dev0 to 4.1.1, and update the date.
Mark the pull request ready.
If tests pass, merge.
On the repository page, click “Releases” to go to the releases page.
Click “Draft a new release” on the top right.
In the tag dropdown, enter v4.1.1 as a new tag. Leave the target as main.
Set the release title to v4.1.1.
Generate release notes automatically, and then edit further as required.
Click “Publish release” to deploy, which will update PyPI and build and upload the latest documentation.
Create a new release candidate branch (e.g. rc4.1.2), and make a draft pull request.

title: Developer guide
text:
In the design record

18-conformance.md: every claim of the spec and the test that checks it, and the corpus
12-backends.md: how closely the solvers agree, and why
constitution.md: the principles the tests ultimately serve

title: Code of conduct
text:
Our pledge
In the interest of fostering an open and welcoming environment, we as contributors and maintainers pledge to making participation in our project and our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

title: Code of conduct
text:
Our standards
Examples of behavior that contributes to creating a positive environment include:

Using welcoming and inclusive language
Being respectful of differing viewpoints and experiences
Gracefully accepting constructive criticism
Focusing on what is best for the community
Showing empathy towards other community members

Examples of unacceptable behavior by participants include:

The use of sexualized language or imagery and unwelcome sexual attention or advances
Trolling, insulting/derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
Public or private harassment
Publishing others’ private information, such as a physical or electronic address, without explicit permission
Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

title: Code of conduct
text:
Our responsibilities
Project maintainers are responsible for clarifying the standards of acceptable behavior and are expected to take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any instances of unacceptable behavior.
Project maintainers have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, or to ban temporarily or permanently any contributor for other behaviors that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

title: Code of conduct
text:
Scope
This Code of Conduct applies both within project spaces and in public spaces when an individual is representing the project or its community. Examples of representing a project or community include using an official project e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event. Representation of a project may be further defined and clarified by project maintainers.

title: Code of conduct
text:
Enforcement
Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported by contacting the project team at info@starsim.org. All complaints will be reviewed and investigated and will result in a response that is deemed necessary and appropriate to the circumstances. The project team is obligated to maintain confidentiality with regard to the reporter of an incident. Further details of specific enforcement policies may be posted separately.
Project maintainers who do not follow or enforce the Code of Conduct in good faith may face temporary or permanent repercussions as determined by other members of the project’s leadership.

title: fit
text:
fit
Fitting sims to data: likelihoods, particle filters, samplers, and what sim.fit() runs
These exist so that a model can be fitted, with its uncertainty, in the same way whichever solver runs it. Parameters are chosen by giving them bounds (ss.par), in declared modules or in the parameters of modules written as code. Some methods are for some solvers only: gradients come from JAX, and particle filters need a stochastic compartmental solver.
Imported when it is first used (by ss.fit.X, sim.fit(), or sim.sensitivity()), not by import starsim.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Fit
The result of fitting a sim to its data; see sim.fit()


ModelComparison
The result of comparing models by how well they predict held-out data; see ss.fit.compare_models()


Optimization
The result of allocating spending to maximize (or minimize) a result; see ss.fit.optimize()


ParticleFilter
An estimate of the likelihood of a stochastic sim’s data, from a bootstrap particle filter (see sim.fit() with method='pmcmc')


Swarm
The parameter values of each particle of IF2, iterated filtering, and the rates of the run that they give (see sim.fit() with method=‘if2’)





fit.Fit(
    sim,
    before,
    pars,
    table,
    trials,
    method,
    mismatch,
    mismatch_before,
    measure,
    samples,
    diagnostics,
    converged,
    why,
    scores,
    study=None,
)
The result of fitting a sim to its data; see sim.fit()





Name
Type
Description

ss.Sim
the calibrated sim: a copy of the original with the best-fit values, already run

dict
the best-fit value of each fitted parameter; can be passed to ss.Sim(pars=...)

df

fit.ParticleFilter(sim, likelihood=None, weights=None)
An estimate of the likelihood of a stochastic sim’s data, from a bootstrap particle filter (see sim.fit() with method='pmcmc')
Many runs of the sim (the particles, ss.solvers.Particles) go forward together. At each data point, each is weighted by the likelihood of the data given its results, and when the weights become uneven, the runs are drawn again in proportion to them, so that runs that have strayed from the data are dropped and those that follow it are copied. The product over the data of the mean weight is an unbiased estimate of the likelihood (Andrieu, Doucet & Holenstein 2010), which is what particle MCMC needs.
Each declared disease is filtered on its own, since the diseases of a sim that the kernels run whole do not affect each other, except those tracked jointly (see ss.solvers.Crossing), which are filtered together, as the runs of their program. An outcome is compared with the data as its expected number (rather than drawn, as a run of the sim draws it), as the likelihood would compare it.
Each particle has random numbers of its own, so the particles are shared between threads (see ss.options.threads; one in the workers of ss.parallel() and of a calibration), and the estimate does not depend on how many there are.

fit.Swarm(sim, fitted, set_pars, to_x, z0, sd=0.05, cooling=0.5, n_points=1)
The parameter values of each particle of IF2, iterated filtering, and the rates of the run that they give (see sim.fit() with method=‘if2’)
Each particle carries values of its own, on the unbounded scale that the fit searches on, which a random walk perturbs at the start of each pass of the filter and before each data point, by steps that shrink geometrically, to cooling of their first size after 50 passes (as pomp’s mif2() and camdl do; Ionides et al. 2015). Sample from a posterior by particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings: a random-walk Metropolis sampler on a log-density that is estimated by a particle filter
Since the estimate of the likelihood is unbiased, the chains sample from the exact posterior (Andrieu, Doucet & Holenstein 2010), however noisy it is; more noise only makes them move more slowly. In the warm-up, the proposal’s covariance is learned from the chain so far (Haario et al. 2001), and its scale is tuned toward accepting 15% of proposals (about the best when the estimate is noisy; Sherlock et al. 2015). In the first half of the warm-up, the estimate where the chain is is made again at each step, so that a chain far from the posterior, where the estimate is noisiest, cannot be held by a lucky one.

fit.ParticleFilter(sim, likelihood=None, weights=None)
An estimate of the likelihood of a stochastic sim’s data, from a bootstrap particle filter (see sim.fit() with method='pmcmc')
Many runs of the sim (the particles, ss.solvers.Particles) go forward together. At each data point, each is weighted by the likelihood of the data given its results, and when the weights become uneven, the runs are drawn again in proportion to them, so that runs that have strayed from the data are dropped and those that follow it are copied. The product over the data of the mean weight is an unbiased estimate of the likelihood (Andrieu, Doucet & Holenstein 2010), which is what particle MCMC needs.
Each declared disease is filtered on its own, since the diseases of a sim that the kernels run whole do not affect each other, except those tracked jointly (see ss.solvers.Crossing), which are filtered together, as the runs of their program. An outcome is compared with the data as its expected number (rather than drawn, as a run of the sim draws it), as the likelihood would compare it.
Each particle has random numbers of its own, so the particles are shared between threads (see ss.options.threads; one in the workers of ss.parallel() and of a calibration), and the estimate does not depend on how many there are.

title: internals.loop
text:
internals.loop
The integration loop: the order in which each module’s code runs in each timestep
It exists so that modules with different timesteps run together in one fixed order, which can be inspected with sim.loop.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Loop
Define the integration loop


LoopEntry
One executable event in the integration loop





internals.loop.Loop(sim)
Define the integration loop
The Loop handles the order in which each function is called in the sim. The order is defined in Loop.collect_funcs(), which searches through the sim and collects all methods to call, in order, in the integration loop.
Each type of module is called at a different time. Within each module type, they are called in the order listed. The default loop order is:
1. sim:               advance()        # Move the time to this step's time point
2. sim:               start_step()     # Initialize the sim, including plotting progress
3. all modules:       start_step()     # Initialize the modules, including the random number distribution
4. sim.custom:        step()           # Run any custom modules
5. sim.demographics:  step()           # Update the demographics, including adding new agents
6. sim.diseases:      step_state()     # Update the disease states, e.g. exposed -> infected
7. sim.connectors:    step()           # Run the connectors
8. sim.networks:      step()           # Run the networks, including adding/removing edges
9. sim.interventions: step()           # Run the interventions
10. sim.diseases:     step()           # Run the diseases, including transmission
11. people:           step_die()       # Figure out who died on this timestep
12. people:           update_results() # Update basic state results
13. all modules:      update_results() # Update any results
14. sim.analyzers:    step()           # Run the analyzers
15. all modules:      finish_step()    # Do any final tidying
16. people:           finish_step()    # Clean up dead agents
17. sim:              finish_step()    # Finish the step
One time index holds for every function of a step, in every module: the step from time point k-1 to k is step k, and throughout it sim.ti == k, where its results go (so the first step has ti == 1): self.results.x[self.ti] is this step’s value, in step() as in update_results(), and a time recorded as self.ti in one is self.ti in the other. sim.now is when the step starts, time point k-1, which it reads time-varying inputs and dates at. At the first time point (ti == 0, now the start) there is no step: only the results of the start are recorded (people’s and every module’s but the interventions’, which have done nothing yet), and the analyzers run (at_start).

Type
Description
Default

Sim
the sim to run (usually made by the sim itself)
required

The list of LoopEntry events in execution order; made the first time it is needed, since a sim run by the kernels in one call never needs it

internals.loop.Loop(sim)
Define the integration loop
The Loop handles the order in which each function is called in the sim. The order is defined in Loop.collect_funcs(), which searches through the sim and collects all methods to call, in order, in the integration loop.
Each type of module is called at a different time. Within each module type, they are called in the order listed. The default loop order is:
1. sim:               advance()        # Move the time to this step's time point
2. sim:               start_step()     # Initialize the sim, including plotting progress
3. all modules:       start_step()     # Initialize the modules, including the random number distribution
4. sim.custom:        step()           # Run any custom modules
5. sim.demographics:  step()           # Update the demographics, including adding new agents
6. sim.diseases:      step_state()     # Update the disease states, e.g. exposed -> infected
7. sim.connectors:    step()           # Run the connectors
8. sim.networks:      step()           # Run the networks, including adding/removing edges
9. sim.interventions: step()           # Run the interventions
10. sim.diseases:     step()           # Run the diseases, including transmission
11. people:           step_die()       # Figure out who died on this timestep
12. people:           update_results() # Update basic state results
13. all modules:      update_results() # Update any results
14. sim.analyzers:    step()           # Run the analyzers
15. all modules:      finish_step()    # Do any final tidying
16. people:           finish_step()    # Clean up dead agents
17. sim:              finish_step()    # Finish the step
One time index holds for every function of a step, in every module: the step from time point k-1 to k is step k, and throughout it sim.ti == k, where its results go (so the first step has ti == 1): self.results.x[self.ti] is this step’s value, in step() as in update_results(), and a time recorded as self.ti in one is self.ti in the other. sim.now is when the step starts, time point k-1, which it reads time-varying inputs and dates at. At the first time point (ti == 0, now the start) there is no step: only the results of the start are recorded (people’s and every module’s but the interventions’, which have done nothing yet), and the analyzers run (at_start).

internals.graph
Not for the user: the graph of one module: its states, transitions, and parameters, collected, named, completed with defaults (each guess recorded), and checked
It exists as the one description of a declared model, which every solver runs and describe() shows, so that a model can be written once.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared modules

The states and transitions of one module

    module,
    args=None,
    members=None,
    init_prev=None,
    init=None,
    init_n=None,
    first=None,
    names=None,
)
The states and transitions of one module
The graph is built when the module is constructed. It names everything, works out which states are people and which transitions are transmissions (from their rates), turns inline values into named parameters, and checks the result. Every guess is recorded, in graph.guessed and in the guessed of each state and transition.

The states and transitions of one module
The graph is built when the module is constructed. title: internals.conditions
text:
internals.conditions
Conditions: who something applies to
A condition is written against the attributes of the people and modules in the sim, e.g. (ppl.age > 65) & ~sir.vaccinated. Written before the sim exists, it is lazy: an expression that is evaluated each time it is needed during a run, on agents in an agent-based run and on groups in a compartmental one. A function of the sim does the same job, for anything the operators cannot say.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Cond
A lazy condition: an unevaluated expression over the arrays of the people and modules in a sim


Event
Something that happens to people at a moment: going through a transition (tr), one branch of it





internals.conditions.Cond(op, *args)
A lazy condition: an unevaluated expression over the arrays of the people and modules in a sim
Conditions are not usually created directly: they are what comparisons and logical operators give when used on arrays that have not been initialized yet, on declared states, and on stratifications.











Name
Type
Description
Default




op
str
the operation: a leaf (‘people’, ‘state’, ‘dim’, ‘kind’, ‘array’, ‘incidence’, ‘event’, ‘memory’, ‘move’), an operator, ‘~’, or ‘isin’
required


args
list
the operands
()






ppl = ss.People(n_agents=10_000)
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.3*I, recovery=ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10))
eligible = (ppl.age > 65) & sir.S






Name
Description




args
The operands; a dimension given as a product (vx.held) is named when it is read, since a product can be named after the condition is written


count
For an event: how many times it has happened to each person, e.g. screening.count >= 2


enter
For a set of states (A \| B): the event of entering it from outside it (moves within the set are not entering it)


ever
For an event (e.g. screening.positive): whether it has happened to each person, as a condition


exit
For a set of states (A \| B): the event of leaving it for a state outside it


since
For an event: the time since it last happened to each person (infinite if never), e.g. cytology.since >= ss.years(5)


time
For a set of states (A \| B): the time since entering it from outside it, in the sim’s unit (moves within the set do not reset it; NaN outside it)


uids
The agents the condition holds for now, in a sim that is running or has run (agents only): e.g. sim.interventions.screening.ever.uids, everyone ever screened (the sim’s copy of the delivery, not the one given, which the sim copies)


values
In a running sim, as agents: the condition’s value for each agent alive, in the order of sim.people.auids (as ss.Arr.values)









Name
Description




arith
Arithmetic on a condition: with an expression (a parameter, a state’s count), a typed value (ss.peryear(0.02)), or a value by level or in time (ss.by, ss.timeseries), it is an expression for a rate, e.g. b*ss.ppl.age; otherwise a condition


clip
The value kept between two values, as an expression for a rate (np.clip(0.5*ss.ppl.age, 0, 1) calls this)


compare
A comparison: with an expression (e.g. a fitted ss.par), an expression that is 1 or 0, for a rate; otherwise a condition


eval
Evaluate the condition; ctx supplies the value of each leaf (see Selector)


evaluate_in
For cond[uids] and cond.values: the value for each agent (by UID), in the sim of a module the condition reads


isin
Whether the value is one of some values, as a condition, e.g. ppl.age.isin([1, 2])





internals.conditions.Cond.arith(op, a, b)
Arithmetic on a condition: with an expression (a parameter, a state’s count), a typed value (ss.peryear(0.02)), or a value by level or in time (ss.by, ss.timeseries), it is an expression for a rate, e.g. b*ss.ppl.age; otherwise a condition



internals.conditions.Cond.clip(min=None, max=None, out=None)
The value kept between two values, as an expression for a rate (np.clip(0.5*ss.ppl.age, 0, 1) calls this)











Name
Type
Description
Default




min
float
the lowest value; if None, no lower limit
None


max
float
the highest value; if None, no upper limit
None


out
None
not used; present since np.clip() passes it
None







internals.conditions.Cond.compare(op, other)
A comparison: with an expression (e.g. a fitted ss.par), an expression that is 1 or 0, for a rate; otherwise a condition



internals.conditions.Cond.eval(ctx)
Evaluate the condition; ctx supplies the value of each leaf (see Selector)



internals.conditions.Cond.evaluate_in(sim_only=False)
For cond[uids] and cond.values: the value for each agent (by UID), in the sim of a module the condition reads



internals.conditions.Cond.isin(values)
Whether the value is one of some values, as a condition, e.g. ppl.age.isin([1, 2])











Name
Type
Description
Default




values
list
the values
required









internals.conditions.Event(kind, obj, dst=None)
Something that happens to people at a moment: going through a transition (tr), one branch of it (tr.to(B)), or entering or leaving a state or a set of states (X.enter, (A | B).exit), where entering a set means arriving from outside it
An event is a condition, true for the agents it happened to from the moment they moved until the same point in the next step; it can be given to where= or ss.on(); and in a running sim, .uids are those agents.





Name
Type
Description
Default




kind
str
‘tr’, ‘to’, ‘enter’, or ‘exit’
required


obj
Transition / list
the transition; or the states, as ss.States or (module, name) pairs
required


dst
State
for ‘to’, the destination
None









Name
Description




names
For entering or leaving: the names of the states


uids
The agents the event happened to, in a running sim









Name
Description




spec
What the engine is asked for: see ss.solvers.Agents.event_uids()





internals.conditions.Event.spec()
What the engine is asked for: see ss.solvers.Agents.event_uids()









Name
Description




state
A state of a module by its path, resolved when the condition is evaluated: for a module made before the others exist





internals.conditions.state(path)
A state of a module by its path, resolved when the condition is evaluated: for a module made before the others exist
It is a condition (the people in the state), and .enter and .exit are its events, as for a declared state. A path to a transition ('ng.cure') is the condition of having gone through it.











Name
Type
Description
Default




path
str
the module and the state, e.g. 'hpv18.X'
required






canceled = (S + P + C + L) >> Z @ ss.on(ss.state('hpv18.X') | ss.state('hpv31.X'))
seek = ss.treat(drug, where=ss.state('ng.C').enter) # For a module made from a string

title: internals.debugtools
text:
internals.debugtools
Tools for debugging and profiling Starsim runs: sim.profile(), detailed diagnostics, and mock objects for testing a module without a sim
They exist so that a slow or surprising run can be looked into without changing the model.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules

title: interop
text:
interop
Import models from other frameworks
ss.import_from(filename, format=...) reads another framework’s model into a sim; see v4_design/design/16-interop.md. Each importer reads its format into an ss.io.Source, and ss.io.build() writes that as Starsim code by the same rules for every format (ss.io.write()) and runs the code to make the sim: the code is kept in sim.imported.code, how each rate was read is printed, and what could not be translated is listed as ss.errors.ImportIncomplete and kept in sim.imported.





Name
Description




Code
Python to write as it is, for a value an importer gives that code_value() does not write, e.g. a network


Source
A model read from another framework, before it is built into a sim





interop.Code()
Python to write as it is, for a value an importer gives that code_value() does not write, e.g. a network



interop.Source(name, format, file=None)
A model read from another framework, before it is built into a sim
An importer fills this in from the source, then build() writes it as Starsim code (write()) and runs the code to make the sim. Every rate is an expression in Python syntax, in which a state’s name means the number of people in it.











Name
Type
Description
Default




name
str
the model’s name
required


format
str
the format it was read from, e.g. ‘emulsion’
required


file
str
the file it was read from, if any
None









Name
Description




add_flow
A flow between states


add_outcome
A reported quantity: a share of a flow, or of another outcome, with a delay (see ss.outcome)


add_par
A parameter: a number in the sim’s unit, maybe with bounds and a prior (ss.Dist) for calibration


add_state
A state; init is a number of people


skip
Something in the source that was not translated


stratify
A stratification of the disease, as the arguments to ss.Disease.stratify()

interop.to_hub(
    msim,
    targets,
    origin_date=None,
    by=None,
    every='week',
    output_type='quantile',
    quantiles=hub_quantiles,
    location=None,
)
The runs of a MultiSim as a submission to a hub (in the hubverse format): each target, by scenario, location, and period
Each scenario (the label of its sim) is its own scenario_id, and the periods are counted from origin_date. A target’s name says what it is: one starting “cum” is the total since the origin date, one starting “peak size” is the largest value of a period (with no horizon), and any other is a flow’s total over each period, or a count at its end.





Name
Type
Description
Default




msim
ss.MultiSim
the runs
required


targets
dict
the hub’s name (or a list of names) for each result, e.g. dict(incidHosp=['inc hosp', 'cum hosp', 'peak size hosp'])
required


origin_date
date
the date the periods are counted from (default: the start of the runs); for runs without dates, a time, which the origin_date column then holds
None


by
str
the dimension whose levels are the locations (default: one location, the total)
None


every
str
the period: ‘day’ or ‘week’ (of the sim’s steps, which must then be days)
'week'


output_type
str / list
‘quantile’ (of the runs of each scenario), ‘sample’ (each run, by its position in its scenario), or both
'quantile'


quantiles
list
the quantiles (default: the 23 that the US hubs ask for)
hub_quantiles


location
str
the name of the single location, if by is not given
None



Returns a long dataframe with columns origin_date, scenario_id, location, target, horizon, output_type, output_type_id, and value.
Example:
msim = ss.parallel(baseline=s1, lockdown=s2, n_runs=20)
hub = ss.io.to_hub(msim, targets=dict(infection=['inc inf', 'cum inf']), origin_date='2020-03-01', by='patch')




interop.write(sources, **kwargs)
The Starsim code of one or more models read from another framework
Each source becomes a declared disease (ss.Disease), with its parameters, states, and transitions as variables; the code ends with the sim (sim = ss.Sim(...)). It says where the model came from, how each rate was read, and what was not translated. This is the code build() runs, kept as sim.imported.code.











Name
Type
Description
Default




sources
Source / list | the model, as read by an importer, or several (e.g. one for each state machine) | required |


kwargs
dict
passed to ss.Sim(), after each source’s config
{}














Name
Type
Description






An sc.objdict of the code, how each flow was read (choices, a line each), and what was guessed about each transition (guessed, by disease and transition)

title: interventions
text:
interventions
Interventions, which change the course of a sim during a run
Interventions typically include things like testing, treatment, and vaccination. A delivery (ss.Delivery, and ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat()) gives a product to the people chosen, and exists so that the same intervention can be written once and run under any solver. It also works with a disease written as code, as agents.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Delivery
Deliver a product, or move people along a stratification; see ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat()


Intervention
Base class for interventions.


screen
Deliver a diagnostic test; see ss.Delivery for the arguments


treat
Deliver a treatment; see ss.Delivery for the arguments


vaccinate
Deliver a vaccine; see ss.Delivery for the arguments





interventions.Delivery(
    what=None,
    who=None,
    move=None,
    increment=None,
    start=None,
    stop=None,
    at=None,
    interval=None,
    where=None,
    coverage=None,
    capacity=None,
    when=None,
    deliver=None,
    trace=None,
    priority=None,
    queue=None,
    delay=None,
    disease=None,
    at_age=None,
    strain=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Deliver a product, or move people along a stratification; see ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat()
Who receives it is who=: a condition on people (who is eligible), or an event (the people it happened to); where= is anything else it depends on, including an event, and when= a condition on time. With an event in who= or where=, delivery is triggered: it reaches the people the event happened to on this step who meet the conditions. Otherwise, with at or interval, delivery happens in rounds, and in each round every eligible person is offered the product once; and with neither, delivery is routine: each person is offered the product once, at the first step on which they are eligible.
A delivery is an event too (the people it reached on the step), and so is each outcome of it (a test’s positive and negative, a cure’s cured, failed, and unneeded): a follow-up is a step of its own, triggered by one (ss.treat(drug, who=screening.positive)), and runs after it in the same step. Each event remembers per person whether (.ever), how often (.count), and how long ago (.since) it happened, including on this step once the delivery has run. With no product and no move, a delivery is a step people attend (e.g. a clinic visit): its event is who attended, which several steps can take. delivery.reached() is the UIDs of the people it reached on the step (agents only).
Its methods are how it runs as agents; in a compartmental run, what differs is delivery.in_compartments (see ss.solvers.CompartmentalDelivery). A product whose effect is code of your own is an ss.Product with an administer(uids) method.
Note: CRN safe as agents.





Name
Type
Description
Default




what
ss.Product
what is delivered: an ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, or ss.Treatment, or a product written as code (an ss.Product with an administer()), which any of them can give (also the first argument); ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat() instead take the product’s own keywords and make it, e.g. ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, ...)
None


who
Cond / event
who receives it, which must choose people or compartments: a condition on them (e.g. ss.ppl.age < 5), an event (e.g. sir.infection, screening.positive, or a delivery), or a combination with & and \| (an event \| a condition raises, being neither triggered nor routine); a condition on the population or a function goes in where=
None


move
Transition / dict / StrainMove
instead of a product, a move between two states for the people reached, written with the states, e.g. move=S >> V (a one-off campaign), or from any of several (move=U + P + W >> P: a re-dose, which restarts the time in P of those already there); or the level of a stratification they move to, e.g. move=dict(vaccinated=True), or from one level to another, move=dict(risk=('low', 'high')); or a change of strains, e.g. move=DS >> RIF
None


strain
str / Strain
with move= into a state where people carry a strain (e.g. move=S >> E), the strain they arrive with: the import of a strain on a date, e.g. ss.Delivery(move=S >> E, strain='alpha', at=['2021-01-01'], capacity=20)
None


increment
str / dict
instead of a product, a counter that goes up for the people reached: its name, which adds 1 (increment='doses'), or a dict of the amount for each (dict(doses=2))
None


at_age
dur / float
routine delivery to people as they reach this age (a bare number is in years), e.g. at_age=ss.months(9); not to people already past it when delivery starts, nor (as agents) to those who arrive past it later, e.g. immigrants. As compartments, people reach it by aging into the age group it starts, so the sim needs age groups with an edge at the age (an error otherwise)
None


start
date / float
when delivery starts, within the sim (default: the start of the sim); a number is a calendar year from 1900 on (e.g. 2030), and otherwise a time in the sim’s unit (in a sim with dates, that long after the start)
None


stop
date / float
when delivery stops (default: never); a stop after the end of the sim never stops it
None


at
list
deliver in rounds at these times (a campaign), each within the sim: dates, or numbers, read as start is
None


interval
dur
deliver in rounds this far apart, between start and stop
None


where
Cond / event / str / func
anything else it depends on, joined to who= with &: a condition on the population (e.g. sir.I.n > 1000), an event, which triggers it (e.g. where=sir.infection, or a transition by its path, where='sir.infection', found when the sim is initialized), a condition on people, or a function of the sim
None


coverage
float
the fraction of eligible people reached; also ss.by(...), a function of the sim returning a probability per person, or a typed rate or probability (e.g. ss.perday(0.1), ss.probperyear(0.5)): the chance over the step or the round (and, for routine delivery, offered at every step to those eligible)
None


capacity
float
the number that can be delivered: a number per round (or per step, for delivery on events or by a function), or a rate (e.g. ss.peryear(50_000)), which routine delivery needs; a rate in rounds gives what accrues between them
None


priority
Cond / list / Expr / func
who is served first when not everyone can be (under capacity=): a condition, or a list of them served in order (all of the first, then the second); a score, highest first: an expression (e.g. -hiv.cd4, the lowest CD4 first) or a function of the sim (or of (sim, uids), agents only); or a list of conditions and scores, each breaking the ties of the ones before (e.g. [due, ss.ppl.age], those due first, and among them the oldest); other ties are broken at random
None


queue
bool / dur
what happens to people not served for lack of capacity (agents only): None (the default), they are lost; True, they wait until served; a duration, they wait at most that long, and those still waiting then are the outcome never_ran. Those waiting are served before anyone newly reached in their class (longest first), and leave the queue if they stop being eligible (left)
None


delay
dur / Dist
for a triggered step, the time from the trigger to delivery (agents only): a duration, or a distribution of durations, drawn per person (e.g. ss.uniform(ss.months(1), ss.months(8))). The people triggered receive it then if they are eligible then (who=’s condition, and coverage=, are applied when it is due); someone waiting is not triggered again
None


trace
str / Network / list
contact tracing: deliver to the contacts, in this network (or these), of the people that the event in who= selects, instead of to them; the condition and coverage= then apply to the contacts. Agents only, since only networks know who someone’s contacts are. A network with memory= also gives the partnerships of that long ago that have ended (e.g. ss.DegreeNet(..., memory=ss.months(12)), to notify the partners of the past year)
None


when
func
deliver only on the steps where this function of the timeline returns True (e.g. lambda t: t.ti % 7 == 0); a condition on anything but time goes in where=
None


deliver
func
a function of the sim returning who receives it this step (UIDs, or a number per group in a compartmental run); replaces where, coverage, and the rounds
None


disease
str
the disease the product acts on (default: the only one)
None


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the variable the delivery is assigned to
None


label
str
a human-readable name
None






# Seeding: three people, chosen from everyone susceptible, infected every 30 days for ten years
seeds = ss.Delivery(move=S >> I, capacity=3, start=ss.days(30), interval=ss.days(30), stop=ss.years(10))

# A move along a stratification for 70% of people in two rounds, e.g. a campaign that leaves a mark
rollout = ss.Delivery(move=dict(vaccinated=True), coverage=0.7, at=[5, 30], who=~sir.vaccinated)

# Each round of a campaign adds a dose (with sim.stratify(doses=[0, 1, 2, 3]))
campaign = ss.Delivery(increment='doses', coverage=0.6, at=[2025, 2026, 2027])

# A test, and a treatment of those who test positive, as two steps
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.95, who=ss.ppl.age > 30, coverage=0.4, interval=7)
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.95, who=screening.positive, coverage=0.8)

title: interventions
text:
Name
Description




Delivery
Deliver a product, or move people along a stratification; see ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat()


Intervention
Base class for interventions.


screen
Deliver a diagnostic test; see ss.Delivery for the arguments


treat
Deliver a treatment; see ss.Delivery for the arguments


vaccinate
Deliver a vaccine; see ss.Delivery for the arguments





interventions.Delivery(
    what=None,
    who=None,
    move=None,
    increment=None,
    start=None,
    stop=None,
    at=None,
    interval=None,
    where=None,
    coverage=None,
    capacity=None,
    when=None,
    deliver=None,
    trace=None,
    priority=None,
    queue=None,
    delay=None,
    disease=None,
    at_age=None,
    strain=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Deliver a product, or move people along a stratification; see ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat()
Who receives it is who=: a condition on people (who is eligible), or an event (the people it happened to); where= is anything else it depends on, including an event, and when= a condition on time. With an event in who= or where=, delivery is triggered: it reaches the people the event happened to on this step who meet the conditions. Otherwise, with at or interval, delivery happens in rounds, and in each round every eligible person is offered the product once; and with neither, delivery is routine: each person is offered the product once, at the first step on which they are eligible.
A delivery is an event too (the people it reached on the step), and so is each outcome of it (a test’s positive and negative, a cure’s cured, failed, and unneeded): a follow-up is a step of its own, triggered by one (ss.treat(drug, who=screening.positive)), and runs after it in the same step. Each event remembers per person whether (.ever), how often (.count), and how long ago (.since) it happened, including on this step once the delivery has run. With no product and no move, a delivery is a step people attend (e.g. a clinic visit): its event is who attended, which several steps can take. delivery.reached() is the UIDs of the people it reached on the step (agents only).
Its methods are how it runs as agents; in a compartmental run, what differs is delivery.in_compartments (see ss.solvers.CompartmentalDelivery). A product whose effect is code of your own is an ss.Product with an administer(uids) method.
Note: CRN safe as agents.





Name
Type
Description
Default




what
ss.Product
what is delivered: an ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, or ss.Treatment, or a product written as code (an ss.Product with an administer()), which any of them can give (also the first argument); ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat() instead take the product’s own keywords and make it, e.g. ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, ...)
None


who
Cond / event
who receives it, which must choose people or compartments: a condition on them (e.g. ss.ppl.age < 5), an event (e.g. sir.infection, screening.positive, or a delivery), or a combination with & and \| (an event \| a condition raises, being neither triggered nor routine); a condition on the population or a function goes in where=
None


move
Transition / dict / StrainMove
instead of a product, a move between two states for the people reached, written with the states, e.g. move=S >> V (a one-off campaign), or from any of several (move=U + P + W >> P: a re-dose, which restarts the time in P of those already there); or the level of a stratification they move to, e.g. move=dict(vaccinated=True), or from one level to another, move=dict(risk=('low', 'high')); or a change of strains, e.g. move=DS >> RIF
None


strain
str / Strain
with move= into a state where people carry a strain (e.g. move=S >> E), the strain they arrive with: the import of a strain on a date, e.g. ss.Delivery(move=S >> E, strain='alpha', at=['2021-01-01'], capacity=20)
None


increment
str / dict
instead of a product, a counter that goes up for the people reached: its name, which adds 1 (increment='doses'), or a dict of the amount for each (dict(doses=2))
None


at_age
dur / float
routine delivery to people as they reach this age (a bare number is in years), e.g. at_age=ss.months(9); not to people already past it when delivery starts, nor (as agents) to those who arrive past it later, e.g. immigrants. As compartments, people reach it by aging into the age group it starts, so the sim needs age groups with an edge at the age (an error otherwise)
None


start
date / float
when delivery starts, within the sim (default: the start of the sim); a number is a calendar year from 1900 on (e.g. 2030), and otherwise a time in the sim’s unit (in a sim with dates, that long after the start)
None


stop
date / float
when delivery stops (default: never); a stop after the end of the sim never stops it
None


at
list
deliver in rounds at these times (a campaign), each within the sim: dates, or numbers, read as start is
None


interval
dur
deliver in rounds this far apart, between start and stop
None


where
Cond / event / str / func
anything else it depends on, joined to who= with &: a condition on the population (e.g. sir.I.n > 1000), an event, which triggers it (e.g. where=sir.infection, or a transition by its path, where='sir.infection', found when the sim is initialized), a condition on people, or a function of the sim
None


coverage
float
the fraction of eligible people reached; also ss.by(...), a function of the sim returning a probability per person, or a typed rate or probability (e.g. ss.perday(0.1), ss.probperyear(0.5)): the chance over the step or the round (and, for routine delivery, offered at every step to those eligible)
None


capacity
float
the number that can be delivered: a number per round (or per step, for delivery on events or by a function), or a rate (e.g. ss.peryear(50_000)), which routine delivery needs; a rate in rounds gives what accrues between them
None


priority
Cond / list / Expr / func
who is served first when not everyone can be (under capacity=): a condition, or a list of them served in order (all of the first, then the second); a score, highest first: an expression (e.g. -hiv.cd4, the lowest CD4 first) or a function of the sim (or of (sim, uids), agents only); or a list of conditions and scores, each breaking the ties of the ones before (e.g. [due, ss.ppl.age], those due first, and among them the oldest); other ties are broken at random
None


queue
bool / dur
what happens to people not served for lack of capacity (agents only): None (the default), they are lost; True, they wait until served; a duration, they wait at most that long, and those still waiting then are the outcome never_ran. Those waiting are served before anyone newly reached in their class (longest first), and leave the queue if they stop being eligible (left)
None


delay
dur / Dist
for a triggered step, the time from the trigger to delivery (agents only): a duration, or a distribution of durations, drawn per person (e.g. ss.uniform(ss.months(1), ss.months(8))). The people triggered receive it then if they are eligible then (who=’s condition, and coverage=, are applied when it is due); someone waiting is not triggered again
None


trace
str / Network / list
contact tracing: deliver to the contacts, in this network (or these), of the people that the event in who= selects, instead of to them; the condition and coverage= then apply to the contacts. Agents only, since only networks know who someone’s contacts are. A network with memory= also gives the partnerships of that long ago that have ended (e.g. ss.DegreeNet(..., memory=ss.months(12)), to notify the partners of the past year)
None


when
func
deliver only on the steps where this function of the timeline returns True (e.g. lambda t: t.ti % 7 == 0); a condition on anything but time goes in where=
None


deliver
func
a function of the sim returning who receives it this step (UIDs, or a number per group in a compartmental run); replaces where, coverage, and the rounds
None


disease
str
the disease the product acts on (default: the only one)
None


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the variable the delivery is assigned to
None


label
str
a human-readable name
None






# Seeding: three people, chosen from everyone susceptible, infected every 30 days for ten years
seeds = ss.Delivery(move=S >> I, capacity=3, start=ss.days(30), interval=ss.days(30), stop=ss.years(10))

# A move along a stratification for 70% of people in two rounds, e.g. a campaign that leaves a mark
rollout = ss.Delivery(move=dict(vaccinated=True), coverage=0.7, at=[5, 30], who=~sir.vaccinated)

# Each round of a campaign adds a dose (with sim.stratify(doses=[0, 1, 2, 3]))
campaign = ss.Delivery(increment='doses', coverage=0.6, at=[2025, 2026, 2027])

# A test, and a treatment of those who test positive, as two steps
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.95, who=ss.ppl.age > 30, coverage=0.4, interval=7)
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.95, who=screening.positive, coverage=0.8)

delay= is the step’s, the time from its trigger to the test, as for any step; the time from the test to its result is the test’s (ss.Diagnostic(delay=...)).

solvers.deliveries
Not for the user: deliveries in a compartmental run
ss.Delivery is the one class for deliveries, and its methods are how it runs as agents. In a compartmental run, a delivery also makes a CompartmentalDelivery (delivery.in_compartments), which holds what only that needs: a selection is the share of the people in each state and group, so who is reached, served, moved, cured, or tested is a share of each, and moving them moves shares of the engine’s compartments between groups, carrying the events of the step along. title: library.econ
text:
library.econ
Health economics: the costs of a sim, disability-adjusted life years, discounting, and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules
Costs are not part of every sim, so these live in the library rather than in core Starsim: ssl.Costs adds a sim’s costs up as results, ssl.DALYs does the same for disability-adjusted life years, ssl.discount() discounts a result over time, and ssl.ICER compares the costs and effects of scenarios, after they have run or as a sim runs.





Name
Description




Costs
The costs of a sim, from its results, with their total


DALYs
The disability-adjusted life years of a sim: the years lived with disability, plus the years of life lost


ICER
Compare the costs and effects of scenarios: incremental cost-effectiveness ratios





library.econ.Costs(
    unit_costs=None,
    fixed=0,
    start=None,
    deliveries=True,
    **kwargs,
)
The costs of a sim, from its results, with their total
Each delivery made with a cost= (e.g. ss.vaccinate(..., cost=5)) already has a cost result; this adds them up, along with a cost for each event of any other result (e.g. care for each infection) and a fixed cost per year. Every cost is a result of this analyzer, named after where it came from, and total is their sum.

Type
Description
Default




unit_costs
dict
the cost of each event of a result, by the result’s path, e.g. {'measles.infection': 50} for $50 of care for each infection, or {'routine.delivered': 5} for $5 a dose of a delivery made without its own cost=
None

float
a cost per year that does not depend on any result, such as running a program (staff, cold chain, training)
0

float / str
when the fixed cost starts, read as any time is (see ss.connectors.to_time(): a number from 1900 on is a year; default: the start of the sim)
None

bool
whether to include the cost result of every module that has one
True






import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

vx = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, coverage=0.5, where=ss.ppl.age < 5, interval=ss.years(1), cost=5)
costs = ssl.Costs(unit_costs={'sir.infection': 50}, fixed=1000)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sir', networks='random', interventions=vx, analyzers=costs)
sim.run()
sim.results.costs.plot()
print(sim.results.costs.total.sum())

library.econ.ICER(
    sims=None,
    outcome='dalys.dalys',
    cost='costs.total',
    baseline=None,
    rate=0,
    start=None,
    window=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Compare the costs and effects of scenarios: incremental cost-effectiveness ratios
Each scenario’s cost and outcome are totaled (discounted if rate is given), and the outcome averted is that of the baseline less the scenario’s. The scenarios are ordered by cost, and each is compared with the next cheaper one that isn’t dominated. A scenario is dominated if it costs more and averts no more than a cheaper one, and extendedly dominated if a mix of two others would avert more for the same cost. With several runs of each scenario, their means are compared.
This works in two ways. After the scenarios have run, give them to ssl.ICER(), and read icer.df. Or add it to a sim as an analyzer, after ssl.Costs and ssl.DALYs: the sim then counts as one more scenario, compared at each step with the scenarios given over the same period, so that what runs in the sim can act on the comparison, for example an intervention that follows icer.best(wtp=1000).

msim = ss.parallel({'Nothing': base, 'Vaccine': base.new(interventions=vx)}, n_runs=20)
icer = ssl.ICER(msim, rate=0.03, start=2010)
icer.df

library.econ.ICER(
    sims=None,
    outcome='dalys.dalys',
    cost='costs.total',
    baseline=None,
    rate=0,
    start=None,
    window=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Compare the costs and effects of scenarios: incremental cost-effectiveness ratios
Each scenario’s cost and outcome are totaled (discounted if rate is given), and the outcome averted is that of the baseline less the scenario’s. The scenarios are ordered by cost, and each is compared with the next cheaper one that isn’t dominated. A scenario is dominated if it costs more and averts no more than a cheaper one, and extendedly dominated if a mix of two others would avert more for the same cost. With several runs of each scenario, their means are compared.
This works in two ways. After the scenarios have run, give them to ssl.ICER(), and read icer.df. Or add it to a sim as an analyzer, after ssl.Costs and ssl.DALYs: the sim then counts as one more scenario, compared at each step with the scenarios given over the same period, so that what runs in the sim can act on the comparison, for example an intervention that follows icer.best(wtp=1000).
