title: solvers.compartmental
text:
solvers.compartmental
Not for the user: the compartmental engine: a declared model run as groups of people (ode, binomial, gillespie, and tau-leaping)
It exists so that a model with nothing per person can run faster than as agents, from the same declaration.
Used with: compartments; declared modules





Name
Description




Compartmental
Runs a graph as compartments: deterministically (ode) or stochastically





solvers.compartmental.Compartmental(module, sim, solver=None)
Runs a graph as compartments: deterministically (ode) or stochastically (binomial, gillespie, or tau, the exact solver’s fallback for long runs)
It exists so that the deterministic and stochastic forms share one engine.
The states are expanded into compartments (one per branch and sub-stage) and the transitions into a flat list of flows, each with a source compartment, a rate, and the compartments it feeds. Every solver steps the same list of flows.





Name
Description




engines
The engines whose people its program holds, as a crossing’s: this one


owner
What holds the people and the program that runs them: this engine, or the crossing its disease is tracked jointly in (see ss.solvers.Crossing), whose program steps them all


shared
Whether this engine moves people in ways that belong to the sim rather than to the module (aging, relocating, the movement register): in a crossing, only one does (see ss.solvers.Crossing.lead), since they all see the same people


smooth
Whether any parameter varies smoothly in time (not as a step function), so is taken at the middle of each step


transfer_index
The position of each transfer among the flows of a whole run (after the transitions, with the other movers)









Name
Description




add_per_births
After a step: the children of those who went through a transition with births driven by its flow (ss.birth(per=)), n for each, in the youngest groups of their parents’ place


aging_rates
The rate per year at which people age out of each age group (but the last): the density of people in the year below


apart_shares
For several non-exponential dwell times out of a state, each for other people (where=): the share of each group that enters each one’s track, 1 for the one it has (the first, if none)


arrive
Add an amount to a state, split between its tracks; with before=True, as if they arrived a step before (people infectious at the start, who have been so for the first step, as agents date them), so one slot along a conveyor


at_home
Whether a time share between places (a sparse array) keeps everyone at home, as np.allclose(share, np.eye(P)) would say, without forming either


at_middle
Take values that vary smoothly in time at the middle of the step, which runs from time point ti-1 to ti, as tables() does, so that a stepped run takes the same values as a whole one


attr
An attribute in a compartmental run: a trait is the mean of its distribution, as a parameter that is a distribution is (see trait_mean())


backfill_burnin
A module’s people who start part way through (ss.Pregnancy(burnin=True): see its burnin_plan()): each group’s


binomial_substeps
The substeps the chain-binomial solver takes in each step, from the fastest total rate out of a compartment of people at the start (see substeps())


birth_map
Where the children of the people in each group are born (rows to columns): the youngest group of each dimension, by the split of the others, in their parents’ place


births_of
The engine and inflow of each declared module with an ss.birth(per=) of the same transition as tr (this module’s own first)


branch_where
Whether a transition is a branch out of each of its sources whose where= is on states and strata, so closes it at entry (see branch_mult()) rather than changing its rate


build
Lay out the compartments (after init_dims()): the dwell times, the protection between strains, and the compartments and flows; raises a CapabilityError for what has no compartmental form yet


build_layout
Expand the states into compartments and the transitions into flows


call_uids
A function that takes uids, which a compartmental run does not have (see Agents.call_uids())


certain
The name of a transition with an infinite rate (a probability of 1 over the period) at the start, which the kernels take as everyone moving at once (see ss.kernels.certain()), and which JAX and the exact solver by place do not; or None


changes
The rate of change of each compartment from new infections (new=True: arrivals only), or from every other flow; see next_generation()


clock
A clock, which a compartmental run does not keep (see Agents.clock())


collect
The results of many runs, from the number in each state and the flow along each transition and mover


constant_transfer
Whether a transfer’s rate holds for the whole run, so its mover can be set once before it (see run_args()): a rate or duration of plain values, with no modifiers


count_deaths
For a split between states and ss.null (with no ss.stay): those who died are its flow less those who went to a state, so the two agree in each run; flows are by flow along the axis before the last (the groups)


count_weighted
A weighted count ((ss.by(biting=w)*I).n, A.n_trans): the people in each state and group counted by the group’s weight (and infectiousness), in the same place


coverage
A product’s coverage (itn.coverage): the share of the people in the same place who hold it, by what each level of holding it counts as (see ss.expressions.Coverage.level_weights())


current
Whether the layout holds for the sim’s groups now, and for its solver (or the one given): one made to choose the solver is used by the run unless the groups changed since (see ss.solvers.make_engine())


define
Replace the declared states on the module with their run-time form


delay_steps
The length of a fixed delay (ss.constant), plus any minimum stay before it, in whole steps: agents leave at the start of the step nearest its end


derived
The results that are worked out from the number in each state and the flow along each transition


derived_outcomes
What step_outcomes() does on each step, for every step at once (with expected, outcomes of whole events are their expected number, rather than drawn); only the outcomes in names, if given (with those they are worked out from); for many runs (the first dimension of the flows), each drawn from the random numbers of its seed in seeds


det_flow
Whether a flow is of a state that is not people, so is never drawn as whole events


drawn_outcomes
The outcomes of derived_outcomes() when they are drawn: a step at a time, by Engine.report_outcome(), with the runs and groups (all but the last dimension of the flows) side by side


eval
An expression’s value: from the tape, if it is on it (see init_tape()), else worked out here


event_frac
The people who went through a transition in the last step (or one of its branches, to), as a fraction of the state they are now in


exit_rate
The rate at which people leave a state other than by infection (one over their mean time in it), as a mean over groups


exposure
Exposure to people in a state through the sim’s mixing: the chance that a contact is with someone in that state


expr_key
What a function’s expression is made of, to tell when it changes: its text, and the exact value of each number in it (None if it is not an expression)


flatten_rates
The operations of the kernels for each rate: what they act on, in order; the operations, and where each flow’s start; the size of stack they need; and the row of consts of each mover’s rate (see init_program())


flow_base
The rate of a flow before its multipliers: the only part that can depend on the number in each compartment


flow_mult
The multipliers on a flow’s rate, which hold for the whole step


flows_of
The flows of each engine its program holds, as a crossing’s: this one’s


force
Move a fraction of the people in each state a transition leaves from (or in srcs), and each group, to a state, counted in the transition’s flow if there is one (as when a treatment cures); a synchronized flow moves other modules’ coordinates too; with y, of those people (by compartment and group) rather than the engine’s


gives_back
In a branching process, whether a move from one state to another is from the infected side back into the uninfected side, which it takes people out of the model by instead


group_needs
The states and flows (by position) that are needed by group: those of the results that keep their values by group, and what they are worked out from


held
Whether a value that varies in time is a step function (so is held for each step)


init_exposures
What each operation that reads an exposure needs, kept for each run, and the parameters of the operations


init_func_exprs
Call each value that is a function of the sim, to find those that give an expression of the model’s states, which are worked out within the step


init_movers
Movement between groups: aging, and the declared transfers


init_post
Set the initial conditions


init_program
Flatten the flows into arrays for the kernels: see ss.kernels


init_register
The movement register as arrays for the kernels (with no events, if there is none): see ss.kernels.Register


init_shifts
The deliveries that the kernels take in a whole run (see ss.Delivery.tabulated), as arrays: see ss.kernels.Shifts


init_syncs
Synchronized flows (proposal 03 §2.3): a transition of another module triggered by a transition of this one


init_tape

solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.binomial_substeps()
The substeps the chain-binomial solver takes in each step, from the fastest total rate out of a compartment of people at the start (see substeps())
People who arrive in a compartment within a substep leave it from the next, so a compartment holds about x/2 too many, with x its total rate out times the substep, and R is that much too high (TC1). So x is kept to binomial_bias (5%), which bounds the bias in each compartment to about 2.5%; and near the epidemic threshold, where the prevalence moves by the bias in R over R0 - 1 (an SIS’s endemic prevalence is 1 - 1/R0), to 0.1 × |R0 - 1|, for a bias of about 5% (TB3: TBsim’s resistance model, +12% at 3 substeps a month, is +3% at 12; an SIS with R0 = 1.05 gave 0.083 for 0.048 at whole steps). A fixed delay doesn’t count, since its people don’t leave at a rate: a model whose only exits are fixed delays takes whole steps, which keeps its final size but lowers its peak (by about 15% for an SIR at a fifth of the delay a step); substeps=3 gives about 5%, for about twice the time.

The next-generation matrix at the disease-free state, F V⁻¹, over the infected compartments of every group
The infected compartments are those of the states people are infected into or infect from, of any count (such as a reservoir, or infectious mosquitoes) that the rate of an infection uses, and of the counts that infected people’s numbers move a count into (mosquitoes biting them). A new infection is a flow from any other compartment into one of these. At the disease-free state, everyone is in the first state (so R0 is in a population with no immunity; with start=True, only the infected are moved there, for the reproduction number at the start), each group keeping its size, the infected counts are empty, and the other counts that are filled by an inflow (mosquitoes not infected) are at their equilibrium. Under the partner-change model (see ss.solvers.Mixing.partnerships()), the chance that a partnership with someone in a source state, formed now, transmits to the people in each group before it stops being able to: H/(H + k) with k = 1/D̄ + c, for partnerships that end at a constant rate, or H/(H + c)·(1 − E[exp(−(H + c)·T)]) over their duration T otherwise; H is the hazard per unit time in the partnership (acts per unit time times the hazard per act in the direction from the partner’s side, or the beta itself on a network without acts), and c the rate at which the partner leaves the source state or the person leaves the state they are infected from

solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.rates()
The rate of every flow, per unit time and per member of its source compartment (or in total, for an inflow)



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.ratio_names()

After a step: the flow along each transition and mover over it, by group, and the people at its end



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.record_stocks()
As ss.solvers.Engine.record_stocks(), for every state at once



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.reduce(value, state=None, what=None)

solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.refresh_program()

solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.restart()
Go back to the start of the run, with the current values of the parameters and the seed: see ss.Sim.restart()



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.restart_movement()
Put the movement between places, worked out again from new values of its parameters (see ss.geo.Mobility.fitted()), into the program, as a restart with them needs (see ss.Sim.restart()); False if the new values move people between places the old ones did not, so the sim must be built again

Whether modifiers act on a transmission on some of its routes (ss.modify(..., route=))

The multiplier on the contacts through each term of the mixing, from the modifiers of a transmission on that route: 1 − share·(1 − multiply), a number or one for each group (of the people who would be infected)

solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.settled()
Whether the program from the last step still holds, so the rates of this one need not be worked out again
A module with a step of its own stops a run being taken whole, but usually changes nothing the rates depend on. So, if nothing else needs Python between the steps (kernel_reason()), the only thing that can change them is a parameter set by that module, which is looked for at each step, as is the amount of a modifier. Values that vary in time then come from the tables of a whole run. A modifier added during the run is seen at the step it is added, and from then on, as a modifier may do anything, each step works out its own values.

For solver=‘ide’: a dwell time as it is, as a conveyor of whole steps, with the rate of leaving each slot that gives the distribution’s own chance of leaving after that many steps (rounded to the nearest), out to the step by which all but 1e-6 have left, whose slot is the last: everyone left there leaves in the next step, as from a fixed delay
Returns the rates of the slots before the last, or None for a distribution whose CDF is not known (which is left as Erlang stages, with a note)

The number of people in each state (rows) and group (columns)

The compartment of a state for people who stay in it with no exit of their own



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.stays(
    name,
    exits,
    competing,
    staged,
    branches,
)
For each transition out of a state with a minimum stay (after=): the first slot of a conveyor it acts on
A person in slot j has been in the state j whole steps, and agents count a stay as whole steps too (see Agents.stayed()). A dwell time with a minimum stay starts after it, so its stages come after the conveyor; a fixed delay with one is a longer conveyor (see delay_steps()).



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.step()

Store a result of a whole run: its total at each time point, and its values by group if it keeps them; returns the totals



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.substeps()
The number of substeps to take in each timestep (0 to let the solver choose)
The chain-binomial solver takes enough substeps that its step bias is small, as far as the rates are known at the start (at most max_binomial): see binomial_substeps(). Each substep is off the ODE by an amount of order rate × dt (ST55: an acute stage of 1.7 months at monthly steps took everyone infected from 9% to 51%). It moves people through as many stages of a dwell time as they pass in a substep (see ss.kernels.draw_chain()), so it is the dwell’s mean that counts, not its stages; a fixed delay is a conveyor of whole steps, so its length doesn’t count. substeps=1 takes whole steps, as most chain-binomial models (and frameworks’ discrete-time models) do.



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.sweep_triggers()
At each step: move the people a trigger holds for who are still in its source (who arrived by aging, a transfer, or another disease’s move, or for whom a condition on time or counts has come to hold)

The parts of the program that can change over time, at each step (or as a single entry, if nothing varies)

Some of the people in a compartment: a fraction, or a draw where the solver keeps whole numbers

The value of each expression on the tape, worked out once a step (or again, whenever the values it uses can have changed, as the engine’s other cached values are)

The group that each group’s people move to when their level in some dimensions is changed ({dimension index: level})

title: solvers.compartmental
text:
Name
Description




Compartmental
Runs a graph as compartments: deterministically (ode) or stochastically





solvers.compartmental.Compartmental(module, sim, solver=None)
Runs a graph as compartments: deterministically (ode) or stochastically (binomial, gillespie, or tau, the exact solver’s fallback for long runs)
It exists so that the deterministic and stochastic forms share one engine.
The states are expanded into compartments (one per branch and sub-stage) and the transitions into a flat list of flows, each with a source compartment, a rate, and the compartments it feeds. Every solver steps the same list of flows.





Name
Description




engines
The engines whose people its program holds, as a crossing’s: this one


owner
What holds the people and the program that runs them: this engine, or the crossing its disease is tracked jointly in (see ss.solvers.Crossing), whose program steps them all


shared
Whether this engine moves people in ways that belong to the sim rather than to the module (aging, relocating, the movement register): in a crossing, only one does (see ss.solvers.Crossing.lead), since they all see the same people


smooth
Whether any parameter varies smoothly in time (not as a step function), so is taken at the middle of each step


transfer_index
The position of each transfer among the flows of a whole run (after the transitions, with the other movers)









Name
Description




add_per_births
After a step: the children of those who went through a transition with births driven by its flow (ss.birth(per=)), n for each, in the youngest groups of their parents’ place


aging_rates
The rate per year at which people age out of each age group (but the last): the density of people in the year below


apart_shares
For several non-exponential dwell times out of a state, each for other people (where=): the share of each group that enters each one’s track, 1 for the one it has (the first, if none)


arrive
Add an amount to a state, split between its tracks; with before=True, as if they arrived a step before (people infectious at the start, who have been so for the first step, as agents date them), so one slot along a conveyor


at_home
Whether a time share between places (a sparse array) keeps everyone at home, as np.allclose(share, np.eye(P)) would say, without forming either


at_middle
Take values that vary smoothly in time at the middle of the step, which runs from time point ti-1 to ti, as tables() does, so that a stepped run takes the same values as a whole one


attr
An attribute in a compartmental run: a trait is the mean of its distribution, as a parameter that is a distribution is (see trait_mean())


backfill_burnin
A module’s people who start part way through (ss.Pregnancy(burnin=True): see its burnin_plan()): each group’s


binomial_substeps
The substeps the chain-binomial solver takes in each step, from the fastest total rate out of a compartment of people at the start (see substeps())


birth_map
Where the children of the people in each group are born (rows to columns): the youngest group of each dimension, by the split of the others, in their parents’ place


births_of
The engine and inflow of each declared module with an ss.birth(per=) of the same transition as tr (this module’s own first)


branch_where
Whether a transition is a branch out of each of its sources whose where= is on states and strata, so closes it at entry (see branch_mult()) rather than changing its rate


build
Lay out the compartments (after init_dims()): the dwell times, the protection between strains, and the compartments and flows; raises a CapabilityError for what has no compartmental form yet


build_layout
Expand the states into compartments and the transitions into flows


call_uids
A function that takes uids, which a compartmental run does not have (see Agents.call_uids())


certain
The name of a transition with an infinite rate (a probability of 1 over the period) at the start, which the kernels take as everyone moving at once (see ss.kernels.certain()), and which JAX and the exact solver by place do not; or None


changes
The rate of change of each compartment from new infections (new=True: arrivals only), or from every other flow; see next_generation()


clock
A clock, which a compartmental run does not keep (see Agents.clock())


collect
The results of many runs, from the number in each state and the flow along each transition and mover


constant_transfer
Whether a transfer’s rate holds for the whole run, so its mover can be set once before it (see run_args()): a rate or duration of plain values, with no modifiers


count_deaths
For a split between states and ss.null (with no ss.stay): those who died are its flow less those who went to a state, so the two agree in each run; flows are by flow along the axis before the last (the groups)


count_weighted
A weighted count ((ss.by(biting=w)*I).n, A.n_trans): the people in each state and group counted by the group’s weight (and infectiousness), in the same place


coverage
A product’s coverage (itn.coverage): the share of the people in the same place who hold it, by what each level of holding it counts as (see ss.expressions.Coverage.level_weights())


current
Whether the layout holds for the sim’s groups now, and for its solver (or the one given): one made to choose the solver is used by the run unless the groups changed since (see ss.solvers.make_engine())


define
Replace the declared states on the module with their run-time form


delay_steps
The length of a fixed delay (ss.constant), plus any minimum stay before it, in whole steps: agents leave at the start of the step nearest its end


derived
The results that are worked out from the number in each state and the flow along each transition


derived_outcomes
What step_outcomes() does on each step, for every step at once (with expected, outcomes of whole events are their expected number, rather than drawn); only the outcomes in names, if given (with those they are worked out from); for many runs (the first dimension of the flows), each drawn from the random numbers of its seed in seeds


det_flow
Whether a flow is of a state that is not people, so is never drawn as whole events


drawn_outcomes
The outcomes of derived_outcomes() when they are drawn: a step at a time, by Engine.report_outcome(), with the runs and groups (all but the last dimension of the flows) side by side


eval
An expression’s value: from the tape, if it is on it (see init_tape()), else worked out here


event_frac
The people who went through a transition in the last step (or one of its branches, to), as a fraction of the state they are now in


exit_rate
The rate at which people leave a state other than by infection (one over their mean time in it), as a mean over groups


exposure
Exposure to people in a state through the sim’s mixing: the chance that a contact is with someone in that state


expr_key
What a function’s expression is made of, to tell when it changes: its text, and the exact value of each number in it (None if it is not an expression)


flatten_rates
The operations of the kernels for each rate: what they act on, in order; the operations, and where each flow’s start; the size of stack they need; and the row of consts of each mover’s rate (see init_program())


flow_base
The rate of a flow before its multipliers: the only part that can depend on the number in each compartment


flow_mult
The multipliers on a flow’s rate, which hold for the whole step


flows_of
The flows of each engine its program holds, as a crossing’s: this one’s


force
Move a fraction of the people in each state a transition leaves from (or in srcs), and each group, to a state, counted in the transition’s flow if there is one (as when a treatment cures); a synchronized flow moves other modules’ coordinates too; with y, of those people (by compartment and group) rather than the engine’s


gives_back
In a branching process, whether a move from one state to another is from the infected side back into the uninfected side, which it takes people out of the model by instead


group_needs
The states and flows (by position) that are needed by group: those of the results that keep their values by group, and what they are worked out from


held
Whether a value that varies in time is a step function (so is held for each step)


init_exposures
What each operation that reads an exposure needs, kept for each run, and the parameters of the operations


init_func_exprs
Call each value that is a function of the sim, to find those that give an expression of the model’s states, which are worked out within the step


init_movers
Movement between groups: aging, and the declared transfers


init_post
Set the initial conditions


init_program
Flatten the flows into arrays for the kernels: see ss.kernels


init_register
The movement register as arrays for the kernels (with no events, if there is none): see ss.kernels.Register


init_shifts
The deliveries that the kernels take in a whole run (see ss.Delivery.tabulated), as arrays: see ss.kernels.Shifts


init_syncs
Synchronized flows (proposal 03 §2.3): a transition of another module triggered by a transition of this one


init_tape
Put the expressions that are worked out once a step for every group alike (the branch probabilities, and the rates


init_triggers
Triggers (ss.on()): on states and strata, the compartments where they hold vanish; on time or counts, they are applied at each step


kernel_reason
Why the whole run cannot be taken in one call to the kernels (something in Python needs to see the model between one step and the next), in a few words, or None if it can: see ss.solvers.why_not()


kernels
The kernels to take the run (or runs runs) with, compiled or as plain Python, chosen once for a run: see ss.kernels.choose()


make_program

mother
ss.mother(x), which needs agents (see Agents.mother())


move_share
Move a share of each state and group (within the sources srcs) along a triggered transition: with p=, that share of them; with several destinations, split between them


move_some
A one-off move from code (ss.move()): a share p of the people in some states (or n of them, exactly where the solver keeps whole people; of those for whom where holds) to a state, or of a count, to and from outside the model too (dst or srcs empty); returns the number moved

Move a fraction of the people in each of some states, and each group, to a state: along a transition (see force()), or along none, as a one-off move (ss.vaccinate(move=S >> V)); with syn (synchronized flows), also returns the moves in this module’s own groups; with y, of those people rather than the engine’s; with given, the number to move from each compartment instead (see move_some())

The rates of a mover from group to group, as a sparse matrix (each group’s people move along one dimension, so to only a few groups)

note_counter
In a compartmental run, a note when a counter’s levels are not one apart, so people within a wider level are taken to be at its lower edge when it goes up


note_stages
In a compartmental run, a dwell time that is not exponential or Erlang is approximated by Erlang stages, which is said in one line

par_transfer
Whether a transfer’s rate is a parameter that varies in time (e.g. aging at a rate given for each year), and nothing else of it does,


par_values
What the rates are worked out from, to compare with those of the last step (see settled())


partnership_chance
Under the partner-change model (see ss.solvers.Mixing.partnerships()), the chance that a partnership with


pass_syncs
After a step, or a move by an intervention: give each module whose transition is triggered by one of this one’s the people its flow moved, as its transition’s flow


plain_seconds
About how long the run would take as plain Python, from the size of its program and its rates at the start (see ss.kernels.plain_seconds())


prog_value
The value of a parameter in the program: a beta for each route is 1 here (with any modifiers), since it is applied to the exposure through each (see set_contacts())


program_mixing
The mixing as the kernels take it: the groups of each place, and the arrays of each term


prop
A property of people or a condition, in a rate (see ss.expressions.Prop): its value for each group (for a condition, the share of the group it holds for; on states, of the people in the state the flow leaves)


rates
The rate of every flow, per unit time and per member of its source compartment (or in total, for an inflow)


ratio_names
The results given as expressions, and the standard prevalence if it is kept by group as a ratio (see init_results())


record_flows
After a step: the flow along each transition and mover over it, by group, and the people at its end


record_stocks

reduce
A modified value is a scalar or one value per group; if it differs by state, the row for the state it is used for


refresh_program
Set the numbers in the program that hold for this step: the rates that do not depend on the compartments, and the values the others use


restart
Go back to the start of the run, with the current values of the parameters and the seed: see ss.Sim.restart()


restart_movement
Put the movement between places, worked out again from new values of its parameters (see ss.geo.Mobility.fitted()), into the program, as a restart with them needs (see ss.Sim.restart()); False if the new values move people between places the old ones did not, so the sim must be built again


round_preserving
Round to whole numbers, keeping the total


route_betas
For a transmission with a beta for each route (beta=dict(home=…, school=…)), or with a route that has acts: the beta


route_mods
Whether modifiers act on a transmission on some of its routes (ss.modify(..., route=))


route_mults
The multiplier on the contacts through each term of the mixing, from the modifiers of a transmission on that route: 1 − share·(1 − multiply), a number or one for each group (of the people who would be infected)


run_all
Take every step of the run in one call to the kernels (or to JAX: see ss.gradients), and fill in the results from what comes back


run_args
What the kernels need for a whole run, apart from the seed (and the tables, unless tables=False)


run_many

solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.binomial_substeps()
The substeps the chain-binomial solver takes in each step, from the fastest total rate out of a compartment of people at the start (see substeps())
People who arrive in a compartment within a substep leave it from the next, so a compartment holds about x/2 too many, with x its total rate out times the substep, and R is that much too high (TC1). So x is kept to binomial_bias (5%), which bounds the bias in each compartment to about 2.5%; and near the epidemic threshold, where the prevalence moves by the bias in R over R0 - 1 (an SIS’s endemic prevalence is 1 - 1/R0), to 0.1 × |R0 - 1|, for a bias of about 5% (TB3: TBsim’s resistance model, +12% at 3 substeps a month, is +3% at 12; an SIS with R0 = 1.05 gave 0.083 for 0.048 at whole steps). A fixed delay doesn’t count, since its people don’t leave at a rate: a model whose only exits are fixed delays takes whole steps, which keeps its final size but lowers its peak (by about 15% for an SIR at a fifth of the delay a step); substeps=3 gives about 5%, for about twice the time.

The next-generation matrix at the disease-free state, F V⁻¹, over the infected compartments of every group
The infected compartments are those of the states people are infected into or infect from, of any count (such as a reservoir, or infectious mosquitoes) that the rate of an infection uses, and of the counts that infected people’s numbers move a count into (mosquitoes biting them). Whether the program from the last step still holds, so the rates of this one need not be worked out again
A module with a step of its own stops a run being taken whole, but usually changes nothing the rates depend on. So, if nothing else needs Python between the steps (kernel_reason()), the only thing that can change them is a parameter set by that module, which is looked for at each step, as is the amount of a modifier. Values that vary in time then come from the tables of a whole run. A modifier added during the run is seen at the step it is added, and from then on, as a modifier may do anything, each step works out its own values.

Type
Description
Default

arr
the fraction to move, states by groups
required


changes
dict
the level to move them to, for each dimension that changes
required







solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.slot_rates(tr, dwell, most=5000)
For solver=‘ide’: a dwell time as it is, as a conveyor of whole steps, with the rate of leaving each slot that gives the distribution’s own chance of leaving after that many steps (rounded to the nearest), out to the step by which all but 1e-6 have left, whose slot is the last: everyone left there leaves in the next step, as from a fixed delay
Returns the rates of the slots before the last, or None for a distribution whose CDF is not known (which is left as Erlang stages, with a note)

    name,
    exits,
    competing,
    staged,
    branches,
)
For each transition out of a state with a minimum stay (after=): the first slot of a conveyor it acts on
A person in slot j has been in the state j whole steps, and agents count a stay as whole steps too (see Agents.stayed()). A dwell time with a minimum stay starts after it, so its stages come after the conveyor; a fixed delay with one is a longer conveyor (see delay_steps()).

The results of a whole run, from its compartments and flows at each time point, taken in one part or a part at a time; the results by group are kept at each time point, or every few steps (see ss.solvers.group_rows())

Type
Description
Default

iterable

required

The results of the deliveries of a run taken in JAX, worked out again from the compartments at each time point they happened at (exact, since the run is an ODE)

Store a result of a whole run: its total at each time point, and its values by group if it keeps them; returns the totals



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.substeps()
The number of substeps to take in each timestep (0 to let the solver choose)
The chain-binomial solver takes enough substeps that its step bias is small, as far as the rates are known at the start (at most max_binomial): see binomial_substeps(). Each substep is off the ODE by an amount of order rate × dt (ST55: an acute stage of 1.7 months at monthly steps took everyone infected from 9% to 51%). It moves people through as many stages of a dwell time as they pass in a substep (see ss.kernels.draw_chain()), so it is the dwell’s mean that counts, not its stages; a fixed delay is a conveyor of whole steps, so its length doesn’t count. substeps=1 takes whole steps, as most chain-binomial models (and frameworks’ discrete-time models) do.



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.sweep_triggers()

The synchronized flows of a transition (to a destination), with their maps worked out

The value of each expression on the tape, worked out once a step (or again, whenever the values it uses can have changed, as the engine’s other cached values are)

title: analyzers
text:
analyzers
Define analyzers, which are used to track variables when the sim is run.
Analyzers typically include things like additional tracking states by age or another conditional.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Analyzer
Base class for Analyzers. Analyzers are used to provide more detailed information


infection_log
Log infections – see ss.diseases.InfectionLog for detail





analyzers.Analyzer(name=None, label=None, **kwargs)
Base class for Analyzers. Analyzers are used to provide more detailed information about a simulation than is available by default – for example, pulling states out of sim.people on a particular timestep before they get updated on the next step.
The key method of the analyzer is step(), which is called at each time point: at the end of each step, once its results are recorded (with self.ti the step’s, as in every module), and at the first time point (self.ti == 0), before any step, to record the start.



analyzers.infection_log(**kwargs)
Log infections – see ss.diseases.InfectionLog for detail
This analyzer activates an infection log running in each disease. This is different than other analyzers, but is required since the information required to create an infection log isn’t kept outside of the disease’s transmit() step.
Each entry has the time (t), the person infected (target), who infected them (source), and the route (network). The source is known only for transmission over a network, where each infection is drawn along an edge: seeds have a source of -1, and infections by a mixing pool (ss.MixingPool), a contact matrix, or mixing with everyone (no network) have a source and network of NaN, since they come from the share infectious in a group rather than from a particular person. As agents only.
Note: CRN safe.


import starsim as ss
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=1000, dt=0.2, dur=15, diseases='sir', networks='random', analyzers='infection_log')
sim.run()
sim.analyzers[0].plot()

Description

    sims=None,

    label=None,

    inplace=True,
    debug=False,
    **kwargs,
)
The runs of one or more sims: every result of the sims with a run axis first, and the sims that were run
Made and run by ss.parallel(), the way to run many sims (or by sim.run(n_runs=...), a shortcut for running one sim many times). Making a MultiSim and calling msim.run() does the same.

Type
Description
Default

None

None

int
the number of runs of each sim, each with its own seed (by default, 4 for a single sim given as sims, otherwise 1)
None

sets of values of parameters to run each sim with; see ss.parallel()
None

bool / dict
draw n_runs sets of values from the priors of the parameters, or the draws to run; see ss.parallel()
False

False

{}



By default (verbose not given: the sims’ own verbose, if they share one, else ss.options.verbose) the runs print nothing of their own, and the MultiSim shows their progress: nothing for runs that are done within a second, a bar for each run if there are up to 10 that each take more than 10 seconds, and otherwise one bar with the number of runs done (to a file, a line every tenth); then a line on what was run.
Once run, a MultiSim has:

results: every result with a run axis first (see ss.Result), e.g. msim.results.sir.I.quantiles();
runs: one row per run, with its scenario (the label of its sim), the values of any parameters swept or drawn, and its seed (rand_seed);
sims: the sims that were run (for runs restarted from one compartmental sim, that sim, as it was after its last run).

len(msim) is the number of runs.
A subclass changes the sim of each run by overriding make_run(), and can take options of its own for it by adding them to run_options (see the last example).



import starsim as ss

s1 = ss.Sim(networks='random', diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.02), label='Low transmission')
s2 = ss.Sim(networks='random', diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.05), label='High transmission')
msim = ss.parallel(s1, s2, n_runs=5)
msim.plot() # The median and a 95% interval of each scenario
msim.results.sis.prevalence.select(scenario='Low transmission').median()

class NoisyMultiSim(ss.MultiSim): # Each run with its own beta, drawn around 0.05
    run_options = ss.MultiSim.run_options + ['noise']

    def make_run(self, sim, values, seed, noise=0.1):
        beta = 0.05*np.exp(noise*np.random.default_rng(seed).normal())
        return super().make_run(sim, dict(values or {}, beta=beta), seed)

msim = NoisyMultiSim(s1, n_runs=10, noise=0.2).run()

Put the results of the sims together as runs (msim.results), if they have the same time points (msim._same_times)
Sims with different time points (e.g. different steps) are kept as they are: each can be plotted on its own time axis (msim.plot()), but their results can’t be put together, so what combines the runs raises an error.



run.MultiSim.combine()
Combine the sims into a single sim, whose results are those of one population made of all of them, e.g. to treat several smaller sims as one larger population
Only the output is combined. Results that scale with population size (res.scale=True, e.g. counts) are summed; other results (e.g. prevalence) are averaged, weighted by each sim’s total_pop. The population sizes (n_agents and total_pop) are summed, and pop_scale is updated to match. The people are not joined: the combined sim keeps the people (if any) of the first sim, so it is not a larger population of agents that interact, and cannot be run again as one. To keep the runs as runs, see ss.MultiSim.merge().

By default (verbose not given: the sims’ own verbose, if they share one, else ss.options.verbose) the runs print nothing of their own, and the MultiSim shows their progress: nothing for runs that are done within a second, a bar for each run if there are up to 10 that each take more than 10 seconds, and otherwise one bar with the number of runs done (to a file, a line every tenth); then a line on what was run.
Once run, a MultiSim has:

results: every result with a run axis first (see ss.Result), e.g. msim.results.sir.I.quantiles();
runs: one row per run, with its scenario (the label of its sim), the values of any parameters swept or drawn, and its seed (rand_seed);
sims: the sims that were run (for runs restarted from one compartmental sim, that sim, as it was after its last run).

len(msim) is the number of runs.
A subclass changes the sim of each run by overriding make_run(), and can take options of its own for it by adding them to run_options (see the last example).



import starsim as ss

s1 = ss.Sim(networks='random', diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.02), label='Low transmission')
s2 = ss.Sim(networks='random', diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.05), label='High transmission')
msim = ss.parallel(s1, s2, n_runs=5)
msim.plot() # The median and a 95% interval of each scenario
msim.results.sis.prevalence.select(scenario='Low transmission').median()

class NoisyMultiSim(ss.MultiSim): # Each run with its own beta, drawn around 0.05
    run_options = ss.MultiSim.run_options + ['noise']

    def make_run(self, sim, values, seed, noise=0.1):
        beta = 0.05*np.exp(noise*np.random.default_rng(seed).normal())
        return super().make_run(sim, dict(values or {}, beta=beta), seed)

msim = NoisyMultiSim(s1, n_runs=10, noise=0.2).run()

run.MultiSim.combine()
Combine the sims into a single sim, whose results are those of one population made of all of them, e.g. to treat several smaller sims as one larger population
Only the output is combined. Results that scale with population size (res.scale=True, e.g. counts) are summed; other results (e.g. prevalence) are averaged, weighted by each sim’s total_pop. The population sizes (n_agents and total_pop) are summed, and pop_scale is updated to match. The people are not joined: the combined sim keeps the people (if any) of the first sim, so it is not a larger population of agents that interact, and cannot be run again as one. To keep the runs as runs, see ss.MultiSim.merge().

Lactation, as declared states: N (not breastfeeding) and L (breastfeeding)
A sibling of ss.Pregnancy (or of a subclass of it, by any name), since lactation overlaps the next pregnancy. A live birth starts it (with p_breastfeed), or restarts it for a woman breastfeeding already; it ends after dur_breastfeed, or at once if a child of hers dies before the age of 1. A BreastfeedingNet pairs each newborn with a mother who is in L and ends the pair when she leaves it. Added by ss.Pregnancy when the sim has a BreastfeedingNet (lactation='auto'). pregnancy.Pregnancy(
    pars=None,
    fetus='auto',
    lactation='auto',
    metadata=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Pregnancy, as declared states and transitions
Everyone is in NP (not pregnant: men and children too) or P (pregnant). Gestational age is P.time. Conception is one transition, so contraception, HIV, or LAM are modifiers of it (ss.modify(preg.conception, multiply=...)). A pregnancy ends in an abortion (at once, with p_abortion), a miscarriage or stillbirth (a hazard before or after loss_threshold), a maternal death (antepartum), or a delivery at the end of a dwell of dur_pregnancy. Each delivery gives embryos_per_pregnancy children (birth): as agents, new agents whose parent is the mother, placed in each declared module’s state given by its own ss.birth(per=preg.delivery) (or else its first state). Children die before the age of 1 at infant_rate (infant_mortality; 0 by default). It runs as agents under solver='auto'; a compartmental solver named explicitly runs a small approximate form (see compartmental_form()).
For other modules, preg.delivery happens to the mother, and to her fetuses (if they are agents: see _init_fetus()) before they are born, so a death of a fetus on=preg.delivery is a stillbirth; preg.birth happens to the newborns, so a neonatal death is on=preg.birth.
Its parameters are listed in __init__(); code reacts to its events with add_callback(), e.g. preg.add_callback(preg.birth, fn). Its states and results are P (pregnant), ti_P, the scheduled delivery ti_exit_P (set_delivery() reschedules it), and the flows conception, birth, miscarriage, stillbirth, and abortion.

pregnancy.Pregnancy.burnin_plan(engine)
burnin=True (the default): women pregnant at the start. Each woman who could conceive has the chance of having conceived in the mean duration of a pregnancy before the start, at her conception hazard then (1 - exp(-h*dur)), at a step uniform over it, and is run forward by the pregnancy’s own transitions (abortion, losses, and delivery, with no births), so the start has the gestational ages and the first steps their deliveries. In the compartmental form, the same share of each group, less the abortions and the losses on the way, is spread evenly over gestation (see ss.solvers.Compartmental.backfill_burnin()).



pregnancy.Pregnancy.compartmental_form(sim)
The small compartmental form, used only when a compartmental solver is named (solver='auto' runs a pregnancy as agents): the states NP and P, conception, abortion, maternal deaths, and the delivery at the end of dur_pregnancy (a fixed delay, or Erlang stages for a distribution), with n children per delivery (ss.birth(per=preg.delivery)). The losses do not read the gestational age (P.time): the loss rate is split between miscarriage and stillbirth by the share of the mean gestation below loss_threshold. It has no fetuses, no links between mothers and children, no lactation, no preterm risk, and no deaths at delivery (p_maternal_death). Returns the note that says so



pregnancy.Pregnancy.compute_asfr()
The age-specific fertility rates of the step (per 1000 women: deliveries by the mother’s age, over the women of that age), and the TFR from them. As compartments, by the age of each group, so it needs an age stratification (otherwise NaN)



pregnancy.Pregnancy.conception_rate(sim)
The hazard of conception, per year, for each agent (by UID) or each group: the fertility rate (in the year a pregnancy starting now would end, if given by year), rescaled from all fecund women to those not pregnant; 0 for anyone not fecund
An override can instead take (sim, uids) and return a rate for each of those agents (as agents only), e.g. ss.peryear(table[self.method[uids]]), rather than one for every slot of the raw arrays.



pregnancy.Pregnancy.link(sim)
lactation='auto': add an ss.Lactation to a sim that has none, if it has a BreastfeedingNet (or lactation=True), with this module’s breastfeeding parameters; called by ss.solvers.choose_solver()



pregnancy.Pregnancy.make_children(tr, parents, ti)
As agents, at a delivery: the children of the mothers (see ss.solvers.Agents.step_per()), and the events on the mothers



pregnancy.Pregnancy.preterm_risk(uids)
At conception: each woman’s relative risk of preterm birth (rel_ptb), her baseline (rr_ptb) times the risk at her age (rr_ptb_age), multiplies her probability of a preterm duration (below preterm_threshold), capped at 1; the durations within the preterm and the term ones keep their shares. For dur_pregnancy as an ss.choice (the default), each duration is drawn so (one uniform number, by inverse transform), kept in weeks (dur_gestation, the gestational age at birth), and the delivery scheduled by it, as the engine schedules a dwell time (agents only)



pregnancy.Pregnancy.run_callbacks()
The callbacks (see add_callback()) see the step’s new pregnancies once their fetuses and preterm risk are set, so a callback’s set_delivery() is kept



pregnancy.Pregnancy.set_delivery(uids, ti, weeks=None)
Reschedule the deliveries of some pregnant women to a step (its index, as ti_exit_P reads; each scheduled exit of P is the delivery: losses are rates, which compete with it), with the gestational age they will have then (dur_gestation): weeks if given, otherwise the weeks from conception to that step



pregnancy.Pregnancy.step()
The pregnancy’s transitions, at the start of the step, before the diseases’



pregnancy.Pregnancy.step_die(uids)
As agents: take the dead out of the states. The death of the last fetus of a pregnancy is a miscarriage or a stillbirth for the mother, by gestational age; a mother who dies while pregnant loses her fetuses, counted the same way; and a death before the age of 1 is an infant death for the mother.

Pregnancy, as declared states and transitions
Everyone is in NP (not pregnant: men and children too) or P (pregnant). Gestational age is P.time. Conception is one transition, so contraception, HIV, or LAM are modifiers of it (ss.modify(preg.conception, multiply=...)). A pregnancy ends in an abortion (at once, with p_abortion), a miscarriage or stillbirth (a hazard before or after loss_threshold), a maternal death (antepartum), or a delivery at the end of a dwell of dur_pregnancy. Each delivery gives embryos_per_pregnancy children (birth): as agents, new agents whose parent is the mother, placed in each declared module’s state given by its own ss.birth(per=preg.delivery) (or else its first state). It runs as agents under solver='auto'; a compartmental solver named explicitly runs a small approximate form (see compartmental_form()).

pregnancy.Pregnancy.burnin_plan(engine)
burnin=True (the default): women pregnant at the start. Each woman who could conceive has the chance of having conceived in the mean duration of a pregnancy before the start, at her conception hazard then (1 - exp(-h*dur)), at a step uniform over it, and is run forward by the pregnancy’s own transitions (abortion, losses, and delivery, with no births), so the start has the gestational ages and the first steps their deliveries. In the compartmental form, the same share of each group, less the abortions and the losses on the way, is spread evenly over gestation (see ss.solvers.Compartmental.backfill_burnin()).



pregnancy.Pregnancy.compartmental_form(sim)
The small compartmental form, used only when a compartmental solver is named (solver='auto' runs a pregnancy as agents): the states NP and P, conception, abortion, maternal deaths, and the delivery at the end of dur_pregnancy (a fixed delay, or Erlang stages for a distribution), with n children per delivery (ss.birth(per=preg.delivery)). The losses do not read the gestational age (P.time): the loss rate is split between miscarriage and stillbirth by the share of the mean gestation below loss_threshold. It has no fetuses, no links between mothers and children, no lactation, no preterm risk, and no deaths at delivery (p_maternal_death). Returns the note that says so

An override can instead take (sim, uids) and return a rate for each of those agents (as agents only), e.g. ss.peryear(table[self.method[uids]]), rather than one for every slot of the raw arrays.

At conception: each woman’s relative risk of preterm birth (rel_ptb), her baseline (rr_ptb) times the risk at her age (rr_ptb_age), multiplies her probability of a preterm duration (below preterm_threshold), capped at 1; the durations within the preterm and the term ones keep their shares. The pregnancy’s transitions, at the start of the step, before the diseases’

As agents: take the dead out of the states. The death of the last fetus of a pregnancy is a miscarriage or a stillbirth for the mother, by gestational age; a mother who dies while pregnant loses her fetuses, counted the same way; and a death before the age of 1 is an infant death for the mother.

Places and the movement between them: a geography (ss.geo.geography), and movement between its places (ss.geo.Mobility, from a matrix, a data file of moves, or a movement model: ss.geo.gravity or ss.geo.radiation)
These exist so that a model of more than one place can be built from named places and a standard movement model. Movement applies to a declared model stratified by place (sir.stratify(patch=...)); a geography can also be used by a network (ssl.GeoNet), for a disease of either kind.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules

Description

Movement between the levels of a spatial stratification

gravity
The gravity model of movement: the share of their time that a person from place i spends in place j (or, for migration,


radiation

geo.Mobility(model=None, matrix=None, kind=None, away=None, data=None)
Movement between the levels of a spatial stratification
People either commute (they keep their home, and spend a share of their time in other places, where they are exposed and expose others), visit (the same, but they are exposed to the residents of the places they go to and do not expose anyone there, as flepiMoP has it), or migrate (they relocate). Or, with kind='force', nobody moves and the force of infection does, as in LASER: with M[i,k] the movement from place i to place k, each place keeps 1 − Σ_k M[i,k] of its own force of infection and receives M[k,i] of each other place’s.
Other forms are written with the general pieces. Commuters who come back at a finite rate (Keeling and Rohani’s model 7.3) are a second spatial dimension of where people are now, with transfers between its levels at rates by home.
A movement register (data=) is a table of events on given dates, with columns date, from, to, n, and optionally states. Each row moves n people from one place to another; a row with no from adds them to to (births, purchases), and one with no to removes them from from (deaths, sales out of the model). The people who move or leave are chosen at random from those in states (by default, everyone); people who are added go into states (by default, the first state). Each event happens at the start of the first step that begins on or after its date, before that step’s transitions, and the events of a step happen in the order of the table.
Note: CRN safe as agents.

Type
Description
Default

gravity / radiation
a movement model (instead of matrix)
None


matrix
array
the movement from each place (rows) to each place: for commuting the share of time spent there, and for migration the rate of moving there (a SciPy sparse array for many places, most pairs of which share no one)
None

str / df

None


kind
str
‘commute’, ‘visit’, ‘migrate’, or ‘force’; by default ‘migrate’ for a register and ‘commute’ otherwise
None


away
float
for commuting and visiting, the share of their time people spend away from home (for ‘force’, the share of each place’s force of infection that goes to the others); the movement is rescaled to give every place that share (to keep the differences between places, scale the matrix by hand and give no away=)
None

The gravity model of movement: the share of their time that a person from place i spends in place j (or, for migration, the rate at which they move there) is k × pop[i]^(a−1) × pop[j]^b / distance[i,j]^c
Populations and distances come from the geography of the dimension it is used on (ss.geo.geography). The model gives the shape of the movement, and away= its amount: the share of their time that people spend away from home, split between the other places by gravity. k has units of distance^c / pop^(a+b−1), so no default fits both three towns and a country; give it only if it has been calibrated. With neither, people spend 10% of their time away.

geo.gravity(away=None, k=None, a=1.0, b=1.0, c=2.0)
The gravity model of movement: the share of their time that a person from place i spends in place j (or, for migration, the rate at which they move there) is k × pop[i]^(a−1) × pop[j]^b / distance[i,j]^c
Populations and distances come from the geography of the dimension it is used on (ss.geo.geography). The model gives the shape of the movement, and away= its amount: the share of their time that people spend away from home, split between the other places by gravity. k has units of distance^c / pop^(a+b−1), so no default fits both three towns and a country; give it only if it has been calibrated. The radiation model of movement (Simini et al. 2012), which has no parameters to fit: of the people from place i who travel, the share who go to place j is pop[i] × pop[j] / ((pop[i] + s) × (pop[i] + pop[j] + s)), where s is the population of the other places nearer to i than j is
It is used as ss.geo.gravity is, with the populations and distances of the geography of the dimension it is used on (ss.geo.geography): the model gives where people go, and away= how much they travel. A state that a dimension does not apply to (a count, or a state left out of states=) is kept at the first level of that dimension.

The protection between the strains of a disease with shared states (ss.Strains(immunity=...), see ss.immunity)

Due to a state (due_to=R): its people are protected by the strains they carry in it, against each strain; a multiplier for each level of the strain dimension and strain, in protect. A state people are not infected in (R) can be infected again, moving on as from the first state (immune_states); one they are infected in (L) can carry another strain as well (see ss.strains.add_superinfection()).

Work out the sources and delay of each outcome, and the order to compute them in

Set the starting values, once the people are initialized



solvers.engine.Engine.init_pre()
Lay out what the run needs, before the people are initialized

One count per state, one flow per transition (res.infection.cum is its cumulative total), and for the library’s diseases, Starsim’s standard disease results



solvers.engine.Engine.init_strain_weights()
The share of the infectiousness of the people at each level of the strain dimension that goes to each strain (levels by strains)
Someone who carries one strain passes it on; someone who carries several passes on each in proportion to its infectiousness (its rel_trans); their own infectiousness is that of their level.

solvers.engine.Engine.n_people(total=True)

solvers.engine.Engine.note_fast_steps()

In a run that takes whole steps, say which transitions are fast compared with the timestep: by the parameters’ own values, without their modifiers, which may read what does not exist until the run (e.g. a property of people another module adds)



solvers.engine.Engine.outcome_share(flow, weight, draw)
The events of an outcome from those of one of its sources, times its weight: a fraction of whole events is a draw if draw, and the part of an event left over (from agents who stand for a fraction of a person) is kept as its mean



solvers.engine.Engine.own_moves(tr)
The moves of move= and increment=: see moves()



solvers.engine.Engine.plain_value(val)
A value written inside another (a direction of ss.peract, or a route of a beta dict) as a number, or a value for each group



solvers.engine.Engine.plausible_density(tr)
Whether a transition is density-dependent transmission as meant (S >> I @ beta*I.n, see ss.graph.Graph.density_sources), rather than a count written for a share: whether one infectious person infects each susceptible at a rate under 5% a step. A beta meant for a share (0.3 per day) is far above one for density dependence, R0/(N × the time infectious), unless the population is a handful of people

The sim’s copy of the product of a coverage (itn.coverage, see ss.expressions.Coverage)



solvers.engine.Engine.prop(cond)

One step of an outcome: its events in the step (amount, for each group, or each run and group) are reported after its delay, and stay in it for its duration, each drawn for each event if draw. buf keeps the events still to be reported (pending) and to leave (leaving), each a ring over the next steps, and the number in the outcome (n). The value of a transmission’s beta on the route it is being worked out for (self._route, as agents): a beta for each route gives its value for this one; on a network with acts, a probability per act (ss.peract, or a bare number) gives the hazard per act, −ln(1 − p), in each of the network’s directions (see act_hazards())

Some states split into this disease’s own and other diseases’ (e.g. syph.I in a rate of HIV), by the name of each other disease

title: demographics
text:
demographics
Births, deaths, migration, and pregnancy
These exist so that the population can change during a run. ss.Births and ss.Deaths are written as code, ss.birth() and the like declare the same flows for the whole population, and ss.Pregnancy is declared, so that conception and delivery are transitions that other modules can modify or respond to.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules

Configure disease-independent “background” deaths.
The probability of death for each agent on each timestep is determined by the death_rate parameter and the time step. The default value of this parameter is 0.01, indicating that all agents will face a 1% chance of death per year.
However, this function can be made more realistic by using a dataframe for the death_rate parameter, to allow it to vary by year, sex, and age. The separate ‘metadata’ argument can be used to configure the details of the input datafile.

Base class for demographic modules.
A demographic module typically handles births/deaths/migration and takes place at the start of the timestep, before networks are updated and before any disease modules are executed. demographics.Pregnancy(pars=None, fetus='auto', metadata=None, **kwargs)
Pregnancy, as declared states and transitions
Everyone is in NP (not pregnant: men and children too) or P (pregnant). Gestational age is P.time. Conception is one transition, so contraception, HIV, or LAM are modifiers of it (ss.modify(preg.conception, multiply=...)). A pregnancy ends in an abortion (at once, with p_abortion), a miscarriage or stillbirth (a hazard before or after loss_threshold), a maternal death (antepartum), or a delivery at the end of a dwell of dur_pregnancy. Each delivery gives embryos_per_pregnancy children (birth): as agents, new agents whose parent is the mother, placed in each declared module’s state given by its own ss.birth(per=preg.delivery) (or else its first state). Children die before the age of 1 at infant_rate (infant_mortality; 0 by default). It runs as agents under solver='auto'; a compartmental solver named explicitly runs a small approximate form (see compartmental_form()).
For other modules, preg.delivery happens to the mother, and to her fetuses (if they are agents: see _init_fetus()) before they are born, so a death of a fetus where=preg.delivery is a stillbirth; preg.birth happens to the newborns, so a neonatal death is where=preg.birth.
As agents, a live birth starts breastfeeding (lactating, with p_breastfeed), or restarts it for a woman breastfeeding already; it ends after dur_breastfeed, or at once if a child of hers dies before the age of 1. It is a state of each woman rather than one of the module’s exclusive states (NP, P), since it overlaps the next pregnancy. A BreastfeedingNet pairs each newborn with a mother who breastfeeds, and ends the pair when she stops.
As agents, a woman who leaves P (a delivery, a loss, or an abortion) faces conception again in the same step, for what is left of it (half a step); the children and records of a delivery (ti_delivered, since_birth, lactating) are made first, so a rate or a modifier that reads them sees this delivery. A rate given as a function (e.g. an override of conception_rate()) can be called more than once a step, for those who arrive in NP within it, so it should not draw random numbers.
Its parameters are listed in __init__(); code reacts to its events with add_callback(), e.g. preg.add_callback(preg.birth, fn). Its states and results are P (pregnant), ti_P, the scheduled delivery ti_exit_P (set_delivery() reschedules it), and the flows conception, birth, miscarriage, stillbirth, and abortion; as agents, lactating (breastfeeding).
Note: CRN safe as agents.

demographics.Pregnancy(pars=None, fetus='auto', metadata=None, **kwargs)
Pregnancy, as declared states and transitions
Everyone is in NP (not pregnant: men and children too) or P (pregnant). Gestational age is P.time. Conception is one transition, so contraception, HIV, or LAM are modifiers of it (ss.modify(preg.conception, multiply=...)). A pregnancy ends in an abortion (at once, with p_abortion), a miscarriage or stillbirth (a hazard before or after loss_threshold), a maternal death (antepartum), or a delivery at the end of a dwell of dur_pregnancy. Each delivery gives embryos_per_pregnancy children (birth): as agents, new agents whose parent is the mother, placed in each declared module’s state given by its own ss.birth(per=preg.delivery) (or else its first state). Children die before the age of 1 at infant_rate (infant_mortality; 0 by default). It runs as agents under solver='auto'; a compartmental solver named explicitly runs a small approximate form (see compartmental_form()).
For other modules, preg.delivery happens to the mother, and to her fetuses (if they are agents: see _init_fetus()) before they are born, so a death of a fetus where=preg.delivery is a stillbirth; preg.birth happens to the newborns, so a neonatal death is where=preg.birth.
As agents, a live birth starts breastfeeding (lactating, with p_breastfeed), or restarts it for a woman breastfeeding already; it ends after dur_breastfeed, or at once if a child of hers dies before the age of 1. It is a state of each woman rather than one of the module’s exclusive states (NP, P), since it overlaps the next pregnancy. A BreastfeedingNet pairs each newborn with a mother who breastfeeds, and ends the pair when she stops.
As agents, a woman who leaves P (a delivery, a loss, or an abortion) faces conception again in the same step, for what is left of it (half a step); the children and records of a delivery (ti_delivered, since_birth, lactating) are made first, so a rate or a modifier that reads them sees this delivery. A rate given as a function (e.g. an override of conception_rate()) can be called more than once a step, for those who arrive in NP within it, so it should not draw random numbers.
Its parameters are listed in __init__(); code reacts to its events with add_callback(), e.g. preg.add_callback(preg.birth, fn). Its states and results are P (pregnant), ti_P, the scheduled delivery ti_exit_P (set_delivery() reschedules it), and the flows conception, birth, miscarriage, stillbirth, and abortion; as agents, lactating (breastfeeding).
Note: CRN safe as agents.

title: gradients
text:
gradients
gradients
The ODE run in JAX: gradients of results with respect to parameters, and many runs at once
A compartmental engine flattens its flows into a ss.kernels.Program. The Numba kernels step through it; run() here takes the same program and runs the same fourth-order Runge-Kutta (or Euler) steps in JAX, so that the run can be differentiated (gradient()) and many runs with different values can be taken in one call (run_sets()). JAX is imported only when one of these is used.
What JAX differentiates is the run: the program’s numbers, and the compartments at the start, to the compartments and flows at every step. The steps either side of it are Python (working out those numbers from the parameters, and the results from the run, including outcomes and the goodness of fit), and are differentiated by central differences along the direction the run is differentiated in. They are cheap and smooth, so this is accurate to about 1e-9 of the value.

people.People.request_death(uids, cause=None, hazard=None)
External-facing function to request an agent die at the current timestep
In general, users should not directly interact with People.ti_dead to minimize interactions between modules (e.g., if a module requesting a future death, overwrites death due to a different module taking place at the current timestep).
Modules that have a future time of death (e.g., due to disease duration) should keep track of that internally. When the module is ready to cause the agent to die, it should call this method, with itself as the cause.
The actual deaths are resolved after modules have all run, but before analyzers. That way, regardless of whether removing dead agents is enabled or not, analyzers will be able to see and record outcomes for agents that died this timestep.

title: API
text:
analyzers
Define analyzers, which are used to track variables when the sim is run.


connectors
Define connectors, which are used to mediate interactions between modules when the sim is run.


data
Data by place: ages, populations, birth and death rates, contact matrices, and administrative units


demographics
Births, deaths, migration, and pregnancy


diseases
Diseases: the base class (ss.Disease), diseases with transmission written as code (ss.Infection), and the textbook models (ss.SIR, ss.SIS, ss.SEIR)


distributions
The distributions to choose from: ss.uniform, ss.normal, ss.poisson, and so on, each a random-number-safe ss.Dist


fit
Fitting sims to data: likelihoods, particle filters, samplers, and what sim.fit() runs


geo
Places and the movement between them: a geography (ss.geo.geography), and movement between its places (ss.geo.Mobility, from a matrix, a data file of moves, or a movement model: ss.geo.gravity or ss.geo.radiation)


interventions
Interventions, which change the course of a sim during a run


networks
Networks and mixing pools: who meets whom, and so who can infect whom


people
The people in a sim (ss.People), lazy references to their properties (ss.ppl), and how they are made


products
Products: vaccines, treatments, and diagnostics, and the protection people hold from them


results
Results: the values a sim records at each time point (ss.Result), the containers that hold them (ss.Results), and how they are compared with data (ss.simdata)


run
Running many sims: ss.parallel() and ss.MultiSim


settings
Options for Starsim, and the plotting style


sim
The sim (ss.Sim) and its parameters (ss.SimPars)


strains
Strains of a disease (ss.Strains), and protection between them (ss.immunity)


transitions
States, transitions, and the expressions that drive them.


utils
Numerical utilities and other helper functions

title: internals.gradients
text:
internals.gradients
Not for the user: the ODE run in JAX: gradients of results with respect to parameters, and many runs at once
A compartmental engine flattens its flows into a ss.kernels.Program. The Numba kernels step through it; run() here takes the same program and runs the same fourth-order Runge-Kutta (or Euler) steps in JAX, so that the run can be differentiated (gradient()) and many runs with different values can be taken in one call (run_sets()). JAX is imported only when one of these is used.
What JAX differentiates is the run: the program’s numbers, and the compartments at the start, to the compartments and flows at every step. The steps either side of it are Python (working out those numbers from the parameters, and the results from the run, including outcomes and the goodness of fit), and are differentiated by central differences along the direction the run is differentiated in. They are cheap and smooth, so this is accurate to about 1e-9 of the value.
Used with: compartments; declared modules

internals.gradients.jax()
Import JAX (imported only when first used, since it takes a few tenths of a second)
If JAX has not been imported yet, it is given a device for each core of the CPU (as numpyro.set_host_device_count() does), so that the chains of a posterior run on cores of their own; everything else runs on the first, as before. The platform it runs on is ss.options.jax (e.g. “cpu”), if not “auto”. The first time, its devices are started here, so that a GPU that fails to start (e.g. with a CUDA plugin of another version than jaxlib) says what to do.

whether the result scales with the population (by pop_scale, the people each agent stands for): by default (‘auto’), by its kind, so a flow or stock (a count, e.g. infections) does, and a ratio (e.g. prevalence) does not
'auto'

kind
str
what the result is, which decides how it behaves: ‘flow’ (a number of events in each step, e.g. new infections; it has a cumulative total, and is summed over each period of data it is compared with), ‘stock’ (a quantity at each time point, e.g. the number infected), ‘ratio’ (one quantity divided by another, e.g. prevalence; one that keeps its numerator and denominator sums each over a period, then divides), or None for a result with no meaning over time. The kind also sets the default scale. By default (‘auto’) it is guessed from summarize_by if only that is given, or else from the name (new_... is a flow; n_..., cum_..., and cumulative are stocks), or else from the dtype: an integer is a count, guessed to be a flow (a count over each step, e.g. doses given), and anything else is a ratio. Give kind='stock' for a count of people at each time point with no such name (e.g. ss.Result('vaccinated', dtype=int, kind='stock')), and kind= for anything else the guess gets wrong
'auto'


summarize_by
str
how the result is summarized over time (and resampled): by default (‘auto’), by its kind: ‘sum’ for a flow, ‘last’ for a stock, ‘mean’ for a ratio, and None for none; or another way, e.g. ‘mean’ to average a flow over time, or any other key of ss.Result.summarizers
'auto'

list
if provided, make a 2D result of shape (npts, len(columns)), with these names for the columns, e.g. ['wild', 'alpha']
None


runs
dataframe
for a result across the runs of a MultiSim: one row per run, with its scenario (and the values of any parameters swept); the values then have a run axis first, of shape (n_runs, npts)
None


groups
bool
for a module written as code in a stratified sim: keep the values by group too, so they can be selected (res.select(sex='female'), res.by('age')) as a declared module’s are; set them with set_groups()
False



In most cases, ss.Result behaves exactly like np.array(), except with the additional fields listed above. To see everything contained in a result, you can use result.disp().
For a 2D result, res.alpha or res['alpha'] returns a 1D result for that column (which shares data with the 2D result), and res[ti] returns the row for that timestep.



res = ss.Result('infection', columns=['wild', 'alpha'], shape=10)
res[3] = [20, 5] # Set the values for timestep 3
res['alpha'][4] = 8 # Set one value for timestep 4
res['alpha'].label # Returns 'infection (alpha)'
A result across the runs of a MultiSim (msim.results.sir.I) is the same result with a run axis first: select() also takes run= (a position), scenario=, and the parameters swept; quantiles(), median(), and mean() summarize over the runs of each scenario; and plot() draws the median and a 95% interval of each scenario (lines=True draws every run).
```python
msim = sim.run(n_runs=10)
I = msim.results.sir.I # Runs by time points
I.select(run=3) # One run, as a result of one sim
low, mid, high = I.quantiles([0.025, 0.5, 0.975])
I.median().plot()
```

results.Result.resample(new_unit=None, summarize_by=None, use_years=False)
Resample the result to a longer time unit, by its summarize_by (which by default follows its kind)
A flow is summed over each period, a stock takes its value at the end of each period, and a ratio sums its numerator and denominator over each period (by group, if it has them) and divides them (one with no parts is averaged over the period). Periods start at the sim’s start and include their end, as for data; calendar months and years are used instead for a sim with dates. Each period is labeled by its end: for calendar months and years, the first day of the next (so a year of weekly steps is labeled 1 January of the next year, not the week ending after it), or the end of the run if sooner; otherwise its last time point. The values by group (select() and by()) are resampled too.

def init_results(self):
    super().init_results()
    self.define_results(ss.Result('n_infected', groups=True), ss.Result('prevalence', scale=False, groups=True))

def update_results(self):
    super().update_results()
    alive, infected = self.sim.groups.count(), self.sim.groups.count(self.infected)

    self.results.prevalence.set_groups(self.ti, infected, alive)

By default (‘auto’) it is guessed from summarize_by if only that is given, or else from the name (new_... is a flow; n_..., cum_..., and cumulative are stocks), or else from the dtype: an integer is a count, guessed to be a flow (a count over each step, e.g. doses given), and anything else is a ratio. In most cases, ss.Result behaves exactly like np.array(), except with the additional fields listed above. To see everything contained in a result, you can use result.disp().
For a 2D result, res.alpha or res['alpha'] returns a 1D result for that column (which shares data with the 2D result), and res[ti] returns the row for that timestep.



res = ss.Result('infection', columns=['wild', 'alpha'], shape=10)
res[3] = [20, 5] # Set the values for timestep 3
res['alpha'][4] = 8 # Set one value for timestep 4
res['alpha'].label # Returns 'infection (alpha)'
A result across the runs of a MultiSim (msim.results.sir.I) is the same result with a run axis first: select() also takes run= (a position), scenario=, and the parameters swept; quantiles(), median(), and mean() summarize over the runs of each scenario; and plot() draws the median and a 95% interval of each scenario (lines=True draws every run).
```python
msim = sim.run(n_runs=10)
I = msim.results.sir.I # Runs by time points
I.select(run=3) # One run, as a result of one sim
low, mid, high = I.quantiles([0.025, 0.5, 0.975])
I.median().plot()
```
