results.Result.resample(new_unit=None, summarize_by=None, use_years=False)
Resample the result to a longer time unit, by its summarize_by (which by default follows its kind)
A flow is summed over each period, a stock takes its value at the end of each period, and a ratio sums its numerator and denominator over each period (by group, if it has them) and divides them (one with no parts is averaged over the period). Periods start at the sim’s start and include their end, as for data; calendar months and years are used instead for a sim with dates. Each period is labeled by its end: for calendar months and years, the first day of the next (so a year of weekly steps is labeled 1 January of the next year, not the week ending after it), or the end of the run if sooner; otherwise its last time point. The values by group (select() and by()) are resampled too.

# In a module written as code, in a sim stratified by sex and age
def init_results(self):
    super().init_results()
    self.define_results(ss.Result('n_infected', groups=True), ss.Result('prevalence', scale=False, groups=True))

def update_results(self):
    super().update_results()
    alive, infected = self.sim.groups.count(), self.sim.groups.count(self.infected)
    self.results.n_infected.set_groups(self.ti, infected)
    self.results.prevalence.set_groups(self.ti, infected, alive)

internals.time.DateConverter()
Starsim date conversion interface for matplotlib
It exists so that Matplotlib can plot ss.date and ss.dur values directly.
This class gets registered with matplotlib as the converter for Starsim date and DateArray types, allowing them to be used directly as axis values. This achieves two outcomes

When Starsim date or DateArray values are plotted, the x-axis values are automatically converted to float years for plotting. If this class is not used, matplotlib will instead convert them to days since 1970-01-01, which is the default behavior for pd.Timestamp.
If the first plotting command used on an axis has date/DateArray as the x-axis, our standard custom date locators and formatters will be used, so that the float years will automatically be labeled with dates.

Together, this means that users can freely plot both Starsim date/DateArray values and plain float years on the same axis without needing any conversions, and they’ll also automatically get date-based ticks without needing to set the locator, even if they are using custom plotting code rather than ss.Result.plot().

internals.time.FloatYearLocator(unit)
Locator to calculate tick positions for float year axes
It exists so that a plot against decimal years gets tick marks at sensible dates.
Matplotlib’s AutoDateLocator is the standard way to calculating date-based tick positions, incorporating a lot of functionality around sensibly setting the tick intervals e.g., to whole months. This class wraps AutoDateLocator to allow it to be used with float year axis values, by converting the float year values to matplotlib date values before calling the locator, and then converting the calculated tick positions back to float years before returning them.



internals.time.MockAxis(axis)
Emulator for Axis.get_view_internal() to return converted values
Matplotlib’s date locators (AutoDateLocator, YearLocator, MonthLocator etc.) call Axis.get_view_internal() to get the current axis limits. These locators all expect the values to be returned in matplotlib dates (i.e., days since 1970-01-01). This helper class is bound to the actual axis, and emulates Axis.get_view_interval() performing the conversion to return the values in the expected units. That way, the Locator instances can be used directly without needing any other changes.
When this class is instantiated, it is bound to an actual Axis instance. The axis instance would have our custom date units and values in floating point years. Then MockAxis.get_view_interval() converts these years to standard matplotlib date values before they get passed to the Matplotlib locators.

Convert this rate to one with a different denominator
As well as the rate classes (e.g. ss.permonth), a duration unit can be supplied (e.g. 'month' or ss.months), in which case the matching rate class of the same subtype is used – so ss.peryear(1).to('month') gives permonth(0.0833), while ss.probperyear(1).to('month') gives probpermonth(...).

internals.time.per(value, unit=None)
A per represents an instantaneous rate of an event occurring. Rates must be non-negative, but need not be less than 1.
Through multiplication, rate can be modified or converted to a probability, depending on the data type of the object being multiplied.
When a per is multiplied by a scalar or array, the rate is simply scaled. Such multiplication occurs frequently in epidemiological models, where the base rate is multiplied by “rate ratio” or “relative rate” to represent agents experiencing higher (multiplier > 1) or lower (multiplier < 1) event rates.
Alternatively, when a per is multiplied by a duration (type ss.dur), a probability is calculated. The conversion from rate to probability on multiplication by a duration is 1 - np.exp(-rate/factor), where factor is the ratio of the multiplied duration to the original period (denominator).
For example, consider >>> p = ss.per(0.8, ss.years(1)) When multiplied by a duration of 1 year, the calculated probability is 1 - np.exp(-0.8), which is approximately 55%. >>> p*ss.years(1)
When multiplied by a scalar, the rate is simply scaled. >>> p*2
The difference between prob and per is subtle, but important. per works directly with the instantaneous rate of an event occurring. In contrast, prob starts with a probability and a duration, and the underlying rate is calculated. On multiplication by a duration, * per: rate -> probability * prob: probability -> rate -> probability
The behavior of both classes is depending on the data type of the object being multiplied.
ss.per is identical to ss.freq, except by default multiplication returns a probability rather than a number of events. Use ss.per for probabilities (e.g., probability of death per year), and ss.freq for events (e.g., number of acts per year).



internals.time.peract(value=None, **directions)
A probability per act, for a transmission over a network that defines acts (e.g. ss.SexualNet)
It is not a time value: it has no unit and no conversion, so it means the same at any timestep. A partnership with a acts per unit time transmits over a step dt with probability 1 − (1 − p)^(a·dt). Modifiers, rel_trans, rel_sus, and source weights multiply the per-act hazard −ln(1 − p), so beta=0.03 with rel_trans=10 is 1 − 0.97^10 = 0.263 per act.

internals.time.prob(value=None, unit=None, rate=None)
prob represents the probability of an event occurring during a specified period of time.
The class is designed to allow conversion of a probability from one duration to another through multiplication. However, the behavior of this conversion depends on the data type of the the object being multiplied.
When multiplied by a duration (type ss.dur), the underlying constant rate is calculated as rate = -np.log(1 - self.value). Then, the probability over the new duration is p = 1 - np.exp(-rate/factor), where factor is the ratio of the new duration to the original duration.
For example, >>> p = ss.prob(0.8, ss.years(1)) indicates a 80% chance of an event occurring in one year.



p*ss.years(1) When multiplied by the original denominator, 1 year in this case, the probability remains unchanged, 80%.






p * ss.years(2) Multiplying p by ss.years(2) does not simply double the probability to 160% (which is not possible), but rather returns a new probability of 96% representing the chance of the event occurring at least once over the new duration of two years.



When a prob object is multiplied by a number, the underlying rate is scaled, not the probability, so the result is always a valid probability: >>> p * 2 is ss.prob(0.96, ss.years(1)), the same as p + p (two competing hazards), and p * 0.2 is 0.275, not 0.16. A probability of 1 is an infinite rate, so it stays 1 whatever it is multiplied by; as the rate of a declared transition, it moves everyone in the step (as agents, those who arrive in the step too; in compartments, the whole compartment at the start of each step or substep).
Use per instead if prob if you would prefer to directly specify the instantaneous rate.

internals.time.DateConverter()
Starsim date conversion interface for matplotlib
It exists so that Matplotlib can plot ss.date and ss.dur values directly.
This class gets registered with matplotlib as the converter for Starsim date and DateArray types, allowing them to be used directly as axis values. This achieves two outcomes

When Starsim date or DateArray values are plotted, the x-axis values are automatically converted to float years for plotting. If this class is not used, matplotlib will instead convert them to days since 1970-01-01, which is the default behavior for pd.Timestamp.
If the first plotting command used on an axis has date/DateArray as the x-axis, our standard custom date locators and formatters will be used, so that the float years will automatically be labeled with dates.

Together, this means that users can freely plot both Starsim date/DateArray values and plain float years on the same axis without needing any conversions, and they’ll also automatically get date-based ticks without needing to set the locator, even if they are using custom plotting code rather than ss.Result.plot().

When this class is instantiated, it is bound to an actual Axis instance. The axis instance would have our custom date units and values in floating point years. internals.time.per(value, unit=None)
A per represents an instantaneous rate of an event occurring. Rates must be non-negative, but need not be less than 1.
Through multiplication, rate can be modified or converted to a probability, depending on the data type of the object being multiplied.
When a per is multiplied by a scalar or array, the rate is simply scaled. Such multiplication occurs frequently in epidemiological models, where the base rate is multiplied by “rate ratio” or “relative rate” to represent agents experiencing higher (multiplier > 1) or lower (multiplier < 1) event rates.
Alternatively, when a per is multiplied by a duration (type ss.dur), a probability is calculated. The conversion from rate to probability on multiplication by a duration is 1 - np.exp(-rate/factor), where factor is the ratio of the multiplied duration to the original period (denominator).
For example, consider >>> p = ss.per(0.8, ss.years(1)) When multiplied by a duration of 1 year, the calculated probability is 1 - np.exp(-0.8), which is approximately 55%. >>> p*ss.years(1)
When multiplied by a scalar, the rate is simply scaled. >>> p*2
The difference between prob and per is subtle, but important. per works directly with the instantaneous rate of an event occurring. In contrast, prob starts with a probability and a duration, and the underlying rate is calculated. On multiplication by a duration, * per: rate -> probability * prob: probability -> rate -> probability
The behavior of both classes is depending on the data type of the object being multiplied.
ss.per is identical to ss.freq, except by default multiplication returns a probability rather than a number of events. Use ss.per for probabilities (e.g., probability of death per year), and ss.freq for events (e.g., number of acts per year).



internals.time.peract(value=None, **directions)
A probability per act, for a transmission over a network that defines acts (e.g. ss.SexualNet)
It is not a time value: it has no unit and no conversion, so it means the same at any timestep. A partnership with a acts per unit time transmits over a step dt with probability 1 − (1 − p)^(a·dt). Modifiers, rel_trans, rel_sus, and source weights multiply the per-act hazard −ln(1 − p), so beta=0.03 with rel_trans=10 is 1 − 0.97^10 = 0.263 per act.

Type

None

a value for each direction of the network, named <side>2<side> from the network’s sides (net.directions), e.g. m2f and f2m on ss.SexualNet
{}



Each value is a number in [0, 1], an ss.par, an expression of them, an ss.timeseries, or an ss.by over a dimension of the susceptible. A direction can also be written as a pair of sides, {('m', 'f'): 0.3}, which is the same as m2f=0.3. Every direction of the network needs a value (unless one is given for all), and a direction it does not have raises; both are checked when the sim is initialized. On a route without acts (ss.RandomNet, mixing pools), it raises a ValueError.



S, I = ss.states(2)
hiv = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ dict(sexualnet=ss.peract(m2f=0.001, f2m=0.0005), needles=ss.peract(0.006))*I)

internals.time.prob(value=None, unit=None, rate=None)
prob represents the probability of an event occurring during a specified period of time.
The class is designed to allow conversion of a probability from one duration to another through multiplication. However, the behavior of this conversion depends on the data type of the the object being multiplied.
When multiplied by a duration (type ss.dur), the underlying constant rate is calculated as rate = -np.log(1 - self.value). Then, the probability over the new duration is p = 1 - np.exp(-rate/factor), where factor is the ratio of the new duration to the original duration.
For example, >>> p = ss.prob(0.8, ss.years(1)) indicates a 80% chance of an event occurring in one year.



p*ss.years(1) When multiplied by the original denominator, 1 year in this case, the probability remains unchanged, 80%.






p * ss.years(2) Multiplying p by ss.years(2) does not simply double the probability to 160% (which is not possible), but rather returns a new probability of 96% representing the chance of the event occurring at least once over the new duration of two years.



When a prob object is multiplied by a number, the underlying rate is scaled, not the probability, so the result is always a valid probability: >>> p * 2 is ss.prob(0.96, ss.years(1)), the same as p + p (two competing hazards), and p * 0.2 is 0.275, not 0.16. A probability of 1 is an infinite rate, so it stays 1 whatever it is multiplied by; as the rate of a declared transition, it moves everyone in the step (as agents, those who arrive in the step too; in compartments, the whole compartment at the start of each step or substep).
Use per instead if prob if you would prefer to directly specify the instantaneous rate.

title: internals.timeline
text:
internals.timeline
Timelines: the time vectors of a sim and of each of its modules
They exist so that sim.t and module.t give the current step and date, and a module can step at its own rate.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Timeline
Handle time vectors and sequencing (“timelines”) for both simulations and modules.





internals.timeline.Timeline(
    start=None,
    stop=None,
    dt=None,
    dur=None,
    name=None,
    init=None,
    sim=None,
)
Handle time vectors and sequencing (“timelines”) for both simulations and modules.
Each module can have its own time instance, in the case where the time vector is defined by absolute dates, these time vectors are by definition aligned. Otherwise they can be specified using dur objects which express relative times (they can be added to a date to get an absolute time)





Name
Type
Description
Default




start
str/int/float/ss.date/ss.dur
when the simulation/module starts, e.g. ‘2000’, ‘2000-01-01’, 2000, ss.date(2000), or ss.years(2000)
None


stop
str/int/float/ss.date/ss.dur
when the simulation/module ends (note: if start is a date, stop must be too)
None


dt
int/float/ss.dur
Simulation step size
None


dur
int/float/ss.dur
If “stop” is not provided, run for this duration
None


name
str
if provided, name the Timeline object
None


init
bool
whether or not to immediately initialize the Timeline object (by default, yes if start and stop or start and dur are provided; otherwise no)
None


sim
Sim
if provided, initialize the Timeline with this as the parent (i.e. populating missing values)
None



The Timeline object, after initialization, has the following time vectors, each representing a different way of representing time:

tvec: ground truth simulation time, either as absolute ss.date instances, or relative ss.dur instances, e.g. DateArray([<2021-01-01>, <2021-01-03>, <2021-01-05>, <2021-01-07>])
tivec: the vector of time indices (np.arange(len(tvec)))
timevec: the “human-friendly” representation of tvec: same as tvec if using ss.date, else floats if using ss.dur
yearvec: time represented as floating-point years
datevec: time represented as ss.date instances
relvec: relative time, in the sim’s time units

The Timeline object also has the following attributes/methods:

ti (int): the current step, which is also the time point where its results go: step ti runs from time point ti-1 to ti (0 before the first step)
npts (int): the total number of time points in the timeline (one more than the number of steps; see note below)
now() (ss.date/float/str): the current time, the start of the step (time point ti-1; the start of the run before the first step), based on tvec by default or a different vector if specified

Note: the time vectors include both the start and stop endpoints, so npts (the number of time points) is one more than the number of steps taken. For example, start=0, stop=1, dt=1 runs a single step but produces two time points ([0, 1]), since the state is recorded at both the start and the end. Specifying the length via dur is exactly equivalent to specifying stop (internally, stop = start + dur), so e.g. start=2000, dur=1 and start=2000, stop=2001 produce identical timelines. See the time user guide for the rationale behind the inclusive endpoint.



t1 = ss.Timeline(start=2000, stop=2020, dt=1.0)
t2 = ss.Timeline(start='2021-01-01', stop='2021-04-04', dt=ss.days(2))

title: errors
text:
errors
Errors, warnings, and notes.
Each error is an exception class, e.g. ss.errors.UnknownState, and each warning a warning class, e.g. ss.errors.ImportIncomplete. A note is a line about something that was assumed or approximated: it is kept in sim.notes and printed when verbose is 1 or more (see ss.note()). The docstring of each class says when it is raised, and is what the catalog in the specification (15-errors.md) is made from: see ss.errors.catalog().





Name
Description




AlreadyRunError
A sim that has already run (or been finalized) is stepped, finalized, or added to again; sim.run() runs it again from the start


CapabilityError
The requested solver cannot run part of the model. Three cases: there is no sensible approximation (contact tracing,


CodedError
Base class for Starsim’s named errors, e.g. ss.errors.UnknownState; except ss.CodedError catches any of them


Note
Base class for Starsim’s named notes, e.g. ss.errors.UnitInferred; a note is said with ss.note()


StarsimWarning
Base class for Starsim’s named warnings, e.g. ss.errors.ImportIncomplete





errors.AlreadyRunError(*args)
A sim that has already run (or been finalized) is stepped, finalized, or added to again; sim.run() runs it again from the start



errors.CapabilityError()
The requested solver cannot run part of the model. Three cases: there is no sensible approximation (contact tracing, transmission trees, agent-only custom code); a function or condition asked for something that exists only per agent in a compartmental run; or an approximation would be needed and approx=False. Names the part, what it asked for, and what would fix it

internals.modules.Module(name=None, label=None, **kwargs)
The main base class for all Starsim modules: diseases, networks, interventions, etc.
By convention, keyword arguments to modules are assigned to “_“, which is an alias for None. These are then populated with defaults by mod.define_pars(), which are then updated with mod.update_pars(), which inspects the __init__ function to get these arguments.
Note that there is no functional difference between specifying arguments this way rather than simply via **kwargs, but having the arguments shown in the function signature can make it easier to read, and “_” is a convention to indicate that the default is specified below.
It is also of course OK to specify the actual values rather than “_“; however module arguments are often complex objects (e.g. ss.bernoulli) that can’t be easily specified in the function signature.
Finally, note that you can (and should) call super().__init__() with no arguments: the name, label, and time arguments get correctly updated via self.update_pars().

class SIR(ss.Module):
    def __init__(self, pars=_, beta=_, init_prev=_, p_death=_, **kwargs):
        super().__init__() # Call this first with no arguments
        self.define_pars( # Then define the parameters, including their default value
            beta = ss.peryear(0.1),
            init_prev = ss.bernoulli(p=0.01),
            p_death = ss.bernoulli(p=0.3),
        )
        self.update_pars(pars, **kwargs) # Update with any user-supplied parameters, and raise an exception if trying to set a parameter that wasn't defined in define_pars()
        return

internals.modules.Module.define_aliases(overwrite=False, **kwargs)
Define aliases for states, e.g. self.define_aliases(infectious='infected')
An alias is only used if the attribute isn’t otherwise defined, so it acts as a default that a subclass overrides simply by defining a state of the same name. This is how ss.Infection treats everyone infected as infectious, while letting a subclass define infectious as a state (or another alias) in its own right.
Each alias is either the name of another state, or a callable taking the module as its only argument. A callable behaves like a property: it is recomputed on each access, so it can be read but not written to.
Note: a callable alias defined as a lambda can’t be saved with plain pickle (sc.save() and ss.MultiSim are both fine, since they use dill). Use a module-level function, or a property, if plain pickling is required.
A callable alias also generates an automatic result, in the same way a BoolState does: an alias named infected produces the result infected. A string alias does not, since the state it points to is already counted under its own name.

internals.modules.Module.from_func(func)
Create a module from a function
Wraps a plain function into a module of the calling class, so that simple, one-off logic can be used anywhere a module is expected without writing a full class. The function must take the sim as its only argument; it becomes the module’s step() method and is therefore called once on every timestep (so it must do its own time gating, e.g. if sim.now == 2015:). The module’s name is taken from the function’s name.
This is the mechanism behind “function-based” interventions and analyzers: passing a function to interventions=, analyzers=, or custom= automatically calls from_func() on the appropriate class (ss.Intervention, ss.Analyzer, or ss.Module respectively), so usually you don’t need to call this method directly. Call it explicitly when you want to construct the module yourself, e.g. to add it to a sim later.
Keyword arguments of the function with defaults are the module’s parameters, passed to it at each call; one given as ss.par with bounds can be fitted (sim.fit()), sampled (sim.sensitivity()), and set by name (ss.Sim(pars=...), ss.parallel(pars=...)) as any other. This is how to fit a value that is not a parameter of any module, e.g. one set in code (see the second example).
Function-based modules are otherwise minimal: they have no states or results of their own. As soon as you need define_states() or define_results(), write a proper subclass instead.











Name
Type
Description
Default

callable
a function taking the sim, and optionally keyword arguments with defaults (its parameters)
required









Name
Type
Description




mod
Module

Example::
import starsim as ss

def knockdown(sim): # Halve transmission for one year starting in 2015
    if sim.now == 2015:
        sim.diseases.sis.rel_trans[:] *= 0.5

# Explicit construction ...
intv = ss.Intervention.from_func(knockdown)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks='random', interventions=intv)

# ... or equivalently, let the sim convert it automatically:
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks='random', interventions=knockdown)

# A value set in code, fitted: the share of transmission left in 2015
def knockdown(sim, share=ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.1, 1])):
    if sim.now == 2015:
        sim.diseases.sis.rel_trans[:] *= share

internals.modules.required()
Decorator to mark module methods as required.
A common gotcha in Starsim is to forget to call super(), or to mistype a method name so it’s never called. This decorator lets you mark methods (of Modules only) to be sure that they are called either on sim initialization or on sim run.


import starsim.library as ssl

class CustomSIS(ssl.AgentSIS):

    def step(self):
        super().step()
        self.custom_step() # Will raise an exception if this line is not here
        return

    @ss.required() # Mark this method as required on run
    def custom_step(self):
        pass

internals.modules.Module.define_aliases(overwrite=False, **kwargs)
Define aliases for states, e.g. self.define_aliases(infectious='infected')
An alias is only used if the attribute isn’t otherwise defined, so it acts as a default that a subclass overrides simply by defining a state of the same name. This is how ss.Infection treats everyone infected as infectious, while letting a subclass define infectious as a state (or another alias) in its own right.
Each alias is either the name of another state, or a callable taking the module as its only argument. A callable behaves like a property: it is recomputed on each access, so it can be read but not written to.
Note: a callable alias defined as a lambda can’t be saved with plain pickle (sc.save() and ss.MultiSim are both fine, since they use dill). Use a module-level function, or a property, if plain pickling is required.
A callable alias also generates an automatic result, in the same way a BoolState does: an alias named infected produces the result infected. A string alias does not, since the state it points to is already counted under its own name.

internals.modules.Module.from_func(func)
Create a module from a function
Wraps a plain function into a module of the calling class, so that simple, one-off logic can be used anywhere a module is expected without writing a full class. The function must take the sim as its only argument; it becomes the module’s step() method and is therefore called once on every timestep (so it must do its own time gating, e.g. if sim.now == 2015:). The module’s name is taken from the function’s name.
This is the mechanism behind “function-based” interventions and analyzers: passing a function to interventions=, analyzers=, or custom= automatically calls from_func() on the appropriate class (ss.Intervention, ss.Analyzer, or ss.Module respectively), so usually you don’t need to call this method directly. Call it explicitly when you want to construct the module yourself, e.g. to add it to a sim later.
Keyword arguments of the function with defaults are the module’s parameters, passed to it at each call; one given as ss.par with bounds can be fitted (sim.fit()), sampled (sim.sensitivity()), and set by name (ss.Sim(pars=...), ss.parallel(pars=...)) as any other. This is how to fit a value that is not a parameter of any module, e.g. one set in code (see the second example).
Function-based modules are otherwise minimal: they have no states or results of their own. As soon as you need define_states() or define_results(), write a proper subclass instead.

Type
Description
Default

required

Type
Description

import starsim as ss

def knockdown(sim): # Halve transmission for one year starting in 2015
    if sim.now == 2015:
        sim.diseases.sis.rel_trans[:] *= 0.5

# Explicit construction ...
intv = ss.Intervention.from_func(knockdown)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks='random', interventions=intv)

# ... or equivalently, let the sim convert it automatically:
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks='random', interventions=knockdown)

# A value set in code, fitted: the share of transmission left in 2015
def knockdown(sim, share=ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.1, 1])):
    if sim.now == 2015:
        sim.diseases.sis.rel_trans[:] *= share

internals.modules.required()
Decorator to mark module methods as required.
A common gotcha in Starsim is to forget to call super(), or to mistype a method name so it’s never called. This decorator lets you mark methods (of Modules only) to be sure that they are called either on sim initialization or on sim run.


import starsim.library as ssl

class CustomSIS(ssl.AgentSIS):

    def step(self):
        super().step()
        self.custom_step() # Will raise an exception if this line is not here
        return

    @ss.required() # Mark this method as required on run
    def custom_step(self):
        pass

The sides of the network and the property of people it matches or counts partners by must be dimensions of the model. Partners are drawn from the population at random, in proportion to the partners each person has, within the other side for a network between men and women, and with match=, the share at the same level that it gives.

Exposure of each group through one term of the mixing: see exposure()



solvers.mixing.Mixing.within_places(term)
Make a contact matrix act within each place
The cells of the matrix become pairs of a place and a level, and the movement between places applies to each level: people mix by the matrix with the people present where they are. A matrix that is given over the places themselves already says who meets whom across them, so it is used as it is.
The mixing is the product of the time share between places and the matrix between levels (np.kron(share, matrix)), but is kept as the two factors, which is much smaller and faster with many places: see term_exposure().

Make a contact matrix act within each place
The cells of the matrix become pairs of a place and a level, and the movement between places applies to each level: people mix by the matrix with the people present where they are. A matrix that is given over the places themselves already says who meets whom across them, so it is used as it is.
The mixing is the product of the time share between places and the matrix between levels (np.kron(share, matrix)), but is kept as the two factors, which is much smaller and faster with many places: see term_exposure().

library.networks
Additional network types: household, cluster, spatial, and theoretical.
HouseholdNet builds households from DHS-style survey data; ClusterNet divides agents into fully connected clusters, and HybridNet is Covasim’s population of households, schools, workplaces, and community; DiskNet connects agents that are spatially close, GeoNet connects them across real places, and GridNet puts them on a lattice; ErdosRenyiNet and NullNet are useful for theoretical work and debugging, SmallWorldNet and ScaleFreeNet are the classic graphs, and StaticNet turns a NetworkX graph into a network. Core network classes (ss.RandomNet, ss.DegreeNet, ss.SexualNet, etc.) live in starsim.networks.
Most of these networks run as agents only. Those a compartmental run can approximate by a mean number of contacts are marked in their files.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules

Description

Fully connected clusters of agents, e.g. households, schools, or workplaces

Disk graph in which edges are made between agents located within a user-defined radius.

Fully connected clusters of agents, e.g. households, schools, or workplaces
Each agent (optionally, only those within an age range) is assigned to one cluster, with cluster sizes drawn from cluster_size, and every pair of agents within a cluster is connected. Agents are assigned to clusters in a random order (from a CRN-safe random number per agent), so clusters are not correlated with other networks. library.networks.ErdosRenyiNet(pars=None, **kwargs)
In the Erdos-Renyi network, every possible edge has a probability, p, of being created on each time step.
The degree of each node will have a binomial distribution, considering each of the N-1 possible edges connection this node to the others will be created with probability p.
Please be careful with the dur parameter. When set to 0, new edges will be created on each time step. If positive, edges will persist for dur years. Note that the existence of edges from previous time steps will not prevent or otherwise alter the creation of new edges on each time step, edges will accumulate over time.
Warning: this network is quite slow compared to ss.RandomNet.
Note: CRN safe.

library.networks.GeoNet(
    places='Kenya',
    level=1,
    local=0.9,
    c=2.0,
    pars=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Random contacts between real places
Each agent lives in a place, in proportion to its population. Most of an agent’s contacts are in their own place, and the rest are in other places, more of them in places that are large and near, as in a gravity model: the share going from place i to place j is in proportion to pop_j/distance_ij**c. Within each place, contacts are paired at random. A country’s places need no download (see ss.geo.geography).
The place of each agent is the state place, an index into geo.names. Like ss.RandomNet, this is not CRN safe when people are born or die.

library.networks.HouseholdNet(
    pars=None,
    dhs_data=None,
    dynamic=True,
    prob_move_out=_,
    update_freq=_,
    **kwargs,
)
A household contact network built from DHS-style survey data.
When initialized, this network overrides the age (and optionally sex) of all agents in the sim and assigns each agent a household ID. Use with caution if other modules depend upon or alter age and sex.
Households are created by selecting a random household from the provided data and setting the age and sex of agents to match, repeating until all agents have been assigned to a household. Ages in the data are typically in integer years; a random fractional year is added so agents don’t share exact ages.
This network assumes only one mother per household. Births are automatically added to their mother’s household network.
Note: not CRN safe unless dynamic=False (the partners who move out are drawn together).





Name
Type
Description
Default




dhs_data
DataFrame / str
A pandas or Sciris dataframe with columns hh_id and ages. Optionally also sexes. The ages column should contain comma-separated age strings (e.g. "72, 17, 30"). If sexes is included, it should contain comma-separated values using DHS convention (1 = male, 2 = female) with the same number of entries as ages. Pass 'default' to use synthetic data (see make_default_data()), e.g. for demos and testing.
None


dynamic
bool
If True (default), households evolve over time: one female is assigned as head of each household, pregnant non-head females may move out to form new households, and births are added to the mother’s household. Requires the Pregnancy module. If False, the network is static and step() is a no-op.
True


prob_move_out
float
Probability a non-head female moves out to start her own household, evaluated once at the start of each pregnancy. Default 0.7. Only used when dynamic=True.
_


update_freq
int
How often (in timesteps) to update the network. Default 1. Only used when dynamic=True.
_


pars
dict
the same parameters, as a dict
None



The expected dataframe format is::
    hh_id                ages          sexes
0       0          72, 17, 30        1, 1, 2
1       1                  37              2
2       2          13, 55, 36        2, 1, 2
3       3  52, 13, 12, 64, 53     1, 2, 1, 2
4       4              30, 66           1, 1
Data in this format can be obtained from the DHS Program <https://dhsprogram.com>_. To prepare a DHS household dataset:

Register and request access at https://dhsprogram.com
Download a Household Recode (HR) dataset in Stata format (e.g. XXHR7xDT.zip)
Use HouseholdNet.load_dhs() to extract the data::
import starsim as ss; import starsim.library as ssl dhs_data = ssl.networks.HouseholdNet.load_dhs(‘XXHR7xDT/XXHR7xFL.DTA’) sim = ss.Sim(networks=ssl.networks.HouseholdNet(dhs_data=dhs_data)) sim.run()

If real data are not available, synthetic data can be constructed::
import numpy as np
import sciris as sc
import starsim as ss; import starsim.library as ssl

n = 1000
age_strings = []
for i in range(n):
    household_size = np.random.randint(1, 6)
    ages = np.random.randint(0, 80, household_size)
    age_strings.append(sc.strjoin(ages))
dhs_data = sc.dataframe(hh_id=np.arange(n), ages=age_strings)

household = ssl.networks.HouseholdNet(dhs_data=dhs_data)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks=household)
sim.run()
sim.plot()

library.networks.HybridNet(
    pars=None,
    household_size=_,
    contacts=_,
    beta=_,
    school_ages=_,
    work_ages=_,
    dynamic=_,
    method=_,
    clustered=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Covasim v3’s “hybrid” population: households, schools, workplaces, and community
When added to a sim, this expands into four separate networks: households (h), schools (s), and workplaces (w), each an ssl.ClusterNet, and community (c), an ss.RandomNet with Poisson-distributed contacts. Schools and workplaces are restricted by age. As in Covasim v3, the networks are static; unlike it, schools and workplaces are clusters by default, so that a person’s contacts also know each other (use clustered=False for Covasim v3’s random networks). With the default Poisson sizes, clusters give the same mean number of contacts as a random network. Each network can then be modified separately, e.g. sim.networks.s.
The default beta values are Covasim v3’s per-layer relative transmissibility, and are applied to the edges of each network; for per-network transmissibility on the disease instead, set them to 1 and use e.g. ss.SIS(beta=dict(h=0.3, s=0.06, w=0.06, c=0.03)).
Note: CRN safe, unless dynamic=True and people are born or die.

if True (default), schools and workplaces are ssl.ClusterNets, sized to give contacts for Poisson and constant distributions (other distributions are used directly as cluster sizes, which gives a different mean); if False, they are ss.RandomNets, as in Covasim v3

library.networks.StaticNet(graph=None, pars=None, **kwargs)
A network class of static partnerships converted from a networkx graph. There’s no formation of new partnerships and initialized partnerships only end when one of the partners dies. The networkx graph can be created outside Starsim if population size is known. Or the graph can be created by passing a networkx generator function to Starsim.

    pars=None,
    dhs_data=None,
    dynamic=True,
    prob_move_out=_,
    update_freq=_,
    **kwargs,
)
A household contact network built from DHS-style survey data.
When initialized, this network overrides the age (and optionally sex) of all agents in the sim and assigns each agent a household ID. Use with caution if other modules depend upon or alter age and sex.
Households are created by selecting a random household from the provided data and setting the age and sex of agents to match, repeating until all agents have been assigned to a household. Ages in the data are typically in integer years; a random fractional year is added so agents don’t share exact ages.
This network assumes only one mother per household. Births are automatically added to their mother’s household network.
Note: not CRN safe unless dynamic=False (the partners who move out are drawn together).





Name
Type
Description
Default




dhs_data
DataFrame / str
A pandas or Sciris dataframe with columns hh_id and ages. Optionally also sexes. The ages column should contain comma-separated age strings (e.g. "72, 17, 30"). If sexes is included, it should contain comma-separated values using DHS convention (1 = male, 2 = female) with the same number of entries as ages. Pass 'default' to use synthetic data (see make_default_data()), e.g. for demos and testing.
None


dynamic
bool
If True (default), households evolve over time: one female is assigned as head of each household, pregnant non-head females may move out to form new households, and births are added to the mother’s household. Requires the Pregnancy module. If False, the network is static and step() is a no-op.
True

float
Probability a non-head female moves out to start her own household, evaluated once at the start of each pregnancy. Default 0.7. Only used when dynamic=True.
_


update_freq
int
How often (in timesteps) to update the network. Default 1. Only used when dynamic=True.
_

dict
the same parameters, as a dict
None



The expected dataframe format is::
    hh_id                ages          sexes
0       0          72, 17, 30        1, 1, 2
1       1                  37              2
2       2          13, 55, 36        2, 1, 2
3       3  52, 13, 12, 64, 53     1, 2, 1, 2
4       4              30, 66           1, 1
Data in this format can be obtained from the DHS Program <https://dhsprogram.com>_. To prepare a DHS household dataset:

Register and request access at https://dhsprogram.com
Download a Household Recode (HR) dataset in Stata format (e.g. XXHR7xDT.zip)
Use HouseholdNet.load_dhs() to extract the data::
import starsim as ss; import starsim.library as ssl dhs_data = ssl.networks.HouseholdNet.load_dhs(‘XXHR7xDT/XXHR7xFL.DTA’) sim = ss.Sim(networks=ssl.networks.HouseholdNet(dhs_data=dhs_data)) sim.run()

If real data are not available, synthetic data can be constructed::
import numpy as np
import sciris as sc
import starsim as ss; import starsim.library as ssl

n = 1000
age_strings = []
for i in range(n):
    household_size = np.random.randint(1, 6)
    ages = np.random.randint(0, 80, household_size)
    age_strings.append(sc.strjoin(ages))
dhs_data = sc.dataframe(hh_id=np.arange(n), ages=age_strings)

household = ssl.networks.HouseholdNet(dhs_data=dhs_data)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks=household)
sim.run()
sim.plot()

library.networks.HybridNet(
    pars=None,
    household_size=_,
    contacts=_,
    beta=_,
    school_ages=_,
    work_ages=_,
    dynamic=_,
    method=_,
    clustered=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Covasim v3’s “hybrid” population: households, schools, workplaces, and community
When added to a sim, this expands into four separate networks: households (h), schools (s), and workplaces (w), each an ssl.ClusterNet, and community (c), an ss.RandomNet with Poisson-distributed contacts. Schools and workplaces are restricted by age. As in Covasim v3, the networks are static; unlike it, schools and workplaces are clusters by default, so that a person’s contacts also know each other (use clustered=False for Covasim v3’s random networks). With the default Poisson sizes, clusters give the same mean number of contacts as a random network. Each network can then be modified separately, e.g. sim.networks.s.
The default beta values are Covasim v3’s per-layer relative transmissibility, and are applied to the edges of each network; for per-network transmissibility on the disease instead, set them to 1 and use e.g. ss.SIS(beta=dict(h=0.3, s=0.06, w=0.06, c=0.03)).
Note: CRN safe, unless dynamic=True and people are born or die.

title: products
text:
products
Products: vaccines, treatments, and diagnostics, and the protection people hold from them
A product says what something does (e.g. its efficacy), and a delivery (ss.vaccinate(), ss.treat(), ss.screen()) says who gets it and when. They are kept apart so that one product can be delivered in several ways. A product written as code (administer()) runs as agents.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Diagnostic
A diagnostic test: what ss.screen() delivers


Effect
The effect of a product on one quantity, for the people who hold it: a multiplier of 1 - efficacy


EventSource
What a delivery and a product share as events: the people it reached on the step (screening), its outcomes (screening.positive), and their memory


Held
Base class for products that change rates for the people who hold them


Product
Generic product base class: see ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, and ss.Treatment


StrainEffect
The effect of a product against acquiring each strain of a disease with shared states, for the people who hold it: on each strain’s force of infection (see ss.solvers.Engine.strain_effect())


Treatment
A treatment: what ss.treat() delivers


Vaccine
A vaccine: what ss.vaccinate() delivers


box
Protection that is full for a time, then lost at once, or (with decay=) fading exponentially: the waning= of a product


held_cond
The condition vx.held (whether each person holds this product), which on a class is whether they hold any product of that kind (where=ss.Vaccine.held), for a model built before its products





products.Diagnostic(
    sensitivity=1.0,
    specificity=1.0,
    results=None,
    delay=None,
    detects=None,
    cost=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    **kwargs,
)
A diagnostic test: what ss.screen() delivers
A test gives each person one of its results: by default positive or negative, from sensitivity and specificity; or one of results=, each with its probability given the state a person is in. Each result is a result of each delivery of it, and an event (screening.positive for one delivery, hiv_rdt.positive for any delivery of the product), which triggers the steps that follow.
Note: CRN safe as agents.





Name
Type
Description
Default




sensitivity
float / dict
the probability that someone with the condition tests positive; a dict gives one for each state (each a number or an ss.by), and the test then detects being in those states. The states can be of several diseases ({hpv16.I: 0.9, 'hpv18.CIN': 0.95}), and the boolean states of a disease written as code ('hpv16.cin'); delivered with disease=[...], a state with no disease ('cin') is that state of each
1.0


specificity
float
the probability that someone without it tests negative
1.0


results
dict
instead of sensitivity and specificity, the results in order of severity, most severe first, each with its probability for people in each state (a dict by state, of any disease, as for sensitivity; a number is for those with what detects= says); the last is None, everyone the others do not take. A key None in a result’s dict is for people in none of the states keyed in any result (of any disease the test is keyed by), e.g. a false positive: it is counted once, whereas a result for a state (susceptible=0.1) is one for each disease. For someone in states of several diseases, there is a result for each disease, and the most severe of them is theirs (for a positive and a negative result, each disease is detected independently)
None


delay
dur / dict
the time from the test to the result (agents only); a dict gives one for each result
None


detects
Cond / func
the condition the test detects (default: being in an infected state of the disease)
None


cost
float
the cost of each delivery
None


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the variable the test is assigned to
None


label
str
the label, for plots and printing
None


kwargs
dict
passed to ss.Product
{}






pcr = ss.Diagnostic(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, cost=4.00, delay=ss.days(2))
xpert = ss.Diagnostic(sensitivity=dict(symptomatic=0.91, asymptomatic=ss.by(age=[0.73, 0.78]))) # By state, and by age group within a state
hpv_dna = ss.Diagnostic(sensitivity={hpv16.I: 0.9, hpv16.CIN: 0.95, hpv18.I: 0.9}, specificity=0.97) # Across diseases
cytology = ss.Diagnostic(results=dict(high_grade=dict(cin=0.9, cancer=1.0), ascus={'cin': 0.1, None: 0.1}, normal=None)) # ASCUS for 10% of people with neither CIN nor cancer

Description

The names of the diseases whose states it is keyed by

The names of its results from the least severe to the most (the order of tails()): for a positive and a negative result, negative first

A test has no step of its own (its deliveries give it), so it does not stop a whole run in the kernels

Description

The delay of each result, from the least severe to the most (None for none)

Each disease’s states: a value for its infected (or for detects=) becomes one for the infected of each, and one by state, for that state of each that has it; a person’s result is the worst over the diseases


key_ref
A key of a dict by state, as (disease name, or None for the delivery’s; state name): a declared state, a state of a disease written as code (hpv16.cin, an ss.BoolState), or text ('hpv16.cin')

products.Treatment(
    cure=None,
    efficacy=None,
    transition=None,
    to=None,
    moves=None,
    **kwargs,
)
A treatment: what ss.treat() delivers
A treatment can cure (cure=, once, when it is given), change rates for as long as it is held (efficacy=), or both. By default it is given to the people who are infected. A treatment that cures has the outcomes cured, failed (infected, and not cured), and unneeded (not infected), which are results and events of its deliveries.
A treatment can instead name the transitions it moves people along (moves=), usually undriven ones (cure = A + C >> S, with no @). Each person treated who is in a source of one of them moves along it with its probability (cured), or does not (failed); one in no source is unneeded. The transitions can be of several diseases, and the probability for each can differ; a modifier of an undriven transition (ss.modify(ng.cure, multiply=0.5, where=...)) multiplies the probability for the people it applies to. It is then given to the people in their sources. What happens at failure (resistance) is a transition of the disease triggered by the outcome: ss.Transition(I, R_res, where=drug.failed, p=0.05).

products.Treatment(
    cure=None,
    efficacy=None,
    transition=None,
    to=None,
    moves=None,
    **kwargs,
)
A treatment: what ss.treat() delivers
A treatment can cure (cure=, once, when it is given), change rates for as long as it is held (efficacy=), or both. By default it is given to the people who are infected. A treatment that cures has the outcomes cured, failed (infected, and not cured), and unneeded (not infected), which are results and events of its deliveries.
A treatment can instead name the transitions it moves people along (moves=), usually undriven ones (cure = A + C >> S, with no @). Each person treated who is in a source of one of them moves along it with its probability (cured), or does not (failed); one in no source is unneeded. The transitions can be of several diseases, and the probability for each can differ; a modifier of an undriven transition (ss.modify(ng.cure, multiply=0.5, where=...)) multiplies the probability for the people it applies to. It is then given to the people in their sources. What happens at failure (resistance) is a transition of the disease triggered by the outcome: ss.Transition(I, R_res, where=drug.failed, p=0.05).

title: connectors
text:
connectors
Define connectors, which are used to mediate interactions between modules when the sim is run.
While most of the coupling between disease modules happens automatically via shared states (e.g., shared susceptibility), connectors allow explicit cross-module logic such as seasonal forcing or co-infection effects; ss.modify() changes a named quantity, e.g. a seasonal ss.modify(sir.rel_trans, multiply=ss.seasonal(amplitude=0.2, peak='January')).

A number from 1900 on (see ss.time.assume_cal_year()) is a calendar year, as start=2000 is: in a sim with dates, 2005 is the start of 2005, and 2005.5 the middle of it. A number from 1900 on (see ss.time.assume_cal_year()) is a calendar year, as start=2000 is: in a sim with dates, 2005 is the start of 2005, and 2005.5 the middle of it. Any other number is a time in the sim’s unit: in a sim with dates, that long after the start; otherwise, a time on the sim’s own axis (which, for a sim whose start and stop are years, is the year). title: transitions
text:
transitions
States, transitions, and the expressions that drive them.
A model is a set of ss.State objects and the ss.Transition objects between them. A transition can be written with operators or in full, which build the same object:
S >> I @ 0.3 * I                                # Operators
ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.3 * I)               # In full
The ss.graph.Graph class (in internals/graph.py) collects the states and transitions of one module, names them, fills in defaults (recording each guess), and checks them. The expressions are in ss.expressions, the values that vary (ss.by, ss.timeseries, ss.seasonal) in ss.parameters, how a model is shown in ss.display, and its stratifications in ss.dimensions.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared modules





Name
Description




State
Something a person can be in, or a count of something that is not people


Transition
A movement between states


lifetable
A life table: how many die at each age, from which each person’s age at death is drawn, given their age (see ss.death(lifetable=))


outcome
A reported quantity: a flow worked out from other flows, which moves nobody





transitions.State(
    name=None,
    init=None,
    init_n=None,
    people=None,
    rel_sus=1.0,
    rel_trans=1.0,
    keep_time=False,
    label=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Something a person can be in, or a count of something that is not people
A state is a compartment when the model runs as an ODE and a boolean array over agents when it runs as agents; the declaration is the same.











Name
Type
Description
Default




name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the keyword or the variable the state is assigned to
None


init
float
the share of people who start in the state (1.0 is everyone); for a state that is not people, its starting amount
None


init_n
int
instead, the number of people who start in the state
None


people
bool
whether this state holds people (the default), or is a count of something else (people=False: bacteria in the water, mosquitoes); people=True says so explicitly, for a group of people that only an inflow fills
None


rel_sus
float
susceptibility multiplier while in this state
1.0


rel_trans
float
infectiousness multiplier while in this state
1.0


keep_time
bool
as agents, keep the time each person entered the state (ti_<name>) for code to read, e.g. the years since onset; by default it is kept only if the model reads it (a clock, a scheduled exit), to save memory
False


label
str
a human-readable name, for plots
None






S, R = ss.states(2)
I = ss.State(init=0.01)     # 1% of people
E = ss.State(init_n=10)     # 10 people
V = ss.State(rel_sus=0.2, label='Vaccinated')
A = ss.State(keep_time=True) # Code reads mod.ti_A

Description

The event of entering this state: for where= or ss.on(), or .uids


exit
The event of leaving this state


given_init
Whether a starting value is given (init= or init_n=)

The share of the scheduled dwell time in this state that has elapsed, from 0 to 1 (NaN outside it)

Time since this person last entered the state, in the sim’s unit (NaN outside it)

The number in these states in the whole population: in a model with places, in every place, not only the same one as with .n







transitions.Transition(
    src=None,
    dst=None,
    rate=None,
    dur=None,
    p=None,
    stages=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    where=None,
    move=None,
    increment=None,
    after=None,
    acquisition=None,
    per=None,
    alone=False,
)
A movement between states
Usually built with the operators (S >> I @ rate); ss.birth() and ss.death() also return an ss.Transition.





Name
Type
Description
Default




src
State / list
the source state, several states (a list, or a sum I + R), or ss.null for an inflow
None


dst
State / list
the destination state, a list of states (branching), or ss.null for an outflow
None


rate
any
a hazard: a number, ss.per, ss.prob, an expression of states and parameters, or a function; a transmission is a rate with the source of infection in it (rate=beta * I)
None


dur
any
a dwell time: a duration or a distribution of durations (instead of rate); with an event in where=, the time after it that people move
None


p
float / list
branch probability
None


stages
int
number of sub-stages used to realize the dwell time
None


where
Cond / Event / func
who it applies to: a condition (e.g. ppl.age > 30), as for ss.modify(where=); for everyone else its rate is 0. With no rate= or dur=, a trigger (see ss.on): people move as soon as a condition holds. An event moves the people it happens to (where=preg.delivery), or dur= after it (a time drawn for each person), as agents; joined to a condition with &, those who meet it
None


move
dict / StrainMove
a change of level in a dimension as well as of state: the dimension, and the level people move to, or a pair of levels (e.g. move=dict(risk=('low', 'high')), which applies only to people at the first); or a change of strains (move=DS >> (DS, RIF), see ss.strains.Strain)
None


increment
str / dict
a counter that goes up as well: its name, which adds 1 (increment='parity'), or a dict of the amount for each (increment=dict(parity=2) for twins, dict(doses=-1)); a counter is a dimension with integer levels, whose last level is open-ended
None


after
dur
a minimum stay: nobody leaves by this transition until they have been in its source state this long (a rate applies from then on, and a dwell time starts then)
None


acquisition
bool
whether it is an acquisition of the disease, which rel_sus, a product’s efficacy against acquisition, and ss.treat act on. If not given: a contact-mediated transition is, and so is any other transition out of the disease’s first state if none out of it is contact-mediated (an infection by a bite rate or an EIR)
None


per
str
'strain', for an event of a disease with strains (ss.Strains) in a state they share, with an outcome for each strain carried: with p=, each strain carried takes the first destination with its own probability (p= times the strain’s value for the transition, or p='<value>', the strains’ values of that name, with their values for the transition then multiplying its rate), and anyone left with a strain takes the second (or stays), carrying those left, e.g. cure by treatment
None


alone
bool
with per='strain' and a rate: each strain carried has its own rate (the rate times its value), and the first to happen moves on alone (the others are dropped), e.g. one of two strains progressing
False


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the keyword or the variable it is assigned to
None


label
str
a human-readable name
None






S, I, R = ss.states(3)
infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.05 * I)
cure      = ss.Transition(I, S) # No driver: only by treatment
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(10))
maturing  = ss.Transition(J, A, rate=ss.perday(1), where=ppl.age > 1) # Only adults
failure   = ss.Transition(Tx, I, rate=ss.peryear(0.1), move=DS >> (DS, RIF)) # Treatment fails, and the strain acquires resistance (DS, RIF = strains)
twins     = ss.Transition(P, PP, dur=ss.months(9), p=0.02, increment=dict(parity=2)) # Parity goes up by 2
weaning   = ss.Transition(NB, W, rate=ss.perday(0.5), after=ss.days(21)) # At least 21 days old first, as EMULSION's duration
postpartum = ss.Transition(PP, NP, where=preg.delivery, dur=ss.months(6)) # Six months after each woman's own delivery
importation = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=ss.perday(1e-4), acquisition=True) # An infection from outside, alongside one by contact

Whether it has no wait (dur=0, or ss.constant(0)): people go through it in the step they arrive in its source, or, with where=, in the step the condition first holds for them

The time since each person last went through this transition (infinite if never; agents only), e.g. where=tb.diagnosis.since <= ss.years(2)

transitions.pars(defaults, **kwargs)
Create several parameters at once, from defaults and the values given, as a class’s declared parameters are made
For a disease whose states and transitions depend on its options, and so are made in __init__() rather than declared on the class (e.g. beta = ss.par(...), as ss.SIR does). Each parameter is an ss.par named after its key, so it can be fitted or set by name (ss.Sim(pars=...)). A value given takes the default’s bounds and description unless it has its own; a bare number for a typed default keeps its unit (e.g. 2 for a default of ss.peryear(1) is 2 per year); a default of None is an optional parameter, None unless given. A name that is not a default is an error.

transitions.Transition(
    src=None,
    dst=None,
    rate=None,
    dur=None,
    p=None,
    stages=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    where=None,
    move=None,
    increment=None,
    after=None,
    acquisition=None,
    per=None,
    alone=False,
)
A movement between states
Usually built with the operators (S >> I @ rate); ss.birth() and ss.death() also return an ss.Transition.





Name
Type
Description
Default




src
State / list
the source state, several states (a list, or a sum I + R), or ss.null for an inflow
None


dst
State / list
the destination state, a list of states (branching), or ss.null for an outflow
None


rate
any
a hazard: a number, ss.per, ss.prob, an expression of states and parameters, or a function; a transmission is a rate with the source of infection in it (rate=beta * I)
None


dur
any
a dwell time: a duration or a distribution of durations (instead of rate); with an event in where=, the time after it that people move
None


p
float / list
branch probability
None


stages
int
number of sub-stages used to realize the dwell time
None


where
Cond / Event / func
who it applies to: a condition (e.g. ppl.age > 30), as for ss.modify(where=); for everyone else its rate is 0. With no rate= or dur=, a trigger (see ss.on): people move as soon as a condition holds. An event moves the people it happens to (where=preg.delivery), or dur= after it (a time drawn for each person), as agents; joined to a condition with &, those who meet it
None


move
dict / StrainMove
a change of level in a dimension as well as of state: the dimension, and the level people move to, or a pair of levels (e.g. move=dict(risk=('low', 'high')), which applies only to people at the first); or a change of strains (move=DS >> (DS, RIF), see ss.strains.Strain)
None


increment
str / dict
a counter that goes up as well: its name, which adds 1 (increment='parity'), or a dict of the amount for each (increment=dict(parity=2) for twins, dict(doses=-1)); a counter is a dimension with integer levels, whose last level is open-ended
None


after
dur
a minimum stay: nobody leaves by this transition until they have been in its source state this long (a rate applies from then on, and a dwell time starts then)
None


acquisition
bool
whether it is an acquisition of the disease, which rel_sus, a product’s efficacy against acquisition, and ss.treat act on. If not given: a contact-mediated transition is, and so is any other transition out of the disease’s first state if none out of it is contact-mediated (an infection by a bite rate or an EIR)
None


per
str
'strain', for an event of a disease with strains (ss.Strains) in a state they share, with an outcome for each strain carried: with p=, each strain carried takes the first destination with its own probability (p= times the strain’s value for the transition, or p='<value>', the strains’ values of that name, with their values for the transition then multiplying its rate), and anyone left with a strain takes the second (or stays), carrying those left, e.g. cure by treatment
None


alone
bool
with per='strain' and a rate: each strain carried has its own rate (the rate times its value), and the first to happen moves on alone (the others are dropped), e.g. one of two strains progressing
False


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the keyword or the variable it is assigned to
None


label
str
a human-readable name
None






S, I, R = ss.states(3)
infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.05 * I)
cure      = ss.Transition(I, S) # No driver: only by treatment
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(10))
maturing  = ss.Transition(J, A, rate=ss.perday(1), where=ppl.age > 1) # Only adults
failure   = ss.Transition(Tx, I, rate=ss.peryear(0.1), move=DS >> (DS, RIF)) # Treatment fails, and the strain acquires resistance (DS, RIF = strains)
twins     = ss.Transition(P, PP, dur=ss.months(9), p=0.02, increment=dict(parity=2)) # Parity goes up by 2
weaning   = ss.Transition(NB, W, rate=ss.perday(0.5), after=ss.days(21)) # At least 21 days old first, as EMULSION's duration
postpartum = ss.Transition(PP, NP, where=preg.delivery, dur=ss.months(6)) # Six months after each woman's own delivery
importation = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=ss.perday(1e-4), acquisition=True) # An infection from outside, alongside one by contact

Each parameter is an ss.par named after its key, so it can be fitted or set by name (ss.Sim(pars=...)). A value given takes the default’s bounds and description unless it has its own; a bare number for a typed default keeps its unit (e.g. 2 for a default of ss.peryear(1) is 2 per year); a default of None is an optional parameter, None unless given. title: settings
text:
settings
Options for Starsim, and the plotting style
These exist so that behavior that isn’t part of a model (how much to print, how to treat warnings, which kernels to use) is set in one place. All options should be set using set() or directly, e.g.:
ss.options(verbose=False)
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Options
Set options for Starsim.





settings.Options()
Set options for Starsim.
Use ss.options.set('defaults') to reset all values to default, or ss.options.set(verbose='default') to reset one parameter to default. See ss.options.help(detailed=True) for more information.
See ss.options.context() to set options temporarily, and ss.style() to set the plotting style temporarily.
Common options are (see also ss.options.help(detailed=True)):
- verbose:        default verbosity for simulations to use
- warnings:       how to handle warnings (e.g. print, raise as errors, ignore)


ss.options(verbose=True) # Set more verbosity
ss.options(warnings='error') # Be more strict about warnings

The states and transitions of one module
The graph is built when the module is constructed. It names everything, works out which states are people and which transitions are transmissions (from their rates), turns inline values into named parameters, and checks the result. Every guess is recorded, in graph.guessed and in the guessed of each state and transition.

graph.Graph.bad_splits(exits)
The groups of branches with constant p= whose shares do not sum to 1: those that apply to the people at each level named by a move= arrow are summed within that level; returns [(branches, total)]



graph.Graph.check()
Checks that do not need the sim



graph.Graph.check_counts()
Refuse a forgotten people=False (MA35): a group of states of people that no transition links to the first state and that only an inflow (not a birth) fills, as mosquitoes are, would otherwise silently become agents



graph.Graph.check_first(why=None)
Raise if the module has states of people but no first state (see resolve_people()), which every solver needs: it is where people start unless they are put elsewhere, and where those added later (born, or seeded from) come from



graph.Graph.check_read(state)
Refuse a state that an earlier module only read in a rate, so took as a state of its own that nothing fills, e.g. Rb.frac in disease a, declared before the disease b that Rb was meant to belong to

For the name of one destination of a transition with several, '<transition>.<state>' (e.g. 'progression.C'): the transition; otherwise None

The names of the destinations of the transitions with several, as destination() takes them



graph.Graph.dwell_not_branch(name, how, modname)
For a multiplier (how, e.g. ‘the modifier “m”’) on a transition with several destinations chosen with p= and a dwell time: a note that it changes the dwell, not a branch (TL16), naming the destinations that would; otherwise None



graph.Graph.expand_rows()
Entries of p= with a to axis (an ss.by over to, whose labels are destination states): one Share of the entry for each destination it covers
Entries without one are one destination each, in order, skipping the destinations that a to axis names; an entry whose to axis gives values by position only covers the destinations left. The entries as given are kept as tr.p_given.



graph.Graph.fill_people(tr)
Fill in what depends on which states are people: the sources of the deaths of everyone (ss.death() with no state), and the people a birth rate is per person of (ss.birth())



graph.Graph.leaves()
The leaves of the rates and branch probabilities of its transitions



graph.Graph.modifier_kind(name)
What a modifier on a transition acts on: its probability if it is one branch of several with p= (chosen on entry) or one destination of a transition with several ('recovery.R'), and otherwise its rate



graph.Graph.resolve_acquisition()
Work out which transitions are an acquisition of the disease, which rel_sus, a product’s efficacy against acquisition, and ss.treat act on
A contact-mediated transition is one. So is any other transition of people out of the first state that is not an outflow, whatever its rate (a bite rate, an EIR, a count of bacteria), unless a transition out of that state is contact-mediated, which is then the acquisition (so S -> V alongside S -> I @ beta * I is a vaccination). acquisition= on the transition says it outright.



graph.Graph.resolve_attrs()
Resolve each attribute: another attribute given by name, the cases of a derived one by state (a state, a sum of states, or a | of them), and its events



graph.Graph.resolve_exits()
Group the transitions out of each state: those with p= split on entry, the rest compete



graph.Graph.resolve_init_prev()
By default, 1% of people start infected, seeded through the transmission (frequency- or density-dependent), unless a state is given a starting value



graph.Graph.resolve_pars()
Turn inline values in the standard slots into named parameters (beta, dur, rate, p)



graph.Graph.resolve_people()
Which states are people: every state, unless it is declared a count (ss.State(people=False), e.g. mosquitoes or bacteria in the water); and the first state, where people are unless they are put elsewhere: first= if given, else the state named S or susceptible (in any case). Nothing else is guessed: with neither, check_first() raises when the sim is initialized (a birth into a state of its own, ss.birth(X), needs no first state, but the people who start in no state do)



graph.Graph.resolve_rest()
Work out where the people not given an initial state start: the first state, unless it is given an initial value of its own, which is then kept (init=dict(S=0.1, I=1e-4) starts 10% susceptible). Then it is the one state of people with no initial value, with a note in guessed; with none or several, there is no such state, and the initial values must sum to 1 (see Engine.init_fractions())



graph.Graph.resolve_states()
Find the states: the ones declared, and those the transitions use



graph.Graph.resolve_transitions()
Give every transition a name, a source, and a rate or a dwell time



graph.Graph.set_keywords()
A value given as a keyword sets the parameter of that name; there is nothing else for it to be



graph.Graph.set_slots(tr)
Record the kind of value each parameter of a transition is, as par.slot (which describe() and the model spec use): ‘rate’ or ‘dur’, or None for a plain number (e.g. a factor of a rate); returns the standard slots it fills, as (slot name, parameter)



graph.Graph.spread_pars()
The parameters whose value is a distribution across people (e.g. beta=ss.lognorm_ex(0.3, 0.1)), other than dwell times, which are stages or are sampled on entry



graph.Graph.stratify(**kwargs)
Stratify the graph by one or more dimensions; see ss.Disease.stratify()



graph.Graph.unit_values()
All the typed values (durations and rates) in the graph, used to infer the sim’s unit



graph.Graph.unset_default_init_prev()
Remove the default init_prev, e.g. of a strain that its disease seeds

title: distributions
text:
distributions
The distributions to choose from: ss.uniform, ss.normal, ss.poisson, and so on, each a random-number-safe ss.Dist
These exist so that a model can use any distribution for a parameter or a draw, with the same random numbers for the same agent across scenarios. How they work is in ss.dists. As agents, they are drawn for each agent; in a compartmental run, most are read for what they say about the group, such as their mean.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules

distributions.choice(a=2, p=None, replace=True, **kwargs)
Random choice between discrete options
The probabilities can differ by agent: give p as a 2D array with one row per agent drawn for (or a function returning one), and one column per choice. Each row is normalized to sum to 1. Each agent’s choice is found from their own random number by the inverse CDF of their own row, so the draw is one vectorized call, and keeps common random numbers: an agent’s choice doesn’t depend on who else is drawn for, or on other agents’ probabilities.

Type
Description
Default

int or array
the number of choices, or the choices themselves (default 2)
2


p
array / func
if supplied, the probability of each choice (default, 1/a for a choices); or a 2D array (or a function returning one) with a row of probabilities (or weights) for each agent
None


replace
bool
whether an option can be chosen more than once (default True)
True






# Simulate 10 die rolls
ss.choice(6, strict=False)(10) + 1

# Choose between specified options each with a specified probability (must sum to 1)
ss.choice(a=[30, 70], p=[0.3, 0.7], strict=False)(10)

# A row of probabilities per agent: here by age group, from a table of age groups × choices
table = np.array([[0.7, 0.2, 0.1], [0.3, 0.4, 0.3]])
def p_by_age(self, sim, uids):
    return table[(sim.people.age[uids] >= 18).astype(int)]
method = ss.choice(a=['none', 'pill', 'iud'], p=p_by_age) # In a module's __init__()
chosen = self.method.rvs(uids) # In its step()
Note: although Bernoulli trials can be generated using a=2, it is much faster to use ss.bernoulli() instead.

distributions.choose_n(n=1, weights=None, die=False, **kwargs)
Choose exactly n agents (without replacement) from a set of candidate UIDs
Like ss.bernoulli, use the filter() method, which returns the chosen UIDs. One random number is drawn per candidate (based on its slot), and the n candidates with the smallest numbers are chosen. This means that if the candidates change slightly (e.g. between two scenarios), most of the same agents are still chosen (unlike e.g. ss.choice(replace=False)).
If weights are supplied, candidates are chosen with probability proportional to their weight, via the Efraimidis–Spirakis key (1-u)**(1/w). This is computed as -log(1-u)/w, so the n smallest are chosen as before, and equal weights give the same agents as no weights. Candidates with zero weight are never chosen, so fewer than n UIDs are returned if fewer than n candidates have nonzero weight.











Name
Type
Description
Default




n
int / func
the number of agents to choose (or a function returning it); if more than the number of candidates, all are chosen
1

array / func
if supplied, the relative weight of each candidate (or a function returning them), matching the UIDs passed to filter()
None


die
bool
if True, raise an exception if fewer than n agents can be chosen (default: False)
False






# Seed exactly 20 infections of a disease written as code
sir = ssl.AgentSIR(init_prev=ss.choose_n(20))

# Choose 5 agents, weighted by age
chooser = ss.choose_n(5, weights=lambda self, sim, uids: sim.people.age[uids])

The probabilities can differ by agent: give p as a 2D array with one row per agent drawn for (or a function returning one), and one column per choice. Each row is normalized to sum to 1. distributions.choose_n(n=1, weights=None, die=False, **kwargs)
Choose exactly n agents (without replacement) from a set of candidate UIDs
Like ss.bernoulli, use the filter() method, which returns the chosen UIDs. One random number is drawn per candidate (based on its slot), and the n candidates with the smallest numbers are chosen. This means that if the candidates change slightly (e.g. between two scenarios), most of the same agents are still chosen (unlike e.g. ss.choice(replace=False)).
If weights are supplied, candidates are chosen with probability proportional to their weight, via the Efraimidis–Spirakis key (1-u)**(1/w). This is computed as -log(1-u)/w, so the n smallest are chosen as before, and equal weights give the same agents as no weights. Candidates with zero weight are never chosen, so fewer than n UIDs are returned if fewer than n candidates have nonzero weight.

Fast inverse-CDF sampling for the common-random-number (ppf) path.
SciPy’s generic discrete ppf is very slow (it root-finds per element), and for CRN draws it is called every time an ss.poisson is sampled by UID. For a scalar lam we instead precompute the CDF once and map each uniform via np.searchsorted, which is 30-60x faster and produces bitwise-identical results. Array-valued lam is inverted by ss.solvers.backends.draws (SciPy’s above a mean of 30, and for unusual values).
