title: solvers.choose
text:
solvers.choose
Not for the user: choosing the solver: which engine runs a declared model, and why (choose_solver()), and the steps that build a declared model before it is run (parameters by name, births and deaths of the population, a named population, the unit, life tables)
It exists so that a model need not say how it runs: the choice is made from what it holds, and the reason is kept. Modules written as code are taken into account, and get an engine too.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Undeclared
The engine of a disease that declares no states or transitions (see ss.Disease): there is nothing for it to run, so the disease’s own





solvers.choose.Undeclared(module, sim)
The engine of a disease that declares no states or transitions (see ss.Disease): there is nothing for it to run, so the disease’s own code is all of it. It gives that code what a declared disease’s engine gives its own, as agents: the modifiers and products on its rel_sus, rel_trans, and parameters (dis.current_value(), and self.pars while it runs), transmission over the networks (ss.Infection.transmit_route(); see Transmission), and, for a delivery, the people its conditions select and a cure (force())
It exists so that code written for a disease can act on any disease in the same way.





Name
Description




define
With strains, the distributions of who infects whom and of protection (see Transmission.pick_sources()), by the names a declared disease’s transmission called infection (e.g. ss.SIR’s) gives them, so the same model draws the same numbers both ways


eval
An expression of parameters (e.g. a modifier’s amount, ss.par(2, bounds=[1, 4])), at their values


force
A cure by a delivery (see ss.Delivery.cure()): the disease’s own clear_infection()


nothing
Nothing to run: each step of the lifecycle is the disease’s own code


start_step
Values held for a step (e.g. the modifiers of a network’s contacts) are worked out again: at the step’s start, and once the interventions have run (the disease’s step())


unapplied
Why the disease would not apply the modifiers (mods) on a parameter (name) or on its rel_sus or rel_trans (kind), or None if it would: a transmitted ss.Infection reads those in transmit_route() (see ss.connectors.check_applied())


update_results
The count of each ss.BoolState, as for any module


value
A parameter given as ss.par (e.g. with bounds, to be fitted) is its value, which the disease’s code reads





solvers.choose.Undeclared.define()
With strains, the distributions of who infects whom and of protection (see Transmission.pick_sources()), by the names a declared disease’s transmission called infection (e.g. ss.SIR’s) gives them, so the same model draws the same numbers both ways

solvers.choose.Undeclared.value(p)
A parameter given as ss.par (e.g. with bounds, to be fitted) is its value, which the disease’s code reads









Name
Description




auto_reasons
The reasons, from the capability record, that solver='auto' runs the model as agents (none if it runs it as compartments)


choose_engine
Whether JAX takes the sim’s whole run of the ODE, as ss.gradients runs it, rather than the kernels, and why


choose_solver
Work out the sim’s unit and solver; see ss.Disease for declaring a model that can be run with different solvers


flows_of
The transitions of a declared disease that are births, arrivals, or deaths of everyone, so are the population’s


group_people
In a compartmental run, one row per group: the properties that are not dimensions have no values to give, so are removed, as are the active agents (auids), and counting who is alive counts the people, not the groups


init_capabilities
One record for each ingredient that changes which solvers can run the model, read by solver='auto', sim.describe(), and the CapabilityError of a compartmental solver that was asked for


init_crossings
In a compartmental run: track jointly the states of diseases that refer to each other, or whose people are born or die (see crossing_groups())


init_group_values
The values of the dimensions in the people: as agents, each person’s level of each; in a compartmental run, with one row per group, the age of each group (the middle of its age group) and its sex


kernel_seconds
About how long the compiled kernels would take for a whole run of the ODE, from the size of its model alone: its time


make_engine
Create the engine that runs a module’s graph under the sim’s solver: in a compartmental run, the one laid out to choose the solver (see lay_out()), unless the groups changed since; for a disease that declares nothing, one that runs nothing


set_par_values
Apply parameter values given by name (pars=dict(beta=0.1), or ‘sir.beta’ if the name is used by more than one module; for a parameter with a value per level, ‘beta[a]’ for one level)


settle_start
Once every module has its people: as agents, those placed in a state nobody waits in move on at once; and the diseases tracked jointly take their initial conditions


solver_table
What decides which engine runs a model, as a dataframe: a row for each rule, in the order they are read, with a column for each


why_not
Why an engine ('kernels', a whole run in one call; or 'jax', the ODE in JAX, as for gradients) cannot run the sim, in a few words, or None if it can





solvers.choose.auto_reasons(sim)
The reasons, from the capability record, that solver='auto' runs the model as agents (none if it runs it as compartments)



solvers.choose.choose_engine(sim)
Whether JAX takes the sim’s whole run of the ODE, as ss.gradients runs it, rather than the kernels, and why
By sim.jax: True for JAX, False for the kernels, or None (the default) to choose: JAX if the run would take the kernels more than jax_after seconds (see kernel_seconds()). Once started, JAX takes 0.1 to 0.3 times as long as the kernels for the ODE over many groups, but starting it takes about half a second in a session (0.3 s to import it, and 0.1 to 0.25 s to trace a model; compiled code is kept on disk), which a short run would notice. The choice depends on the model only (kernel_seconds() is worked out from its size, never timed), not on what has run before, whether the kernels are compiled, or the load on the machine (and an ODE run in JAX agrees with the kernels to about 1e-14). The other solvers are run by the kernels, as is a model JAX does not cover (see why_not()), with a note if JAX was asked for.
Returns whether to use JAX, and the reason, also kept as sim.engine_reason.



solvers.choose.choose_solver(sim)
Work out the sim’s unit and solver; see ss.Disease for declaring a model that can be run with different solvers
Agents are made only when something needs them, whether the model is declared or written as code: a sim of modules written as code with nothing per person (e.g. an ODE of its own in NumPy) has no agents, and one with per-person arrays (Starsim 3’s diseases written as code) runs as agents. title: solvers.crossing
text:
solvers.crossing
Not for the user: diseases whose states are tracked jointly in a compartmental run
It exists since a condition in one disease on a state of another (e.g. coinfection) needs the people counted by both.
Used with: compartments; declared modules





Name
Description




Crossing
Diseases whose states are tracked jointly in a compartmental run, since a condition in one refers to a state of another (e.g. ss.modify(hiv.rel_trans, multiply=3, where=syph.I))


Joint
An engine’s compartments by its groups (engine.y), when its disease is tracked jointly with others: a view of the





solvers.crossing.Crossing(sim, names, reasons=None)
Diseases whose states are tracked jointly in a compartmental run, since a condition in one refers to a state of another (e.g. ss.modify(hiv.rel_trans, multiply=3, where=syph.I))
Each disease in the crossing is a dimension of the sim, named after it, whose levels are its compartments and which applies to the people of the others. Each keeps its own engine, which works out its rates and its results, and sees the people as it has them: by its own compartments, and by groups that include the compartments of the others (with its own dimension at its first level).
They are run by one program: its compartments are the product of the diseases’ compartments of people (and, for a compartment that is not people, such as a reservoir, one for each combination of the others’), and its groups are those of the sim’s other dimensions. Each flow of a disease is a flow of the program for each combination of the others’ compartments, so every rate is worked out from the people as they are at the start of the step (not each disease in turn), and a whole run, many runs, a particle filter, and a run in JAX take a crossing as they take one disease. The solvers that draw whole events in steps draw each disease’s in turn, from those rates, so each disease’s moves (e.g. through the stages of a dwell time) are drawn as they would be for it alone. The program’s compartments (y) are the one copy of the people: each engine’s (engine.y) are a view of them (Joint), so a change made in Python (e.g. by an intervention) is seen by all of them at once. The crossing is run as one engine is (see ss.solvers.Compartmental.step() and run_all(), where it is the engine’s owner): the last disease to step takes the step for all of them, and the first to take a whole run takes it for all of them, and gives each its part. Its size is counted before it is made (see ss.solvers.choose.joint_layout()), and kept within ss.options.max_joint; sim.describe() shows it, with the memory a whole run takes.

solvers.crossing.Crossing(sim, names, reasons=None)
Diseases whose states are tracked jointly in a compartmental run, since a condition in one refers to a state of another (e.g. ss.modify(hiv.rel_trans, multiply=3, where=syph.I))
Each disease in the crossing is a dimension of the sim, named after it, whose levels are its compartments and which applies to the people of the others. Each keeps its own engine, which works out its rates and its results, and sees the people as it has them: by its own compartments, and by groups that include the compartments of the others (with its own dimension at its first level).
They are run by one program: its compartments are the product of the diseases’ compartments of people (and, for a compartment that is not people, such as a reservoir, one for each combination of the others’), and its groups are those of the sim’s other dimensions. Each flow of a disease is a flow of the program for each combination of the others’ compartments, so every rate is worked out from the people as they are at the start of the step (not each disease in turn), and a whole run, many runs, a particle filter, and a run in JAX take a crossing as they take one disease. The solvers that draw whole events in steps draw each disease’s in turn, from those rates, so each disease’s moves (e.g. through the stages of a dwell time) are drawn as they would be for it alone. The program’s compartments (y) are the one copy of the people: each engine’s (engine.y) are a view of them (Joint), so a change made in Python (e.g. by an intervention) is seen by all of them at once. The crossing is run as one engine is (see ss.solvers.Compartmental.step() and run_all(), where it is the engine’s owner): the last disease to step takes the step for all of them, and the first to take a whole run takes it for all of them, and gives each its part. Its size is counted before it is made (see ss.solvers.choose.joint_layout()), and kept within ss.options.max_joint; sim.describe() shows it, with the memory a whole run takes.

title: strains
text:
strains
Strains of a disease (ss.Strains), and protection between them (ss.immunity)
These exist so that one disease can have several strains, with their own values and with protection between them, without being written as several diseases. The strains of a declared disease share its states; a disease written as code carries one strain at a time, as agents (ss.Infection.define_strains()).
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Strains
The strains of a disease: ss.Disease(..., strains=ss.Strains(...)), which is then dis.strains


immunity
Protection between strains: what having (or having had) one strain does against each strain





strains.Strains(
    strains,
    immunity=None,
    max_strains=None,
    transmit='one',
    split=None,
    name='strain',
    label=None,
    **values,
)
The strains of a disease: ss.Disease(..., strains=ss.Strains(...)), which is then dis.strains
The strains share the disease’s states: a person is in a state once, carrying their strains, with one course. The engine chooses how to run what is declared (one strain at a time, or sets of strains carried together), and describe() says which.
With no immunity=, a person carries one strain at a time, being infected (or recovered) protects against every strain, and a new infection takes its source’s strain. ss.immunity(due_to=...) changes that: protection from a state. With max_strains above 1, people carry sets of strains (the levels of the strain dimension, e.g. ‘DS+RIF’), and a set takes the largest of its strains’ values for a transition; once full, a new strain replaces the oldest (counted in the flow that brought it).
Values for each strain are multipliers on the disease’s transitions (by name: their rate, a duration divided, or a branch’s probability) and on rel_trans. They can be given two ways, which are the same thing: by strain, as a dict of dicts; or by parameter, as lists, one entry per strain.

strains.immunity(*args, due_to=None, rel_sus=None, combine='max')
Protection between strains: what having (or having had) one strain does against each strain
rel_sus= is the protection against being infected: a matrix, with rows from the strain held and columns against the strain (1 is complete), or a single number, the same protection from any strain held against every strain. Each person’s protection against a strain is combined over the strains they hold by combine=, and multiplies rel_sus by 1 − protection. Several ss.immunity objects, and any modifier or product on rel_sus, multiply.
due_to= is a state (due_to=R) whose people are protected, by the strains they hold there. A state protects against every strain completely unless an ss.immunity says otherwise; partial protection in a state people are infected in (due_to=L) lets them carry another strain as well (superinfection), up to max_strains. A relative rate of superinfection that is a parameter (to fit), or above 1, is written as the transmission itself, e.g. L >> L @ rr*foi, which carries the new strain as well in the same way.

Type
Description
Default




due_to
State / str

None

array / float

None

'max'

internals.dists
The machinery of random-number-safe distributions: ss.Dist, and how the distributions of a sim are found, seeded, and drawn from
It exists so that each decision in a sim has its own random stream, which keeps two runs comparable (common random numbers). As compartments, a distribution mostly describes a dwell time or a parameter: the engine draws from its own generator.
The distributions themselves are in ss.distributions.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Dist
Base class for tracking one random number generator associated with one distribution,


Dists
Class for managing a collection of Dist objects


scipy_dist
A distribution of scipy.stats, by name, and its parameters (kwds), as a frozen one holds them





internals.dists.Dist(
    dist=None,
    distname=None,
    name=None,
    unit=None,
    round=False,
    seed=None,
    offset=None,
    strict=True,
    sim=None,
    module=None,
    mock=False,
    **kwargs,
)
Base class for tracking one random number generator associated with one distribution, i.e. one decision per timestep.
See ss.distributions.dist_list for a full list of supported distributions. Parameter inputs tend to follow SciPy’s, rather than NumPy’s, definitions (although in most cases they’re the same).
Distributions scale in different ways, such as converting between time units, given by scaling. Some distributions can’t be scaled at all (e.g. ss.beta_dist() or ss.choice()). For distributions that can be scaled, some distributions can only be (linearly) scaled before the random numbers are generated (called “predraw”), some can only be scaled after (called “postdraw”), and some can be scaled in either way (both).
For example, a normal distribution is both since 2Normal(a, b) = Normal(2a, 2b). A Poisson distribution is “predraw” since 2Poisson(λ) ≠ Poisson(2λ), and there is no way to get the correct shape of a different Poisson distribution once the numbers have been drawn. Finally, distributions with unitless shape parameters as well as parameter that can have units (e.g. a gamma distribution with shape and scale parameters) are referred to as “postdraw” since scaling all input parameters is invalid (i.e. 2Gamma(shape, scale) ≠ Gamma(2shape, 2scale)), but they can still be scaled (i.e. 2Gamma(shape, scale) = Gamma(1shape, 2*scale)).
So scaling is one of:
- 'postdraw' (after the random numbers are drawn, e.g. `ss.weibull()`)
- 'predraw' (before the draw, e.g. `ss.poisson()`)
- ['predraw', 'postdraw'] (either, e.g. `ss.normal()`)
- None (not at all, e.g. `ss.beta_dist()`)
Note: by default, ss.Dist is initialized with an ss.Sim object to ensure random number reproducibility. You can override this with either ss.Dist(strict=False) on creation, or dist.init(force=True) after creation. A distribution with a unit (e.g. ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10))) draws in that unit outside a sim, with neither.
Although it’s possible in theory to define a custom distribution (i.e., not one from NumPy or SciPy), in practice this is difficult. The distribution needs to have both a way to return random variates (easy), as well as the probability point function (inverse CDF). In addition, the distribution must be able to take a NumPy RNG as its bit generator. It’s easier to just use a default Dist (e.g., ss.random()), and then take its output as input (i.e., quantiles) for whatever custom distribution you want to create.

internals.dists.Dist.check_unitless_pars()
Check that parameters that must be dimensionless have not been given time units
Some distribution parameters are inherently unitless, such as the shape parameter of ss.weibull() or ss.gamma(); these are listed in the distribution’s unitless_pars attribute. Supplying a timepar for these is always an error, since scaling them by dt would change the shape of the distribution rather than its location or spread. Distributions with unitless_pars = None are not checked.

internals.dists.Dist.convert_timepars()
Convert time parameters (durations and rates) to scalars
This function converts time parameters into bare numbers that will be returned by rvs() depending on the timestep of the parent module for this Dist. The conversion for these types is

Durations are divided by dt (so the result will be a number of timesteps)
Rates are multiplied by dt (so the result will be a number of events, or else the equivalent multiplicate value for the timestep)




internals.dists.Dist.crn_key()
For a compiled loop that draws the uniforms itself (e.g. ss.solvers.backends.passes.infect()), in place of rvs(uids): the seed and index of this call’s draws, which are hash_uniforms(seed, ind, slots) at dtype, with the bookkeeping of one call to rvs(); not for the user. None if they cannot be drawn that way (without common random numbers, or while the draws are being recorded), in which case rvs() is called instead.

internals.dists.Dist.harmonize_par_units()
Ensure that parameters that share dimensions also share time units
Some distributions have several parameters with the same dimensions (e.g. the mean and standard deviation of ss.lognorm_ex()); these are listed in the distribution’s unit_pars attribute. Supplying units for only some of them is the expected usage, since the units of the others follow from it: for example, ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(10)) means the same thing as ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(10), std=ss.years(1)). Any plain numbers are therefore converted to the same timepar as their siblings. (Without this, they would be interpreted as numbers of timesteps, and would give different answers for different values of dt.) Mixing durations and rates cannot be resolved this way, so it raises an exception. Distributions with unit_pars = None are not checked.

internals.dists.even_out(rands, seed, ind)
Evenly spaced uniforms in the same order as rands, for ss.Sim(even_draws=True); not for the user
The smallest of n uniforms becomes (0 + v)/n, the next (1 + v)/n, and so on, with one offset v for the call. Each number is still exactly uniform, so every distribution keeps its shape, but together they have the mean and spread they should. Each stays close to its original value, so CRN keeps working, though less well (see ss.Sim).

internals.dists.hash_uniforms(seed, ind, slots, dtype=None, even=False)
Generate one uniform random number in (0, 1) per slot via a counter-based (splitmix64) hash keyed by (seed, ind); not for the user.
This is the engine behind Starsim’s common random numbers (CRN). Because each output depends only on its slot (plus the per-draw key), the same slot always yields the same value regardless of how many other agents are drawn – so structural differences between scenarios don’t ripple into unrelated agents. Unlike the stream-based approach (draw slots.max()+1 numbers and gather), this generates exactly len(slots) numbers, avoiding the slot_scale blowup.
The result is returned at dtype (default ss.dtypes.float) so the CRN path matches the dtype of the native draw path (Dist.rand). The mantissa width is matched to the float width (24-bit for float32, 53-bit for float64) so every value stays strictly < 1 – a plain float64->float32 cast would round the largest values up to exactly 1.0 and break the [0, 1) contract (e.g. expon.ppf(1.0) is inf). The float64 stream is unchanged from earlier versions. With even, the numbers of the call are evenly spaced (see even_out()).

internals.dists.Dist(
    dist=None,
    distname=None,
    name=None,
    unit=None,
    round=False,
    seed=None,
    offset=None,
    strict=True,
    sim=None,
    module=None,
    mock=False,
    **kwargs,
)
Base class for tracking one random number generator associated with one distribution, i.e. one decision per timestep.
See ss.distributions.dist_list for a full list of supported distributions. Parameter inputs tend to follow SciPy’s, rather than NumPy’s, definitions (although in most cases they’re the same).
Distributions scale in different ways, such as converting between time units, given by scaling. Some distributions can’t be scaled at all (e.g. ss.beta_dist() or ss.choice()). For distributions that can be scaled, some distributions can only be (linearly) scaled before the random numbers are generated (called “predraw”), some can only be scaled after (called “postdraw”), and some can be scaled in either way (both).
For example, a normal distribution is both since 2Normal(a, b) = Normal(2a, 2b). A Poisson distribution is “predraw” since 2Poisson(λ) ≠ Poisson(2λ), and there is no way to get the correct shape of a different Poisson distribution once the numbers have been drawn. Finally, distributions with unitless shape parameters as well as parameter that can have units (e.g. a gamma distribution with shape and scale parameters) are referred to as “postdraw” since scaling all input parameters is invalid (i.e. 2Gamma(shape, scale) ≠ Gamma(2shape, 2scale)), but they can still be scaled (i.e. 2Gamma(shape, scale) = Gamma(1shape, 2*scale)).
So scaling is one of:
- 'postdraw' (after the random numbers are drawn, e.g. `ss.weibull()`)
- 'predraw' (before the draw, e.g. `ss.poisson()`)
- ['predraw', 'postdraw'] (either, e.g. `ss.normal()`)
- None (not at all, e.g. `ss.beta_dist()`)
Note: by default, ss.Dist is initialized with an ss.Sim object to ensure random number reproducibility. You can override this with either ss.Dist(strict=False) on creation, or dist.init(force=True) after creation. A distribution with a unit (e.g. ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10))) draws in that unit outside a sim, with neither.
Although it’s possible in theory to define a custom distribution (i.e., not one from NumPy or SciPy), in practice this is difficult. The distribution needs to have both a way to return random variates (easy), as well as the probability point function (inverse CDF). In addition, the distribution must be able to take a NumPy RNG as its bit generator. It’s easier to just use a default Dist (e.g., ss.random()), and then take its output as input (i.e., quantiles) for whatever custom distribution you want to create.

Each number is still exactly uniform, so every distribution keeps its shape, but together they have the mean and spread they should. internals.dists.hash_uniforms(seed, ind, slots, dtype=None, even=False)
Generate one uniform random number in (0, 1) per slot via a counter-based (splitmix64) hash keyed by (seed, ind); not for the user.
This is the engine behind Starsim’s common random numbers (CRN). Because each output depends only on its slot (plus the per-draw key), the same slot always yields the same value regardless of how many other agents are drawn – so structural differences between scenarios don’t ripple into unrelated agents. Unlike the stream-based approach (draw slots.max()+1 numbers and gather), this generates exactly len(slots) numbers, avoiding the slot_scale blowup.
The result is returned at dtype (default ss.dtypes.float) so the CRN path matches the dtype of the native draw path (Dist.rand). The mantissa width is matched to the float width (24-bit for float32, 53-bit for float64) so every value stays strictly < 1 – a plain float64->float32 cast would round the largest values up to exactly 1.0 and break the [0, 1) contract (e.g. expon.ppf(1.0) is inf). The float64 stream is unchanged from earlier versions. With even, the numbers of the call are evenly spaced (see even_out()).

Whether two lists hold the same objects, or plain values that are equal and of the same type



internals.dists.some(x)
np.any(x), likewise



internals.dists.str2int(string, modulo=1000000000)
Convert a string to an int to use as a random seed; not for the user
Cannot use Python’s built-in hash() since it’s randomized for strings. Hashlib (sc.sha) is 5x slower than int.from_bytes(string.encode(), byteorder=‘big’), but should only add a couple milliseconds to a typical sim.



internals.dists.timepar_of(val)
The time parameter that a distribution’s parameter is, or holds in an array of them (which is slow, but allowed); else None

title: converters
text:
converters
Import models from other frameworks, and export sims to them
ss.import_from(filename, format=...) reads another framework’s model into a sim, and ss.export_to(sim, format) writes a sim in another framework’s format; see docs/design/16-interop.md in the lingua_franca_design repo. Each importer reads its format into an ss.converters.Source, and ss.converters.build() writes that as Starsim code by the same rules for every format (ss.converters.write()) and runs the code to make the sim: the code is kept in sim.imported.code, how each rate was read is printed, and what could not be translated is listed as ss.errors.ImportIncomplete and kept in sim.imported.

    msim,
    targets,
    origin_date=None,

The runs of a MultiSim as a submission to a hub (in the hubverse format): each target, by scenario, location, and period
Each scenario (the label of its sim) is its own scenario_id, and the periods are counted from origin_date. A target’s name says what it is: one starting “cum” is the total since the origin date, one starting “peak size” is the largest value of a period (with no horizon), and any other is a flow’s total over each period, or a count at its end.

Type
Description
Default

ss.MultiSim
the runs

required

None

str

None


every
str
the period: ‘day’ or ‘week’ (of the sim’s steps, which must then be days)
'week'


output_type
str / list

'quantile'

list
the quantiles (default: the 23 that the US hubs ask for)
hub_quantiles


location
str
the name of the single location, if by is not given
None

title: sim
text:
sim
The sim (ss.Sim) and its parameters (ss.SimPars)
This is what a user runs. It exists to gather the people, modules, and settings of a model in one object; to choose how to run it (the solver); and to hold the results. It works the same way for every kind of model.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Sim
The Sim object


SimPars
Create the parameters for the simulation. Typically, this function is used





sim.Sim(
    *models,
    label=None,
    people=None,
    demographics=None,
    connectors=None,
    networks=None,
    diseases=None,
    interventions=None,
    analyzers=None,
    custom=None,
    modules=None,
    data=None,
    pars=None,
    **kwargs,
)
The Sim object
All Starsim simulations run via the Sim class. It is responsible for initializing and running all modules and generating results. The sim orchestrates ss.People, ss.Network, ss.Disease, ss.Intervention, ss.Demographics, and other modules via the ss.Loop integration loop.





Name
Type
Description
Default




model
Module / list / dict
the model: a module or a list of modules, which are sorted by type as for modules; transitions, alone or in a list (or in diseases=), are one disease, named from its states (e.g. sim.sir). Alternatively, the sim parameters as an ss.SimPars object or a nested dictionary, which can include all other arguments
required


pars
dict
the values of model parameters by name, e.g. pars=dict(beta=0.1) or pars=fit.pars (see ss.par), and of sim settings by their own names (e.g. stop) where no parameter of the model has the name; a name that is neither raises a KeyError
None

str
the human-readable name of the simulation
None


people
People
if provided, use this ss.People object
None

sim.Sim.fit(
    pars=None,
    data=None,
    weights=None,
    likelihood=None,
    gof=None,
    penalty=None,
    method=None,
    n_runs=None,
    reseed=None,
    rand_seed=None,
    nopython=True,
    verbose=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Fit every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data
Fits every parameter that has bounds (see ss.par) to every result that has data (see ss.Sim(data=...)). The original sim is not changed. The fitting itself is in ss.fit, which is imported when it is first used.
A parameter can be one of a declared model, of a module written as code (ssl.HIV(beta=ss.par(...)), also a value in a dict parameter, fitted as e.g. cin_fn.k, or a setting kept as an attribute), a modifier’s amount (ss.modify(..., multiply=ss.par(...))), or a keyword argument of a function given as a module (def set_testing(sim, symp_prob=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 0.5])), for a value set in code); one named alike in several modules is fitted with its module’s name, e.g. hpv16.rel_beta. A parameter whose value is an array, with bounds for each element (ss.par(np.array([...]), bounds=[lows, highs])), has each element fitted, as knots[0], …, except those whose bounds are equal. A data column names a result, as sim.results has it: e.g. prevalence, sir.prevalence, an analyzer’s by_age.cancers_0_15, a result nested deeper (hpv.genotype.cancers), or a column of a result with columns (sis.infection.alpha).





Name
Type
Description
Default




pars
list
the names of the parameters to fit (default: all that have bounds)
None


data
df
the data to fit to (default: the sim’s data)
None


weights
dict
the relative weight of each data series (default: equal)
None


likelihood
dict
the likelihood of a data series, by its name (e.g. dict(prevalence=ss.normal(scale=0.02))), for series whose outcome does not declare one. If every series has a likelihood, the fit maximizes their sum (plus the log of the priors of the parameters that have one, for the methods that find a best fit: the most probable values)
None


gof
str / func
the goodness of fit: ‘nae’ (normalized absolute error, the default), ‘rmse’, or a function of the sim; any other name is an error
None


penalty
func
a function of the parameter values (a dict by name, an array whole) returning a number added to what a best fit minimizes, e.g. a smoothness penalty, lambda pars: 10*np.sum(np.diff(pars['knots'], 2)**2)
None


method
str / list
by default, a best fit (a point estimate), by the method that suits the sim, which is printed with the reason: ‘l-bfgs-b’ for a deterministic sim with gradients (from JAX; see ss.gradients), ‘nelder-mead’ for one without them, or with one or two fitted parameters (where it is faster than gradients), and ‘optuna’ for a stochastic sim, including an agent-based one. A posterior is asked for by name: ‘nuts’ (the No-U-Turn sampler, for a deterministic sim with gradients whose data series all have a likelihood, with each chain started from one of the best points of a scan over the bounds that are apart), ‘pmcmc’ (particle MCMC, for a stochastic compartmental sim whose data series all have a likelihood: a random-walk Metropolis sampler on the likelihood estimated by a particle filter; see ss.fit.ParticleFilter), or ‘abc-smc’ (approximate Bayesian computation by sequential Monte Carlo, for any sim, with no likelihood needed); the priors are the parameters’ prior=, or uniform over their bounds. Also: ‘if2’ (iterated filtering, for the sims that ‘pmcmc’ fits: the maximum-likelihood values, from passes of a particle filter in which each particle’s values are perturbed by a shrinking random walk; see ss.fit.Swarm), ‘powell’ (no gradients) or ‘slsqp’ (with gradients, like ‘l-bfgs-b’), or a list of methods, each started from the best fit of the one before (a stage that does not converge stops the list; see ss.fit.fit_stages())
None


scan
int
for the SciPy methods, NUTS, and particle MCMC, the number of points spread over the bounds to try first (default: 10 per parameter, at most 100); the search starts from each of the best restarts=3 of them that are apart (for SciPy; 1 for a single parameter of a deterministic sim), each NUTS chain from one of the best that are apart, and particle MCMC from the best
required


n_runs
int
runs per evaluation, for a stochastic sim (default 4 for a stochastic compartmental sim, and 1 for agents and for a deterministic one); every point is scored by the mean over the same seeds (common random numbers), except under Optuna, where each point takes fresh seeds so that its search averages over chance (see reseed=); fit.mismatch is the score at the best fit over the first seeds
None


reseed
bool
whether each point takes fresh seeds (default: True for Optuna, False otherwise); reseed=False with Optuna scores every point with the same seeds, e.g. for a rare outcome, where with fresh seeds the search favors values whose runs were lucky
None


rand_seed
int
the random seed for the fitting method (default: the sim’s, so a fit gives the same answer each time)
None


nopython
bool
for a deterministic sim with gradients and a likelihood for every series, whether the gradients (and a NUTS posterior) have to be taken with the log-likelihood as one function in JAX; if the model has something JAX does not cover yet, the fit is then an error that says what, and with nopython=False it takes them with Python in the loop instead, which is much slower
True


verbose
bool
whether to print progress
None


kwargs
dict
passed to the fitting method (each method’s settings are in the docs of ss.fit.fit_scipy(), fit_optuna(), fit_if2(), fit_pmcmc(), fit_abc_smc(), and fit_nuts(), and one the method does not take is an error), e.g. n_trials=200 for Optuna (and n_workers=4 to run trials in 4 processes at once, and storage='fit.log' to keep the trials in a file, so that calling it again resumes the fit; see ss.fit.fit_optuna()), maxiter=500 for SciPy, draws=500, warmup=500, and chains=4 for NUTS (the defaults; 1,000 draws and 1,000 warm-up draws for particle MCMC, whose draws are more correlated), particles= for particle MCMC (default: chosen by each chain in its warm-up; see ss.fit.pmmh()), or parallel=False to run its chains one after another; for IF2, particles=1000, iterations=50 (passes of the filter), cooling=0.5 (the share of the first size of the random walk’s steps that is left after 50 passes, as pomp’s cooling.fraction.50), sd=0.05 (that first size, on the scale searched on: the logit of each value’s place between its bounds, of its log for wide bounds), and chains=4 (each from its own start: the best of the initial values and a spread of points over the bounds, by the filter)
{}









Name
Type
Description






An ss.fit.Fit, with the calibrated sim as fit.sim and the best-fit values as fit.pars






beta = ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 0.5])
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sir = ss.Disease(S >> I @ beta * I, I >> R @ ss.days(10), init_prev=0.01)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, data='cases.csv', start='2020-01-01', stop='2020-06-01')
fit = sim.fit() # A best fit
post = sim.fit(method='nuts') # A posterior, given a likelihood for each data series
fit.sim.plot()

sim.Sim.rescale()
Dynamically rescale the population; only used if pars.rescale=True
The scale factor starts at 1. Once the fraction of agents who are not naive (i.e. have ever been infected with any disease) exceeds pars.rescale_threshold, the scale factor is increased by at least pars.rescale_factor (up to pars.pop_scale), and the same fraction of non-naive agents are made naive again (via disease.make_naive()), so that each agent now represents more people. Based on Covasim’s dynamic rescaling.
The people no agent stands for yet are counted as one number, results.unrepresented: pop_scale - 1 for each agent at the start, less the people the agents alive take on at each rescaling (from scale s to s', s' - s for each); the deaths and births of agents do not change it. So alive is scale people for each agent alive, plus these.

    *models,

The Sim object
All Starsim simulations run via the Sim class. It is responsible for initializing and running all modules and generating results. The sim orchestrates ss.People, ss.Network, ss.Disease, ss.Intervention, ss.Demographics, and other modules via the ss.Loop integration loop.

the model: a module or a list of modules, which are sorted by type as for modules; transitions, alone or in a list (or in diseases=), are one disease, named from its states (e.g. sim.sir). Alternatively, the sim parameters as an ss.SimPars object or a nested dictionary, which can include all other arguments

None

as above, for connectors

as above, for interventions

as above, for diseases

None

str
how to run modules with declared states and transitions (see ss.Disease): ‘auto’ (the default: an ODE if every part of the model has a compartmental form, otherwise agents), ‘ode’, ‘ide’ (deterministic, with each dwell time as it is rather than as stages), ‘binomial’ (chain-binomial), ‘gillespie’ (exact, one event at a time), ‘tau’ (tau-leaping: close to exact, and much faster for a run of many events), or ‘abm’
required

run the declared model as a branching process, under any solver: infection takes no one from the states of the uninfected and gives no one back, so the susceptible side stays as it would be with no infection (agents are made only for the infected); see sim.branching for the size and outcome of each run, and sim.run(until=) to stop one

Modules can be supplied either via individual keyword arguments (diseases, networks, etc.) or all together via the modules argument. When using modules, Starsim automatically sorts them by type. The individual kwargs and modules can be mixed; they are merged together.

sim.Sim.fit(
    pars=None,
    data=None,
    weights=None,
    likelihood=None,
    gof=None,
    penalty=None,
    method=None,
    n_runs=None,
    reseed=None,
    rand_seed=None,
    nopython=True,
    verbose=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Fit every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data
Fits every parameter that has bounds (see ss.par) to every result that has data (see ss.Sim(data=...)). The original sim is not changed. The fitting itself is in ss.fit, which is imported when it is first used.
A parameter can be one of a declared model, of a module written as code (ssl.HIV(beta=ss.par(...)), also a value in a dict parameter, fitted as e.g. cin_fn.k, or a setting kept as an attribute), a modifier’s amount (ss.modify(..., multiply=ss.par(...))), or a keyword argument of a function given as a module (def set_testing(sim, symp_prob=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 0.5])), for a value set in code); one named alike in several modules is fitted with its module’s name, e.g. hpv16.rel_beta. A parameter whose value is an array, with bounds for each element (ss.par(np.array([...]), bounds=[lows, highs])), has each element fitted, as knots[0], …, except those whose bounds are equal. A data column names a result, as sim.results has it: e.g. prevalence, sir.prevalence, an analyzer’s by_age.cancers_0_15, a result nested deeper (hpv.genotype.cancers), or a column of a result with columns (sis.infection.alpha).





Name
Type
Description
Default




pars
list
the names of the parameters to fit (default: all that have bounds)
None


data
df
the data to fit to (default: the sim’s data)
None


weights
dict
the relative weight of each data series (default: equal)
None


likelihood
dict
the likelihood of a data series, by its name (e.g. dict(prevalence=ss.normal(scale=0.02))), for series whose outcome does not declare one. If every series has a likelihood, the fit maximizes their sum (plus the log of the priors of the parameters that have one, for the methods that find a best fit: the most probable values)
None


gof
str / func
the goodness of fit: ‘nae’ (normalized absolute error, the default), ‘rmse’, or a function of the sim; any other name is an error
None


penalty
func
a function of the parameter values (a dict by name, an array whole) returning a number added to what a best fit minimizes, e.g. a smoothness penalty, lambda pars: 10*np.sum(np.diff(pars['knots'], 2)**2)
None


method
str / list
by default, a best fit (a point estimate), by the method that suits the sim, which is printed with the reason: ‘l-bfgs-b’ for a deterministic sim with gradients (from JAX; see ss.gradients), ‘nelder-mead’ for one without them, or with one or two fitted parameters (where it is faster than gradients), and ‘optuna’ for a stochastic sim, including an agent-based one. A posterior is asked for by name: ‘nuts’ (the No-U-Turn sampler, for a deterministic sim with gradients whose data series all have a likelihood, with each chain started from one of the best points of a scan over the bounds that are apart), ‘pmcmc’ (particle MCMC, for a stochastic compartmental sim whose data series all have a likelihood: a random-walk Metropolis sampler on the likelihood estimated by a particle filter; see ss.fit.ParticleFilter), or ‘abc-smc’ (approximate Bayesian computation by sequential Monte Carlo, for any sim, with no likelihood needed); the priors are the parameters’ prior=, or uniform over their bounds. Also: ‘if2’ (iterated filtering, for the sims that ‘pmcmc’ fits: the maximum-likelihood values, from passes of a particle filter in which each particle’s values are perturbed by a shrinking random walk; see ss.fit.Swarm), ‘powell’ (no gradients) or ‘slsqp’ (with gradients, like ‘l-bfgs-b’), or a list of methods, each started from the best fit of the one before (a stage that does not converge stops the list; see ss.fit.fit_stages())
None


scan
int
for the SciPy methods, NUTS, and particle MCMC, the number of points spread over the bounds to try first (default: 10 per parameter, at most 100); the search starts from each of the best restarts=3 of them that are apart (for SciPy; 1 for a single parameter of a deterministic sim), each NUTS chain from one of the best that are apart, and particle MCMC from the best
required


n_runs
int
runs per evaluation, for a stochastic sim (default 4 for a stochastic compartmental sim, and 1 for agents and for a deterministic one); every point is scored by the mean over the same seeds (common random numbers), except under Optuna, where each point takes fresh seeds so that its search averages over chance (see reseed=); fit.mismatch is the score at the best fit over the first seeds
None


reseed
bool
whether each point takes fresh seeds (default: True for Optuna, False otherwise); reseed=False with Optuna scores every point with the same seeds, e.g. for a rare outcome, where with fresh seeds the search favors values whose runs were lucky
None


rand_seed
int
the random seed for the fitting method (default: the sim’s, so a fit gives the same answer each time)
None


nopython
bool
for a deterministic sim with gradients and a likelihood for every series, whether the gradients (and a NUTS posterior) have to be taken with the log-likelihood as one function in JAX; if the model has something JAX does not cover yet, the fit is then an error that says what, and with nopython=False it takes them with Python in the loop instead, which is much slower

whether to print progress

passed to the fitting method (each method’s settings are in the docs of ss.fit.fit_scipy(), fit_optuna(), fit_if2(), fit_pmcmc(), fit_abc_smc(), and fit_nuts(), and one the method does not take is an error), e.g. n_trials=200 for Optuna (and n_workers=4 to run trials in 4 processes at once, and storage='fit.log' to keep the trials in a file, so that calling it again resumes the fit; see ss.fit.fit_optuna()), maxiter=500 for SciPy, draws=500, warmup=500, and chains=4 for NUTS (the defaults; 1,000 draws and 1,000 warm-up draws for particle MCMC, whose draws are more correlated), particles= for particle MCMC (default: chosen by each chain in its warm-up; see ss.fit.pmmh()), or parallel=False to run its chains one after another; for IF2, particles=1000, iterations=50 (passes of the filter), cooling=0.5 (the share of the first size of the random walk’s steps that is left after 50 passes, as pomp’s cooling.fraction.50), sd=0.05 (that first size, on the scale searched on: the logit of each value’s place between its bounds, of its log for wide bounds), and chains=4 (each from its own start: the best of the initial values and a spread of points over the bounds, by the filter)

sim.Sim.rescale()
Dynamically rescale the population; only used if pars.rescale=True
The scale factor starts at 1. Once the fraction of agents who are not naive (i.e. have ever been infected with any disease) exceeds pars.rescale_threshold, the scale factor is increased by at least pars.rescale_factor (up to pars.pop_scale), and the same fraction of non-naive agents are made naive again (via disease.make_naive()), so that each agent now represents more people. Based on Covasim’s dynamic rescaling.
The people no agent stands for yet are counted as one number, results.unrepresented: pop_scale - 1 for each agent at the start, less the people the agents alive take on at each rescaling (from scale s to s', s' - s for each); the deaths and births of agents do not change it. So alive is scale people for each agent alive, plus these.

A value for each person: drawn at an event, recorded at an event, drawn once when the person is made (a trait), or derived
Which it is depends on value and on=: a distribution with on= is drawn when the event happens to someone; an expression (or the name of another attribute) with on= is recorded then, as it was just before the move; a dict of them by event (a transition, tr.to(B), X.enter, …) records each event’s own value, with no on=; a distribution with no on= is a trait; and an expression, or a dict of one by state (states not listed give NaN), with no on= is derived, worked out when it is read. title: library.diseases
text:
library.diseases
Example disease models: cholera, COVID, dengue, Ebola, gonorrhea, HIV, influenza, malaria, measles, pertussis, polio, RSV, syphilis, TB, typhoid, and a non-communicable disease (NCD), and Starsim 3’s SIR, SEIR, and SIS written as code.
These are illustrative, lightly-parameterized models intended as starting points for building your own disease modules, not as validated models for any specific setting. Each one says in its docstring where its structure and its default parameters came from. Core disease base classes (ss.Disease, ss.Infection, ss.SIR, etc.) live in starsim.diseases.





Name
Description




ART
Scale up antiretroviral therapy over time.


AgentSEIR
An SEIR model written as code: Starsim 3’s ss.SEIR (see ssl.AgentSIR), with its lognormal dur_exp and dur_inf and p_death=0.01; for an SEIR model, use ss.SEIR


AgentSIR
An SIR model written as code: Starsim 3’s ss.SIR


AgentSIS
An SIS model with waning immunity, written as code: Starsim 3’s ss.SIS (see ssl.AgentSIR), with its lognormal dur_inf


CD4_analyzer
Record the CD4 count of every agent at every timestep.


COVID
COVID-19, as a SECIR model: a chain of increasingly severe states, each of which some people leave by recovering


Cholera
Cholera, with both direct and environmental (waterborne) transmission.


Ebola
Ebola, including severe disease and transmission from unburied bodies.


Gonorrhea
Gonorrhea, as an SIS model on a sexual network


HIV
Simple HIV model with CD4 count dynamics and ART.


Influenza
Seasonal influenza, as a SEIRS model with a yearly cycle in transmission


Malaria
Malaria as the Ross-Macdonald model of humans and mosquitoes


MalariaImmunity
Malaria with immunity, as the Garki model


Measles
Measles, as an SEIR model.


NCD
Example non-communicable disease


Pertussis
Pertussis (whooping cough), as a SEIRS model with slowly waning immunity


Polio
Poliovirus, with a paralytic fraction


RSV
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), as a seasonal MSEIRS model


Syphilis
Syphilis, as a staged infection, wholly declared


TB
Tuberculosis, as the LSHTM model of the spectrum of TB disease


Typhoid
Typhoid fever, with chronic carriers

An SEIR model written as code: Starsim 3’s ss.SEIR (see ssl.AgentSIR), with its lognormal dur_exp and dur_inf and p_death=0.01; for an SEIR model, use ss.SEIR
This class extends AgentSIR with an exposed state: agents who are infected but not yet infectious. exposed and infectious are the literal E and I compartments, and infected is derived from them: an agent is infected from the moment it acquires the infection, whether or not it is yet transmitting. So infected and prevalence count E plus I, while transmission depends on infectious alone.
Correspondingly, ti_exposed is the time of acquisition and ti_infectious is the time of becoming infectious. ti_infected is deliberately not defined, since it is too easily confused with ti_infectious.

    beta=_,
    init_prev=_,

    p_death=_,

)
An SIR model written as code: Starsim 3’s ss.SIR
This class implements a basic SIR model with states for susceptible, infected/infectious, and recovered, as per-agent arrays updated in code (see ss.Infection). It also includes deaths, and basic results. It is an example of writing a disease as code, and a base class for diseases with per-agent behavior (e.g. ssl.Ebola); for an SIR model, use the declared ss.SIR, which runs with every solver. A Starsim 3 subclass of ss.SIR that overrides its methods can subclass this class instead, unchanged.
Its defaults are Starsim 3’s: a lognormal dur_inf (a mean of 6 years, std 1 year) and p_death=0.01, where the declared ss.SIR is the textbook SIR, with an exponential dur_inf and no deaths. Use it to keep a Starsim 3 model’s parameters; its timing is the agent engine’s (see above), so each case is infectious for half a step longer on average than in Starsim 3.

    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,
    _names=None,

COVID-19, as a SECIR model: a chain of increasingly severe states, each of which some people leave by recovering
People who are infected are exposed (E), then infected without symptoms (INS), and then either recover or develop symptoms (ISy); of those, some become severe (ISev, in hospital), then critical (ICr, in intensive care), and some of those die. People without symptoms and with symptoms are both infectious, at rel_ins and rel_sym of the contact rate.

This version is not age-structured. Since the severity of COVID-19 rises steeply with age, a real model would be: covid.stratify(age=[0, 20, 60], split=[0.25, 0.5, 0.25], adjust=dict(severe=[0.2, 1, 4])), with a contact matrix given to the sim (see the user guide on stratification).

    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,
    _names=None,
    **kwargs,

Gonorrhea, as an SIS model on a sexual network
Gonorrhea leaves no lasting immunity: people clear the infection, by treatment or on their own, and are susceptible again at once. Most infections in women go without symptoms and so last much longer than those in men, which is why a fuller model gives the duration and the transmission probability by sex.
Source: the parameters are those of the gonorrhea module of STIsim (https://github.com/starsimhub/stisim, stisim/diseases/gonorrhea.py), whose own sources are cited there: a transmission probability per act from men to women of 0.06, and durations to clearance of a few months to about a year, from which dur_inf here is a single average.
Nobody is treated here, so the level gonorrhea settles at is above what a setting with treatment would show, and it depends strongly on the network: with few partners and few acts it dies out instead.

library.diseases.HIV(pars=None, **kwargs)
Simple HIV model with CD4 count dynamics and ART.
Infected agents have a CD4 count that declines towards cd4_min while untreated and recovers towards cd4_max while on ART, at a rate set by cd4_rate. Seasonal influenza, as a SEIRS model with a yearly cycle in transmission
Transmission follows a smooth yearly cycle (ss.seasonal), highest in January in the northern hemisphere, and immunity wanes within a year or so, as the virus drifts. library.diseases.Malaria(
    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,
    _names=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Malaria as the Ross-Macdonald model of humans and mosquitoes
People are susceptible, infectious, or recovered, and are born and die; mosquitoes are susceptible or infectious, and stay infectious until they die. Mosquitoes are a count, not people (Sv, Iv), and start at their density of m per person, all susceptible.
Source: the Ross-Macdonald model, in the form of Keeling MJ, Rohani P, Modeling Infectious Diseases in Humans and Animals, Princeton University Press, 2008, section 4.4. Every default here is from its Program 4.4: the biting rate a (its r of 0.5 per 1,000 humans), the transmission probabilities b and c (its transmission matrix), gamma, mu_h, mu_v, and m (its 10,091 mosquitoes per 1,000 people). The model is originally that of Ross R, The Prevention of Malaria, Murray, 1911, and Macdonald G, The Epidemiology and Control of Malaria, Oxford University Press, 1957.
R0() is 14.6 with these values, which is the square root of the classical Ross-Macdonald value, m·a²·b·c/(γ·μ_v) = 213, since each passage through a mosquito and back is two generations.

library.diseases.MalariaImmunity(
    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,
    _names=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Malaria with immunity, as the Garki model
The states keep the source’s names: x1 (nonimmune and negative), x2 (nonimmune, incubating), y1 (positive and infectious), y2 (positive, not infectious, recovering slowly), y3 (immune positive, recovering fast), x3 (immune and negative), and x4 (immune, incubating). People lose infectivity before they gain a fast recovery rate, and are detected less often once immune (q3). Everything about the mosquitoes is in one number, the vectorial capacity C: the potentially infective contacts each person makes per day through them. Inoculation saturates as C rises (h = g(1 − exp(−C·y1))), and superinfection slows recovery (R(h) = h/(exp(h/r) − 1)).
Source: the Garki model of Dietz K, Molineaux L, Thomas A, “A malaria model tested in the African savannah”, Bull World Health Organ 1974;50(3-4):347-357, in the form given by Molineaux L, Gramiccia G, The Garki Project, WHO, 1980, chapter 10. The defaults are its Table 31: g, alpha2, and r1 were fitted to the Garki data, and alpha1, delta, dur_inc, ratio (r2/r1), and q3 were assumed. C varied by season and village from below 0.01 to above 2 (its Fig. 77), so the default here is a constant chosen for illustration; give an ss.seasonal() for a seasonal one.
Malaria dies out below the critical vectorial capacity, (alpha1 + delta)/g, which is 0.022 per day with these values, as the source gives.

Syphilis, as a staged infection, wholly declared
People who are infected incubate (E), then have a primary chancre (P), then secondary syphilis (Se), and then early latent syphilis (El), from which some relapse to secondary syphilis and the rest pass to late latent syphilis (Ll). A share of those develop tertiary syphilis (T), which can kill; the rest are no longer infectious (R).
How infectious a person with latent syphilis is falls with the time since their latent stage began, a quantity each person carries: two modifiers of rel_trans, members of the disease. Since it acts on each person, this disease runs as agents.
Source: the natural history and its parameters are those of the syphilis module of STIsim (https://github.com/starsimhub/stisim, stisim/diseases/syphilis.py), whose own sources are cited there: the incubation period, primary and secondary stages from Garnett GP et al. (1997), the definition of early latent syphilis as up to two years after infection from WHO Europe, and the share developing tertiary syphilis. The half-life of latent infectiousness is STIsim’s.
Nobody is treated here, and the latent and tertiary stages last for years and count towards prevalence, so the level it settles at is well above what a setting with treatment and screening would show; add ss.screen() and ss.treat() to the sim for that. How far it spreads also depends on the network: the partnerships, how long they last, and the acts in them.

Tuberculosis, as the LSHTM model of the spectrum of TB disease
People who are infected either clear the infection, or develop disease that moves back and forth between non-infectious, asymptomatic (infectious, but at trans_asymp of a symptomatic person), and symptomatic. People who cleared or recovered can be infected again, at their own relative rate. Only symptomatic people die of TB; every death is replaced by a birth, so the population stays the same size, as in the source.

Treatment is off in that reference, and is left out here; TBsim adds treatment, drug resistance, and preventive therapy.
With the reference’s beta of 9, TB declines slowly over centuries (R0() is 0.23, since most infections are cleared and few reach disease), reproducing that reference exactly; beta is what a model of a particular place fits to its data.
Rates are per year, so a step of a year or a month suits it.

Dengue: several serotypes, each passed on by mosquitoes, with partial cross-protection between them
Each serotype is a disease of its own, den1 to den4, with the host and vector structure of ssl.Malaria, plus the extrinsic incubation period in the mosquito, so this returns a list of diseases, and the results are sim.results.den1 and so on. Having had one serotype gives complete protection against that one and partial protection against the others (cross), a modifier of each serotype’s rel_sus.
Sources: the host-vector structure is the Ross-Macdonald model as given by Keeling MJ, Rohani P, Modeling Infectious Diseases in Humans and Animals, Princeton University Press, 2008, section 4.4 (see ssl.Malaria). The dengue values are indicative ones from the literature rather than one source’s fitted set: about 6 days of viremia in people and an extrinsic incubation period of about 10 days in Aedes aegypti at tropical temperatures, with a mosquito lifetime of about 10 days. That infection with one serotype gives lasting protection against it and temporary, partial protection against the others is the finding of Reich NG et al., “Interactions between serotypes of dengue highlight epidemiological impact of cross-immunity”, J R Soc Interface 2013;10(86):20130414 (https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2013.0414); here that cross-protection does not wane, which is a simplification, and its size (cross) is illustrative.

An SEIR model written as code: Starsim 3’s ss.SEIR (see ssl.AgentSIR), with its lognormal dur_exp and dur_inf and p_death=0.01; for an SEIR model, use ss.SEIR
This class extends AgentSIR with an exposed state: agents who are infected but not yet infectious. exposed and infectious are the literal E and I compartments, and infected is derived from them: an agent is infected from the moment it acquires the infection, whether or not it is yet transmitting. Correspondingly, ti_exposed is the time of acquisition and ti_infectious is the time of becoming infectious. ti_infected is deliberately not defined, since it is too easily confused with ti_infectious.

library.diseases.MalariaImmunity(
    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,
    _names=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Malaria with immunity, as the Garki model
The states keep the source’s names: x1 (nonimmune and negative), x2 (nonimmune, incubating), y1 (positive and infectious), y2 (positive, not infectious, recovering slowly), y3 (immune positive, recovering fast), x3 (immune and negative), and x4 (immune, incubating). People lose infectivity before they gain a fast recovery rate, and are detected less often once immune (q3). Everything about the mosquitoes is in one number, the vectorial capacity C: the potentially infective contacts each person makes per day through them. Inoculation saturates as C rises (h = g(1 − exp(−C·y1))), and superinfection slows recovery (R(h) = h/(exp(h/r) − 1)).

The defaults are its Table 31: g, alpha2, and r1 were fitted to the Garki data, and alpha1, delta, dur_inc, ratio (r2/r1), and q3 were assumed. C varied by season and village from below 0.01 to above 2 (its Fig. 77), so the default here is a constant chosen for illustration; give an ss.seasonal() for a seasonal one.
Malaria dies out below the critical vectorial capacity, (alpha1 + delta)/g, which is 0.022 per day with these values, as the source gives.

    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,

)
Typhoid fever, with chronic carriers
Most people recover from typhoid, but a small share become chronic carriers, who shed for life and are much less infectious than an acute case (rel_carrier), while contributing to transmission for decades. Immunity after infection wanes slowly, if at all.
Sources: the values of the carriers are from Pitzer VE et al., “Predicting the impact of vaccination on the transmission dynamics of typhoid in South Asia”, PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2014;8(1):e2642 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0002642): a relative infectiousness of carriers of 0.01, a share becoming carriers within their 0.3% to 10% by age, and a rate of waning immunity estimated as close to zero, so immunity is lifelong by default. beta is set to give their estimated R0 of 2.8 for Kolkata and Vellore. The duration of acute infection, 4 weeks, is a standard value.

Dengue
Dengue: several serotypes, each passed on by mosquitoes, with partial cross-protection between them





library.diseases.Dengue(
    n_serotypes=4,
    cross=0.3,
    a=ss.perday(0.5),
    b=0.5,
    c=0.5,
    m=2.0,
    dur_inf=ss.days(6),
    eip=ss.days(10),
    mu_v=ss.perday(0.1),
    init=0.001,
    **kwargs,
)
Dengue: several serotypes, each passed on by mosquitoes, with partial cross-protection between them
Each serotype is a disease of its own, den1 to den4, with the host and vector structure of ssl.Malaria, plus the extrinsic incubation period in the mosquito, so this returns a list of diseases, and the results are sim.results.den1 and so on. Having had one serotype gives complete protection against that one and partial protection against the others (cross), a modifier of each serotype’s rel_sus.
Sources: the host-vector structure is the Ross-Macdonald model as given by Keeling MJ, Rohani P, Modeling Infectious Diseases in Humans and Animals, Princeton University Press, 2008, section 4.4 (see ssl.Malaria). The dengue values are indicative ones from the literature rather than one source’s fitted set: about 6 days of viremia in people and an extrinsic incubation period of about 10 days in Aedes aegypti at tropical temperatures, with a mosquito lifetime of about 10 days. That infection with one serotype gives lasting protection against it and temporary, partial protection against the others is the finding of Reich NG et al., “Interactions between serotypes of dengue highlight epidemiological impact of cross-immunity”, J R Soc Interface 2013;10(86):20130414 (https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2013.0414); here that cross-protection does not wane, which is a simplification, and its size (cross) is illustrative.

library.mnch.CongenitalDisease.set_congenital(target_uids, source_uids=None)
Assign congenital outcomes during in-utero infection (called when transmission occurs via PrenatalNet).
Does nothing unless the disease defines birth_outcome_keys and birth_outcomes in its pars. Diseases that need fully custom logic (e.g. syphilis, which has stage-dependent outcomes) can override this method entirely.
To use it, define in the disease’s __init__:
self.define_pars(
    birth_outcome_keys = ['stillborn', 'congenital', 'normal'],
    birth_outcomes     = sc.obj(default=ss.choice(a=3, p=[0.3, 0.4, 0.3])),  # Illustrative placeholder
)
Each outcome name needs a matching ti_<name> FloatArr state; non-lethal outcomes also need a BoolArr of the same name. Death outcomes (‘miscarriage’, ‘neonatal_death’, ‘stillborn’) fire via request_death; others set a bool state.
Outcomes are scheduled for the mother’s delivery timestep, except for fetal losses (‘miscarriage’, ‘stillborn’), which are scheduled one timestep earlier so that they occur before the fetus is delivered and are classified as fetal losses rather than neonatal deaths. A fetus infected within one timestep of delivery is therefore born alive, and a lethal outcome for it counts as a neonatal death.
For state- or GA-dependent probabilities, provide multiple keyed distributions in birth_outcomes and override _assign_congenital_outcomes.

library.mnch.FetalHealth(pars=None, **kwargs)
Track fetal health outcomes during pregnancy.
Works alongside the Pregnancy module to model birth weight outcomes (low birth weight, small for gestational age) based on fetal growth restriction. Disease-agnostic by design: external modules (connectors, interventions) modify fetal health via the public API methods.
Preterm classification is handled by the Pregnancy module (based on gestational age at birth). This module focuses on the weight/growth axis.
Integrates with Pregnancy via its callbacks (add_callback()): Pregnancy calls on_conception when new pregnancies begin and on_delivery when births occur. External modules (e.g. disease connectors) can register their own on preg.conception, after this module’s, to act on new pregnancies after baseline initialization.
During pregnancy, weight_percentile, growth_restriction, timing_shift, and n_exposures are tracked on the mother. At delivery, birth_weight, lbw, vlbw, and sga are stored on the newborn.
Each pregnancy gets a baseline weight percentile drawn at conception. Two modification levers are available:
1. **Delivery timing**: bring the delivery (`ti_exit_P`) forward (preterm birth risk)
2. **Growth restriction**: accumulate fractional weight reduction
At delivery: birth_weight = baseline_for_GA × percentile × (1 - restriction)
The results are counts of births and outcomes on each step, and means and rates over a step’s births (mean_birth_weight, lbw_rate, …), which are NaN on a step with no births, and are left out of a mean over time (e.g. res.mean_birth_weight.resample('year')).
Note: CRN safe.

library.mnch.fetal_infection(pars=None, **kwargs)
Connect a disease to fetal health outcomes during pregnancy.
Monitors for infections in pregnant women and applies fetal damage: - Timing shift: brings delivery forward (increases preterm birth risk). Drawn from a lognormal distribution per affected pregnancy. - Growth restriction: reduces birth weight by a fixed fractional penalty.
Damage is applied at two points: 1. At conception, if the mother is already infected (via a conception callback registered with the pregnancy, after FetalHealth’s). 2. During pregnancy, when a new infection occurs (detected in step() by checking ti_infected == self.ti: an infection in the previous step is dated at its end, which is this step’s start).
Requires ssl.mnch.FetalHealth() in custom and an SIR disease written as code (ssl.AgentSIR(name="sir")) in diseases.
Note: CRN safe.

Type
Description
Default

required

required

dict
the same parameters, as a dict
None



To adapt for a different disease::
class my_fetal_connector(fetal_infection):
    def init_pre(self, sim):
        # Register with FetalHealth, but check for your disease instead
        ...

    def _apply_damage(self, uids):
        # Custom damage logic, e.g. stage-dependent penalties
        fh = self.fh
        disease = self.sim.diseases.my_disease
        severe = disease.severe[uids]
        mild_uids   = uids[~severe]
        severe_uids = uids[severe]
        fh.apply_growth_restriction(mild_uids, 0.05)
        fh.apply_growth_restriction(severe_uids, 0.25)
        ...

library.mnch.fetal_infection(pars=None, **kwargs)
Connect a disease to fetal health outcomes during pregnancy.
Monitors for infections in pregnant women and applies fetal damage: - Timing shift: brings delivery forward (increases preterm birth risk). Drawn from a lognormal distribution per affected pregnancy. - Growth restriction: reduces birth weight by a fixed fractional penalty.
Damage is applied at two points: 1. At conception, if the mother is already infected (via a conception callback registered with the pregnancy, after FetalHealth’s). 2. During pregnancy, when a new infection occurs (detected in step() by checking ti_infected == self.ti: an infection in the previous step is dated at its end, which is this step’s start).
Requires ssl.mnch.FetalHealth() in custom and an SIR disease written as code (ssl.AgentSIR(name="sir")) in diseases.
Note: CRN safe.

Type
Description
Default

required

required

the same parameters, as a dict
None



To adapt for a different disease::
class my_fetal_connector(fetal_infection):
    def init_pre(self, sim):
        # Register with FetalHealth, but check for your disease instead
        ...

    def _apply_damage(self, uids):
        # Custom damage logic, e.g. stage-dependent penalties
        fh = self.fh
        disease = self.sim.diseases.my_disease
        severe = disease.severe[uids]
        mild_uids   = uids[~severe]
        severe_uids = uids[severe]
        fh.apply_growth_restriction(mild_uids, 0.05)
        fh.apply_growth_restriction(severe_uids, 0.25)
        ...

internals.parameters.by(table=None, dims=None, **kwargs)
A value for each level of one or more stratifications, or of people’s own properties
With several dimensions as keywords, the value of a group is the product of its value in each. A table gives every combination directly: it has a column for each stratification (holding the labels of its levels) and a column of values.
A property of people that is not a dimension of the sim (e.g. sex, read from people.female, or a property such as urban) is read from each person, as agents: give its values by name (sex=dict(female=..., male=...)), or as a table. A column of numbers in a table holds the lower edges of bins (the last one open-ended), so a table by single year of age works as agents whatever the model’s age groups (a compartmental run needs bins whose edges are those of the groups, or coarser: a group split by a bin has no one value, and is refused); a row whose key is None gives the value for people with no value of the property, who otherwise get the mean over the levels.











Name
Type
Description
Default




table
df / array
a dataframe (or a dict of columns) with a column per stratification or property and a column named value; or, with dims, an array with one axis per dimension
None


dims
list
the dimensions of the axes of an array given as table
None


kwargs
dict
each dimension, and one value per level (a list, by position), or a dict of values by label (or, for one dimension, by lower bin edge if the keys are numbers, as in a table: ss.by(age={0: 0, 15: 0.3}))
{}



A value may itself vary in time (ss.timeseries or ss.seasonal), in the keyword and table forms.
Arithmetic with a number, or with another ss.by over the same levels, gives an ss.by; anything else (e.g. tables by different bins, a count, or np.minimum(by, 1)) is an expression, worked out where it is used.



beta = ss.by(age=[0.08, 0.05, 0.03])
beta = ss.by(age=[0.08, 0.05, 0.03], sex=[1.0, 0.8]) # One per age group and sex: the product
init = ss.by(pd.DataFrame(age=['child', 'adult'], patch=['north', 'north'], value=[10, 5])) # Every other combination is 0
pop = ss.by([[3000, 1000], [5000, 2000]], dims=['age', 'patch']) # Ages by row, places by column
beta = ss.by(age=[ss.timeseries({2020: 0.08, 2021: 0.04}), 0.05, 0.03]) # Children's value changes in 2021
mu = ss.by(sex=dict(female=0.008, male=0.011)) # From people.female, with or without a dimension by sex
p = ss.by(dict(age=range(15, 50), value=vals)) # By single year of age (bins with these lower edges)

internals.parameters.by(table=None, dims=None, **kwargs)
A value for each level of one or more stratifications, or of people’s own properties
With several dimensions as keywords, the value of a group is the product of its value in each. A table gives every combination directly: it has a column for each stratification (holding the labels of its levels) and a column of values.
A property of people that is not a dimension of the sim (e.g. sex, read from people.female, or a property such as urban) is read from each person, as agents: give its values by name (sex=dict(female=..., male=...)), or as a table. A column of numbers in a table holds the lower edges of bins (the last one open-ended), so a table by single year of age works as agents whatever the model’s age groups (a compartmental run needs bins whose edges are those of the groups, or coarser: a group split by a bin has no one value, and is refused); a row whose key is None gives the value for people with no value of the property, who otherwise get the mean over the levels.











Name
Type
Description
Default

df / array
a dataframe (or a dict of columns) with a column per stratification or property and a column named value; or, with dims, an array with one axis per dimension
None

list

None


kwargs
dict
each dimension, and one value per level (a list, by position), or a dict of values by label (or, for one dimension, by lower bin edge if the keys are numbers, as in a table: ss.by(age={0: 0, 15: 0.3}))
{}



A value may itself vary in time (ss.timeseries or ss.seasonal), in the keyword and table forms.
Arithmetic with a number, or with another ss.by over the same levels, gives an ss.by; anything else (e.g. tables by different bins, a count, or np.minimum(by, 1)) is an expression, worked out where it is used.



beta = ss.by(age=[0.08, 0.05, 0.03])
beta = ss.by(age=[0.08, 0.05, 0.03], sex=[1.0, 0.8]) # One per age group and sex: the product
init = ss.by(pd.DataFrame(age=['child', 'adult'], patch=['north', 'north'], value=[10, 5])) # Every other combination is 0
pop = ss.by([[3000, 1000], [5000, 2000]], dims=['age', 'patch']) # Ages by row, places by column
beta = ss.by(age=[ss.timeseries({2020: 0.08, 2021: 0.04}), 0.05, 0.03]) # Children's value changes in 2021
mu = ss.by(sex=dict(female=0.008, male=0.011)) # From people.female, with or without a dimension by sex
p = ss.by(dict(age=range(15, 50), value=vals)) # By single year of age (bins with these lower edges)

internals.errors
Errors, warnings, and notes.
Most errors are Python’s own (ValueError, TypeError, a KeyError for a name that is not found); the few kept as classes here are those that code may want to catch by kind, e.g. ss.CapabilityError. A note is a line about something that was assumed or approximated: it is kept in sim.notes and printed when verbose is 1 or more (see ss.note()).

internals.dates.datedur(value=None, **kwargs)
A calendar duration, e.g. ss.datedur(months=1): a thin wrapper of pd.DateOffset
Added to a date, it follows the calendar, so a month from 31 January is the end of February and a year from 1 March 2020 is 1 March 2021; dt=ss.datedur(months=1) steps a sim by calendar months. It takes whole numbers of years, months, weeks, and days (as keywords), or one of: a pd.DateOffset, a dateutil.relativedelta, a number of years, or a duration in one of these units (e.g. ss.days(7)). As a number (.years, .days, or divided by another duration) it is approximate, as other durations are: a year is 365 days, and a month a twelfth of a year. The time between two dates (date - date) is ss.days, not a datedur.


ss.date('2020-01-31') + ss.datedur(months=1) # 2020-02-29
ss.datedur(years=1)/ss.datedur(months=1) # 12
