title: internals.arrays
text:
internals.arrays
Arrays of agents’ values: states such as age or infection status, and the UIDs that index them
A state holds a value for every agent, and reads only the active ones, so code can use it like a NumPy array as agents are born and die. A few classes here stand in for them when a run has groups of people rather than agents (GroupAges, GroupAlive).
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Arr
Store a state of the agents (e.g. age, infection status, etc.) as an array.


BaseArr
An object that acts exactly like a NumPy array, except stores the values in self.values.


BoolArr
Subclass of ss.Arr with defaults for booleans.


BoolState
A boolean array being used as a state.


FloatArr
Subclass of ss.Arr with defaults for floats and ints.


GroupAges
people.age in a compartmental run: one row per group, at the middle of its age group


GroupAlive
people.alive in a run without agents: one row per group of people, not one per person


IndexArr
A special class of Arr used for UIDs and RNG IDs; not to be used as a general integer array (for that, use IntArr)


IntArr
Subclass of ss.Arr with defaults for ints.


TimeArr
Times, as step numbers of the module’s timeline: when something happened or is due for each agent, e.g. a declared disease’s ti_X (when each entered state X) and ti_exit_X, as agents, and people.ti_dead


UIDArr
The UIDs of all agents (people.uid), which take no memory: a UID is the agent’s index, so raw is made when read


Unkept
A declared disease’s time of entering a state (ti_X) that is not kept, since the engine does not need it (see ss.options.keep_times)


Watch
The link from a state to the engine that keeps count of who is in it (BoolState.watch), which is told of


uids
Class to specify that integers should be interpreted as UIDs.





internals.arrays.Arr(
    name=None,
    dtype=None,
    default=None,
    nan=None,
    label=None,
    raw=None,
    skip_init=False,
    people=None,
    mock=None,
    columns=None,
    shared=False,
)
Store a state of the agents (e.g. age, infection status, etc.) as an array.
In practice, Arr objects can be used interchangeably with NumPy arrays. They have two main data interfaces: Arr.raw contains the “raw”, underlying NumPy array of the data. Arr.values contains the “active” values, which usually corresponds to agents who are alive.
By default, operations are performed on active agents only (specified by Arr.auids, which is a pointer to sim.people.auids). For example, sim.people.age.mean() will only use the ages of active agents. Thus, sim.people.age.mean() is equal to sim.people.age.values.mean(), not sim.people.age.raw.mean().
If indexing by an int, integer array, or ss.uids object, Arr.raw is used (i.e. the ints are treated as UIDs). If indexing by a full slice ([:]) or a boolean array, Arr.values is used. Arr objects can’t be directly indexed by a list, as this would be ambiguous about whether values or raw is intended. For example, if there are 1000 people in a simulation and 100 of them have died, sim.people.age[999] and sim.people.age[ss.uids(999)] both return the age of the agent with UID 999, whereas sim.people.age.values[899] returns the age of the last active agent.
Note on terminology: the term “states” is often used to refer to all ss.Arr objects, (e.g. in module.define_states(), whether or not they are BoolStates.

A callable, with a single argument for the number of values to produce;
A ss.Dist instance.

None

None

int
if provided, create a mock People object (of length mock, unless raw is provided) to initialize the array (for debugging purposes)
None


columns
int / list
if provided, create a 2D array with this many columns (e.g. one per variant), or a list of column names (e.g. ['wildtype', 'mutant'])
None


shared
bool / Arr
if True, the array takes no memory per agent until a value is set (other than by its default, which must be a scalar): until then every agent has the default, and raw is a read-only view of it; if an Arr, the same with that array’s values (as people.slot reads people.uid)
False



For 2D arrays (i.e. if columns is supplied), arr[uids] returns an array of shape (len(uids), ncols), arr[uids, v] or arr[:, v] returns column v, and arr.col(v) returns column v as a 1D Arr. If the columns are named, v can also be a name, e.g. arr.col('mutant'), arr['mutant'], or arr.mutant. A scalar default fills every column, and a callable default should return an array of shape (n, ncols). Arrays with more dimensions are also supported via a tuple, e.g. columns=(2,3) gives a raw array of shape (len_tot, 2, 3).



# Create a standalone Arr for quick testing
age = ss.Arr('age', default=0, mock=5) # 5 = length if not supplying a real People object
age[:] = [20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
age.mean()  # Returns 40.0

# Use within a simulation
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=100).init()
sim.people.age.mean()  # Mean age of active agents

# Create a 2D array, e.g. immunity to each of 3 variants
imm = ss.FloatArr('imm', default=0, columns=3, mock=5)
imm[ss.uids([0, 1]), 2] = 0.8 # Set immunity to variant 2 for agents 0 and 1
imm[ss.uids([0, 1])] # Returns an array of shape (2, 3)
(imm.col(2) > 0.5).uids  # Returns ss.uids([0, 1])

# Create a 2D array with named columns
imm = ss.FloatArr('imm', default=0, columns=['wildtype', 'mutant'], mock=5)
imm[ss.uids([0, 1]), 'mutant'] = 0.8 # Same as imm[ss.uids([0, 1]), 1] = 0.8
(imm.col('mutant') > 0.5).uids  # Returns ss.uids([0, 1])

Times, as step numbers of the module’s timeline: when something happened or is due for each agent, e.g. a declared disease’s ti_X (when each entered state X) and ti_exit_X, as agents, and people.ti_dead
Stored as float32 step numbers, NaN for “never” (not set), so ti_I > 0 and (sim.ti - ti_I)*sim.t.dt give the right answer. due() gives whose time has come, with a time between steps rounded up or down at random in proportion (by each agent’s phase, as the agent engine rounds a dwell time: see ss.People.phase()), so it keeps its mean; isclose(sim.ti) gives whose time is taken at this step, and .years converts them to years. == and != raise, since a time between steps never equals a step: eq() is exact equality. For plain arithmetic on the times, compare them: e.g. ti_x < sim.ti + 0.5 is due at the nearest step, and ti_x <= sim.ti at the first step at or after it.
A declared state’s time of entering (ti_X) reads as the index of the step the move happened in, whatever kind of move it was (a progression at the step’s start, an infection by contact at its end), so ti_X.isclose(sim.ti) is “entered this step”. The engine keeps its own time of the move, which .raw gives (see shift). So the difference of two of them is not always a duration: an infection by contact happens at the end of its step and a scheduled move at the start of its step, so ti_I - ti_E of an SEIR reads one step longer than the latent period was. For the time people spent in a state, use the state’s stays (e.g. np.mean(seir.E.stays), the mean latent period), which is built from the engine’s times.


sim = ss.Sim(ss.SIR(), unit='day', stop=100).run()

self.define_states(ss.BoolState('exposed'), ss.TimeArr('ti_infectious'))

internals.arrays.uids()
Class to specify that integers should be interpreted as UIDs.
It exists so that indexing an ss.Arr with these reads those agents by UID, not by position.
For all practical purposes, behaves like a NumPy integer array. However, has additional methods uids.concatenate(), uids.remove(), and uids.intersect() to simplify common UID operations.
The following operators are supported:

+ / +=: if the RHS is a uids, concatenation (equivalent to uids.concatenate()); otherwise element-wise addition (e.g. uids([1,2]) + 1 → uids([2,3])). Concatenation preserves duplicates.
- / -=: set difference — equivalent to uids.remove(). Duplicate entries in the original will also be removed (uses np.setdiff1d internally).
| / |=: union (unique elements from both arrays). Note that duplicate entries in the original are removed (use + instead to keep them).
& / &=: intersection
^ / ^=: symmetric difference

Note: because uids is a subclass of np.ndarray, set-like in-place operators (+= with a uids RHS, -=, |=, &=, ^=) must return a new array and rebind the variable. However, += with a scalar or array RHS modifies the array in-place and preserves id(self).


a = ss.uids([1, 2, 3])
b = ss.uids([3, 4, 5])
a + b   # Concatenate: uids([1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5])
a | b   # Union:       uids([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
a & b   # Intersect:   uids([3])
a - b   # Difference:  uids([1, 2])

internals.arrays.Arr(
    name=None,
    dtype=None,
    default=None,
    nan=None,
    label=None,
    raw=None,
    skip_init=False,
    people=None,
    mock=None,
    columns=None,
    shared=False,
)
Store a state of the agents (e.g. age, infection status, etc.) as an array.
In practice, Arr objects can be used interchangeably with NumPy arrays. They have two main data interfaces: Arr.raw contains the “raw”, underlying NumPy array of the data. Arr.values contains the “active” values, which usually corresponds to agents who are alive.
By default, operations are performed on active agents only (specified by Arr.auids, which is a pointer to sim.people.auids). For example, sim.people.age.mean() will only use the ages of active agents. Thus, sim.people.age.mean() is equal to sim.people.age.values.mean(), not sim.people.age.raw.mean().
If indexing by an int, integer array, or ss.uids object, Arr.raw is used (i.e. the ints are treated as UIDs). If indexing by a full slice ([:]) or a boolean array, Arr.values is used. Arr objects can’t be directly indexed by a list, as this would be ambiguous about whether values or raw is intended. For example, if there are 1000 people in a simulation and 100 of them have died, sim.people.age[999] and sim.people.age[ss.uids(999)] both return the age of the agent with UID 999, whereas sim.people.age.values[899] returns the age of the last active agent.
Note on terminology: the term “states” is often used to refer to all ss.Arr objects, (e.g. in module.define_states(), whether or not they are BoolStates.

For 2D arrays (i.e. if columns is supplied), arr[uids] returns an array of shape (len(uids), ncols), arr[uids, v] or arr[:, v] returns column v, and arr.col(v) returns column v as a 1D Arr. If the columns are named, v can also be a name, e.g. arr.col('mutant'), arr['mutant'], or arr.mutant. A scalar default fills every column, and a callable default should return an array of shape (n, ncols). Arrays with more dimensions are also supported via a tuple, e.g. columns=(2,3) gives a raw array of shape (len_tot, 2, 3).



# Create a standalone Arr for quick testing
age = ss.Arr('age', default=0, mock=5) # 5 = length if not supplying a real People object
age[:] = [20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
age.mean()  # Returns 40.0

# Use within a simulation
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=100).init()
sim.people.age.mean()  # Mean age of active agents

# Create a 2D array, e.g. immunity to each of 3 variants
imm = ss.FloatArr('imm', default=0, columns=3, mock=5)
imm[ss.uids([0, 1]), 2] = 0.8 # Set immunity to variant 2 for agents 0 and 1

# Create a 2D array with named columns
imm = ss.FloatArr('imm', default=0, columns=['wildtype', 'mutant'], mock=5)
imm[ss.uids([0, 1]), 'mutant'] = 0.8 # Same as imm[ss.uids([0, 1]), 1] = 0.8
(imm.col('mutant') > 0.5).uids  # Returns ss.uids([0, 1])

internals.arrays.TimeArr(name=None, **kwargs)
Times, as step numbers of the module’s timeline: when something happened or is due for each agent, e.g. a declared disease’s ti_X (when each entered state X) and ti_exit_X, as agents, and people.ti_dead
Stored as float32 step numbers, NaN for “never” (not set), so ti_I > 0 and (sim.ti - ti_I)*sim.t.dt give the right answer. due() gives whose time has come, with a time between steps rounded up or down at random in proportion (by each agent’s phase, as the agent engine rounds a dwell time: see ss.People.phase()), so it keeps its mean; isclose(sim.ti) gives whose time is taken at this step, and .years converts them to years. == and != raise, since a time between steps never equals a step: eq() is exact equality. For plain arithmetic on the times, compare them: e.g. ti_x < sim.ti + 0.5 is due at the nearest step, and ti_x <= sim.ti at the first step at or after it.
A declared state’s time of entering (ti_X) reads as the index of the step the move happened in, whatever kind of move it was (a progression at the step’s start, an infection by contact at its end), so ti_X.isclose(sim.ti) is “entered this step”. The engine keeps its own time of the move, which .raw gives (see shift). So the difference of two of them is not always a duration: an infection by contact happens at the end of its step and a scheduled move at the start of its step, so ti_I - ti_E of an SEIR reads one step longer than the latent period was. For the time people spent in a state, use the state’s stays (e.g. np.mean(seir.E.stays), the mean latent period), which is built from the engine’s times.


sim = ss.Sim(ss.SIR(), unit='day', stop=100).run()
sir = sim.diseases.sir
infected_today = sir.ti_I.isclose(sim.ti).uids
years = sir.ti_I.years # The year of infection of each agent (NaN if never infected)

# In a disease written as code
self.define_states(ss.BoolState('exposed'), ss.TimeArr('ti_infectious'))
self.ti_infectious[uids] = self.ti + dur # In steps
mask = self.exposed & self.ti_infectious.due() # Those whose time has come

internals.arrays.uids()
Class to specify that integers should be interpreted as UIDs.
It exists so that indexing an ss.Arr with these reads those agents by UID, not by position.
For all practical purposes, behaves like a NumPy integer array. However, has additional methods uids.concatenate(), uids.remove(), and uids.intersect() to simplify common UID operations.
The following operators are supported:

+ / +=: if the RHS is a uids, concatenation (equivalent to uids.concatenate()); otherwise element-wise addition (e.g. uids([1,2]) + 1 → uids([2,3])). Concatenation preserves duplicates.
- / -=: set difference — equivalent to uids.remove(). Duplicate entries in the original will also be removed (uses np.setdiff1d internally).
| / |=: union (unique elements from both arrays). Note that duplicate entries in the original are removed (use + instead to keep them).
& / &=: intersection
^ / ^=: symmetric difference

Note: because uids is a subclass of np.ndarray, set-like in-place operators (+= with a uids RHS, -=, |=, &=, ^=) must return a new array and rebind the variable. However, += with a scalar or array RHS modifies the array in-place and preserves id(self).


a = ss.uids([1, 2, 3])
b = ss.uids([3, 4, 5])
a + b   # Concatenate: uids([1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5])
a | b   # Union:       uids([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
a & b   # Intersect:   uids([3])
a - b   # Difference:  uids([1, 2])

solvers.agents.Agents(module, sim, solver=None)
Runs a graph as agents
It exists so that a declared model can run with individuals, for what compartments cannot hold.
Each state that holds people is a boolean array over agents. A dwell time is sampled when an agent enters a state and the exit is scheduled; rates that depend on the state of the model are drawn each step, with competing rates out of one state resolved in a single draw; and contact-mediated transitions are drawn over the sim’s networks. States that are not people stay plain counts.

solvers.agents.Transmission(module, sim)
Transmission as agents, the same for a declared disease (Agents, for its transmissions) and one written as code (ss.Infection.transmit_route(), through its engine, ss.solvers.Undeclared): who can transmit and be infected, with the modifiers and products on rel_trans and rel_sus applied (current_value()); who is infected over a network (over_network()); and who infected whom (first_infections())
Where the two differ, the caller says how:

Hazard or probability. over_network() takes the chance of an edge in the step. A declared disease gives 1 − exp(−β·dt) from its rate, or, on a network with acts, works out a hazard per act (Agents.transmit_acts()); one written as code gives its beta as the probability in the step, converting a rate the same way (ss.Rate.to_prob()).
Order and attribution. The routes are taken in the order of sim.networks, and on each, p1 to p2 and then p2 to p1; someone reached by several is infected by the first (first_infections()), which is the source in the infection log. With strains, every strain is passed on in one pass, and someone reached by several is infected by one of them drawn at random, whose strain they take (pick_sources()), and then only if they are not protected against it (unprotected()): declared or written as code, by the same code.
Random numbers. Each edge’s is drawn by its source and target from the disease’s trans_rng, so the same disease, by the same name, gives the same edges the same numbers, declared or written as code; and so are the draws of who infects whom, and of protection, which are keyed by the step alone (step_draw()).

solvers.agents.Agents(module, sim, solver=None)
Runs a graph as agents
It exists so that a declared model can run with individuals, for what compartments cannot hold.
Each state that holds people is a boolean array over agents. A dwell time is sampled when an agent enters a state and the exit is scheduled; rates that depend on the state of the model are drawn each step, with competing rates out of one state resolved in a single draw; and contact-mediated transitions are drawn over the sim’s networks. Under homogeneous mixing: the infectiousness-weighted fraction of people in the state

Move agents who are in a state a transition leaves from (or in srcs) to a state, counted in the transition’s flow if there is one (as when a treatment cures), with its change of level (ST30); dated at the step’s start, or at ti

The group of each agent; given a state, the group they are counted in while in it (which leaves out the dimensions the state does not have)

Infect some agents now, from code (ss.Disease.infect()): those in the first state, along its first transmission (with the strain given), counted in its flow, dated as infections are (at the step’s index, its end), and logged as seeds

See Engine.init_dwell_mods(); and the distributions each set= draws from, before the sim initializes the distributions



solvers.agents.Agents.init_post()
Sample the agents into the states

Whether a value (an expression of parameters, or a condition) is the same for each person for the whole run, so it can be worked out for everyone once (see fixed_edges()): numbers, parameters with no modifiers whose values are numbers or values by sex (see is_lifelong()), and conditions on sex



solvers.agents.Agents.is_lifelong(by)
Whether a value by people’s properties is the same for each person for the whole run: by sex alone, with values that do not change in time



solvers.agents.Agents.lifelong_mods(mods)
Whether modifiers only say who a quantity is for, by something that never changes (e.g. a transition with where=ss.ppl.female), so each person’s multiplier stays the same for the whole run

Values for everyone, by UID, kept for the run (see is_lifelong()), from values(uids); those for agents added since are worked out as they are needed



solvers.agents.Agents.live_counts()
The number of agents in each state of people now, by group (not collapsed): kept from the last census (with any changes of group since: see moved_groups()), or counted again



solvers.agents.Agents.local_count(states)
In a model with places: the number in the same place as each agent, or, when the counts are being advanced, as each group

The agents in a state, as UIDs
Read from the state’s array directly rather than through the living agents (.uids), which is several times faster for a large population: anyone who has died has already left every state (see die()).

    dst,
    p=None,
    n=None,
    uids=None,
    where=None,

A one-off move from code (ss.move()): a share p of the agents in some states (or n people, as the nearest whole number of agents; or of uids, those given; or of those for whom where holds), chosen at random, to a state; or of a count, to and from outside the model too (dst or srcs empty); returns the number of people moved

Move the agents who are in some states to a state: along a transition (see force()), or along none, as a one-off move, dated at the step’s start (or at ti); returns those moved

The multiplier on a quantity for some agents, from its modifiers



solvers.agents.Agents.mult_raw_extra(kind)
Whether mult_raw() has a multiplier on a kind of quantity other than its modifiers: the adjust= of the stratifications

The number of people some agents stand for, before the population scale: their number, or, if agents are weighted (people.scale), the sum of their weights



solvers.agents.Agents.note_counter(strat, what)
Agents add to each person’s own value, so a counter’s levels need not be one apart (see Compartmental.note_counter())



solvers.agents.Agents.place_newcomers()
Put agents made by other modules since the last step (e.g. born of ss.Births or ss.Pregnancy), who are in no state, in the first state



solvers.agents.Agents.place_raw()
The place of each agent, as an array indexed by UID



solvers.agents.Agents.prop(cond)
A property of people or a condition, in a rate (see ss.expressions.Prop): its value for each agent being evaluated, as it was when first asked for in the step



solvers.agents.Agents.put_first(uids)
Put some agents in the first state, and in no other (e.g. fetuses made after the start, whose states would otherwise be their arrays’ defaults)



solvers.agents.Agents.record_stocks()
As for the other engines (see Engine.record_stocks()), with the number in each state of people as it has been kept since the last census (see census())



solvers.agents.Agents.regroup(uids=None)
The groups of some agents (or of anyone, if uids is None) have changed: if any of them are in a state, the counts by group are taken again when next needed

Seed some agents who are in the first state: put them where a new infection puts them, the destinations of the first transmission in its shares, as init_prev does; returns those seeded

Type
Description
Default




uids
uids
the agents; those not in the first state are left where they are
required


log
bool
whether to record them as seeds in an ss.infection_log
True

As agents, an init_prev that chooses who starts infected one by one: a function of the sim (and the agents), or ss.by over a property of people that is not a dimension

The time of entering a state for someone put in it at the start: as if they had entered it in the step before the first, so that a seed with a dwell of d steps is a source for d steps, as anyone who enters later is (HP62). Contacts (a network, a mixing pool, or beta*I well mixed) are made after the step’s state changes, and a rate (beta*I.n) reads the people at its start, so a source by contact entered at 0 (in the first step’s contacts, leaving at the start of the second), and anyone else at -1 if they are where an infection puts people (in the first step’s rates, then counted at the start only, as under the ODE: CR4), else at 0

The strain each agent carries, as an array indexed by UID

Whether a branch (or one destination of a transition) has no modifiers and no adjust= of the stratifications

As counted(), with each agent counted by its weight (people.scale)

solvers.agents.Transmission(module, sim)
Transmission as agents, the same for a declared disease (Agents, for its transmissions) and one written as code (ss.Infection.transmit_route(), through its engine, ss.solvers.Undeclared): who can transmit and be infected, with the modifiers and products on rel_trans and rel_sus applied (current_value()); who is infected over a network (over_network()); and who infected whom (first_infections())
Where the two differ, the caller says how:

Hazard or probability. over_network() takes the chance of an edge in the step. A declared disease gives 1 − exp(−β·dt) from its rate, or, on a network with acts, works out a hazard per act (Agents.transmit_acts()); one written as code gives its beta as the probability in the step, converting a rate the same way (ss.Rate.to_prob()).
Order and attribution. The routes are taken in the order of sim.networks, and on each, p1 to p2 and then p2 to p1; someone reached by several is infected by the first (first_infections()), which is the source in the infection log. With strains, every strain is passed on in one pass, and someone reached by several is infected by one of them drawn at random, whose strain they take (pick_sources()), and then only if they are not protected against it (unprotected()): declared or written as code, by the same code.
Random numbers. Each edge’s is drawn by its source and target from the disease’s trans_rng, so the same disease, by the same name, gives the same edges the same numbers, declared or written as code; and so are the draws of who infects whom, and of protection, which are keyed by the step alone (step_draw()).

Description




current_value
rel_sus or rel_trans (kind) of every agent (by UID), times the factors (e.g. whether each is susceptible), with the modifiers and products active on it applied; may be the array itself, so it is not to be changed


first_infections
Each agent infected, once, with who infected them and over which route: the first of pairs to reach them. Each pair is the sources, the


over_network
Who is infected over a network in the step: an edge from u to v transmits with probability rel_trans[u]·rel_sus[v]·net_beta(beta),


pick_sources
With strains, each agent reached in the step, once, with who infected them and the rest of that pair’s values: one of those who reached


route_mult
The multiplier on a transmission over a route, as a function of the edges and of the people who would be infected (see ss.connectors.route_mult()); name is that of a declared disease’s transmission, or rel_sus for a disease written as code


step_draw
Uniforms for some agents from one of the transmission’s distributions (self.dists[key]), keyed by the step alone, so the same agents get the same numbers, declared or written as code; without common random numbers, its next draws


unprotected
Which of some agents reached by a strain are infected by it: each with the chance kept, the share of the force of infection of the strain that reaches them (1 − their protection against it), drawn from protect_<name>





solvers.agents.Transmission.current_value(kind, *factors)
rel_sus or rel_trans (kind) of every agent (by UID), times the factors (e.g. whether each is susceptible), with the modifiers and products active on it applied; may be the array itself, so it is not to be changed



solvers.agents.Transmission.first_infections(pairs)
Each agent infected, once, with who infected them and over which route: the first of pairs to reach them. Each pair is the sources, the targets, and the index of the route (one, or one for each), and any more values (e.g. a strain); returns the targets (sorted), and for each, the source (ss.dtypes.int_nan where not known), the route, and the more values, of the first pair to reach them

    i,
    route,
    rel_trans,
    rel_sus,
    betas,
    name,
)
Who is infected over a network in the step: an edge from u to v transmits with probability rel_trans[u]·rel_sus[v]·net_beta(beta), times the modifiers on the route for v (see ss.Network.transmit()). On a network with acts, these all scale the hazard of each act, as for a declared disease (see transmit_acts()), not the chance over all the acts, so net_beta() is given the chance per act they leave

required

required

A list of (sources, targets, i), for each direction that transmits

With strains, each agent reached in the step, once, with who infected them and the rest of that pair’s values: one of those who reached them, each as likely (the first to happen is as likely to be any of them), drawn from pick_<name>. Each pair is the sources, the targets, the index of the route (one, or one for each), and any more values (e.g. a strain), as for first_infections()

The multiplier on a transmission over a route, as a function of the edges and of the people who would be infected (see ss.connectors.route_mult()); name is that of a declared disease’s transmission, or rel_sus for a disease written as code

Uniforms for some agents from one of the transmission’s distributions (self.dists[key]), keyed by the step alone, so the same agents get the same numbers, declared or written as code; without common random numbers, its next draws

Which of some agents reached by a strain are infected by it: each with the chance kept, the share of the force of infection of the strain that reaches them (1 − their protection against it), drawn from protect_<name>

expressions.attr(

    init=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
)
A value for each person: drawn at an event, recorded at an event, drawn once when the person is made (a trait), or derived
Which it is depends on value and on=: a distribution with on= is drawn when the event happens to someone; an expression (or the name of another attribute) with on= is recorded then, as it was just before the move; a distribution with no on= is a trait; and an expression, or a dict of one by state (states not listed give NaN), with no on= is derived, worked out when it is read. Attributes set on the same event are set in the order they are declared, and each sees the ones before it. As agents only.

Type

Default

None

None

cd4_preart = ss.attr('cd4', on=start_art)                               # Recorded, just before starting

cd4        = ss.attr({latent: cd4_latent, falling: cd4_latent*(1 - falling.progress)}) # Derived
nab        = ss.attr(ss.uniform(0.5, 0.95), on=clearance, combine='max', init=0)

expressions.mother(x, born=False)
A condition or expression evaluated on each unborn agent’s mother (1/0 for a condition, or its value), and 0 for anyone born, unless born=True
Usable in rates, p=, where=, who=, ss.on(), and modifier conditions. Agents only: solver='auto' chooses them, and a compartmental solver stops with a CapabilityError.

required

title: networks
text:
networks
Networks and mixing pools: who meets whom, and so who can infect whom
A network holds the contacts (edges) between people, over which a disease spreads. Mixing pools (ss.MixingPool, ss.MixingPools) and contact matrices (ss.contacts()) spread it between groups instead, without edges. These exist so that a model’s contacts are separate from its diseases, and one network can carry several diseases. networks.DegreeNet(
    pars=None,
    n_contacts=_,
    dur=_,
    concurrency=_,
    max_contacts=_,
    match=_,
    acts=_,
    where=_,
    between=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Partnerships that form and dissolve, with a target number of partners at a time
The number of partners people have at any moment (n_contacts) is a target for the whole population, not a fixed number for each person: partnerships end at random, and people look for new ones at a rate that depends on how many they already have, chosen so that the distribution of the number of partners stays at the target. Everyone moves through it over time, as in EpiModel’s networks fitted to target statistics: this covers the same ground as a dyad-independent exponential random graph model (ERGM), with the terms for edges, degree, and mixing, but not terms such as triangles. The network starts at the target. In an open population, partnerships that end at a constant rate (dur a mean) end less often by as many as are ended by a partner leaving (dying), as EpiModel’s d.rate correction does, so they last as long as given on average; with any other distribution of durations, people look for partners more (or less) often, by a factor that keeps the mean number of partners at the target. Partnerships are not only sexual: people who share needles have partners too. For sexual partnerships, with an age of debut, see ss.SexualNet.
Each partnership can be between one person of each of two groups (between), e.g. a man and a woman, so a disease’s beta on it can differ by direction; each group can then have its own number of partners (n_contacts as a dict). With no target (n_contacts=None), people who have no partner are paired on every step, so nobody has more than one at a time.
A subclass that overrides step() forms its own partnerships: the base starts none for it, and has none of the parameters for forming them, only between.
Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die.

networks.RandomNet(
    pars=None,
    n_contacts=_,
    dur=_,
    beta=_,
    age_range=_,
    dynamic=_,
    method=_,
    remove_self_loops=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Random connectivity between agents
Each agent has a number of contacts (n_contacts), and the other end of each is drawn from the other agents’ contacts (method='fast', the default), so an agent’s chance of being picked is proportional to its own number of contacts. This keeps the mixing structure of risk-stratified networks (a small high-risk core with many contacts forms most of its edges with itself).
method says how the other end of each contact is drawn:

'fast' (the default): by sampling the contacts with replacement. The source side of each edge is exactly n_contacts, while the target side is Poisson-distributed with mean n_contacts, so agents have somewhat more variable numbers of contacts than with 'exact'; about 1.8x faster than 'exact'.
'exact': by shuffling the contacts (sampling without replacement), so each agent has exactly n_contacts contacts.
'uniform': uniformly from all eligible agents, regardless of their own n_contacts, as in Covasim v3’s random networks. This gives less variable numbers of contacts (e.g. with n_contacts=ss.poisson(20), a variance of about 15, rather than 30 for 'fast' or 20 for 'exact'), but loses the mixing structure above.
'safe': by giving each contact a random place on a line, from the agent’s own random numbers, and joining it to its nearest neighbor there. Adding an agent then changes only the contacts next to theirs, which suits scenario comparisons, but it is slower, and does not yet work within places.

Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die, unless dynamic=False: with any of these methods but 'safe', one death rewires almost every edge.

networks.SexualNet(
    pars=None,
    between=_,
    dur=_,
    debut=_,
    acts=_,
    participation=_,
    n_contacts=_,
    concurrency=_,
    max_contacts=_,
    match=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Sexual partnerships that form and dissolve, between two groups of people: by default, men and women
A ss.DegreeNet between men and women (between='mf'), in which people take part after their debut (debut), if they do (participation, drawn at their debut). By default, people who have no partner are paired on every step, so nobody has more than one at a time. With n_contacts, the number of partners people have at a time is a target instead (among people who take part, after their debut), as for ss.DegreeNet; with partnerships much longer than people’s time in the network, it takes a few decades to settle.
Each partnership is between one person of each of two groups (between): a man and a woman, two men, or e.g. a female sex worker and a client, and each group can have its own number of partners (n_contacts as a dict). With match=, a share of partnerships is between people at the same level of a property of people, such as a risk group.
Each partnership has a number of acts per step (acts), so a disease’s beta on it is a probability per act (see ss.peract), and the share of them in which a condom is used (condoms, 0 unless set, e.g. by a subclass in add_pairs()), which a modifier of the transmission on the network reads, e.g. ss.modify(hiv.infection, efficacy=0.8, share=lambda net: net.edges.condoms, route='sexualnet').
A subclass that overrides step() forms its own partnerships: the base starts none for it, and has none of the parameters for forming them, only between.
For several types of partnership with their own rules, see STIsim; for partnerships that are not sexual (e.g. needle sharing), ss.DegreeNet.
Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die.

networks.fisher_yates_shuffle(arr, randvals)
In-place Fisher-Yates shuffle using precomputed uniform random values.
Equivalent to np.random.permutation (a uniform random shuffle), but ~1.3x faster for the large arrays used in network generation. randvals should be uniform on [0, 1) and the same length as arr.
Note: randvals is consumed in order (randvals[k] for the k-th swap), not indexed by position. This means that changing the array length (e.g. adding one agent) shifts every swap, so the shuffle is not random-number safe – matching ss.RandomNet(method='exact')’s intended behavior (see ss.RandomNet(method='safe') for the CRN-safe version).



networks.nb_transmit(src, trg, rel_trans, rel_sus, beta, randvals)
Optimized transmission kernel: returns the (source, target) UIDs of transmitting edges.
Fuses the gather/multiply/compare and the UID extraction into a single branchless pass. This avoids the full-length boolean temporary and the two separate gather passes (trg[mask], src[mask]) of the previous approach – ~1.4x faster at typical transmission rates, more when transmission is common. UIDs are emitted in edge order, preserving CRN behavior.

networks.DegreeNet(
    pars=None,
    n_contacts=_,
    dur=_,
    concurrency=_,
    max_contacts=_,
    match=_,
    acts=_,
    where=_,
    between=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Partnerships that form and dissolve, with a target number of partners at a time
The number of partners people have at any moment (n_contacts) is a target for the whole population, not a fixed number for each person: partnerships end at random, and people look for new ones at a rate that depends on how many they already have, chosen so that the distribution of the number of partners stays at the target. Everyone moves through it over time, as in EpiModel’s networks fitted to target statistics: this covers the same ground as a dyad-independent exponential random graph model (ERGM), with the terms for edges, degree, and mixing, but not terms such as triangles. The network starts at the target. In an open population, partnerships that end at a constant rate (dur a mean) end less often by as many as are ended by a partner leaving (dying), as EpiModel’s d.rate correction does, so they last as long as given on average; with any other distribution of durations, people look for partners more (or less) often, by a factor that keeps the mean number of partners at the target. Partnerships are not only sexual: people who share needles have partners too. For sexual partnerships, with an age of debut, see ss.SexualNet.
Each partnership can be between one person of each of two groups (between), e.g. a man and a woman, so a disease’s beta on it can differ by direction; each group can then have its own number of partners (n_contacts as a dict). With no target (n_contacts=None), people who have no partner are paired on every step, so nobody has more than one at a time.
A subclass that overrides step() forms its own partnerships: the base starts none for it, and has none of the parameters for forming them, only between.
Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die.

Type

Default

# EpiModel's introductory network: 175 partnerships among 500 people, 110 people with two or more partners, nobody with four or more, and partnerships lasting 50 steps
net = ss.DegreeNet(n_contacts=0.7, concurrency=0.22, max_contacts=3, dur=50)

# Most partnerships within a risk group, and over half within a region
net = ss.DegreeNet(n_contacts=0.7, dur=50, match=dict(risk=0.8, region=0.6))

# And four times as many partners in the high-risk group (with sim.stratify(risk=['low', 'high']))
net = ss.DegreeNet(n_contacts=ss.by(risk=[0.4, 1.6]), dur=50, match=dict(risk=0.8))

# Needle sharing among people who inject drugs (a boolean property of people), with 20 injections a month in each partnership
needles = ss.DegreeNet(name='needles', where=ss.ppl.pwid, n_contacts=2, dur=ss.months(6), acts=ss.freqpermonth(20))

# Sex work, between female sex workers and their clients (boolean properties of people)

networks.RandomNet(
    pars=None,
    n_contacts=_,
    dur=_,
    beta=_,
    age_range=_,
    dynamic=_,
    method=_,
    remove_self_loops=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Random connectivity between agents
Each agent has a number of contacts (n_contacts), and the other end of each is drawn from the other agents’ contacts (method='fast', the default), so an agent’s chance of being picked is proportional to its own number of contacts. This keeps the mixing structure of risk-stratified networks (a small high-risk core with many contacts forms most of its edges with itself).
method says how the other end of each contact is drawn:

'fast' (the default): by sampling the contacts with replacement. The source side of each edge is exactly n_contacts, while the target side is Poisson-distributed with mean n_contacts, so agents have somewhat more variable numbers of contacts than with 'exact'; about 1.8x faster than 'exact'.
'exact': by shuffling the contacts (sampling without replacement), so each agent has exactly n_contacts contacts.
'uniform': uniformly from all eligible agents, regardless of their own n_contacts, as in Covasim v3’s random networks. This gives less variable numbers of contacts (e.g. with n_contacts=ss.poisson(20), a variance of about 15, rather than 30 for 'fast' or 20 for 'exact'), but loses the mixing structure above.
'safe': by giving each contact a random place on a line, from the agent’s own random numbers, and joining it to its nearest neighbor there. Adding an agent then changes only the contacts next to theirs, which suits scenario comparisons, but it is slower, and does not yet work within places.

Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die, unless dynamic=False: with any of these methods but 'safe', one death rewires almost every edge.

networks.SexualNet(
    pars=None,
    between=_,
    dur=_,
    debut=_,
    acts=_,
    participation=_,
    n_contacts=_,
    concurrency=_,
    max_contacts=_,
    match=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Sexual partnerships that form and dissolve, between two groups of people: by default, men and women
A ss.DegreeNet between men and women (between='mf'), in which people take part after their debut (debut), if they do (participation, drawn at their debut). By default, people who have no partner are paired on every step, so nobody has more than one at a time. With n_contacts, the number of partners people have at a time is a target instead (among people who take part, after their debut), as for ss.DegreeNet; with partnerships much longer than people’s time in the network, it takes a few decades to settle.
Each partnership is between one person of each of two groups (between): a man and a woman, two men, or e.g. a female sex worker and a client, and each group can have its own number of partners (n_contacts as a dict). With match=, a share of partnerships is between people at the same level of a property of people, such as a risk group.
Each partnership has a number of acts per step (acts), so a disease’s beta on it is a probability per act (see ss.peract), and the share of them in which a condom is used (condoms, 0 unless set, e.g. by a subclass in add_pairs()), which a modifier of the transmission on the network reads, e.g. ss.modify(hiv.infection, efficacy=0.8, share=lambda net: net.edges.condoms, route='sexualnet').
A subclass that overrides step() forms its own partnerships: the base starts none for it, and has none of the parameters for forming them, only between.
For several types of partnership with their own rules, see STIsim; for partnerships that are not sexual (e.g. needle sharing), ss.DegreeNet.
Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die.

Mixing between groups from a contact matrix; returns ss.MixingPools
A matrix, and what it is over:

a country’s, by name (ss.contacts('Kenya')), from starsim_data, by 5-year age group;
its own age groups, given by their lower edges (ss.contacts(matrix, ages=[0, 15, 65])), which need not be the model’s (it is regrouped to them);
the model’s own stratifications: its age groups (ss.contacts(matrix)), another one (ss.contacts(matrix, dims='risk')), or several together (ss.contacts(matrix, dims=['sex', 'risk'])), for mixing that is not a product, e.g. men mix with women, and by risk differently for each sex.

Mixing that is a product over stratifications takes a matrix for each, by name (ss.contacts(dict(age=..., area=...))): the contacts between two groups are the product of the entries for each. The matrix by age can have its own age groups here too (ss.contacts(dict(age=..., area=...), ages=[0, 15, 65])).

S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.05*I, recovery=ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10), init_prev=0.01)
mixing = ss.contacts([[10, 3], [3, 5]], ages=[0, 18])
sim = ss.Sim(sir, networks=mixing, unit='day', stop=100).run()

sir.stratify(risk=['low', 'high'])
mixing = ss.contacts([[2, 1], [1, 8]], dims='risk')

home, school = ss.contacts('Kenya', layer=['home', 'school']) # Contacts a day, by 5-year age group
sim = ss.Sim(sir, networks=[home, school], stratify=dict(age=[0, 5, 18, 65]), unit='day', stop=100)

# A product: by age, then 90% of contacts within one's own area
mixing = ss.contacts(dict(age=[[10, 3], [3, 5]], area=[[0.9, 0.1], [0.1, 0.9]]), ages=[0, 18])

# Men mix with women, and the high-risk with each other more among men than among women: a matrix over sex and risk together
matrix = np.zeros((2, 2, 2, 2)) # [sex, risk, sex, risk], with sex ['female', 'male'] and risk ['low', 'high']
matrix[0, :, 1, :] = [[0.8, 0.2], [0.5, 1.5]] # Women's contacts with men
matrix[1, :, 0, :] = [[0.8, 0.5], [0.2, 2.0]] # Men's contacts with women
mixing = ss.contacts(matrix, dims=['sex', 'risk'])

networks.fisher_yates_shuffle(arr, randvals)
In-place Fisher-Yates shuffle using precomputed uniform random values.
Equivalent to np.random.permutation (a uniform random shuffle), but ~1.3x faster for the large arrays used in network generation. randvals should be uniform on [0, 1) and the same length as arr.
Note: randvals is consumed in order (randvals[k] for the k-th swap), not indexed by position. This means that changing the array length (e.g. adding one agent) shifts every swap, so the shuffle is not random-number safe – matching ss.RandomNet(method='exact')’s intended behavior (see ss.RandomNet(method='safe') for the CRN-safe version).



networks.nb_transmit(src, trg, rel_trans, rel_sus, beta, randvals)
Optimized transmission kernel: returns the (source, target) UIDs of transmitting edges.
Fuses the gather/multiply/compare and the UID extraction into a single branchless pass. This avoids the full-length boolean temporary and the two separate gather passes (trg[mask], src[mask]) of the previous approach – ~1.4x faster at typical transmission rates, more when transmission is common. UIDs are emitted in edge order, preserving CRN behavior.

    data=None,

    min_year=1800,
    out_of_range=0,
    default_age=0,
    default_year=2024,
)
Standardize formats of input data
Input data can arrive in many different forms. This function accepts a variety of data structures, and converts them into a Pandas Series containing one variable, based on specified metadata, or an ss.Dist if the data is already an ss.Dist object.
The metadata is a dictionary that defines columns of the dataframe or keys of the dictionary to use as indices in the output Series. It should contain:

metadata['data_cols']['value'] specifying the name of the column/key to draw values from
metadata['data_cols']['year'] optionally specifying the column containing year values; otherwise the default year will be used
metadata['data_cols']['age'] optionally specifying the column containing age values; otherwise the default age will be used
metadata['data_cols'][<arbitrary>] optionally specifying any other columns to use as indices. These will form part of the multi-index for the standardized Series output.

If a configured column is not present in the data, a known synonym is used instead if one is available (see ss.col_synonyms); for example, year data labeled “Time” (as in UN World Population Prospects data) is used for a data column configured as “Year”. Explicitly configured column names always take precedence over synonyms.
If a sex column is part of the index, the metadata can also optionally specify a string mapping to convert the sex labels in the input data into the ‘m’/‘f’ labels used by Starsim. In that case, the metadata can contain an additional key like metadata['sex_keys'] = {'Female':'f','Male':'m'} which in this case would map the strings ‘Female’ and ‘Male’ in the original data into ‘m’/‘f’ for Starsim.

Standardize formats of input data
Input data can arrive in many different forms. This function accepts a variety of data structures, and converts them into a Pandas Series containing one variable, based on specified metadata, or an ss.Dist if the data is already an ss.Dist object.
The metadata is a dictionary that defines columns of the dataframe or keys of the dictionary to use as indices in the output Series. It should contain:

metadata['data_cols']['value'] specifying the name of the column/key to draw values from
metadata['data_cols']['year'] optionally specifying the column containing year values; otherwise the default year will be used
metadata['data_cols']['age'] optionally specifying the column containing age values; otherwise the default age will be used
metadata['data_cols'][<arbitrary>] optionally specifying any other columns to use as indices. These will form part of the multi-index for the standardized Series output.

If a configured column is not present in the data, a known synonym is used instead if one is available (see ss.col_synonyms); for example, year data labeled “Time” (as in UN World Population Prospects data) is used for a data column configured as “Year”. Explicitly configured column names always take precedence over synonyms.
If a sex column is part of the index, the metadata can also optionally specify a string mapping to convert the sex labels in the input data into the ‘m’/‘f’ labels used by Starsim. In that case, the metadata can contain an additional key like metadata['sex_keys'] = {'Female':'f','Male':'m'} which in this case would map the strings ‘Female’ and ‘Male’ in the original data into ‘m’/‘f’ for Starsim.

title: diseases
text:
diseases
Diseases: the base class (ss.Disease), diseases with transmission written as code (ss.Infection), and the textbook models (ss.SIR, ss.SIS, ss.SEIR)
ss.Disease exists so that one class can hold a disease declared from states and transitions, written as code, or both. A declared disease runs with any solver; ss.Infection and other code that works on individual agents runs as agents.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




BuiltAfterInit
Build what a disease declares in its __init__() (define_states(), define_transitions()) once that has finished


Disease
A disease: states people are in and the transitions between them (declared), code, or both


Infection
A disease with transmission written as code


InfectionLog
Record infections


SEIR
An SEIR model: as ss.SIR, with an exposed (latent) state before people become infectious


SIR
An SIR model: susceptible, infected, and recovered, optionally with deaths from infection


SIS
An SIS model: people recover from infection and are susceptible again





diseases.BuiltAfterInit()
Build what a disease declares in its __init__() (define_states(), define_transitions()) once that has finished



diseases.Disease(
    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,
    _names=None,
    **kwargs,
)
A disease: states people are in and the transitions between them (declared), code, or both
Declared from its states and transitions, no methods need to be defined, and the disease can be run with any solver (see ss.Sim):
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I,
    recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
The same disease can be declared in a class body (the class form), which can also add behavior by defining methods; ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR are written this way.
A disease can also be written as code: a subclass that declares nothing, defines its per-agent arrays (define_states()), and changes them in its own step_state() and step(); it runs as agents. One class can mix the two, e.g. a declared natural history and a coded array that its step() updates after super().step() has taken the declared transitions. Each lifecycle method runs the declared part through the disease’s engine (which, for a disease that declares nothing, has nothing to run), so an override calls super() as for any module. ss.Infection adds transmission written as code.
Note: CRN safe as agents.

required

required

required

The results are the number in each state (I), the flow along each transition by its name (infection, with its cumulative total as res.infection.cum), and the results and outcomes declared (e.g. prevalence=I/(S + I + R), as ss.SIR declares).



# Operator form: declare the states, then the transitions
S, I, R   = ss.states(3)
infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)
ss.Sim(sir, stop=100).run().plot()

# Class form: for when there is behavior that is not a transition
class SIR(ss.Disease):
    S, I, R   = ss.states(3)
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)

# Written as code: a disease that is not transmitted
class Anemia(ss.Disease):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(p_onset=ss.bernoulli(0.01))
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(ss.BoolState('anemic', label='Anemic'))

    def step_state(self):
        self.anemic[self.pars.p_onset.filter()] = True

diseases.Disease.R0(matrix=False)
The basic reproduction number, from the next-generation matrix at the disease-free state
By definition it is in a population with no immunity: everyone is taken to be in the first state (e.g. S), each group keeping its size, whoever starts immune (init=dict(R=0.9)). The reproduction number at the start, with that immunity, is in the line a run prints as it starts, when it differs (R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible)).
The model is laid out as an ODE: if the disease is in a sim, a copy of that sim is made with solver='ode', with its mixing and stratification; otherwise a sim with the disease alone, under homogeneous mixing, with the default number of people. Values that vary in time are taken at the start. A sim runs a copy of the disease it is given, so the R0 of a sim’s model is sim.diseases.<name>.R0(); this matters where a count is a number rather than a share of the people (mosquitoes per person).
This is the largest eigenvalue of the next-generation matrix. Where infection passes through a vector (people infect mosquitoes, which infect people), each passage is a generation, so R0 is the square root of the classical Ross–Macdonald value. Shedding into a reservoir that is a count (such as water) is not an infection, so there R0 is the number of people infected through the reservoir by one person.

sir.R0() # 3.0

class SIRS(ss.Disease):
    def __init__(self, waning=True, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(init_prev=0.01, **kwargs)
        self.define_states(ss.states('S I R'))
        beta = ss.par(0.3)
        self.define_transitions(
            infection = self.S >> self.I @ beta*self.I,
            recovery  = self.I >> self.R @ ss.days(10),
        )
        if waning:
            self.define_transitions(waning=self.R >> self.S @ ss.days(100))

diseases.Infection(pars=None, strains=None, **kwargs)
A disease with transmission written as code
An ss.Disease that adds network-based transmission with directional beta values (transmit(), transmit_route()), the susceptible and infected states, the attributes that other modules act on (rel_sus, rel_trans), set_prognoses() for the people infected, and the prevalence and infection results. The rest of the disease is written as for any other module: its own per-agent states (define_states()) and how they change (step_state(), set_prognoses()), so it can hold anything an agent can have: a CD4 count, an immunity level that wanes, a time since infection. It runs as agents. A disease with no beta (such as ssl.NCD) is not transmitted; one that has no use for these states at all is a plain ss.Disease.
An infection in a step happens at its end, so a course scheduled from it starts at the next step: schedule a move dur steps after an infection at self.ti + 1 + dur, in an ss.TimeArr, and take it when due() (as in the example below). Each case is then infectious for dur steps on average, as a declared disease’s is; the seeds are dated at the start (self.ti is 0), the end of the step before the first, so they are too.
A disease that can be written as states and transitions is declared instead, with ss.Disease (see ss.SIR), which gives it every solver and describe(), equations(), and R0(). The v4 verbs that act on arrays work on both: ss.modify(hiv.rel_trans, ...), conditions such as hiv.cd4 < 200, and fitting the values in pars.
With strains=ss.Strains(...), each person carries one strain at a time (self.strain, the index of the strain of their current or last infection, -1 if none), which the disease’s code reads (e.g. in set_prognoses(), and strain_value() for a strain’s values). The strains are transmitted in one pass, each by those infectious with it at its rel_trans; each new case is infected by one of those who reached them in the step, at random, and takes their strain, unless protected against it (strain_sus(): protection from ss.immunity(due_to=<state>, rel_sus=matrix) by the strain they had, or the disease’s own), as a declared disease’s strains are passed on, by the same code (ss.solvers.Transmission).
Note: CRN safe.

class SIRS(ss.Infection):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(beta=ss.perday(0.05), init_prev=ss.bernoulli(0.01), dur_inf=10)
        self.define_states(ss.BoolState('recovered'), ss.TimeArr('ti_recovered'))
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)

    def step_state(self):
        done = (self.infected & self.ti_recovered.due()).uids
        self.infected[done] = False
        self.recovered[done] = True
        self.susceptible[done] = True # Protected only by the immunity of their strain, if any

    def set_prognoses(self, uids, sources=None):
        super().set_prognoses(uids, sources)
        self.infected[uids] = True
        self.recovered[uids] = False
        self.ti_infected[uids] = self.ti
        self.ti_recovered[uids] = self.ti + 1 + self.pars.dur_inf # Infected at the end of this step, so infectious from the next

# Two strains, the second more transmissible; recovering from one protects fully against it, and partly against the other
strains = ss.Strains(['H1', 'H3'], rel_trans=[1, 1.5], immunity=ss.immunity(due_to='recovered', rel_sus=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]))
sim = ss.Sim(diseases=SIRS(strains=strains, name='flu'), networks='random', n_agents=2000, unit='day', stop=100).run()
sim.diseases.flu.strain # The strain of each person's current or last infection

diseases.InfectionLog(disease=None, networks=None)
Record infections
The infection log records transmission events and optionally other data associated with each transmission. Entries are stored as one chunk of arrays per call, so logging is cheap; they are combined when the log is read. Basic functionality is to track transmission with



Disease.infection_log.add_entries(targets, sources, t)



or, for a single infection,



Disease.infection_log.append(source, target, t)



Seed infections can be recorded with a source of None (or NaN), although all infections should have a target and a time. Other data can be captured in the log, either at the time of creation, or later on. For example



Disease.infection_log.add_entries(targets, sources, t, variant=variants)



records extra data for each infection (ss.Infection records the network this way). Modules can optionally add per-infection outcomes later as well, for example



Disease.infection_log.add_data(uids, t_dead=2024.25)



This would be equivalent to having specified the data at the original time the log entry was created - however, it is more useful for tracking events that may or may not occur after the infection and could be modified by interventions (e.g., tracking diagnosis, treatment, notification etc.)
A table of outcomes can be returned using InfectionLog.to_df(), and a NetworkX graph with InfectionLog.to_graph().

diseases.Disease(
    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,
    _names=None,
    **kwargs,
)
A disease: states people are in and the transitions between them (declared), code, or both
Declared from its states and transitions, no methods need to be defined, and the disease can be run with any solver (see ss.Sim):
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I,
    recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
The same disease can be declared in a class body (the class form), which can also add behavior by defining methods; ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR are written this way.
A disease can also be written as code: a subclass that declares nothing, defines its per-agent arrays (define_states()), and changes them in its own step_state() and step(); it runs as agents. One class can mix the two, e.g. a declared natural history and a coded array that its step() updates after super().step() has taken the declared transitions. Each lifecycle method runs the declared part through the disease’s engine (which, for a disease that declares nothing, has nothing to run), so an override calls super() as for any module. ss.Infection adds transmission written as code.
Note: CRN safe as agents.

# Written as code: a disease that is not transmitted
class Anemia(ss.Disease):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(p_onset=ss.bernoulli(0.01))
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(ss.BoolState('anemic', label='Anemic'))

    def step_state(self):
        self.anemic[self.pars.p_onset.filter()] = True

diseases.Disease.R0(matrix=False)
The basic reproduction number, from the next-generation matrix at the disease-free state
By definition it is in a population with no immunity: everyone is taken to be in the first state (e.g. S), each group keeping its size, whoever starts immune (init=dict(R=0.9)). The reproduction number at the start, with that immunity, is in the line a run prints as it starts, when it differs (R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible)).
The model is laid out as an ODE: if the disease is in a sim, a copy of that sim is made with solver='ode', with its mixing and stratification; otherwise a sim with the disease alone, under homogeneous mixing, with the default number of people. Values that vary in time are taken at the start. A sim runs a copy of the disease it is given, so the R0 of a sim’s model is sim.diseases.<name>.R0(); this matters where a count is a number rather than a share of the people (mosquitoes per person).
This is the largest eigenvalue of the next-generation matrix. Where infection passes through a vector (people infect mosquitoes, which infect people), each passage is a generation, so R0 is the square root of the classical Ross–Macdonald value. Shedding into a reservoir that is a count (such as water) is not an infection, so there R0 is the number of people infected through the reservoir by one person.

Type
Description
Default

bool
if True, return the next-generation matrix (over the infected compartments of every group) rather than its largest eigenvalue

sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.3*I, recovery=ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10))
sir.R0() # 3.0

diseases.Infection(pars=None, strains=None, **kwargs)
A disease with transmission written as code
An ss.Disease that adds network-based transmission with directional beta values (transmit(), transmit_route()), the susceptible and infected states, the attributes that other modules act on (rel_sus, rel_trans), set_prognoses() for the people infected, and the prevalence and infection results. The rest of the disease is written as for any other module: its own per-agent states (define_states()) and how they change (step_state(), set_prognoses()), so it can hold anything an agent can have: a CD4 count, an immunity level that wanes, a time since infection. It runs as agents. A disease with no beta (such as ssl.NCD) is not transmitted; one that has no use for these states at all is a plain ss.Disease.
An infection in a step happens at its end, so a course scheduled from it starts at the next step: schedule a move dur steps after an infection at self.ti + 1 + dur, in an ss.TimeArr, and take it when due() (as in the example below). Each case is then infectious for dur steps on average, as a declared disease’s is; the seeds are dated at the start (self.ti is 0), the end of the step before the first, so they are too.
A disease that can be written as states and transitions is declared instead, with ss.Disease (see ss.SIR), which gives it every solver and describe(), equations(), and R0(). The v4 verbs that act on arrays work on both: ss.modify(hiv.rel_trans, ...), conditions such as hiv.cd4 < 200, and fitting the values in pars.
With strains=ss.Strains(...), each person carries one strain at a time (self.strain, the index of the strain of their current or last infection, -1 if none), which the disease’s code reads (e.g. in set_prognoses(), and strain_value() for a strain’s values). The strains are transmitted in one pass, each by those infectious with it at its rel_trans; each new case is infected by one of those who reached them in the step, at random, and takes their strain, unless protected against it (strain_sus(): protection from ss.immunity(due_to=<state>, rel_sus=matrix) by the strain they had, or the disease’s own), as a declared disease’s strains are passed on, by the same code (ss.solvers.Transmission).
Note: CRN safe.

class SIRS(ss.Infection):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(beta=ss.perday(0.05), init_prev=ss.bernoulli(0.01), dur_inf=10)
        self.define_states(ss.BoolState('recovered'), ss.TimeArr('ti_recovered'))
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)

    def step_state(self):
        done = (self.infected & self.ti_recovered.due()).uids
        self.infected[done] = False
        self.recovered[done] = True
        self.susceptible[done] = True # Protected only by the immunity of their strain, if any

    def set_prognoses(self, uids, sources=None):
        super().set_prognoses(uids, sources)
        self.infected[uids] = True
        self.recovered[uids] = False
        self.ti_infected[uids] = self.ti
        self.ti_recovered[uids] = self.ti + 1 + self.pars.dur_inf # Infected at the end of this step, so infectious from the next

# Two strains, the second more transmissible; recovering from one protects fully against it, and partly against the other
strains = ss.Strains(['H1', 'H3'], rel_trans=[1, 1.5], immunity=ss.immunity(due_to='recovered', rel_sus=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]))
sim = ss.Sim(diseases=SIRS(strains=strains, name='flu'), networks='random', n_agents=2000, unit='day', stop=100).run()
sim.diseases.flu.strain # The strain of each person's current or last infection

title: Tutorials
text:
Core tutorials
The core tutorials build models of compartments: groups of people, by state and by age or place. Starsim runs them as equations, as stochastic models, or as agents.


T1 – Getting started
A measles outbreak as an SIR model: run it, plot it, and check what Starsim built.


T2 – Building a model
The first model in more depth: states, transitions, parameters, time, and results.


T3 – Building a disease
A latent period, how long people stay in each state, waning immunity, and deaths, with the diagram and equations.


T4 – Age groups and contacts
Who mixes with whom: age groups, contact matrices, and real populations.


T5 – Interventions and scenarios
Vaccination, school terms, and comparing scenarios across many runs.


T6 – Geography and mixing
Several towns, and how an outbreak travels between them.


T7 – Data and calibration
Fitting the model to reported cases, and projecting from the fit.


T8 – Stratification and co-transmission
Splitting a model by more than age, and two diseases that affect each other.


T9 – Custom modules
Writing your own behavior as code, while keeping the model compartmental.

title: Tutorials
text:
Agent-based modeling
These tutorials are for models that need individual people: contact networks, individual histories, births and deaths, and interventions that target individuals.


A1 – Diseases
A disease as agents: individual states, histories, and differences between people.


A2 – Networks
Who meets whom, one contact at a time: random, sexual, and other networks.


A3 – Demographics
Births, deaths, and pregnancy for individual people.


A4 – Interventions
Interventions that target individuals: eligibility, testing, and treatment.


A5 – Custom modules
Writing agent-level logic of your own, from a small change to a new module.


The answers to the exercises are in the solutions.






TipRunning tutorials locally



Each tutorial can be downloaded as a Jupyter notebook: look for the download button at the top of the page. Or, to run them all locally: clone the Starsim repository, install Starsim (pip install -e .), go to docs/tutorials, and open them in Jupyter (jupyter lab, with jupytext installed to open .qmd files directly, or run ./convert_notebooks first).

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
This page is a ten-minute tour of Starsim. It builds one model step by step: a simple epidemic, then the same epidemic with age groups, an intervention, data to fit it to, and many runs to show the uncertainty. Each step is a few lines of code, and each step says what the code means in the terms of an epidemiological model. The parameters are illustrative, not estimates for any particular disease or setting.
To follow along, install Starsim with pip install "starsim[jax]", and paste each block into a notebook or a Python script, in order.

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
An SIR model
In an SIR model, everyone is in one of three compartments: susceptible (S), infectious (I), or recovered (R). People move between them along two transitions:

Infection, from S to I. Each susceptible person is infected at a rate of β times the share of people who are infectious, so the number infected per day is β S I / N (frequency-dependent transmission).
Recovery, from I to R. People stay infectious for 10 days on average, so they recover at a rate of 1/10 per day.

In Starsim, the compartments are states, and each transition says where people move from, where they move to, and at what rate (after @):

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I        # From S to I, at a rate of 0.3 times the share infectious
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)  # From I to R, after 10 days on average
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery)

Starsim kernels: Rust, OUT OF DATE (built before its source last changed, so results may be wrong): run "./build" in starsim/solvers/rust/


A state in a rate, like I in 0.3*I, is the share of people in it. A duration, like ss.days(10), is the average time spent in a state before leaving it. Since the duration is in days, β = 0.3 is per day. The model is the standard set of equations:

sir.equations()

dS/dt = -beta * S * I / N
dI/dt =  beta * S * I / N - I / dur_I
dR/dt =  I / dur_I


The basic reproduction number is R0 = β × the duration = 0.3 × 10 = 3. To run the model, give it to a sim with how long to run for:

sim = ss.Sim(sir, stop=ss.days(100))
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: sir, 10,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 100
  sir: R0 = 3, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.003 s; sir: 9,309 infections; at most 3,036 infectious, on day 27









The sim says what it ran and what happened: 10,000 people (the default population) as an ODE, R0 = 3 as expected, and the size and timing of the peak. Since nothing in this model is about individual people, Starsim runs it as a deterministic compartmental model (an ODE). The same model can also be run as a stochastic model or as agents, as the last section shows.

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
How the epidemic starts
By default, 1% of people start infected, and everyone else starts in the first state, S. The share that starts infected is init_prev, the initial prevalence:
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)  # 0.1% start infected
init_prev puts people in the state that an infection leads to: I here, but E in an SEIR model, where people are exposed before they are infectious. To start people in any state, give init (the share of people in each state) or init_n (the number of people in each):
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001, R=0.2))  # 0.1% infectious, 20% already immune
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10))         # 10 people infectious

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
Age groups and contacts
Most respiratory infections spread differently between age groups. stratify() splits each state by age: here into three groups, with the share of the population in each. ss.contacts() says how much each group mixes with each other one: a contact matrix, in which row i, column j is the number of contacts a day that a person in group i has with people in group j. With contacts, β is the chance of infection per contact. This model also has an outcome, cases: the infections that are reported, here one in five.

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(0.02, bounds=[0.005, 0.1]) # A parameter that can be fitted, between these bounds

infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
cases     = ss.outcome(0.2*infection) # One infection in five is reported
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, cases, init_prev=0.0001)
sir.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the share of people in each

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]])
pars = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=1e6, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01')
sim = ss.Sim(sir, **pars)
sim.run()
sim.results.sir.I.by('age').plot()

Sim: sir, 1,000,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2025-07-01
  sir: R0 = 2.82, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0026 s; sir: 907,068 infections; at most 262,517 infectious, on 2025-02-25









Every state and transition has a result of the same name (S, I, R, infection, recovery), and so does each outcome (cases). by('age') splits a result by age group, and select() picks one group, e.g. sim.results.sir.I.select(age='65+').

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
Interventions
An intervention changes the course of the epidemic from some point on. Here are two: vaccinating 80% of people aged 65 and over on 1 February, with a vaccine that cuts their chance of infection by 90%, and masks, which cut transmission by 40% from the same day:

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, where=sir.age >= 65, coverage=0.8, at='2025-02-01')
masks = ss.modify(sir.pars.beta, multiply=0.6, start='2025-02-01')

To compare them, make a sim for each scenario, and run them together with ss.parallel():

scenarios = {'No intervention': None, 'Vaccine': vaccination, 'Masks': masks}
sims = {}
for label, intervention in scenarios.items():
    sims[label] = ss.Sim(sir, interventions=intervention, **pars)

msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot()

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (No intervention, Vaccine, Masks)

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
Data and fitting
A model is fitted by finding the values of its parameters that make its results match data. To try this where the right answer is known, make data from the model itself: run it with β = 0.025, and draw weekly counts of cases from it, with random noise as in real reporting. The noise is drawn with the true sim’s own random seed (rand_seed=2), not the default seed of the sims being fitted, since the noise in real data has nothing to do with the model’s.

truth = ss.Sim(sir, pars=dict(beta=0.025), rand_seed=2, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_data('cases', resample='week')
data.head()

Sim: sir, 1,000,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2025-07-01

Data is matched to results by name: the column cases is compared with the result cases, and since the data is weekly, each row is compared with the total of the model’s cases over its week. sim.fit() then fits every parameter that has bounds (here, β) to every result that has data:

sim = ss.Sim(sir, data=data, **pars)
fit = sim.fit()
fit.plot()

Searching on a log scale: beta

The goodness of fit is 0.002704 at the best values and 1.015 at the initial values









The plot shows the model’s cases with the starting value of β (before) and the fitted one (after), against the data. As in the fit, the model’s cases are added up over each week, so that each point is compared with a week of data. fit.pars has the values found: β is close to the 0.025 the data was made with.

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
Uncertainty and many runs
The ODE gives one answer: the epidemic as expected on average. A real epidemic varies by chance from one outbreak to the next, and more so in a small population or when there are few cases. To see this, run the model as a stochastic model, in which the number of people who move between states each day is random, and run it many times. solver='binomial' runs the same model this way (as a chain-binomial model), and n_runs=20 runs it 20 times, each with its own random seed:

msim = fit.sim.run(solver='binomial', n_runs=20)
msim.plot()








The plot shows the median of the runs, and the range that holds 95% of them. msim.summarize() gives the same for each result over the whole run: the median, the low and high ends of that range, the mean, and the standard deviation:

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
Next steps

The tutorials cover each of these steps in more depth, one at a time, with a model of a measles outbreak.
The user guide covers each topic in full, including networks, demographics, custom modules, and solvers.
The gallery has complete models to start from.
If you have a model in another framework, the conversion guides show how to bring it into Starsim.
Starsim can also be used from R, with R-Starsim.
